The Agni Purāṇa.
Chapter One.
Now begins the first chapter.
In the introduction to the work,
I pay homage to Śrī, Sarasvatī, Gaurī, Gaṇeśa, Skanda, Īśvara, Brahmā, Vahni, Indra and the other gods, and Vāsudeva.
In Naimiṣa, the ṛṣis headed by Śaunaka, who were performing a sacrifice to Hari, spoke a welcome greeting to Sūta while on the occasion of their pilgrimage. The ṛṣis said:
O Sūta, you have been honored by us; tell us the essence of essences,
by the mere knowledge of which omniscience is produced.
Sūta said:
Viṣṇu, the all-pervading Lord who performs creation and the other cosmic functions, is indeed the essence of essences;
by knowing that "I am Brahman," omniscience arises.
"Two Brahmans are to be known: the Brahman of sound and that which is the Supreme.
"Indeed, two types of knowledge are to be known"—thus says the Atharvaṇa Śruti.
I, Śuka, Paila, and the others went to the hermitage of Badarikāśrama.
Having bowed to Vyāsa, they questioned him; he then spoke to us the essence.
Vyāsa said:
O Sūta, listen as I relate what Vasiṣṭha told me, as well as Śuka and the others.
For he was asking the sages about the supreme Brahman-sāra, which is higher than the highest;
[the reading in the manuscript marked with *gha* is "lakṣmīm"].
2. "By mere cognition" (vijñātamātreṇa) is the reading of the marked manuscript (gha); 3.
"That which is both the other and the beyond" (aparañca parañca yat) is the reading of manuscript (kha).
The reading "yadabravīt" (what he said) is found in the two manuscripts marked Kha and Gha;
this is the reading of page 1.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O Vyāsa, listen as I declare the twofold nature of Brahman, which follows all things in their entirety.
Just as Agni previously told me, together with the sages and the gods:
"The supreme *Āgneya Purāṇa* is the supreme imperishable knowledge of Brahman;
it is the lower Brahman consisting of the *Ṛgveda* and other scriptures, which brings happiness to all the gods. (3)
The Agni Purāṇa, which was spoken by Agni, is equal to the Veda;
it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those men who read or hear this divine work.

Vasiṣṭha said: He questioned the god Viṣṇu, who is the form of the fire of time, the light of Brahman, higher than the highest, and who is worshipped by sages through knowledge and action. AP 1.011ab.
Speak, O Brahmā, of the Lord (Īśvara), who is the boat for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra;
[speak of] the essence of knowledge, by knowing which a man becomes omniscient.
Agni said:
"I am Viṣṇu, Kālāgnirudra; I shall declare to you the essence of knowledge."
The ancient essence of knowledge,
which is everything and the cause of all— of creation, re-creation, genealogy, and the periods of the Manvantaras.
And from the accounts of the dynasties [he is known] as the one who assumes the forms of the fish, the tortoise, and so forth.
Lord Viṣṇu is indeed the two-fold knowledge: both the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā).
The Vedas, known as Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharvan, along with the six auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), O twice-born one; [and] the two types of knowledge regarding Brahman— thus [it is said].
The reading in the marked manuscript is "akhilātmagam";
this is the reading in manuscript Kha.
3. "The supreme mouth of all the Vedas," according to the reading of the manuscript marked Kha;
4. "Equal to the Vedas," according to the manuscripts marked Kha and Gha.
The reading "puṇyam" is found in manuscript *kha*;
this is the reading of the marked manuscript.
6. "Having spoken thus," is the reading found in the manuscript marked *ga*.
7. "Precisely because of the illumination of knowledge," is [the reading] in *ga*.
The reading "Brahmāgneya Purāṇa" is found in the two manuscripts marked Ga and Gha.
9. "O twice-born one"—this is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter *kha*:
"The Śikṣā, Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, and Jyotiṣa constitute the limbs [of the Veda]."
Prosody, grammar, hermeneutics, the treatises on dharma, the Purāṇas,
logic, medicine, music, archery, and the science of statecraft—
this is the lower knowledge; the higher knowledge is that by which Brahman is attained.
That which is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage or conduct, and eternal—
just as it was told to me by Viṣṇu from Brahmā in the past,
so shall I relate to you the reason for his forms such as the Fish and others.
Thus ends the first chapter, named "The Question," in the Āgneya Purāṇa, the Great Purāṇa.
Chapter 2:
Description of the Fish Incarnation (Matsyāvatāra)
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Tell me of Viṣṇu in the forms of the Fish and others, the cause of creation and so forth,
and the ancient Brahman as described in the Āgneya Purāṇa, just as it was heard by you from Viṣṇu in the past."
Agni said:
O Vasiṣṭha, listen as I describe the Fish incarnation of Hari;
for the performance of an incarnation is indeed for the destruction of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous.

At the end of the past kalpa, O Sage, there occurred the occasional dissolution (naimittika-laya) pertaining to Brahmā. Therein, the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ were submerged by the oceans. Then, Vaivasvata Manu performed austerities for the sake of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Once, while he was performing water-libations at Kṛtamālā,
a single tiny fish entered the water in his joined palms.
As he was about to cast it back into the water, it said to him, "O best of men, do not throw me away!"
"Brahman is realized"— this is the reading found in the three manuscripts marked Kha, Ga, and Gha.
2. "The practice of those without lineage is supreme"—this is the reading found in the manuscript marked *ga*.
3. "Do not revile me, O best of kings"—this is the reading found in the manuscripts marked *kha*, *ga*, and *gha*.
The reading of the three marked manuscripts:
"Today I have fear from crocodiles and the like";
having heard that, he threw [the child] into a water-jar.
But that old fish spoke again to him: "Give me a large place.

Now begins the fifth chapter,
the Description of the Śrī Rāma Incarnation.
Agni said:
I shall recount the Rāmāyaṇa as it was spoken of old by Nārada to Vālmīki; thus recited, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Nārada said:
From Viṣṇu was born Brahmā from his navel-lotus; Marīci was the son of Brahmā; from Marīci came Kaśyapa; from him, Sūrya; and from him, Vaivasvata Manu.
From him likewise came Ikṣvāku, and in his lineage was Kakutstha.
From Kakutstha came Rāghava; from him, Aja; and from him, Daśaratha.
For the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa and the others, Hari himself manifested in four forms.
From King Daśaratha, Rāma was born of Kauśalyā.
Bharata was born to Kaikeyī and Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna to Sumitrā; these sons were born from the milk-rice (*pāyasa*) offered by Ṛṣyaśṛṅga,
which had been consecrated for the sacrifice and partaken of by them, and they were equal to their father Rāma.
Requested by Viśvāmitra for the destruction of the obstacles to the sacrifice,
the king dispatched Rāma along with Lakṣmaṇa to be with the sage.
Rāma, having gone there, was instructed in missiles and weapons; he became the slayer of Tāḍakā.
With the Mānava missile, he sent Mārīca far away, bewildered;
and the powerful one killed Subāhu, the destroyer of sacrifices, along with his army.
Dwelling at Siddhāśrama together with Viśvāmitra and the others,
he went to the sacrifice of the King of Mithilā along with his younger brother, having been urged by Viśvāmitra on account of Śatānanda, in order to see the bow.
The king related [the matter] to Rāma, and the sage was honored at the sacrifice;
he effortlessly drew the bow and broke it. Then Janaka gave Sītā, his daughter not born from a womb, who was pure with heroism, to him.
Rāma also gave [the maidens] to Rāma when his father and the others had arrived;
he married that Jānakī, and likewise Lakṣmaṇa married Urmilā,
as well as Śrutakīrti and Māṇḍavī, the two daughters of Kuśadhvaja.
Both Śatrughna and Bharata, the younger brothers of Janaka,
married his two daughters after being highly honored by Janaka. Having defeated the son of Jamadagni, Rāma departed with Vasiṣṭha and the others.
Bharata, along with Śatrughna and Yudhājit, arrived at Ayodhyā.
Thus ends the description of the Bālakāṇḍa in the Rāmāyaṇa within the Āgneya Purāṇa, the foremost of the great Purāṇas.

Thus ends the twelfth [chapter], titled "The Description of the *Harivaṃśa*," in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*, the first great Purāṇa.

Chapter Thirteen:
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
A narration beginning with the origins of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas;
Agni said:
"I shall fully proclaim the Bhārata, characterized by the majesty of Kṛṣṇa."
Viṣṇu removed the burden of the earth, making the Pāṇḍavas the instrumental cause.
From Viṣṇu was born Brahmā from his navel-lotus; from Brahmā came his son Atri; from Atri came Soma; from Soma came Budha; and from him was born Purūravas, the son of Ila.

From him came Puru; in his lineage was Bharata, then King Kuru.

Citrāṅgada, Vicitravīrya, and Satyavat were the sons of Śāntanu. When Śāntanu had gone to heaven, Bhīṣma, remaining celibate, protected the kingdom of his brothers; meanwhile, the young Citrāṅgada was slain.

Because his death occurred at the hermitage of Śataśṛṅga due to the union with his wife as a result of a sage’s curse, Yudhiṣṭhira was born to Pāṇḍu from Kuntī through Dharma;
Bhīma from Vāta; Arjuna from Śakra; and [the twins] from the Aśvin-kumāras to Mādrī.

The evil-minded Duryodhana burned the Pāṇḍavas in the house of lac;

Then, having slain the Rākṣasa Vaka, they all remained in the house of a Brāhmaṇa in Ekacakrā, disguised as ascetics; thereafter,

In battle, Arjuna obtained the divine bow Gāṇḍīva from Agni, an excellent chariot, Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer, and inexhaustible arrows;

The Description of the Battle between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas.
Agni said:
The armies of Yudhiṣṭhira and Duryodhana marched toward Kurukṣetra.
Seeing Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the others, Pārtha said, "I will not fight my teachers. To him, the Blessed One replied: "Bhīṣma and the other leaders are not to be grieved for;

1. "Endowed with Vidura" is the reading found in the manuscript marked Kha;
"This self is the Supreme Brahman; know that 'I am Brahman.

Bhīṣma was the commander-in-chief at the outset of Duryodhana’s army,

The Pāṇḍavas, led by Śikhaṇḍin, slew the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with Bhīṣma in battle; the conflict between the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas was like the war between the gods and the asuras.
As the gods looked on, it became a source of increasing joy for those who were well-disposed;
yet Bhīṣma, with his weapons, struck down the Pāṇḍava army over ten days,
for on the tenth day, Arjuna indeed rained arrows upon the heroic Bhīṣma.
Śikhaṇḍin, as instructed by Drupada, rained down weapons like a cloud;
and Bhīṣma, who possesses death at his own will, having demonstrated the path of battle,
remained lying on a bed of arrows as directed by the Vasus for the sake of the world of the Vasus.
Looking toward the northern solstice, meditating on Viṣṇu, and offering praise,
Droṇa remained stationed as the commander-in-chief while Duryodhana was afflicted with grief; meanwhile,
when the Pāṇḍava army was exultant, Dhṛṣṭadyumna was the commander of their host.
A fierce battle took place between them, increasing the population of Yama’s kingdom;
Virāṭa, Drupada, and the others were submerged in the ocean that was Droṇa.
The great army of Duryodhana, consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, [was likewise overwhelmed].

On the second day, Karṇa was struck down by Arjuna;

The king, the crusher of enemies, became devoted to the duties of kingship, the duties of liberation, and the duties of charity;

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Mahābhārata," in the Āgneya Purāṇa, the foremost of the Great Purāṇas.

Chapter 16.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Account of the Incarnations of the Buddha and Others.
Agni said:
I shall describe the descent of the Buddha, which bestows wealth upon those who read or hear it.
Long ago, in a war between the gods and the asuras, the gods were defeated by the daityas;
crying out for protection, "Save us! Save us!", they went to the Lord for refuge.
This son of Śuddhodana was the embodiment of illusion and delusion;
he deluded those Daityas and caused them to abandon the Vedic dharma. Indeed, they became Buddhists, while others besides them were deprived of the Vedas.
He himself subsequently became an Arhat, and he caused others to become Arhats as well;
thus were the heretics born, devoid of the Vedic dharma and other such traditions.
They will perform deeds worthy of hell and will seize even from the lowest;
at the end of the Kali age, all will become of mixed caste (saṅkara),
robbers, and devoid of virtue, [and] the Veda will be the Vājasaneyaka.
Indeed, there will be fifteen branches by measure;
clothed in the mantle of dharma yet delighting in adharma,
these Mlecchas in the form of kings will devour human beings.
Kalkī, the son of Viṣṇuyaśas, with Yājñavalkya as his domestic priest,
having taken up missiles and equipped with weapons, will exterminate the Mlecchas and establish the proper boundaries for the four social orders as they ought to be.
And in all the hermitages, he will establish the subjects on the path of the true Dharma;
then, casting off his form as Kalkin, Hari will go to heaven,
and thereafter the age named Kṛtayuga will come into being just as it was in ancient times.
O best of beings, the castes and stages of life will remain established in their respective duties;
thus it shall be in all kalpas and in all manvantaras.
There have been, and there will be, innumerable incarnations—past, future, and so forth.
The man who reads or hears the accounts of Viṣṇu’s ten incarnations shall have his desires fulfilled, become pure, and, together with his family, attain heaven;
for Hari thus indeed establishes the order of righteousness and unrighteousness.
And that Hari, the cause of creation and so forth, has descended.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Buddha and Kalki Incarnations," in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*, the Great Purāṇa.
Chapter 17:
Description Concerning Creation
Agni said:
"I shall now describe the pastimes of Viṣṇu, such as the creation of the world; listen.
He is the creator of heaven and so forth; he is the beginning of creation, the source of emanation, possessed of qualities and yet devoid of qualities."
In the beginning, there was the unmanifest Brahman alone; there was no ether, night, day, or the like,
nor Prakṛti, Puruṣa, or Viṣṇu.
Then, having entered, he agitated the Great Principle (mahat-tattva) at the time of heaven; from that, the ego (ahaṃkāra) arose, which is threefold:
the Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Bhūtādi, which is Tāmasa.
From egoity (ahaṅkāra), space arose as mere sound;
from that, wind as mere touch; from that, fire as mere form;
from this, water as mere taste; and the earth is traditionally held to be mere smell. (17.004–005ab)
From the *tāmasa* ego arise the sense organs (*indriya*), which are *taijasa*;
the ten deities are *vaikārika*, as is the mind, the eleventh organ.
From that [proceeds] the Lord, the Self-existent (*svayambhū*).
Desiring to create various beings, he first emitted the waters alone; into them he cast his seed. The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara.
At the end of that eon, Nārāyaṇa is remembered as being at its eastern limit; in that egg resting upon the waters,
Brahmā himself was born, whom we have heard is called Svayambhū.
Having dwelt there for a full year, the Blessed One divided that single mass into two parts— both heaven and earth—
and between those two fragments, the Lord created space.
In the waters, he established the earth floating upon them and the ten directions;
therein he placed time, mind, speech, desire, anger, and likewise delight—
[and] Viṣṇu.

Chapter 20.
Now begins the twentieth chapter, the description concerning the process of creation;
Agni said:

The first creation is to be known as that of Mahat, belonging to Brahmā; the second is the creation of the subtle elements (tanmātras), which is recorded as the creation of the gross elements (bhūtas);
and the third is the creation of the Vaikārika, which is recorded as the creation of the senses (aindriyaka).
Thus this primary creation (prākṛta-sarga) has arisen preceded by intelligence;
the fourth is the principal creation (mukhya-sarga), and the immovable beings are indeed known as the principal ones.
That which was called the "sideways-streamed" (tiryak-srotas) is therefore known as the animal creation (tairyag-yonya).
Likewise, the sixth creation of the gods is known as that of the "upward-streamers" (ūrdhvasrotas); thereafter, the seventh creation is that of the "downward-streamers" (arvāksrotas), which is human;
and the eighth is the creation of grace (anugrahasarga), which consists of both the pure (sāttvika) and the dark (tāmasa).
These five are known as the modified (vaikṛta) creations, and three as the primary (prākṛta) ones; thus, the primary, the modified, and the ninth, the Kaumāra creation.

From Brahmā, there are nine creations which are the root causes of the world; Khyāti and the others, the daughters of Dakṣa, married Bhṛgu and the other sages. Creation is declared by people to be threefold: eternal, occasional, and [periodic].
The ordinary daily creation occurs after the intermediate dissolution;
that in which [creation] arises day by day is indeed recognized as the constant creation (*nitya-sarga*).
Khyāti gave birth to the two gods Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ from Bhṛgu.

Śrī, the wife of Viṣṇu, was praised by Śakra for the prosperity of Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ; they had two sons in succession, Prāṇa and Mṛkaṇḍuka. From Mṛkaṇḍu was born Mārkaṇḍeya, and from him was born Vedaśiras.

[Soma] begot Soma, Durvāsas as a son, and the yogi Dattātreya.

From Pulaha and Kṣamā were born Sahiṣṇu and the Karmapādins.

% Chapter 22.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter,
the description of the rules for bathing;
Nārada said:

I shall describe the ritual bathing for the purpose of performing rites and so forth. Having taken earth with the *Nṛsiṃha* mantra and divided it into two parts, one should perform the mental bath (*manaḥ-snāna*) with one part;
then, having immersed oneself, sipped water (*ācamana*), and performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*), one should have protection established by means of the *Siṃha* mantra. (2)ab: n.
1. Hrīṃ to Tvaritā,
hrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sau Tripurā— thus is the reading marked with the letter Kha in the manuscript.
2. "Having performed the protection ritual" (kṛtarakṣaṇa) is the reading found in manuscript Gha;
Then one should perform the ritual bath preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma),
while meditating in the heart upon the knowledge of Hari with the eight-syllable mantra.

Having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) by reciting the *siṃha-mantra* three times over the clay on the palm of the hand, and having consecrated the sacred site (*tīrtha*) by reciting the *vāsudeva-mantra*, one should touch it; then, having cleansed the body with mantras beginning with the Vedas and worshipped it with the *mūrti-mantra*.
Having performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite and put on his garment, he should proceed;
having applied the mantras and sprinkled the water held in his hand twice,
and having restrained the breath with the *nārāyaṇa* mantra and smelled it, he should release it.
After meditating on Hari while in the water and offering the *arghya* oblation, one should recite the twelve-syllable mantra hundreds of times; then, from the *yogapīṭha* onwards in sequence,
one should recite the mantras ending with those of the guardians of the directions, as well as those of the sages and the hosts of ancestors.
Having placed all beings, from humans down to the stationary,
within himself and having withdrawn his limbs, he should enter the sacrificial chamber while reciting the mantras;
likewise, in other forms of worship, he should perform the ritual bath with the root-mantra and the others.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for Bathing," in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*, the foremost of the great Purāṇas.
Chapter 23.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter,
the Exposition of the Ritual of Worship.
Nārada said:
O Brahmins, I shall describe the procedure for worship, by performing which one obtains everything;
having washed one's feet, sipped water, restrained speech, and performed the protection ritual.

Meditating on the god Hari, facing east and having assumed the svastika posture, as well as the lotus and other postures— this is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter Gha, page 56.

One should meditate on the seed-syllable located in the center of the navel, smoke-colored and consisting of fierce wind; then, remembering the seed-syllable *kṣauṃ*, a treasury of splendor situated in the middle of the heart-lotus, one should expel all impurity from the body.
One should burn away impurity with flames spreading downward, upward, and across; then,
visualizing [the moon] in the form of the crescent situated in the sky, the wise one should drench his own body with nectar-water pervading the heart-lotus.
Having purified [the body] by means of the path of the *suṣumnā* womb, which spreads through all the channels (*nāḍī*),
one should then place the *tattva*, followed by the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) and the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
First, the pervasive [mantra] is placed on both hands, beginning from the right thumb, and then the limbs [are assigned].
One should place the twelve limbs upon the body with the mantras consisting of two syllables each:
the heart, the head, the crest, the armor, the weapon, and the eyes; as well as the belly, the back, the arms, the thighs, the knees, and the feet.

Having performed the mudrā, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu; having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, one should worship. Having placed the *vardhanī* vessel on the left and the materials for worship on the right, one should wash them with the *astra-mantra* and the *arghya*, and then place them together with perfumes and flowers.

Having sprinkled with water over which the mantra has been recited eight times— ending with *phaṭ*— the all-pervading light of consciousness (*caitanya*), one should meditate on Hari in the hand; then,
facing the directions of fire (southeast), one should [place] virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), detachment (*vairāgya*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
On the yoga-seat, starting from the east, are the limbs beginning with Adharma;
on the seat are Kūrma, Ananta, Yama,
and the mandalas of the Sun and so forth.
"One should dry it up entirely"— this is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter *ṅa*.
"A wise man should cause his own desires to burn"— this is the reading in the manuscript marked *kha*; "A wise man should gladden himself"— this is the reading in manuscript *ṅa*.
The reading of the marked manuscript (ṅa) states:
"But having sprinkled that spot with water and meditated on Hari in one's hand, one should recite [the mantra]."
4. "Padmam" is the reading found in the three manuscripts marked kha, ga, and ṅa:

Having first meditated upon Vimalā and the others situated on the filaments, and Karṇikā situated on the pericarp within one's own heart, one should then invoke them into the mandala and worship them with water for the guest-offering (arghya),
water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
One should offer the bath, clothing, sacred thread, ornaments, perfumes, flowers,
incense, lamps, and the articles for the altar with the Puṇḍarīkākṣa-vidyā.
One should worship the limbs starting from the east, and at the eastern door, one should worship the son of Aṇḍaja (the Garuḍa-mantra).
One should place the discus and mace in the right corner, and the conch and bow in the left corner;
on the left and right of the deity, one should place the two quivers and the sword,
and on the left, the shield and Śrī.
One should place Puṣṭi on the right, and on the left and in front,
the forest garland, the Śrīvatsa, and the Kaustubha; outside, one should worship all the guardians of the directions with their respective mantras, beginning with Viṣṇu and ending with Arghya.
One should worship with the limbs and the seed-syllable, both individually and collectively;
having recited the mantra, circumambulated, praised, and offered the *arghya*, one should meditate upon the heart and perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), thinking: "I am Brahman, I am Hari."
The words "Come" (āgaccha) are to be employed for the invocation, and "Forgive me" (kṣamasva) for the dismissal.
Having performed worship in this manner with the eight-syllable mantra and others, one becomes a partaker of liberation.
Thus the worship of the single form has been declared; now hear the worship of the ninefold manifestation (navavyūha).

Having placed Vāsudeva on the two thumbs and Balarāma and the others on the index fingers and so forth, one should then worship them in order— beginning from the east— in the body, specifically in the head, forehead, face, heart, navel, private parts, knees, and feet. (21)
The single seat, the ninefold array, and the nine seats are as before.
[Note 1: In the left hand is armor; "Śrī" is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter *kha*.]
In some small manuscripts, the readings "viṣṇurarghauvasānataḥ" and "viṣṇāvarghau ca mānataḥ" occur; however,
these appear to be incorrect.
The reading "viṣṇum arghyāsanādibhiḥ" is indeed appropriate; however,
the reading "madhyagulphāditaḥ pi sphaca" belongs to the manuscript marked with the letter Ṅa.
In a nine-petaled lotus, one should worship the Ninefold Form (Navamūrti) and the Ninefold Array (Navavyūha) as before;
having performed the desired worship, one should then worship Vāsudeva in the central position.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of the Primordial Form and Others," in the Āgneya Purāṇa, the foremost among the great Purāṇas.
Chapter 24.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter: the procedure for the construction of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and so forth.
Nārada said:

I shall explain the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) by which one may partake in all desired objects. Having marked out a square measuring twenty-four finger-breadths with a cord, one should dig a level pit of that same size.
The girdle of the pit should be made, leaving a space of two finger-breadths;
it should be twelve finger-breadths high in the eastern direction,
then eight, two, and four finger-breadths [respectively], and four finger-breadths in width.
The beautiful vulva, ten fingers in length, should be made with its tip extending six, four, and two fingers respectively, gradually receding and situated toward the western direction;
it should resemble an *aśvattha* leaf and be slightly inserted into the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
The tube is four finger-breadths long; it is fifteen finger-breadths long [in total],
with the base being three finger-breadths and its tip being six finger-breadths.
The measurement for a single cubit is doubled for two cubits and so forth.
I shall now describe the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), which may be circular or otherwise, having one or three girdles.
[Note 1: "designations such as 'sadmā' and so on," according to manuscript *kha*.]
The reading of the marked manuscript is "malantu dvyaṅgulam" (let there be two finger-breadths [of space]), as found in manuscript Ga.
This is the reading of the marked manuscript.
The thread situated at half the pit, which extends beyond the corner—
that half of it, having been placed in the direction and rotated, shall form a circle.
Having carefully marked the center from the north, outside the directions, at half the distance of the pit (kuṇḍa) and half the distance of the corner (koṇa),
one should rotate the line drawn from that center; thus the auspicious half-moon pit is formed.
The petals should be in the shape of a lotus, while the girdles are circular.
One should have the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) made to the measure of a staff-like arm, or five or seven finger-breadths; it should also be made square. AP 24.010ab–24.011ab.

One-third of that [measurement] should form a beautiful circular pit in the center. One should excavate it so that it is equal in width and height; furthermore, one should reduce the outer part by half, then by a fourth of an angula, and finally by half of that half again.
One should cause a beautiful girdle for the pit to be made with half of the remaining material;
the neck should have a width of three parts and a length equal to one thumb,
or it may be one and a half thumbs, and at its tip there should be a mouth.
It should be four finger-breadths in width, or perhaps five;
its three [sections] should be two finger-breadths each, which is very beautiful in the middle. Its length should be equal to that, with a well-formed depression in the center.
There should be a hollow at the neck region extending as far as the little finger;
the remaining portion of the vessel should be fashioned according to one's taste and decorated. The *sruva* ladle should be one cubit in length and provided with a handle.
The *vaṭuka* should be made two finger-breadths in height, circular, and very beautiful.
1. "Equipped with a *kuṇḍaka*" is the reading found in manuscript Kha;
2. "The *kaṇṭhaka* is two finger-breadths [in length]" is [the reading found in] Kha.
The reading of the marked manuscript is "candrābhaṃ dvyaṅgulam" (shining like the moon, two finger-breadths), according to manuscript Ṅa.
This is the reading of the marked manuscript.
Just as a cow’s hoofprint might be submerged in shallow mud, so it should be;
having smeared [the ground], one should draw a line one finger-breadth wide with a vajra-tip.
The first line should be drawn facing north; between those two lines facing east, one who knows the mantra should likewise draw three lines in the sequence starting from the south.
Having thus drawn them and sprinkled them with water while reciting the *praṇava*, the knower of mantras [proceeds].
One should prepare a seat for Him; having empowered that [seat] with the Vaiṣṇavī power and adorned it as an embodied form, one should cast the fire while remembering Hari.
Then, having offered fuel-sticks of the length of a span and having swept around the fire, [one should proceed].
Having strewn *darbha* grass threefold starting from the east, he should place there the vessels, the fuel, and the fire on the ground, as well as the pair of *śruk* and *śruva* ladles,
the vessel for clarified butter (*ājya-sthālī*), the vessel for the sacrificial porridge (*caru-sthālī*), the *kuśa* grass, and the clarified butter along with the *praṇītā* water.
Having sprinkled [the materials] and taken the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, having filled it with water and poured that water through the *pavitra* blades held in his hand,
he should carry it toward the east and place the vessel before the light.
Having sprinkled that [water] three times with those waters and having placed the fuel (idhma) in front,

one should meditate on Viṣṇu in the *praṇītā* vessel adorned with beautiful flowers; then, having filled the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) with clarified butter, one should place it in front to the north.
One should perform the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*) by means of both pouring together (*samplava*) and straining (*utpavana*).
With two *kuśa* blades that have unbroken tips, are without internal nodes, and are a span (*prādeśa*) in length,
one should hold them with upturned hands using the thumbs and ring fingers.
Having taken the clarified butter from those two, he should pour it out twice and then cast it down three times;
likewise, having taken the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, he should sprinkle water upon them with those two.
1. "Rudranāsikām" is the reading found in the manuscript marked Kha; "Vaktranāsikām" is the reading found in the manuscript marked Ṅa.
2. "Having worshipped the first of those two, one should toss [the flower] upwards three times"— this is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter *ṅa* on page 61.
Having heated it with darbha grass, wiped it clean, and washed it again,
the practitioner, having heated it once more, should place it down while reciting the Praṇava alone.
Thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) beginning with the syllable *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*,
according to the established order of the rites starting from conception (*garbhādhāna*) and so forth;
[the sequence] ending with the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), ending with the initiation into vows (*vratabandha*), and concluding with the return home (*samāvartana*).
Or he may conclude at the end of the section, according to the [extent of the] ancillaries.
The practitioner should perform the ritual service with the *praṇava* in all cases;
however, the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the ancillaries should be performed according to one's means.

First is the ceremony for entering the womb; then the *puṃsavana* (rite for ensuring a male child) is prescribed; followed by the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair), the *jātakarma* (birth rite), the naming ceremony, the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*), the initiation into the vows (*vratabandha*), and all the Vedic observances (*vedavrata*) in their entirety.
The return ceremony (*samāvartana*), the union with the wife, and then the qualification [for ritual acts]—
having meditated upon each one in the sequence beginning with the Heart-mantra and having worshipped it,
one should again offer eight oblations for each rite.
Then the practitioner should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with the *śruci* ladle using the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, pronouncing it with a protracted vowel and a beautiful tone;
having thus consecrated the fire of Viṣṇu, he should cook the *vaiṣṇava-caru*.
Having propitiated Viṣṇu on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and recollecting the mantras,
one should cook [the offering] according to the sequence beginning with the seat, including the limbs and the supreme enclosure;
having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, the meditator should contemplate the God, the best of deities.
Having placed the fuel and then the two *āghāra* libations of clarified butter, which are situated at the *agnīdh* fire;
[the word] "having yoked" (*niyujya*) means "having established," according to the reading in the manuscript marked with the letter *kha*.
2. "The divine vows in their entirety" is the reading found in the manuscript marked Kha. 3. "And yoga according to its respective domains" is [the reading found in] Kha.
The reading of the manuscript marked with the letter *ca* is "mantrān santarpya saṃtarpyet";
the reading of the two manuscripts marked with the letters *kha* and *gha* is as follows.
When proceeding from the northwest, the southwest, the east, and so forth, in due order,
one should then offer the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) for the eyes in the south and the north.
One should offer all the mantras into the middle [fire] according to the sequence of worship;
one should satisfy the deity with clarified butter, and perform the limb-homa (aṅgahoma) as a tenth part of the [main] oblation for the form.
One may offer a hundred or a thousand [oblations] with clarified butter and other substances, or with sacrificial wood and sesame seeds.
Having completed the ritual up to the end of the oblations, he should summon the pure disciples who have fasted,
seat them before him, and then sprinkle those "beasts" with the weapon-mantra.
Having united the disciples with his own self, [he should release them] from the bonds of ignorance and karma.
Consciousness, which follows the subtle body (*liṅga*) and is bound together with it,
should be sprinkled with the path of meditation and purified by the seed-syllable of wind (*vāyu-bīja*).
Then, by means of the seed-syllable of fire, one should [dissolve] the creation known as the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
One should meditate on the entire [universe] as completely burnt, remaining like a heap of ashes;
or one should flood that ash with water, making the world consist of water,
and then one should place upon it the earthly power (śakti) known by the name of the seed-syllable (bīja).

One should meditate upon that auspicious cosmic egg (aṇḍa), composed of earth and enveloped by all the subtle elements (tanmātras) together; it arises from that [egg], has that as its support, and has that as its essence.
In the center of that, one should contemplate the anthropomorphic form (pauruṣī mūrti), which is identical with the Praṇava.
One should subsequently transfer the *liṅga*, which resides within oneself and has been previously consecrated,
and contemplate it as gradually growing until its organs and form are fully differentiated.
Then, having remained for one year as an egg, it becomes divided into two parts.
1. "Or likewise with fuel-sticks or sesame seeds"—this is the reading found in the manuscript marked *gha*. 2.
"It is shown together with the *liṅga* (linguistic mark)"—this is the reading found in the manuscript marked *ṅa*.
The reading of the marked manuscript is "saṃsārañcākṣayaṃ smaret" (and one should remember saṃsāra as inexhaustible),
according to manuscript kha.
4. "On the sacrificial ground, previously consecrated"—this is the reading found in manuscript *kha* and in the marked manuscript.
Having meditated upon the two fragments as heaven and earth, and Prajāpati born between them, he should sprinkle him again with the *praṇava* and,
according to the previously mentioned ritual placement (*nyāsa*), make his body consist of the essence of the mantras.
Then Viṣṇu, having placed his hand upon [the disciple’s] head and meditated upon the Vaiṣṇava [mantra],
having thus generated one or even many [disciples] through the yoga of meditation,
should grasp both hands with the root-mantra and bind the eyes with a cloth.
The Guru, who knows the reality of the God of gods, having performed the worship correctly with the Netra-mantra and an unstruck (anāhata) sound,
should seat the disciples, who hold handfuls of flowers, facing the east.
And they too, being thus instructed by their teacher, should worship Hari;
having first offered a handful of flowers there, they should immediately perform a worship with flowers and other offerings, even without the recitation of mantras.
Thereafter, having performed the worship of the Guru’s feet, one should give him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), whether it be one's entire possession or even half of it.
The Guru should thoroughly instruct the disciples, and Hari is to be worshipped by them under His various names.

One should worship the Lord Viṣvaksena, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace; and while reciting his mantra, one should dismiss him from the mandala with the index finger. One should offer all of Viṣṇu’s remains (nirmālya) to Viṣvaksena.
Having likewise consecrated himself with the *praṇītā* waters and having merged the fire residing in the sacrificial pit into his own self, he should dismiss Viṣvaksena.
One who desires enjoyment attains everything; one who desires liberation is absorbed into Hari.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fire-Rite and Other Rituals," in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*, the Great Purāṇa.
[Variant reading in manuscript *kha*: "Having performed the worship of Vāsudeva..."]
The reading of the marked manuscript: p.
64, Chapter 25.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter, the Exposition of the Mantras of Vāsudeva and Others.
Nārada said:
I shall describe the characteristics of the worship of the mantras beginning with Vāsudeva:
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha;
preceded by "Obeisance to the Blessed One" (namo bhagavate), followed by the syllables A, Ā, AṂ, and AḤ, which are their respective seed-syllables.
Beginning with the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, followed by *namo nārāyaṇāya*;
then *oṃ tat sat brahmaṇe caiva*, *oṃ namo viṣṇave namaḥ*;
and *oṃ kṣauṃ oṃ namo bhagavate narasiṃhāya vai namaḥ*.

Oṃ bhūḥ! Homage to the Blessed One, Varāha! O lords of men, these nine beloved leaders possess the luster of the javā flower, the dawn, and turmeric; they are blue, dark-green, and red, with complexions like a cloud, fire, and honey. AP 25.004–25.005ab.
Those who know the tantras should fashion the limbs, beginning with the heart, from the seed-syllables of the vowels together with their own names in due order;
the consonants and so forth are their seeds, while their characteristics are otherwise.
The limbs (*aṅga*) are described as being distinguished by long vowels and ending with the word *namaḥ*, while the secondary limbs (*upāṅga*) are joined with short vowels.
The supreme seed-syllable (*bīja*) is situated at the end of the syllables of the divided name.
Combined with long and short vowels in their proper sequence, along with the primary and secondary limbs (*aṅga* and *upāṅga*),

this is the order of the consonants for the arrangement of the heart and other [limbs]. They are divided by means of their own seed-syllables and the names of the limbs ending in their respective names.
1. "The twelve-syllable seed-mantras" is the reading found in manuscript *kha*. 2.
"The supreme [mantra] for the purpose of the established seed-mantra" is the reading found in manuscript *kha*.
The reading of the marked manuscript (kha) is:
"And the limbs and sub-limbs, joined with long vowels, [should be recited] in sequence according to the vowels. This is the reading of the marked manuscript.
"In the seed-syllables of the vowels, [the names] are divided by the names of the limbs with different endings"— this is the reading marked as "ṅa" on page 65.
Having joined the heart and the other limbs up to the *dvādaśānta* in five groups,
one should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to the requirements for accomplishment:
the heart, the head, the crest, the armor, the eye, and the weapon.

One should sequentially assign the six limbs of the seed-syllables to the twelve parts of the root-mantra: the heart, the head, the crest, the armor, the weapon, and the eyes; then the belly, the back, the arms, the thighs, the knees, the shanks, and the feet.
Kaṃ ṭaṃ paṃ śaṃ is Vainateya; khaṃ ṭhaṃ phaṃ ghaṃ gaṃ ḍaṃ baṃ saṃ are those possessed of nourishment; ghaṃ ḍhaṃ bhaṃ haṃ, obeisance to Śrī.
Vaṃ śaṃ maṃ kṣaṃ for Pāñcajanya; chaṃ taṃ paṃ for the Kaustubha gem.
Jaṃ khaṃ vaṃ to Sudarśana; śrīvatsāya saṃ vaṃ daṃ caṃ oṃ dhaṃ vaṃ to the Vanamālā and Mahānanta; salutations!
(6) One should fashion the limbs [of the deity] by means of the words of the seedless (nirbīja) pada-mantras.
The five [limbs], beginning with the heart, are joined with the names of the other castes;
then the *praṇava* (oṃ) and the limbs beginning with the heart are likewise declared in five ways.
First, the *praṇava* is the heart, followed by "parāya" for the head and the tuft (*śikhā*).
But by means of one's own name, the armor-mantra and the weapon-mantra become the "End-of-Name" (Nāmāntaka).
1. "The twelve syllables with effort" is the reading found in the manuscript marked Ṅa; 2.
"the great mace" is [the reading] in Ṅa.
The reading of the marked manuscript is "ṭhaṃ ṇaṃ maṃ kṣaṃ," whereas [the other version] is "ṅa. This is the reading of the marked manuscript.
4. "daṃ bhaṃ pam iti" is the reading of the marked manuscript (kha);
5. "śrīvatsāya ca pañcamam" is [the reading] in manuscript (ṅa).
The reading marked in the manuscript is "śrīvatso vaṃ caṃ daṃ ṭhaṃ laṃ" as found in the *ga* [manuscript];
this is the reading marked in the manuscript.
6. "Salutation indeed to the Infinite; salutation," thus is the reading in the manuscript marked Ṅa.
7. "But by this name," thus is [the reading] in Kha and Ṅa.
The reading from the two marked manuscripts: p. 66 oṃ parāstrādisvanāmātmā(1)
The mantra of that Self, beginning with Ekavyūha and ending with Ṣaḍviṃśavyūha, consists of names ending in the dative case;
one should meditate upon the primordial nature (prakṛti) within the body, from the little finger to the tips of the fingers.
The Supreme Self may be the Puruṣa-self; the two-fold form is the Prakṛti-self.
Oṃ, likewise for the Supreme-Light Self, Vāyu and Arka are the two-fold form.
[One should place] Agni in the Trimūrti.
Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) upon the hands and the body,
one should place Vāyu and Arka on the fingers of both the left and right hands.
This [deity] is embodied in the heart within the threefold manifestation (*trivyūha*), which is the fourth form.

One should place the pervasive *Ṛgveda* on the hand and the *Yajurveda* on the fingers; the form of the *Atharvaveda* is placed on the two palms, extending from the head and heart to the feet. Having placed the pervasive *Ākāśa* (Ether) on the hand as before, one places it upon the body.
In the fingers, and in the head, heart, private parts, and feet, wind,
fire, water, earth, and ether are declared as the fivefold array (pañcavyūha).
Mind, ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose are declared as the sixfold array (ṣaḍvyūha).

Having established the pervasive mental [deity], one should then sequentially place it starting from the thumbs upon the head, mouth, heart, genitals, and feet; this is said to be the compassionate self.
The primordial form, however, is all-pervasive and is designated as the "living soul" (jīva).
One should assign the sevenfold [mantra]— bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svar, mahaḥ, janaḥ, tapaḥ, and satyam—
to the hands and the body, beginning with the thumb;
the seventh is located on the palms.
Lokeśa [is placed] on the body in sequence.
(AP 25.027cd) Note 1: "Oṃ parāstrādityanāmātmā" is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter *gha*.
2. Thus, the twenty-sixth [chapter] begins with the *vyūha*; "from that *vyūha*, Manu [arose] from the Self"—this is the reading found in the manuscript marked *kha*.
3. "Agni [arose] from the two forms"—this is the reading found in the manuscript marked *kha*.
The reading found in the marked manuscript is "talasthaḥ saptamaś caiva," as in manuscript Ṅa;
this is the reading of the marked manuscript.
In the body, [the fires] are situated in the head, forehead, mouth, heart, private parts,
and feet; likewise, they are the Agniṣṭoma, the Uktha, the Ṣoḍaśin, and the Vājapeya.
The self of sacrifice consists of seven forms:
the intellect, the ego, the mind, sound, touch, form, and taste;
from that [follow] smell and the pervasive intellect. One should place these in sequence upon the hands and the body.
One should place [the mantras] on the two palms, the forehead, the mouth, the heart,
the navel, the secret place, and the feet; thus the Person is said to consist of eight arrays (aṣṭavyūha).
Seed-syllable, intellect, ego, mind, sound, the quality [of space], and wind;
form, taste—this ninefold self is the *jīva* located in the two thumbs.
Following the sequence beginning with the index finger, the remainder extends as far as the left forefinger.
In the body— namely, in the head, forehead, mouth, heart, navel, private parts,
knees, and the two feet— this tenfold Indra is established as the pervasive one.
Fire resides in the two big toes, and in the others, beginning with the index fingers.
On the head, forehead, face, heart, navel, genitals,
knees, and the two feet, there are eleven principles: the mind, the ear,
the skin, the eye, the tongue, the nose, speech, the hand, the foot, and the anus.

The *upastha* [is assigned] to the mind (*mānasa*), the pervasive [element] to the ears, and the eight [other elements] to the two thumbs and the fingers beginning with the index finger in sequence; the remaining one is on the palms of both hands. Then, [the elements are assigned] to the head, the forehead, the mouth, the heart, the navel, and the secret place.
Likewise, on the two thighs, the shanks, and sequentially on the ankles and feet, [the deities are placed].
(The reading *atirātrāptayāmaśca* is found in the manuscript marked with the letter *kha*.)

Chapter 29:
The Description of the Sarvatobhadra Maṇḍala
Nārada said:
The practitioner should accomplish the mantra in a temple of the deity or similar place;
having worshipped Hari, the Lord, in a mandala within a house on pure ground.
One should indeed draw the mandalas and other designs upon a square field;
one should delineate the *sarvatobhadra* in thirty-six squares,
and the lotus with its pedestal in a row of squares.
It should extend outward;
from those two [parts] comes the pathway, and from two [more] come the gates in the cardinal directions.
Having rotated the previously described lotus-field into a circle,
and having rotated half of that lotus, one should divide the outer twelfth part and rotate the remainder into four circular fields.
First is the field of the pericarp, the second is that of the filaments,
the third is that of the joints of the petals, and the fourth is that of the tips of the petals; having extended the diagonal threads from the corners to the intermediate directions at the end.
Having placed [the compass] at the tip of the filaments, one should mark the junctions of the petals;
then, having cast the lines, one should draw the eight petals there.
Having fixed the measurement for the space between the petal-junctions at the center, however—
One should rotate the tip of the petal; immediately after that,
having placed its tip and the intervening space on its side according to the outward sequence,
one should then draw two [lines] upon each filament in the middle of each petal.
This lotus-design, characterized by twelve petals, is called the *sāmānya* (general).
One should draw it starting from the east, rotating gradually with a measurement equal to half the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
By means of circular rotations on its sides, six coils (*kuṇḍalī*) indeed come into being.
In this way, there shall be twelve fish and two sets of six lotus-petals;
having thus formed a lotus with five petals for the sake of accomplishment,
one should erase the squares within the pedestal outside the lines of the void.

Three [squares] at the corners are for the feet, while the others are two by two; furthermore, those smeared in the four directions become the limbs. Then, one should erase two rows in the directions for the sake of the courtyard (vīṭhī).
One should construct four doors in each of the four directions;
a wise person should fashion eight ornaments on the sides of those doors.
"One should employ two rows [of squares] in each of the directions for the purpose of the pathways"— this is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter *ṅa* on page 80.
The secondary ornaments (*upaśobhā*) are proclaimed to be equal in number to those [primary ones]. The corners (*koṇa*) are proclaimed to be near the secondary ornaments.
Then, one should contemplate two [cells] in each of the four directions by means of the central squares.
One should polish four [petals] on the exterior, and likewise one on each of the two sides.
For the sake of beauty, one should remove three petals from each side; thereafter, one should similarly create the secondary ornament (*upaśobhā*) by reversing that process.
One should contemplate three [squares] inside and outside the corner, divided twice;
thus there shall be sixteen squares. In this manner, another mandala consists of thirty-six squares in twelve divisions, including the lotus and the pathway.
There should be one row for these two; the door-decorations and so forth are as before.
In a mandala of one cubit, the lotus should be twelve finger-breadths;
in a two-cubit [mandala], it should be one cubit, or one should proceed by increasing [the size] according to the door.

The pedestal (apīṭha) should be square; the wheel (vikara) consists of a lotus with nine parts, of which half is said to be the lotus and three are remembered as the nave (nābhi). One should fashion the doors with eight parts, and the rim (nemi) with four finger-breadths (aṅgula).
Having divided the field into three parts, one should then mark two of them; having stretched the cords across those [sections],
one should draw spokes shaped like the petals of a blue lotus or like a citron fruit.
Or one may also draw [the spokes] as broad as lotus petals, according to one's desire.
Having rotated [the wheel], while standing within the interval between the inner rim (*nemi*) and the outer rim,
one should rotate the base of the spokes while stationed in the middle of the joints.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Characteristics of Mandalas and Other Matters," in the Agni Purāṇa, the Great Ancient Lore.
Chapter 30:
The Ritual Procedure for the Maṇḍala (Maṇḍalavidhi)
Nārada said:

One should worship Brahmā together with his limbs in the central lotus; one should worship the Navel-born [Viṣṇu] in the eastern lotus, Prakṛti in the south-eastern lotus, and Puruṣa in the southern lotus.
To the south of Puruṣa, one should place Vahni; to the southwest, Anila;
Āditya in the lotus of Aindava; and the Ṛg and Yajur Vedas in the lotus of Īśa.
Likewise, Indra and the other deities are placed in the sixteen-petalled lotus of the second [layer].
One should worship the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda, space, wind, fire, water, earth, mind, ear, skin, eye,
tongue, and likewise the nose, as well as the sixteenfold worlds of Bhūḥ and Bhuvaḥ.
Having fully honored Mahā, Janas, Tapas, Satya, as well as Agniṣṭoma, Coktha, Ṣoḍaśī, Vājapeya,
Atirātra, and likewise Aptoryāma, one should worship them.
Mind, intellect, ego, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell [are placed] in the twenty-four lotuses in sequence. (AP 29.007ab) Note 1:

The reading in the marked manuscript is *jyotiṣṭomakam* (in manuscript Ṅa);

The nose, speech, hands, and feet— these thirty-two [deities] on the lotuses are to be worshipped in the fourth enclosure, together with their limbs and retinues;
and having fully worshipped the anus and genitals, one should worship the twelve lords of the months.
One should worship the twenty-six deities beginning with Puruṣottama in the outer enclosure;

Then one should perform the scattering of colored powders upon the drawn mandala; listen:
the pericarp shall be yellow in color, and all the lines shall be white, even, two cubits long, and one thumb-breadth wide; for a single cubit, they shall be half that size and white.
One should join the petals with white [pigment] and the joints with black or dark blue;
the filaments should be red and yellow, and one should fill the corners with red. One should then adorn the yoga-pīṭha as desired with all colors.
One should adorn the pathway with creepers, canopies, leaves, and so forth;
at the gateway of the pedestal, one should use white for the primary ornament (*śobhā*),
red for the secondary ornament (*upaśobhā*), and yellow for the corners (*koṇa*), while the conch-patterns (*śaṅkhya*) should indeed be white.
In the Bhadraka [mandala], the filling is prescribed as follows; likewise is the filling in other [mandalas].
One should adorn the triangle with white, red, and black;
the double-triangle with red and yellow; and the nave of the wheel with black.
The spokes are yellow and red; the rim, however, is dark green.
On the outside, the lines are white, dark green, reddish-brown, black, and yellow.
The white [powder] should be made from rice flour and the like; the red, from safflower and similar substances.
By means of turmeric, it becomes yellow; by means of burnt grain, it becomes black;
and by means of *śamī* leaves and so forth, it becomes dark grey through the recitation of the mantra one hundred thousand times over the seeds.
For four hundred thousand recitations of mantras and one hundred thousand for vidyās; ten thousand for the vidyās of the Buddhas and one thousand for hymns.
First, by means of one hundred thousand recitations, there is the purification of the mantra as well as of oneself.
Likewise, by another hundred thousand [recitations], the mantra becomes consecrated as a field;
previously, an incomparable homa of seeds has been proclaimed.
The preliminary service (pūrvasevā) for the mantras and so forth is proclaimed to be one-tenth [of that number].
But in the practice of another mantra, one should observe the vow for a month;
one should place the left foot on the ground and not accept gifts.
In this way, by doubling or tripling [the duration], the middling and supreme accomplishments are attained.
I shall now explain the meditation on the mantra, by which the fruit born of the mantra may be attained.
The gross form consists of sound and is considered external;
the subtle form consists of light and exists within the heart as the nature of thought.
That which is devoid of thought is proclaimed as the Supreme.
The gross form of Varāha, Siṃha, and Śakti is primarily [the form] of Vāsudeva, which is declared to be devoid of thought.
The form of the others is traditionally held to be within the heart, consisting of thought and always gross; that which is called Vairāja is subtle,
while the form of the Lord (Īśvara) is proclaimed to be devoid of thought.
One should meditate upon consciousness as the imperishable light residing in the lotus of the heart— the seed that is the essence of all seeds— having the form of a *kadamba* flower,
like a lamp placed within a jar whose flame is stilled.
Thus the Lord of Mantras remains concentrated and alone within the heart;
just as rays of light extend outward through the many apertures of a jar to that same extent,
so too do the seed-rays [of consciousness] radiate out through the channels.
86. Then, having made the divine body their own through manifestation, they remain;
the channels (nāḍīs) have set out from the heart and fall within the range of the faculty of sight.

Having properly conquered the breath of the body through the secret yoga, the practitioner of mantra, devoted to recitation and meditation, attains the characteristic of mantra within those two channels consisting of Agni and Soma, which are situated at the tip of the nose.
One who practices yoga while still possessing desire, having purified the elements and their subtle counterparts (*tanmātra*),

attains powers such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and the like; but one who is dispassionate transcends them and, within the divine self, is liberated from the elements, the subtle counterparts, and the grasp of the senses.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Mandalas and Other Matters," in the Āgneya Purāṇa, the foremost among the great Purāṇas.

Chapter 32:
An Exposition on the Formative Forces (Saṃskāra)
Agni said:
"In the initiations for the Nirvāṇa and other rites, the wise man should cause forty-eight purificatory ceremonies (saṃskāras) to be performed; listen to how by these others one may become a god."

One should perform the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) in the womb, and thereafter the *puṃsavana* (male-making rite); then the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair), the *jātakarma* (birth rite), and the naming ceremony; then the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure (*cūḍā*), and the vows of studentship (*brahmacarya*).
The four [sacrifices] are the Vaiṣṇavī, the Pārthī, the Bhautikī, and likewise the Śrautikī; then there is the gift of a cow, the impurity due to birth, and the seven *pākayajñas*.
(1) The *aṣṭakās*, the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, the *śrāvaṇī*, and the *āgrāyaṇī*—these are the others.
The Caitrī and the Āśvayujī; hear now of those seven *haviḥ-yajñas*:
the *ādhāna*, the *agnihotra*, the *darśa*, the *paurṇamāsa*, the *cāturmāsya*, the *paśubandha*, and the *sautrāmaṇi*.
Listen to the seven Soma-sacrifices; the Agniṣṭoma is the best of rites,
followed by the Atyagniṣṭoma, the Uktha, the Ṣoḍaśin, the Vājapeya,
the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma— these are the Savas that rule over a thousand.
Hiraṇyāṅghri, Hiraṇyākṣa, and Hiraṇyamitra— from these [seven];

With golden hands, golden eyes, golden limbs, and golden necklaces;
with a golden mouth, golden body, golden tongue, and possessing gold.

compassion toward all beings, patience, as well as uprightness, purity, lack of exertion, and auspiciousness is another quality.
One should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra, accompanied by freedom from miserliness and lack of longing.
These initiations—Saura, Śākteya, Vaiṣṇava, and Īśa—are declared to be equal;
one who is purified by these purificatory rites shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Freed from all diseases, the man lives like a god;
through recitation, burnt offerings, worship, and meditation upon the Lord, he attains his desired objects.
Thus ends the account of the forty-eight purificatory rites in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*, the foremost among the great Purāṇas.

Then, by means of drying and other such methods, one should effect the purification of the body; subsequently, one should meditate upon the withered physical frame, starting from the feet up to the crown of the head.

Having meditated upon a drop (*bindu*) of nectar, one [should drench] that body of ashes with it.
Having transformed the body into a divine one by pronouncing "laṃ," one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and the body, and then carry out the mental sacrifice (*mānayāga*).
One should worship Viṣṇu, together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), within the lotus of the heart using mental flowers and other offerings.
One should worship the Lord of Gods, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, with the root mantra:
"Welcome, O Lord of the God of Gods; be present here, O Keśava!
Accept this mental worship according to its true purpose."
The foundational power (*ādhāra-śakti*) is worshipped, followed by Kūrma, then Ananta, and then the Earth; then,
in the center and in the directions starting with the southeast (Agni), one worships Dharma and the others, and Adharma and the others located at Indra and the other principal directions.

The Gaṇa, Sarasvatī, Nārada, and Nalakūvara are to be worshipped;

Having established Acyuta with the root mantra— [accompanied by] Dhṛti, Śrī, Rati, Kānti, and the others— and having entreated him with "Oṃ, be present before me," [one says] "be near. Having offered the arghya and other items, one should worship with perfumes and so forth using the root mantra.
Oṃ, terrify, terrify! O heart, strike fear into the head!

Then, [reciting] "Oṃ hrūṃ phaṭ, obeisance to the weapon," one should worship the limbs with the root seed-syllable, and worship the enclosure of the forms in the east, south, west, and north.
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha— along with Śrī, Dhṛti, Rati, and Kānti— are the forms of Hari located in the southeast and the other directions.

Then Airāvata, the goat, the buffalo, the monkey, and the fish;

Having bowed to Hari, Pṛśnigarbha, Kumuda, and the others—the door-keepers, two by two, starting from the east and ending at the northern gate—one should offer an oblation outside on the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), saying: "Obeisance to the attendants of Viṣṇu; obeisance, [I give] this oblation."
One should worship Viśvaksena Īśānaka for the sake of the universe;
one should tie a protective thread on the right hand of the deity.
To the teachers who have served for a year and who bestow the complete fruit [of the rite], [one should offer gifts].

Homage to the God who is the friend of Brahman, to Śrīdhara, the imperishable Self.

To the one whose body is sound, consisting of the forms of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
having drawn the mandala in the evening, one should bring the sacrificial materials and so forth.
Having washed his hands and feet and arranged the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), the person,
holding the *arghya* vessel in hand, should sprinkle his head and the area around the doorway with the *arghya* and other substances;
then he should begin the sacrifice of the door and worship the lords of the archways (*toraṇeśas*).
The trees of the east are the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Vaṭa, and Prakṣa; in the east,
the Ṛgveda is adorned by Indra, the Yajurveda is most auspicious with Yama,
the Sāmaveda is called Sudhanvan, and the Atharvaveda belongs to Soma and Suhotra.
Within the archways, the banners beginning with Kumuda and the two jars should be worshipped at each door by their respective names; in the east, Pūrṇa and Puṣkara;
on the right, Ānanda and Nandana; and Vīrasena and Suṣeṇaka.
O gentle one, one should worship Sambhava and Prabhu, as well as the door-keepers.
Having dispelled obstacles by scattering flowers consecrated with the Astra-mantra, one should enter.
Then, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and made the ritual gestures (mudrās), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Having recited the *śikhā* mantra ending with the syllable *phaṭ*, one should scatter mustard seeds in the various directions.
With Vāsudeva, one should [offer] cow urine; with Saṅkarṣaṇa, cow dung;
with Pradyumna, milk; from that [milk], curd; and from Nārāyaṇa, ghee.

One, two, three, or more days' worth of ghee, in a quantity exceeding that [of the other ingredients], is placed together in a vessel of ghee; this is declared to be the *pañcagavya*. One portion is for the sprinkling of the pavilion, and the other is for consumption.

Having brought the world-protectors, Indra and the others, into ten jars, one should worship them; having honored them, one should proclaim this command to them: "You must remain here by the command of Hari. Then, having secured the sacrificial materials and other items, one should scatter the *vikiro* offerings.

Having consecrated eight hundred blades of *kuśa* grass with the root-mantra, one should place those [blades] belonging to Hari in the northeastern direction, and there, one should set down the pitcher (*kumbha*) and the *vardhanī* vessel.
Having worshipped Hari along with His limbs (aṅgas) in the pitcher (kumbha), one should worship the weapon (astra) in the vardhanī vessel;
then, sprinkling the sacrificial hall with a continuous stream from the vardhanī while circumambulating it, one should thereafter worship the pitcher upon a stable seat.
One should worship Hari with perfumes and other offerings in a jar enriched with the five jewels and fine cloth;
and to the left, one should worship the Weapon-mantra in a *vardhanī* vessel containing gold,
and nearby, one should worship Vāstu-Lakṣmī and Bhū-Vināyaka.
One should likewise perform the ritual ablution (srapana) for Viṣṇu on occasions such as the solar transits;
having placed nine flawless full jars in the nine corners, one should place the five nectars, water, and so forth, in the jars starting from the east and continuing toward the southeast.
Curd, milk, honey, and warm water constitute the fourfold *pādya*.
The lotus, *śyāmāka* grain, *dūrvā* grass, and the consort of Viṣṇu (the *tulasī* leaf) constitute the *pādya*.
Likewise, barley, fragrance, fruit, and unbroken rice grains are declared to be the eightfold *arghya*.

One should offer kuśa grass, white mustard seeds, flowers, sesame seeds, and other substances as an act of worship; one should also present water for rinsing the mouth accompanied by cloves and kakkola. One should bathe the deity with the root mantra and also with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
One should pour pure water from the central jar onto the head of the deity;
the person should touch the tip of the *kūrca* grass with the water flowing out from the jars.
He should offer water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and water for sipping that is pure;
having wiped his limbs with a cloth, he should lead [the deity] along with the cloth to the mandala.
Having worshipped there, he, restraining his breath, should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the sacrificial pit or other such place.
Having washed his hands, he should [draw] three lines directed toward the east;
these are called *arhaṇā*.
The reading "dūrvāgram" belongs to manuscript Ṅa;
it is the reading of the marked manuscript.
Having sprinkled with the water for the guest-offering (arghyodaka) the three lines from south to north and the three from north to the tip, one should display the yoni-mudrā.
Having meditated upon fire in the form of Agni, the man should cast it into the womb of the sacrificial pit;
thereafter, he should arrange the vessels along with the *darbha* grass, the *śruk* and *śruva* ladles, and so forth,
as well as the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the fuel-wood (*idhma*), each measuring one cubit in length.
One should place the *praṇītā* vessel, the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, the clarified butter pot, the ghee and other materials,
and two measures of rice— each pair placed face down—
into the *praṇītā* and *prokṣaṇī* vessels, with *kuśa* grass laid across them pointing toward the east.
Having filled the *praṇītā* vessel with water, meditated upon the deity, and worshipped him,
one should place the *praṇītā* in front, in the middle of the ritual materials.
Then, having filled the *prokṣaṇī* vessel with water and worshipped it, one should place it on the right.
One should cook the *caru* offering in the fire and place Brahmā to the south;
having spread *kuśa* grass starting from the east, one should then set up the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
Thereafter, a person should perform the *vaiṣṇavīkaraṇa* rite through the sequence beginning with *garbhādhāna*.

For the rites of conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), birth (janman), and those beginning with the naming ceremony up to the return home from studentship (samāvartana), he should offer eight oblations with each ritual act using the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles joined together, followed by the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Having visualized Lakṣmī in her menses in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should perform the fire-oblation;
she is known as Kuṇḍalakṣmī, the primordial nature consisting of the three qualities (guṇas).
She is the womb of all beings and of the multitude of sciences and mantras.
Fire is the cause of liberation, and the Supreme Self (Paramātman) is the bestower of liberation.

The head is declared to be in the east; the two arms are situated in the corners, namely the northeast (Īśāna) and southeast (Āgneya); while the two shanks are in the northwest (Vāyavya) and southwest (Nairṛta).
The belly is said to be the *kuṇḍa*, and the womb (*yoni*) is prescribed as the *yoni*.
The three qualities (*guṇatraya*) are the girdles (*mekhalā*); having meditated thus, one offers ten fuel-sticks (*samidh*).
One should offer five additional oblations with the *praṇava* using the *muṣṭi-mudrā*.
Then one should again offer the two *āghāra* libations from the northwest to the southeast, and subsequently cook [the offering].
One should offer the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) with the root mantra, extending from the northeast to the southwest.
With the syllable *uttare* at the limit of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*) and with that same syllable at the south,
one should meditate from the center upon the consecrated fire situated in the middle of the lotus—
belonging to Viṣṇu, having seven tongues, and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.

One should offer one hundred and eight oblations, or half of that (fifty-four), or eight, into the solar eye with the root mantra; and for the limbs, one should offer a tenth part [of those oblations].
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fire-Rite," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Chapter Thirty-Six:
