"O God, O Lord of the Suras, by your grace I become pure;
having consecrated myself with the *hṛdaya* and other mantras,
and having sprinkled the Viṣṇu-vessel, one should proceed to the presence of the God."
Having released the protective cord, one should give the purifier to oneself:
"O Lord, please accept the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) which has been prepared by me,
so that through the completion of my rites, no fault may befall me."
One should offer the *pavitraka* to the gatekeepers, the seats, and the chief preceptor;

then, starting from the little finger, one should offer the *vanamālā* to the Deity from the base upwards. One should present the *pavitra*s beginning with the *hṛdaya* mantra and ending with Viśvaksena.
Having offered the *pavitraka* into the fire for Agnivarti, Viṣṇu, and the others,
and having worshipped them, one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra for the sake of expiation;
or else, one hundred and eight [oblations] with the five Upaniṣads.
With garlands of jewels and coral, and with mandāraka flowers and the like—
may this annual worship be yours, O Garuḍa-bannered One!
Just as the forest garland and the Kaustubha gem are always upon your chest, O Lord.
In that same way, carry within your heart the sacred threads and the worship;
may whatever was performed in the ritual of observance and worship— whether intentionally or unintentionally—
be complete for me, even if it was deficient due to obstacles.
Having prayed, bowed, and asked for forgiveness, one should then place the sacred thread upon one's head;
having offered the bali-oblation along with sacrificial fees, one should satisfy the preceptor, who is devoted to Viṣṇu.

1. "And having released the *rakṣābandha*"—this is the reading found in the manuscript marked *kha*. "Having released that [thread], one should give the *pavitra* from its base for the sake of protection"—this is the reading found in the manuscript marked *ṅa*.
The reading of the marked manuscript is:
"And you, O Pavitraka, carry [this] in your heart during worship," as found in manuscript Ṅa. This is the reading of the marked manuscript.
One should honor the Brahmins with food, clothing, and other gifts for a day or even for a fortnight;
and at the time of bathing, one should offer them a sacred thread (*pavitra*) after having it worn.
One should give food and other provisions without restriction, and then eat oneself;
on the day of dismissal, having honored the sacred threads (pavitra),
one should dismiss them after duly performing this annual worship of mine.
"Go now, O Purifier, to the world of Viṣṇu, having been dismissed.
Having worshipped Viṣvaksena between Someśa and [the other deity],
and having duly honored the sacred threads (pavitrāṇi), one should offer them to a Brāhmaṇa."
For as many threads as are fashioned in that strainer,
for that many thousands of yugas he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu,
having uplifted a hundred lineages— ten preceding and ten succeeding.

"Having established [the deity] in the world of Viṣṇu, one shall oneself attain liberation. Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Sacred Thread Offering for Viṣṇu," in the Āgneya Purāṇa, the foremost of the great Purāṇas.
Chapter 37:
The Ritual for the Ascension of the Pavitra of All the Gods (Sarvadevapavitrārohaṇavidhi)
Agni said:

Listen briefly to the consecration of the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇa*) for all the gods; the *pavitra* should possess all the required characteristics and be made of cotton (*svarasa*) or gold (*analaga*).
O Source of the World, come together with your retinue of attendants;
I invite you for tomorrow morning and shall offer you the purificatory thread (*pavitraka*).
O Creator of the World, homage to you; please accept this purificatory thread.
In the manuscript marked with the letter *kha*, the reading is "pavitrāropaṇam" (the offering of the sacred thread).
2. "jagatsūte" is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter Ṅa;
O Lord Śiva, salutations to you; for the sake of purification and to bestow the fruit of a year’s worship,
please accept this sacred thread (*pavitraka*) adorned with garlands of gems and coral, mandāra flowers, and other blossoms.
"O Lord of the knowers of the Vedas, let this annual worship be yours.
Having completed this annual worship according to my ritual injunctions, O Pavitra, you are now dismissed; go to the heavenly world."
O God Sūrya, homage to you! Accept this purifier for the sake of purification, which bestows the fruit of the year-long worship.
O God Śiva, homage to you! Accept this purifier.
For the sake of purification, bestowing the fruit of the annual worship—
O Vāṇeśvara, salutations to you; please accept this sacred thread for the sake of purification,
bestowing the fruit of the annual worship.
O Śaktideva, salutations to you! Accept this sacred thread (*pavitraka*), which grants the fruit of a year’s worship for the sake of purification;
it is a sublime thread consisting of Nārāyaṇa and Aniruddha.
I bestow upon you this thread, which consists of Kāmadeva and is the excellent embodiment of Saṅkarṣaṇa; it grants wealth, grain, long life, and health,
and it bestows knowledge, lineage, and good fortune.
I bestow upon you this thread consisting of Vāsudeva, which grants dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa, and is the means for crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra;
it is a thread consisting of the universal form (viśvarūpa), the giver of all, and the destroyer of sin.
Regarding "Lord of the Multitude" (gaṇeśvara), it is [the letter] ga,
gha, and ṅa.
The reading "param" is found in manuscript Ṅa;
this is the reading of the marked manuscript.
I grant you the extraction of the past and future lineages;
I bestow the four [lineages] beginning with Kaniṣṭha, in sequence, by means of the mantras.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Concise Ritual of the Pavitrārohaṇa," in the Āgneya Purāṇa, the foremost of the great Purāṇas.
Chapter 38:
The Fruit of Constructing a Temple for the Devas
Agni said:
I shall describe the fruits and other benefits of constructing a temple for Vāsudeva and others;
for one desiring to build a divine abode and the like, it destroys the sins of a thousand births.
Even those men who, with their minds, rejoice in the house being built for Kṛṣṇa— which destroys the sins of a hundred lifetimes for its builders—
are themselves freed from all evils and go to the world of Acyuta.
A man who has a temple of Hari constructed quickly leads ten thousand generations of his family— both those past and those yet to come— to the world of Viṣṇu;
and having seen it, his ancestors dwell there.

Indeed, adorned in the world of Viṣṇu and liberated from the sufferings of hell, they go to the abode of the creator Kṛṣṇa, a temple of the gods that destroys the multitude of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
That fruit which is not obtained through sacrifices is obtained by making a temple;

when a temple is built, one obtains the fruit of bathing in all sacred fords (*tīrtha*). Furthermore, whatever fruit and other rewards belong to those slain in battle for the sake of the gods and others— [that too is attained].
Even a dwelling built with deceit or with dust,
such as a house and so forth, bestows the realm of heaven.
The reading "nandanti" is found in the texts marked with the signs kha and ga.
"valganti" is the reading in the manuscript marked as Ṅa; "hṛṣṭā" is the reading in manuscripts Kha and Ga.
The reading of the two marked manuscripts:
"One who has established a single abode becomes a dweller in heaven; one who has established three abodes partakes in the world of Brahmā. (AP 38.008ab)

One who maintains five houses attains the world of Śambhu; one who maintains eight houses finds stability on earth; but he who maintains sixteen abodes shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having caused the temple of Hari to be built as small, medium, or excellent,
one attains heaven, the Vaiṣṇava world, and liberation respectively; moreover,
by constructing an excellent abode for Viṣṇu, a wealthy person obtains that which is most supreme.
Even a man without wealth obtains that same merit by building a temple for the gods with very little expenditure after first acquiring the necessary funds.
By having a temple of Hari constructed with one thousand, a hundred, or even fifty characteristic marks, one attains abundant and excellent merit;
by building such a dwelling, one goes to where the one whose banner is Garuḍa resides.
Even those who, while playing in their childhood, build a house for Hari Vāsudeva out of dust, go to his world; likewise,
those who do so at a sacred ford (tīrtha), a holy shrine (āyatana), or in a virtuous field (saddhakṣetra), or in the eighth [type of place].
The fruit for the builder of a temple for Viṣṇu is three times that which has been described.
Those who smear a Vaiṣṇava temple with plaster mixed with the paste of bandhūka flowers go to the city of the Blessed One.
A person who, having rescued one who has fallen, one who is falling, or likewise one who has half-fallen,
attains the abode of Hari and receives double the fruit. Furthermore,
he who is the rescuer of the fallen and the protector of the fallen [attains the same].
A man who builds a temple for Viṣṇu here becomes a partaker of the world of Viṣṇu; as long as the pile of bricks remains in the abode of Hari,
the builder, together with his family, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
1. "But the one who builds sixteen houses" is the reading of the manuscript marked *ga*.
2. "By even a very small [amount]" is the reading of the manuscript *kha*.
He alone is meritorious and worthy of honor in this world and in the next. (AP 38.019cd)
He who causes a temple to be built for Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva is born truly virtuous; by him alone is his lineage purified.
He who builds a house for Viṣṇu, Rudra, the Sun, the Goddess, or others, shall be a possessor of fame.
Of what use are the hoards of wealth guarded by that fool,
acquired through suffering, who does not cause a temple to be built for Kṛṣṇa, nor whose wealth is enjoyed by his ancestors, brahmins, and the gods?

The acquisition of wealth by one who cannot enjoy it for his kinsmen is useless; just as death is certain for men, so too is the loss of wealth certain. Yet the fool remains attached to that fickle life and to transient riches.
When wealth serves neither for giving nor for the enjoyment of embodied beings,
nor for fame, nor for the sake of Dharma— what benefit is there in its ownership?
Therefore, having acquired wealth, whether by fate or through human effort, [one should employ it for these purposes].

One should properly give gifts to the foremost of the twice-born and cause sacred recitations (*kīrtana*) to be performed. Since that which is superior to gifts is the excellence found in recitations,
the wise person should therefore cause temples and other such structures for Viṣṇu and the other deities to be built.
When established in the abode of Hari by the best of men who are endowed with devotion,
the entire triple world— including all that is moving and unmoving,
as well as the past, present, and future, the gross, the subtle, and that which is otherwise— becomes truly established.
Everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass originates from Viṣṇu,
that great-souled one who is the god of gods and is omnipresent.
Having established a temple for Viṣṇu, one is not born again on earth;
the fruit obtained from constructing a shrine for Viṣṇu is equal to that of constructing one for the gods.
1. *Tathaiva ca*—this is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter *ga*. 2. *Sarveśasya*—this is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter *kha*.
The reading marked in the manuscript (p.
111): "Of those whose nature is Śiva, Brahmā, Arka, Vighneśa, Caṇḍī, Lakṣmī, and so forth..."
The merit from constructing a temple is great, but that from making an image is greater;
there is no end to the fruit of the sacrifice performed for the installation of an image.
The merit from an image made of wood is greater than one made of clay, and that from one made of bricks is greater than one made of wood.
The fruit obtained from a temple built of stone is greater than that from one made of bricks, gold, or other materials;
even the sins committed over seven lifetimes perish from the very commencement [of the work].
One who builds a temple becomes an inhabitant of heaven and does not go to hell.
"Having delivered a hundred lineages, a man shall lead them to the world of Viṣṇu.
Yama said to the messengers of Yama who build temples for the gods: Yama spoke.
Those men who perform worship of images and the like shall not be led to hell;
however, those who do not build temples and such shall be brought into my presence.
Depart with confidence, and let my command be carried out according to the law.
Nowhere shall living beings ever violate your commands;
they have taken refuge solely in you, the infinite Father of the world.
You must exclude them from this [assembly], for they have no place here.

And those who, with their minds fixed on Him and devoted solely to Him, always worship Viṣṇu— the one whom the Blessed One has declared in the world to be the ultimate refuge— those persons should be avoided from afar.
Whether standing, sleeping, walking, rising, stumbling, or remaining still, [they worship Him].
Those who praise Govinda and those people who worship the god Janārdana with daily and occasional rites— these must be shunned by you from afar;
they are not to be looked upon by you, for being absorbed in Him, they go to His state.
1. "They are to be brought without distinction," according to the reading of the manuscript marked Ga; 2. "Let my rule be observed," according to the manuscript marked Kha.
The reading in the marked manuscript is "jantavaḥ kvacid" (in some places, living beings),
[as found] in manuscript Kha.
Those men who worship with flowers, incense, garments, and most beloved ornaments are not to be accepted when they have come to the abode of Kṛṣṇa. (1)
Those who perform the smearing [of the temple] and those devoted to sweeping it,
as well as their sons and their entire lineage, are to be spared from the abode of Kṛṣṇa; likewise, so too is anyone born of the family by whom a sanctuary for Viṣṇu was caused to be built.
One hundred men with wicked minds should not even look upon you; however,
he who causes a temple of Viṣṇu to be built— whether made of wood,
stone, or even clay— is liberated from all sins.
Whatever great fruit one obtains by performing sacrifices day after day,
that same fruit he who causes a temple for Viṣṇu to be built attains;
[he delivers] a hundred future lineages as well as a hundred past ones.

He who causes a temple for the Blessed One to be built leads [his ancestors] to the world of Acyuta; Viṣṇu, who consists of the seven worlds, belongs to him who constructs his abode. He delivers [them] to imperishable worlds and attains those imperishable realms himself.
For as many years as the arrangement of the brick-pile remains standing,
for that many thousands of years does its maker reside in heaven.
The maker of the image goes to the world of Viṣṇu, and the installer is absorbed into Hari.

Agni said: "O Hari, those who have performed the installation of a replica of the abode of the gods within their field of vision, yet do not bring [the deity] there as prescribed by Yama, [are at fault]."
Hayaśīrṣa spoke to Brahmā for the sake of the installation of the gods: "E" and so forth.
Thus ends the description of the majesty of temples and other such matters, titled [Chapter X] in the Āgneya Purāṇa, one of the great ancient scriptures (Mahāpurāṇa).

Chapter 39:
The Procedure for the Seizing of the Ground (Bhūparigraha-vidhāna)
Hayagrīva said:
O Brahmin, listen to me as I shall describe the installation and other rites for Viṣṇu and the others;
indeed, the Pañcarātras and Saptarātras have been proclaimed by me.
These have been divided by the sages in the world into twenty-five in number:
the *Hayaśīrṣatantra*, the primordial *Tantra*, the *Trailokyamohana*,
the *Vaibhavatantra*, the *Pauṣkaratantra*, and those of *Prahrāda*, *Gārgya*, and *Gālava*.
The Nāradīya and the Sampraśna, the Śāṇḍilya and the Vaiśvaka, as well as the Satyokta, the Śaunaka-tantra, the Vāsiṣṭha, the Jñānasāgara,
the Svāyambhuva, the Kapila, the Tārkṣa, and the Nārāyaṇīyaka.
The Ātreya, the one called Nārasiṃha, the one called Ānanda, as well as the Āruṇa, the Baudhāyana, and the Viśvokta which is of Ṛṣi origin— [I shall summarize] the essence of these.
For a twice-born man born in the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa) and other such regions should perform the consecration;
however, one born in the marshy lands (nakaccha), originating from the Kāverī or Koṅkaṇa,
or hailing from Kāmarūpa, Kaliṅga, Kāñcī, Kaśmīra, or Kosala, [should not].

Space, wind, fire, water, and earth—these five nights are insentient and dominated by *tamas*. That teacher should know: "I am Brahmā, I am Viṣṇu, I am the stainless one," which is free from the five nights.
Even if he is devoid of all [physical] characteristics, that guru has mastered the tantras. (AP 39.009ab) Note:
The reading "ca īśvaram tathā" is found in the three manuscripts marked as Ga, Ṅa, and Gha.

114, "The deities should be established facing toward the city, and not turned away from it."
In Kurukṣetra, at Gayā and other such places, and in the vicinity of rivers;
in the center of the city is Brahmā, while in the east is the beautiful abode of Śakra.

One should construct a temple for Agni in the southeast, for the Mothers and the Bhūtas in the south, and for Yama; for Caṇḍikā in the southwest, and for the Pitṛs, Daityas, and others in the west; and for Varuṇa and Āpaḥ in the northwest.
In the northwest, one should build for Vāyu and Nāga; in the north, for Yakṣaguhā;
in the northeast, for Caṇḍīśa and Maheśa; and in every direction, for Viṣṇu.
However, having avoided the site of an ancient temple, one may then construct a small palace.
A wise person should neither construct [a building] that is equal nor one that exceeds [the established limit].
Having left a boundary twice the height of the intended structure,
the wise man should have another palace built so as not to cause suffering to either party.

Once the ground has been purified, one should perform the ritual appropriation of the site (bhūmiparigraha) extending as far as the boundary of the enclosure wall; thereafter, one should offer a bali-oblation to the spirits consisting of black gram, turmeric powder, parched grain, curd, and flour.
Having caused the barley meal to be scattered with the eight-syllable mantra in the eight directions,
may all those *rākṣasas* and *piśācas* who dwell upon this earth depart; I shall prepare a place for Hari.
Having driven the ox with a goad, one should cause it to plow with the oxen.
Eight *paramāṇus* are proclaimed to constitute a *trasareṇu*.
Eight of those [trasareṇus] make a hair-tip (*bālāgra*), and eight of those are considered to be a *likhyā*.
Eight of those [yūkās] are known as one *yava*; and eight of those [yavas] are a *yavamadhyama*.
(Regarding the phrase "in rivers and mountains," the reading is found in the manuscripts kha, ga, and ṅa.)

Thus ends the "Acquisition of the Ground" (*bhūparigraha*) within the section on consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*, the Great Ancient Scripture.

Chapter 40:
The Ritual Procedure for Offering the Arghya Water of Honor.
The Blessed One said:
"In former times there was a great being who caused fear to all beings;
cast down by the gods upon the earth, he is known as Vāstupuruṣa."
In a field of sixty-four squares, one should satisfy Īśa, situated in half of a corner,
with ghee and unbroken rice; then Parjanya,
located on two squares, and Jayanta, situated on two squares, with blue lotuses and the like, and with a banner.
One should worship Mahendra located in a single square with all red substances; Ravi in a square with a canopy;
Satya in a square with abundant clarified butter;
and Vyoman in a square with the meat of birds.
One should worship Agni situated on half a square with the *sruc* ladle; Pūṣan on half a square with parched grain (*lāja*);
Vitatha on two squares with gold; and Gṛhakṣata with fire produced by friction.
With meat and rice, one should worship Dharmeśa; on each [altar] stands a pair:
a Gandharva with two feet worshipped with perfumes, and a bird-like tongue; likewise, a deer standing upright with its head held high is worshipped with blue cloths.
One should offer to the ancestors with *kṛsara* while standing on the ground; [one should offer] with tooth-sticks while standing on a foot.
(Regarding the term "nṛhasta," the reading in manuscript *kha* is "nṛhasta").
The reading of the marked manuscript is "with the flesh of a śākulā bird" (vyoma śākulamāṃsena), according to manuscript KHA. The reading of the marked manuscript is [as follows].
One should worship Dauvārika and Dvisaṃstha with *yāvaka*, Sugrīva with *puṣpa* flowers, Puṣpadanta with bundles of *kuśa* grass, and Varuṇa with lotuses on one side.
One should pacify an *asura* situated on a full square with liquor; the remainder (*śeṣa*) with ghee and water; sin with barley grains on half a square; disease with *maṇḍaka* cakes on half a square;
a serpent with *nāgapuṣpa* flowers on a square; and a principal [deity] situated on two squares with various foods.
One should worship Bhallāṭa at one step with *mudga* rice, and likewise Soma at another step;
then the Ṛṣi at two steps with honey and milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and Diti at one step with lotus roots (*śālūka*),
and the other half of Diti with fried cakes (*lopikā*).
Then, with *pūrikās*, there is a bow below Īśa; in the [next] square, with milk;
then below that, with *apavatsa*; and in one square, it stands with curd.
And with *laḍḍukas*, there is *marīci* in the four eastern squares.
One should offer red flowers to Savitṛ in the square at the bottom-left corner,
and in the square below that, one should offer kuśa-water to Sāvitrī;
to Vivasvat, one should offer reddish flowers and sandalwood in the four outer corners.
In the southwestern corner cell, one should offer food with rice for Indra;
below that, in the corner cell, food with ghee for Indrajaya.
In the four-square sections, jaggery-milk porridge (guḍapāyasa) should be given to Indra.
In the lower-left corner, one should offer cooked meat to Rudra;
in the cell of the corner below that, raw fruit to Yakṣa; and in the four corners, meat-rice and *māgha* to Mahīdhara.
In the center, on a four-legged stand, one should place sesame and rice for Brahmā;
for Carakī, beans and ghee; for Skanda, *kṛsara* and blood; for Vidārī and Kandarpa, red lotuses and meat-rice.
One should [worship] Pūtanā with fat and bile, and Jambhaka with flesh and blood,
in the four central [squares].
The reading from the marked manuscript (p.
117): "With bile, blood, and bones, [he creates] the wicked Pilipiñja; with a garland of blood..."
One should worship Īśa and the others with blood and flesh, or, in their absence, with unbroken grains (akṣata).
One should offer oblations (bali) at will to the hosts of Rākṣasas and Mātṛs, as well as to the Piśācas and others, to the ancestors (pitṛs), and to the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas).
Having offered oblations and fully satisfied these [deities], one should not construct palaces and other such structures.
In the Brahma-sthāna, one should first worship Hari and Lakṣmī, and afterwards Gaṇa and Mahīśvara, who consists of the Vāstu-deity.
One should place the jar together with the *vardhanī* vessel,
Brahmā in the center of the *kumbha*, and the deities beginning with Brahmā along with the lords of the directions;
thereafter, one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), recite the benediction (*svasti-vācana*), and prostrate.
Having properly grasped the water-jar, O Brahmin, one should circumambulate the mandala clockwise; with a moist thread, one should whirl a stream of water,
and by that same path as before, one should sow the seven seeds.
One should cause the commencement of that excavation by means of that path. Then, one should dig a pit in the middle measuring one cubit in size;
having smeared its bottom with four finger-breadths [of paste], one should thereafter worship it.
Having meditated upon the four-armed Viṣṇu, one should offer the arghya from the water-pot; one should fill the cavity with a small pitcher (karkarī), place white flowers within it,
and fill it with seeds and earth, ensuring it is turned clockwise, which is most excellent.
Having completed the offering of the *arghya*, one should present cows, clothing, and other gifts to the preceptor;
then one should worship the architect who knows the proper time, as well as the Vaiṣṇavas and others. Thereafter, one should diligently cause the pit to be dug down to the water-level.
An arrow lodged beneath a person does not cause harm within the house.
1. "Pilipiccham" is the reading in manuscript Ṅa; 2. "Mahīdharaṃ vāstumayam" is the reading in manuscripts Kha and Ṅa.

When there is a bone-thorn, there is indeed a wall for the householder and suffering;
whatever name one hears, the thorn arises from that.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Offering of Arghya," in the Āgneya Purāṇa, the foremost of the great Purāṇas.
Chapter 41:
The Procedure for the Laying of Stones (Śilāvinyāsavidhāna)
The Blessed One said:
"I shall describe the foundation of the pedestal and the characteristics for the arrangement of the stones.
First, a pavilion should be constructed, with four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas)."

In the placement of the *kumbha* jars and the laying of bricks, one should fill the excavation to a height auspiciously three-quarters of the elevation of the door-pillars; there, on level ground, one should worship the *vāstu* deity. The bricks should be well-baked and measured at twelve finger-breadths.
It should be endowed with a width equal to one-third of its length; furthermore,
in the case of a stone [stūpa], an excellent stone slab measuring one cubit should be used.
One should place nine copper jars made of bricks, well-filled with water,
using water mixed with the five decoctions, water with all medicinal herbs,
and likewise water with fragrant substances.
With [offerings] consisting of gold and rice, anointed with fragrant sandalwood,
[one should recite] the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," as well as "śanno devīr" and "tarat samandī."
And with the *pāvamānī* verses,
with "ud uttamaṃ varuṇa," and likewise with the *kathāna* hymns;
[this should be done] very extensively, according to their divisions, with skill.
The reading in the marked manuscript is "śilā syān na śilāmaye" (it should be stone, not made of stone), as found in manuscript Ga.

Chapter 42:
Description of the Characteristics of Palaces (Prāsāda-lakṣaṇa-kathana)
Hayagrīva said:
I shall now fully describe the temple plan which is common to all; listen.
A wise man should divide the square site into sixteen parts.
In its center, one should construct [a structure] made of iron with four [pillars],
according to the measurement of an equal palace; this is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter *ṅa*.
One should calculate twelve parts for the purpose of the walls;
the height of the plinth (jaṅghā) should be made four parts in length.
The wise one should fashion the *mañjarī* on the shank with a height double [that of the base];
a proper circumambulation should be made for the *mañjarī* using a fourth part [of its height],
and an equal projection of that measurement should be made on both sides.
The front extension should be made equal to the pinnacle,
or it may be made double that size according to what is aesthetically pleasing.
In front of the pavilion, [the measurement] from the width should be by means of two lines of the inner sanctum (garbha).
One should make it one-quarter longer than its width and adorned with central pillars;
or else, one should construct the front pavilion (mukhamaṇḍapa) according to the measurement of the interior of the temple.
Then, having divided the area into eighty-one squares, one should begin the construction of the pavilion from the rear.
One should worship the deities located at the end of the feet in the arrangement of the eastern door as parrots;
likewise, in the arrangement of the enclosure wall, one should worship those situated within the thirty-two [divisions].
This is the general characteristic of a temple.

Now hear about another temple [measured] by the *māna* or by the image. The auspicious pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) should be made according to the measurement of the image; the inner sanctum (*garbha*) should be half the size of the pedestal, and the walls should be measured according to the size of the sanctum.
One should determine the height according to the measurement of the wall's length; the wise man should fashion the spire to be twice the height of the wall,
and the circumambulatory path (bhramaṇa) should be fashioned as one-fourth of the spire.
The entrance porch (mukhamaṇḍapa) should be [constructed] at the front with one-fourth of the spire (śikhara),
or else joined with one-eighth [of it]; this is the reading found in the manuscript marked *kha*.
"Combined with a fourth part"— this is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter *ga*.

Forty-second Chapter.

Regarding the installation of deities in a temple, the Blessed One said:

One should first place Lakṣmī and Vaiśravaṇa; on the south, the group of Mothers; Skanda, Gaṇeśa, and Īśāna; on the west, the planets beginning with the Sun;

Chapter 44:

The Blessed One said:

Having established, worshipped, and offered the sacrificial oblation (bali), the artisan should then divide the stone marked by the central line into nine parts; on the stone,

A sphere measuring two finger-breadths is called by the name Kālanetra. Having divided one part into three, one should fashion the portion for the heels;
likewise, one part is for the knees and one part for the neck.
The crown of the head should be one *tāla* in measure; likewise, the face is one *tāla*.
The throat is one *tāla*, and the heart is likewise one *tāla*. The distance from the navel to the genitals is one *tāla*, and the two thighs are each two *tālas*.
The shank should be two tālas; now hear the lines:

Likewise, another [line] should be made on the penis, another thread on the waist,
and another on the navel for the purpose of accomplishing the binding of the girdle.
In the same way, two threads should be placed at the heart and at the throat; another should be placed on the forehead, and yet another on the head.
Wise practitioners should place a single thread above the crown of the head.

The forehead, nose, and mouth should each be made four finger-breadths [in width];

The forehead is proclaimed to be eight finger-breadths in width;

The distance between the ear and the eye is declared to be four finger-breadths.

Chapter 45:

The Blessed One said:

"I shall describe the characteristics of the pedestal (piṇḍikā). Its length should be equal to the height of the image, and its height should be half that of the image; it should consist of sixty-four layers."
Having omitted two rows below and above,
that which is the square [in the middle] is one and a half finger-breadths in width; thus [it is stated] in manuscript Ṅa.

the girdle (mekhalā) shall consist of one part, and the excavation (khāta) shall be half that measure.

excluding the eyes, however, the thighs, knees, and the calf-muscle (piṇḍikā) have the same widths. One should fashion the back of the feet, the buttocks, and the hips according to their respective proportions.
The length [of the feet] is seven fingers minus one-seventh; the thigh and the shank have a circumference multiplied by their width and a length reduced by one eye (two);
likewise the hip, the middle of the side, and that rounded, thick, and full pair of breasts.
In this context, the reading "iyam" is found in manuscript *ṅa* and in the edition marked with a cipher.
The breasts should be made one *tāla* in measure, and the waist should be one and a half *kalās* more;
the remaining characteristics should be as before, and there should be a lotus in the right hand.
To the left are two auspicious female figures holding chowries at their sides;
then there is Garuḍa with a long beak. Next, I shall describe those beginning with Cakrāṅga. Thus ends the description of the pedestal, Lakṣmī, and other features in the *Āgneya-mahāpurāṇa*.
The forty-fifth chapter, named [so-and-so].
Now begins the forty-sixth chapter.
The Blessed One spoke concerning the description of the characteristics of the Śālagrāma and other forms:
"I shall now describe the Śālagrāma and other forms which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
Vāsudeva is dark at the door and possesses two wheels of Śālagrāma; Saṅkarṣaṇa is known by his two joined wheels and is excellent when red;
Pradyumna has fine wheels, many perforations, and is blue and elongated.
The yellow [mark] is suppressed, has a lotus as its limb, is circular, and possesses two or three lines;
the black [mark] is Nārāyaṇa, with a raised navel, hollow and long;
the supreme [mark] has a lotus and a disc, a hole on the back, and possesses a dot.
Viṣṇu is black with a thick circle; in the center, there is a line in the shape of a mace.
Nṛsiṃha has a thick curve and five dots; Varāha has the mark of a spear. Those two discs are uneven and extended.
Auspicious is the tortoise-shaped mark (kūrma), which resembles a sapphire, is thick, marked with three lines,
and has a raised back with circular whorls;
likewise auspicious is the horse-necked mark (hayagrīva), which is blue, marked with a goad and a plow, and possesses a dot.
1. "Pṛthuśchidraśca" is the reading found in the marked manuscript (Ṅa), page 134.
Vaikuṇṭha has one wheel and a lotus; Abjī has lines on its tail; Matsya is long with three dots and filled with the color of glass;
Śrīdhara is marked by a forest garland, circular, and has five lines.
Vāmana is round, extremely short, dark blue, and marked with a dot;
Trivikrama is dark-brown, with a line on the right and a dot on the left;
Ananta has limbs like the coils of a serpent, possessing many colors and many forms.
Sthūla, Dāmodara, Madhyacakra, and Dvāḥsūkṣmavinduka; Sudarśana has a single disc, while Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa arises from two; the god Acyuta has three discs, or Trivikrama likewise possesses three discs.
Janārdana has four wheels, Vāsudeva has five;
Pradyumna has six wheels, and Saṅkarṣaṇa has seven.
Puruṣottama has eight wheels, and Navavyūha is marked with nine.
The ten incarnations [are worshipped] with ten [stones], and Aniruddha with eleven;
the twelve-fold self with twelve, and beyond that, the infinite [is worshipped] with more.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Characteristics of the Śālagrāma and Other Images" in the Āgneya Purāṇa, the Great Purāṇa.
The Forty-sixth Chapter.
Now begins the Forty-seventh Chapter.
The Blessed One spoke concerning the worship of the Śālagrāma and other [objects]:
"I shall tell you of the worship of the Śālagrāma and other [stones] marked with discs for the sake of spiritual accomplishment."
The worship of Hari may be of three kinds— desirous, undesirous, or both;
however, for the five [incarnations] beginning with the Fish, it is either desirous or both.
1. "Below the middle wheel is the subtle bindu" (madhyacakrādhaḥ sūkṣmavindukaḥ) is the reading of the marked manuscript (Ṅa).
2. "For the sake of desired objects, it is of both natures" (kāmyārtheṣūbhayātmakaḥ) is the reading of manuscript (Gha).
The reading marked in the manuscript:
"For the liberation of Varāha, Nṛsiṃha, and Vāmana" (AP 47.002cd).

Now hear concerning the worship of the three, beginning with the *cakra* and the *śālagrāma*: worship of the *śālagrāma* is the highest, yet it is fruitless; worship of the *arcana* is the lowest, yet it is fruitful; worship of the image (*mūrti*) is the middle way, performed upon the four-cornered lotus of the *cakra*.
Having placed the *praṇava* in the heart and performed the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) ritual upon the hands and body,
and having formed the three mudrās, one should worship the Guru outside the *cakra* in the east;
one should worship Gaṇa in the west and Dhātṛ in the northwest.
One should worship Vidhātṛ, Kartṛ, and Hartṛ in the northeast; Viṣvaksena in the southeast; and Kṣetrapāla in the southeast.
One should worship the Vedas beginning with the Ṛgveda in the east and other directions, as well as Ādhāra, Ananta, and Bhūmi.
Having established the seat— the triple mandala known as the sun, moon, and fire, consisting of a lotus— there with the twelve-syllable [mantra], one should worship the stone.
One should worship it sequentially with the individual seed-syllables and then with the entire [mantra] together.

Then, starting from the east and so forth, one should worship with the Vedas and other mantras, with two *gāyatrīs*, and with the *jita* mantra; finally, one should worship with the *praṇava* and display three mudrās:
those of Viṣvaksena, the Discus, and the Guardian of the Field (*kṣetrapāla*).
The first worship of the Śālagrāma is said to be fruitless.
As before, one should draw a sixteen-spoked maṇḍala with a lotus;
one should worship the preceptor and others as before, using the conch, discus, mace, and sword.
In the east and north, one should offer a seat with the [mantras] beginning with the Vedas and the bow and arrows;
one should place the stone with the twelve syllables. Now hear the third [stage], the worship: one should draw an eight-spoked lotus, beginning with the Guru.
One should sacrifice as before;
"one should sacrifice with four as before" is the reading in manuscript Ṅa.
The reading "gandhādyaiḥ" is found in manuscript Ṅa;
this is the reading of the marked manuscript.
Having offered a seat with the eight-syllable mantra, one should likewise place the stone with that same mantra;
one should worship it ten times with that [mantra], as well as with the two Gāyatrīs and the Jitam.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of Śālagrāma and Other Sacred Objects," in the Āgneya Purāṇa, the foremost among the Great Purāṇas.
Chapter 48:
Narration of the Hymn to the Twenty-four Forms (Caturviṃśatimūrtistotra)
The Blessed One said:
"Oṃ-rūpa Keśava, the bearer of the lotus, conch, discus, and mace;
Nārāyaṇa, the possessor of the conch, lotus, mace, and discus, [should be circumambulated] clockwise."
Then I bow to Gada, Mādhava, Ari, Śaṅkhin, and Padmin;
to Govinda, the powerful one who holds the discus, the Kaumodakī mace, the lotus, and the conch;
to Viṣṇu, the bestower of enjoyment, who holds the glorious mace, the lotus, the conch, and the discus.
May Madhusūdana, who holds the conch, discus, lotus, and mace, protect me;
may Trivikrama, who possesses the lotus, mace, discus, and conch, [protect me];
and may Vāmana, who holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, always protect me with devotion.
May Śrīdhara, Padmī, Cakraśārṅgin, and Śaṅkhin protect us;
may Hṛṣīkeśa, Gadācakrī, Padmī, and Cakraśaṅkhin protect us; and may Varada Padmanābha, the bearer of the conch, lotus, discus, and mace, protect us.

I bow to that Dāmodara, who holds the lotus, conch, mace, and discus. By him, the world is protected: Vāsudeva, bearing the mace, conch, and discus, and holding the lotus; may Saṅkarṣaṇa, bearing the mace, conch, lotus, and discus, protect you all.
"Then it was conquered," is the reading found in the three manuscripts marked kha, ga, and ṅa.
2. "The discus, and likewise the conch," according to the reading of the manuscript marked with the letter Ṅa;
May Gadī, Cakrī, Śaṅkhagadī,
Pradyumna the lord who bears the lotus, Aniruddha who holds the discus, mace, conch, and lotus, protect us.
May the Lord Puruṣottama, the Sovereign of the Gods, who is enriched with the lotus and conch, bearing the glorious mace,
Adhokṣaja, who holds the lotus, mace, conch, and discus— protect you!
I bow to that Lord Nṛsiṃha, who bears the discus, lotus, mace, and conch.
May Acyuta—bearer of the mace, the lotus, the discus, and the conch—protect you;
may Upendra, who has the form of a child and bears the conch and mace, as well as the discus and lotus, protect you;
and may Janārdana, who holds the lotus, the discus, the conch, and the mace, protect you.
Hari holds the conch, the lotus, and the discus, and bears the Kaumodakī mace;
Kṛṣṇa, the holder of the conch, mace, lotus, and discus, bestows upon me both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
From that primordial form, Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa came into being.
From Saṅkarṣaṇa comes Pradyumna, and from Pradyumna comes Aniruddha;
through the divisions beginning with Keśava, each one is sequentially threefold.
This twelve-syllable hymn possesses twenty-four forms.
Whoever should read or even hear this shall become pure and obtain everything.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Hymn to the Twenty-four Forms," in the Āgneya Purāṇa, the Great Purāṇa.
Chapter 49:
Description of the Characteristics of Fish and Other Creatures.
The Blessed One said:
"I shall describe to you the ten incarnations, characterized by the Fish and the others.
The Fish incarnation shall have the form of a fish, and the Tortoise incarnation shall have the form of a tortoise."
n 1 The reading "śaṅkhapadmī" is found in the two manuscripts marked as Ga and Gha.
Alternatively, Bhūvarāha may be fashioned with a human body, bearing a mace and other weapons;
on his right side there is a conch, and on his left either Lakṣmī or a lotus.
The Earth and Ananta are situated at his left elbow, following after his feet;
by the installation of Varāha, there shall be sovereignty and the crossing of the ocean of existence.
Narasiṃha has his mouth wide open, with the demon wounded upon his left thigh.
Tearing open his chest, Mālī appeared with a shimmering discus and mace;
he might have a parasol and a staff, or be a dwarf, or perhaps four-armed; Rāma might be depicted with bow and arrow in hand, or equipped with a sword and an axe.
Rāma is also remembered as having two arms, bearing a bow, an arrow, a sword, and a conch; or else Rāma may have four arms, holding a mace and a plow.
One should place the plow in the upper left hand and a beautiful conch in the lower [left] hand.
With a pestle in his upper right hand and a most beautiful wheel below it,
the Buddha— whose nature is peaceful, whose ears are long, whose body is fair, and who is clothed in garments—
stands upon an upward-pointing lotus, bestowing the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Kalkī, the twice-born who will destroy the Mlecchas,
or else mounted upon a horse, bearing a sword and equipped with a conch, a discus, and arrows—
I shall now describe to you the characteristics of the nine [incarnations] beginning with Vāsudeva.
In the upper right [hand] is a mace, and in the upper left is the supreme discus;
Brahmā and Īśvara are his constant attendants on the sides. Vāsudeva is as before, either holding a conch, granting boons, or having two or four arms.
Lāṅgalin is known as Rāma, who bears the club and the lotus;
he is the one who seized the Dānava from the left thigh.

The reading "cihnitapustakapāṭhaḥ" (the reading of the marked manuscript) is found in manuscript *kha*; the reading "gaurāṅgaścāyudhāvṛtaḥ" (fair-complexioned and equipped with weapons) is found in the two marked manuscripts *ga* and *kha*.
3. "Equipped with bow and arrows" is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter Ṅa;
Pradyumna holds a vajra in his right hand and a conch in his left;
alternatively, Pradyumna may hold a bow and arrow in his hands, being yellow in color.
The all-pervading Nārāyaṇa likewise becomes four-armed and restrained;
Brahmā has four faces, four arms, and a large circular belly,
and he possesses matted hair with a swan as his foremost vehicle.
In the right [hand] is a rosary and a *sruva* ladle, while in the left is a *kuṇḍikā* water-pot;
Sarasvatī and Sāvitrī are on the left and right [respectively].
Viṣṇu has eight arms; upon Tārkṣya [is his seat], and in his hand is a sword in the right.
Holding a mace and an arrow, granting boons, with a bow and a shield in his left hands,
and a discus and a conch— thus is the four-armed Narasiṃha; or he may have four arms while bearing the conch and the discus, having torn asunder the great asura.
The Boar, however, is not four-armed; Śeṣa is held in the palm of his hand.
Supporting the earth with one arm, the Holder of Kamalā stands with his left foot resting on the earth and Lakṣmī established at his feet.
Trailokyamohana is on Tārkṣya; he has eight arms,
with a discus, sword, mace, and goad in his right hands,
and a conch, bow, club, and noose in his left hands, together with a lotus and a lute.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Viśvarūpa; furthermore, [the deity holds] a mallet and a noose in the right hands, while in the left hands [he holds] a spear, a trident, and an arrow,
as well as a conch, a Śārṅga bow, a mace, a noose, and a tomara-weapon.
In the manuscript marked with the symbol Ṅa, the reading is "a wheel on the right."
2. "Covered with red lead" is the reading in the manuscript marked Ṅa;

"Holding the agitated earth with his left hand and Kamalā below. This is the reading of the marked manuscript (ṅa).
Holding a plow, an axe, a staff, a knife, and a shield-throws,
he has twenty arms and four faces; he stands on the right, while [the other] is on the left.
The three-eyed one, who does not lie on his left side even when reclining upon the waters;
whose single foot is supported by Śrī and who is praised by Vimalā and others;
whose navel-lotus is the four-faced Brahmā; Hari is both Viṣṇu and Śiva.
Holding a trident and a spear in his right hand, and bearing a mace and a discus in his other hands;
his body marked by the hair of Rudra, he is accompanied by Gaurī and Lakṣmī;
Hari has the horse-head, with a conch, discus, mace, and the Vedas in his hands.
His left foot is held up while his right rests upon the back of a tortoise;
Dattātreya has two arms and is accompanied by Śrī on his left lap.
Viṣvaksena, the attendant of Hari, holds a discus, a mace, a plow, and a conch.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Icons," in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*, the Great Purāṇa.
Chapter 50:
Description of the Characteristics of the Goddess’s Image
The Blessed One said:
Caṇḍī shall have twenty arms; with her right hands she holds a trident, a sword, a spear, a discus, a noose, a shield, a weapon, and displays the gesture of fearlessness.
With her left hands, Caṇḍī has ten arms, holding a *ḍamaru* drum, a spear, a snake-noose, a shield, an axe, a goad, a bow, a bell, a banner, a mace, a mirror, and a mallet. AP_50.003ab.
Below that is Mahiṣa, with his head severed and his skull fallen;
[and] the supreme hide— this is the reading found in the manuscript marked Ṅa.
A man born from his neck, enraged, with a weapon raised in hand, holding a trident, vomiting blood, with blood-streaked hair and eyes; AP_50.004cd/
Being devoured by a lion while her neck is tightly bound with a noose,
with her right foot treading upon a lion and her left foot upon a low-caste asura—
this Caṇḍikā is three-eyed, armed, and the crusher of enemies.
In the place consisting of nine lotuses, Durgā is to be worshipped according to her own form:
first in the center, and likewise in the directions starting with Indra, by means of the [mantras] consisting of the nine principles (tattvas) in sequence.
She has eighteen arms; in her right hands, she holds a severed head and a shield.
The goddess holds a mirror, a threatening finger, a bow, a banner, and likewise a hand-drum (ḍamaruka) in her left hands; she also bears a noose, a spear, a mallet, and a trident,
as well as a vajra, a sword, a goad, and arrows, along with a chakra and a probe.
The remaining sixteen [deities] are likewise equipped with these same weapons;
however, the nine beginning with Rudracaṇḍā, having abandoned the *ḍamaru* and the raised index finger, are as follows:
Rudracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, and Caṇḍanāyikā.
Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavatī, Caṇḍarūpā, Aticaṇḍikā,
Ugracaṇḍā, and Madhyasthā— [these] are yellow, reddish, and black;
Nīlā, Śuklā, Dhūmrikā, Pītā, and Śvetā ride upon lions.
Then the buffalo, the man, the swordsman, the seizing of the hair, the fist,
and the *ālīḍha*— these nine should be established as the *durgās* for the increase of sons and other blessings.
Likewise, Gaurī, Caṇḍikā, and others hold a water-pot, a syllable, a tusk, and fire;
she herself is Rambhā in the forest, Siddhā when devoid of fire, and likewise Lalitā. Her left hand rests upon her shoulder, while the second holds a mirror.
1. "By means of the nine principles (*navatattva*) and so forth" is the reading found in manuscript *Ṅa*.
2. "Nine [images] in the halls" is the reading found in manuscript *Ṅa*.
The reading marked in the manuscript:
"On the south [is] Phalāñjali-hastā, and there Saubhāgyā is upright. (AP 50.015ab)
Lakṣmī has a lotus in her right hand and holds a *śrīphala* fruit in her left;
Sarasvatī holds a book and a rosary in her hands and a lute;
and Jāhnavī is white in complexion, holding a jar and a lotus, and is seated upon a crocodile.

Kūrmagā, Yamunā, Kumbhakārā, and Śyāmā are worshipped. Tumburu, white in color and holding a lute, stands before Mātṛkā; Gaurī is four-faced and holds a rosary and a vessel of liquor, while Brāhmī is on a bull.

Śāṅkarī, white in color and mounted on a swan, holds a sacrificial vessel and a skull-bowl in her left hands; she holds a bow and an arrow in her right hands, and a discus and a bow in her left hands,
while standing upon a bull.
Kaumārī is red, mounted on a peacock, with two arms and a spear in her hand;
Lakṣmī holds a discus and a conch in her right hands, while holding a mace and a lotus in her left; and Vārāhī, holding a mace, is mounted upon a buffalo.
For the sake of accomplishment, Aindrī is on the left, holding a vajra in her hand and possessing a thousand eyes;
Cāmuṇḍā is the destroyer of the hollows, fleshless and three-eyed,
or else fleshless with marrow in her bones, with hair standing erect and a lean belly.
She wears an island-skin on her left side, while in her right hands she holds a skull-cup, a *paṭṭiśa* spear, a trident, and a flaying knife; she is mounted upon a corpse and adorned with bones.
Vināyaka is human in form, with a massive belly and an elephant’s face.
The trunk is large and wrapped with a sacred thread; its mouth shall consist of seven *kalās*.
In both width and length, the trunk is thirty-six finger-breadths;
the neck is twelve *nāḍīs* and one and a half *kalās* in height.
The neck is thirty-six finger-breadths [in length], and the secret part is one and a half finger-breadths. *makareddhari jāhnavī* (as found in manuscript kha).
The reading in the three manuscripts marked Gha, Ṅa,
and Ca is "vāme vajram" (a vajra on the left); this is [also] in Kha and Ṅa.
The reading of the two marked manuscripts is "śaṅkhāri," whereas the reading of the marked manuscript [alone] is [as follows].
The navel and thighs are twelve [finger-breadths], as are the shanks; on the right foot he holds his own tusk and an axe, while on the left he rests upon a sweetmeat and a blue lotus.
Sumukhī and Viḍālākṣī are at his sides; Skanda is mounted upon a peacock;
the Lord Śākha and Viśākha are two-armed and assume the form of children;
in the right hand is a spear and a cock; then there is Ekavaktra and Ṣaṇmukha.
He may have six arms or twelve; in a village he is two-armed, while in the forest he holds a spear, arrows, a noose, a sword,
a goad, and a raised index finger in his six right hands, and likewise in his left.

Rudracarcikā holds a peacock-feather bow, a shield, a banner, and the gestures of fearlessness and the cock; she carries a skull, a flaying knife, a trident, and a noose in her southern and northern hands; she wears an elephant hide, has her face turned upward, and her feet are raised.
That same eight-armed goddess, endowed with a skull-topped drum upon her head, is therefore Rudracāmuṇḍā; she then dances as Nāṭeśvarī. This very same one, seated and four-faced, is Mahālakṣmī.
She devours men, horses, buffaloes, and elephants held in her hands;
she has ten arms and three eyes, and she bears a weapon, a sword,
and a *ḍamaru* drum in her right hands, while holding a bell and a shield in her left.
The goddess Siddhayogeśvarī, known as Siddhacāmuṇḍā, bestows all accomplishments;
she may have this form, or another red form endowed with a noose and a goad.
Bhairavī is the Vidyā of Form, endowed with twelve arms;
these fierce goddesses born of the cremation grounds are known as the Eight Mothers (Ambāṣṭaka).
"This is the first group of eight" is the reading found in the three manuscripts marked kha, ga, and gha;
Kṣamā is surrounded by auspiciousness;
she is aged, has two arms, a wide-open mouth, and protruding teeth.
She brings security and stands upon the ground with her knees and hands touching it.
The Yakṣiṇīs have steady, long eyes; the Śākinīs have crooked glances;
the Rūpiṇīs are tawny-eyed and exceedingly beautiful; and the Apsarases are ever-present.
Nandīśa, holding a rosary and a trident, is the guardian of the gate.
Mahākāla, Īśa, Muṇḍī, as well as Śūla and Khaṭaka;
likewise Kṛśa, Bhaṅgī, and the dancing Kuṣmāṇḍa, who is stout and dwarfish;
Gajakarṇa, Gokarṇa, Vaktra, and others—these are the Gaṇas such as Vīrabhadra and the rest.
Ghaṇṭākarṇa has eighteen arms, tearing asunder sinful diseases;
he holds a vajra, sword, staff, discus, arrow, mace, goad,
and hammer in his right hands, while his left hands hold a threatening gesture, shield, spear, severed head, and noose.

The god, who crushes the Visphoṭakas, holds a bow, a bell, and an axe, and with two [other hands] holds a trident; he is adorned with garlands of bells. (4) Thus ends the chapter titled "Characteristics of the Images of the Goddess" in the Āgneya Purāṇa, the Great Purāṇa.
The fiftieth chapter.

he holds an ink-pot and a pen, while in his right hand he carries a water-pot."
On the left, at the door, is Piṅgala, the bearer of the staff, who belongs to the host of the Sun;

2. "Vajradṛṣṭayaḥ" is the reading in manuscript Kha; 3. "Mahārathyā rūpiṇyo 'psarasaḥ" is [the reading] in manuscript Kha.

gha) is *visphoṭakarunardana*.

Varuṇa, he who is named Sūrya, and another, Sahasrāṃśu;
Dhātṛ known as Tapana, Savitṛ, and Gabhastika;
Ravi, Parjanya, Tvaṣṭṛ, Mitra, and Viṣṇuka.

In the rite of bringing forward the fire, the mantra is: "O Agni, you are indeed called Agni.

One should offer sesame seeds with clarified butter using the *vyāhṛtis* and the root mantra;
then one should perform the *śānti*-oblation with the three sweet substances (*madhuratraya*).
With the twelve-syllable mantra, one should touch the feet, the navel, the heart, and then the head.

Having burnt [the offerings] with the Viṣṇugāyatrī, one should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Gāyatrī;
one should perform the fire-oblation, present the bali-offering, and feed the twice-born in the north.
For the sake of pleasing the lords of the Sāman, one should give gold and a cow to the preceptor.

Having offered the *bali* to the guardians of the quarters, one should perform a vigil at night with the sound of the *brahmagītā* and other chants, for the purpose of consecrating all the portions. Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Consecration," in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*.

Chapter 60:

the wise man should place the image in the portion belonging to Brahmā.
O Bird-born One, never in the portions belonging to the gods, humans, or *piśācas*,
nor having abandoned the portion of Brahmā or relying on anything else,
should the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) be established with effort within the portions of the gods and humans.
One should perform the ritual placement of gems upon the neuter stone;
having offered oblations with the Nārasiṃha mantra, one should indeed perform the placement of gems with that very mantra.

One should place rice, gems, the three minerals, metals and so forth, and sandalwood and other substances into the nine pits starting from the east, or in the center according to one's preference. AP 60.005ab
Then, having covered the pit with guggulu resin while reciting the mantras of Indra and the other deities,
and having performed the ritual for the placement of jewels,
the preceptor should touch the image with bundles of *darbha* grass together with sticks, accompanied by the *sahadeva* plants.

Having consecrated it with both external and internal rites, one should purify it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and with water from a river or a sacred bathing place (tīrtha). For the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa), one should prepare a sacrificial mound (khaṇḍila) all around with sand.
One should construct a very beautiful square measuring one and a half cubits;

then, one should arrange water-pots (kalaśas) in the eight directions according to the prescribed placement. Having brought fire from the east and so forth, it should be consecrated with the eight-syllable mantra.
One should offer fuel-sticks with the *gāyatrī* verse beginning "tvamagne dyubhiḥ";
one should cause clarified butter to be offered in full measure,
and [sprinkle] the water for pacification using mango leaves.

One should sprinkle [the deity] on the head with water consecrated one hundred times with the root mantra; for by means of this *ṛc*, "And may Fortune be yours," and having lifted [the image] with the verse, "Arise, O Lord of Brahmā," [one should perform the rite].
With the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ," one should lead [the deity] facing the temple;
having placed Hari upon a palanquin, one should cause him to circumambulate the city and other areas,
accompanied by the sounds of songs, the Vedas, and so forth.
One should hold [the vessel] at the door of the palace;
one should sprinkle it with scented water— thus [it is said] in the versions *kha*,
*gha*, and *ṅa*.

instrumental music, and so forth," as found in manuscript Ṅa.
One should have Hari bathed by women and Brahmins with eight auspicious jars.

Then, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings using the root mantra, the preceptor should present garments and so forth, as well as the eightfold *arghya* offering, while reciting "ato devā... (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.7.4.2). When the ascendant is stable, he should install [the deity] upon the pedestal while reciting "devasya tvā... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.2.4.1).
"Oṃ, salutations to you, O Trivikrama, who have traversed the three worlds!

Having bathed [the deity] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and washed it with scented water,
one should worship Hari, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, together with his limbs and retinue.
One should meditate on one's own form as his image, while the earth serves as his pedestal.
One should fashion his body from luminous atoms;
I shall invoke the living soul, which resides within the twenty-five principles,
which is consciousness and supreme bliss, and which is devoid of the states of waking and dreaming.
Free from body, senses, mind, intellect, vital breath, and ego,
and established within the hearts of all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—
O Supreme Lord, remain steadfast within the image in this heart.
"Bring the image to life; you must abide within it, both externally and internally.

Having performed the act of enlivening, one should awaken [the deity] with the *praṇava*.
Having touched the heart, one should indeed mutter that which is called "bringing about presence. While meditating upon the *Puruṣasūkta*, one should mutter this secret mantra.
Salutations to you, the Lord of the Gods, whose nature is the power of contentment.

Chapter Sixty-One:
The Ritual for the Installation of the Door, the Hoisting of the Banner, and Other Related Procedures.
The Blessed One said:
"Having bowed to Viṣṇu, one should perform the *avabhṛtha* (concluding) bath;
having established the pitchers upon the eighty-one squares (*ekāśītipada*), one should install Hari."
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; having presented the *bali* offering, one should honor the preceptor (*guru*).
I shall now describe the consecration of the door: beneath the door, one should indeed place gold;
the preceptor, having established the two *udumbara* door-posts with eight jars, [should proceed].

Having worshipped thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings using mantras from the Vedas and other sources, the Guru should offer oblations into the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) with fire, using sacrificial wood, parched grain, sesame seeds, and so forth. Having provided a bed and other such items, he should then place the *Ādhāraśakti* (the Foundation Power) below.
One should place the two deities Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa at the base of the two branches;
and upon the upper *udumbara* fruit, one should worship the goddess Lakṣmī, who is honored by the hosts of gods,
according to the prescribed rule with the Śrīsūkta, and likewise the four-faced Brahmā.
Having offered the *śrīphala* and other items as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor and others,
the preceptor should install Hari at the gateway of the perfected consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).

Know the flagstaff to be the primordial nature (prakṛti), and the staff in human form;
understand from me that the palace is a specific manifestation of the form of Vāsudeva.
Know that space is characterized by voidness;
know that fire is its radiance; likewise, know wind to be that which possesses touch.
Know water to be within stones and the like, consisting of earth and possessing the qualities of earth.
Sound arises from an echo; touch would be that which is rough and so forth;
form would be white and so forth; taste is the perception of food and the like;

The nose is known to rest upon the nose-tip (śukanāśā); the two arms are considered to be its two chariots.

Chapter Sixty-Two:
The Ritual Procedure for the Installation of Lakṣmī (Lakṣmīpratiṣṭhāvidhi)
The Blessed One said: "In summary, I shall declare to you the installation of the deities and so forth;
first is the installation of Lakṣmī, and likewise that of the host of goddesses."
One should perform everything as before, including the pavilion and the ceremonial bathing (maṇḍapasnāna).
Having placed Śrī upon the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha), one should indeed set out eight jars;
having anointed [the image] with clarified butter using the root mantra, one should bathe it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should open the eyes of the golden-hued, tawny Śrī with [the mantra] beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇā*.
(Note: The reading in the manuscript marked with the letter *ṅa* is *maṇḍalasnapanādikam*.)
2. "One should place the jars in the direction of Varuṇa"—this is the reading found in the manuscripts marked with the letters gha and ṅa, p. 182.

with the mantra "aśvapūrvā," one should consecrate her with that pitcher from the east.
One should consecrate him from the south with "I am desire" (kāmosmi),
and from the west with "Candra and Prabhāsā," and from the north with "Of the color of the sun" (ādityavarṇa).
One should consecrate him from the southeast with "May he come to me" (upaitu mā), and from the southwest with "Hunger and thirst" (kṣutpipāsā).
At the northwest direction, [he should worship] Gandhadvārā, who is the mental form of desire;
with the Īśāna jar alone, he should perform the head-anointing with golden clay;
and with eighty-one jars, while releasing the waters upon the earth with the mantra, he should perform the ritual bath.

With the mantra beginning "ārdrāṃ puṣkariṇīṃ gandhaiḥ" and "ārdrām," and with flowers such as *puṣpaka*, one should bring forth that [divinity] consisting of those [mantras]. Having projected the power of consciousness (cicchakti) by means of the Lakṣmī-bīja, one should worship again with the Śrīsūkta.
Then, in the pavilion and in the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should offer lotuses or karavīra flowers, having performed a thousand or even a hundred oblations.
One should offer the household utensils and all other items with the Śrīsūkta alone.
Then, having performed the entire consecration of the temple as before,

The Blessed One spoke on the consecration of wells and so forth:
"I shall describe the consecration of wells, step-wells, and tanks; listen to it."
For Hari is Varuṇa, the supreme Soma, in the form of water; the universe consists of Agni and Soma, and Viṣṇu is water. A man should have an image of Varuṇa fashioned from gold, silver, or gems.
Two-armed, seated upon the back of a swan, granting fearlessness with the right hand and holding a serpent-noose with the left, accompanied by river-deities, nāgas, and others;
there shall be an altar adorned with a sacrificial pit in the center of the sacrificial pavilion.
One should place the Varuṇa-pitcher along with the water-jar at the archway;
and at the gate, one should place pitchers upon a Bhadraka, an Ardhacandra, or a Svastika diagram.
Having performed the establishment of the fire in the sacrificial pit, one should cause the full oblation to be offered.
At the bathing pedestal, one should touch Varuṇa with the mantra "ye te śata...

Having washed [the vessels] with the mantra *śanno devī* and with auspicious waters purified by the *śuddhavatī* verses, one should consecrate eight jars: sea water in the eastern jar, Ganges water in the southern, rainwater in the western, and mountain spring water in the northern.
River water should be placed in the west, river water in the northwest, water from plants in the north, and water from a sacred ford (tīrtha) in the northeast; however,

Over those [goddesses] he should mutter the mantra "yāsāṃ rājā" (64.009cd). Having wiped and cleansed the deity with the mantra "durmitriyā" (64.009d), the wise one should open the eyes with the "citra" mantra and the three sweets (64.010cd).
One should fill the golden vessel with light and then present a cow to the preceptor.

One should consecrate [the disciple] with water from the eastern pitcher using the mantra "samudrajyeṣṭhāḥ," with water from the Varuṇa pitcher using "samudraṃ gaccha," with water from the Gaṅgā-related pitcher using "gāṅgeya," and with water from the Soma pitcher using "somo dhenu."

One should perform purification with the *devīrāpaḥ* [mantra] using water from mountain springs and from rivers; with the *pañcanadyaḥ* [mantra], water from the five rivers; with the *udbhid* [mantra], water from a spring; then with the *pāvamānī* verses and water from sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*).
One should use the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* [mantra] for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and the *hiraṇyavarṇā* [mantra] for gold dust.
With water from rain-clouds, reciting the *vyāhṛtis*, and with water from wells;

One should perform the bath with the mantra "snāpayed varuṇasya"; the *arghya* with "tvanno varuṇa"; the *madhuparka* with the *vyāhṛtis*; the garment with "bṛhaspate";
the purifier (*pavitra*) with "varuṇa"; and the upper garment with the *praṇava*.

Having offered an oblation of barley,
one should perform the rite of pacifying water;
one should sprinkle it upon the head of the deity and perform the rite of restoration to life.
One should meditate upon Varuṇa joined with Gaurī and the hosts of rivers and streams;

Having raised [the image] from the back of an elephant or other [vehicles], one should cause it to be carried around by those [processions] accompanied by auspicious rites.

The sixty-fourth chapter.
Chapter Sixty-Five: An Account of the Establishment of the Assembly Hall (Sabhā)
The Blessed One said: "I shall describe for you the location of the assembly hall as well as its construction; one should perform the Vāstuyāga sacrifice on ground that has been duly examined."
Having constructed the assembly hall according to his own will, he should install the deities according to his own will;
thus he should offer water.
The reading in the marked manuscript (Ṅa) is:
"one should cause the twice-born to drink [the milk] from Gokula."
One should not have an assembly hall constructed at a crossroads, in a village, or in a deserted place.
Stainless, having uplifted his lineage, the builder rejoices in heaven.
According to this procedure, one should construct a seven-storied temple for Hari;
as it is for kings, so it is for others, with the directions starting from the east and the banners and other ornaments.
Excluding the corner-arms, one should construct a four-winged house (*catuḥśāla*),
or a three-winged, two-winged, or even a single-winged house.
One should not make it with excessive expenditure (*vyayādhika*), for that brings about the fault of financial loss.

If there is an excess in the [first] term, there will be suffering; therefore, the Guru, who is expert in the science of Garga, should make both terms equal and multiply the total sum by eight (eight Vasus).
Then, one should divide by seven (the seven-flamed fire). AP_65.006cd–65.007ab/
When that [sum] is divided by eight, whatever remains is the elapsed expenditure (*vyaya*).
Alternatively, the wise one should multiply the heap of *kara* by seven;
when the portion is divided by eight, [the remainder represents] earth and so forth.
One should visualize them as follows:
a banner, smoke-colored [a goat], a lion, a dog, a bull, a donkey, an elephant, and likewise a crow; these arise in the east and the other directions, and one should thus conceptualize them.

A house with three wings on all sides is recommended, provided it is devoid of openings to the north and east; a two-winged house is always obtained when it is joined with another's house to the south.
Alternatively, there may be a single-winged house to the south, or even one facing west.
A house with two wings on one side is praised; all others are bringers of fear.
A four-winged house is always praised, being free from all defects.
One may construct a residence with one story up to seven stories.

A temple for a deity, devoid of gates, altars, and the like, and free from the [earth] filling-in process, should always be established according to the ritual procedure for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). (Note:
*pūś* refers to the earth-filling in the context of cities, crossroads, villages, and so forth.)
The reading of the marked manuscript is "dhvajādi" (and so forth), according to manuscript *kha*.
This is the reading of the marked manuscript.
Having established the people through the rites prescribed by the assembly,
and having performed a bath with all medicinal herbs in the morning, being pure and vigilant;

Having fed the twice-born with sweet foods and having had the Brahmins recite auspicious blessings, the householder— adorned with full water-jars and other ornaments, and featuring an arched gateway (toraṇa)— should enter his home while holding a cow's tail; then, after honoring the astrologers, he should retire to rest.
With a concentrated mind, one should recite this mantra for prosperity in the home:
Oṃ! O Nandā, daughter of Vasiṣṭha, grant us joy together with the Vasus and our progeny!
O Jayā, descendant of Bhṛgu, bring about the victory of our offspring!
O Pūrṇa, heir of Aṅgiras, fulfill my every desire;
O Bhadra, heir of Kāśyapa, form an auspicious resolve for me.
[This is] you who are endowed with all seeds and medicinal herbs, and surrounded by all jewels and medicinal herbs.

O Goddess, daughter of Prajāpati, may you take delight here in this beautiful, joyful, and vast abode of Vasiṣṭha; O fortunate and virtuous Goddess, daughter of Kaśyapa, may you find pleasure in this home.
O Goddess, daughter of Bhṛgu, who bestows worldly prosperity, may you dwell in this home adorned with perfumes and garlands, honored by supreme teachers;
O unmanifest one, made manifest, full, daughter of the sage Aṅgiras.
O brick, grant what is desired; I am establishing you within the possession of the lord of the land, the lord of the city, and the lord of the house.
May you be the bringer of increase in men, wealth, elephants, horses, and cattle.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Establishment of the Assembly Hall," in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*, the Great Purāṇa.

Chapter Sixty-Six:
Now begins the sixty-sixth chapter.
The Blessed One has spoken the ritual procedure for common consecration;
now I shall describe the consecration of a collective [image], which is like that of Vāsudeva.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and likewise the two Aśvins,
as well as all the Ṛṣis— I shall describe their specific [mantras] to you; taking the first syllable of whichever deity's name it may be, [one should proceed].
Having divided [the mantra] by its morae (mātrās), one should then divide the long limbs.
First, one should arrange the seed-syllable with the bindu, the Praṇava, and the salutation.
Likewise, the worship and installation of all [deities] should be performed with the root-mantra.
I shall describe the installation of observances, vows, and penances, as well as monasteries, bridges, and temples, beginning with the fasting for a month on the twelfth lunar day;
thereafter, one should establish a stone slab, a full water-pot, a bronze vessel, and the necessary ritual materials.

Having collected the *brahmakūrca* materials, the practitioner should cook a sacrificial porridge (*caru*) made of barley in the milk of a tawny cow, reciting the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ". Then, having sprinkled it with clarified butter while reciting the *praṇava*, he should stir it with a ladle.
Having prepared [the oblation] and poured it out, one should then worship Viṣṇu and perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).

One should offer with the *vyāhṛtis*, with the *gāyatrī*, and with the verse beginning "tad viprāsaḥ. Likewise, one should offer with the verses beginning "viśvataścakṣuḥ," "vedyaiḥ," and "bhūr agnaye."
One should offer oblations to Sūrya, Prajāpati, and the intermediate space (antarikṣa).
With "Dyaus svāhā! To Brahmā svāhā! To Pṛthivī, the Great King!
one should perform the oblation to King Soma and to Indra and the other deities.
1. "One should fashion the limbs"—this is the reading found in the two manuscripts marked Kha and Ṅa.

Having offered oblations in this manner, one should respectfully present portions of the sacrificial porridge as offerings to the quarters.

Having offered one hundred and eight fuel-sticks (*samidh*) made of *pālāśa* wood, he should perform an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya-homaka*) with the *Puruṣasūkta*. Then, having offered eight sesame seeds (*tilāṣṭaka*) with the verse beginning "irāvatī," he should [offer] to those who follow the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa.

as well as to the mountains, the rivers, and the oceans,
one should offer the *vyāhṛtis* and three full oblations with the *sruva* ladle.

The wise man should conclude his vow by saying, "May the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu be pleased.

having gratified the Lord of Gods with a sacrifice, he should cook the Vaiṣṇava caru.

and having poured it out, one should perform the oblation (*homa*) with the mantras of the deities;
at the end of that, one should again offer oblations to Viṣṇu and the other guardians of the months.
Oṃ, svāhā to Viṣṇu! Oṃ, svāhā to Viṣṇu, the one who has gone down! Oṃ, svāhā to Viṣṇu, Śipiviṣṭa!
Oṃ, svāhā to Narasiṃha! Oṃ, svāhā to Puruṣottama!
One should offer twelve fuel-sticks of the aśvattha tree, saturated with clarified butter, into the fire.
Then, with the *viṣṇo rarāṭam* mantra, one should offer twelve oblations; thus it is stated in the reading of the manuscripts marked Kha and Ṅa.

Having thus set aside the *gopatha*, one should install the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) there; [one should do so] for a ten-cubit post at water-stations, gardens, monasteries, bridges, and the like, as well as in the home. one should worship those who resemble lions and possess white, red, yellow, and blue colors.
In the center of the lotus is Rāṃ, the radiant one; Rīṃ, the subtle one; Raṃ, Jayā; Rūṃ, Bhadrā; Reṃ, Vibhūtī; Vimalā; Raim, Amoghā;
Roṃ, Rauṃ, and Vidyutā—these are the Śaktis facing all directions, beginning from the east.
