Chapter Seventy-Four:
An Account of the Worship of Śiva
Īśvara said:

I shall now describe the worship of Śiva. Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and possessing the *praṇava* and the *arghya*, one should sprinkle the door with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) and worship the guardians of the door through fire-offerings (*homa*) and other rites.
One should worship Gaṇa, Sarasvatī, and Lakṣmī at the *ūrdhvodumbaraka*;
then one should worship Nandin and Gaṅgā situated on the right and left respectively.
Having cast down Mahākāla and Yamunā with his divine gaze,
and having cleared away the divine obstacles moving through the air by scattering flowers,
he struck those stationed on the ground with three blows from the heel of his right foot into the temple of the Āgamas.
One should cross the threshold by resorting to the left side and enter;
having entered, one should place the *astra-mantra* on the threshold-post (*udumbara*) with the right foot.
Then, one should worship Brahmā, the lord of the site (*vāstvadhipati*), in the center with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ vāstvadhipataye brahmaṇe*.
1. "Saṃhāriṇyopasaṃhṛtam" is the reading found in the manuscript marked Kha;
"saṃhāriṣṇopasaṃhṛtam" is the reading in Ga and Ṅa.
The reading of the two marked manuscripts is "abhyarcya ca," whereas the reading of the marked manuscript [in question] is [different].
3. "Located on the right branch" is the reading found in the two manuscripts marked Gha and Ṅa;
Having taken up water-pots that have been purified by means of weapons such as the *nirīkṣaṇa* (inspection) rite,
and having received permission from Śiva, he should proceed silently toward the Gaṅgā or other sacred waters.
With his limbs purified, he should [bathe] with water that has been strained through a cloth and over which mantras have been recited.
One should fill those various [vessels] in the ocean with the *gāyatrī* or with the heart-mantra.
Having gathered all the materials, such as flowers, for the purpose of worship, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth.

Then, having assigned [the deity] to the right side of the body with a gentle face, one should take [the essence] from the body using the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and hold it at the crown of the head with the mantra.
For the sake of experiencing the karma to be enjoyed, one should do so by means of what is called the "tortoise" hand-gesture (*pāṇi-kacchapikā*).
One should purify one's own self within the heart-lotus or at the station of the *dvādaśānta*. Having contemplated the five elements within the hollow interior of the body,
one should visualize the pair of big toes from both the inside and outside of that hollow space.
Then, having placed the power (śakti), which pervades the heart, within the syllable *hūṃ* which has the luster of fire,
the meditator should indeed restrain the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
And with that [mantra] ending in *phaṭ*, having pierced the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā;
(variant reading in manuscript Ṅa: "the essences of fragrance").
The reading in the marked manuscript is "luḍḍukān"; this is the reading in the marked manuscript according to manuscript KHA.
2. "guḍḍukākṣatā" is the reading in manuscript Ṅa;
"gaṇḍūkākṣatā" is the reading in manuscript Gha.
The reading of the marked manuscript is "saumyāsyaḥ svaśarīrataḥ" (gha).
This is the reading of the marked manuscript.
"By the Mūrti-mantra," according to the reading found in the three manuscripts marked with the letters Ga, Gha, and Ṅa.
5. "On one's own head and body" is the reading found in the manuscript marked Ṅa;
6. "Behind the syllable Oṃ" is [the reading found in] Ṅa.

The reading marked with a sign in the manuscript is "candramadhyasthite" (in the center of the moon), while the reading in manuscript *kha* is the same; the reading marked with a sign in the manuscript is "cakramadhyasthite" (in the center of the wheel), while the reading in manuscript *ṅa* is the same.

Having pierced the twenty-one knots and placed the syllable *hūṃ* at the crown of the head, one should then [unite] the life-force with the heart by means of the *sampuṭa* [breathing technique], having directed the consciousness through inhalation (*pūraka*).
Having placed *hūṃ* upon the topknot (*śikhā*), one should contemplate it as pure and consisting of the nature of the drop (*bindu*).

Then, having performed breath-retention (*kumbhaka*) within Śambhu, one should unite [it] with a single upward thrust (*ekodghāta*). Through exhalation (*recaka*) by means of the activity of the seed-syllable, one becomes absorbed in Śiva and should then purify.
In one's own body, however, [one should practice] in reverse order until the *bindu*; there,
having brought the *bindu* to dissolution, the earth and wind, as well as water and fire, [merge] with one another.
Two by two are to be accomplished, as well as space; hear that without contradiction.
The earthly mandala is yellow, solid, marked with a thunderbolt, and consists of the portion of its own cessation.
Having visualized a square shape starting from the feet up to the head,
one should contemplate it as having become wind by means of five upward thrusts;
[it is] a gentle liquid half-moon, marked with a white lotus.
By means of this seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, it has attained the state of being established;
conjoined with the Rāma-mantra,
it is the causeless end of the Person (*puruṣānta*).
One should purify the fire element with four exhalations using the *arghya* water.
One should visualize the fiery mandala as triangular, red, marked with a swastika, and having the form of the Vidyā, by means of this seed-syllable: *HŪM*.
One should purify the water-element by means of three fierce *udghātas*,
[conceiving it] as having Viṣṇu as its essence; this is the reading found in the manuscript marked "kha."

The hexagonal mandala of Vāyu is marked with six dots,
black in color, born from the seed-syllable *hrem*, and consists of the digit of pacification (*śāntikalā*).
Having meditated upon it, one should purify the earth element with a pair of upward-pointing [triangles].
[One should visualize] a circle composed of the space-bindu, adorned with the bindu and śakti;
it has the form of the void, is perfectly round, and is as pure as clear crystal.

Having meditated on that which consists of the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*) with the syllable *Hauṃ* ending in *Phaṭ*, one should contemplate it as perfectly pure through the yoga of a single exhalation (*ekodghāta*). Then, one should nourish everything with the root mantra that rains down nectar (*amṛta*).

Having meditated upon that which is called the support (ādhāra), Ananta, and the lotus of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and so forth, one should then invoke the form [of Śiva] consisting of Śiva from the dvādaśānta into that [lotus] by means of emanation.

Then, having drenched that [deity] on all sides with divine nectar using the Śakti-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the infusion of limbs) upon the fingers beginning with the little finger.

The ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) of the mantras beginning with the heart-mantra is considered to be the process of "making complete" (*sakalīkaraṇa*). Having protected the perimeter with the weapon-mantra (*astra*),
one should then display the net of power (*śaktijāla*) both below and above that mantra, and exhibit the great mudrā (*mahāmudrā*).

One should worship Śiva with the flowers of the elements from the feet up to the crown of the head within the lotus of the heart by means of inhalation (pūraka); then, one should satisfy the fire of Śiva in the sacrificial pit of the navel with the mantras of Śiva and the excellent clarified butter of nectar drawn [upward].

One should contemplate on the forehead a single auspicious form in the shape of a drop (bindu).

One vessel among vessels made of gold and other materials, purified with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astra), should be filled with water, unbroken rice (akṣata), and so forth, which takes the form of nectar produced from that drop.
Having filled [the vessel] with the heart-mantra and worshipped it with the six limbs, one should consecrate it;
having protected it with the *heti* mantra, one should veil it with the armor (*kavaca*) mantra.
Having prepared the eight-limbed offering (*arghya*), one should sprinkle it with the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*).
Then one should consecrate oneself by sprinkling a drop of that water upon the head;

with the water of the weapon-mantra (*astravāri*), one should sprinkle the sacrificial materials situated there; having consecrated them with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), one should envelop them with the *piṇḍas* while reciting the armor-mantra (*tanutrāṇa*).
Having displayed the *amṛta-mudrā* and offered a flower, and having placed [the deity] upon his own seat,
one should apply a *tilaka* on the head and join the flower with the root mantra.
[This applies] during bathing, worship of the deity, fire-offerings (*homa*), eating, sacrifice, and yoga.
In the obligatory recitation, the steadfast one should always remain silent;
having purified the mantra by reciting it neither too softly nor too loudly, and having worshipped it well-prepared during the ritual, he should offer the general *arghya* with the *gāyatrī*.
Having repeated the five Brahma-mantras and taken the garland from the *liṅga*,
one should offer it to Caṇḍa in the northeastern direction with the Heart-mantra.
Then, having washed the pedestal and the *liṅga* with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra, one should [proceed] with the Heart-mantra.
One should sprinkle with water from the *arghya* vessel; this is the purification of the *liṅga*.
Once the self, the substances, the mantras, and the *liṅga* have been purified, one should worship all the deities.
To Gaṇapati in the northwest and to the Gurus, O Śivā, one should offer worship with the syllable *Hāṃ*.

"One should worship the Foundation Power (Ādhāraśakti), which resembles a sprout and rests upon the Tortoise-stone (Kūrmaśilā). (AP 74.044ab)
One should worship the infinite seat (āsanam) of Śiva mounted upon the Brahma-stone;
the sandals of Śiva’s seat are described as having variegated hair, facing one another with their backs visible, and appearing in the forms of the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages.
One should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya— shining like saffron, saffron, gold, and collyrium respectively— in the directions starting from the southeast, in sequence.

The Śaktis have hands granting boons and fearlessness, and they hold chowries;

Balavikaraṇī, and Balapramathanī are to be worshipped in sequence.

One should place the Lord upon the lion-throne as his seat, which pervades the principles from Earth up to Śuddhavidyā—the white, all-pervading one with five faces.

Holding a ten-armed form with a crescent moon in his right hands, he displays a spear, a double-edged sword, a trident, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and the gesture of granting boons; in his left hands, he holds a hand-drum,
a citron, a blue lotus, a rosary, and a water lily.
In the center, one should place the form of Śiva endowed with the thirty-two marks,
reciting "Hāṃ Haṃ Hāṃ, to the form of Śiva," while remembering Śiva as self-luminous;
having led the mantra to the abode of Śiva by abandoning the causal deities beginning with Brahmā.
Then, having meditated upon the supreme Śiva in the form of a drop (bindu), situated in the middle of the forehead, possessing the shimmering radiance of the moon, endowed with the six limbs,
and placed within a handful of flowers, one should cause him to enter the image of Lakṣmī.
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva; having first invoked [the deity] with the heart-mantra (hṛd) using the invocation-mudrā (āvāhanī),

and having established [him] with the establishment-mudrā (sthāpanī), one should bring Śiva into close proximity and then bind him with the firm mudrā (niṣṭhurā), ending with "phaṭ" while visualizing the dark splendor of Time (kālakānti).
Having dispelled the obstacles with the *viṣṭi* [mudrā], one should then perform the salutation with the *liṅga* mudrā.
Afterwards, one should veil [the deity] with the heart-mantra; then follows the invocation (*āvāha*), whereby the deity becomes face-to-face.
Then there should be the seating (*niveśana*) and the stabilization (*sthāpana*). "O Lord, I am yours"—this is the presence (*sannidhāna*).
Until the conclusion of the ritual manual (*karmakāṇḍa*), the dissolution of the deity remains upon that which is present.
The manifestation of one's own devotion is the veiling (avaguṇṭhana).
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa with the six mantras, one should then achieve oneness.
One should perform the rite of immortalization for the limbs together with the possessor of the limbs;
[one should contemplate] the heart of Śambhu as the power of consciousness, the eightfold sovereignty of Śiva, invincible mastery as the crest-lock, and the divine splendor as the impenetrable armor.
"Pratāpa," "Duḥsaha," and "Astra"— which removes obstacles—

and likewise "Namaḥ," "Svadhā," "Svāhā," and "Vauṣaṭ," should be uttered in their proper order, preceded by the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), and one should present the water for the feet (pādya) and the other offerings.

Having thus consecrated the Supreme Lord with the ten purificatory rites— offering water for the feet to His pair of lotus-feet, water for sipping to His faces, and the respectful offering (arghya) along with dūrvā grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains to the head of the God— AP 74.063ab.

having first worshipped them with substances consecrated by the mantras of Īśa and the others.

Chapter 75:
The Ritual for the Installation of the Fire and Other Procedures.
The Lord said: Holding the vessel for the *argha* offering, one should proceed to the fire-sanctuary well-concealed;
and with divine vision, one should prepare all the implements for the sacrifice.
Facing north, he should gaze at the sacrificial pit; he should perform the sprinkling and the striking with *kuśa* grass using the *astra-mantra*,
while the sprinkling [of water] is considered to be performed with the *varma-mantra*.
One should perform the excavation and removal with the sword, the filling and leveling with armor, the sprinkling with arrows, the pounding with the nature of the shafts,
the sweeping, the smearing, and the fashioning of the forms of the digits.
One should always perform the donning of the three threads and the worship with armor;
one should draw three lines toward the north— with one facing downward toward the east—
using *kuśa* grass and the *Śivāstra* mantra, or else their arrangement may be reversed.
With the *vajrīkaraṇa* mantra and the heart-mantra, one should place darbha grass at the crossroads;
with the armor-mantra, one should set down the vessel of seeds, and with the heart-mantra, the seat (*viṣṭara*).
Having invoked the Mistress of Speech (*Vāgīśvarī*) there with the heart-mantra, one should worship the Sovereign (*Īśā*).

Having brought the fire from its constant source and placed it upon a pure vessel, one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyāda), purify it through inspection and other rites,
and then unify the three fires— the digestive (audarya), the lunar (aindava), and the elemental (bhauta).

Oṃ hūṃ; one should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) for the consciousness of fire (*vahnicaitanya*) by means of the seed-syllable of fire. Chapter 78: The Account of the Pavitrārohaṇa Rite.
Īśvara said:
I shall describe the *pavitrārohaṇa* (the rite of offering the sacred thread), which fulfills the ritual worship and other rites;
that is declared to be the daily (*nitya*), and there is another, the occasional (*naimittika*).
It should be performed on the fourteenth days of the months beginning with Āṣāḍha, as well as during the bright and dark fortnights of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada;
or alternatively, one may perform it starting from the first lunar day (pratipad) until the fourteenth day of the month of Kārttika.
For the deities of Fire, Brahmā, Ambikā, Īśāna, Nāga, Skanda, Arka, and Śūlin,
[the threads] are made of gold, silver, and copper respectively in the Kṛta and following ages; in the Kali age, they may also be made of cotton or of silk, lotus-fiber, and so forth.
The Praṇava, the Moon, Fire, Brahmā, the Nāga, Guha, Hari,
the Lord of All, and all the gods reside respectively within the nine threads;
[the number of strands] is one hundred and eight, fifty-four, or twenty-seven for the superior and other grades.
Alternatively, [it is] by eighty-one or thirty-six sūtras;
"the winds of bodily insanity" (śarīronmādavāyavaḥ) is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter *gha*.

Jayā, Vijayā as the sixth, Ajitā, and Sadāśivā;

The pavitraka for the liṅgas shall range from one cubit up to nine cubits.

Chapter Eighty-One:
The Ritual Procedure for Initiation into the Samaya Vow.
Īśvara said:

I shall explain the initiation that brings about the destruction of sin for the sake of enjoyment and liberation— that by which the separation from the bonds of *mala*, *māyā*, and so forth is effected.

And when knowledge is generated in the disciple, that initiation bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. In the scripture, the recipient of grace is considered to be of three kinds: the first is the *vijñānakala*, the second is the *pralayākala*, and the third is the *sakala*.

Among these, the first is liberated by mere impurity (*mala*), while the other is liberated from both impurity and karma. Since [the latter] is associated with the principles beginning with *kalā* and ending with the earth (*bhūmi*) through hymns of praise, initiation (*dīkṣā*) is likewise considered to be of two kinds: without support (*nirādhārā*) and with support (*sādhārā*).

For those two, it is without support; for the whole [of the path], however, it has a support. By the conduct of Śambhu, which is independent of any support, it is brought about through the descent of the intense power (*tīvra-śakti*); thus it is known as "without support" (*nirādhārā*).
Assuming the form of the Teacher (Ācārya), Śambhu performs through his power—which is divided into *māyā*, *tīvra*, and so forth—that which is called the "possessor of instruments" (*sādhikaraṇa*).
(Note 1: In manuscript *kha*, the reading is *pralayānala*.)
The reading in the marked manuscript is *pralayātmaka*; this is the reading in manuscript Ṅa.
This [emptiness] is said to be fourfold: with seed and without seed;
with functional capacity and without functional capacity—how this is so shall now be explained.

For men, [the initiation] accompanied by the observance of the rules (samayācāra) is "with seed" (savīja); however, for those who are incapable, it is "without seed" (nirvīja), being devoid of the observance of the rules. For through this, one becomes qualified for the obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites.
Therefore, initiation for the *sādhaka* and the *ācārya* should possess an office (*sādhikārā*);
however, for those who have been initiated as my sons, it is "seedless" (*nirbījā*).
Because it consists solely of the obligation to perform daily rites, their initiation is one that lacks an office (*niradhikārikā*).
This [meditation] is of two kinds, for it arises in two forms respectively:
one there is "possessed of action," preceded by the drawing of a circle or mandala;
that which occurs through mental activity alone is considered "possessed of knowledge."

Thus, by the initiation-teacher who has obtained authority, the *skandadīkṣā* is accomplished; the Guru, having performed his daily rites (*nityakriyā*), should then perform the worship of the Lord of the Gate with the *praṇava* and the water-lotus of the *arghya* in his hand. (AP 81.014ab)

Having dispelled obstacles and placed the weapon-mantra (astra) upon the threshold, he should remain seated on his own seat and perform the purification of the elements (bhūta-śuddhi) and the yoga of mantras as prescribed.
[He should prepare] water mixed with sesame seeds, rice, white mustard, kuśa grass, dūrvā grass, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Then, this special *arghya* consisting of barley, milk, and water;
with that water, the purification of the ritual materials, the *tilaka*, and the worship of one's own seat and self;
as well as the accomplishment of the mantra and the *pañcagavya*, all as before.

He scattered parched grain, sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice; he scattered kuśa grass, pure parched grain, and incense, all consecrated with the weapon-mantra. (AP 81.018ab) [Note: "Having performed the two daily rites" is the reading in manuscript kha.]
The reading of the marked manuscript (2) is "bhasmadūrvākṣatān" (ashes, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice grains);
this is the reading of manuscript Ṅa.
These [deities], sprinkled with water from the ritual vessel, enveloped by the armor-mantra, appearing in various forms of seizing, and warding off the flood of obstacles— AP_81.019ab.
Having fashioned a supreme sword of awakening (bodhāsi) from thirty-six palm-lengths of *darbha* grass, consecrated seven times with the *Śivāstra* mantra,
and having placed the auspicious [mantra] within oneself as the desired support for creation; AP 81.020ab.
Having placed the partless Śiva [therein], one should contemplate, "I am Śiva.
Having placed the *uṣṇīṣa* on the head, one should adorn one's own body.
One should apply fragrant ointment to one's own right hand.
One should worship the Lord here according to the prescribed rite;
thus, having placed the radiant Śiva upon one's own head with the Śiva-mantra,
one should contemplate oneself as the agent, non-different from Śiva.

The Lord who has six supports— acting as the witness of the rites in the mandala, the protector of the sacrifice in the jar, the locus of the fire-oblation in the fire, the liberator from bonds in the disciple, and the one who bestows grace upon his own self— is the Sovereign. (AP 81.025ab)
He should then cultivate a very firm conviction that "I am indeed he.
Standing with the sword of knowledge in hand and facing the southwest,
the man should sprinkle the sacrificial pavilion with water for offering (arghya) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should consecrate [the site] with the purificatory rites at the four crossroads, beginning with the rite of inspection (*īkṣaṇa*).
Having scattered the *vikara* offerings there, one should collect them together with a bundle of *kuśa* grass.
One should then prepare those [offerings] as a seat in the *vardhanī* vessel located in the direction of the Lord (the northeast).
In the southwest, one should worship the deities of the site (vāstugīrvāṇas), and at the door,
one should worship Lakṣmī with gems— her who is filling [the space] and whose form is that of the pavilion— with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
1. "Astrāmbu" is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter Ṅa; 2. "Śiṣye pāpavimocaka" is [the reading] in the manuscript marked with the letter Ṅa.
The reading marked [in the manuscript]:
"On a cloth with water, containing gems, placed upon grain, facing west" (AP 81.029cd).
One should worship Śambhu in the eastern pitcher; Śakti to the south of the pitcher;
and in the west, Vardhanī, who is seated upon a lion and has the form of a sword.
In the cardinal directions, one should worship the guardians of the quarters, beginning with Indra and ending with Viṣṇu, seated upon the Praṇava.
Having worshipped with the heart-mantra those [deities] equipped with vehicles and weapons by their respective names,
one should first take up that [water] which flows into the front of the jar, and having caused it to circulate clockwise with an uninterrupted stream of water; AP_81.032cd.
Uttering the root mantra, he should cause the world-protectors to hear the command of Śiva:
"Protect [this] according to the proper method. Then, having placed that [vessel], he should hold the *kumbha*;
thereafter, having worshipped Śaṅkara along with his limbs (*aṅga*) within the *kumbha* upon a stable seat.
Having deposited the path to be purified [into the *vardhanī*], one should worship the Weapon (*astra*) with:
*oṃ haḥ astrāsanāya hūṃ phaṭ*;
*oṃ oṃ astramūrtaye namaḥ*.
Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ, homage to the Pāśupata weapon!
Oṃ oṃ, homage to the heart, hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ śrīṃ, hūṃ phaṭ, homage to the head! Oṃ yaṃ, hūṃ phaṭ, homage to the crest-lock! Oṃ gūṃ, hūṃ [homage to the armor!]
*Phaṭ namaḥ*. *Oṃ phaṭ astrāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ*.
One should visualize the Weapon (Astra), which has four faces and fangs, together with its spear, mallet, trident, and sword, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
One should perform the union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga* by means of the *liṅgamudrā*. Oṃ aṃ haḥ, for the subduing of weapons, hraṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ aṃ, to the embodiment of the weapon!
Homage! Oṃ paśūṃ huṃ phaṭ, homage to the Pāśupata weapon. Oṃ hṛdayāya hraṃ phaṭ, homage.
Oṃ śrīṃ śirase hrūṃ phaṭ.
Namaḥ! Oṃ maṃ, phaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhā), namaḥ!
Oṃ, phaṭ to the weapon (astra), hūṃ phaṭ, namaḥ!
Thus reads the manuscript marked with the letter *ga*: *oṃ haḥ astrāsanāya krūṃ phaṭ / oṃ oṃ astramūrtaye namaḥ / oṃ svāṃ*.

Oṃ paṃ, to the crest-lock, krūṃ phaṭ, homage! Oṃ khaṃ, to the armor, krūṃ phaṭ, homage!
Oṃ haṃ phaṭ, to the weapon!
*phaṭ namaḥ*. Thus [ends the section]; this is the reading found in the marked manuscript (p.
One should touch the *kumbha* with the thumb and the *vardhanī* with the fist while reciting the *hṛdaya* and *astra* mantras;

for the sake of enjoyment (*bhukti*) or liberation (*mukti*), one should first touch the *vardhanī* with the fist and then offer the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) to protect the mouth of the *kumbha*.
One should place a hundred recitations of the root mantra upon the ritual pitcher (*kumbha*);
then, with a tenth part of that, one should perform the protection for the *vardhanī* vessel and announce the safeguarding:

"O Lord of the World, O Sustainer of all sacrifices, you must protect [this]!
(81.39cd) One should worship the four-armed [deity] situated in the *praṇava* in the northwest, along with the host [of attendants].

Seated for the purpose of satisfying the mantra, having placed the *arghya*, fragrance, ghee, and so forth on his left, and the fuel sticks (*samidh*), *darbha* grass, sesame seeds, and so forth on his right;
having consecrated the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the fire, the ladle (*sruc*), the clarified butter (*ājya*), and so forth as before, he should meditate upon them.
One should worship Śiva in the fire within the heart of the upward-facing [liṅga] as the primary [object]; likewise,

having performed the placement (nyāsa) according to the rite of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa) upon one's own body, the Śiva-pitcher, the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), the fire, and the disciple, the paths (adhvan) to be purified should be established according to the rules.
Having visualized the mouth as the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should recite the seeds of the seven-tongued fire for the desired oblations with heart-mantras.
The last two letters [of the alphabet], devoid of the vowel *ṛ*, are joined with the letter *ṛ* and the sixth vowel (*ū*).
Joined with the moon (indu), the drop (bindu), and the crest (śikhā), following the sequence of the seed-syllables of the tongues:
Hiraṇyā, Vanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, and thereafter Suprabhā;
Atiriktā and Bahurūpā, facing the directions of Rudra, Indra, Agni, and Āpya respectively.
One should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with sweet substances such as milk for rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*);
but for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), one should use oil-cakes, barley-meal, husks,
sour gruel, salts, goat’s buttermilk, pungent oils, and thorny plants.
1. "One should worship Kāla in the northwest"—this is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter *ga*:
Even with crooked fuel-sticks, one who is angry may sacrifice with the *bhāṣyā* mantra;
through the oblation of *kadamba* buds and so forth, the Yakṣiṇī is certainly accomplished.
For the sake of subjugation and attraction, one should offer oblations of *bandhūka*, *kiṃśuka*, and other such flowers.

The *bilva* is for sovereignty, the *pāṭala* and *campaka* flowers for the sake of prosperity (*lakṣmī*), and lotuses for the status of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*); edible foods and delicacies are for the attainment of wealth. *Dūrvā* grass is for the destruction of disease and for the subjugation of all living beings.
The flowers of *priyaṅgu* and *pāṭalī*, and the leaf of the mango tree, are the ender of fever;
*mṛtyuñjaya* is the conqueror of death. Prosperity comes from the oblation of sesame seeds, and the *rudra-śānti* is for the sake of all peace. Now, that which is at hand shall be explained.
One should satisfy the root mantra with one hundred and eight oblations and the limbs with a tenth part; then, as before, one should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra.
Likewise, for the initiation of disciples, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times for each disciple.
To ward off ill omens and likewise for the sake of auspicious signs,
two hundred oblations should be offered with the root mantra as before; furthermore,
there should be a single libation with the root and the other seven mantras, ending each with "svāhā."
The kindling [of the fire] is performed with the seed-syllables encased by the *śikhā* (the crest-mantra) ending in *hrūṃ phaṭ*;
the satiation (*tarpaṇa*) is performed with mantras such as *oṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā*, and so forth,
as well as *oṃ hrūṃ hrauṃ hrīṃ śivāya hrūṃ*.
Then, having performed the illumination with *phaṭ* and other mantras,

one should tie a bracelet around the neck of the vessel— which has been washed with auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*), enveloped in the armor-mantra (*varma*), and anointed with sandalwood paste and other substances. (AP 81.058ab)
For the preparation of the *caru* offering, one should use two blades of sacred *darbha* grass over which the armor-mantra (*varma*) and weapon-mantra (*astra*) have been recited;
[this is done] with mantras ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, according to the reading marked with the letter *kha*.
2. Oṃ hūṃ hauṃ hūṃ śivāya hūm iti kha; the reading in the marked manuscript is:
oṃ kraṃ hauṃ kraṃ śivāya krūṃ iti ṅa.
The reading of the marked manuscript is "dharmaguṇṭhitām" (as found in manuscript kha).
When a seat has been offered with the armor-mantra (*varman*) and others, upon a mandala fashioned with a half-moon; AP_81.059ab.
When the image has been installed and has become manifest, one should worship Śiva with flowers of meditative intent (*bhāva*).
Alternatively, when a vessel with its mouth covered by cloth has been placed upon a hearth facing west, one should worship with externally grown flowers, conceiving it as having a human nature.

When the vessel has been purified by means of inspection and other rites, when the seed-syllable of egoity has been deposited within it, and when its body of merit and demerit has been recited over, one should place the vessel— cleansed with cow-products and water and consecrated with the Astra-mantra— upon the human self.
Cow’s milk, purified by mantras and consecrated with a hundred recitations of the *Prāsāda* mantra,
should be poured therein along with grains such as *tuṇḍala* and *śyāmāka*;
specifically, five handfuls of these should be used for the rite of a single disciple.

Thereafter, one should gradually increase the portion by one *prasṛti* for each subsequent [deity] starting from two; one should perform the covering with the *analamantra* and the protection with the *kavaca-mantra*.
Facing east, one should cook the *caru* in the fire of Śiva using the *mūlamantra*.
When it has been well-heated there in that cauldron, having filled the ladle with clarified butter,

and having offered the heated oblation while reciting the *saṃhitā* mantras ending with "svāhā," he should place the pot within the mandala upon sacred grass (*darbha*) prepared with the *astra* mantra.
Having covered that ointment on her body with the syllable *praṇava* and [the mantra] addressed to the Heart,
she becomes truly cool upon receiving this cooling sprinkling; thus,
he should apply it to the disciple once each with the *saṃhitā* mantras.
Having offered oblations upon the seats of Dharma and the others (3),
and having offered the *sampāta* into the fire-pit to the west of the mandala with the *sruva* ladle, one should perform purification with the *saṃhitā* mantra. AP_81.069ab/
Having once touched the *caruka* with that same [mantra] ending in *vaṣaṭ*, [one should offer it] on the seat with [the mantras] beginning with *dharma*.
(Note 1: The reading in the marked manuscript is *dharmādyair āsane*.)
2. "In the mandala made with water and earth" is the reading found in manuscript *kha*.

One should lead [the offering], which has become nectar through the *dhenumudrā*, to the presence of the Lord of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍileśa*). (1)

One should offer the portion for one's own disciples and the portion for the god Vahni; then, with the mantra ending in "namaḥ" and using the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should present this triad— clarified butter mixed with honey— for the *stokapāla* and others, and likewise offer the water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamanīyaka*).
Having offered a hundred oblations with clarified butter while reciting the mantra, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) according to the prescribed rite.
To the east or in the middle of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), or between the two jars of Śambhu,
one should perform the internal offering (antarbali) for Rudra, the group of Mothers, and the others, using the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra).
Even while within Śiva, one who has not yet attained full realization should cultivate the meditation on oneness, thinking:
"I am endowed with omniscience and other qualities, standing everywhere and above;
I am the portion of [Śiva], the locus of conjunction, presiding over the sacrifice."

Identifying himself with the thought "I am Śiva," he should emerge from the sacrificial pavilion onto a mandala fashioned according to the weapon-mantra, upon which the tips of the darbha grass have been previously laid down. There, on a seat of the *praṇava*, he should place the disciple, who is wearing a white upper garment.
Having bathed, one should face north for liberation, but face east for worldly enjoyment.
Having raised the body upward, one should gaze at it facing east;
from the feet up to the crest-lock for liberation, and in reverse order for worldly enjoyment.
Having sprinkled [the disciple] with the water from the vessel using the eye that reveals the abode of Śiva, for the sake of accomplishing the ritual bath with mantra-water,
for the ash-bath, for the pacification of obstacles, and for the destruction of evil; AP_81.078cd–81.079ab.
One should strike [the disciple] with the ashes of the weapon-mantra through the yoga of creation and withdrawal; then,
having sprinkled him again with the water of the weapon-mantra, one should lead him to the edge of the sacrificial mound for the sake of the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the rite of making him complete).

Kha, and Ga.
The reading of the three marked manuscripts is "pāśabhittaye" (for the destruction of the bonds),
according to the reading of the marked manuscript.

Above the navel, while reciting the Astra mantra, one should wipe three times with the tips of Kuśa grass; below the navel, for the expiation of sins (aghamarṣaṇa), one should touch [the body] three times with the roots of the grass.
And for the twofold purpose of the bonds, one should offer [the victim] with the *śara* mantra;

then, one should install Śiva, together with his limbs and his teaching, into that body. Then, having worshipped him with flowers and other offerings, one should [bind] his eyes with the *netra* mantra or the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Having tied [the thread] with a consecrated white cloth that has a border,
and having caused him to enter by way of circumambulation from left to right, one should give a seat together with the cloth to the auspicious southern side, according to his caste.

having restrained [the breath] and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the purified body, one should worship that [deity].
The Śiva-hand (śivahasta), which bestows the station of Rudreśa, should be placed upon the head of the disciple facing east by means of the root mantra; this hand, granted by the Śiva-mantra,
is the means for undertaking service to Śiva.
Having removed the worshipper from the forest of obstacles, he should cast the flower upon Śiva.
Rich with mantras, situated in that vessel, and followed by the hosts of the gods of Śiva,
the Guru should then assign names to the Brahmins and others either in sequence or according to his own will.
Having caused him to perform prostrations before the water-pots and the fire,
he should likewise seat him on a seat provided with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), facing the north.
One should contemplate [the disciple] as if emerging from the body through the *suṣumṇā* channel;
and [one should offer] gold consecrated with the mantra using the root of *darbha* grass, which has been dissolved into one's own *graha*.

O Śikhidhvaja, having reached the heart of the disciple by means of the *recaka* breath with the *śiva-āṇu* mantra, [the root of that mantra] is at the disciple's own shanks and the tip [of the nose]; then,
returning by means of the *pūraka* breath, it enters the interior of one's own heart.
Having again performed such a junction of the channels with the fire of Śiva, one should offer three oblations into the heart for the sake of its proximity;
one should perform a hundred oblations with the root mantra.
"In this way, one shall become fit for the worship of Bhava through the initiation of the *samaya*.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Initiation of the *Samaya*," in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*, the Great Purāṇa.
Chapter Eighty-Two:
An Exposition on the Consecration of Refinement (*saṃskāradīkṣā*)
Īśvara said:
O Ṣaṇmukha, listen; I shall declare the procedure for the initiation of purification (saṃskāradīkṣā).
One should invoke the head of Maheśa, who resides within the fire, into the heart.
Having worshipped those two who are joined together and having gratified them with the heart-mantra, one should offer five oblations into their presence with that very mantra.
One should strike the child with the heart-mantra.
One should contemplate consciousness there in the form of a throbbing star;
[the reading in the two manuscripts marked Kha and Ga is "śivātmanā"].
2. "And for the sake of stability in the hand of Śiva"—this is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter *ga*.
3. "With a flower over which the mantra has been recited eight times"—this is the reading found in the manuscript marked with the letter *ṅa*.
The reading marked in the manuscript:
Having entered there, one should utter the syllable *huṃ* through the practice of exhalation (*recaka*). (AP 82.004ab)
Having drawn that [energy] upward with the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā], one should place it in the heart by means of the *pūraka* [breath-retention].
Then, with the *udbhava*-named mudrā belonging to Vāgīśvarī,
one should cast it out by means of the *recaka* [exhalation].
Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Self (ātmane namaḥ).
One should offer oblations into a blazing fire that is free of smoke for the sake of accomplishing one's desired goal;
however, if the fire is not fully kindled and emits smoke, the homa will not succeed.
A fire that is oily, turning clockwise, fragrant,
and accompanied by sparks that do not touch the ground is praised;
having offered oblations with such signs and others, one burns away the disciple's impurity.

Or he may burn him with his own being for the sake of producing the state of the twice-born; likewise, when established for the purpose of conception, he should contemplate himself as a portion of Rudra.

One should perform oblations with the root mantra five hundred times for the sake of the parting of the hair (*sīmanta*) and the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), according to the ten-part proportion beginning with *vauṣaṭ*. Furthermore,
there is the extraction [of the mantra] from its power when its bonds have become loosened.
The conception (*garbhādhāna*) is said to be the state of being Rudra’s son for the Self;
the manifestation of the three qualities of one's own mind is considered here to be the *puṃsavana* rite;
and the knowledge arising from the discrimination between Māyā and the Self is the *sīmantonnayana*.

The acceptance of the purification of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Śiva is considered to be "birth" (janana), performed by means of the mantra consisting of the self enclosed within the heart [mantra]. We do not consider awakening to be the realization of one who is already Śiva as being Śiva;
rather, having grasped oneself with the *saṃhāramudrā* as resembling a shimmering spark of fire,
one should place it within the lotus of one's own heart.
Then, by means of the *kumbha* (retention) yoga, one should utter the root mantra; at that time,

one should bring about the state of complete absorption within the hearts of Śiva and Śivā through the process of exhaling (*recaka*) while sequentially abandoning the causal deities beginning with Brahmā.
Having led the self to the end of Śiva and taken it up with the *udbhava-mudrā*,
the knower of the ritual procedure should, by means of the mantra encapsulated within the heart and through exhalation (*recaka*),
cast it into the pericarp of the disciple’s heart-lotus.

Then the Guru should perform the appropriate worship of Śiva, of the fire, and of himself; he should likewise cause the disciple to prostrate and to hear the rules of conduct (samayas). He must not revile the deity nor the scriptures, and he must not step over the remains of offerings (nirmālya) and so forth.
One should perform worship of Śiva, the fire, and the guru for as long as one lives.
To children, the ignorant, the elderly, women, those addicted to sensual pleasures, and those afflicted by disease,
one should give wealth according to one's ability.
For one who is capable, having consecrated the complete constituent elements of the elements— matted hair, ashes, staff, loincloth, and self-restraint—
with the mantras of Īśāna and the others, or with the *hṛdaya* and other [mantras], in their proper order; AP_82.021cd.

Having placed [the substances] into the vessels as before with mantras ending in "svāhā," and having offered the melted portion thus prepared, one should show it to the Lord of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍileśa). Then,
for the sake of protection, one should place it beneath the water-jar for a mere moment.
Having received the command from Śiva, the Guru should bestow it upon the ascetic;
thus especially in the case of the distinguished initiation into the *samaya*.

The disciple becomes fit for the knowledge of the fire-sacrifice and the scriptures. (AP 82.024cd)
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Initiation into the Observances," in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*, the foremost of the Great Purāṇas.
Chapter Eighty-Three: An Account of the Initiation into Nirvāṇa (Nirvāṇadīkṣākathana)

The Lord said: Now, in the initiation of liberation (nirvāṇadīkṣā), one should perform the kindling of the root [mantra] and so forth for the purpose of severing the power that binds the fetters, or by means of the striking and other rites.
Then, with each individual oblation, or with each of those three [syllables] respectively,
one should offer the seed-syllable *garbha* and the half-śikhā-mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*, preceded by the *dhruva*-mantra:
*oṃ hrūṃ hrauṃ hauṃ hrūṃ phaṭ*.
The illumination of the root mantra is *oṃ hrūṃ hauṃ hauṃ hrūṃ phaṭ* (three times);
likewise for the heart, the head, and the face.
One should perform the individual illumination for every cruel rite; likewise,
in rites of pacification and nourishment, one should use this mantra ending with *vaṣaṭ* and so forth, accompanied by *vaṣaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ*, which stand above all desired objects.
One should perform the oblation with the vows in all rites of nourishment and the like.
Then, [one should visualize] the pure form within the mandala situated on one's own left side.
1. "With *hrīṃ phaṭ* at the end and *dhruva* at the beginning"—this is the reading marked as *kha*. 2. *Oṃ hūṃ hauṃ hauṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—this is [the reading] marked as *kha*.
The reading of the marked manuscript is:
*oṃ hūṃ hoṃ hūṃ phaṭ* (as in Ga); this is the reading of the marked manuscript.
3. Oṃ hūṃ hāṃ hāṃ hūṃ phaṭ iti kha; the reading marked with a dot is:

The reading of the marked manuscript (cihnitapustaka) 4 is "vaṣaḍantādinātmanā," as found in manuscripts marked kha and ga.
Having worshipped the disciple and visualized that thread as the *suṣumṇā*,
one should bring it from the root-mantra to the binding of his topknot, down to the big toe.
By means of the withdrawal [mantra], one should bind it upon the body of the disciple who desires liberation;
for a man, one should apply it on the right side, and for a woman, on the left.
And one should worship the Śakti with the Śakti-mantra upon his head.
Having taken up the thread with the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should join it with that very [mantra].

Having taken up the channel (*nāḍī*) with the root mantra and placed it upon the thread, one should worship it with the heart mantra. Then, having veiled it with the Rudra-mantra, one should offer three oblations with the heart mantra.
One should likewise offer [these] even when one has the capacity, for the sake of bringing about presence:
*Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the path of phonemes; hāṃ, obeisance to the path of worlds; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the path of time.* (1)
Having projected the path to be purified onto the thread, and having sprinkled the disciple with water consecrated by the *astra* mantra,
one should strike him on the heart with a flower empowered by the *astra* mantra, and then enter the body of the disciple.

And there, by means of the yoga of exhalation (recaka), the Guru should separate the consciousness— situated within the seed-syllable *haṃsa* and joined with the syllable *hūṃ*— from its form as a weapon,
[uttering]: *oṃ hauṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.

Having severed [the connection] with the thread of power (śaktisūtra) using the mantra "Hāṃ Haṃ Svāhā," one should join it to the thread that has become a channel (nāḍī) by means of the withdrawal mudrā (saṃhāramudrā), reciting:
"Oṃ Hāṃ Haṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the Self (ātman)."
One should meditate upon this as all-pervasive and envelop it with the armor-protection:
(3) Oṃ dvām, homage to the path of the feet.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the path of creative energies (kalādhvan). Thus.

One should offer three oblations with the heart-mantra for the purpose of invoking the presence [of the deity].

Having projected the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) and performed the visualization of the Śāntyatītā [kalā], one should contemplate within that [kalā] the other principles (*tattva*) and so forth, which have become mantra:
*oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the bond of the Śāntyatīta kalā*.
By this one should observe:
O Tattva, there is also a single mantra-word and sixteen syllables;
likewise, within this [tattva] are eight worlds, two seed-syllables, and two channels.
Having internalized the object, the quality, the single cause, and Sadāśiva within the white [thread] of the Śāntyatītā [kalā], one should press it:
*oṃ hauṃ śāntyatītakalāpāśāya hūṃ phaṭ*.
Having taken [the thread] with the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should place it upon the tip of the thread.
One should worship it and offer three oblations (*āhuti*) for the sake of bringing about its presence (*sannidhi*).
There are two principles (*tattva*), two syllables, and the pair of seed-syllables and channels (*vīja-nāḍī*).
One should meditate upon the two qualities, the two mantras, the single Lord (Īśvara) seated upon a lotus,
the seven and ten worlds which are the solar stations (*padāni*), and the one object of tranquility— Acyuta— within the dark [syllable].
Having struck it and taken hold of it, one should attach it to the mouth-thread;
one should offer three oblations with one's own seed-syllable for the sake of its presence.
In the Vidyā, there are seven principles and twenty-one feet.
Having internalized the six phonemes, the single transmigrating one, the twenty-five qualities of the worlds, the triad as the one object, and the cause of Rudra,
[he perceives] the two stories concerning the life-channel within the transcendent [reality].
Having taken up the weapon, one should place it upon twenty-two squares,
sixty worlds, and sixty digits, along with the four qualities.
1 Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hoṃ, [for the sake of] the noose of the kalā beyond peace (śāntyatītakalāpāśa), thus [says] Ga; this is the reading of the marked manuscript, p.
Having included Hari— the object, cause, and the triad and single [mantra]— within the mantras,

and having performed the striking with the white [thread] and other rites during the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), one should worship the oblations while [the deity] is present, stationed at the line of the navel.
Hrīṃ: [it purifies] more than a hundred worlds, the vital winds of the seed-channels, and also those of the two sense organs. AP_83.028ab.

Having internalized within the yellow-colored Nivṛtti [kalā] the reality of color, each respective object, the five qualities (guṇas), the cause, and the four Śambaras residing in the Brahmāṇḍa-mantra, one should strike [it].
First, having placed that which is at the end of the portion of reality upon the thread, one should worship it; then,
having established it in the fire, one should offer three oblations.
Having thus taken [the thread], one should join it to the body of the disciple according to the *kalāsūtra*.
In the initiation accompanied by seed-syllables (*sabīja*), this is done in accordance with the conduct of the observance (*samaya*) and the sacrifice;
it is for the sake of protecting the commencement of the body, as well as for the fruit of mantra-perfection.
For the sake of dharma such as *iṣṭāpūrta*, one should meditate upon a separate, continuous,
subtle entity that manifests consciousness within the midst of the *kalās*.
Then, by this very sequence, one should perform the acts of satiation (*tarpaṇa*) and illumination (*dīpana*).
Likewise, with three oblations each by means of one's own mantra—
beginning with "Oṃ hauṃ, svāhā to the noose of the kalā beyond peace (śāntyatīta)" and so forth— one performs the libation with "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ."
For the purpose of binding the *kalās* beyond the state of peace (*śāntyatīta*),
one should perform the illumination with "HŪM PHAṬ" and so forth; that thread is for the realization of pervasion across the five locations of the *kalās*.
1. *Hrīṃ tribhuvanādhipānām iti*—this is the reading marked as "kha";

Having taken [the materials] with saffron and clarified butter,
one should worship Śiva there along with his limbs, piercing the fetters in due order with the *kalā*-mantras ending in *hūm* and *phaṭ*.
Having entered within with [the mantras] ending in *namaḥ*, one should perform the seizing and binding of the *kalās* with such mantras as:
*oṃ hūṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ hūṃ phaṭ śāntyatītakalāṃ gṛhṇāmi badhnāmi*. Thus for the *kalās*.

The employment of nooses and the like for seizing and binding constitutes "seizing" (*grahaṇa*); furthermore, "binding" (*bandhana*) refers to the undertaking of every possible means of action directed toward a person. (AP 83.037ab)
Then, having seated him, one should place that thread upon the disciple's shoulder.

To destroy extensive sins, one should perform a hundred oblations with the root mantra. For a man, [the offering] should be in a pair of shallow bowls (*śarāva*), and for a woman, within the belly of a *praṇītā* vessel.

Having prepared the thread by enclosing it within the *hṛdaya* and *astra* mantras, one should worship it with the *hṛdaya* mantra; then, having purified it by the *sampāta* rite, one should place it beneath the *kalaśa* and announce the protection. AP 83.040ab.
Having placed a flower in the hand of the disciple and having worshipped the jar and other implements, he should lead him out from the center of the sacrificial hall; then,
having drawn three mandalas for those seeking liberation who face the Unsurpassed (Anuttara), [he should proceed].
For the sake of their consumption, he should have the disciples sit there facing east; first,
he should have them eat three small portions of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with his hand joined with kuśa grass, offering it at each interval.
On the third day, however, it should be measured by three morsels,
or eight morsels in size, avoiding contact with the teeth;
[it should be eaten] from a cup of *pālāśa* leaves for liberation, and from a leaf of the *pippala* tree for worldly enjoyment.

Having offered the *sambhojana* with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should cause [the recipient] to sip pure water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*).

Having prepared the tooth-stick with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should cast it into auspicious water for the removal of defects such as deficiencies; then, having performed one hundred and eight recitations with the root-mantra,
the dedication of all rites is made to the Lord of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍileśa*).
One should perform the dismissal of this [deity] and the worship of Caṇḍeśa;
then, having removed the *nirmālya*, one should offer the remainder into the fire of the *caru*.
Having worshipped the jar and the world-protectors (*lokapāla*s) and then dismissed them, [one should proceed].
He should dismiss the assembly and the fire, provided it has been protected outside;
having briefly offered the bali-oblation to the world-protectors (lokapālas) outside,
he should bathe with ashes or pure water and enter the village.
He should place the householders on a bed of *darbha* grass with their heads toward the east, well-protected;
and the ascetics (*yatis*) on a bed of pure ashes with their heads toward the south,
their topknots tied and accompanied by the seven *māṇavaka* mantras of the weapon.
Having understood [this], he should bathe his disciples; then he should go outside again.
[Reciting] "Oṃ hili hili, svāhā to the trident-bearer," and having consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the sacrificial porridge (caru), he should take up the tooth-stick.

Having sipped water for purification and meditated upon Śiva, the Guru should take his place upon the purifying bed and, recollecting the ritual section pertaining to initiation, lie down; thus has the procedure for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of initiation been briefly described.
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Consecration (Adhivāsana)" within the Nirvāṇadīkṣā section of the Āgneya Purāṇa, the foremost among the Mahāpurāṇas. [Variant reading:
"One should go to the sacrificial hall."]

Chapter Eighty-Four: The Eighty-Fourth Discourse.
Regarding the ritual procedure for initiation into Nirvana,
the Lord said: "Then, having risen in the morning, the Guru, having performed his ablutions and other preliminary rites,"
The consumption of curd, fresh meat, wine, and the like is auspicious;
riding elephants and horses in a dream is auspicious; [wearing] white garments and the like is auspicious;
anointing with oil and the like is inferior; and an oblation with a *ghora* mantra serves for pacification.

Having performed the two daily rites and entered the sacrificial pavilion, one who has sipped water for purification should perform the ritual according to the rules for occasional ceremonies as if it were a daily rite;
then, having purified oneself, one should likewise apply the "Hand of Śiva" upon oneself.
Having placed [the deities] within the pitcher and worshipped Indra and the others in their proper sequence,

one should perform the worship of Śiva either upon a mandala or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). This includes the libation and worship of the fire, ending with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and the libation of mantras.

To destroy the affliction of suffering, one should perform the kindling of the mantra by offering one hundred and eight oblations with a weapon while reciting *hūṃ* in the *sampuṭa* (enclosing) manner; furthermore,
the internal offering ritual should be performed between the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and the water-pot (*kumbha*).
Having obtained permission for the entrance of the disciple, he should go outside;
there, in accordance with the ritual rules, he should perform the rites such as the placement [of the disciple] within the mandala,
along with the *sampāta* oblation, accompanied by darbha grass held in the hand in the form of its channels.
Having offered three oblations with the root mantra for the sake of his presence,
and having worshipped Śiva residing within the pitcher, one should bring forward the cord of bonds (pāśasūtra).

Having established that [state] and perceived with his mind the pervasiveness of cessation (nivṛtti), he then beheld one hundred and eight worlds within it:
Kapāla, Aja, Buddha, Vajradeha, and Pramardana.
Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śāstṛ, Pinākin, and Tridaśādhipa;
Agni, Rudra, Hutāśa, Piṅgala, Khādaka, and Hara; Jvalana, Dahana, Babhru, Bhasmāntaka, and Kṣapāntaka.
He is the remover of Yama and death, the sustainer, the ordainer, and the one who delights in all actions;
he is Time, both Dharma and Adharma, the uniter, and the disuniter;
he is Nairṛta, the slayer.
The slayer, of cruel gaze and terrifying appearance,
with upraised shoulders, deformed eyes, and smoke-colored red fangs;
Bala and Atibala, the mighty one with a noose in hand.
Śveta, Jayabhadra, Dīrghabāhu, Jalāntaka,
Vaḍavāsya, and Bhīma— these ten are remembered as the sons of Varuṇa.
Śīghra, Laghu, Vāyuvega, Sūkṣma, Tīkṣṇa, and Kṣapāntaka [are the sons of Vāyu].
The ender of the five, Pañcaśikha, Kapardin, he whose vehicle is the clouds,
the wearer of the matted-lock crown, and likewise the bearer of various jewels;
the lord of treasures, handsome, blessed, possessing a gentle body, and the bestower of grace.
Then there are Prakāśa, Lakṣmīvat, and Kāmarūpa; in the tenth [section] are Vidyādhara, Jñānadhara, Sarvajña, Vedapāraga,
Mātṛvṛtta, Piṅgākṣa, Bhūtapāla, and Balipriya.

In the two channels named Iḍā and Piṅgalā reside both the vital winds, Prāṇa and Apāna; likewise, the sense organs are the nose and the genitals,
and their object is said to be smell among the fivefold qualities beginning with smell.
The earthly mandala is yellow, marked with vajras, and square;
its extent is one hundred times ten million yojanas.
Within this very [mandala], the fourteen wombs (yonis) are to be known as contained.

The first [birth] belongs to all the gods; the second consists of the divine origins such as the Manus; the third includes wild animals, birds, and domestic cattle; the fourth comprises the four types of reptiles;
the fifth is all that is stationary; and the sixth birth is the non-human.
The Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, Aindra, Saumya, Prāṇeśvara,
and the Brāhma are proclaimed as the eighth.
The earth-element (pārthiva-tattva) is considered the locus of authority for the eight [tattvas];
its dissolution occurs in primordial nature (prakṛti), while experience (bhoga) and Brahmā reside in the intellect (buddhi).
From that [earth-element] arise all the worlds and so forth belonging to the waking state.
Having meditated upon the *nivṛtti* [kalā] as being pregnant with the embryo and having joined it with its own mantra—
namely, *oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ nivṛttikalāpāśāya hūṃ phaṭ*— then...

By means of the *saṃhāramudrā* and *kumbhaka*, [the breath is drawn] downward: the seed-syllable *oṃ* and the crocodile (*makara*)— this is the reading marked with the letters *ga* and *ṅa* in the manuscript.

Having established [the deity] within the *kumbha* by means of this *udbhavamudrā* and the *recaka* breath, one should offer the *arghya* with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the noose of the *nivṛtti-kalā*" and worship [the deity]. Then, with the face turned away,
one should offer three oblations for the purpose of making [the deity] present (*sannidhāna*) and three oblations for the purpose of gratification (*santarpaṇa*), ending each with "svāhā."
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā"— having thus invoked and worshipped Brahmā,
and having gratified him with the mantra ending in svāhā, [one says]: "O Brahmā, within your jurisdiction, I shall initiate this seeker of liberation."
"You must remain favorable; thus one should inform the ritual procedure.
Then, one should invoke with the heart-mantra the Goddess Vāgīśvarī, who is the sixfold form of will, knowledge, and action, and who is the single cause.
Then, one should worship and satisfy the Goddess Vāgīśvarī by this method:

with the weapon-mantra (śarāṇu) ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*, preceded by the seed-syllable (*vīja*) whose meaning is the heart-enclosure (*hṛtsampuṭa*), which is the cause for agitating all wombs (*yoni*) without exception.
The knower of the ritual procedure should strike him on the heart, and he shall enter [the disciple];
then the consciousness of the disciple, resembling a spark of fire, [resides] in the heart.
One should divide that which stands in cessation and is joined with the fetters by means of the Jyeṣṭhā [mudrā],
using this [mantra]: *oṃ hāṃ hūṃ haḥ hūṃ phaṭ oṃ hāṃ svāhā*, and then, by means of inhalation (*pūraka*) and the hook-gesture (*aṅkuśamudrā*).
Having drawn that out and grasped it with one's own mantra, one should unite it with oneself:
*oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ hāṃ ātmane namaḥ*.
Having visualized the union of the two parents, one should lead that consciousness out by means of the *recaka* breath,
leading it through the sequence of abandoning the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, up to the abode of Śiva;
[there, one should utter] "Oṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hāṃ" in the void (*kha*).

Having taken [the seed] for the purpose of conception, one should simultaneously cast it into all wombs,
or into the womb of Vāgīśvarī by means of the left-hand Udbhava-mudrā,
reciting: *oṃ hāṃ hāṃ hāṃ ātmane namaḥ*.
One should worship with this very [mantra] and also satisfy [the deity] in five ways.
For all other wombs, one should perform the purification of the body with the *hṛdaya* [mantra].
There is no *puṃsavana* (rite for ensuring a male child) here, because the bodies of females and others are also possible.
Or else, one should perform the *sīmantonnayana* rite for the divine limbs as if they were a body;
then, feeling aversion toward all embodied beings, one should effect their birth with the head [of the deity].

Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ haṃ phaṭ! Having entered by means of this very [mantra], one should then separate the consciousness with the weapon-mantra, while it is bound by its fetters, using the *jyeṣṭhā* hook-mudrā.

Having drawn that [deity] forth with the mantra ending in *svāhā*— namely, *oṃ hāṃ hūṃ haṃ phaṭ svāhā*— and having grasped it by enclosing oneself with that very same mantra, one should unite it with one's own self using the mantra ending in *namaḥ*.
Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hīṃ, salutation to the Self (ātmane namaḥ).
Oṃ hāṃ huṃ haḥ phaṭ— this is the reading marked as "kha" in the manuscript.
2. Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hrīṃ ātmane namaḥ; thus [it is stated] in the manuscript marked "kha," p.
As before, having meditated upon the union with the Father by means of the goddess named Udbhavā on the left, one should then place [the seed] into the womb by this very same method.

One should perform all the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* according to the previously stated procedure. When the bonds have been loosened by means of the root mantra, one should recite it a hundred times as an expiation for the concealment by the power of impurity (*mala-śakti*) and for the severing of the bonds.

One should offer five oblations for each of the five [limbs] with the weapon-mantra as before. With the noose-mantra, consecrated by the *pravāra* rite, one should sever [the bonds] with the sword-mantra using scissors joined with the *kalā* and *vīja* mantras, as prescribed.
Oṃ hāṃ, for the bond of the *kalā* beyond peace, haḥ hūṃ phaṭ!
Having released and coiled the bonds as before with the weapon-mantra (*astra*),
and having placed them in a ladle filled with ghee, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with that very same *kalā*-mantra.
One should offer oblations with the Astra-mantra five times for the removal of the nooses and the goad;
then, to prevent the need for expiation, one should offer eight oblations.
Having invoked Sadāśiva into the heart and performed worship and libation, [one should proceed].
One should perform the transfer of authority according to the previously stated procedure:
"Oṃ hāṃ, O Sadāśiva, accept the bride-price of the mind-drop, svāhā!
O Sadāśiva, for this bound soul whose fetters have been entirely burnt away..."
"You must not remain for the sake of bondage; rather, you should cause the command of Śiva to be heard.
Having offered the full oblation with the root mantra, one should dismiss Sadāśiva.
Then, one perceives the self as purified, like the risen autumn moon.

Having joined [the disciple] with the fierce *saṃhāramudrā* within himself, the Guru should extract [the disciple's essence] residing in the disciple's body by means of the *udbhavamudrā*. He should then place a drop of *arghya* water upon the disciple's head for the sake of nourishment.
Having asked for forgiveness with great devotion, he should likewise dismiss his parents;
[the reading in the manuscript marked *ga* is: "with the left hand and with the heart itself"].
"O parents, since you were distressed by me for the sake of initiating my disciples,
I have liberated you through compassion; therefore, go now to your own abode."
With a pair of scissors consecrated by the *śikhā-mantra*, which is the very nature of the power of consciousness (*bodhaśakti*),
he should cut the disciple’s tuft of hair (*śikhā*) to the length of four finger-breadths with the *śivāstra-mantra*:
*oṃ klīṃ śikhāyai hūṃ phaṭ*.
Oṃ haḥ astrāya hūṃ phaṭ!
Having placed that cow-dung ball into the ladle filled with clarified butter,
one should offer it into the fire while reciting the Astra-mantra ending in hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ hauṃ haḥ, for the weapon, hūṃ phaṭ!
Having washed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and having bathed the disciple and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) himself,
he should strike the site of the union and himself with the weapon-mantra.
Having separated [the deity], drawn [it forth], and worshipped it as before, one should cause it to enter the pericarp of the lotus of one's own heart from the *dvādaśānta*.

Having filled the *śruva* ladle with clarified butter using the prescribed downward-facing *śruca* ladle, and having taken it up according to the ritual procedure prescribed for daily rites by means of the mudrā resembling a conch shell,
one should extend the head and neck in accordance with the utterance of the sound (*nāda*).
And having internally attained the auspiciousness of equal vision, endowed with the supreme state,
one should take from the disciple as well as from one's own self the sixfold ritual procedure at the tip of the ear, [extending] through the channel of the vital breath.

Having meditated with full intent upon the drop (*bindu*), one should contemplate it sequentially in seven ways, beginning first with the nature of the union of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and ending with the other [aspects].
*Oṃ hūṃ śikhāyai hūṃ phaṭ*—thus [is the mantra for] the tuft of hair (*śikhā*). (kha, ṅa)
The reading of the marked manuscript is:
*oṃ hrīṃ śikhāyai hraṃ phaṭ* (as in manuscript *ga*). This is the reading of the marked manuscript.
2. "Going into the midst of Govinda’s world" is the reading found in the manuscript marked Kha. 3.
"Having separated, drawn out, and gathered" is the reading found in manuscripts Kha and Ṅa.
The reading in the marked manuscript is "kuṇḍamaṇḍalavahnibhya" (from the sacrificial pit,
the mandala, and the fire), according to manuscript Kha.

Having performed inhalation (*pūraka*) and retention (*kumbhaka*) of that which is designated as mantra, emitted through the sequential utterance beginning with the heart, one should open the mouth slightly.
The third [state] is the nature of sound (nāda) following the *suṣumṇā* channel;

through the abandonment of the seventh cause, there is dissolution (*laya*) as the subsiding of the diverse sounds (*vikhara*). The upward movement of the power (*śakti*) and the sound is considered to be the "diverse power" (*śakti-vikhara*).
That which is devoid of power and objects of knowledge for the entire vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the sixth, called *vikhara*; and that which transcends power is the seventh.
This very place of union is designated as the principle (*tattva*) of *vikhara*.

Having performed inhalation and retention, opening the mouth slightly and slowly uttering the root mantra, one should effect the dissolution of the disciple’s self into the syllable *Ha*, which has the form of lightning and consists of the vital breath of the six paths.
The letter *ukāra* is situated extending one span from the navel;
beyond that, the letter *makāra* is four finger-breadths from the heart;
and the letter *oṃkāra*, the designator of Viṣṇu, is eight finger-breadths from the throat.
The letter *ma*, which denotes Rudra, resides at the palate four finger-breadths deep;
likewise, the *bindu* residing in the middle of the forehead denotes Īśvara;
and the *nāda* is the deity Sadāśiva, extending as far as the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
Constantly releasing the *śakti* situated at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) in due succession,
and experiencing therein the divine sensation like that of an ant crawling,
one reaches the supreme reality at the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*), which is characterized by supreme bliss.

Having dissolved the mind into that Śiva— who is devoid of objective existence, transcendent, auspicious, and the source of eternal qualities— one should contemplate the disciple’s own self within it;
releasing a stream of clarified butter even into the end of a flame, one should merge into the supreme Śiva.
For the sake of stability lasting for a *yojana*, [one should perform the rite] with the *śivāṇu* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. (1) (Note 1:
The reading in the marked manuscript is *vauṣaḍantaśivātmane*.)
Having offered the full oblation according to the ritual procedure, one should perform the recitation of the qualities and the descent [of the deity]:
*Oṃ hāṃ ātmane*.
Omniscient one, be [fulfilled], svāhā!
Oṃ hāṃ, for oneself,
be completely satisfied, svāhā!
Oṃ hrūṃ, for myself,
become primordial awakening, svāhā!
Oṃ hauṃ, for myself!
Be independent, svāhā!
Oṃ hauṃ, O Self,
be one whose power is unimpaired, svāhā!
Oṃ haḥ! Be possessed of infinite power for oneself, svāhā!

Having thus grasped the self endowed with the six qualities from the supreme syllable according to the ritual procedure, one possessed of meditative cultivation should project it into the body of the disciple,
for the sake of pacifying the exhaustion produced by the impact of the intense power of the atoms.
Having offered the *arghya* water, one should place drops of nectar upon the head of the disciple; then,
having bowed down to the pot of Īśāna and the others, one should station the disciple in the southern mandala to the right of Śiva, facing northward.
"Having assumed my own form, you yourself have favored him;
therefore, increase his devotion toward the god Agni and toward that preceptor.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods and having prostrated himself, the preceptor [spoke] personally.
1. *Oṃ hrīṃ ātman*—this is the reading in the manuscript marked *kha*; *oṃ hauṃ ātman*—this is in manuscript *gha*.
The reading in the manuscripts marked with the signs Kha, Ga, and Ca is:
*oṃ hrīṃ ātmane*; the reading in the manuscript marked with the sign Oṃ is: *oṃ hīṃ*.
