The reading of the marked manuscripts is:
*oṃ ātman* (this is the reading of the manuscripts marked Ga and Gha).
4 Oṃ hrāṃ ātman iti kha; the reading in the marked manuscript is:
Oṃ huṃ ātman iti.
The reading in the manuscripts marked *ga*,
*gha*, and *ṅa* is "oṃ hauṃ ātman."
5. *Oṃ haiṃ ātman*—this is the reading in the manuscript marked Kha;
7. *In the southern mandala of Śiva*—this is the reading in the manuscript marked Ga.
The reading in the marked manuscripts (kha,
ṅa) is: "O Lord, increase his devotion."
One should respectfully utter the blessing, "May it be well with you," to the disciple;
thereafter, with supreme devotion, one should offer the eight flowers to the deity.
Having bathed the "little son" (the disciple) with the Śiva-vessel, he should dismiss the sacrifice.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Completion of the Nirvāṇa-initiation," in the *Ādi-mahāpurāṇa* of Agni.
Chapter 89:
The Exposition of the Initiation into the Single Reality (Ekattvadīkṣā)
Īśvara said:
Now, the initiation based on the single principle (ekatattva) is taught because of its brevity;
one should perform the binding of the thread and so forth according to the requirements, by means of one's own self.
One should meditate upon the principles (tattvas) beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Śiva as being within the Supreme Principle (samatattva),
like a multitude of gems strung upon a thread.
Having invoked the Śiva-principle and so forth, one should perform the rites of impregnation (garbhādhāna) and the rest as previously described.
However, one should perform the offering of all the fees with the root mantra.
Then, one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) infused with the essence of the reality-teachings—
that single [offering] by which the disciple attains nirvāṇa.
Having given another full oblation for the sake of union with Śiva and for the attainment of stability,
one should perform the consecration with the Śiva-pitcher.
Thus ends the section titled "The Description of Initiation into the Single Principle" in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*, the Great Ancient Scripture.
The Ninety-Ninth Chapter:
Chapter 90.
Now begins the ninetieth chapter, the narration of the consecration and other rites. The Lord said:
Having worshipped Śiva, one should perform the consecration for the sake of the prosperity of the disciple and others.
One should place nine jars in order in the directions starting from the northeast (Īśāna):
in them, the ocean of salt water, the ocean of milk, the ocean of curd, and the ocean of ghee.
Then one should install the eight Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) in their respective order:
Śikhaṇḍin Rudra as the first, Śrīkaṇṭha as the second,
Trimūrti, Ekarudrākṣa, Ekanetra, and Śivottama.
One should place the seventh, named Sūkṣma, and the eighth, Ananta Rudra,
in the middle; and one should install Śiva Samudra and the Śiva-mantra within the bathing pavilion constructed for the Lord of the Directions at the sacrificial hall.
One should construct an altar two cubits in length and eight finger-breadths in height;
having placed Ananta upon a seat made of *śrīparṇī* wood or similar materials there,
and having seated the disciple facing east and performed the ritual of totalization (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should worship him.
Then, one should perform the ritual sprinkling (nirmañchana) with sour gruel, rice, earth, ashes, dūrvā grass, balls of cow dung, white mustard seeds,
curd, and water;
subsequently, using the sequence of alkaline waters, one should perform it with the *hṛdaya*, *vidyeśa*, and *śambara* mantras.
One should bathe the disciple with water-pots while he is endowed with the concentration on *svadhā*; having clothed him in two white garments and seated him to the right of Śiva,
one should again worship the disciple on the seat previously described, just as before.

The *uṣṇīṣa*, the *yogapaṭṭa*, the crown, the scissors, the water-pot, the rosary, the book, and so forth; [the authority] over Śiva and others; [and] the gift of sweet milk from the eight oceans—thus [it is said]. (AP 90.011ab) :n 1 Variant readings: "sweet milk" (*svādugargodāna*) in manuscripts *ka* and *kha*.
The reading marked in the manuscript (p.
285): "Having understood initiation, exposition, consecration, and so forth, from this day forward, you [must perform them]."
Having saluted and prostrated before Maheśvara, he should cause the disciple to hear the command that must be performed,
and then he should make a formal request for the sake of dispelling the flames of obstacles.
"I have been commanded by you, who are the embodiment of the Guru, for the sake of consecration.
O Śiva, this one, who has mastered the Saṃhitās, has now been consecrated by me.
For the satisfaction of the circle of mantras, one should offer five oblations for each of the five [mantras]."
Then, having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he should cause the disciple to stand on his own right side;
he should mark the fingers of the disciple’s right hand, beginning with the thumb,
one after another as they are bound with the tips of burnt *darbha* grass and *śambara* fibers.

Having placed flowers in his hand, he should cause him to perform prostration. Then, having performed the rite [of offering] into the pitcher, the fire, and Śiva himself, he should enter into that duty. Disciples who have been well-examined according to the scripture are to be favored by you.
Through the consecration of kings, humans, and others, their desired goals are attained by means of the consecration with the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*), reciting:
*āṃ śrāṃ śrauṃ paśuṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of Consecration and Other Rites," in the *Āgneya-mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter [X].
Chapter Ninety-One: The Exposition of Various Mantras and Other Rituals.
Īśvara said:
Having been consecrated, one should worship Śiva, Viṣṇu, and the Sun and other deities;
one should bathe them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) amidst the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments.
"Having seen for himself," according to the reading of the manuscript marked *ga*.
He who [recites this] goes to the world of the gods, uplifting his own lineage; whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of millions of years— AP_91.002cd.
By anointing the gods with clarified butter, one becomes ash in the fire;
by bathing the gods with an *āḍhaka* measure of clarified butter and other substances, one becomes a god.
Then, having anointed them with sandalwood, one should likewise worship them with perfumes and other offerings.
The gods, when praised with hymns, always grant little effort;
they bestow knowledge of the past and future, mastery of mantras, worldly enjoyment, and liberation.
Having taken the subtle syllables of the question and divided them by two, one discerns the auspicious and the inauspicious.

The life-force (*jīva*) consists of three [syllables], and the root-element (*mūladhātu*) consists of four; the intellect of the Brahmins and others begins with *yañ* and the reality of the elements (*bhūtatattva*), and likewise at the end is the recitation (*japa*) and so forth.
At the end of one, three, and more than three [syllables], in the word ending in *dvipama* and *kāntaka*.
Inauspicious [planets] in the middle [of their periods] cause middling results; among the three Indras, the King (Rāhu) is auspicious.
In a group of years, Yama takes away ten years of life for certain.
One should write [the names] upon a lotus with the mantras of Sūrya, Gajāsya (Gaṇeśa), Īśa (Śiva), Durgā, Śrī, and Viṣṇu.
When touched by the recited *Kaṭhinī* along with lines in the shape of cow-urine,
beginning with one and continuing through the triads up to the conclusion of the four tetrads;
likewise, in the sixty-four squares, [the syllables] *marut*, *vyoma*, and the seeds of *marut* [are arranged].
From the falling and touching of the dice, auspicious and other results [are determined] starting from one or three and so on, up to eight at the end; likewise,
those beginning with the Banner (dhvaja) are equal, deficient, or odd, bestowing auspiciousness and the like.

In that worship, the mantras of the name of Tripurā consist of the consonants beginning with *ka*, preceded by the sixteen vowels; these same consonants from *ka* onwards, joined with their respective vowels,
are preceded by the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* and the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), and end with *namaḥ*.
Then there are twenty thousand and one hundred and sixty mantras beginning with the Śobhana.
The reading marked in the manuscript:
Āṃ Hrīṃ are the mantras of Sarasvatī and likewise of Caṇḍikā.
Likewise, the mantras of Gaurī and Durgā are *āṃ* and *śrīṃ*; similarly, the mantras of Śrī are [the same]; the mantras of Sūrya are *akṣauṃ* and *krauṃ*;
and the mantras [of Gaṇeśa] are *āṃ* and *hauṃ*.

The mantras of Śiva are "Āṃ Gaṃ"; the mantras of Gaṇeśa are "Āṃ"; and likewise those of Hari are formed with the consonants beginning with Ka (Kādi) increased by fifty-one, combined with the sixteen vowels.

All the mantras of the Sun, Īśa, Devī, and Viṣṇu, consisting of those [syllables] beginning with *ka* and accompanied by vowels starting with *a*, are beautiful; through their progression according to the sun, oceans, gods, and Indra,
each mandala consists of three hundred and sixty [mantras] respectively.
Having been consecrated, the Guru should recite mantras, meditate, and initiate his disciples and others.
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of Various Mantras and Other Matters," in the Āgneya Purāṇa, the Great Ancient Lore.
Chapter Ninety-Two:
An Exposition on the Ritual for Consecration (Pratiṣṭhāvidhi)
Īśvara said:
O Guha, I shall explain consecration (pratiṣṭhā) in due order and in brief:
the pedestal (pīṭha), the Śakti, Śiva as the Liṅga, their union, and that [union] by means of the Śiva-mantras.
There are five types of consecration (pratiṣṭhā); I shall describe their nature to you.
That in which there is the application of the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā) is specifically called pratiṣṭhā;
whereas installation (sthāpana) is the placement [of the deity] upon the pedestal (pīṭha) as appropriate.
The stabilization and re-establishment of a shrine whose pedestal has become damaged is called *sthitasthāpana*.
That which is preceded by the removal of the *liṅga* is declared to be *utthāpana*,
in which the wise perform the consecration after having placed the *liṅga* back [upon the pedestal].
Likewise, "kṣau hrau" are the mantras of the Sun; this is the reading found in the manuscripts marked with the letters *ga* and *gha*.
Now, the installation (āthāpana) of Viṣṇu and the others has been described as being of two kinds;
in all these [cases], one should enjoin the supreme Śiva as the consciousness (caitanya).
One should also examine the ground in five ways for the purpose of building a palace. Desiring to construct a palace, one should perform the examination of the earth:
[the ground] that is white with the scent of clarified butter, red with a red scent, and fragrant; (3) AP_92.007ab.
The earth for Brahmins and the other castes is, respectively, yellow, black, and fragrant with wine;
it is auspicious in the east, north, and everywhere, yet the eastern direction is distinguished as the best among them.
When a pit one cubit deep is filled with earth, that soil which remains in excess [is auspicious].
The Guru should know the earth to be excellent if it is sprinkled with water and other substances;
however, if it is defiled by bones, charcoal, and the like, he should thoroughly purify it for the sake of cities, villages, fortresses, houses, and palaces. (5–6)
Having repeatedly performed the ritual in the pavilion— beginning with the worship of the door and ending with the satisfaction through mantras— by means of digging, providing cow-pens, or plowing,
one should recite the Aghora-weapon mantra a thousand times.
One should sacrifice according to the prescribed rite.
Having leveled and smeared the ground, one should purify the directions and draw lines with gold, curd, and unbroken grains of rice.
One should worship Śiva in the full water-pot (pūrṇakumbha) located in the northeast cell from the center, while proceeding clockwise.
Having worshipped the *vāstu*, one should sprinkle the spade and other tools with that water.
[The passage] beginning with "the raising" (*utthāpana*) and ending with "and of Viṣṇu and others" is thus concluded.
The reading consisting of one and a half verses does not exist in manuscript *ga*.
2. According to manuscript *ga*, it reads "yathādhārābhibhedena. 3. According to manuscript *kha*, it reads "raktagandhānugandhi."
4. "It is praised" — thus [it is] in manuscript *gha*.
5. "One should certainly purify" — thus [it is] in manuscript *gha*.
6. The half-verse beginning with "city and village" does not exist in manuscript *gha*.
7. "Ending with the radiance of the mantra," according to manuscript Ga;
"ending with the ground of the mantra," according to manuscript Gha.
8. "Having produced the terrible weapon, the great weapon," according to manuscript Ga.
9. One should draw nine lines—thus [read] Kha and Ga;
10. "In a golden vessel" (svarṇakuṇḍe)—thus Ga;
"in a golden jar" (svarṇakumbhe)—thus Gha and Ṅa.
Outside, having worshipped the hosts of *rakṣas* according to the ritual, one should cast the directional offerings; then,
having sprinkled and bathed the ground.
One should worship another pitcher covered with a pair of cloths, having placed it upon the shoulder of a twice-born man, amidst the din of songs, musical instruments, and Vedic recitations.

Having performed the worship at the water-pot, when the auspicious moment has arrived, one should dig in the southeast corner of the fire-pit with a spade that has been consecrated and smeared with honey;
one should cast the earth from the excavation toward the southwest and pour the water from the pot into the pit.
One should lead [the cord] to the eastern boundary of the city as far as desired;
then, having stood there for a moment, one should cause it to revolve.
Sprinkling water all around the city as far as the region of Īśāna, marking the lines of the parting of the hair,
this is declared to be the offering of the *arghya* through the circumambulation of the jar there.
Having thus taken possession of the ground, immediately thereafter,
one should have it excavated down to the level of gravel or water, out of a desire to destroy the defects of hidden obstacles;
if the ground is occupied by a virgin, one should extract the obstacle according to the prescribed rite.
If the interrogator’s question-letters are *a*,
*ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, *śa*, and *ha*, and they fall from the banner and other [positions] of the fire [diagram], they indicate a stake (*śalya*) in its own location.
One should know [the nature of that stake] by the measurement of the bodily deformity of the agent.
By the entry of cattle and other animals, and by their cries and sounds in the various directions,
one should write the Mātṛkā, enriched with the eight groups of consonants, either on a board or upon the ground;
through the sequence of these groups, starting from the east and ending in the northeast, one gains knowledge of hidden obstacles (śalya).
In the *ava* group there is indeed iron, and in the *ka* group charcoal from fire;
having sprinkled the ground and established [the site],
[one uses] that which is called a spade.
3. "From the east to the northeast" (pūrvamīśāntam) — thus in manuscript kha.

4. "One should cause [the liquid] to flow out" (srāvayet) — thus in manuscript kha. 5. "If nine interrogative syllables are uttered" (nava cet praśnākṣarāṇi bhāṣante) — thus in manuscripts ga and gha.
6. For the directions beginning with the East, [the syllables] from *ta* onwards: in the *ca*-group, there is ash in the South; and in the *ṭa*-group, bone in the Southwest.
In the *tavarga* one finds bricks; in the *pavarga*, a skull; in the *yavarga*, corpses, insects, and the like; in the *śavarga*, one should indicate iron and so forth;
likewise, in the *havarga*, silver, and from the *avarga*, things that cause misfortune.
Having filled the pit— which was three-quarters full— with water mixed with mud eight finger-breadths deep and held in the hollow of the hands, and having struck it with a mallet,
the Guru should have the ground there smeared and made level so that it floats evenly.

Having performed the general *arghya* offering, he should proceed to the pavilion to be described; having worshipped the arches and the guardians of the gates, he should enter through the western door and perform there the purification of himself and the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the pavilion.
One should attach the *kalaśa* to the *vardhanī*, perform the worship of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and Śiva,
and carry out all rites such as the generation and worship of the fire (*agni-jananapūjā*) as previously described.

One should go to the bathing pavilion for the stones; the stones for the base (pāda), the pedestal (dharma), and so forth of the temple-liṅga are recommended to be eight finger-breadths in height, square in shape, and one cubit in length.
In a temple made of stone, slabs of stone should be used; in one made of brick, half that size.
Stone slabs are for a stone temple, and bricks for a brick temple;
they should be marked with nine faces and so forth.
The five [lunar days] known as Paṅkā, Paṅkāṅkitā, Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and the fifth is considered Pūrṇā.
Of these, the [corresponding] signs are the lotus, the great lotus, the conch, and likewise the crocodile.
And Samudra—these five are the treasure-pots located sequentially below;

Chapter Ninety-Six:
The Ritual Procedure for the Consecration (Adhivāsana)
Īśvara said:
Having bathed and performed the two daily rites, the Guru, holding the *praṇava* and the *argha* vessel in his hands, [should proceed].
Accompanied by his assistants, the image-bearers, and the Brahmins, he should go to the sacrificial hall;
there, he should worship the archways beginning with Kṣānti in due order, as previously described.
Following the sequence of circumambulation, one should place the door-keepers on their respective branches:
Nandin and Mahākāla in the east; Bhṛṅgin and Vināyaka in the south;
Vṛṣabha and Skanda in the west; and Devī and Caṇḍa thereafter in the north.

One should worship in successive order two jars each, located at the base of the branches— namely Parjanya and Aśoka— which are tranquil and cool, and which represent the past and the life-sustaining nectar.
With their own names in the dative case, preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*,
[one should worship] two by two.

The dimensions of the body's marks are three times the length of the *liṅga* when divided into parts according to the description of the portions; thus, the mark of the body of the *liṅga* exists on all sides. (96.053cd)
In the case of a *liṅga* measuring one cubit (*hasta*) or more, the *lakṣma-rekhā* (the line of marks) is covered by eight parts of a ninth-parted barley grain, both in depth and in width;
thus, it increases by eight parts for every additional half-cubit of the *liṅga*.

In the case of an eight-cubit [liṅga], the depth of the pedestal (pṛthvī) is one cubit; thus, by increasing [the depth] by one-eighth [of the height] for each increment, the depth of the pedestal becomes eight barleycorns when the liṅga is nine cubits high. (6)
And in the case of the marks on the limbs, where each successive part increases by one-quarter,
the measurement of the body's span (viṣkambha) indeed increases by one barleycorn (yava).
Furthermore, through the addition of eight and six [units] respectively, the lines also increase by one-third.
And in all [these], there should be a subtle mark at the very top of the head;
it is called the "descent of the mark" (lakṣmāvatāraka).

Chapter Ninety-Nine: The Account of the Installation of the Sun Deity (*Sūryapratiṣṭhākathana*)
Īśvara said:
I shall describe the installation of the Sun, including the pavilion and so forth, as well as the ritual bathing and so forth, exactly as before.
Then, according to the previously mentioned procedure,

having projected the Vidyā along with its limbs upon the seat and the bed, one should project the Sun there as the three principles (tritattva), together with the five consonants beginning with *kha* and their corresponding vowels.
Having performed the purification and other rites as before, and having purified the *piṇḍī*, one should install the five principles (*tattva*) as before, extending up to the site and the square,
and then duly establish it with the all-pervading Power (*Śakti*).

The Guru should duly install the Sun, ending with the *śakti*, using his own seed-syllable; or else, he should install Āditya, ending with the name of the master, followed by the word "pāda. AP 99.005ab.
The previously mentioned [details] are to be observed also in the installation (*sthāpana*).
Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Installation of the Sun," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

The Lord said:
Now I shall also describe the ritual procedure for the consecration of the door-deities.
Having purified the components of the door with decoctions and other substances,
one should place the triad— consisting of Ātman and the others, ending with Īśvara— at the base, middle, and top sections of the lintel.
Having performed the ritual placement and established [the deities],
and having offered oblations and recited mantras here according to their forms, one should then worship the Vāstu deity at the door itself, consecrated with the Ananta mantra.

Having placed the five [substances] beginning with jewels and having performed the pacification homa, there are barley, white mustard seeds, *ṛddhi*, *vṛddhi*, great sesame seeds, cow-dung, clay, mustard seeds, the king of *rāga* (datura), *mohanī*, *lakṣmaṇā*, and *amṛtā*.

Having tied a bundle (poṭalī) consisting of yellow pigment (rocanā), *rug-vaca*, and *dūrvā* grass to a naturally grown *udumbara* tree below the palace with the syllable *praṇava* for the sake of protection,
one should place it slightly leaning against the northern door.
Having placed the *ātmatattva* below and the *vidyātattva* on the two branches,
one should place Śiva, the pervader of all auspiciousness, in the region of space;
then, one should install Maheśanātha by means of the root mantra.

When one Brahmin is fed, it is as if ten million have been fed;
how much more so when many have eaten? What is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.

He who gives food on the way to Gayā makes his ancestors possessed of a son.
Having bowed to Vaṭeśvara at the banyan tree, one should worship the great-grandfather;
he obtains imperishable worlds and shall uplift a hundred lineages.
Whether performed sequentially or non-sequentially, a pilgrimage to Gayā yields great fruit.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Pilgrimage to Gayā," within the "Glorification of Gayā" section of the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 116:
The Procedure for the Pilgrimage to Gayā (Gayāyātrāvidhi)
Agni said: Having bathed in the Mahānadī with the Gāyatrī itself,
one should perform the Sandhyā.
Having first performed the morning *śrāddha* with the *gāyatrī*, the *piṇḍa* offering becomes inexhaustible;
and at midday, having bathed while the sun is rising, one should worship with songs and instrumental music.
One should perform the twilight devotions (sandhyā) in front of Sāvitrī and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna) at her feet; and having entered the womb-gate at the foot of Agastya,
one who has emerged shall not enter a womb again and is liberated from worldly existence.
1. *prātaḥ* (in the morning), according to Ka...
2. *madhyāhne sarasi* (at midday in the lake), according to Ga...
3. *mucyate bhayāt* (is released from fear), according to Cha... and Jha... p. 9.
One should offer the *bali* at Kākaśilā and then pay homage to Kumāra;
then, as one who offers the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), one should do so at Svargadvārī, at the Soma-pool, at Vāyutīrtha,
at Ākāśagaṅgā, and at Kapilā.
Having bowed to Śiva Kapileśa and offered the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) at Rukmikuṇḍa,
and having bowed to Koṭīśa at Koṭītīrtha, a man [should offer the piṇḍa] at Amoghapada,
Gadālole, Vānaraka, and Gopracāra.
By bowing to the cow at Vaitaraṇī, there shall be the deliverance of twenty-one generations;
and by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Krauñcapada on the third lunar day, as well as at Viśālā and Niścirā, one likewise effects such deliverance.

In the liberation from debt and the liberation from sin, one who performs a bath with ashes in a pit of ashes is freed from evil; he should bow to the god Janārdana. "O Janārdana, this funeral cake (piṇḍa) is offered by me into your hand."
"May there be inexhaustible [merit] for me who have gone to the other world;
at Gayā, Janārdana himself appears in the form of the ancestors.
Having seen that lotus-eyed one, one is indeed liberated from the three debts."
Having bowed to Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara, a person should bow to Gṛdhreśvara;
at the root-field (mūlakṣetra) of Maheśa, one should offer funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at the stream (dhārā).

and at Puṣkariṇī, at Kardamāla, and at Rāmatīrtha, one who offers the funeral cake.
One should bow to Prabhāseśa and offer funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Pretaśilā;
thus the ancestors, kinsmen, and others— whether residing in heaven, the intermediate space, or on earth, and whether in the form of pretas or otherwise— are liberated.
By the rice-balls offered by me at all three locations— the Pretaśilā at Gayāśiras and the Pretakuṇḍa at Prabhāsa— the giver of the rice-balls shall deliver his entire lineage.
Having paid obeisance to Vasiṣṭheśa, one should offer the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) before him; likewise,
one should offer the piṇḍa at Gayānābhi, Suṣumṇā, Mahākoṣṭhī,
in front of Gadādhara, on Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, and in the presence of the Goddess.
First, one should bow to Muṇḍapṛṣṭha together with Kṣetrapāla and the other deities;
by worshipping him, there shall be no fear, and poisons, diseases, and the like will be destroyed.
Having paid homage to Brahmā, one leads one's lineage to the world of Brahmā.
Having worshipped Subhadrā, Balabhadra, and Puruṣottama,
one who is endowed with all desires shall uplift their lineage and attain the celestial realm;
having paid homage to Hṛṣīkeśa, one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) before him.
And by worshipping Mādhava, one becomes a god dwelling in a celestial chariot (vaimānika).

Having worshipped Mahālakṣmī, Gaurī, Maṅgalā, and Sarasvatī, and having delivered his ancestors, he dwells in heaven; having enjoyed his pleasures there, he returns here with wisdom in the scriptures.

however, this reading ending with "having uplifted the lineage, a partaker of heaven" (*kulamuddhṛtya nākabhāg iti*) does not exist in manuscript *jha*.

Having worshipped Śrī Kapardin Vināyaka, one shall be liberated from diseases and attain heaven;
and having worshipped Kārttikeya, one shall obtain success free from obstacles. One should also worship Somanātha, Kāleśa, Kedāra, and Prapitāmaha.
Having worshipped the eight secret liṅgas— Siddheśvara, Rudreśa, Rāmeśa, and Brahmakeśvara— one indeed partakes of everything.
One should bow to Nārāyaṇa, Varāha, and Narasiṃha for the sake of prosperity;
and having fully worshipped those known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as the destroyer of Tripura, the bestower of all things, Sītā, Rāma, Garuḍa, and Vāmana.
He obtains all his desires and leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
Having fully worshipped the primordial god who wields the mace (Gadādhara) along with the gods,
he is liberated from the three debts and delivers his entire lineage.
The stone is divine in form and meritorious; therefore, the stone embodies the gods.
In Gayā, there is indeed no place where a sacred ford (tīrtha) does not exist. By whose name one casts the funeral cake (piṇḍa), that person shall be led to eternal Brahman.
Having bowed to Phalgvīśa and Phalgucaṇḍī, one who performs the śrāddha at Aṅgārakeśvara, at the site of Mataṅga, and at Bharatāśramaka,
as well as at Haṃsatīrtha, Koṭitīrtha, and where the Pāṇḍuśilānnada is located, [attains the highest goal].

One who offers funeral cakes at the Sarasvatī shall deliver all his ancestors;
having performed the evening twilight devotion, he should bow to the goddess Sarasvatī.
A Brahmin who performs the three daily devotions becomes a master of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Having circumambulated Gayā and honored the Brahmins of Gayā, all acts such as the giving of food performed there become inexhaustible;
having offered praise, one should thus pray to Gadādhara, the Primordial God: *AP_116.035ab*

and who is devoid of body, senses, mind, intellect, vital breath, and ego.
I bow to the eternally pure, awakened, true Brahman—
the non-dual God, the Lord worshipped by both gods and demons.

and whose mind is intent on uplifting the lineage.

may you be my witness here today that I am now free from the three debts."

likewise, having reached Gayā, I have performed the expiation for my ancestors.

"The Śrāddha for the ancestors becomes inexhaustible and bestows the eternal world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Pilgrimage to Gayā," in the section on the Greatness of Gayā within the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 117:
The Ritual for Śrāddha Offerings (Śrāddhakalpa)
Agni said:

Kātyāyanī told the sages that one should perform the śrāddha rite just as prescribed; one should perform the śrāddha at Gayā and other such places, especially on occasions such as the sun’s transit (saṅkrānti).
Either at the proper time or during the dark fortnight, on the fourth day or later,
having properly prepared the site and the lunar mansion, one should invite [the guests] on the preceding day.
Ascetics, virtuous householders, or *snātaka* Brahmins learned in the Vedas— those who are blameless, devoted to their duties, disciplined, and endowed with proper conduct.
1. "And having completed [the rites] under the supreme asterism," thus [in the manuscript] *cha*.
2. "Those purified by conduct (*ācāra*)," thus [in the manuscripts] *ga* and *ja*;
page 14.
One should avoid those afflicted by leprosy, skin diseases, and the like; one should not accept those who have been invited [if they are otherwise disqualified].
Instead, for rites to the gods, one should seat three persons who are bathed, pure, self-controlled, and facing east; or for rites to the ancestors and others, one may seat one person on each side.
In this same manner, one should also perform [the rites] for the maternal grandfather and others, even with vegetables.
On that day, one should remain celibate, free from anger, unhurried, gentle,
truthful, vigilant, not traveling on a road, refraining from Vedic recitation, and restrained in speech.
He should question all those seated at the head of the rows regarding their questions and their seats;

having spread double-folded *darbha* grass for the ancestors, he should proceed with the rites beginning with the gods. He should ask, "Shall I invoke the Viśvedevas? and [the others] should say, "Invoke them! (117.007cd–117.008ab).
Having invoked the Viśvedevas and scattered barley, he should then mutter:
"O Viśvedevas, hear this! I shall invoke the ancestors.
When told, "Invoke them," he should call out, "uśantas tvā."
Then, having scattered sesame seeds, one should recite the mantra beginning with "āyāntu" for the ancestors (*pitṛka*).
Or, one should sprinkle water over the vessel for the ancestors while reciting the three-verse hymn beginning with "śanno devīr abhiṣṭaye.
Having offered barley with the mantra "yavo 'si," one should offer sesame seeds everywhere for the ancestors.

"You are sesame, having Soma as your deity, born from the sacrifice of cows, fashioned by the gods; anciently mixed with waters and accompanied by *svadhā*, may you gratify the worlds of our ancestors with *svadhā*. Thus.
One should offer a flower with the words "śrīś ca te," using a vessel made of gold,
silver, udumbara wood, or rhinoceros horn, or a leaf-cup, while moving it clockwise.
However, for the gods one should perform the rite counter-clockwise (apasavya), whereas for the ancestors one should perform it clockwise (savya).
1. "Not hurried" and "not too straightforward" [are the readings] in manuscript Ṅa.
2. "Resorted to truth" and "not on the path" and "without Vedic study" are the readings in manuscripts Kha and Gha;
And for each person, with one [offering] into their hands which hold the *pavitra* grass, [he recites]:
"Those divine waters which were produced from milk, those which are from the atmosphere, and those which are from the earth."
May those waters, golden-hued and worthy of sacrifice, be auspicious, most comfortable, and favorable to us.

"O Viśvedevas, this is your arghya; Svāhā! And O Pitṛs, this is for you. Having thus offered [the water] to the grandfather and the others, he should first pour out the remnants (saṃsrava). With the words, "Thou art the place for the Pitṛs," he places the vessel face down.

In this rite, having offered perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and garments, and having set aside food mixed with ghee, he asks, "I shall perform the offering in the fire; please grant permission. Being thus authorized, the one who maintains the sacred fire should offer oblations into the flame.
In the absence of fire, however, [he should offer] into the hand of the father, which holds the *pavitra* grass, with the mantra:
"Svāhā to Agni Kavyavāhana! (117.016cd).
The first oblation is for Soma accompanied by the ancestors, and then for Yama Aṅgiras;
having placed the remnants of the offering into the food vessel, he should touch the vessel.

Having recited, "The earth is your vessel, the sky is your lid; I offer nectar into the nectar in the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa, svāhā," he should place his thumb into the food while reciting, "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ."
Having scattered sesame seeds while reciting "apahatā" (the demons are struck down), one should cause the food to be offered;
then, having said "juṣadhvam" (be pleased), one should thereafter mutter the Gāyatrī and other mantras.
[The phrase] "for each one," etc., refers to this.
1. The reading ending with "prathame caret" is not present in manuscript *jha*.
2. "anagniko jale caiva" is found in manuscript *ṅa*. 3. "svadhā" is found in manuscript *ka*.
Salutation to the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis; salutation always and again to Svadhā and to Svāhā.
Knowing them to be satiated, he should scatter food and offer water once each;
having recited the Gāyatrī as before, he should indeed mutter, "Honey! Honey!
He should ask, "Are you satisfied? and they should reply, "We are satisfied."
Having obtained permission regarding the remaining food, one should then gather all the food together;
having set it aside near the leavings and performed the ritual rinsing (avanejana), one should offer three pindas upon kusha grass. Others say this should be done after the guests have sipped water.
When they have sipped water, one should cause water, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata) to be offered.
Then, a man should offer the water for imperishability (akṣayyodaka) and pray for blessings:
"May the ancestors be non-terrible; may our lineage always increase. (AP 117.025ab)
May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give.
May food be abundant for us, and may we receive guests.
"May we have those who ask from us, and may we not have to ask anything from anyone.
Having spread out the *kuśa* grass used for the *svadhā* invocation along with the *pavitra* strainers, he should say,
"I shall pronounce the *svadhā*," and being permitted, he should say, "Let it be pronounced."

"Let the *svadhā* be uttered for the fathers, the grandfathers, and those headed by the great-grandfathers; let there be *svadhā*. And while this is being said, he should pour water out, having turned the vessel face upwards, and then give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
"May they always belong to Svāhā"— thus [he should pray], according to the *kha*,
*cha* manuscripts; "he should then pray"— thus according to the *gha*, *ja*, and *jha* manuscripts.

The passage beginning with "The ancestors are not terrible" (*aghorāḥ pitaraḥ*) and ending with "having spread [the grass] along with the *pavitra* blades" (*āstīrya sapavitrakān*) is absent from the two manuscripts Kha and Cha.
One should give according to one's ability to the deities and the ancestors, or else have [the Brahmins] recite:
"May the Viśvedevas be pleased," and then release them with the word "vāja."

Having followed [the Brahmins] while reciting "āmāvāja-sya" and having circumambulated the Brahmins, he should enter his home; he should perform this likewise every month on the new moon day (amāvāsyā).
I shall now describe the Ekoddiṣṭa Śrāddha; one should perform it as previously prescribed.
One should cause a single purifier, a single half [of a blade], and a single ball of food to be offered.
There is no invocation (āvāhana) nor the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa), for the Viśvedevas are not present here.
When asked about satisfaction, the twice-born should say "It is well-savored" (svaditam); he should say "It is pleasantly tasted" (sukhaditam).
"May [the ancestors] be present," [he says]; at the pouring out of the inexhaustible water, "May you be pleased.
To the others, "We are pleased"; he should perform the remainder as previously described.
I shall now describe the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, which may be performed at the end of the year or even in the middle.
There are three vessels for the ancestors and one vessel for the deceased; these four, together with the *pavitra* grass, are filled with sesame seeds, flowers,
and scented water.
Having filled [the vessel], he sprinkles [the water].

From the two verses beginning with "Those who are equal in the vessel of the preta and the vessel of the ancestors" (ye samanāḥ), the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and so forth is performed as before; thus the state of being an ancestor (*pitṛtā*) arises for the *pretas*.

Now I shall describe the *abhyudayika* śrāddha; everything is as before, but one should mutter [the mantras] excluding those addressed to the ancestors (*pitṛ*). It is performed in the forenoon, and it is circumambulated clockwise.
Here, the ritual services include straight *kuśa* grass, and *yava* grains are used in place of sesame seeds.
When asked about satisfaction, the twice-born should say, "It is well-prepared; it is perfectly prepared.
[Note:
1. *gandhodakena siktāni* means "sprinkled with scented water."]
2. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "athābhyudayikam" and ending with "yavair iha" does not exist in manuscript Jha.
"Oṃ, I shall invoke the Nāndīmukha ancestors for the rice-balls"; he should ask, "May they be pleased," and [recite] "inexhaustible."
"I shall cause the Nāndīmukha ancestors to be addressed," he says;
then [the officiant] asks him, and he should reply, "May the groups of Nāndīmukha ancestors be gratified.
The Nāndīmukha ancestors are his father, his grandfather, and his great-grandfather.
The maternal grandfather, the great-maternal grandfather, and the great-great-maternal grandfather should not employ the word *svadhā*; one should feed an even number of Brahmins.
I shall now describe the satisfaction of the ancestors through cultivated plants and herbs.
Likewise, one is satisfied for a month by forest roots, tubers, fruits, and the like;
for two months by fish; for three months by venison; and for four months by the meat of birds.
Then four by means of the Raurava [skin],
five by the [skin of] the goat, six by the tortoise,
seven and eight by the boar, and nine indeed by the [skin of the] blue jay.
With the meat of a ram, or with that of ten buffaloes, deer, or boars, one is satisfied for a year; with cow's milk or milk-rice (pāyasa),
or with the meat of a vārdhīnasa bird, satisfaction lasts for twelve years.
Rhinoceros meat, black potherb, red goat, honey,
and large-scaled fish— these constitute an inexhaustible *śrāddha* offered during the month of Maghā in the rainy season.

Furthermore, one who studies the mantras, one who maintains the *agnihotra*, one who studies a Vedic branch (*śākhā*), and one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*) [are worthy recipients].
One who has kindled the sacred fire with grass (Tṛṇāciketa), one who knows the Trimadhu, a reciter of the Dharmadroṇa,
and one who possesses knowledge of the Triṣuparṇa and the Jyeṣṭhasāman— these are purifiers of the company at a meal.
1. *Dadhyakṣatavadaryādyā* according to Ga. and Cha.
2. *Tathā vanyaiḥ* according to Kha. and Ṅa. 3. *Vatsaraṃ rauraveṇātha* according to Gha.
4. "But by a goat-stealer, [the group] of five"—thus in manuscript Ṅa.
5. "A red goat"—thus in manuscripts Ga, Gha, and Ṅa. 6. "The *māgha* śrāddha here is inexhaustible"—thus in manuscript Jha.
7. Regarding "of a droṇa of water," [the manuscript reads] "jha...":
I shall now declare the ritual procedure for the desire-yielding trees (kalpavṛkṣas).
On the [first] lunar days, there is much wealth;
on the second, women are supreme; on the fourth, one grants dharma and desire; on the fifth, one desiring a son; and on the sixth, one attains preeminence.
In the seventh [lunar day] one shares in agriculture; in the eighth, there is the gain of wealth; in the ninth, there are single-hoofed animals;
and in the tenth, there will be a herd of cattle.
On the eleventh day, there is a retinue; on the twelfth, wealth and grain;
on the thirteenth and fourteenth, preeminence among kinsmen; and the Śrāddha for those who died by the sword is declared to yield all attainments on the new moon day (Amāvāsyā).
The seven hunters became deer in the Daśārṇa forest; on Mount Kālañjara they were cakravāka birds; in Śaradvīpa they were haṃsas; and in Lake Mānasa they were swans.
They too were born in Kurukṣetra as Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas;
they set out on a long journey—do not despair of them. When recited at the beginning of a *śrāddha* ceremony, the *śrāddha* becomes complete and bestows the world of Brahmā.

A son or other descendant should perform the *śrāddha* for his father; if that father is still living, he should perform it for his grandfather; if that grandfather is also living, he should perform it for his great-grandfather.
Then [I shall speak] of the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather; [I shall declare] the time—thus [he said]. (9) *śreṣṭhabhāgy api* according to manuscript *kha*.

Likewise, for one's mother and others, as well as for one's maternal grandfather and others— he who recites this ritual manual for the *śrāddha* shall obtain the fruit of performing the *śrāddha*.
A śrāddha offered at a sacred ford (tīrtha), at the beginning of a Yuga, or at the beginning of a Manvantara, becomes inexhaustible;
as do those offered on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, the twelfth of Kārttika,
the third of Māgha, and likewise the third of Bhādrapada.
The new moon of Phālguna, as well as the eleventh day of Pauṣa;

the Manus beginning with Svāyambhuva, who are indeed the foremost and imperishable among them;
and Gayā, Prayāga, the Gaṅgā, Kurukṣetra, and the Narmadā.
Śrīparvata, Prabhāsa, Śālagrāma, Vārāṇasī,

Chapter 118:
Bhāratavarṣa (The Land of Bharata)
Agni said:
That region which lies north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains is named Bhārata; it extends for nine thousand [yojanas].
This is the land of action for those proceeding toward heaven and liberation; it is Vārāṇasī, where one may obtain the fruit of the merit performed by the faithful.

p. 21 Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimān, and Hemaparvata. (1)
The Vindhya, the Pāripātra, and seven other principal mountain ranges are here. Indradvīpa, Kaseru, Tāmravarṇa, Gabhastimān,

This, however, is the ninth among them, an island surrounded by the ocean;
this island extends for nine thousand yojanas from south to north. There are nine divisions of Bhārata.
Furthermore, in the Madhyabheda region, there are the Kirātas and Yavanas to the east, while the Brāhmaṇas and others dwell in the center;
likewise, there are rivers originating from the Pāripātra mountains that have the Vedas and Smṛtis as their mouths.
From the Vindhya mountains flow the Narmadā and others; from the Sahya, the Tāpī, Payoṣṇikā, Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Kṛṣṇaveṇā, and so forth;
likewise, from Malaya flow the Kṛtamālā and others, while the Trisāmā and others are born from Mahendra.
The regions beginning with Kumāra, Śuktimat, and Himādri, as well as Candrabhāgaka, Kuru, Pāñcāla, Madhyadeśa, and others, are situated to the west.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "Bhāratavarṣa," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.

[The world] is surrounded by the ocean of wine (suroda);

Dvairatha, Laṃvana, Dhairya, Kapila, and Prabhākara—
these, beginning with the Brahmins and headed by Dadhimukha, worship that form of Brahmā.
Likewise, Vidruma, Hemaśaila, Dyutimān, and Puṣpavān [worship him].

It is encompassed by Śākadvīpa, where the sons of Havya are the lords of Śāka.
Jalada, Kumāra, Sukumāra, Maṇīvaka,
Kuśottara, Modākī, and Druma are the regions named after them.
Udaya, Jaladhara, Raivata, Śyāmaka, and Odraka [are likewise].
Āmvikeya, as well as Ramya, Keśarī, and the seven rivers;
[and] Rudrābha—so it is in manuscript *ka*;
Vikrama—so it is in manuscripts *kha* and *ga*.

In Puṣkalāvatī there are sacred fords;
the Magas [are] of the mind of Magadha.
And the twice-born, moving slowly,
worship the form of the Sun,
while Śāka is surrounded by the ocean of milk.
That [continent] is also surrounded by Puṣkara; it has two sons of Savana, Masāvīta and Dhātaki, each marked by their respective region for two years.
Here, in the center, is one mountain named Mānasa, which is ring-shaped.
It is equal in extent and height, measuring thousands of *yojanas*.
Its inhabitants have a lifespan of ten thousand years, and Brahmā is worshipped there by the gods.
It is surrounded by an ocean of sweet water, equal in size to the continent itself.
Neither deficiency nor excess occurs in the waters of the oceans;
during the rising and setting of the moon in both the bright and dark fortnights,
[the increase] is exactly fifty digits.
O Great Sage, the increase and decrease of the waters of the oceans are seen to be measured in hundreds of finger-breadths;
they are sweet-tasting and possess many virtues.
The earth is golden and devoid of living beings;
beyond that is the Lokāloka mountain, ten thousand yojanas in width.
The Lokāloka is enveloped in darkness, and beyond it lies the shell of the cosmic egg.
The earth, together with its shell and crust, is fifty crores [yojanas] in extent.

Chapter 120:
The Structure of the Universe (Bhuvanakoṣa)
Agni said:
"The breadth of the earth is remembered as seventy thousand [yojanas],
its height is ten thousand, and each of the netherworlds (pātāla) is likewise one [ten thousand]."
Aṭala, Vitala, Nitala, Gabhastimat, the one called Mahātala, Sutala as the foremost, and Pātāla as the seventh;
these are [respectively] black, yellow, reddish-brown, white, sandy, rocky, and golden.
In those delightful regions, the Daityas and others dwell in happiness.
Below the netherworlds (pātālas) resides Śeṣa, who is Viṣṇu in his aspect of darkness (tāmasa);
because of the infinity of his qualities, he is infinite, and he supports the earth with his head.
Below the earth there are many hells, yet a Vaiṣṇava shall certainly not fall there. As far as the earth is illuminated by the sun, that much is considered the sky.
One hundred thousand *yojanas* from the earth is the distinguished solar orb.

The Moon is one hundred thousand [yojanas] from the Sun; the lunar mansion is one hundred thousand from the Moon; Mercury resides two hundred thousand from the Sun; Venus is two hundred thousand from Mercury;
Mars is two hundred thousand from Venus; and Jupiter is two hundred thousand from Mars.

Two hundred thousand [yojanas] from Guru (Jupiter) is the orbit of Saturn; seven hundred thousand from Saturn is Dhruva. From the sages (the Seven Seers), however, the three worlds extend upward by one million [yojanas] from Dhruva, where Maharloka is located, the inhabitants of which dwell for an eon (kalpa).
Twenty-six yojanas from there is the place where Sanaka and the others reside.
From Janaloka, by eighty million [yojanas] is Vairāja, where the deities reside;
by ninety-six million [yojanas] from Tapas is Satyaloka.
That is indeed remembered as Brahmaloka, where there is no more death.

The terrestrial world (bhūr-loka) is accessible on foot; the atmospheric world (bhuvar-loka) is said to extend from the earth to the sun; and the heavenly world (svar-loka) extends from there to the pole star (dhruva), spanning fourteen hundred thousand [yojanas].
This expansion of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is enclosed by the shell of the mundane egg (aṇḍakaṭāha);
it is surrounded on the outside by water, fire, air, and ether, and beyond those by the source of the elements (bhūtādi),
each ten times greater than the preceding, and likewise by the Great Principle (mahat).
O Sage, each of the remaining [elements] increases tenfold over the preceding one;
and having encompassed all these great ones, the Pradhāna stands established.
Of that infinite [Pradhāna], there is no end, nor is its number known.
O Sage, that supreme primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is the cause of everything without exception;
countless classes of beings born therein are like fire in wood or oil in sesame seeds— such is the person (*puruṣa*).
Abiding in the *pradhāna*,
all-pervading, conscious by nature, and self-knowing; both the *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa* indeed sustain the selves of all beings.
O one of great wisdom, enveloped by the power of Viṣṇu, these two possess the nature of mutual dependence;
that very power is both the cause of their separation and of their union.

Indeed, having attained the power of Viṣṇu, the gods and others come into being;
and that Viṣṇu is himself Brahman, from whom this entire world proceeds.
The chariot of the sun consists of nine thousand yojanas.
O best of sages, its axle is likewise twice as long as the Īśā staff—
specifically one and a half koṭis and seven hundred thousand yojanas— and upon it the wheel is established.
The wheel of time, consisting entirely of the year— having three naves, twelve spokes, six rims, and the nature of the two solstices—
is established upon the second axle of Vivasvat, which measures forty thousand [years].
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are five other [parts] of the chariot, each measuring one and a half axle-lengths;
the measurement of both the two yoke-halves is equal to that of the axle;
the axle is short, and the yoke-half is likewise short, serving as the support for the chariot’s pole.
O observer of noble vows, the seven meters beginning with Gāyatrī are the horses;
the rising and setting of the sun should be understood as its appearance and disappearance.
Within the limited space where the steadfast Vasiṣṭha is situated, [the sun moves].
It comes forth by itself from the earth until the dissolution of all beings;
it rises higher than the Ṛṣis to where Dhruva is established.
This is the divine third station of Viṣṇu, radiant in the sky.
This is the supreme abode for ascetics who have shaken off the mire of faults,
[a place] where there is no destruction of the earth.
Then the Gaṅgā originates, destroying sins through mere remembrance.
The form of Hari in heaven, O Lord, should be known as having the shape of a porpoise.
The Pole Star (Dhruva) is situated at its tail; revolving there, it causes the planets to revolve.
That chariot is presided over by the gods, the Ādityas, the eminent ṛṣis, the Gandharvas, the Apsarases, the Grāmaṇīs, the Sarpas, and the Rākṣasas.
The Lord Sun is the cause of snow, heat, and the rains;
he is Viṣṇu, consisting of the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas, and is the cause of both auspicious and inauspicious results.
His chariot has three wheels, and his horses are as white as jasmine.
Accompanied on the left and right by ten [thousand], he moves through thirty-three thousand, thirty-three hundred,
and thirty-three gods who drink the moon.
O Father, one part [of the chariot] is composed of water and one part is situated in light;
the chariot of the son of the Moon (Budha) is produced from the substances of wind and fire,
and Budha moves by means of it, yoked to eight horses.
The chariot of Śukra also has eight horses, and the chariot of Bhauma likewise; the chariot of Bṛhaspati has eight horses, the chariot of Śani has eight horses,
the chariot of Svarbhānu has eight horses, and the chariot of Ketu has eight horses.
O Brahmin, because that body today belongs to Viṣṇu, the Earth is the destroyer of all sins.

Hari is the source from which the lotus-ponds arise, together with the mountains and other features; he is the light, the worlds, the rivers, the mountains, the oceans, the forests, and the groves.
That which exists and that which does not exist is Viṣṇu; it is the manifestation of the knowledge of Viṣṇu.
There is nothing whatsoever apart from consciousness; knowledge is Viṣṇu, the supreme state.
May He grant that by which one becomes Viṣṇu—He who is truth, knowledge, and infinite.
Indeed, he who recites this *Bhuvanakoṣa* shall possess a self that has attained happiness;

Chapter 121:
Jyotiḥśāstra (The Science of Astrology)
Agni said:
"I shall proclaim the science of light (jyotiḥśāstra), which provides discernment between the auspicious and the inauspicious;
it is the essence of the four hundred thousand [verses], and by knowing it, one becomes all-knowing."
In the sixth and eighth houses there is no marriage; nor [is there marriage] in the second and twelfth houses for the woman.
Indeed, there is no affection in the trines (triangles), nor in the remaining even-seventh positions.
1. "The unfolding of knowledge and discernment" (jñānavijñānajṛmbhitam) is [the reading in] Ja...
2. "Hari is the intention of the auspicious and inauspicious" (śubhāśubhāśayo hariḥ) is [the reading in] Kha... and Cha...
3. "In the group of six and eight" (ṣaṭkāṣṭake) is [the reading in] Kha...
Ga, Gha, Ṅa, Ja, Ca—
there will be affection among these four in the triangles; thus says Ja.
If there is mutual friendship, a common field, or a common water-sign between the second and twelfth houses and the trines,
and if there is a single lordship or even a friendly aspect between the stars, [the yoga is formed].

Nevertheless, a union should be performed; however, it should not be done when the six or eight [planets] are again [in such positions], nor when Jupiter and Venus have set, nor when a man dies along with his wife.
When the Sun has entered Jupiter’s sign, or when Jupiter has entered the Sun’s sign—*AP_121.005ab*—[these are times for marriage].
They do not praise marriage [at such times], for it may result in the widowhood of the bride.
During retrograde motion (*aticāra*), there should be a period of three fortnights; during direct retrogression (*vakra*), four months.
One should not perform vows or marriages while Jupiter is in retrograde or direct retrogression.

In the month of Caitra or Pauṣa, during the waning phases of the moon (riktās), while Hari is asleep, on Tuesdays or Sundays, and at the time of the new moon, it shall be inauspicious; however, the period of twilight brings auspiciousness.
Furthermore, the asterisms Rohiṇī, the three Uttarās, Mūla, Svātī, Hasta, and Revatī are favorable.
Marriage is declared to be auspicious when [the moon] does not enter Gemini.
Furthermore, in the case of marriage, ear-piercing, religious vows, the *puṃsavana* rite,
the first feeding, and the first tonsure, one should avoid asterisms that are pierced by planets.
The *puṃsavana* rite is prescribed under the asterisms Śravaṇa, Mūla, and Puṣya; when the Sun, Mars, or Jupiter is in transit; and when the Moon is in Aquarius, Leo, or Gemini.
Expiation (*niṣkṛti*) is performed under the asterisms Hasta, Mūla, and Mṛgaśiras, and under the asterism Revatī (Pauṣṇa), as well as on Wednesday and Friday.
The chewing of betel-leaf is auspicious under the asterisms of Arka (Kṛttikā), Indu (Mṛgaśiras), Jīva (Punarvasu), and Bhṛguja (Śravaṇa).
The first tasting of food is auspicious under Śukra (Śukra), Jīva (Puṣya), Mṛga (Mṛgaśiras), and Maunaka (Mūla);
likewise under the five beginning with Hasta, under Puṣya, and under the three beginning with Kṛttikā.
One should avoid a pierced bear; thus [it is stated] in the manuscripts kha,
ga,
and gha.
Ṅa, cha, ja, and ca are the two [letters] for Jupiter;
"jha" refers to Capricorn and Pisces.
(Page 31)
One should consume new grain and fruit under Aśvinī and Revatī;
one should administer medicine under Puṣya, Hasta, Jyeṣṭhā, Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Aśvinī, Svāti, and Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), and avoid doing so under any other [asterisms].

On the days of Mars, the Sun, or Saturn, one who has been freed from illness should bathe under the asterisms of Maghā, Bharaṇī, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, and the three [asterisms] beginning with Śravaṇā, which are purifying.
On a clay tablet, one should write the syllable *hrīṃ* eight times, with the name in the center and *hrīṃ* in the cardinal directions;

on a birch bark or cloth, one should write the *hrīṃ*-enclosed *pārthiva* mantra in the cardinal directions and the *vasus* in the intermediate directions using yellow pigment and saffron; when worn around the neck, it grants protection.
By this mantra, enemies will certainly come under one's control.
*Śrīṃ hrīṃ* is called the "encasement" (*sampuṭa*); it should be placed sequentially upon the eight petals. *Śrīṃ hrīṃ*.
On a birch leaf covered with cow-dung and turmeric,
using *gorocanā* and saffron, one may write the arrival of cattle; furthermore, by means of the juice of turmeric on a stone slab, one paralyzes enemies when it is placed face-down upon the ground.
Oṃ hūṃ saḥ (3) [is] the name of the *sampuṭa*; oṃ hūṃ saḥ (4) [is placed] on the eight petals in sequence.
On birch bark, using *gorocanā* and saffron, one should write the "Death-Averting" [mantra]. The twelve yogas of the enemy are as follows:
gain occurs at the third, seventh, and eleventh houses; at the fourth, eighth, and twelfth, there is an enemy.
The body, wealth, siblings, friends, children, enemies,
likewise wife, death, dharma, action, income, and expenditure follow in sequence;

Oṃ hraṃ sa;
thus [is it] for the sake of one, five, nine, and peace—thus [it is].
One should clearly state the strength of the nine stars for the ascendants beginning with Aries;
they are known as Janma, Sampat, Vipat, Kṣema, Pratyari, Sādhaka, Nidhana, Mitra, and Pramitra, respectively. This is the strength of the stars.
During the six months beginning with Māgha, milk is praised as the primary food for those under the influence of Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, the Sun, and the Moon.
The piercing of the ears should be performed on a Wednesday or Thursday, under the asterisms of Puṣya, Śravaṇa, or Citrā.

In the fifth year, one should undertake formal study; one should avoid the sixth lunar day, the first of the month, the "empty" days (the 4th and 9th), and the fifteenth; and having worshipped Bhauma (Mars), Vāṇī (Sarasvatī), Hari, and Śrī, [one should begin] during the six-month period beginning with Māgha.
The auspicious tying of the hair-braid, the tonsure ceremony, and other such rites are not recommended when the moon is in the asterisms of Śravaṇā and so forth,
nor when Jupiter, Venus, or the moon have set or waned.

One should predict death or mental dullness for a Brahmin who has been initiated [for the Vedas] under an inauspicious lunar mansion or on an inauspicious day. The *samāvartana* (the rite of returning home) is prescribed for an auspicious weekday and under a favorable lunar mansion; it should take place when the signs of the zodiac are auspicious and are conjoined with or aspected by benefic planets.

The science of archery (dhanurveda) is recommended under Aśvinī, Maghā, Citrā, Svātī, Yāmya (Bharaṇī), the two Uttarās (Uttaraphalgunī and Uttarabhādrapadā), Punarvasu, and Puṣya; likewise under Bharaṇī,
Ārdrā, Maghā, Āśleṣā, Vahni (Kṛttikā), and the asterism Bhaga (Pūrvaphalgunī).

A man desiring to live should not wear a new garment when Jupiter, Venus, or Mercury are [in unfavorable positions]; nor should he do so during a marriage ceremony or similar rites on the day of Bhadra (Pūrvabhādrapadā) and others.
However, it is auspicious during the asterisms of Revatī, Aśvinī, Dhaniṣṭhā, and the five beginning with Hasta.
The wearing of conch shells, coral, and gems is praised during the six months beginning with Māgha.
If a purchased article is sold during the three preceding [nakṣatras] or under Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), it will cause loss; however,
if sold under Aśvinī, Svāti, Citrā, Revatī, Vāruṇa, or Harī (Aśleṣā), it will bring profit.
If goods purchased are profitable, those sold will result in loss.
Under the asterisms of Bharaṇī, the three Pūrvas, Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Svātī, Kṛttikā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Viśākhā, the owner does not remain in possession [of the property].
Where wealth is deposited, whether as a gift or as a loan,
one should perform the royal consecration under the asterisms of Uttarā-Śravaṇā and Śakra (Jyeṣṭhā),
as well as in the months of Caitra, Jyeṣṭha, Bhādra, Āśvina, and Pauṣa.
Having avoided the month of Māgha, the auspicious house may be built during the remaining months;
for the commencement of a house, the asterisms Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Mūla, the three Uttaras, Mṛgaśiras, Svātī, Hastā, and Anurādhā are recommended.
One should avoid [the construction of] ponds and palaces on Sundays and Tuesdays; likewise,
when Jupiter has entered the sign of Leo, during the month of Āśleṣā (Gurvāditya), during an intercalary month (Malimluca),
and when Venus is in its infancy, in its old age, or is heliacally set, one should avoid all house-building activities.
There will be fire, fear, disease, oppression by the king, and loss of wealth.
When the five-day period of Śravaṇa has concluded, one should perform the entry into the house under Dhaniṣṭhā, the Uttarās, or Śatabhiṣaj (Vāruṇa).
The occurrence of a shipwreck occurs under the twenty-second, twenty-third, twenty-fifth, twenty-seventh, or thirteenth lunar day;
it is observed by the king when the moon is in Dhaniṣṭhā, Hasta, Revatī, or Aśvinī,
or when it is in the three Pūrvas, Dhaniṣṭhā, Ārdrā, Kṛttikā, Mṛgaśiras, or Viśākhā.

Chapter 139:
The Sixty-Year Cycle of Years (Ṣaṣṭisaṃvatsara)
Īśvara said:
I shall now proclaim the auspicious and inauspicious [effects] of the sixty-year cycle; listen to this.
In the year *Prabhava*, there will be sacrificial rites, and in *Vibhava*, people will be happy.
And in the Śukla year, all crops flourish, and people are gladdened with joy.
Under Prajāpati there is prosperity; under Aṅgiras, the increase of enjoyments;
under Śrīmukha, the world prospers; and under Bhāva, existence itself increases.
Pūraṇa fulfills; Śakra is the Ordainer who produces all medicinal herbs.
Īśvara brings security, health, abundant grain, and plenty.
Pramāthin brings moderate rain, while during Vikrama there is an abundance of crops.
Vṛṣa brings rain to all, Citrabhānu brings variety,
Svarbhānu brings security and health, and the clouds are auspicious for crossing over.
Under Pārthiva, there is an abundance of crops, as well as excessive rain and victory.
Under Sarvajit, the rain is excellent; under Sarvadhārī, it bestows plenty.
Virodhin destroys the clouds, and Vikṛta is terrifying.
In Khara, one becomes a heroic man; in Nandana, the subjects rejoice.
In Viṣaya, one is a slayer of enemies and shall crush foes, diseases, and the like.
In Jvarārta, the world is afflicted by passion; in Duṣkara, the subjects are difficult to manage.
In the Durmukha year, the world is ill-disposed; in the Hemalamba year, there is no prosperity. O Great Goddess, the Saṃvatsara year brings abundance, while the Vilamba year bestows plenty of food.
In the *vikārī* [year], there is constant anger among enemies; in *vijaya*, [there is prosperity] at some time or other.
In *plava*, the waters overflow; in *śobhana*, the subjects perform auspicious deeds.
In *rākṣasa*, the world is cruel; in *anala* (referred to as *vividha-dhānya*), various grains flourish.
In the *Piṅgalā* [year], there is good rain at some point, but indeed, loss of wealth is said to occur;
in the *Siddhārthā*, everything is accomplished; in the *Raudrī*, fierce events prevail;
in the *Durmati*, there is moderate rain; and the *Duṇḍubhī* brings security and abundance of grain.
During the *krodhana* year, blood flows and men vomit it; they have red eyes and are victorious.
During the *kṣaya* year, however, the world’s wealth is exhausted for sixty years.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Sixty-Year Cycle," in the *Yuddhajayārṇava* section of the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Chapter One Hundred and Forty-One:
The Chapter on the [One] Hundred and Forty-First [Topic]
The Lord spoke this knowledge of the thirty-six words:
"I shall declare the fruit of the medicinal herbs established in the thirty-six positions."
This is the method for making humans immortal, served by Brahmā, Rudra, and Indra:
*harītakī*, *akṣa*, *dhātrī*, *marīca*, the root of *pippalī*,
*vahni*, *śuṇṭhī*, *pippalī*, *guḍūcī*, *vacā*, and *nimba*.
Vāsaka, śatamūlī, rock salt (saindhava), sindhuvāraka,
kaṇṭakārī, gokṣuraka, bilva, punarnavā, balā,
eraṇḍa, muṇḍī, rucaka, bhṛṅga, alkali (kṣāra), and then parpaṭa.
Dhanyāka, jīraka, śatapuṣpī, and javānikā;
viḍaṅga, khadira, kṛtamāla, along with haridrā,
vacā, and siddhārtha— these indeed constitute the thirty-six words.
Indeed, these great medicinal substances, known by names such as *ekā* and so forth, sequentially remove all diseases and grant immortality;
they penetrate into every part of the body.
Their powder may be made into pills (vaṭikā) processed with juice, or into an electuary (avaleha), a decoction (kaṣāya), a bolus (modaka), or a piece of jaggery (guḍakhaṇḍaka).
[Note: 1. "cavyanimbakā" is found in manuscripts Ja and Jha.]
2. [The section] on the removal of wrinkles and grey hair: Honey or ghee, or even ghee and oil. (AP 141.008cd)
For when it is consumed with one's whole being, it becomes a reviver of the dead;
by using half a *karṣa*, one *karṣa*, half a *pala*, or one *pala* [of this substance],
one shall live for three hundred years.
Indeed, in the *Mṛtasañjīvanī-kalpa*, there is no yoga superior to this.
By the first ninefold yoga, one is liberated from all diseases;
by the second and the third, and by the fourth, one is freed from ailments.
Thus, from the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth hexads; likewise from the nine-tetrad;
and from the wind [elements] numbered one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, and eight.
One is released from bile by [the planets] Agni (3), Bhāskara (12), 26, and 27; one is released from phlegm by 5, 6, 7, 8, and 15 [years].
When held under control, it occurs at 4, 3, 5, and 6 [years].
One is liberated from all [afflictions] beginning with the planets and ending with the seizing spirits, by means of the numbers one, two, three, six, seven, eight, nine, eleven, thirty-two, fifteen,
and twelve, respectively; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
The knowledge of the thirty-six steps should not be given to just anyone.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Knowledge of the Thirty-Six Steps," in the *Yuddhajayārṇava* of the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter [X]:

Chapter 142:
Mantras, Medicinal Herbs, and Other [Rituals]
Īśvara said:
I shall describe mantras, medicinal herbs, and yantras that bestow all things.

The qualities of the letters in the thief’s name are doubled and the syllables are quadrupled; when divided by the name, the remainder indicates the thief. Now I shall declare the *jātaka*: those odd-numbered letters in the query that correspond to the [odd] positions in the womb grant the birth of a son.

If the syllables of the name are equal [in number], one is blind in the left eye; if they are unequal, the right eye shall be blind. Furthermore, for a female or male name, the measures (mātrās) and syllables (varṇas) are multiplied by four, and when added to the total sum of the syllables, [the result determines the degree of blindness].

If the female [sign] is even and the male [sign] is odd, there will be no [danger]; however, in the case of a specific [configuration], the woman dies first. If [the configuration] is devoid of form, then the man dies first.
Having grasped the question with subtle syllables and determined the matter through all its constituent parts,

I shall now explain the Saturn-wheel (Śanichakra); one should disregard its aspect when it is situated in the seventh house from the sign occupied by the query, as its aspect exceeds one hundred and forty degrees.
The first, second, eighth, and twelfth [houses] are the aspects of the feet; the lord of the day should abandon that [house], while the remaining [lords] possess half a watch (yāmārdha).
1. "The wheels of mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth" (mantrauṣadhādicakrāṇi) — thus in the manuscripts *gha* and *ña*.
2. "Specifically" (viśeṣeṇa) — thus in manuscript *kha*.
3. "Those who enjoy half a watch [of the night]" (yāmārdhabhoginaḥ) — thus in manuscript *ka*.
O Gaṇeśa, O Nandin, O Jayanta:
I shall tell you how to abandon Saturn’s portion in battle; I speak of the day-Rāhu to you. AP 142.008ab.
When the Sun is in the east, Mars in the northwest, Saturn in the south, Jupiter in the southeast,

Venus in the fire-quarter (southeast), Mars in the southeast, and Rāhu is always situated in the north with Mercury; when the serpent-Rāhu is in the northeast, the southeast, and the southwest for one *prahara* each.
Having encircled the wind, one slays the enemy facing the Lord;
I shall now declare the lunar days and Rāhu: on the full moon, Rāhu is in the domain of Agni, and on the new moon, he is in the northwest (Vāyu), destroying the enemy who faces him.
The letters from *ka* to *ja* should be in the front; those from *sa* to *da* and from *dha* to *na* should be in the south.
One should avoid the groups of letters from *ka* to *la* in the east, while those from *ya* to *ha* should be in the north; one must avoid the aspect of the lunar day (*tithi*).

In the *Mūlabhedaka* [diagram], one should draw three lines toward the east and three toward the south, marking the solar zodiac signs and so forth; in such a view, there is loss, whereas otherwise there is victory. I shall now describe *Viṣṭi* and Rāhu: one should cause eight lines to fall [therein].
From Śiva one should lead to Yama, from Yama to Vāyu, from Vāyu to Indra, and from there to Varuṇa;
from Nairṛta one should lead to Candra, from Candra to Agni, and from there to Water (Jala);
from Jala to Īśa moves Rāhu, together with Viṣṭi, possessing great power.
In the northeast on the third and so forth, and in the south on the seventh and so forth— likewise in the dark or bright fortnight— in the northwest, Rāhu destroys enemies,
as well as Indra and the others, Bhairava and the others, the Brahmāṇīs and the others, and the planets and so forth.

The eight groups of eight [mantras] are in the east and so forth; in the south and so forth, one should station the Vātayoginī in whichever direction the wind blows and there cause the enemies to be slain.
I shall now describe the method for strengthening [the rite]: it consists of wearing [the mantra] on the neck, the arms, and other parts of the body.
The Śarapuṅkhikā plant, uprooted during the Puṣya asterism, wards off the aim of arrows;
likewise, both Parājitā and Pāṭhā ward off the sword.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, O Vajra-Chain! Strike, strike! Oṃ, devour, devour! Oṃ, eat! Oṃ, you red-eyed one, you wearer of the red garment, you whose limbs are smeared with ashes, you whose body is anointed with ashes, you whose weapon is the vajra, you who are densely arrayed in the form of a vajra: bind, bind the eastern direction! Oṃ, drink the blood with your skull-cup! Oṃ, are! Oṃ, khāda! Oṃ, are! Oṃ, raktaṃ piba kapālena raktākṣi raktapaṭe bhasmāṅgi bhasmaliptaśarīre vajrāyudhe vajrākāranicite pūrvāṃ diśaṃ bandha 2.

Oṃ, bind the southern direction! Bind, bind! Oṃ, bind the western direction! Bind, bind! Bind the northern direction! Bind the nāgas! Bind, bind! Bind the wives of the nāgas! Bind, bind! Oṃ, bind the asuras!
Oṃ, bind the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas! Bind, bind! Oṃ!

Protect, protect from whatever afflictions there may be—such as those caused by *pretas*, *bhūtas*, *gandharvas*, and others! Oṃ, protect above! Protect below! Oṃ, bind the razor-edged blade! Oṃ, blaze, O you of great power! Strike, strike! Oṃ, Moṭi, Moṭi! O you who possess a mass of flames like a vajra-fire wall, Huṃ Phaṭ Hrīṃ Hrūṃ!
Śrīṃ phaṭ hrīṃ haḥ phūṃ pheṃ phaḥ! From all planetary influences (grahas), from all diseases, and from all evil afflictions—hrīṃ! Protect [me] from them all!
One should employ this in all rites against planetary influences, fevers, spirits, and the like. //20//
Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "Mantras, Medicines, and the Like," in the *Yuddhajayārṇava* of the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 143:
The Worship of Kubjikā (Kubjikāpūjā)
Īśvara said:
I shall declare that which accomplishes all aims,
by means of which the gods were conquered by the deities using weapons and other implements combined with clarified butter.
And from the worship of the Kubjikā-cakra; thus [it is stated] in the manuscripts marked kha and cha,
page 95.
One should place the seed-syllable of Māyā on the secret organ, the sixfold weapon-mantra on the hands,
"Kālī Kālī" as the heart-mantra, "Duṣṭacāṇḍālikā" as the head-mantra,
and the syllable "Oṃ" (as well as "Hrauṃ Spheṃ Ha Sa Kha Ka Cha Ḍa") as Bhairava, the crest-mantra.
One should worship Bhelakhī as the armor, Dūtī as the eyes, and Raktacaṇḍikā;
thereafter, one should worship Guhyakruñjikā as the weapon within the positions of the mandala:
Kūrcaśiras in the southeast, Śikhā in the northeast, and [the weapon] in the southwest and northwest.
In the center of the armor-mantra is the eye, and the weapon-mantra is in the directions within the mandala;
in the pericarp, there are thirty-two syllables: *sroṃ*, *ha-sa-ṣa-ma-la-na-va-va-ṣa-ḍa-sa-cā*, which are the seed-syllables of the self-mantra.

One should worship Brahmāṇī, Māheśī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Caṇḍikā, along with Indra, from the directions of Śiva (North), Indra (East), Agni (Southeast), and Yama (South). AP 143.007ab.
In the water [element], one should worship the garland of flowers and the five mountains;
one should worship Jālandhara, Pūrṇagiri, and Kāmarūpa in sequence.
One should worship Vajrakubjikā in the northwest, southeast, southwest, and in the center.
Anādivimala, who is worthy of worship and praised by Sarvajñavimala;
then Prasiddhavimala, and Saṃyogavimala;
then the one called Samaya-vimala—this is the group of five Vimalas.
In the northwest, southwest, and southeast, and on the northern peak,
are Kubjārtha, Khiṅkhinī as the sixth, Sopannā, Susthirā,
and Ratnasundarī; these are the eight Lords of the Days on the peaks in the northeast and the others.
Mitra, Oḍīśa, and the one called Ṣaṣṭha shall preside over the rainy season; Gaganaratna shall be in fire, water, and wind; and Kavacaratnaka shall be in the western quarter.
Bruṃ: the mortal named Pañca, located in the directions of Marut, Īśāna, and Agni;
the five jewels in the south and southeast; likewise Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Antikā.
For three of these are the Great-Aged (Mahāvṛddhā), while all [the others] consist of five *praṇavas*.
The worship is twofold, according to the division of twenty-seven and twenty-eight.
One should worship the *Krama-Gaṇapati* with *oṃ aiṃ gūṃ*, and the *Vaṭuka* with the *praṇava*.
In the square mandala, one should worship Gaṇapa in the south,
Vaṭuka in the north, and the sixteen Gurus in the corners;
then, starting from the northwest, [one should worship] eight [deities], and ten in each hexagon.
Brahmā and the other eight [deities] are around it, and in its center is the Ninefold Self (Navātman);
Kubjikā and Kulaṭā—this is indeed the perpetual Krama-worship.
Thus ends the section titled "The Krama-Worship of Kubjikā" in the *Yuddhajayārṇava*, the Great Purāṇa of Agni.
The one hundred and forty-third chapter.
Chapter 144:
Kubjikāpūjā (The Worship of Kubjikā)
Īśvara said:
I shall describe the illustrious Kubjikā, who bestows dharma, wealth, and victory;
one should worship her with the root mantra, either alone or together with her retinue.
Oṃ aiṃ hrauṃ śrīṃ khaiṃ hreṃ hasakṣamalavayambhagavati ambike hrāṃ hrīṃ kṣrīṃ kṣauṃ kṣrūṃ krīṃ kubjike hrāṃ oṃ ṅañanaṇame aghoramukhi vrāṃ chrāṃ.

STRĪṂ, O you who attract the three worlds, HRĪṂ; O you who melt the limbs of Kāma, HRĪṂ;
STRĪṂ, O you who cause great agitation, AIṂ HRĪṂ KṢRĪṂ AIṂ HROṂ ŚRĪṂ PHEṂ KṢAUṂ;

[One should meditate on] Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī in the sequence of the three twilights.
O Kulavāgīśī, may we know you; O Mahākālī, may we meditate upon you;
may that Kaulī inspire us.

The five mantras begin with the *praṇava* (oṃ); one worships the *pādukā*, and in the center is the name in the dative case (*caturthyanta*). There are nine seed-syllables (*bīja*) consisting of two [parts] each; or else they end with *namaḥ*. All of them should be known as being in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*); I shall now declare them.
Kaulīśanātha, Sukalā, Kubjikā from birth, then Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, Kauleśa, Gaganānandanāthaka,
the goddess Caṭulā, Maitrīśī, Karālī, and Tūrṇanāthaka.
Then, these [deities] ending with the goddess Śrīcandrādevī [should be worshipped].
One should worship the sandal (pādukā) that deludes the host of gods, including Bhaga, Ātman, and Puṅga;
one should worship the sandal enriched by the jewels of bliss from the transcendent worlds.
Brahmajñānātha, Kamalā, and Paramā along with Vidyā;
I shall proclaim to you the triple purity consisting of the purity of the Goddess of Knowledge, the Guru, and [the self].
Gaganacaṭulī, Ātman, Padmānanda, Maṇi, and Kalā.
*Vahnikubjinī*, as found in manuscripts *kha* and *cha*,
