Kamala, Māṇikyakaṇṭha, Gagana, and then Kumuda;
Śrīpadma, Bhairavānanda, and the Lord Kamala—these are the nine Siddhas, and together with [the others], they are sixteen.
Śiva, Bhava, and Kṛṣṇa are the [other] nine Siddhas, making sixteen in total.
Candrapūra, Gulma, Śubha, Kāma, Atimuktaka,
Kaṇṭha, Vīra,
Prayoga, Kuśala, and Devabhogaka.
Viśvadeva, Khaḍgdeva, Rudra, Dhātṛ, and Asireva,
Mudrāsphīṭī, Vaṃśapura, and Bhoja— these are the sixteen Siddhas.
One who has pledged the observances (samaya) should have their body constrained by the sixteenfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa).
Having cast a flower into the maṇḍala, one should then worship the maṇḍalas:
Ananta, Mahānta, and always Śiva’s sandals;
as well as Mahāvyāpti and Śūnya—the maṇḍala consisting of the five principles (pañcatattva).
One should worship the sandals of Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, as well as Śaṅkara and Anantaka; one should worship Sadāśiva, Piṅgala, the Lord Bhṛgvānanda,
Lāṅgūlānanda, and Saṃvarta in the location of the mandala.
In the southwest, one should worship Śrī Mahākāla, Pinākin, Mahendraka,
Khaḍga, Bhujaṅga, Vāṇa, Aghāsin, Śabdaka,
Vaśa, Ājñārūpa, and Nandarūpa, having offered oblations in due order.
Hrīṃ khaṃ khaṃ hūṃ sauṃ! O Vaṭuka, accept twice the water for sipping (argha), flowers, incense, lamp, perfume, offering (bali), and worship; salutations to you!
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ kṣeṃ! O Kṣetrapāla, descend, descend!
O you with the mass of matted hair of Mahākāpila, whose three eyes blaze with flaming mouths, come, come! Accept, accept this offering of incense, flowers, and bali! Khaḥ khaḥ! Oṃ kaḥ!
Oṃ laḥ! Oṃ, to the Great Lord of the Ḍāmaras, svāhā! (3) n.
1. *Kāma* and *Muktaka* are designated as *ja*, *cha*, and *ña*.
2. *Vaṭa* and *Vīra* are designated as *ja* and *cha*.

"To the Lord of Mahāmāyā"— thus [is the mantra].
Then, with the remainder of the *bali* offering, one should worship Trikūṭaka with *hrīṃ hrūṃ hāṃ śrīṃ*.

On the left and on the right, at the front and in the south, are the sandals of the Lord of Night; on the right is that of the Lord of Darkness, and at the front is that of Kālānala. [These are] Oḍḍiyāṇa, Jālandhara, Pūrṇagiri, and indeed Kāmarūpa.
And Gaganānandadeva, Svargānanda with his retinue;
the sandals of Satyānanda;
and Nāgānanda called Varga—these are the five jewels at the end of the Muktā [lineage].
In the auspicious and benevolent [direction], one should worship the sixfold sandals of the Lord of the Gods;
one should worship Śrīmatsamayakoṭīśa, Vidyākoṭīśvara,
Koṭīśa, Vindukoṭīśa, and likewise Siddhakoṭīśvara.
One should worship the four Siddhas in the southeast;
one should worship Amarīśeśvara, Cakrīśanātha, Kuruṅgeśa, Vṛtreśa, and Candranāthaka with perfumes and other offerings; and in the south, the five Vimalas.
One should worship Anādivimala, and thereafter Sarvajñavimala;
one should worship Yogīśavimala, as well as those known as Siddha and Samaya—
these four deities in the southwest.
One should conquer Kandarpanāthaka,
all the eastern Śaktis,
and worship the sandals (pādukā) of Kubjikā.
1. *svargānanda* and *devaka* (according to the manuscripts *gha* and *ña*). 2.
*pannagānandadeva* (according to manuscript *ña*).

One should always worship Viṣṇu, the thousand-eyed, the blameless, the auspicious Śiva, with the nine-syllable mantra or the five-praṇava mantra;
[and likewise] Brahmā and the others, from Śiva at the beginning to Brahmāṇī and Maheśvarī at the end.
One should worship Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Śakraśaktikā,
Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī, starting from the east and ending in the northeast;
likewise, Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, and Kākinī are to be worshipped.
Śākinī and Yākinī are to be worshipped in the six fierce [directions] beginning from the northwest;
then, having meditated upon the Goddess who consists of thirty-two syllables,
one should worship her with the five *praṇavas*, or else with the syllable *hrīṃ*.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, six-faced and of sixfold nature,
she is known as the eighteen-fold power of consciousness (cicchakti), endowed with twelve arms.
Seated comfortably upon a lion-throne, she stands atop a corpse-lotus;
she is enriched by thousands of millions of families, with Karkoṭaka positioned as her girdle,
Takṣaka above, and Vāsuki as a necklace around her neck.
She whose earrings are Kulikas, whose circular earrings are Kūrmakas,
whose two eyebrows are Padmas and Makāpadmas, and who holds a Nāga, a skull-cup, a rosary, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a conch, and a book in her left and right hands respectively.
[She holds] a trident, a mirror, a sword, a jewel-garland, a goad, and a bow.
The upper face of the Goddess is white and upward-facing; likewise, the other [face] is white;
the eastern face is pale-white and wrathful; and the southern face is black in color.

Chapter 145:
The Various Mantras of Mālinī
Īśvara said:
I shall proclaim various mantras preceded by the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhā-nyāsa).
The placement is indeed threefold, and the sixfold types are the Śākta, the Śāmbhava, and the Yāmala.
In the Śāmbhava [tradition], there is the *śabdarāśi* consisting of six and sixteen knots;
the *trividyā*, its grasping (*tadgraha*), the *nyāsa*, and that which is designated as the nature of the three *tattvas*.
The fourth [element] consists of the twelve verses of the *vanamālā*.
The fifth is said to consist of the five jewels, and the sixth of the nine-fold self;
in the Śākta tradition, the second is the essence of the threefold knowledge (trividyā) of Mālinī,
while [the third] possesses the sixteen forms.
The other [form] is the twelve-limbed lower staff (adhoryaṣṭaka), which is the fourth;
the fifth should be the six-limbed one, while the others are Śakti and the weapon Caṇḍikā.
*Krīṃ hrauṃ klīṃ śrīṃ krūṃ phaṭ*—these three constitute that which is called the Fourth (*turya*).
*Mālinī* ends with the letter *na*; *Nādinī* is known as the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
*Agrasenī* is on the head; *Śiromālā* is *nivṛtti*, and *śaḥ*.
Ṭa shall be Śānti and shall become the head; Cāmuṇḍā resides in the three eyes.
Ḍha is Priyadṛṣṭi in the two eyes; Guhyaśaktinī is in the nose.
Nārāyaṇī is in the two ears, and Mohanā is in the right ear.
Prajñā resides in the left ear and Vajriṇī is said to be in the mouth;
Ka is Karālī at the right tusk, Kha is Kapālinī at the left shoulder,
Ga is Śivā at the upper tusk, and Gha is Ghorā at the lower left tusk.
U is the crest-lock (śikhā) and the arrangement of teeth; Ī is known as Māyā by means of the tongue.
A is Nāgeśvarī in the speech; Va is Śikhivāhinī in the throat. Bha is Bhīṣaṇī on the right shoulder; Ma is Vāyuvegā on the left.
The syllable *ḍa* is on the right arm, while *ḍha* is on the left; Vināyakā is on both hands.
*Pa* is on the full moon [of the head], while the syllables beginning with *o* are on the fingers.
*Aṃ* is on the left finger, and *aḥ* is on the hand as Sañjīvanī.
*Ṭa* is Kapālinī with a skull; *ta* is Dīpanī on the staff of the trident;
*ja* should be Jayantī on the trident; and *yaḥ* is known as Vṛddhi, the means of accomplishment.

Chapter 148:

*oṃ haṃ khaṃ khaśoklāya svāhā*,

Hrōṃ Kreṃ!

One should worship the abundant, stainless, and most excellent face, which is the essence of essences and worthy of adoration, as well as the eightfold qualities beginning with sovereignty: Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, Aiśvarya, and so forth.
The infinite seat, the lion throne, and beyond that the lotus seat;
within the pericarp and filaments are the circles of the sun, moon, and fire.

One should worship sattva, rajas, and tamas, as well as prakṛti and puruṣa;
one should worship the self, the inner self, and the supreme self.
All of these are joined with the bindu and accompanied by māyā and the vital breath (anila).
One should worship with perfumes and other offerings the eight gatekeepers— Uṣā, Prabhā, Sandhyā, Sāyā, Māyā, and Balā— as well as Sūrya, Caṇḍa, and Pracaṇḍa.
Through worship, recitation, burnt offerings, and other rites, victory shall be attained in battle and similar endeavors.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "Worship for Victory in Battle," in the *Yuddhajayārṇava* of the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 149:
The One Hundred and Forty-Ninth Chapter.
Regarding the Lakṣakoṭi-homa, the Lord said:
"From this fire-offering, there is victory in battle and other such endeavors, the attainment of a kingdom, and the destruction of obstacles."
Having produced purification through hardship and by means of a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma),
[the fire] becomes radiant, like smoke...
"Two dots joined together"—thus it is said.
Having recited the Gāyatrī mantra while submerged in water, one should perform the rite sixteen times. AP 149.002ab.
In the forenoon, he should offer oblations into the fire while performing breath-control (prāṇāyāma). Subsisting on alms, barley-gruel, or fruits and roots,
he should take only a single meal consisting of milk, parched grain flour, or clarified butter.
O Pārvatī, this continues until the completion of the hundred-thousand-fold oblation (*lakṣahoma*).
At the conclusion of the *lakṣahoma*, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of cows, garments, and gold.
In the event of the occurrence of all kinds of portents, [the rite should be performed] by five or ten twice-born men.
There is no calamity in the world that is not pacified by this.
There is no supreme auspiciousness that exceeds it. Furthermore, a king should have a *koṭihoma* sacrifice performed by brahmins as previously described.
His enemies never stand against him in battle at any time;
nor does any plague or disease arise anywhere in his land.
Excessive rain, drought, rats, locusts, and parrots [do not afflict him].

Rākṣasas and others are pacified, as are all enemies in battle. At a *koṭihoma* sacrifice, one should likewise invite twenty Brahmins, or a hundred, or even a thousand; thus one shall obtain prosperity according to one's desire.
If a twice-born man, a king, or even a merchant should perform a *koṭihoma*, whatever he desires he shall obtain; he shall go to heaven in his very body.
[He should do so] with the *gāyatrī*, the planetary mantras (*grahamantra*), the *kuṣmāṇḍī* verses, or the *jātavedas* hymns.
Then, through oblations and worship with mantras dedicated to Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Viṣṇu, Śakti, Śambhu, and Sūrya,
one obtains minor accomplishment with ten thousand [oblations], while a hundred thousand oblations (lakṣahoma) removes all afflictions.
The *koṭihoma* sacrifice bestows all desired objects and brings about the destruction of all afflictions;
it consists of barley, rice, sesame, milk, ghee, *kuśa* grass, and *pramātīkā*.
The petals of the lotus, uśīra, bilva, and mango are prescribed for the oblation (homa).
For ten million oblations (koṭihoma), the pit should be eight cubits in measure;
for one hundred thousand oblations (lakṣahoma), it is ordained to be half that size.
A *homa* is proclaimed as being performed with ten thousand (*ayuta*), a hundred thousand (*lakṣa*), or ten million (*koṭi*) oblations of clarified butter and other substances.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The *Homa* of Ten Thousand, Hundred Thousand, and Ten Million," in the *Yuddhajayārṇava* section of the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 150:

Agni said:

The eighth Manu will be Chāyāja, the son of Sūrya;
he will be Savarṇi, the eighth [Manu] who is of the same nature as the previous one.
The groups of gods will be the Sutapas and others, and the Dīptimats, Drauṇikas, and so forth.
The sages were Bali and Indra, and the sons were headed by Viraja;
the ninth was Dakṣasāvarṇi, and the gods at that time were the Pārās and others.
Their Indra was Adbhuta, and the best of the twice-born were Savana and the rest.
Dhṛtaketu and others will be the sons [of Brahmā], and from that [period] comes Brahmasāvarṇi;
the hosts of gods will be Sukha and others, and Śatakratu will be their Indra.

The sages were Haviṣya and others, and their sons were Sukṣetra and others;
then Dharmasāvarṇika was the Manu, and the gods were Vihaga and others;

his Indra will be Ṛtadhāman; the deities will be Harita and others;
the seven ṛṣis will be Tapas and others; and his sons will be Vaideva-vanmukha and others.

Manu Bhautya, the fourteenth, shall be the pure Indra;
the hosts of gods beginning with Cākṣuṣa and the twice-born beginning with Agnibāhu are the sons of Manu Bhautya, the fourteenth, headed by Ūru.
The seven ṛṣis from heaven impel the gods on earth;

At the end of the Dvāpara age, Hari divided the Veda for Manu and the others.
That original Veda had four quarters and consisted of one hundred thousand verses. There was originally only one Yajurveda, which he then divided into four parts.
The sage performed the duties of the Adhvaryu with the Yajus formulas, the Hotr’s duties with the Rks, the Audgātra with the Samans, and the office of the Brahman with the Atharvans.
First, Paila, a disciple of Vyasa who had mastered the Rigveda, [was appointed].
Indra gave the *Saṃhitā* to Pramati and Vāskala;
he, in turn, gave his own *Saṃhitā* in four parts to Baudhya and others.
The highly intelligent disciple of Vyāsa named Vaiśampāyana indeed composed twenty-seven branches of the Yajurveda tree;
these include the Kāṇvas, Vājasaneyins, and others, as recorded by Yājñavalkya and his followers.
From the tree of the Sāmaveda, Vyāsa’s disciple Jaimini, along with Sumantu and Sukarman, each took one *saṃhitā* from it;
then the teacher named Sukarman [further] compiled a thousand *saṃhitās*.
Sumantu, a disciple of Vyāsa, divided that Atharvataru and taught it to thousands of pupils known as the Paippalādas;
by the grace of Vyāsa, Sūta composed a Purāṇa-saṃhitā.
Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Manvantaras," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 151:
Duties Other Than Those of the [Four] Castes.
Agni said:
"Manu and the others, having practiced the dharmas leading to enjoyment and liberation, attained those which Puṣkara proclaimed to Paraśurāma as spoken by Varuṇa."
Puṣkara said: I shall now describe for you all the duties of the castes, the stages of life, and others, as proclaimed by Manu and other sages, which grant satisfaction to Vāsudeva and the rest.
Non-violence, truthful speech, compassion, benevolence toward all beings,
visiting sacred fords, generosity, celibacy, and freedom from envy.
O best of the Bhṛgus, service to the gods and the twice-born, as well as to one's gurus;
listening to all the dharmas, likewise the worship of the ancestors, constant devotion toward the king, and being guided by the true scriptures— [these are the duties].
Compassion, forbearance, and likewise faith—
these are declared to be the common dharma for all social classes and stages of life.
Sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, and the act of teaching the Vedas and so forth [are the specific duties].
One should prescribe receiving gifts, teaching,
and [performing sacrifices] as the duties of a Brāhmaṇa; likewise, giving, studying, and sacrificing according to the rules are proclaimed as the duties of a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya.
The specific duty of the Kṣatriya is protection and the suppression of the wicked;
agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are proclaimed as the duties of the Vaiśya;
and for the Śūdra, service to the twice-born or all types of crafts are prescribed.

For the Brahmins and the other [twice-born] castes, birth is the second from the tying of the girdle of muñja grass. According to the natural order (ānulomya) of the castes, birth is traditionally held to be the same as that of the mother; however, the son of a Brāhmaṇī woman born from a Śūdra is a Caṇḍāla, due to the inverse order (pratiloma).
A Sūta is born from a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother; likewise, a Devala is born from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother.
A Pukkasa is the son of a Kṣatriya woman by a Śūdra, born in the reverse order (pratiloma);
similarly, a Māgadha is born from a Vaiśya woman by a Śūdra, and an Āyogava likewise.
From the Vaiśya woman, thousands of those born in the reverse order (pratiloma) arise from those of the reverse order;
[regarding this, some read] "the form of dharma" (dharmarūpa).
Gha..., Ṅa..., and Ña...:
Their marriage should be with those of equal status, and not with those who are superior or inferior.
The occupation of the Caṇḍāla is prescribed as the execution of those condemned to death; likewise,
the livelihood of the Vaidehaka is said to be the protection of women.

The profession of charioteers for horses is for the Sūtas; that of hunters for the Pukkāsas; the performance of praise for the Māgadhas; likewise, the practice of yoga for the Āyogavas; the entering of the arena is prescribed for them, as well as living by means of crafts.
Dwelling outside the village, wearing the clothes of the deceased,
and likewise not being touched by others— such is the rule prescribed for the Caṇḍāla.
Furthermore, the abandonment of the body here for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow [is ordained].
Or, in the case of the procreation of women, children, and so forth by outsiders,
the castes resulting from such mixture are to be known by the actions of both the father and the mother;
thus ends the section on the duties of mixed castes in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "Nāma."
Chapter 152:
The Conduct of the Householder (*Gṛhasthavṛtti*)
Puṣkara said: A Brāhmaṇa, living by his own prescribed duty,
may indeed live according to the dharma of the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, but he should never live like one of the Śūdra caste.
A twice-born man may practice agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and moneylending;
however, he should avoid cow-products, molasses, salt, lac, and meat.
Furthermore, it is said therein that his livelihood should consist of [the sale of] auspicious goods.
Having pierced the earth, having cut through medicinal plants, and having offered oblations, [one kills] insects and ants.
Indeed, farmers purify themselves through sacrifice by worshipping the gods.
A plow with eight oxen is righteous; one with six oxen is for those seeking a livelihood;
one with four oxen is for the cruel; and one with two oxen is for those who destroy dharma.

One may live by means of *ṛta* and *amṛta*, or by *mṛta* and *pramṛta*, or even by *satya* and *anṛta*; but one should never live by one's own improper livelihood. Thus ends [the section on] the "Lifestyles of the Householder" in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The one hundred and fifty-first chapter.
Chapter 153:
The Duties of the Stage of Studentship (Brahmacarya-āśrama-dharma)
Puṣkara said:
I shall declare the dharma of those belonging to the stages of life, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; listen.
Of the sixteen nights of women during their fertile period, the first three are censured.
One desiring a son should approach [his wife] during the even nights; the rite of *ādhāna* (conception) is thus prescribed.
Once the presence of the embryo is clearly known, the *savana* rite should be performed before the fetus moves.
In the sixth or eighth month, the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) should be performed, using an auspicious name that favors the birth of a son.
The wise should perform the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) while the umbilical cord is still uncut;
however, once the period of impurity has passed, the naming ceremony (*nāmakarman*) is prescribed.
For a Brāhmaṇa, it is said that the name should end with the word *śarman*, whereas for a Kṣatriya, it should end with *varman*.
Names consisting of *gupta* or *dāsa* are indeed recommended for Vaiśyas and Śūdras;
that ending in *śarman* is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa, and that ending in *varman* for a Kṣatriya.
A name consisting of the word *gupta* or *dāsa* is indeed recommended for Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
Furthermore, one should present the child to the master, saying, "This is your son.
The tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*) should be performed according to family custom, and the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) for a Brāhmaṇa [should follow].

In the eighth year from conception, or in the eighth year [after birth], for a Kṣatriya in the eleventh year from conception, and for a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception; beyond the sixteenth year, however, [the initiation] does not take place. The girdles made of muñja grass, bark, and [other materials] are prescribed respectively for these classes.
The skins of the black antelope (*mṛga*), the spotted deer (*vaiyāghra*), and the *vasta* are prescribed for those observing the vow;
the staffs made of *parṇa*, *pippala*, and *vilva* wood are proclaimed in sequence,
and they are said to be respectively equal in length to the hairline, the forehead, and the mouth.
All [the bamboo staffs] should be unblemished, with their bark intact, and not scorched by fire;
as for the garments and sacred threads, they should be made of cotton, flax, or wool respectively;
and at the beginning, middle, and end [of these items], they should be marked with the word "bhavat."
First, one should beg for alms where alms are certain;
those [acts] for women are without mantras, but marriage is with mantras. Having initiated the pupil, the teacher should first instruct him in ritual purity (śauca).
One should perform one's conduct, the fire-ritual, and the twilight worship;
one who eats facing the east gains longevity, facing the south gains fame,
facing the west gains prosperity, and facing the north eats according to truth.
One should offer oblations both evening and morning; one should not offer what is impure, nor with hands apart,
and one should indeed abandon honey, meat, singing, and dancing in the company of worldly people.
1. And one should avoid dancing— thus [it is stated] in the manuscripts marked Kha,
Ga,
and Gha.
Ṅa,
cha, ña, ṭa, and ca: these are the evening [vowels].
The passage beginning with "prātaśca" and ending with "nṛtyañca vai tyajet" does not exist in manuscript Ja.
Indeed, one who is intent on violence, slander, and especially vulgar speech,
should not carry a staff or similar items; having cast what was lost into the water, he should take up another.

Having mastered the Vedas and having given the prescribed sacrificial fee, he should indeed bathe; or, as a lifelong celibate student (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī*), he may dwell with his teacher until the end of his body. Thus ends the section on the stage of studentship (*brahmacaryāśrama*) in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The one hundred and fifty-third chapter.
Chapter 154:
Marriage (Vivāha)
Puṣkara said: A Brahmin may take four wives, a king three,
a Vaiśya two, and a man of the lowest caste may take even one wife according to his desire.
All religious duties should not be performed by one of a different caste;

the hand should be taken in marriage from women of the same caste. A Kṣatriya woman should take hold of an arrow, a Vaiśya woman should take hold of a goad, and likewise, a woman of the lowest caste should take hold of the hem of the garment.
A daughter should be given away only once; one who takes her away incurs the punishment of a thief.
No atonement is ordained for one addicted to the sale of offspring.
The giving of a daughter [is like] union with Śacī.
Then the marriage and the fourth-day rite;
[the reading] *satīyoga* is found in manuscripts *kha* and *cha*.
This marriage, consisting of four types of name-giving rites, has been described.
When the husband is lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has fallen from his caste—
under these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women.
If the husband has died, she should give [the bride] to the brother-in-law; in his absence, she may do as she wishes.

The group of constellations consisting of the three preceding [Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā], the fiery [Kṛttikā], the wind-related [Svātī], the three following [Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla], and Rohiṇī is always recommended for marriage.

O Bhārgava, one should not choose a bride from the same lineage (*gotra*) nor from the same ancestral line (*ārṣeya*). Beyond the seventh generation on the father’s side and beyond the fifth on the mother’s side,
the *brāhma* form of marriage consists of inviting a man endowed with noble family and character and giving her to him.
One born of that [marriage] constantly delivers men by the giving away of a maiden;
likewise, the Ārṣa marriage is said to be from the gift of a pair of cattle. That performer of dharma is the Prājāpatya in which the bride is given when she has been requested.
The Āsura [form] is through a bride-price and is base; the Gāndharva is from mutual choice;
the Rākṣasa is from abduction by force; and the Paiśāca is from the deception of the maiden on the wedding day.
One should fashion [an image] from the clay of a potter;
having worshipped it with musical instruments and other offerings at a reservoir of water, one should cause a woman to carry it home.
Indeed, a marriage must certainly not be performed while Keśava is asleep;
nor during the months of Pauṣa or Caitra, on a Tuesday, or under the asterisms of Riktā or Viṣṭi.
Nor when Venus or Jupiter have set, nor when the Moon is afflicted by a planet.
When a lunar mansion is conjoined with Arka (Sunday), Arkabhauma (Tuesday), or afflicted by Vyatīpāta, it is not auspicious;
likewise, the Somya, Pitrya, Vāyavya, Sāvitra, and Rohiṇī mansions [are also inauspicious].
1. "In the year of marriage" is found in manuscripts Gha, Ṅa, Ña, and Ṭa.
2. "With floods of musical instruments" is found in manuscripts Ga, Gha, and Ña.
The three Uttarās, Mūla, Anurādhā, Revatī, and the asterism of marriage (Śatabhiṣaj), as well as a lagna called human and a human portion, are auspicious.

Likewise, in the third, sixth, tenth, eleventh, and eighth houses, the Sun, Venus, and Mercury are praised; Mars is not praised in the eighth house. In the seventh, twelfth, and eighth divisions, the remaining excellent planets are praised.
Likewise, among those [asterisms], the sixth, Śukra (Venus), is not commended for a marriage; likewise, the fourth lunar day (caturthī) should be avoided.
The planets should not be placed there, nor should four or more planets occupy a single house.
One may approach a woman for sexual union except on forbidden days; when she is given with truth, there is always delight.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Marriage," in the Agni Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 155:
Conduct (Ācāra)
Puṣkara said:
Having risen during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā, one should remember Viṣṇu and the other deities;
one should void both urine and feces facing north during the day.
At night, one should perform [the ritual] on the south side, and during both twilights as one does by day.
One should never perform it on a path, at the beginning of a road, in water, or in a pond containing grass.

Having performed purification with earth and sipped water, one should regularly consume a tooth-stick. Thus, bathing is proclaimed to be sixfold: daily, occasional, optional, that which is an auxiliary to ritual acts, that which removes impurities, and the sixth, the ritual bath.
The ritual action of one who has not bathed is fruitless; therefore, one should perform the morning bath.

Water drawn from the ground is more meritorious than [water] left on the surface; water from a spring is more meritorious than that; water from a lake is more meritorious than that; and water from a river is said to be even more meritorious than that.
The water of a sacred ford is meritorious, but the water of the Gaṅgā is meritorious in every respect.
Having first purified his impurities and immersed himself in the reservoir of water,
he should then perform the ritual sipping (*upaspṛśya*) and the wiping of the body with water (*parimārjana*).

Then, with the three verses beginning "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," and also with "śanno devī," and with the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā," as well as with "idam āpaḥ," he should then immerse himself in a body of water and perform the recitation (*japa*) while submerged within the water.
In that regard, one should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn or likewise the Drupadā;
or else the hymn beginning with "yuñjate manaḥ," or even the Puruṣa hymn;
but the Gāyatrī is especially [recommended] for the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn.
The deity is Bhāvavṛtta, and the seer is Aghamarṣaṇa;
its meter is Anuṣṭubh, and Hari is remembered as the Bhāvavṛtta [deity].
While wearing a turban, one should perform the libation to the gods and ancestors with a cloth.
One should offer a handful of water with the *Puruṣasūkta*,
and then, having given a gift, one should perform the fire-oblation (*agnihavana*).
But according to one's ability:
therein, beginning with "The Aghamarṣaṇa" and ending with "the libation to the deities and ancestors."
The reading is not found in manuscript *jha*.
2. "Then the carrying of the fire" (*tato 'gniharaṇam*) is found in manuscripts *ṅa* and *cha*.
3. "Having offered a lamp" (*dīpaṃ datvā*) is found in manuscript *jha*.
Then, for the sake of security and well-being, one should approach the Lord;
[one's] seat, bed, vehicle, wife, children, and water-pot [are all dependent upon Him].
These things are pure for oneself, but they would not be pure for others;
one should yield the path even to those who are heavy with burdens or pregnant women,
and one should not look at the sun when it is rising or setting, nor while it is reflected in water.
One should not look at a naked woman, a well, a slaughterhouse, or one who is a flood of sin; one should not step over cotton, ashes, or anything that is contemptible.
One should certainly not enter the inner apartments, a treasury, or go on an embassy for another.
One should not board an unsteady boat, nor climb a tree or a mountain; likewise, one should not be curious about treatises on worldly gain.
One who crushes clods of earth, cuts grass, or bites their nails comes to ruin.
One should not play musical instruments here, nor go out at night without a lamp;
one should not enter a house by a way other than the door, nor should one expose one's private parts. One should not interrupt a conversation, nor should one change one's clothes in public.
One should say "Bhadraṃ bhadram" (May there be welfare, may there be welfare); one should never utter what is undesirable.

One should avoid a seat made of *pālāśa* wood; one should walk by the shadow of a deity or the like; one should not pass between two persons worthy of worship; and one should not look at the stars and so forth while impure from eating.

One should not speak of one river while standing in another; one should not scratch oneself with both hands; and one should not go to the other side of a river without first having gratified the ancestors and the gods. One should not perform a ritual bath naked.
1. "For he would not be supported by another" (parabhṛtaḥ) — this is the reading in manuscript Jha...
2. The text beginning with "loṣṭamaddī" and ending with "na rātrigaḥ" is found in manuscript Ga.
3. "There is no shadow of Devādri" is found in manuscripts kha, cha, and ga.
4. "One should not cast impurities and so forth into the waters" is found in manuscripts kha and ṭa.
Then, for the sake of security and well-being, one should approach the Lord;
one should remove the garland from oneself and discard the dust from the feet of the donkey and other such animals.

One should not mock those who eat inferior food; one should not go to improper places, nor dwell with them [in such places]. One should not speak with physicians, kings, those near rivers, barbarians, women, leaders of many, those in their menses, or the fallen; instead, one should remember Keśava.
One should not laugh, yawn, or sneeze with the mouth uncovered.
A wise man should protect his master’s honor as he would his own sword;
he should not act in accordance with the impulses of his senses, nor should he allow the obstruction of the Vedas.
A disease, even if it be slight, must never be neglected, for it may become an enemy.
O Bhārgava,
one who has crossed the road should always perform ācamana; he should not carry fire and water together.

One should not utter the sound "huṃ" while worshipping Śiva; one should not step over his foot with one's own foot. Whether in his presence or out of sight, one should never speak unpleasantly to anyone.
One should avoid censuring the Vedas, the scriptures, kings, sages, or deities.

One should not perform [these acts] during the three periods of twilight; one should avoid listening to the Dharma [at such times], but should always take delight in the gods and constantly practice virtue and so forth.
On one's birth star, one should perform the worship of Soma and the honoring of Brahmins, deities, and others; this brings about laughter [or joy].
(Variant readings: *kuryāddhāsyam* in Kha and Ṭa;
*ripurvatsopi* in Ṅa.)
3. *samācāmed iti* (cha);
4. *strīṇām iccheti* (ka); 5. *devanartim iti* (ga).
Gha, ṅa, ña, ṭa, and ca;
"the ocean of sensation" (vedanātim) is kha and cha.
The passage beginning with "One should say 'bhadraṃ bhadram'" and ending with "one should constantly perform dharma and so forth" does not exist in manuscript *jha*.
On the sixth, fourteenth, and eighth days of the lunar fortnight, one should avoid oil massage; likewise,
one should keep urine and feces far from the house and never engage in enmity with superior persons.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Conduct," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 156:
Purification of Substances (Dravya-śuddhi)
Puṣkara said:
I shall now declare the purification of objects: an earthen vessel becomes pure by being fired again;
gold and copper purified when touched by urine, feces, and the like.
Copper is purified by being turned over and washed with water;
bell-metal and iron by means of alkaline substances; pearls and the like by washing; and likewise for lotuses, vessels, and everything made of stone.
Likewise, for vegetables, ropes, roots, fruits, and bamboo vessels, as well as for sacrificial implements used in a ritual, purification is by wiping with the hand;
for those that are oily, it is by washing with hot water; and in the case of a house, it is by sweeping.
"Of the wicked," thus [it is said].

The purification of earthenware is by means of earth and water; that of many-layered cloth is by sprinkling; that of wooden objects is by planing and sprinkling; and that of solid masses and liquids is likewise by sprinkling and by skimming.
The purification of beds, seats, vehicles, winnowing baskets, and carts should be known to be by sprinkling; likewise for fuel made of leaves,
and for objects intended for purity made of horn or ivory, it is by means of a paste.
For vessels made of leather, for bones, and likewise for things like horns;
for resinous exudations, for molasses, and for salts—purification occurs through drying;
and likewise for safflower, for wool, and for cotton.
Water flowing from a pure river is as meritorious as that which has been poured forth; likewise,
a cow is pure except for her mouth, while the mouths of horses, goats, women, calves, birds, and dogs are pure.

One should sip water (perform ācamana) after the mouth has been used for spitting, while engaged in hunting, and always after eating, sneezing, sleeping, drinking water, wading through water, stepping onto a road, and changing one's clothes.
A cat becomes pure by walking; a woman who has had her menses is purified by bathing on the fourth day and is fit for rites pertaining to the gods and ancestors on the fifth day.
For the anus, there should be five applications of clay; for one [the left hand], ten; and for both together, seven.
One should apply a single application of clay to the penis, and three or two applications to the hands;
for students, forest-dwellers, and ascetics, it is fourfold. For garments made of bark-fiber or silk, one should use white mustard seeds.
"From the cleansing and sprinkling of the cloth," as found in manuscripts *gha* and *ṅa*,
page 129.

Purification by sprinkling with water using a deer-hair brush is prescribed for flowers and fruits; indeed, everything is purified by sprinkling with water. Thus ends the section on the purification of substances in the Agni Mahāpurāṇa.
The one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter.
Chapter 157:
On Impurity Due to Death and Other Matters (Śāvāśaucādi)
Puṣkara said:
I shall now declare the purification for the deceased as well as the purification for a woman who has given birth;
the impurity (āśauca) due to death is ordained for ten days among those who are sapinda relations.
O best of the Bhṛgus, the purification for Brāhmaṇas upon birth is likewise [immediate];

for a Kṣatriya it is after twelve days, for a Vaiśya after a fortnight, and for a Śūdra after a month. In the case of a slave born in the natural order (anuloma), the period of impurity is equal to that of the master.

A Brāhmaṇa attains purification by [confessing] six, three, or one [offense] when [the victim belongs to] the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes; and a Kṣatriya likewise attains purification in the same manner. For those born of the Vaiśya and Śūdra castes, purification occurs according to the sequence [of offenses], O Paraśurāma.

For a Śūdra, [the period is] six nights; for a Vaiśya, three nights; until the eruption of teeth, it is immediate; until the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*), the Vedic tradition prescribes a one-night period.
For a Śūdra who has died within three years [of initiation], purification is desired after three nights until the formal instruction of the vows, and for ten nights thereafter;
if more than three years have passed, purification shall occur after twelve days.
It is declared that purification for women occurs after six years have passed, while for those whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed, purification is said to take one night;
likewise, for those whose tonsure has been performed, the relatives become pure after three days.
No impurity is prescribed for the paternal side when women have been married.
For those who give birth in their father’s house, purification is declared to be after one night;
however, a woman in childbirth attains purity only after ten nights, and not otherwise.

If a betrothed maiden dies in her father’s house, her kinsmen are purified after three nights; there is no doubt about this. However, if the period of impurity has already begun, one should complete it according to the first [period] that was incurred.
The word of the King of Dharma is not to be treated as equal to anything else. However,
if one residing in another region hears of the death or birth of a kinsman,
he shall remain impure for only as long as remains of the ten-day period.
If ten nights have passed, one shall remain impure for three nights;
likewise, once a year has passed, one becomes pure simply by bathing. This is also the case when a maternal grandfather has passed away, or when a teacher has died.
In the case of a miscarriage, purification lasts for as many nights as there were months [of pregnancy];
this applies without distinction to all castes when the deceased is a *sapinda* Brāhmaṇa.
1. Regarding the *ācaṇḍāla-naiśikī* [impurity], it is likewise; thus [says] Ṭa...:
"In ten nights they are purified; in twelve days, the king."
O Bhārgava, Vaiśyas [become pure] in fifteen days, and Śūdras in a month;
in the presence of the remnants, one should likewise offer a single *piṇḍa* and,
being composed, recite the name and lineage of that person.
When the best of the twice-born had finished eating and were honored with wealth,
and when they had been dismissed with offerings of unbroken rice and water while their lineages and names were proclaimed,
[he prepared] a trench four fingers wide and of that same depth.
One should make three furrows, each one span (vitasti) long;
and near those furrows, O Rāma, one should briefly kindle three fires for Soma, Agni, and Yama.
One should properly offer oblations everywhere, three times four;
one should perform the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) as before, separately for each, filling them with rice, curd, honey, and likewise with meat.
If an intercalary month should occur in the middle [of the year], one should perform that additional [rite];
or else, one should complete all of this within twelve days.
And if an intercalary month should occur in the middle of the year...
Then, at the twelfth *śrāddha*, that [rite] should be performed even more extensively;
when the year is completed, one should perform the *śrāddha* for the deceased as prescribed for a *śrāddha*, and thereafter for his three male descendants.
In the same manner, being composed, one should offer four balls of food (piṇḍas).
Having honored them and offered them with the mantra "The earth is equal," and also [with] "And among riches" (*dhaneṣu ca*).
kha,
gha,
ṅa.
O Bhārgava, one should offer the *preta-piṇḍa* among the other *piṇḍas* at the sixth, ninth, and twelfth [positions].

And one should likewise employ the vessel for the *preta* among the vessels; this rite should be performed separately in the ritual vessel (*karmapātraka*). This rite is prescribed for a *śūdra*, however, without the use of mantras.
The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for women should likewise be performed at that time;

one should offer the annual *śrāddha*, and for a year after death, one should offer a vessel of food (*kumbhānna*) as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges or drops of rain when Indra pours down.
It is possible to count the grandfathers in this world, but not those who have passed away;
since there is no stability in time that is ever-flowing, one should therefore perform the ritual action.
A deceased ancestor, whether in a divine state or in a place of torment, shall receive the *śrāddha* offering performed for him.

A man who grieves does not benefit either the deceased or himself. There is no period of impurity for those who have committed suicide by means of leaping from a precipice, fire, a rope, or water; nor for those who have been outcasted, nor for those killed by lightning or weapons.
Ascetics, those observing vows, celibates, kings, artisans, and consecrated priests— these,
as well as one who has gone to the funeral pyre, must indeed bathe.
Immediate bathing is prescribed after sexual intercourse and from the smoke of a funeral pyre.
One should never have a deceased twice-born man carried out by a Śūdra,
nor a Śūdra by a twice-born man; for a fault arises from such an act for both of them.
By carrying out the funeral rites for a destitute person, a pauper, or a deceased one, one partakes in the heavenly world;
thus it should be done,
so that this purpose may be fulfilled.
jha..

"In battle one attains victory, and one who gives wood to a deceased person without a protector [attains merit]."
Having designated the deceased as a kinsman and circumambulated that funeral pyre while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya),
they should all then bathe with their clothes on;
and likewise, they should offer three handfuls of water each for the deceased.
Having placed their foot upon a stone at the threshold, they should thus enter the house;
they should cast unbroken grains into the fire and bite a neem leaf.
They should sleep separately on the ground and subsist on food that has been purchased or obtained [without begging].
On the tenth day, however, having performed the shaving of the beard, one becomes pure; the wise man, wearing another garment, should bathe with white mustard seeds and sesame seeds.
This applies likewise when a son is born whose teeth have not yet emerged, or when a child dies, or when there has been a miscarriage.
For him, no cremation with fire should be performed, nor should the water-libation rite;
on the fourth day, however, the collection of the bones must be carried out.
After the collection of the bones, the touching of the limbs is prescribed.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "Impurity due to Death," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 158:
Impurity Arising from Discharge and Other Causes of Flowing Fluids (Srauvādy-aśauca)
Puṣkara said:
I shall declare the impurity resulting from discharges, as approved by the sages beginning with Manu.
1. "With *siddhārthaka* [white mustard seeds] and sesame seeds, one should worship the Brahmins while wearing another garment," so read the manuscripts gha, ṅa, and ña;
"The learned man, wearing another garment, should bathe with *siddhārtha* and sesame seeds," so read the manuscripts ga and ṭa.

In the case of a miscarriage, the period lasts for as many nights as there were months of pregnancy; for three days in the case of a four-month miscarriage, and ten days from the fifth month onwards. For a Kṣatriya, it is four nights, and for a Vaiśya, it is five days.
For a Śūdra, purification is declared to occur after eight days; for women, it is after twelve days;
and for the father, it is by mere bathing alone.

Indeed, there shall be no bathing for the sapinda relatives; there is a three-night impurity for those in the seventh and eighth generations, while for sapindas there is immediate purification until the eruption of teeth. Likewise, until the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā), it shall be one night, and until the initiation (vrata), it shall be three nights.
From this [impurity] for ten nights, there shall be a three-night period for the mother and father. However,
when a child dies before the eruption of teeth, or likewise when a child who has undergone the tonsure ceremony dies,
or when one dies before reaching three years of age, purification occurs after a single night.

Purification occurs in two days for a Kṣatriya and in three for a Vaiśya upon the death [of a relative]; likewise, purification for a Śūdra shall be in five days. Prior to marriage, where a three-night period of impurity is observed for Brāhmaṇas, it lasts twelve days for others.

In that regard, for a Śūdra there is a period of twelve days; for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, it is six or nine days. For one who dies before two years have passed, there is no consecration with fire; one should bury him in the earth. There is no water-libation rite for him, even if the naming ceremony has been performed.
Or, for one whose teeth have appeared, the period may extend until the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
A Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires and is learned in the Vedas becomes pure in one day;
for one deficient in these, or even more deficient, it is three days and four days respectively.

"One who has neglected the *agnihotra* for five days is purified in ten days; such is the declared purification for one who merely calls himself a *brāhmaṇa*. (Variant readings: "purification is declared" in manuscripts gha, ṅa, and ña.)
Twelve days;
a Kṣatriya shall be purified in nine days, and a Brāhmaṇa endowed with virtues in seven days.
A virtuous Vaiśya is purified in ten days, and a Śūdra likewise in twenty;
a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve,
a Vaiśya in fifteen, and a Śūdra is purified in a month.

In the case of an excellence of qualities, when ten days are obtained [as the period of impurity], there is three-day impurity; in the case of three days, one-day impurity; and when one day is obtained, immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*). One should apply this principle in all cases accordingly.
Furthermore, in this context, slaves, resident pupils, hired laborers, and students living at home are included.

Impurity shall be equal to that of the master; it should be observed separately for each person whose connection with the sacred fires was not through marriage. For one who follows the ritual of the three sacred fires (*vaitānika*), impurity begins after the cremation.
For all the classes, the touching occurs at the third part; however,
the letters to be touched are, in sequence, by three, four, five,
ten, four, five, ten, and five, in the fourth, fifth, seventh, and ninth [syllables].
The collection of bones should be performed for the castes in their respective order;

however, there shall be no [waiting period] for unmarried girls, while for those who have been given away in marriage, it shall be three days. For sisters and other such relatives who have undergone the sacramental rites, a period of two nights and the intervening day is prescribed.

The lineage of unmarried daughters belongs to their father's family, while for those who are married, it belongs to the husband's family; however, the offering of water is performed for both at the time of marriage.
If the death of a daughter occurs after ten days have passed since the death of her parents, the period of impurity lasts for three days.
O twice-born one, for the sapindas there is immediate purification before the performance of the tonsure ceremony;
however, until marriage, it lasts for one day, and after that, until the offering of water with the hand, it lasts for three days.
For the son of a brother, it lasts for two days (pakṣiṇī), and for other sapindas, it is immediate.
A Brahmin is purified in ten days upon the birth or death of a relative born of his own caste;
for those born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, he is purified in six, three, and one day respectively.
This should be known regarding sapindas; I shall now speak concerning those who are not legitimate sons and so forth— namely,
in the case of non-legitimate sons, wives who have gone to another man,
and women previously married to others, purification is held to occur after three nights.
The water-libation ceremony shall be withheld for those born of improper unions, for those who persist in the life of a wandering mendicant, and for those who have committed suicide;
likewise for those who have only one mother, for two fathers, and for brothers who have gone to another [wife].
In that case, there is one day of impurity for birth, but for death it shall be two days.
Indeed, I shall now declare the period of impurity for *sapiṇḍas* and for those who share the same water (*samānodaka*).
When a child dies, when one resides in another country, or when a person outside the *sapiṇḍa* circle passes away; 158.028ab.
Having immersed oneself in water while still wearing one's clothes, one becomes pure immediately.
However, those who share the funeral cake (sapiṇḍas) become pure after ten days following the death or birth of a relative;
whereas those of the same lineage (sukulyas) become pure after three nights, provided they have bathed.
Those belonging to the same lineage (gotra) become pure;
however, the status of being a sapinda ceases with the seventh person.
The state of being a samānodaka, however, ceases with the fourteenth person.
If one has forgotten the name of the birth, that [period] is called the supreme lineage-period (*gotra*). However,
if one hears of a death occurring in a foreign land within ten days,
he shall remain impure only for as long as remains of those ten nights.
But when ten days have passed, one shall remain impure for three nights;
however, once a year has elapsed, one becomes pure simply by touching water. (Variant reading:
"In the case of a death-impurity, it shall be for three days.")
But for Mata, it should be thus:

For a maternal uncle, a bird, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, as well as for a son-in-law, a deceased grandson, or a sister’s son, the impurity lasts for one night. (158.34ab)
For a brother-in-law and his son, only bathing is prescribed.
Likewise for maternal grandmothers and a teacher; when a maternal grandfather has died, or during a famine, a national calamity, or when a time of distress has arrived, [the same applies].

Immediate purification is prescribed for those who die from an affliction, as well as for those who know the Brahman when cremated; likewise in a battle against those who attack the Veda, during a national calamity, at a gift-giving, a sacrifice, or a marriage.
For those who kill a Brahmin, a horse, or a king, for suicides,
for one afflicted with an incurable disease, and for one incapable of Vedic study,
the entry into fire or water is prescribed as an expiation.
Whether it be a woman or a man, if they commit suicide by hanging due to anger, affection, humiliation, or fear,
that self-killer shall dwell for one hundred thousand eons in the Śuci hell.
If an aged man who has fallen away from the Śruti and Smṛti gives up his life, there is a period of impurity for three nights; on the second day, the collection of bones should be performed;
on the third day, the water libation should be offered; and on the fourth day, one should perform the Śrāddha.
For those killed by lightning or fire, purification occurs after three days for their *sapiṇḍa* relatives.
Women who have joined heretical sects, those who kill their husbands, or those who do not perform the water-libation rite are not subject to impurity.
However, upon the death of a father, mother, or other such relative, one should remain in wet clothes and fast.
1. "A hungry ghost, or even a sister’s son," so says Ṭa;
2. "One who observes the vow of an ascetic," so says Ja;
3. "Or [it occurs] after dishonor," so says Kha.

And for those struck by lightning and the like, purification is prescribed after three days; thus says Ṭa...
One should perform the funeral rites according to the rules once the year has passed. (AP 158.043cd)
Whoever should carry a deceased person who is not a sapinda by any means,
he becomes pure after bathing with his clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter;
however, if he eats their food, he becomes pure only after ten days.

One should not eat food in that house, nor indeed should one dwell there for even a single day. Those twice-born who carry a deceased Brahmin who is without a protector obtain the fruit of a sacrifice at every step; their purification occurs simply by bathing.
A twice-born man who follows a Śūdra who has become a corpse becomes pure after three days;
however, having performed lamentation together with the kinsmen of the deceased,
he should voluntarily avoid giving gifts, performing Śrāddhas, and other such rites for that day and night.
If the birth of a Śūdra woman occurs in the house, or likewise the death of a Śūdra,
one becomes pure after three days by abandoning the vessels and smearing the ground with cow-dung; however,
while one's own [kinsmen] are present, one must not have a deceased Brāhmaṇa carried away by a Śūdra.
One should lead the deceased, having bathed him and honored him with flowers, to the cremation ground;
one must never burn a naked body nor abandon any part of the body.
Then, a kinsman from the same lineage, having taken hold of it, should place it upon the pyre.
One who has maintained the sacred fires should be cremated according to rule with the three fires;
one who has not maintained them with a single worldly fire, and another likewise. "From this you were born; from you may he be born again."
This son bestows the fire of happiness for the sake of the heavenly world;
the kinsmen pour water once, pronouncing his name and lineage.

And likewise, the performance of water-libations for maternal grandfathers, teachers, and deceased ancestors; such is the ritual action of giving, ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*), and so forth. (AP 158.054ab)
The son should offer the water for the optional rite, as well as for a deceased friend, sister’s son, mother-in-law, or officiating priest;
he should offer the water with the mantra "apo naḥ śośucad agham" for ten days.
It is traditionally taught that there should be ten funeral cakes (piṇḍas) for a Brāhmaṇa, and twelve for a Kṣatriya.
Fifteen [days] are prescribed for a Vaiśya, and thirty are proclaimed for a Śūdra;
whether it be a son, a daughter, or another, one should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) just like a son.
Having placed neem leaves at the door of the house, one should remain self-restrained.
Having sipped water and having touched fire, water, cow dung, and white mustard seeds, they should enter [the house];
having rubbed themselves with earth, they should step slowly upon a stone.
They should abstain from salted food and meat, and sleep on the ground.

Those who have eaten food purchased or obtained, those who have bathed, the original performer of the rite, or one who has completed the ten-day period— should there be no such person, a religious student (brahmacārī) shall perform the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa), the water libation, and so forth;
for in this manner, the impurity (āśauca) arising from death is ordained for the sapindas.

The same would apply to birth for those who desire complete purity. For all [relatives], there is impurity due to death (śāva), but for the mother and father, there is impurity due to birth (sūtaka). The impurity due to birth belongs to the mother alone; the father becomes pure by performing ritual ablution.
It is settled that a *śrāddha* ceremony must be performed on the day of a son’s birth; on that day, for the purpose of making those offerings, one should give cows, gold, garments, and so forth.
Death [is purified] by death alone, and the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) by birth-impurity.
One is purified by whichever of the two periods of impurity occurred first.
If a death-impurity (mṛtaka) should occur during a birth-impurity (sūtaka), or a birth-impurity during a death-impurity,
one should perform purification with respect to the death-impurity, not the birth-impurity.
One should complete a period of impurity that is equal [to another] with the first [period],
but one that is unequal with the second, according to the word of Dharmarāja.
When a death-impurity occurs within another period of impurity, one is purified by the earlier impurity;
the light is sublated by the heavy, but the heavy is never sublated by the light.

If another impurity should occur during the night—whether it be due to a birth or a death—one shall be purified by the remainder of that [first] period; if it occurs in the final watch of the night, purification requires two additional days. If the impurity should occur at dawn, one shall be purified in three days.
In both cases, for ten days the food of the family is not to be eaten.
Giving and other such acts should cease, and the food of the family is not to be eaten.
There is no sin in eating when it is unknown; otherwise, there is a fault for the eater for one day.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "Impurity Arising from Birth and Death," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 159:
Purity Beginning with the Unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and Other Forms of Purification.
Puṣkara said:
For one who has been consecrated or not, heaven and liberation come through the remembrance of Hari;
by casting the bones of the deceased into the waters of the Gaṅgā, his spiritual welfare is secured.
"At first" (*āpāta*) refers to [the view] that even in the absence [of a cause],
it would be exactly thus, and so forth.
The reading "bhokturekamanyathā" does not exist in the three manuscripts gha, jha, and ña.
As long as a man's bones remain in the waters of the Gaṅgā, for that long he dwells in heaven; however,
there is no such rite for those who commit suicide or for those who have fallen from their status.
Likewise, for them as well, it is beneficial for their bones to fall into the waters of the Gaṅgā;
yet the water and food offered to them dissolves in the sky,
due to the great compassion shown toward the deceased who has fallen [into such a state].
The Nārāyaṇa-bali should be performed; by that, one receives grace.
The lotus-eyed Lord is inexhaustible; what is given to him does not perish.
Since he protects one from falling, Janārdana is the worthy recipient.

Hari alone is certainly the bestower of enjoyment and liberation to those who fall [into worldly existence]. Seeing that all worlds are subject to death, one should practice Dharma as one's companion;
for even when dead, a kinsman is not able to follow a deceased man.
For, with the exception of one's wife, the path leading to Yama diverges for everyone;
Dharma alone follows that person wherever they may go.
One should do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's task in the forenoon.
For death does not wait to see whether one's work is finished or unfinished;
having seized one who is attached to fields, shops, and homes, or whose mind is elsewhere,
death departs like a she-wolf snatching a lamb.
Time has no one dear to it, nor is there anyone who is its enemy.
When the lifespan and the karma [that sustains it] are exhausted, it forcibly carries people away.
One does not die before the time has come, even if pierced by hundreds of arrows.
Even when touched by the tip of a blade of kusha grass, one whose time has come does not live.
The path is divided.
Only the Dharma;
medicinal herbs do not protect one who is overtaken by death, nor do mantras and the like.
Just as a calf finds its own mother, so does ordinary karma certainly find its doer.
The world is unmanifest in its beginning, manifest in its middle, and unmanifest in its end.
Just as childhood and other stages occur within a single body, so too is the transition to another body.
Just as one takes up a new garment, so does the embodied soul take up a new body; since this [soul] is eternally indestructible, one should therefore abandon grief.
Thus ends the section on purity in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "Nāma."
Chapter 160:
The Stage of the Forest-Dweller (Vānaprasthāśrama)
Puṣkara said:
"I shall now speak of dharma; listen:
matted hair, maintaining the sacred fire, sleeping on the ground, and wearing deerskin."
Dwelling in the forest, subsisting on milk, roots, wild rice, and fruits,
abstaining from accepting gifts, bathing three times a day, and maintaining celibacy;
the worship of gods and guests— this is the dharma of the forest-dweller.
1. "Medicine and so forth" (auṣadhādi) [is the reading in] manuscript ka...
2. "But for the ascetics" (yatīnāṃ tu) [is the reading in] manuscript ṅa;
page 143.
A householder, having seen his offspring and the offspring of his offspring, should resort to the forest during the third stage of life, either alone or with his wife.
In summer he should constantly practice the penance of the five fires; during the rains, he should live under the open sky;
and in winter, clothed in wet garments, the strong one should perform fierce austerity.
Adopting a state of non-return, he should go straight ahead in a single direction.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Stage of the Forest Hermit," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 161:
The Duties of an Ascetic (Yatidharma)
Puṣkara said:
I shall proclaim the dharma of the ascetic, which reveals knowledge, liberation, and so forth;
having reached the fourth part of one's lifespan, one should completely abandon attachment.
On the very day a steadfast man becomes disenchanted with worldly life, on that same day he should go forth into homelessness,
having performed the Prajāpati sacrifice accompanied by the gift for all the gods.

Having internalized the sacred fires within himself, a Brahmin should depart from his home to the life of a wandering mendicant; he must certainly do so, seeing that he should practice severe austerity in the forest.
3. "One should resort to a direction that is not crooked," so says Ṅa. 4. "One should abandon attachments," so says Ṅa.
5. "Or one should become detached on that very day," so says Ṅa.
One should always wander alone and depend on alms for one's sustenance;
the sage, endowed with wisdom, should be indifferent and free from accumulation.
A skull, the root of a tree, ragged garments,
and solitude;
and equanimity toward all things— this is the state of one who is liberated.
One should neither rejoice in death nor rejoice in life;
one should simply await the time, just as a servant awaits his master's command.
One should step with feet purified by vision, drink water purified by a cloth,
speak words purified by truth, and act with a mind that is pure. For an ascetic, [the vessels] are made of bottle-gourd, wood, clay, or belonging to Viṣṇu.
When the smoke has ceased, the pestle is set aside, the embers are extinguished, the people have finished their meal,
and the removal of the dishes has occurred, the ascetic should always go for alms— like a bee, unattached, not having been invited beforehand, and not having previously requested it.
Alms obtained at that very time are traditionally said to be of five kinds;
one may either use the hollow of the hand as a bowl or practice using a vessel from another vessel.
One should contemplate the destinies of men, which arise from the defects of their karma.
One who possesses pure intent should practice dharma, regardless of which stage of life (āśrama) he is devoted to; being equal toward all beings, outward marks are not the cause of dharma.
Just as the fruit of the *kataka* tree, though it clarifies water, [is effective regardless of its external form].
The water does not become clear merely by uttering its name. (Variant readings: *vṛkṣamūlāni* for *tasya vāri*)
"at the foot of a tree, etc. (as in manuscript ṭa);
"of this pure one" (as in manuscript ṅa);
"life" (as in manuscript kha).
Gha, ṅa, cha, ja; p. 145.
The one who is not crooked, the eunuch, the lame, the blind, and the deaf—
such a twice-born man is released from the cycle of existence by the virtuous, even if he has been born there through ignorance.
Whatever creatures a mendicant kills during the day or night through ignorance, [he is freed from that].
For the sake of their purification after bathing, one should perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas):
[the body] which has bones for its pillars, is bound together by sinews, plastered with flesh and blood,
covered with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and excrement.
One should abandon this abode of the elements, which is beset by old age and sorrow, a dwelling place of disease, afflicted, full of passion, and impermanent;
[and cultivate] fortitude, forbearance, self-control, and non-stealing.
Purity, restraint of the senses, modesty, knowledge, truthfulness, and freedom from anger—these ten constitute the characteristics of dharma.
There are four types of mendicants: the kuṭīcaka, the bahūdaka, [the haṃsa, and the paramahaṃsa].
The Haṃsa and the Paramahaṃsa— whichever comes later is superior;
whether he carries a single staff or three staves, such a yogi is liberated from bondage.

Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the five *yamas*. Then the *niyamas* are purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and worship of the Lord. For the ascetic, there are postures such as the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) and others.

Prāṇāyāma is of two kinds: with seed (sagarbha) and indeed without seed (agarbha). That which is joined with recitation (japa) and meditation (dhyāna) is "with seed," while the opposite is "without seed. Each of these is further threefold, by means of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka).
It is called *pūraka* because of filling, and *kumbhaka* because of the immobility of the breath.
(161.022cd) (Note 1: "One should practice" is found in manuscripts *kha* and *cha*. Note 2: "Compassion and non-stealing" is found in manuscript *ṅa*.)
3. And [the posture] called *tridaṇḍī*—thus in manuscript Ṅa;
4. "The great lotus (*padmaka*) and other postures"—thus in manuscript Ṭa.
Exhalation (*recaka*) is said to be of three kinds according to the division of *mātrās*:
one consisting of twelve [mātrās], another of twenty-four, and another of thirty-six.
A *mātrā* is the duration of a short syllable (*laghvakṣara*), measured by the beat (*tāla*); one should perform the *praṇava* and so forth slowly.

Withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is for those who recite mantras; meditation (*dhyāna*) is the contemplation of the Lord. Concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is the steadying of the mind; absorption (*samādhi*) is abiding in Brahman.
This Self is the Supreme Brahman—truth, knowledge, and infinite.
Consciousness, bliss, Brahman—“That thou art; I am That.
Vāsudeva is the Supreme Brahman, the Light, the Self, the Liberated One, Om.
He is devoid of body, senses, mind, intellect, vital breath, and ego.
The Brahman is the fourth state.
I am the Brahman, the supreme light, the imperishable, the all-pervading Hari. He who is that Person in the sun, he is that very me, the indivisible Om.
Abandoning all undertakings, equanimous in pain and pleasure, patient,
and pure in intention, a man shall pierce the cosmic egg and become Brahman;
he should observe the Cāturmāsya vow on the full moon of Āṣāḍha.
Then one should exert oneself; indeed, starting from the ninth day, or at the junctions of the seasons, one should cause [the hair] to be shaved.
The expiation for ascetics consists of meditation, breath control, and self-restraint. Thus ends the section on the duties of ascetics in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The one hundred and sixty-first chapter. [In some versions, such as ṅa, cha,

and ña, it is titled "That which was stated concerning the end of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep,"] and in the Āgneya Purāṇa, it begins with "The Determination of Impurity" (Aśaucanirṇaya), and so forth.
