Chapter 162:
The Exposition of the Treatise on Dharma (Dharmaśāstra)
Puṣkara said: Manu, Viṣṇu, Yājñavalkya, Hārīta, Atri, Yama, Aṅgiras,
Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, Saṃvarta, Śātātapa, and Parāśara.
Āpastamba, Uśanas, Vyāsa, Kātyāyana, Bṛhaspati, Gotama, Śaṅkha, and Likhita— just as these [sages] have declared the Dharma,
so shall I speak in brief; listen to that which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Vedic action is twofold: that which leads to worldly involvement (*pravṛtta*) and that which leads to withdrawal (*nivṛtta*).
Action performed for the sake of desired results is *pravṛtta*, while action preceded by knowledge is *nivṛtta*.
[The latter consists of] the study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, and the restraint of the senses.
Non-violence and service to the guru are the supreme means for attaining the highest good;
yet among all these, self-knowledge is recorded as the highest.
For that is the foremost of all sciences, and through it, indeed, immortality is attained.
Seeing himself in all beings and all beings in himself,
the one who sacrifices to the self attains self-sovereignty (*svārājya*).
He should be equal-minded regarding the knowledge of the self and diligent in the study of the Vedas.
Especially for a Brāhmaṇa;
[this is] the foremost of the twice-born— thus [it is stated] in manuscript *kha*.
Ṅa,
jha, ña, and ṭa;
these constitute the totality of the twice-born (dvijanman), according to Gha.
One who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, dwelling in whatever stage of life he may be,
is indeed fit for becoming one with Brahman while remaining in this very world.

The commencement of the private Vedic recitations (*svādhyāya-upākarma*) takes place on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, or under the asterism Hasta in the month of Śrāvaṇa, or on the day of the herbs (*oṣadhivāra*), or on the fifth day of Śrāvaṇa; or it may be performed under the asterism Rohiṇī in the month of Pauṣa, or on the Aṣṭakā day.
At the end of the rainy season, one should perform the ritual dismissal (*utsarga*) of the Vedic texts outside [the village] according to the rules.
There is a suspension of study for three days upon the death of a pupil, an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a teacher (*guru*), or a relative;
likewise upon the performance of the *upākarma* ceremony and the *utsarga*, as well as when a master of one’s own Vedic branch (*svaśākhā-śrotriya*) has died.
Upon thunder at twilight, a crash of lightning, an earthquake, or the fall of a meteor;
having completed the Veda, or having studied the Āraṇyaka during the night;
on the fifteenth, fourteenth, or eighth lunar days; and during an eclipse of Rāhu.

Having eaten during the junctions of the seasons, or having accepted food at a *śrāddha* ceremony, one must observe a fast for a day and night; likewise after a ritual for Indra (*śakrapāta*) or for prosperity (*ucchriya*), and when there is the howling of dogs, jackals, donkeys, or owls, or the sound of musical instruments out of season.

In the vicinity of impure things, corpses, Śūdras, outcastes, cemeteries, or those who have fallen [from their status]; under inauspicious stars; during a downpour of lightning and thunder; with wet hands after eating; amidst water; at midnight; or in a violent wind—[one should not study].
During a rain of dust, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, during the fears of twilight or mist,
when fleeing from the harassment of living beings, or when a distinguished guest has arrived at one's home.
1. "It is suitable for the holy life (*brahmacarya*)," according to manuscript ṅa.
2. "When a learned scholar (*śrotriya*) of one's own Vedic branch (*svaśākhā*) has died," according to manuscripts gha, jha, ña, and ṭa.
3. [The same applies] for [eating meat from] rabbits, cats, and pigs;
and [for the same offense] in mounting a donkey, a camel, a vehicle, an elephant, a horse, a boat, or a tree, etc. (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 1.28.18).
These thirty-seven occasions are known as temporary times when study is forbidden.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Treatise on Dharma," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 163:
Narration of the Ritual for Śrāddha Offerings (Śrāddhakalpa)
Puṣkara said:
I shall proclaim the ritual for the Śrāddha ceremony, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; listen.
Having invited the Brahmins on the preceding day during the afternoon, one should welcome them with a hospitable greeting.
One should seat an even number on the pedestal for the rite to the gods (*daiva*), and an odd number for the rite to the ancestors (*pitrka*).
For the gods, they should face east, being three in number; for the ancestors, one may seat only one.
The same applies to the maternal grandfathers, or the *vaiśvadevika* ritual may be performed as a single collective offering.
Having offered water for the washing of the guests' feet and also *kuśa* grass for their seats,
he should, being permitted, invoke [the ancestors] with the verse beginning "O Viśvedevas," and then scatter barley grains.
In a vessel containing a purifier (*pavitraka*),
having poured water with the mantra *śanno devīḥ*, and likewise barley grains with the mantra *yavo 'si*,
one should then pour the *argha* offering into the hand with the mantra *yā divyāḥ*.
Having offered water, fragrance, garlands, incense, and a lamp,
one should then perform the rite with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) and circumambulate the ancestors counter-clockwise (apradakṣiṇa).
Having doubled the *kuśa* grasses and having invoked the ancestors with the verse "uśantas tvā," he should, being permitted by them, recite the mantra "āyāntu naḥ.
Wherever barley would normally be used, sesame seeds should be employed; he should perform the offering of water (*arghya*) and the other rites as before.
Having offered the *arghya* water and having placed the remaining portions of the *saṃsrava* into a vessel according to the rule,
he turns the vessel face down below with the words, "Thou art the place for the ancestors.
Then, taking up food soaked in ghee, he asks, "I shall perform the offering in the fire (*agnau kariṣye*)."
Having been thus authorized with the words "Do so," he should offer oblations into the fire according to the ritual for the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*);
then, with a concentrated mind, he should place the remnants of the offering into vessels,
especially those made of silver, as they may be available.

Having given the food and consecrated the vessel with the mantra "The earth is the vessel," he should place the thumb of the twice-born guest into the food while reciting the verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, and the three verses beginning with "madhu vātā."
Having recited [the mantra] as desired, they should speak; they too should eat while remaining restrained in speech.
Having recited the *pavitraka* mantra, one should offer desirable and sacrificial food (*haviṣya*).
Then, taking the food, one should ask: "Are you satisfied? And what remains of this food?"
He should scatter that food on the ground and offer water once for each [portion]; then,
taking all the food together with sesame seeds, facing south,
he should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) near the remains of the meal, as in the Pitṛyajña.
In the same manner, one should offer water for sipping (ācamana) to the maternal grandfathers;

then one should cause the benediction "svasti" to be recited, as well as the offering of inexhaustible water (akṣayyodaka). Having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability, one should utter the word "svadhā."
"Let it be spoken," being thus permitted, [he says] "Let the *svadhā* be uttered for my ancestors," beginning with "for the maternal grandfathers," and so forth.
The passage ending with "svapitṛbhyaḥ svadhocyatām" is not present in manuscript *jha*;
page 151.
When it is said, "Let there be *svadhā*," one should then pour water on the ground;
or, saying "May they be pleased," one should offer water for the divine ancestors—the Viśvedevas.
[One should pray: "May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny."
"May our faith not depart, and may we have much to give"—
having spoken these pleasing words, one should bow down and dismiss [the guests].
The dismissal is preceded by the gratification of the ancestors with the mantra "vāje vāje."
But when the remnants have first been poured into the argha-vessel, one should turn that vessel for the ancestors face upwards and dismiss the brahmins;
having circumambulated them clockwise and partaken of what was served to the ancestors.
He should remain celibate for that night together with the Brahmins.
Having thus performed the circumambulation, he should worship the Nāndīmukha ancestors during the rite of prosperity (vṛddhi),
performing the ritual with barley and offering balls (piṇḍas) mixed with curd and jujube fruits.
The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is devoid of the gods; it has a single offering (*argha*) and a single purifier (*pavitraka*);
it is indeed without the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the ritual of placing food in the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).
At the point where the word "imperishable" (*akṣayya*) is used, one says "may [the ancestors] attend" (*upatiṣṭhatām*), and at the dismissal of the ancestors (*pitṛvisarjana*).
He should say, "May you be delighted," and they should indeed reply, "We are delighted.
He should prepare four vessels containing scented water and sesame seeds;
he should pour the vessel of the deceased (preta) into the vessels of the ancestors for the purpose of the *arghya* offering.
With the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ," he should perform the remainder as previously described.
This *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed together with the *ekoddiṣṭa* for a woman.
For one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* occurs before the completion of a year, [the procedure is as follows].
1. "One should dismiss [them] starting with the father," according to manuscripts *kha*, *cha*, and *jha*.
2. "Also for a woman," according to manuscripts *kha* and *cha*.
Page 152.
To that [guest] as well, one should give food along with a water-pot for a year to a twice-born man;
and on the anniversary of the death, it should be performed every month for a year,
and the annual Śrāddha should indeed be performed like the monthly rites.
Indeed, by means of sacrificial food (haviṣya-anna), the ancestors are satisfied for one month; by milk-rice (pāyasa), for a year;
and by the meats of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, the boar, and the hare, respectively, the ancestors are satisfied for an increasing number of months by those offerings.
The meat of a rhinoceros, large-scaled fish, food mixed with honey,
the meat of a red goat, black potherbs, and the flesh of the vārdhrīṇasa crane—
whatever one gives while staying at Gayā is said to be eternal.
Likewise, on the thirteenth day of the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism, there is no doubt that one obtains daughters, progeny, bards, excellent cattle, sons,
ghee, agriculture, commerce, as well as animals with cloven and uncloven hooves.
The giver of *śrāddha* always obtains sons endowed with Brahmanic luster, gold, silver, and base metals, preeminence among kinsmen, and all desired objects—
provided he avoids these [lunar days] beginning with the first (*pratipad*), excluding the fourteenth (*caturdaśī*).
Indeed, for those who have been slain by a weapon, it is offered there [to them]:
heaven, offspring, vigor, heroism, as well as a field, strength,
preeminence among sons, good fortune, progeny, and excellence among children.

[The merit] from those given here with fish, deer, sheep, birds, goats, and spotted deer. (Variant readings: *mātsyāvihāriṇaurabhraśākunacchāgapārṣataiḥ* in manuscript *cha*; *dattair iha* in manuscripts *gha*, *ṅa*, and *ña*).

4. "He attains all infinity," according to manuscripts Gha and Ṅa; 5. "Gold," according to manuscripts Kha and Cha.

He who duly offers a Śrāddha from the Kṛttikās until Bharaṇī obtains these desires: solid wealth, knowledge, success in medicine, silver, cattle, goats and sheep, horses, and long life. AP 163.040ab.
The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors, the deities of the śrāddha;

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Ritual of Śrāddha," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 164:
The Fire-Offering to the Nine Planets (Navagrahahoma)
Puṣkara said:
One who desires prosperity, or one who desires peace, or one who desires rain, long life, or nourishment, as well as one performing malevolent rites, should undertake the sacrifice to the planets.

"the fathers and grandfathers are pleased"—thus [it is said]. (Gha... 3; Ṅa... p.

A wise man should give this meal to the twice-born according to the sequence of the planets, honoring them with hospitality as far as his ability permits and according to what he has obtained, following the prescribed rite. [The gifts are:

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Homa for the Nine Planets," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 165:

We go with five families; the sixth among them is the most eminent.
He cannot be conquered by gods, asuras, or humans.

The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the supreme austerity;

"That Brahman is indeed well-known through self-awareness," so it is said in the Gaṇeśa and Gaṅgā recensions.

Chapter 166:

Puṣkara said:

that which proceeds by relying upon the single factor of caste (varṇa).
Dharma is indeed the supreme nectar;
this is to be understood as the duty of the castes, just as it is in the three [stages] beginning with initiation (upanayana).
Whatever matter is established by relying upon a stage of life (āśrama)—

for the religious student, the householder, the forest-dweller,

Among the six measures of policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), that which has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) has been illustrated;

the sages, the Manus, the cows, and the mothers of the gods likewise do so.
The wives of the gods, the trees, the nāgas, the daityas, and the throngs of apsarases;
all weapons, all scriptures, kings, and vehicles;
medicinal herbs, jewels, and whatever divisions of time there are—[all these emerged].
May the rivers, oceans, mountains, sacred fords, clouds,
and streams consecrate you for the fulfillment of all desires and goals.
Then, having been adorned, he should give gold, cows, food, land, and so forth.
"O Kapilā, you are worthy of worship among all the gods, O Rohiṇī;
since you consist of sacred fords and deities, therefore grant me peace."
O Śaṅkha, you are the merit of merits and the most auspicious of auspicious things;
since you are eternally held by Viṣṇu, grant me peace.
O Dharma, you who take the form of a bull, you are the cause of joy for the world.
The abode of the eightfold form, bestow peace upon me!
O Fire, the golden seed situated within the womb of Hiraṇyagarbha,
which yields the fruit of infinite merit— bestow peace upon me!
Since a pair of yellow garments is dear to Vāsudeva,
may Viṣṇu indeed grant me peace through the gift of them;
for you are Viṣṇu, who appeared in the form of a fish at the origin of the nectar of immortality.
Since you are the constant vehicle of the moon and the sun, therefore grant me peace.
Since you are the entire earth, a cow resembling Keśava,
and the eternal remover of all sins, therefore grant me peace.
Since all iron implements, such as the plow and other weapons, are always under your control, therefore grant me peace;
for you are established as a constituent part of all sacrifices.
Since you are the eternal womb of the fire-god, therefore grant me peace.
Since the fourteen worlds abide within the limbs of cows,
may there be auspiciousness for me in this world and in the next.
For the sake of accomplishing dharma, kāma, and artha,
[one should sleep] where the bed of Keśava and Śiva is not empty.
May my bed also never be empty, granted to me in birth after birth.
Just as all the gods are established within all jewels, so may the deities grant me peace through this gift of jewels.
Just as other gifts do not equal even a sixteenth part of the gift of land, may there be for me here peace through the gift of land;
[may there be] the sacrifice to the planets, the ten-thousand-fold oblation, success through sacrificial fees, and victory in battle.
At marriages, festivals, sacrifices, consecrations, and other such rites,
two types of *lakṣa-homa* and *koṭi-homa* are prescribed for the attainment of all desires,
whether performed in one's home or in a pavilion.

In the case of ten thousand [offerings], the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be one cubit in measure and provided with a girdle and a womb; there should be four officiating priests, or even just one himself.
For in the case of a hundred thousand, all of that is ten times greater.
One should worship Tārkṣya here, measuring four cubits or two cubits;
you are the vehicle of Pameṣṭhin, with the sound of the Sāman as your head.
You are the constant remover of worldly objects; therefore, grant me peace.
As before, having consecrated the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should perform the Lakṣahoma;
then one should offer the stream of wealth (vasordhārā) and give gifts such as a bed and ornaments.
In that case as well, there should be eighteen officiating priests (ṛtvij) for the Lakṣahoma.
Through these sacrificial fees and their fruit, Śatrughna, the performer of the *koṭihoma*, shall obtain [them].
1. "In birth after birth" is found in manuscript ṅa.
2. "In the house or in a pavilion" is found in manuscript kha;
"in the house or likewise in a pavilion" is found in manuscript ña.

"O twice-born ones, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be four cubits, eight cubits, or twelve cubits [in size], for the sake of obtaining sons, wealth, kingdom, victory, enjoyment, liberation, and so forth. (kha, ṅa: p. 165)
Whether twenty-five or sixteen [pots] are on the cloth, and four at the door; one who performs the *koṭi-homa* with all desires fulfilled goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
The *homa* may be performed with the mantras of the planets, or with the *gāyatrī*, or even with those dedicated to Viṣṇu.
By means of oblations offered through the mouths of the Jātavedas, whether according to the Śaiva or the renowned Vedic rites,
with sesame, barley, and clarified butter, one partakes of the fruit of the Aśvamedha and other such merits.
For acts of incantation to cause enmity or malevolent sorcery, a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is prescribed; the fuel-sticks (samidhaḥ) are joined with the bones of a hawk and fire,
while those wearing red ornaments and having disheveled hair meditate upon the misfortune of the enemy.
"May those with evil wives be his who hates [me], *huṃ phaṭ*!"— with these words,
one should cut the image made of flour with a razor and destroy the enemy;
whoever performs this sacrifice against a single oppressor shall go to heaven.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Homas of Ten Thousand, One Hundred Thousand, and Ten Million," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 168:
An Account of the Great Sins (Mahāpātaka) and Others.
Puṣkara said:
"The king should inflict punishment upon men who do not perform penance, whether [the offense was] intentional or unintentional; however, one who has performed penance should practice it."
1. "By those [rays] of the sun with Jātavedas as their mouth," according to Kha...
2. "One should destroy the enemy," according to Ṅa and Ña:
One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted;

nor that which has been touched by those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin), nor that which has been touched by a woman in her courses, nor the food of a group (gaṇa), nor the food of a courtesan.
[The food] of a usurer, a singer, one who has been cursed, a eunuch, and one whose house a paramour frequents;
[the food] of a washerman, a cruel man, a bard, and a gambler.

Likewise, [one should avoid] the food of false ascetics, as well as that of thieves and those who punish with the rod; the food of those born from adultery (kuṇḍa and golaka), of those conquered by women, and of those who sell the Vedas;
as well as the food of actors, weavers, and the ungrateful.
One should avoid the food of a blacksmith, a Niṣāda, and a washerman; the food of one who has falsely entered the religious life, of a libertine, and of an oil-presser;
and the food of one who has fallen from a high estate, as well as food that is detested.
Likewise, one who is not invited by a Brāhmaṇa should not eat the food of a Brāhmaṇa,
nor should one who is invited by a Śūdra eat the food of a Brāhmaṇa; having unintentionally eaten the food of any of these, one should fast for three days.
Having eaten intentionally, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance, as well as for semen, feces, or urine.
Having eaten the food of a *caṇḍāla* or a *śvapaca*, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance;
likewise for food not designated for a deceased person (*anirdiṣṭa*), food for the dead (*pretānna*), or that which has been smelled by a cow.

One should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance for eating the leavings of a Śūdra, the leavings of a dog, or likewise the food of an outcast; one should also practice the *kṛcchra* during a period of impurity. Whoever eats the food of someone who is in a state of impurity likewise becomes impure.
[One becomes pure] from a well containing a dead five-toed animal that has been once touched by impurity; [the same applies] to groups [of outcasts] and courtesans,
as well as to thieves and hypocrites.
Having drunk water, the best of the twice-born should remain fasting for three days;
in all cases, the penance for a Śūdra shall be one quarter, while for a Vaiśya and a Kṣatriya it shall be two and three quarters respectively.
Having consumed the urine or excrement of a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
the same applies if he has eaten dried meats.
The food of pretas, hailstones, and the flesh of carnivorous animals, pigs, camels, jackals, monkeys, crows,
cows, humans, horses, donkeys, and camels; mushrooms and village fowl.
Having eaten the flesh of an elephant, one is purified by the *taptakṛcchra* penance; likewise,
having eaten at an *āmaśrāddha*, a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) becomes pure by consuming honey, meat, garlic, or *guñjana* through the *prājāpatya* and other such penances.

Having eaten meat prepared for oneself, as well as the milk of a cow in heat, colostrum, the śleṣmātaka fruit, clay, or rice-and-sesame porridge, saṃyāva, milk-rice, cakes, or fried pastries prepared in vain, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

Meat that has not been ritually offered, the food of the gods, and sacrificial oblations; likewise, one should avoid the milk of cows, buffaloes, and goats, as well as the milk of all such animals during the ten days following their calving.
The hare, the porcupine, the iguana, the rhinoceros, and likewise the tortoise—these five-toed animals are declared edible; all others are forbidden.
One may eat the *pāṭhīna*, the *rohit*, and the *siṃhatuṇḍa* fish.
All products derived from barley and wheat, as well as transformations of milk—
such as *vāga*, *ṣāḍgava*, *cakrā* and so forth— and likewise anything that has been kept with fat; this second [category] belongs to the Vaiśya and the Śūdra.
kha... ; ṅa... ; ña... ca 2; "dried, burnt meats" is ṅa... 3; "the twice-born becomes pure through the Prājāpatya [penance]" is kha...
A Brāhmaṇa whose sacred fires have been extinguished may, if he acts according to his own will,
perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month; sitting like a hero (vīrāsanam) is beneficial for him.
They declare that killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher’s wife,
and associating with those who commit such acts are the great sins (mahāpātaka). Furthermore,
speaking falsely about one's own excellence and malicious talebearing directed toward the king [are also included].
Forcibly compelling a guru to lie is equal to the murder of a Brahmin; abandoning the Vedas, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, and killing a friend—
these six are equal to the drinking of liquor.
The misappropriation of a deposit, as well as the theft of men, horses, silver, land, diamonds, and gems, is declared to be equal to the theft of gold; likewise,
the emission of semen upon one's own female relatives, virgins, and women of the lowest castes [is equal to violating the Guru’s bed].
They consider violating the bed of a friend or a son's wife to be equal to violating the bed of one's guru; likewise,
the killing of a cow, officiating at a sacrifice for those unworthy to sacrifice, adultery, and the selling of oneself [are equal].

Abandoning one’s guru, mother, or father; neglecting one’s private Vedic study or the sacred fires; being superseded by a younger brother in marriage (parivitti); marrying before an elder brother (parivettṛ); giving a daughter in marriage to either of those two; and officiating as a priest for either of them. AP 168.030ab–cd.
Violating a maiden, usury, the breaking of a vow, the selling of a tank, a garden, a wife, or a child;
becoming a *vrātya*, abandoning one's kin, and teaching for a fee; AP 168.031cd–168.032ab.
Receiving instruction from one who has been supported by oneself, and the sale of what is not to be sold—these are equal to the killing of a Brahmin.
(Variant readings: "equal to the killing of a Brahmin" appears in manuscripts *kha*, *ṅa*, and *ña*;
"eating forbidden food" appears in manuscript *ṅa*.)
3. [The verse] "sakhyaḥ sutasya ceti" (from page 169):
"Supreme authority over all forms and the setting in motion of the great machine. AP_168.033ab/
Harming medicinal herbs, living off women, neglecting one's duties, felling green trees for the sake of fuel, taking another's wife, and associating with those who revile women.
Undertaking actions for one's own sake alone, eating censured food,
not maintaining the sacred fires, theft, failing to discharge debts,
studying improper scriptures, immoral conduct, and engaging in vices; AP_168.035–168.036ab.
The theft of grain, base metals, or cattle; the consumption of liquor and the consorting with women [of forbidden classes];

the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; atheism; causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa; and smelling things that should not be smelt or drinking intoxicants—these constitute minor offenses (upapātaka).
Sexual intercourse with a male is recorded as causing loss of caste; likewise,
the killing of dogs, donkeys, camels, lions,
goats, or sheep, as well as fish, snakes, and mongooses, should be known as causing mixed-caste status.
Accepting wealth from those who are censurable, engaging in trade, serving Śūdras,
speaking untruths, and killing worms, insects, or birds— these are to be known as acts that render one unworthy (apātrīkaraṇa), as is eating food contaminated by liquor.
Stealing fruits, firewood, or flowers, as well as acts of indiscretion that bring about defilement.
//41// Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Great Sins and Other Offenses," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
1. The killing of the cat itself;
thus [ends] chapter 169.
Now begins the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter on expiations.
Puṣkara said:
I shall now declare to you the expiation for these and other sins:
a killer of a Brahmin, having constructed a hut, shall dwell in the forest for twelve years;
for the sake of self-purification, he shall beg for alms while carrying the skull of a corpse as his banner.
Or he should throw himself headlong three times into a kindled fire;
or he should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Svarjit, or the Gosava;
or, reciting one of the Vedas, he should travel a hundred yojanas.
Or one should bestow all one's possessions upon a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas;
by these vows, those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) cast off their impurity.
One who has killed a cow and is thus joined with a minor sin (upapātaka) should drink barley-gruel for a month.
Having shaved his head, he should dwell in a cow-pen, covered with a cow-hide;
he should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent condiments and salt, at every fourth mealtime;
for two months, with his senses restrained, he should perform his ablutions with cow-urine.
He should follow the cows during the day and, standing still, inhale the dust raised by them; having completed this deliberated vow, he should give ten cows and a bull as a gift.
If these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas.
One should perform one quarter of the penance for obstructing [a water source], and two quarters for binding [an animal];
one should give [a gift] as the fulfillment of the vow of good conduct.
In a distance of one *yojana*, it should be reduced by a quarter; this applies to the entire journey in the event of a downfall.
Furthermore, in wildernesses, difficult terrains, uneven places, and times of danger, if an accident should occur there, a reduction of one-quarter is prescribed.
One should likewise assign half [the fine] due to the defect of the bell-ornament.
In cases of being subdued, being subdued again, being confined, or being yoked to a cart,
or if death occurs while in a post, a chain, or a tether, one should perform three-quarters [of the penance].
In the case of a broken horn, a broken bone, or likewise the cutting off of the tail,
one should drink barley-gruel (yāvaka) until the cow has recovered its health;
one should recite the Gomatī-vidyā and contemplate the Gomatī praise of the cow.
If, by chance, one person should be killed by many,
they shall each perform a quarter of the penance for killing separately;
however, when assistance is being rendered, there is no sin in a misfortune that occurs.
Those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) should likewise perform this very vow;
for the sake of purification, they may also perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, with the exception of the student who has broken his vow of chastity (avakīrṇin).
However, the avakīrṇin must, at the proper time, [perform a sacrifice] with a donkey at a crossroads.

One should worship Nirṛti at night according to the procedure for the *pākayajña* sacrifices. Having established the fire according to the rules, the wise man should then offer an oblation of clarified butter with the three verses beginning with *samit*, dedicated to Candra, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Agni.
Alternatively, having donned the skin of a donkey, he should wander the earth for a year;
or, having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, he should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Brahmin. He should offer oblations of clarified butter.
If a twice-born man, out of delusion, drinks *surā* that has the color of fire,
he should drink *surā* that has the color of fire, or he should drink cow-urine that has the color of fire, or even water.
A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king and confessed his own deed, should say, "May your majesty punish me.
Having taken up a club, the king himself shall strike him once as he stands there.

A thief is purified by execution, or a Brāhmaṇa by austerity alone. One who has violated the Guru’s bed shall cut off his own penis and testicles, place them in his joined palms, and walk toward the south-west until he collapses.
Or, with his senses restrained, he should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months after intentionally committing any one of the acts that cause loss of caste;
if he did so unintentionally, he should perform the Śāntapana Kṛcchra or the Prājāpatya.
For acts that cause mixture of castes or those that render one unworthy of receiving alms, purification is the lunar penance (Cāndrāyaṇa) for one month;
for acts that cause defilement, it is boiled barley-gruel (Yāvaka) for three days;
and for the killing of a Kṣatriya, the penance is declared to be one-fourth of that for killing a Brāhmaṇa.

If a Vaiśya who abides by his duty kills [these], it is known as an eighth part; for a Śūdra, it is a sixteenth. Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a crow, a frog, a dog, an iguana, an owl, or a crow, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra.

Having killed a woman of any of the four castes who was not staying with her husband, or having caused the death of a woman unintentionally, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra. For the killing of snakes and other boneless creatures, there is a night-long restraint of breath (vāyusaṃyama).
Having committed the theft of articles of little value from another's house,
one succeeds by performing the Śāntapana Kṛcchra penance and completing the vow.
For the theft of food to be chewed or eaten, as well as vehicles, beds, and seats;
for flowers, roots, and fruits; and for grass, wood, trees, dried grain, and molasses, the purification is the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
For stealing gems, pearls, corals, copper, silver, iron, bell-metal, or stones, one should fast for three nights;
for stealing [other such items], one should subsist on grain-particles for twelve days.
For consuming cotton, silk, or worn-out leather, for eating the meat of cloven-hoofed or single-hoofed animals, or for eating birds, perfumes, or medicinal herbs, one must drink milk for three days;
likewise, having emitted semen within one's own female kin, one must perform the penance prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed.

Having approached the wives of a friend or a son, or women of the lowest castes, or the daughter of a paternal aunt, a sister, the daughter of a paternal aunt, or the daughter of one's mother’s brother,
or the daughter of a maternal uncle who is a close relative— one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

Having discharged semen into non-human females, into a woman in her courses, into those who are not the proper womb, or indeed into water, one should perform the Śāntapana Kṛcchra penance. Furthermore,
having engaged in sexual intercourse with a male or a female, a twice-born man [must likewise perform this].

On a journey, in water, and during the day, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on. Having approached women of the Caṇḍāla or other lowest castes, or having eaten their food, or having accepted gifts from them, a Brahmin falls [from his status] through ignorance; through knowledge, he becomes equal [to them].
A husband shall confine a wife who has become corrupt in a single room;
he shall cause her to perform that same penance which is prescribed for a man regarding the wives of others.
If, however, she should become corrupt again after being exhorted by her husband with words suited to her condition, [he shall punish her].
The Kṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa penances are prescribed as her means of purification.
[The reading *veṇucarmāmiṣāṇām* is noted as a variant.]
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by consorting with a *vṛṣalī* for a single night,
he removes that by constantly subsisting on alms and reciting [mantras] for three years.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "Expiations," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 170:
Expiatory Rites (Prāyaścitta)
Puṣkara said: I shall now declare the expiations for one who, by associating with an outcast for a year, becomes an outcast himself.
Through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or marriage— but not through sharing a vehicle, food, or a seat—
a man who enters into association with any one of those outcasts must perform that very person's penance for the sake of purification from that association.

The sapinda relatives, together with other kinsmen, must perform the water-libation for one who has fallen from his caste on an inauspicious day during the evening, in the presence of agnates, officiating priests, and teachers;
a slave shall overturn a jar full of water with his foot, as if for a deceased person.

One should observe impurity for a day and night together with the kinsmen; however, they should refrain from [participating in] the eldest’s share, conversation, and other such matters. Furthermore, a younger brother who is superior in merit shall receive that eldest’s share.
1. For those who have fallen into great sins... 2. "I shall tell you the expiation," [it is said]. *jha* edition.
3. "Like a hungry ghost" (pretavat) always;
[this is the reading in] Kha, Ga, Gha, and Ṅa:

But when the penance has been performed, they should bathe in a sacred body of water and drink from a new, full jar of water together with him; they should perform this very same rite even in the case of women who have committed such offenses.
They should provide them with clothing, food, and drink, and let them dwell near their houses;
yet, for those twice-born men, the Sāvitrī should not be recited according to the prescribed rule.

Having made them perform three *kṛcchra* penances according to the rule, he should initiate them; this same [penance] should also be prescribed for those who have abandoned their duties or followed improper occupations.
Having meditated with a concentrated mind, one should mutter the *Sāvitrī* three thousand times.

Having drunk milk in a cow-pen for a month, one is released from the sin of accepting gifts from the unworthy; likewise, by performing three *kṛcchra* penances, one removes the guilt incurred by officiating at sacrifices for those who have lost their caste (*brātyas*), performing funeral rites for others, or practicing malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) against those who have not fallen from their status.
Having abandoned one who has sought refuge or having caused the Veda to be corrupted, a twice-born man may cast off that sin by subsisting on restricted food for one year. [Likewise,
he is purified] if bitten by dogs, jackals, donkeys, or by domestic carnivorous animals.
One is purified by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma) after killing a man, a camel, a horse, or a boar;
and for the violation of the vows of a *snātaka* or the abandonment of one's duties, fasting is required.

Having uttered the sound "huṃ" to a Brāhmaṇa, or having addressed a superior with "thou," one should bathe, fast for the remainder of the day, and propitiate him by saluting him. For threatening [a Brāhmaṇa], one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; for striking him, the Atikṛcchra.
Having caused blood to flow from a Brahmin, one should perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance; [otherwise] he would not be fit [for society].
2. "He is purified by difficult penances" (kṛcchraiḥ viśuddhyati) — thus read in manuscripts *ga*, *gha*, and *ṅa*.
3. "By men, camels, dogs, and pigs" (naroṣṭraviḍvarāhaiḥ) — thus read in manuscript *ṅa*.
4. "With the sound 'krūṅ'" (krūṅkāram) — thus read in manuscripts *kha*, *gha*, and *cha*.
"Oṃkāra," so [it is said] in Ga and Ṅa; and "Haṃkāra," so in Kha (p.
If a Caṇḍāla or similar person remains in someone’s house unrecognized,
but is later correctly identified after some time, that person must undergo purification;
for the twice-born, the purification consists of either the Cāndrāyaṇa or the Parāka penance.
The *prājāpatya* penance is for Śūdras; the remainder [of the rules] follows accordingly.
Having placed guḍa, safflower, salt, and whatever grains there may be at the door of the house, one should then offer them into the fire.
For earthen vessels, only their abandonment is prescribed;
for remaining substances, the purification of the substance itself is prescribed. This applies to those who drink from a single well, who are defiled by touch or by mere intention.

They may be purified by fasting or by consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). However, a twice-born man who intentionally touches a Caṇḍāla and then eats food should perform either the Cāndrāyaṇa or the Taptakṛcchra penance.

If one has eaten from or drunk from a vessel mixed with the contents of a broken pot, or from vessels belonging to outcasts such as Cāṇḍālas and others who are objects of loathing, one becomes pure after six nights.
Furthermore, if twice-born men consume the remnants of food left over by those of the lowest castes...

A Śūdra, however, should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow for three nights. If a twice-born man drinks water from a well or a vessel belonging to a Caṇḍāla out of ignorance, he should perform the Śāntapana penance; a Śūdra, on the other hand, should fast for one day.
If a twice-born man drinks water after being touched by a Caṇḍāla,
he must perform a three-night penance; a Śūdra, on the other hand, shall fast for one day.
If a twice-born man is touched by a dog or a Śūdra while he is impure from eating remnants, [he must perform purification].
1. "Adorned with contact and volition" (sparśasaṅkalpabhūṣitā) — thus [in] Jha...
2. "Commingled" (saṃsṛṣṭa) — thus [in] Ka... 3. "When" (yadā) — thus [in] Kha... and Ga...
Having fasted for one night, one is purified by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

A Vaiśya and likewise a Kṣatriya should perform their bath at night. If a Brāhmaṇa traveling on a road in a waterless wilderness should void urine or excrement while carrying cooked food, [he must bathe].
Without setting that object down, but having placed it upon his limb,

he should remain; having performed purification and sprinkled the food with water, he should show it to the sun and to fire for those travelers who have been taken by barbarians or by thieves in the wilderness.
I shall declare their atonement once they have returned to their own country, according to the sequence of the social classes.
At the conclusion of the *kṛcchra* penance, a Brāhmaṇa deserves the performance of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) once more;
at the conclusion of three-quarters [of the penance], a Kṣatriya; and at the conclusion of half, a Vaiśya.
Likewise, a Śūdra becomes purified by performing one-quarter [of the penance] and giving a gift.
If a woman in her courses is touched by another woman of the same caste who is also in her courses,
she undoubtedly attains purity by bathing on that very day. However, a menstruating woman who has been touched by one of a lower caste must not eat.
As long as one does not attain purity, one is purified by a ritual bath;
having passed urine while walking on a path, if one drinks water through a lapse of memory,
one becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
A twice-born man who, having discharged urine or feces, fails to perform his personal purification,
becomes pure by drinking barley-gruel for three nights;

Puṣkara said: [Regarding] Expiations.
I shall now declare the supreme secret expiations that bring about purification. By reciting the *Puruṣasūkta* for a month, one destroys sin;
by reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa* three times, one is liberated from all transgressions.
From Vedic recitation, from muttering prayers, from Vāyu, Yama, Gāyatrī, and from the vow, [one is freed] from the sin of eating on the forbidden day (adyaha).
In all *kṛcchra* penances, there is shaving, bathing, burnt offerings, and sacrifice to Hari.
Having risen, one should remain standing during the day, and likewise seated at night.
This is declared to be the vīrāsana posture; by performing it, one destroys the sins committed during the kṛcchra penance.
Eating eight morsels every day is known as the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*; eating four in the morning and four in the evening is known as the *śiśucāndrāyaṇa*.
One should eat two hundred and forty morsels of food in any manner whatsoever during a month; this is the performance of the *suracāndrāyaṇa*.
One should drink hot water for three days, and one should drink hot milk for three days.

Having drunk hot ghee for three days, one should subsist on air for three days; this is declared to be the *taptakṛcchra*. When performed with cold [substances], it is proclaimed as the *śītakṛcchra*.
The *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of subsisting on milk for twenty-one days.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass;
[these are for one] reciting [the mantra] until the end.
A fast for one night is known as the *kṛcchra* penance, and the *śāntapana*; when this is repeated, it is known as the *mahāśāntapana*.

Then, practicing each one for three days is known as the *atiśāntapana* penance; fasting for twelve days constitutes the penance called *parāka*. Eating once a day for three days, then eating only at night for three days, and then eating only unsolicited food for three days, performed in that sequence, [constitutes another form].
Having fasted according to the Prājāpatya rite, one quarter of the Kṛcchra penance is completed;
a month-long penance with fruits constitutes a Phala-kṛcchra; with Bilva fruits it is declared a Śrī-kṛcchra;
with lotus seeds it is a Padma-kṛcchra, and with flowers it is a Puṣpa-kṛcchra.
Likewise, the *patrakṛcchra* is performed with leaves, while the *toyakṛcchra* is performed with water;

similarly, the *mūlakṛcchra* is performed with roots. By subsisting for a month on curd, milk, or buttermilk, or by eating only as much food as fills the palm of one's hand, there occurs the *vāyavyakṛcchra*.
By consuming sesame seeds for twelve nights, one performs the *āgneya-kṛcchra*, which removes affliction;
likewise, by consuming a handful (*prasṛti*) of parched grain for a fortnight, it becomes the *brahmakūrca*.
Having fasted on the fourteenth day, immediately thereafter on the fifteenth day—
A man who, having first eaten sacrificial food (haviṣya), consumes the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) twice a month for one month, is liberated from all sins;
this applies to one desiring prosperity, one desiring nourishment, one desiring heaven, or one seeking the destruction of evil.
"Devoted to the propitiation of the deities and performing difficult penances, he partakes of all [merits].
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "Expiation for Secret Sins and the Like," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Chapter One Hundred and Seventy-Two: The Story of the Great Sage Agastya and the King of Vidarbha; the Birth of the Elephant and the Boar; the Story of the Great Sage Agastya and the King of Vidarbha; the Birth of the Elephant and the Boar.

Then the one hundred and seventy-second chapter begins. The venerable Sūta said: O Brahmins, I shall now relate the story of the great sage Agastya and the king of Vidarbha, as well as the birth of the elephant and the boar. Listen with attention. Formerly, there was a king named Vidarbha who ruled over the city of Kuṇḍina. He was a performer of sacrifices, a donor, and a protector of his subjects. Once, while wandering through the forest for the sake of hunting, he encountered the great sage Agastya. Seeing that best of sages, the king bowed down and sat before him. The sage, having inquired after his welfare, spoke these words to the king: "O King, you have come here for the purpose of hunting. Why do you roam this forest? Tell me. The king said: "O holy one, I am a king who desires to protect my subjects. I wander this forest for the sake of hunting deer and other wild animals. The sage said: "O King, hunting is not at all a praiseworthy activity for those who desire dharma. It is a source of sin and leads to the destruction of dharma. Therefore, O King, abandon this practice of hunting. Protect your subjects according to dharma, perform sacrifices, give gifts, and practice penance. By doing so, you will attain the highest state. The king said: "O holy one, I am a Kshatriya by birth and duty. For me, the protection of subjects and the subduing of enemies is the foremost dharma. I cannot abandon this way of life. The sage said: "If you are unable to abandon hunting, then listen to my words. In this forest, there is a lake known as Agastyahrada. Go there and bathe in its waters. By the power of that bath, you will be freed from the sin of hunting and will attain great merit. Having been thus instructed by the sage, the king went to that lake and bathed there. By the power of that bath, he was liberated from the sin of hunting and attained great splendor. Then, O Brahmins, the king returned to his own city and ruled righteously. Now, regarding the birth of the elephant and the boar: once, while the king was wandering in the forest, he saw a great elephant and a great boar engaged in a fierce battle. Seeing that wonderful sight, the king was filled with wonder. The elephant was white as a conch shell, possessed large tusks, and was adorned with auspicious marks. The boar was dark like a cloud, possessed sharp fangs, and was endowed with great strength. As they fought, they roared loudly, shaking the earth and the forest. Seeing them, the king approached and asked the sage who was nearby: "O holy one, who are these two beings? Why are they fighting each other? The sage said: "O King, this is the elephant born from the lineage of Airāvata, and this is the boar born from the lineage of the Earth. They are fighting because of a dispute over the sovereignty of the forest. Listen to their ancient history. In former times, the gods and the demons churned the ocean of milk. From it arose the goddess Lakṣmī, the nectar of immortality, the horse Uccaiḥśravas, and the elephant Airāvata. The gods took possession of the nectar and the elephant, while the demons fled. However, the elephant Airāvata remained in the world of the gods. Later, when the gods were oppressed by the demons, Airāvata came down to the earth to help them. He wandered the earth, destroying the armies of the demons. Meanwhile, the Earth, being burdened by the weight of many beings, went to Brahmā and said: 'O Lord, I am oppressed by the weight of creatures. Please relieve me of this burden. Brahmā reflected and said: 'O Earth, go to Viṣṇu. He will take away your burden. Following his advice, the Earth went to Viṣṇu and prayed: 'O Lord, please remove my heavy burden. Puṣkara spoke regarding all expiations for sins:

Chapter 173:
Expiation (Prāyaścitta)
Agni said:
"I shall declare the expiation taught by Brahmā, which brings about the pacification of sin.
Killing is traditionally defined as an act resulting in the separation of the vital breaths."
Whether out of passion, hatred, or negligence, whether by one's own hand or through another,
he who causes a Brahmin to be killed becomes a slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmaghātaka*). This applies to all those among many who share a single purpose and bear weapons.
If there is a single killer therein, they are all considered killers.
Whether reviled, beaten, or oppressed by wealth,
[then] the karmas [arise].
They call him a slayer of a Brahmin who, for his sake, would give up his life.
But there is no sin if medical treatment or other assistance is provided, even if death occurs;
likewise, there is no sin in disciplining a son, a pupil, or a wife.
One who, having carefully considered the place, the time, one's own capacity, and the nature of the offense, acts accordingly, incurs no guilt.
A penance should be prescribed where no expiation has been mentioned.
For the sake of a cow or for the sake of a Brahmin, one should immediately renounce one's life, or cast oneself into fire; thus one is liberated from the murder of a Brahmin.
Carrying a skull as his bowl, bearing a banner, subsisting on alms, and making his deed known,
the slayer of a Brahmin shall attain purification by eating sparingly for twelve years;
a man who is a slayer of a Brahmin is purified by practicing pure conduct for six years.

That penance which has been prescribed for killing me unintentionally is remembered as being doubled for one who acts out of desire; however, for one intent on killing, it shall be a three-year penance.
For killing a Brahmin, the penance for a Kṣatriya is double; for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, it is double again (i.e., fourfold and sixfold respectively).

In other cases, it is considered to be the full amount for a Brahmin, one-quarter less for a Kṣatriya, and half a quarter (one-eighth) for a Vaiśya. For an old man, a woman, a child, or one who is ill, the same applies to a Kṣatriya.
It is traditionally taught that for the killing of a Kṣatriya, the penance is one-fourth of that for killing a Brāhmaṇa;
for a Vaiśya who is established in his duty, it is one-eighth; and for a Śūdra, it should be known as one-sixteenth.
Having killed a woman who is not corrupt, one should perform the vow prescribed for killing a Śūdra.
The killer of a cow shall drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and remain self-restrained for a month;
sleeping in a cow-pen and following the cows, he is purified by the gift of a cow.
Alternatively, he may perform the Kṛcchra or Atikṛcchra penance, with a reduction of one-quarter for each successive social class beginning with the king.
One should not [perform] the consecration for one who is excessively old, excessively emaciated, excessively young, or diseased; [and] in the case of its destruction, however... [text fragment].
Having killed [a bird], a twice-born man should perform the half-vow according to the previously prescribed rule;
he should feed Brāhmaṇas according to his ability and give gold, sesame seeds, and so forth.

One should designate the killing of a cow in that case by means of a fist, a slap, or a blow, as well as by the breaking of its horns and so forth, or by striking it with a club and the like; likewise by restraining, tethering,
or yoking it to a cart and such.
If death occurs due to a pillar, a chain, or a noose, one should perform a penance amounting to three-quarters [of the prescribed rite];
for a wooden object, one should perform the *śāntapana* penance; for a clod of earth, the *prājāpatya*; for a stone, the *taptakṛcchra*; and for a weapon, the *atikṛcchra*.
Having killed a cat, an iguana, a mongoose, a frog, a dog, or a bird, one should drink milk for three days and perform the Cāndrāyaṇa Kṛcchra penance;
this vow applies when the act is committed in secret, as well as when it is done openly.
One hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) should be performed for the removal of all sins.
[The following are] drinks: grape juice, madhuka juice, date juice, palm juice, sugarcane juice, madhvīka, ṭaṅkamādhvīka, and maireya.
Liquors derived from coconut and other grains are not [considered] *madya*, yet *paiṣṭī* liquor is declared the primary *surā*;
it is forbidden for the three twice-born classes, and even after drinking it, one becomes pure by performing penance and drinking water.
For the purpose of removing the sin of drinking liquor, one should eat either grain-husks or oil-cake once at night for a year,
wearing matted hair and carrying a skull-topped staff;
likewise, if one has unknowingly consumed feces, urine, or anything touched by liquor, [the same penance applies].
Furthermore, the three twice-born castes must undergo purification again;
one who has drunk water remaining in a vessel that held liquor must observe a vow for seven days,
while one who has drunk the water of a *caṇḍāla* must observe a vow for six days.
Having drunk from the wells or vessels of Caṇḍālas, a twice-born man should perform the Śāntapana penance;
having drunk the water of outcastes, he should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) at the end of three nights.
Having drunk water containing fish, thorns, snails, conchs, oyster shells, or cowrie shells, or having drunk newly collected rainwater, one is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having drunk water from a well that contained a corpse, one is purified after three nights.
Having eaten the food of those who dwell at the very fringe of society, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
in times of distress, however, one is purified by mental remorse alone after eating in the house of a Śūdra.
A Brāhmaṇa who has eaten from the vessel of a Śūdra is purified by fasting and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Food cooked with roots, food cooked with fats, fat itself, curd, and parched grain flour—these are not blameworthy when received from a Śūdra, as are molasses, milk, meat broth, and the like.
One who eats without having bathed shall fast; however, by reciting prayers at the end of the day, he becomes pure.
Having become impure by voiding urine or excrement, or after eating, one becomes pure after three nights.
Likewise, food that has hair or insects fallen into it, that has been intentionally touched with the foot,
that has been looked upon by a killer of an embryo, or even that which has been touched by a woman in her courses [is purified in the same manner].
Having eaten food that has been pecked at by crows and other such birds, touched by a dog, or smelled by cows and the like, one should fast for three days;
however, one who has consumed semen, feces, or urine should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
For a *navaśrāddha*, a *cāndrāyaṇa* is prescribed; for a monthly (*māsika*) rite, a *parāka* is considered appropriate.
For a three-month period, it should be an *atikṛcchra*; for six months, a *kṛcchra*.
For an annual rite (*ābdika*), it should be a *pādakṛcchra*; and for a subsequent annual rite (*punarābdika*), a single day's penance.

If one has consumed forbidden food on the day preceding the annual *vārṣika* śrāddha, or on the following day when the annual *ābdika* śrāddha is performed, the expiation is fasting; likewise for having eaten *bhūstṛṇa* or garlic.
Having eaten garlic or leeks, one should perform the Śiśuka penance.

One should perform the *śiśukṛcchra* penance; thus it is stated in the Kha...
[text].
Furthermore, having eaten the food of those whose food is unfit to be consumed, or the leavings of women and Śūdras, [one must likewise perform this penance].
Having eaten forbidden meat, one should drink milk for seven nights; likewise,
he who eats honey or meat, or food from a house of impurity due to birth or death,
whether he be a student, an ascetic, or one under a vow, shall perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance.
Theft is defined as the taking of another's property by improper means.
A thief of gold is purified by being struck with a club by the king;
he should sleep on the ground, wear matted hair, and subsist on leaves, roots, and fruits.
Eating [only once] at a single time for twelve years, he is purified.
A thief of gold, a drinker of liquor, a killer of a Brahmin, or one who violates the Guru’s bed—
if a man has committed theft or drunk liquor, he should perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year.
For the theft of gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver,
iron, bronze, or stones, as well as for the abduction of human beings, women, fields, or houses, one should subsist on grain-particles for twelve days.
For the theft of large and small wells or ponds, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed;
likewise for the theft of edible and consumable foods, as well as vehicles, beds, and seats,
and of flowers, roots, and fruits, purification is attained through the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
For grass, wood, trees, dried food, molasses,
clothing, leather, and meat, there shall be a fast for three nights;
likewise for the wife of one's father, a sister, and the daughter of one's teacher.
One who approaches the wife of his teacher, his daughter, or his own [daughter] is a violator of the guru’s bed;
having been addressed as such, he shall be cooked in a heated iron vessel,
and by embracing a blazing iron image of a woman, he is purified at death.
Or, having practiced the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months,
one who has violated the Guru’s bed should perform this same rule even in the case of women who have fallen from their status.
Whatever penance is prescribed for a man who has sexual intercourse with another's wife, that same vow he shall cause her to perform if she has shed semen upon virgins, Cāṇḍāla women, or daughters;
however, in the case of the wives of one’s own sapinda relatives, the abandonment of life is ordained.
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by consorting with a *vṛṣalī* for a single night,
he removes by constantly reciting [the sacred texts] for three years;
the same applies to approaching the wife of a paternal uncle or the wife of a brother.

Whether she be a Cāṇḍālī or a Pukkāsī, a daughter-in-law, a sister, a female friend, a paternal or maternal aunt, one who has been entrusted to him, one who has sought refuge, a maternal uncle’s wife, a sister, a woman of the same lineage, or another woman who desires him; AP 173.055ab.
"Having approached the wife of a disciple or the wife of a guru, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "Expiations," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.

Chapter 174:
Expiatory Rites (Prāyaścitta)
Agni said:
"Regarding the omission of the worship of the deities' hermitages and other such duties, the expiation is as follows:
in the event of an omission of worship, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and perform double the worship."
Having offered oblations with the five Upaniṣadic mantras, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas.
If a deity has been touched by a woman who has recently given birth, an outcaste, or a menstruating woman, one should recite [the mantras] a hundred times;
likewise, worship with the five Upaniṣadic mantras and bathing should be performed twice as much.
If the *homa* is omitted, one should feed the Brahmins; likewise, there should be a purificatory bath (*snāna*) and worship.
If the *homa* materials have been eaten by mice or the like, or are infested with insects, one should discard only that portion, sprinkle [the remainder] with water, and worship the deity and others.
One should discard an offering of sprouts that has been cut,
broken, or touched by those who are untouchable; likewise, at the time of worship, one should offer it in another vessel to destroy obstacles caused by gods and humans.
In the event of a transposition of the mantra, the substances, or other elements, one should recite the root mantra and then recite it again.
If the vessel falls from the hand while the deity is present, one should perform eight hundred recitations.
If the vessel is broken or lost, there must be a fast; through one hundred fire-oblations, auspiciousness shall prevail.
1. "He should offer a hundred oblations," according to the manuscripts *kha*, *cha*, and *ca*.

When remorse indeed arises in a person after a sin has been committed,
the one supreme expiation for him is the constant remembrance of Hari.

The Cāndrāyaṇa, the Parāka, or the Prājāpatya penance destroy the flood of sins; likewise, the chanting of mantras dedicated to Sūrya, Īśa, Śakti, Śrīśa, and others destroys the flood of sins. The chanting of the Gāyatrī, the Praṇava, and hymns and mantras is the ender of all sins.
With the letters beginning with *ka* joined to their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*), and with those initial letters followed by their endings,
there are separately more than ten million mantras for Sūrya, Īśa, Śakti, Śrī, and the others;
