He who provides fuel for the four seasons beginning with the rainy season,
and at the end gives a cow of ghee, shall become a Brāhmaṇa observing the fire-vow;
having observed silence during the twilight, he should give a jar of ghee at the end of the month.
The giver of sesame seeds, bells, and garments becomes happy; one who observes the Sārasvata vow, having performed a bath with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), becomes a king who gives cows for a year;
and one who eats only at night on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) should offer cooked food in the month of Caitra.
At the end of the month, the one who observes the vow of Viṣṇu, eating milk-rice and giving a pair of cows, shall go to the golden abode of Viṣṇu; he who,
having offered [food] to the ancestors and the gods, eats [the remainder], shall become a king.
The annual vows have been declared; now I shall speak of the vow for the solar transits (*saṅkrānti*).
By keeping a night vigil at the time of a transit, a man shall attain the heavenly world.
Likewise, by worshipping Śiva and the Sun on the new moon day and during the solar transits (saṅkrānti),
and by bathing Keśava with a prastha of clarified butter during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa), the wise man becomes a practitioner of the Sārasvata vow.
Ga..., gha..., cha..., and ṭa...;
and "all the vows have been declared" according to kha..., cha..., and ja...
By bathing [the image] with ghee, milk, and other substances at the equinoxes and other auspicious times, one measuring thirty-two *palas* is liberated from all sins.
The Umā-vow, which bestows prosperity upon women, is observed on the third and eighth lunar days;
by worshipping Gaurī and Maheśvara, one shall obtain good fortune.
By propitiating Umā and Maheśvara, one shall attain such things as never being separated [from loved ones].
A woman who observes the fundamental vows (*mūlavrata*), one who performs the vows of Umā and Īśvara,
or a woman who is devoted to the Sun— she shall certainly become a man.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-ninth chapter, titled "Various Vows," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter [Number] on Meditation.
Chapter 200:
The Vow of Offering Lamps (Dīpadānavrata)
Agni said:
I shall describe the vow of offering lamps, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One who offers a lamp for a year at the house of a deity or a member of the twice-born caste partakes in all blessings.
By offering lamps for four months, one attains the world of Viṣṇu; by doing so specifically in the month of Kārttika, one attains even the heavenly realm.
There has been nothing superior to the gift of lamps, nor will there ever be.
Through a lamp, one gains long life and sight; from lamps, one obtains fortune, sons, and other blessings.
The giver of a lamp attains good fortune and does not fall away from the world of heaven;
the daughter of the King of Vidarbha, Lalitā, was herself a recipient of the gift of lamps.
Cārudharman, the king, had more than a hundred wives, but she was the most preeminent among them.
That virtuous woman offered a thousand lamps in the temple of Viṣṇu.
When questioned, she spoke to her co-wives regarding the greatness of the lamp.
Lalitā said:
"In former times, Maitreya was the domestic priest of the king of Sauvīra;
by him a temple of Viṣṇu was caused to be built on the bank of the Devikā."
In the month of Kārttika, a lamp was offered by me,
prompted by fear of a cat that was about to perish at the edge of my mouth;
then, with a mouse as its wick, it blazed forth and attained extinction [of darkness].
The daughter of the king died and was reborn as more than a hundred queens. That which I did for him— an act of instigation even though it was not intended by him—
is the fruit he now enjoys, resulting from that lamp offered at the temple of Viṣṇu.
Indeed, because of this, I remember my past lives; therefore, I offer lamps day and night.
One who gives a lamp on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) truly rejoices in a celestial chariot in heaven.
But one who steals a lamp is born either mute or indeed mentally dull.
"Indeed, one falls into a blind, impassable darkness in hell.
To the men who are crying out, struck by the servants of Yama, [the messengers] say:
'Enough with these lamentations! What fruit is there in your wailing even here?'"
When, after being utterly neglected by the heedless throughout thousands of previous births, a living being finally attains a human birth,
why does that self, still exceedingly deluded, rush headlong toward sensual pleasures?
That which was one's own welfare [was abandoned] for the sake of the relish of sense-objects; now that lamentation has arrived here.
(Note: *harṣitam* is found in the manuscripts kha, ga, and gha.)
"It has been defiled," [so they say].
But what has been done previously is experienced; have you not considered this?

Anointing the breasts of another's wife may bring you pleasure for a moment, but it surely brings suffering; the taste of sensual objects lasts but a brief instant, yet it yields misery for many millions of years.
Alas, mother! Why do you lament over that which is sung as the seizing of another’s wife?
What burden is too great for the tongue in the constant chanting of Hari’s name?
For even when oil is of little cost, fire is always obtained from it.
Since you were unable to give, you took a lamp of Hari; that is what brings you this suffering.
"Now, what is the use of lamentation? Endure that which has come upon you.
Having heard these charming words spoken by Agni, they went to heaven because of their gift of lamps.
Therefore, by the gift of a lamp, the fruit of vows is even greater.
Thus ends the two-hundredth chapter, titled "The Vow of Giving Lamps," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 201:
The Worship of the Ninefold Array (Navavyūhārcana)
Agni said:
I shall describe the worship of the ninefold array as taught by Hari to Nārada.
One should worship Vāsudeva, whose seed-syllable is "a-vī," in the center of the lotus within the mandala.
Āvīja and Saṅkarṣaṇa in the south, Pradyumna in the southwest, Aniruddha in the west, and Nārāyaṇa in the waters.
One should place Sad-Brahmā in the southeast (anila), Huṃ for Viṣṇu, Kṣauṃ for Nṛsiṃha in the north, Bhūḥ for Varāha in the northeast, and at the western door;
then Kaṃ, Ṭaṃ, Saṃ, and Śaṃ for Garuḍa at the eastern face and the south.
*Khaṃ chaṃ vaṃ huṃ phaṭ*, and *khaṃ ṭhaṃ phaṃ śaṃ* for the mace in the rite;
*baṃ ṇaṃ maṃ kṣaṃ* for the Lord of the Corner, and *ghaṃ daṃ bhaṃ haṃ*.
One should worship Śrī;
and in the south and north, Puṣṭi. With their respective seed-syllables—gaṃ, ḍaṃ, baṃ, and śaṃ—at the western side of the seat; and with dhaṃ and vaṃ, one should worship Vanamālā in the west.
One should worship Śrīvatsa with *saṃ*, Haṃsa with *haṃ*, Kaustubha in the water with *laṃ* and *chaṃ*,
and the tenth limb, Taṃ, with *taṃ* and *yaṃ*; one should worship Viṣṇu with "Obeisance to Ananta" below,
and the four pitchers beginning with Mahendra in the east and other directions, starting from the ten limbs.
Having meditated upon the arches and the canopy with the seed-syllables of Fire, Wind, and the Moon,
and having worshipped the body within the mandalas in due order, one should then float upward;
thereafter, one should meditate on the subtle form of the self as situated in the sky.
And that very seed of one's own self, which is nectar prepared by being immersed in white nectar flowing from the lunar disc.
While being generated, one should conceive of oneself as the Person (Puruṣa).
Having arisen, one is Viṣṇu himself; one should then place the twelve seed-syllables:
the heart, the head, the crest, the armor, and the weapon.
One should again assign the *astra* [mantra] to the chest, head, crest, back, and eyes; having assigned it to both hands, one then becomes possessed of a divine body. (krūṃ viṣṇuṃ, kṣauṃ nṛsiṃhakam).
2. And the king of birds on the right—thus [in manuscript] Ṅa. 3. And submerged in the white and black—thus [in manuscripts] Kha and Ja:
Just as one does for oneself, so too should one perform the placement [of mantras] upon the deity and likewise within the body of the disciple.
Worship performed in the heart is known as *anirmālya* (without remains); worship of Hari in a mandala and the like is *sanirmālya* (with remains), and the disciples should have their eyes bound.
One should cause the disciple to take the name of whichever deity the flower falls upon his image.
Having seated the disciples to the left, one should offer sesame, rice, and ghee;
having performed one hundred and eight oblations, one should then perform a thousand for the purification of the body.

Having offered more than a hundred complete oblations for the forms and limbs of the Navavyūha, the Guru should initiate them; and he, being worthy of worship, should be honored by them with those riches.
Thus ends the section titled "The Worship of the Navavyūha" in the Agni Mahāpurāṇa.
The two hundred and first chapter.
Chapter 202: The Narration of the Teacher Puṣpa.
Agni said:
Hari is pleased by flowers, perfumes, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
I shall now tell you which flowers are suitable for the deity and which are unsuitable.

The *mālatī* is the most excellent flower, as is the *tamāla*, which bestows both enjoyment and liberation; the *mallikā* destroys all sins, while the *yūthikā* grants the world of Viṣṇu. Likewise, that which consists of *atimukta* flowers and the *pāṭalā* grant the world of Viṣṇu.

By offering *karavīra* flowers one goes to the world of Viṣṇu; by *javā* flowers one becomes meritorious; and by offering *pāvantī*, *kubjaka*, and other such flowers, as well as *tagara*, one attains the world of Viṣṇu.
Through *karṇikāra* flowers one reaches the world of Viṣṇu; through *karuṇṭha* flowers, the destruction of sins; and through lotuses, *ketakī*, and *kunda* flowers, the supreme goal.
By means of *vāṇa* flowers, *varvarā*, and black flowers, one becomes a partaker of the world of Hari.

Likewise, with *aśoka* flowers, *tilaka*, and similarly with *aṭarūṣa* flowers, one partakes in liberation; with *bilva* leaves, one attains the supreme goal; and with *śamī* leaves, one reaches the world of Viṣṇu.
Likewise, with *bhṛṅgarāja* and the petals of the *tamāla*, one likewise attains the world of Viṣṇu.
Tulasī known as Kṛṣṇa and Gaurā, as well as Kalhāra and Utpala; with a garland of the meritorious Padma, Kokanada, and Śatābja lotuses, and with Nīpa, Arjuna, and Kadamba flowers, Hari [is pleased].
And with fragrant *vakula* trees,
with *kiṃśuka*, *munipuṣpa*, *gokarṇa*, and *nāgakarṇaka*,
with *sandhyāpuṣpa*, *bilvataka*, and those born of the *rañjanī* and *ketakī*— (2)
Through offerings of *kuṣmāṇḍa*, *timira*, and those arising from *kuśa*, *kāśa*, and *śara* grasses;

through *maruvaka* flowers and other fragrant leaves such as those used in gambling rituals—by means of all these offered with devotion, there is enjoyment, liberation, and the destruction of sin; for He is pleased by everything.
A flower exceeding a hundred thousand gold pieces is surpassed ten millionfold by a garland; a fruit from one's own grove is three times more meritorious than flowers from another's grove.
One should not worship Viṣṇu with withered flowers, nor with those that have extra petals, nor with those that are crushed.
Likewise with *kāñcanāra*, *unmatta*, and *girikarṇikā*; and with *kadamba* flowers, one becomes a partaker of liberation. (Variant readings:
"with *rajani* and *ketakī* flowers," as found in manuscript *kha*.)
Ṅa, cha, ja, and ca [are the vowels];
"the fruit is by means of those born in water," thus says Ṅa (fol.
With *kuṭaja*, *śālmalī*,
and *śirīṣa* flowers, as well as fragrant *brahmapadma* flowers, [one worships] from Naraka upwards.
Hara is worshipped with flowers of arka, mandāra, and dhustūra;
one should not offer kuṭaja, karkaṭī flowers, or ketakī to Śiva.
That which arises from the pumpkin gourd or the nimba tree is demonic and devoid of fragrance.
By worshipping the gods with the eight flowers of internal disposition— non-violence, mastery of the senses, compassion, and sacred learning— one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Non-violence is the first flower; the restraint of the senses is a flower;
compassion toward all beings is the flower of all flowers;
tranquility is distinguished as a flower; self-control is a flower; austerity is a flower; and meditation is also a flower.
The seventh is truth, and the eighth is indeed truth; Keśava is pleased by these. Worshipped with these very eight flowers, Hari is truly satisfied.
"O best of men, there are other flowers here that are external;
Viṣṇu is well-pleased when worshipped with devotion by those endowed with compassion. Water from the Varuṇa [ocean], flowers, Soma-juice, ghee, milk, and curd [are also offerings]."
The offering of food and the like belongs to Prajāpati; that of incense and lamps belongs to Agni;
fruits, flowers, and so forth belong to Vanaspati as the fifth;
items such as *kuśa* grass and roots belong to Pṛthivī; and fragrant sandalwood belongs to Vāyu.
And with [flowers] produced from the *śālmali* tree (kha,
ga, ṅa); and with fragrant leaves and flowers (ṅa).
3. Hari is to be worshipped with blue lotuses—thus [it is stated] in the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ṅa*, and *ja*.
4. Non-violence is the restraint of the senses—thus in manuscript *ga*.
5. "Patience is a gift," as in [the verse beginning] "Non-violence is the first flower," and so forth;
[and] "He who is honored is satisfied."
Internal recitation: Kha,
Ga,
Gha.
Ṅa,
cha,
ja, ña, ṭa.
It is not found in the books:
"The flower of Viṣṇu, known as faith, and always these eight flowers."
The seat consists of the five limbs of the image;
or [one may perform] the eightfold flower-offering (aṣṭapuṣpikā) to Viṣṇu with [the mantras of] Vāsudeva and others, or to Śiva with [the mantras of] Īśāna and others.
Thus ends the two hundred and second chapter, titled "The Chapter on Flowers," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 203:
The Nature of Hell (Narakasvarūpa)
Agni said:
"O Deva, by worshipping Viṣṇu with flowers and other offerings, a man does not go to the hells;
at the end of his life, he is liberated from his vital breaths even against his will."
Having encountered some cause— water, fire, poison, a weapon, hunger, disease, or falling from a mountain— the embodied being is deprived of life.
It then assumes another body for its torments, according to its own past actions.
Then the evildoer experiences suffering, while he who is devoted to the Dharma experiences happiness;
the former is led by the messengers of Yama, who strike terror into living beings,
through the southern gate on the evil path, while the righteous one is led through the western gate and the others.
And by the servants commanded by Yama, one is cast into the hells. (2) [Note 1]:
"The seat is the sixfold limb of the form" is the reading in manuscript *kha*.
[Note 2]: "Is cast even into the hells" is the reading in manuscript *kha*.
"Always cast into hell" is the reading in manuscript *ṅa*; "Afflicted in hell now" is the reading in manuscripts *gha* and *cha*:
Through dharma and by relying on the arguments of Vasiṣṭha and others, one is led to heaven;
however, the killer of a cow is tormented for a hundred thousand years in the Mahāvīci hell,
as are the slayer of a Brahmin and the stealer of land, who are cast into a fiercely blazing jar of raw clay.

One who kills women, children, or the elderly is tormented slowly in the Raurava hell until the great dissolution; one who sets fire to houses, fields, and so forth is tormented in the fierce Mahāraurava hell for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
That thief is burned for one kalpa and shall fall into the Tāmisraka hell;
for many kalpas he is pierced with spears and other weapons by the servants of Yama,
and in the Mahātāmisraka hell he is tormented by serpents, leeches, and the like.
As long as one remains on the level of a matricide and the like, one dwells for many eons in the *asipatravana* hell, being struck by swords,
and in the *karambhavālukā* hell,
where people who have been burned there are further scorched by the sands and other such things.
In Kākola, one eats the excrement of worms while eating sweets alone;
in Kuṭṭala, one eats urine and blood, having abandoned the performance of the five sacrifices;
and in Sudurgandha, one eats blood and becomes a consumer of forbidden food.
One who inflicts pain on others is crushed like sesame seeds in the oil-press;
one who kills those who have come for refuge is cooked in the oil-press.
One who destroys gifts and one who sells liquids at a sacrifice is cast into the Nirucchvāsa hell.
The liar falls then into the Vajrakavāṭa hell;
the one of evil intent into Mahājvāla; those who have gone to forbidden women into Krakaca; and the adulterer into Guḍapāka.
He strikes at the vital points of others.
[In the verse] "in the Asipatravana with fires," the reading in manuscript *ṅa* is "gurupāke ca" (and in the intense heat), while manuscripts *kha* and *ja* also contain this.
The killer of living beings [suffers] on a razor-edged blade; the stealer of land on an iron frying pan; the stealer of cows or gold on a tree-cutting thunderbolt weapon.

A stealer of honey is tormented in Kālasūtra; one who steals for the sake of others is in Kaśmala; a consumer of excessive meat is in Ugragandha; and one who fails to offer funeral cakes is in Durdhara. Furthermore, those who were fond of taking captives are in Kācabhakṣī.

O Mañjuśrī, one who reviles the sacred teachings goes to the Loha hell; one who bears false witness goes to the Pūtivaktra hell; one who plunders wealth goes to the Pariluṇṭha hell; one who kills children, women, or the elderly goes to the Karāla hell; and one who causes suffering to Brahmins goes to the Apratiṣṭha hell.
A Brahmin who drinks liquor falls into Vilepa; one who steals land falls into Mahātāmra (20).
Likewise, having violated another's wife, he must embrace a glowing iron slab in Śālmalī;
and a woman who has had intercourse with many men must embrace a blazing iron image of a man in Tamāla.

Those who have sexual intercourse with their mothers, daughters, and others are thrown into a heap of glowing coals; thieves are sliced with razors; and those who eat meat, having consumed their own flesh, have their tongues split open and torn out.
Indeed, a man who observes a month-long fast does not go to hell;
likewise one who performs the vow of Ekādaśī or the vow of Bhīṣmapañcaka.
Thus ends [the section] titled "Description of the Nature of Hell" in the Agni Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Two Hundred and Three.

Chapter Two Hundred and Four: The Chapter on the Four [Additional] Hundreds.
Agni spoke regarding the vow of fasting for a month:
"And the vow of fasting for a month..."
I declare to you that which is most excellent:
having performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice and obtained the permission of one's guru,
and having assessed one's own strength through such penances as the Kṛcchra, one should undertake a month-long fast.
O Sage, whether he be a forest-dweller, an ascetic, or even a widow,
one should fast on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina and undertake this vow for thirty days.
"From this day forward, O Viṣṇu, until your awakening,
I shall indeed worship you while fasting for thirty days—
during the months of Kārttika and Āśvina, until your awakening."
"If I were to die in the interval, may there be no violation of my vow for me.
Bathing three times a day, the man observing the vow should worship Viṣṇu three times with perfumes and flowers,
reciting songs and other hymns to Viṣṇu, and practice meditation.
One should avoid idle talk and abandon the desire for wealth;
one should not touch anyone who does not observe vows, nor should one disturb those engaged in improper actions.
(204.007cd) Note 1: According to the manuscripts *gha* and *ja*, "vow" (*vrata*) refers to the practice known as fasting for a month (*māsopavāsa*).
One should avoid longing for food;
one should remain in the temple of the deity for as many as thirty days.
Having worshipped on the twelfth day and fed the twice-born, the observer of the vow,
having concluded the rite and given the sacrificial fee, should perform the breaking of the fast;
he attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation for thirteen kalpas.
One should cause a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice to be performed and worship thirteen Brahmins;
one should provide them with as many pairs of garments, vessels, and seats,
as well as umbrellas along with sacred grass rings (pavitra), and likewise pairs of sandals.

One should give a yogapaṭṭa and a sacred thread to a brahmin; by these [acts], he is so regarded. Furthermore, having worshipped a golden image of Viṣṇu upon the bed for another brahmin, one should likewise worship one's own image with garments and other offerings.
"Completely liberated from all sins by the grace of Viṣṇu, I shall go to the world of Viṣṇu; I myself become Viṣṇu.
Go, go, O Devabuddhi, to the healthy abode of Viṣṇu!"
There, the observer of the vow, assuming the form of Viṣṇu, should remain in a stainless celestial chariot;
then, he should offer that bed to his guru,
and having delivered a hundred generations of his lineage, he shall lead them to the world of Viṣṇu.
Whatever region a person who observes a month-long fast resides in shall become pure;
how much more so the entire family in which such a practitioner of the month-long fast dwells?
Seeing one established in the vow who has fainted, one should cause them to drink milk and clarified butter.
These do not destroy the vow, nor the oblation approved by the Brahmins.
(Variant readings: *tataḥ pānayutāni* and *vai nata*).
Having bowed to the twice-born, he then [offered] milk, water, roots, and fruits as beneficial medicine for his guru. (AP 204.018ab)
"Viṣṇu, the maker of great medicine, shall deliver one from this vow.
Thus ends the two hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Vow of Monthly Fasting," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 205:
The Bhīṣmapañcaka Vow (The Five-Day Vow of Bhīṣma)
Agni said:
I shall describe the Bhīṣmapañcaka, the king of vows that bestows everything;
one should perform it on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika.

Bathing three times a day for five days, likewise with the five grains and sesame seeds, he should satiate the gods, ancestors, and others; remaining silent, he should worship Hari. Having bathed the deity with the five products of the cow and the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), [he should proceed].
Having anointed [the image] with sandalwood and other unguents, one should burn guggulu resin mixed with ghee.
One should offer a lamp day and night, and present the finest cooked rice as an offering.
One should recite the mantra "Oṃ namo vāsudevāya" one hundred and eight times.
1. "Likewise with barley, rice, and sesame seeds," as found in the manuscripts gha, ṅa, cha, and ja;
Then the observer of the vow should offer oblations of sesame seeds and rice smeared with clarified butter,
using the six-syllable mantra accompanied by the utterance of *svāhā*.
On the second day, he should worship the feet with lotuses, and on the third, with bilva leaves.
On the third day, one should smear the knees and thighs with *bhṛṅgaraja*;
on the fourth and fifth days, with *vāṇa*, *bilva*, and *javā*.
On the eleventh day, one should lie upon the ground and consume cow dung.

Cow’s urine, curd, and milk—on the fifth day, the practitioner of the vow should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); on the full moon day, he should eat only at night; by performing this, the practitioner shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, just as Bhīṣma attained Hari through that very practice.
The Brāhmaṇa [should perform] the Bhīṣmapañcaka vow, consisting of worship and so forth, as well as fasting and other observances;
thus ends the section named Bhīṣmapañcaka in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
The two hundred and fifth chapter.
Chapter 206:
The Narration of the Offering of the Arghya Water to Agastya
Agni said:
"The venerable Agastya is Viṣṇu; by worshipping him, one attains Hari before the sun reaches the sign of Virgo, within three days and three quarters."
1. "He obtained Hari; therefore this [is so]"—thus [it is] Ga... / "He reached Hari; therefore this [is so]"—thus Ṅa... / "He attained Hari; therefore this [is so]"—thus Ja... and Ṭa...
2. From worship [arises] fivefold merit; from fasting, the vow of the goat (ajavrata)—thus in the manuscripts *ga*, *gha*, and *ṅa*.
Having fasted and performed worship, one should offer an *arghya* oblation to Agastya. (AP 206.002ab) ja.. , ña.. , ḍa.. ca :p 249.

At twilight, one should place an image made of kāśa flowers in a jar and worship that sage situated within the vessel; during the night, O tiger among sages, O Agastya of great intellect, mass of splendor, one should keep a vigil.
"Accept this worship performed by me together with your beloved;
having invoked [the deity] and presented the water-offering (arghya), one should worship him face-to-face with sandalwood paste and other substances.
Having brought the arghya in the morning near a body of water, one should offer it."
Resembling a *kāśa* flower, born from fire and wind,
son of Mitra and Varuṇa, O pot-born one, homage be to you! By whom the great asura Vātāpi and Ātāpi were devoured.
"May that Agastya, by whom the ocean was dried up, stand before me.
I shall entreat Agastya with my actions, my mind, and my speech;
I shall honor that friend out of a longing for the world beyond."
Let sandalwood— the king of all trees, born in another continent, most beloved by the gods,
the vessel for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and the destroyer of evil— be accepted.
"May this flower garland, which bestows good fortune, health, and prosperity, be accepted;
may this incense be accepted, O Lord, and grant me unwavering devotion.
Grant me my desired boon and a fortunate rebirth in the hereafter."
O best of sages, O bestower of the fruits of all desires,
O mass of splendor, O you of great radiance!
Cha, ja, jha, ña, ṭa, and ca.
"O mass of splendor, Lord of the World," [is found in] manuscript Ṅa; "arisen from fire and wind," [is found in] manuscript Jha;
and "accept this sandalwood of mine," [is found in] manuscripts Ja and Ña.
"Indeed, this guest-offering has been given by me with garments, rice, fruits, and gold;
I shall now inform Agastya of that which was conceived by my mind."
"I shall offer you an arghya with fruits; accept this arghya, O great sage.

Chapter Two Hundred and Eleven: The Account of the Birth of Kārttikeya from Śiva and Pārvatī and His Conquest of the Asuras. The venerable Sūta said: O Brahmins, I shall now relate the birth of Kārttikeya from Śiva and Pārvatī, as well as his conquest of the Asuras. Listen with focused attention. Formerly, the gods, led by Indra, were oppressed by the Daityas, who had become exceedingly powerful through the boons they had received. Unable to endure that oppression, the gods sought refuge with Brahmā. Having approached him, the gods, their faces downcast, spoke these words to the Grandfather (Brahmā): "O Lord, we have been overcome by the Daityas, who have gained strength through boons. We are unable to withstand them; therefore, please grant us protection. Hearing the words of the gods, the Grandfather reflected for a moment and then spoke to them: "O gods, I shall tell you the means by which you may obtain victory over the enemies of the three worlds. Go to the mountain Himavat; there, you will find the daughter of the Mountain King, Pārvatī, who is endowed with supreme beauty and virtue. She is the wife of Śaṅkara. Together with her, Śiva will perform severe penance on the peak of Himavat. From the union of those two, a son shall be born who will be invincible even to the gods, the Asuras, and the Yakṣas. He will be the slayer of the enemies of the gods and the protector of the three worlds. Having heard these words of the Grandfather, the gods, filled with joy, went to the mountain Himavat. There they saw Pārvatī, the daughter of the Mountain King, who was radiant like ten million moons and possessed of great beauty. Seeing her, they were struck with wonder. Then, accompanied by Nārada, they went to the hermitage of Śiva. Having arrived at the hermitage, they beheld the Lord, whose form was like ten million suns, seated upon a bull and adorned with the crescent moon. Prostrating themselves before him, the gods spoke these words: "O Lord of the Gods, we have been oppressed by the Daityas. Please grant us protection. Hearing the words of the gods, Śiva, the benefactor of the world, spoke to them with a smile: "O gods, I know the cause of your distress. I shall go to the mountain Himavat and perform penance there together with Pārvatī. From our union, a son shall be born who will be the destroyer of the enemies of the gods. Therefore, O gods, you must remain vigilant and protect the three worlds. Having spoken thus to the gods, Śiva departed for the mountain Himavat. Arriving there, he performed severe penance along with Pārvatī. As they practiced their austerities, a great light shone forth, illuminating the entire universe. The gods, seeing that light, were filled with wonder and fear. Then, from the union of Śiva and Pārvatī, a being was born who was like ten million suns. He had six faces, twelve arms, and four feet. He held a spear, a trident, a sword, a shield, a bow, and arrows in his hands. He wore a tiger skin and was adorned with various ornaments. Seeing that extraordinary child, the gods were amazed. They offered him worship and praised him with hymns. Then, having taken leave of Śiva and Pārvatī, the gods returned to heaven. The child, known as Kārttikeya, grew up and became a great warrior. He conquered all the Asuras and established the sovereignty of the gods. Thus ends the account of the birth of Kārttikeya and his victory over the Asuras. May this story bring peace and prosperity. The venerable Sūta said: O Brahmins, I have related to you the wonderful birth of Kārttikeya and his conquest of the Asuras. This narrative bestows merit, fame, and long life. One who hears it with devotion is liberated from all sins. Therefore, one should always listen to this sacred story with a pure heart.

Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Account of the Birth of Kārttikeya from Śiva and Pārvatī and His Conquest of the Asuras," in the Skanda Purāṇa. May there be peace. May there be auspiciousness. May there be well-being. Om Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ. Om.
Regarding various gifts, Agni said:
"One who possesses ten cows should give one cow; one who possesses a hundred cows should give ten."
One who gives a hundred [cows] and one who gives a thousand cows— indeed, they all possess equal fruit.
Where there are palaces made of gold, where there is that stream of wealth (vasordhārā),
and where there are Gandharvas and Apsarases, there go those who give a thousand.

By the gift of a hundred cows, one is liberated from the ocean of hell; by giving even a single heifer, one is glorified in the heavenly world. Through the gift of a cow, one obtains long life, health, good fortune, and heaven.
May she who is the auspicious queen of the world-protectors, Indra and the others,
by virtue of the greatness of this gift of a buffalo, grant all my desires in order to assist Dharmarāja.
May she whose son is established [as a deity],
she who is the mother of Mahiṣāsura, be a granter of boons to me;
through the gift of a buffalo one attains good fortune, and through the gift of a bull one goes to heaven.
The gift known as the "row of yoked plows" bestows all fruits;
a row is said to consist of ten wooden plows joined with oxen.
By giving these, bound with golden bands, one is glorified in heaven.
The passage beginning with "By the gift of a hundred cows" and ending with "granting all desires" does not appear in manuscript Jha.
2. Regarding the majesty of the King of Dharma (Dharmarāja), [it is said]:
"By giving ten tawny cows (kapilā) at Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara... (Folio 265).
The fruit of that is said to be inexhaustible upon the liberation of a bull;
dharma consists of four feet, and these four are dear to you.
Homage to you, O Lord of the gods who are benevolent toward Brahmins, nourisher of the ancestors, spirits, and sages!
Since you are liberated, may my worlds be imperishable and free from affliction.
May I owe no debt to the deities.
The elemental, the ancestral, and the human—
may that dharma which is yours, and whatever destiny belongs to one who has taken refuge in you, be my certain fate.
With this mantra, he should strike with the discus and the trident and release [the victim].

On the eleventh day after the death of a person, for whomsoever a bull is released, he is liberated from the world of the departed (preta). [This applies also] at the six-month and annual rites. A nivartana consists of thirty kuṇḍas, each being ten cubits [in measure].
A "cow-skin" (gocarma) is those same [ten] in extent; one who bestows that becomes a destroyer of sin.
He who offers a black antelope skin accompanied by cows, land, and gold—even if he has performed every kind of evil deed—shall attain union with Brahman.
One should give a vessel filled with sesame seeds and likewise filled with honey,
as well as one Magadhan measure of black sesame seeds; and having given a high-quality bed, one attains merit.
One shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
likewise, by fashioning and giving a golden image, one attains heaven for oneself;
and by constructing and giving a spacious house, one shall partake in both enjoyment and liberation.
The fruit of that shall indeed be inexhaustible;
[this refers to] the release of the bull.
And from the release of the bull—thus [is it said] in Ja;
"then divine" in Kha and Cha; and "the giver of that [is] the dispeller of sin" in Śa.
"tatprado 'ghajiditi" is found in manuscripts Gha and Ṅa; "yastu kṛṣṇājinaṃ dadediti" is in manuscript Ṭa;
and "dattvottamaguṇāmiti" is in manuscript Gha.
By giving a house, a monastery, an assembly hall, or a celestial dwelling, and by providing shelter for travelers and building a cowshed, one becomes free from sin and attains heaven.
By the gift of a buffalo to Yama, one becomes free from sin and attains heaven.
Brahmā, Hara, Hari, and the messengers of Yama stand in the midst of the gods;
having severed his head with a noose, he who gives it [as a gift] shall become a partaker of heaven.

Having accepted this gift called "Three-Faced," the twice-born man who bears sin should fashion a silver disc, place it upon his head, and cause it to be given to another twice-born man; this is the great Kālacakra, joined with gold.
He who gives iron equal in weight to his own body shall not go to hell;
he who offers an iron staff weighing fifty palas, having wrapped it in cloth, to a Brahmin, incurs no punishment from Yama.
One should offer roots, fruits, or other substances, whether combined or individually,
with the intent of conquering death, in order to increase one's lifespan.
A man [representing the deceased] should be fashioned from black sesame seeds, with teeth of silver and eyes of gold.
Long-armed, with a sword raised in his hand, he has a discus of hibiscus flowers;
wearing red garments and garlands, he is adorned with a necklace of bones;
his feet are shod with a pair of sandals, and a black woolen blanket rests at his side.
And having worshipped that Kālapuruṣa on the left, who holds a lump of flesh, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa with perfumes and other offerings.
One shall be free from death and disease and become a sovereign lord of kings;
by giving a cow and a bull to a twice-born man, one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having worshipped [the deity] with garments, perfumes, and other offerings,
and having given a golden horse presided over by Revanta, one does not suffer death.
By giving even a single [gift] such as a bell filled [with grain], one becomes a partaker of enjoyment and liberation;
he who bestows gold attains all desires.
When gold is being given, however, silver is desired as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
For other gifts as well, gold is prescribed as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
as are silver, copper, rice, and grain.
The daily *śrāddha*, the worship of the gods—all this is without a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Silver is the fee for the ancestors, the means for accomplishing dharma, desire, and wealth.
Gold, silver, copper, gems, pearls, and riches [are also such means].
The one of great wisdom who gives land gives all this;
he satisfies the ancestors dwelling in the world of the fathers and the deities in the abode of the gods— he who, with a tranquil soul, bestows the earth.
Whether it be a market town, a hamlet, or a village abounding in grain;
or even a hundred nivartanas, or half of that, or houses and the like;
or even a piece of land the size of a cow-hide—by giving such earth, one becomes a partaker of all things.
Just as a drop of oil spreads upon water,
so does the fruit of all other gifts follow one birth;
but the fruit of gifts of gold, land, and cows follows seven births.
Having rescued twenty-one generations of his lineage, the giver of a maiden partakes in the world of Brahmā.
By giving an elephant along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one becomes stainless and attains heaven.
By giving a horse, one obtains long life, health, good fortune, and heaven.
By giving a maidservant to a preeminent brahmin, one shall attain the world of the Apsarases. AP 211.039ab.
By giving a copper vessel weighing five hundred *palas*,
or half of that, or even half of that again, one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
By giving a cart yoked with oxen, one becomes a partaker of the celestial realm through that vehicle.
By the gift of clothing, one obtains long life, health, and imperishable heaven;
by giving grains such as wheat, rice, and barley, one becomes a partaker of heaven.
[One should also give] a seat, a metallic vessel, salt, and fragrant sandalwood.
By offering incense, lamps, betel, iron, silver,
and gems, as well as various divine substances, one shall partake in both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
and by giving sesame seeds and vessels of sesame, one shall attain heaven.

There is no gift superior to the gift of food; there has been none in the past, nor will there ever be. The gifts of elephants, horses, chariots, female and male slaves, and houses do not equal even a sixteenth part of the gift of food.

Even after committing a very great sin, he who subsequently becomes a giver of food is liberated from all sins and attains imperishable worlds. By providing water and establishing water-stations (*prapā*), one shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
By giving firewood and fuel at crossroads and other such places, one obtains radiance and other benefits;
one is served in a celestial chariot in heaven by goddesses, gandharvas, and women.
By giving ghee, oil, and salt, one obtains everything.
1. "Thereafter, one shall obtain enjoyment increased by half of that half [of the previous amount]," thus it is said in the *Cha* manuscript.
2. "Incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), betel, iron, and gems," thus it is said in the *Kha* manuscript.
3. "One shall obtain a blazing fire," thus it is said in the *Ṅa* manuscript.
By giving an umbrella, sandals, wood, and so forth, one shall dwell happily in heaven on the primary lunar days and during the *yogas* such as *viṣkumbha*.

Having worshipped Hari, Hara, Brahmā, the world-protectors, and others at the beginning of Caitra, at the start of the year, and at the commencement of the asterism Aśvinī, giving gifts yields great fruit;
likewise, [the planting of] trees and groves, providing food and the like, and the construction of roads and rest-houses.
By providing an oil massage for the feet and other such services, one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In this world, cows, land, and the gift of knowledge (*sarasvatī*) yield equal fruits.
By bestowing the divine *sarasvatī* (the Vedic knowledge), one becomes stainless and partakes in the world of Brahmā.
He who bestows the knowledge of Brahman is the giver of the earth with its seven islands;
that man who grants fearlessness to all beings partakes of everything.
Whether it be the Purāṇa, the Bhārata, or even the Rāmāyaṇa— 211.53cd.
By having a book written and giving it as a gift, one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
He who teaches the Vedas, the scriptures, dance, and song becomes a dweller in heaven;
he should provide wealth to his teacher and food and other necessities for his students.

What would be given by one who desires the Dharma and perceives [the truth] that has not been given? One obtains the entire fruit of a thousand Vājapeya sacrifices properly bestowed through the gift of knowledge; of this there is no doubt.
He who causes a book to be read shall always be a giver of all gifts; he does so in a temple of Śiva, a house of Viṣṇu, or likewise in a sanctuary of the Sun.
In the three worlds, there are the four castes and the four stages of life, each distinct.
All deities, beginning with Brahmā, are established in the gift of knowledge;
he is honored in heaven.
"One shall become happy in heaven"—thus [it is stated] in the *Gha* and *Ṅa* manuscripts, p.
Knowledge is a cow that milks all desires; knowledge is the unsurpassed eye. (AP 211.059ab)
By the gift of the Upavedas, one rejoices together with the Gandharvas;
by the gift of the Vedāṅgas, one attains the heavenly world;
and by the gift of the Dharmaśāstras, one rejoices together with Dharma itself.
By bestowing the established doctrines (siddhāntas), one attains liberation without a doubt;
moreover, by the gift of a book, one obtains the merit of imparting knowledge.
By giving the Śāstras and the Purāṇas, one shall obtain everything.
He who instructs his disciples shall obtain the fruit of the *puṇḍarīka* lotus;
by giving that which one lives upon, there is no end to the fruit.
One should give whatever is most excellent in the world and whatever is dear to oneself.
One who desires that [the merit] for the ancestors be inexhaustible should give everything to them;
he who, having worshipped Viṣṇu, Rudra, the Lotus-born [Brahmā], the Goddess, Vighneśvara, and the others, offers the articles of worship, partakes of all [merit].
By having a temple and an image constructed, one shall obtain everything;
by performing sweeping and smearing [the floor], a person becomes stainless;
and by performing various mandala rites, one shall become a sovereign of mandalas.
By offering incense, flowers, incense smoke, lamps, food offerings, circumambulation,
bells, banners, canopies, spectacles, instrumental music,
songs, and garments and other gifts to the deity, one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should offer musk, śihlaka, śrīkhaṇḍa, aguru,
camphor, musta, guggulu, and vijaya. [The passage beginning with "sammārjana" and ending with "maṇḍalādhipatir bhavet" is the reading.]
[This] is not in the manuscript:
Having performed the rite with a prastha of ghee on the occasion of a saṅkrānti and so forth, he partakes of all [merit].

A bath is known to require one hundred palas, while an anointing requires twenty-five palas; a great bath (mahāsnāna) is proclaimed to require a thousand. For ten offenses, [the debt] is removed by water, and for a hundred, by bathing with milk.
By offering a thousand [cows] with milk, curd, and ghee, ten thousand are desired.
Having given female and male slaves, ornaments, cattle, land, horses, elephants,
and so forth to the God, one who possesses good fortune and wealth shall go to heaven.
Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "Various Gifts," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 212:
Meru-dānas (Gifts of Mount Meru)
Agni said:
"I shall describe to you the optional gifts that bestow all desires. Having performed the regular worship month after month, one should then perform the optional worship."
One who worships the Guru with the offering appropriate for the vow, performs a great worship at the end of the year, and in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa offers a horse— or indeed a lotus made of flour—
to Śiva after having worshipped him, shall dwell in the world of the Sun for a long time.
"He shall dwell for a long time in the heavenly world," according to manuscripts *ga*,
*gha*, *ṅa*, and *ṭa*;
"He shall dwell for a long time in the world of Śiva" [according to others].
In the month of Pauṣa, by offering an elephant made of flour, one shall deliver twenty-one generations of one's lineage.
By giving a flour-made horse-chariot in the month of Māgha, one would go to hell;
but by giving a flour-made bull in Phālguna, one becomes a lord of the earth enjoying heaven.
And in Caitra, one should give a cow made of sugarcane, accompanied by male and female slaves.
Having given [these], one dwells for a long time in heaven and, at the end of that, becomes a lord of the earth.
By giving seven grains of rice in Vaiśākha, one becomes identical with Śiva. And by making an offering-circle (*balimaṇḍalaka*) with food in Āṣāḍha, one becomes Śiva.
Having given a celestial chariot made of flowers in the month of Śrāvaṇa, that king then goes to heaven;
having given two hundred fruits and uplifted his lineage,
that king should burn guggulu and other incenses in Bhādrapada, and thereby he shall go to heaven.
A vessel filled with milk and ghee given in the month of Āśvina leads to heaven;
O King, by giving jaggery, sugar-candy, and ghee in Kārttika, one thereafter becomes a dweller in heaven.
I shall now describe the twelve-fold Meru-gift, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, during the Meru-vrata, one should bestow a Meru of jewels upon a brahmin;
hear now the dimensions of all these Merus in order:
they are known as Vajra, Padma, Mahānīla, Nīla, and Sphaṭika.

The best [type of mandala] consists of one *prastha* each of emerald, pearl, and flowers; the middling should be half that, and the lowest half of that again. One should avoid stinginess regarding wealth.
One should place Mount Meru in the pericarp (*kārṇikā*), with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa as its presiding deities.
Mālyavat is to be worshipped in the east, and to its east is the one known as Bhadra;
Aśvakarṇa is declared to be there, and Niṣadha is to the south of Meru.
Then Hemakūṭa and Himavat—these three are likewise in the north.
Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgin are in the west; Gandhamādana, Vaikaṅka, and Ketumāla— Meru is joined by these twelve.
Having fasted and performed his ablutions, he should worship Viṣṇu or Śiva before the deity; and having worshipped Mount Meru with mantras, he should indeed give it to a Brahmin.
To the Brahmin of such-and-such a lineage, he should give this supreme Meru made of material substance.
For the sake of enjoyment, liberation, and purity, I give this Viṣṇu-deity to you.
Having uplifted your lineage, you shall sport in a celestial chariot, honored by the gods, in the worlds of Indra, Brahmā, Śiva, and the city of Hari.
On other occasions as well, such as the solar transits (saṅkrānti) and so forth, one should cause [the gift] to be given.
With a thousand palas of gold, one should fashion Mount Meru,
provided with three peaks and endowed with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
One should cause each of its mountains to be fashioned with one hundred [parts] each;
together with Meru, there are thirteen mountains renowned therein.
During the solstices, eclipses, and so forth, having worshipped Hari in front of Viṣṇu—
Having offered a golden Mount Meru to a brahmin, one shall dwell for a long time in the world of Viṣṇu.
For as many atoms as there are here, so long shall that king remain;
he who, through his resolve, gives a silver Mount Meru accompanied by the twelve mountains [attains the same].
And the previously mentioned fruit is attained by worshipping Viṣṇu and a Brahmin; having assigned the earth, Meru, a region, a mandala, or even a village [as the gift],
the remaining portions are calculated as one-eighth.
As before,
having conceptualized the fruit as being equal to twelve mountains in the form of elephants and Mount Meru,
one should give it.
1. *Gha*, *ṅa*, and *ña* are the maṇḍala; *ga* and *jha* are the village itself; *ṭa* is the remainder of the limbs. Thus [it is said] in the *Kha*.
One should give [a gift] endowed with three persons; having given it, one obtains infinite fruit.
[One should give] the Aśvamedha-Meru with fifty-three horses, joined with twelve horses.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu and the other deities and offered that [gift], the king shall become one who has enjoyed all pleasures.
According to the number of horses, he should give a "mountain of cows" as before;
and in the center, a "mountain of cloth" consisting of silk garments weighing a full *bhāra*.
Having offered twelve garments and mountains, one obtains that inexhaustible fruit;
and with five thousand palas of ghee, there is a mountain of clarified butter.
On each of these mountains, one should worship Hari with five hundred [offerings].
Having offered everything before Viṣṇu to a Brāhmaṇa, one attains Hari;
and likewise, by making and giving a Khaṇḍameru, one obtains the fruit.
A Dhānyameru consists of five khāris, while another consists of single khāris each.
All [the peaks] should have three golden horns; having worshipped Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, or especially Viṣṇu among them all, one obtains inexhaustible fruit.
In this manner, one should fashion a mountain of sesame seeds measuring one-tenth [of the original].
Its peaks are as before, and likewise those on other mountains;
having given Tilameru, one partakes of the world of Viṣṇu along with one's kinsmen.
"Salutations to the one whose nature is Viṣṇu, salutations indeed to the upholder of the earth."
To the one whose peaks are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa; who is situated at the navel of the earth;
the lord of the twelve mountains; the remover of all sins;
the devotee of Viṣṇu; the peaceful one—grant me protection in every way.

"Free from sin, together with my ancestors, I go to Viṣṇu; Om, salutation! [I am] a partaker of the world of Brahmā along with my kinsmen. Thus [it is said]. Ap 212.035ab. n. 1 Jha. reads "bandhubhir brahmalokabhāk".
You are Hari; before Hari, I am Viṣṇu,
and I offer this with devotion to Viṣṇu for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the two hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Gifts of Meru," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 213:
Gifts of Land (Pṛthvī-dāna)
Agni said:
I shall describe the gift of the earth; the earth is considered to be of three kinds:
[the first] consists of seven continents and oceans, measuring one hundred crore yojanas.
That supreme earth is said to extend as far as Jambūdvīpa;
one should fashion it with five bhāras of gold,
and likewise prescribe a tortoise and a lotus made from half that amount.
The earth is said to be excellent when it consists of two parts; it is middling with three parts, and inferior with four parts,
according to the reduction by one-third in the *kūrma* and *paṅkaja* [lotus] types.
One should fashion a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpapādapa*) with a thousand *palas*;
it should be provided with a root, a trunk, leaves, and endowed with fruits and flowers. (Note 1:
*svalpā sā tu tribhāgena* is found in manuscripts Ṅa and Ṭa.)
Having mentally conceived the five aggregates, the wise man should cause the five [offerings] to be given;
the giver of this rejoices for a long time with his ancestors in the world of Brahmā.
In front of Viṣṇu, one should [offer] the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) made of five hundred palas;
within that cow reside the gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
The gift of a cow is the gift of all things, it bestows everything, and it grants the world of Brahmā.
Having given a tawny cow (*kapilā*) before Viṣṇu, one may deliver one’s entire lineage;
having adorned a woman and given her away, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*);
and by giving land that yields all kinds of crops, one shall partake of everything.
Whether giving a village, a city, or even a small settlement, one who performs the rite of releasing a bull becomes happy and delivers his lineage.
Thus ends the two hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "Gifts of the Earth," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 214:
The Narration of the Greatness of Mantras
Agni said:
I shall describe the wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra), by the knowledge of which Hari is known.
Below the navel is the bulb (kanda), from which sprouts have emerged.
1. "One shall obtain the fruit of a human sacrifice" (naramedhaphalaṃ labhet) — thus in manuscripts *ga*, *ṅa*, and *ña*.
2. "Or a city and a pond" (purīṃ vāpīm) — thus in manuscript *kha*.
3. "At the beginning of Kārttika and so forth" (kārttikādau) — thus in manuscripts *kha* and *ṭa*.
"By practicing [this], one may deliver one's lineage"— thus it is stated in the manuscripts *ga*,
*gha*, *ṅa*, and *ṭa* on page 277.
Seventy-two thousand [channels] are situated in the center of the navel;
they pervade everywhere— sideways, upwards, and downwards—
and these ten principal channels are arranged like a wheel.
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, as well as Suṣumṇā; Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā, Pṛthā likewise;
Alambuṣā and Huhu, and Śaṅkhinī is recorded as the tenth.
These ten channels are proclaimed as the carriers of the vital breaths:
prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
The first of the ten winds is indeed *prāṇa*, and it is their sovereign.
Residing in the chest of living beings, this *prāṇa* constantly causes the vital breath to flow from exhalation toward inhalation, perpetually filling it.
Because the vital breath (prāṇa), which rests upon the individual soul (jīva), performs the act of departure through exhalation, inhalation, and coughing, it is therefore proclaimed as "prāṇa.
The downward-moving breath (apāna), however, leads food down into the lower parts of men.
The wind that carries urine and semen is celebrated as apāna;
the wind named samāna brings together what has been drunk, eaten, and smelled, as well as blood, bile, phlegm, and wind within the limbs.
The wind named udāna makes the lower lip and the face quiver and provokes redness in the eyes; it agitates the vital points (marmas). Vyāna causes the limbs to bend and provokes disease.
Likewise, from the throat comes *pratidāna*, and from *vyāpana* it is called *vyāna*;
*nāga* is said to be in belching, and *kūrma* resides in the opening of the eyes.
*Kṛkara* is indeed for eating; *Devadatta* is for yawning.
*Dhanañjaya* resides in the sound and does not leave even when one is dead.
Life (*jīva*) departs in ten ways, for by that [wind] the wheel of channels is [sustained].
The transits, the equinoxes, the days, nights, and solstices;
the intercalary month, the debt, as well as the deficient night and the wealth [of the surplus night].
The deficient night is hiccup, and the intercalary month is yawning.
In this context, coughing is considered a debt and exhalation is called wealth.
The northern [channel] is to be known as the left, while the right is designated as the southern;
that which issues from between the two nostrils is declared to be the equinox (*viṣuva*).
Furthermore, its transition occurs from its own place through the conjunction of places:
O Brahmin, Suṣumṇā is established in the central limb, Iḍā in the left, and Piṅgalā in the right; the upward vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed known as the day.
Apāna is the night; thus, the single vital air is tenfold in nature.
Āyāma, situated in the middle of the body, is considered the lunar eclipse (soma-grahaṇa). They know that āyāma which transcends the body is the solar eclipse (āditya-grahaṇa).

One should fill the abdomen with air as much as desired; this is the *prāṇāyāma* known as *pūraka*, which fills the body. Having closed all the gates [of the senses], one remains free from inhalation and exhalation.
That breath control (prāṇāyāma) in which one remains like a completely filled pitcher is called *kumbhaka*.
Then, the knower of mantras should release the air upward with a single exhalation;
joined with the practice of exhaling, he should expel the air upward.
1. "It is so, it is so" (balantatheti) [is the reading in] Ña... 2. "Power is spoken of" (balamucyate) [is the reading in] Ña... and Jha:
Since Śiva, residing within one's own body, utters [the mantra] spontaneously,
therefore that alone is called "japa" by those who know the reality.
Two tens of thousands, one thousand, and likewise six hundred.

In a single day and night, that lord of yogis performs the recitation of the *ajapā* Gāyatrī, which is [the essence of] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. For one who recites this *ajapā*, rebirth no longer exists.
The primordial Kuṇḍalinī is considered to be conjoined with the Moon, Fire, and Sun;
she is to be known as residing in the region of the heart, situated in the form of a sprout.
Therein occurs the placement of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa), for that indeed depends upon creation.
The best of the virtuous (sāttvika) should contemplate nectar flowing therein;
he who is within the body is to be known as "with parts" (sakala), while he who is devoid of the body is "without parts" (niṣkala).
He who should utter "Haṃsa, Haṃsa" is the Swan, the God Sadāśiva.
Just as oil is contained in sesame seeds and fragrance is inherent in a flower, so does that [Self] abide within and without the body of a person.
Brahmā has his station in the heart; Viṣṇu is established in the throat.
Rudra, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), resides in the forehead;
one should know Śiva to be at the tip of the vital breath (prāṇa), and that which is both supreme and non-supreme (parāpara) is at its end.
He is declared to be "with parts" (sakala) in five ways, but when reversed, he is fruitless (niṣphala).
If one, having raised the *prāsāda* sound, recites the hundred-syllable mantra while engaged in yoga, one attains perfection within six months; of this there is no doubt.
Through the knowledge of the coming and going [of breath], the destruction of all sins occurs.

I have described the *prāsāda* mantra as being gross (*sthūla*), subtle (*sūkṣma*), and supreme (*para*);
one should perceive the *prāsāda* in three ways: short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*).
The short [syllable] burns away sins; the long one bestows liberation;
and the prolated one, adorned with a bindu upon its head, serves for nourishment.
For the purpose of slaying, the syllable *phaṭ* is beneficial at the beginning and end of the short [mantra].
The heart-mantra is proclaimed for both the beginning and the end, as well as for the summoning [of the deity].
One should stand and recite the mantra five hundred thousand times over the southern form of the Lord;

A mantra thus nourished shall effect subjugation, eradication, and other such rites.
That twice-born one who understands the three voids— the void above, the void below, and the void in the middle which is free from affliction— is certainly liberated.

He who does not know the temple (prāsāda) which is the great body of the five mantras, endowed with thirty-eight parts (kalās), is not called an Ācārya; likewise, he who knows the Oṃkāra, the Gāyatrī, Rudra, and so forth, is a Guru.

Regarding the ritual of the twilight prayers (*sandhyāvidhi*), Agni said:
"He who thoroughly understands the syllable *oṃ* is a yogi; he is Hari, the Supreme Person."
Therefore, one should practice the syllable *oṃ*, for it is the essence of all mantras and bestows everything;
in the application of all mantras, the *praṇava* is traditionally held to be the foremost.
Whatever rite is fully completed with that is truly complete, and nothing else.
The three imperishable Great Utterances preceded by the syllable *oṃ*,
together with the three-footed *Sāvitrī*, should be known as the mouth of Brahman.
He who studies these daily for three years without interruption [attains that state].
Becoming like the wind and possessing the form of space, he attains Brahman, the Supreme.

For one who performs supreme austerities through breath control, there is nothing higher than the single-syllable Brahman; and for one devoted to the Sāvitrī, there is nothing higher than silence; truth is superior even to silence.
Seven recitations remove sins; ten bring one to heaven;
but that goddess, when recited twenty times, leads one indeed to the abode of Īśvara.
Having chanted it one hundred and eight times, one has crossed the ocean of saṃsāra.
The Gāyatrī is superior to the recitations of the Rudras and the Kuṣmāṇḍas;
there is no recitation higher than the Gāyatrī, and no oblation equal to that of the Vyāhṛtis.
Even a quarter-verse of the Gāyatrī, or half a verse, or even a single Ṛc-verse [is supreme].
The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, the theft of gold,
and even the violation of the teacher’s wife— she purifies herself from these by means of *japa* alone.
When a sin has been committed, an oblation with sesame seeds and the recitation of the Gāyatrī are prescribed.
Having recited the Gāyatrī a thousand times while fasting, one becomes a destroyer of that sin—
even if he is a killer of cows, a killer of his father, a killer of his mother, a killer of a Brahmin, or one who has violated the teacher’s bed.

A killer of a Brahmin, a thief of gold, or a drinker of liquor is purified by reciting [the Gāyatrī] one hundred thousand times; or else, having bathed, he should recite it one hundred times while submerged within the water.
By drinking water one hundred times while reciting the Gāyatrī, he becomes a destroyer of sin.
The Gāyatrī, when recited one hundred times, is remembered as the pacifier of sins;
when recited one thousand times, that Goddess destroys minor offenses (upapātaka). When recited ten million times, she grants all desires; by this, one attains divinity and sovereignty.
Having first uttered the syllable *oṃ*, as well as *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*,
the *gāyatrī* and the *praṇava* at the end— this is declared for the recitation (*japa*). Viśvāmitra is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *gāyatrī* is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and Savitṛ is likewise the deity.
The application [of the mantra] is for recitation during the ritual of approaching the deity, as well as for silent recitation and for oblation.
[The deities are: Agni, Vāyu, Ravi, Vidyut, Yama, Varuṇa (Lord of Waters), Guru, Parjanya, Indra, Gandharva, and Pūṣan immediately thereafter.
Mitra, Varuṇa, Tvaṣṭṛ, the Vasus, the Maruts, Śaśin,
Aṅgiras, Viśva, the two Nāsatyas, Ka, as well as all the deities,
Rudra, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu are, in order, the presiding deities of the syllables.
At the time of reciting the Gāyatrī, these [parts of the body] are said to destroy sin:
the two big toes, the two ankles, the two shanks, the two knees,
the two calves, the penis, the two testicles, the waist, the navel, and likewise the abdomen.

the two eyes, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, the front of the face, and the right and left sides of the head— these are the locations of the [vital points] in sequence.
Yellow, dark-blue, tawny, emerald-green, resembling fire,
shining like gold, lightning, smoke, black, red, fair, sapphire-blue,
crystal-like, golden, and pale-white; the ruby possesses all these splendors.
Golden, smoky-grey, red, blue, crimson, black, and golden-yellow are the colors of the Gāyatrī in sequence;
when meditated upon at the time of visualization, she removes sins, and when offered oblations, she grants all desires.
An oblation with sesame seeds accompanied by the Gāyatrī mantra destroys all sins.
One desiring peace should perform it with barley; one desiring long life, with clarified butter;
for the success of one's undertakings, with white mustard seeds; and for spiritual luster, with milk.
Likewise, one desiring a son [should offer] with curd; one desiring grain with *śāli* rice;
for the pacification of afflictions by planetary spirits, with fuel-sticks from milk-exuding trees;
likewise, one desiring wealth with *bilva* fruits, and one desiring prosperity with lotuses.

One desiring health should indeed perform it with *dūrvā* grass during a portent involving a preceptor; one desiring good fortune with *guggulu* resin, and one seeking knowledge with milk-rice (*pāyasa*). Through ten thousand recitations, success as described shall be attained; through a hundred thousand, that which is desired by the mind.
By ten million [repetitions], one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin; such a person becomes a Hari who uplifts his lineage.
Alternatively, a sacrifice to the planets (*grahayajña*) is the primary means, or a fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of ten thousand [offerings] accomplishes one's purpose.

Having sipped water again, one should touch the heart, the navel, and the shoulders.
The seer of the *praṇava* is Brahmā, and its meter is indeed the *gāyatrī*.
Its deity is Agni, and it is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); this is indeed the yoga for all ritual acts.
The goddess Śuklā, whose mouth is fire, belongs to the lineage of Kātyāyana.

The divine Trailokyavaraṇā is joined with the support of the earth; the auspicious goddess, bearing the thread of the imperishable, is seated upon a lotus throne. Oṃ! Come, O Goddess Varadā; be present for my recitation.
Prajāpati is indeed the seer of all the vyāhṛtis.
The syllable *oṃ*, the imperishable Brahman, consists of both its individual parts and their combination.
Viśvāmitra, Yamadagni, Bharadvāja, Gautama,
the sage Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Kāśyapa follow in due order.
Agni, Vāyu, Ravi, Vākpati, Varuṇa,
Indra, and Viṣṇu are the deities of the vyāhṛtis in their respective order; likewise, Gāyatrī, Aṣṭi, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, and Paṅkti are the meters.
They say that *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* are the meters for what has not been specifically mentioned;
this applies to the ritual application (*viniyoga*) of the *vyāhṛtis*, as well as to breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and fire offerings (*homaka*).
For these, the verse beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭha" or "drupadād īva" is traditionally prescribed for the water libations.
"Or [the verses] beginning with *drupadādīni* by means of the *ṛc*s," as found in the manuscripts designated as Ṅa, Ja, and Ña,
on page 285.
Likewise, at the end, one should sprinkle eight drops upward with the *hiraṇyavarṇā* and *pāvamānī* verses to overcome the sins committed since birth; then,
while submerged in water, one should recite the *ṛtaṃ ca* verse and the *aghamarṣaṇa* three times.
For this verse beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," Sindhudvīpa is remembered as the seer (*ṛṣi*);
for the purpose of the Brahma-bath, its meter (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī and its deity (*devatā*) is Water;
it is employed for the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) and for the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the horse sacrifice (*kratu*).
For the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta, the seer (ṛṣi) is Aghamarṣaṇa himself;
the meter (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh, and its deity (daivata) is Bhāvavṛtta.
Furthermore, "Āpō jyotī raso 'mṛtam" is remembered as the head (śiras) of the Gāyatrī.
The seer is Prajāpati; his mantra is a *yajus* devoid of meter (*chandas*).
Brahmā, Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya are proclaimed as its deities.
Through the restraint of breath, Vāyu arises, and from Vāyu, Agni is born.
From fire comes water; from that comes purification, and from that one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
He moves within all beings, in the secret cave of those who possess manifold forms.
He is austerity, sacrifice, and the exclamation vaṣaṭ; he is water, light, essence, and the immortal.
The seer of "ud u tyam jātavedasam" is said to be Praṣkanna;
the meter is declared to be Gāyatrī, and Sūrya is indeed the deity. Its application is in the Atirātra sacrifice, and Agniṣoma is the presiding deity.
In the hymn beginning with "citraṃ devānām," the seer is declared to be Kautsa;
its meter is Triṣṭubh, and Sūrya is proclaimed as its deity.

Chapter Two Hundred and Sixteen: The Chapter on the Sixteen [Additions] to Two Hundred.
Agni spoke on the Nirvāṇa of Gāyatrī:
"Having thus performed the ritual of the Sandhyā, one should mutter and meditate upon Gāyatrī."
Because she protects her disciples through song, as well as her wife and her very life-breaths, she is remembered as Gāyatrī;
because she is from the Sun (Savitṛ), she is Sāvitrī; and because she reveals [all things] and consists of the form of speech, she is Sarasvatī.

That light is the supreme Brahman; it is remembered as *bharga* because it is splendor (*tejas*). For the root *bhā* is used in the sense of shining, while the form *bhrasj* is used in the sense of cooking.
Furthermore, it is remembered that it cooks herbs and the like; likewise, the root *bhrāj* would be used in the sense of shining.
*Bharga* is so called because it shines (*bhrājate*); this is frequently stated in the Vedic hymns (*chandas*). It is *vareṇya*, meaning most excellent among all splendors, indeed the supreme state;
for it is always to be chosen by those who desire heaven and liberation.
Because the root *vṛ* has the meaning of "choosing," we meditate upon that Lord— the Truth which is devoid of waking, dreaming, and other states, eternally pure, awakened, and one;
we contemplate "I am Brahman," the supreme light, for the sake of liberation.
That light is the Blessed Viṣṇu, the cause of the birth and other states of the world;
some recite it as Śiva, and others recite it as the form of Śakti;
some, the Vedic scholars who maintain the sacred fires, recite it as Sūrya, and others as Agni.
"From the body and likewise from the vital breaths"—
in the beginning of the Vedas, Viṣṇu, whose form is fire and so forth, is indeed sung as Brahman.
That supreme station of the divine Viṣṇu Savitṛ is remembered as the great clarified butter (*ājya*); for the Lord Hari, the self-luminous,
is pressed out as the rain-god Parjanya, the wind, and the sun, and he ripens [all things] through cold, heat, and so forth.
An oblation duly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, and from rain, food; from that, living beings arise.
Let us hold this in our minds with the thought, "May we support [them]."

Neither glory nor splendor belongs to us; rather, it is He who impels and directs the intellects of all living beings— the intelligence of all experiencers in all their actions regarding both seen and unseen results— He who possesses the forms of Viṣṇu, Sūrya, and Agni.
Impelled by the Lord, one may go either to heaven or even to the pit of dogs;
this entire world, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), is pervaded by the Lord.
Hari, the God who sports with heavens and other realms, is that very Person, the Sovereign.

This Puruṣa, who is within the sun and is indeed called Bharga, should be beheld by those seeking liberation through meditation within the solar orb, for the sake of destroying birth and death and the threefold suffering.
The Reality in the assembly is the Consciousness-Brahman, which is the supreme station of Viṣṇu;
it is indeed the fourth state (*turīya*), the excellent splendor (*bharga*) of the divine Savitṛ.
From the body and the waking state up to Brahman, we meditate with the thought, "I am Brahman."
"That person who is in the sun, he am I—the infinite Om.
He who always sets in motion the knowledge of auspicious actions and the like.

Salutation to the one whose mark is the self of all, to the one whose mark is the limbs of all worlds;

Salutations to the one whose mark is the Puruṣa; indeed, salutations to the one whose mark is the states of being.

Agnī said: Puṣkara then spoke concerning the consecration of a king to Rāma, who was indeed inquiring about the duties of a king.
"Just as it was told at the beginning, so shall I tell you the remainder, O Vasiṣṭha.
Puṣkara said:
"I shall proclaim the duty of kings, which is superior to all other duties of kings."
The king shall be the slayer of enemies and the protector of his subjects; wielding just punishment, he will protect you all and practice his vow while abiding in the Dharma.
After one year, the king should select a priest who is twice-born,

as well as ministers who possess knowledge of the self in its entirety; then, at the proper time and with all necessary materials, he should consecrate his queen, who possesses the characteristics of righteousness.
When the king has died, one should perform [the rites]; no restriction of time is prescribed here.
Having had the astrologer and the domestic priest bathe with sesame seeds and white mustard, and having proclaimed victory for the king, the king shall sit upon the auspicious throne.
The protector of the kingdom should proclaim safety and release [the prisoner] from the dungeon.
Before the consecration, the domestic priest should perform the propitiatory rite dedicated to Indra.
On the day of the consecration, having fasted, he should offer oblations with the sacred mantras into the fire upon the altar.

whose roar is like a multitude of chariots or a cloud; and which is smokeless.

First, O King, the monarch should cleanse his head with earth from the summit of a mountain;

One should likewise cleanse the right arm with earth dug up by an elephant's tusk,
the left arm with earth dug up by a bull's horn,

one should consecrate the king— seated upon an auspicious throne— with the five products of the cow over his head, using four jars filled with water by the four ministers.

Then the preeminent Brāhmaṇa of the Ṛgveda should perform the consecration of the king with honey, and the Brāhmaṇa of the Sāmaveda with water from *kuśa* grass.
Likewise, the domestic priest, having gone to the pitcher containing the collected remnants (*sampāta*), [should perform the rite].
Having duly performed the protection of the fire among the members of the assembly,
O highly fortunate one, he should likewise give [the offerings] to the Brahmins with the sounds of those mantras which have been proclaimed for the consecration of royal glory.
Then the domestic priest should go to the very base of the altar;
he should consecrate [the king] with a hundred-holed golden vessel,
reciting the verse beginning with "yā oṣadhīḥ" for the medicinal herbs and the verse beginning with "ratha" for the fragrant substances.

One should touch [the disciple] with flowers while reciting "puṣpavatī," with seeds while reciting "brāhmaṇī," with gems while reciting "āśuḥ śiśānaḥ," and with kuśa-grass water while reciting "ye devāḥ" and "gandhadvārā."
O twice-born ones, they should anoint the head and throat with yellow pigment (rocanā) and with the waters of all sacred fords;
while accompanied by the sounds of songs, musical instruments, and the like, and by whisks, fans, and other such items,
they should carry a pitcher filled with all medicinal herbs before the king.
The king, having worshipped Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra and the other lords of the planets, and [offered] ghee along with auspicious items and the like, should look into that mirror.
1. And likewise the base of the altar (vedīmūla), as well as the *iri-kha*... 2. With lamps—thus [it is] in manuscript Ṅa. 3. Then the Yajurvedin and the Ṛgvedin—thus [it is] in manuscript Ṅa.
Seated upon a bed covered with a tiger skin, the domestic priest [performs] the rites beginning with the planetary offerings (*grahādika*).
Having offered the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and other honors, one should cause the binding of the turban to be performed;
and for the king, the binding of the crown should be given, followed by five skins.
With the [mantras] beginning with "dhruvādyaiḥ," one should enter the skin of a bull or that of a cat.
Then, upon his seat, there should be skins from a leopard, a lion, or a tiger;
and the usher should present the ministers, counselors, and others,
as well as the astrologer and the domestic priest with gifts of cows, goats, sheep, houses, and so forth.
Having honored the twice-born and worshipped them with offerings of other cattle, grain, and the like;
having circumambulated the fire and bowed to the preceptor; and then, having touched a bull from behind and worshipped a cow and its calf consecrated with mantras.
Having mounted a horse and honored the elephant, he should mount it;
accompanied by his forces, he should circumambulate the royal highway.
He should enter the city and, having honored all with gifts and other honors, dismiss them.
Thus ends the two hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Coronation of Kings," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 219:
The Mantras for Consecration (Abhiṣeka)
Puṣkara said:

I shall now declare the consecration mantras for kings, deities, and others, which destroy all evil. One should sprinkle [the subject] with water from a jar using *kuśa* grass; by that, everything indeed succeeds.
May the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara consecrate you;
may Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha [consecrate you].
