Chapter 220:
The Attainment of Companionship (Sahāyasampatti)
Puṣkara said:
"Once consecrated along with his ministers, that best of kings shall conquer his enemies;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should be appointed as the king's commander-in-chief."
The doorkeeper should be of noble birth, knowledgeable in the treatises on ethics, and wise in policy;
the envoy should be pleasant-spoken, tireless, and endowed with great strength. The bearer of betel—whether a man or a woman—should be devoted, capable of enduring hardship, and beloved.
A minister for peace and war should be appointed who is expert in the sixfold policy and other such matters;
there should be a sword-bearer as a protector, and a charioteer who knows the strengths and weaknesses of the forces;
the superintendent of the kitchen, stationed in the galley, should be a beneficial and wise man.

The members of the assembly should be knowers of the Dharma; the scribe should be skilled in letters; the gatekeepers should be men who know the proper time for summoning and are well-disposed. The superintendent of wealth should be one who knows gems and other valuables, and the man in charge of the treasury should be trustworthy.
A physician who knows the science of Ayurveda, a superintendent of elephants who is an expert in horses and the like,

an elephant-rider who has conquered fatigue, and a superintendent of horses who is like [an expert] in horses and the like; a superintendent of fortresses who is well-disposed and wise, and an architect who knows the science of architecture (vāstuveda).
One who is skilled with weapons released from machines, those released by hand, those not released, and those held while being released; one who is proficient in wrestling and beneficial to the king;
and an elderly superintendent of the inner apartments who is fifty years of age.
Women [should be honored],
while men aged seventy years may engage in all ritual activities.
He should remain awake in the armory; having understood [the situation], his course of action is ordained.
Having discerned actions as superior, inferior, or middling, the king should employ men accordingly as superior, inferior, or middling.
Desiring to conquer the earth, the king brought together allies who were most righteous in their religious duties, heroic in the acts of battle,
and likewise pure in all respects.
He should employ eunuchs among women and fierce men in cruel tasks; whichever man the king knows to be pure in a particular matter, he should appoint that man to it.
He should employ those who are base in matters of dharma, artha, and kāma, while employing the lowly in base tasks.

The king should appoint those who have been tested by means of secret trials according to their merit; and together with his ministers, he should duly appoint forest-rangers for the elephant preserves. He should also station supervisors there, intent upon tracking their footprints.
One should employ each person in that task for which they possess skill;
one should appoint servants inherited from one's father and grandfather to all duties,
except for matters concerning inheritance, for they are already united in those.
He should diligently seek out and provide shelter to people arriving from the capital of another king, whether they be wicked or virtuous; yet,
having recognized one as wicked, he should not trust him, but rather keep him under his control while employing him in his service.
One should indeed honor those who have come from other lands after discovering them through spies;
for enemies, a shower of fire, a serpent, and even a sword are all found together in the pursuit of harmful deeds against one's foes.
"Two [types of] servants are to be known as Vasiṣṭhas through their desire for support, and likewise, bad servants are on the other side. (Kha manuscript, p. 303)
A king should have spies as his eyes; he should constantly employ spies who are not known to the people, who are gentle, and who are unknown to one another— namely,
merchants, those skilled in counsel, astrologers, and physicians.

Likewise, a king should not place his trust in the outward appearance of renunciants who discern strength and weakness; rather, he should rely on the testimony of many regarding the loyalty or disloyalty of his servants and the virtues or vices of the people.
One should apply knowledge of both the auspicious and the inauspicious for the sake of mastery;
one should perform actions that produce affection, yet from straightforwardness, one should cultivate detachment. Through fortune that wins over people, a king becomes a delighter of the people.
Thus ends the two hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Allies," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 221: Then Puṣkara said:
A servant should carry out the king's command like a disciple serving his master;
he should not cast aside the king's word, but speak what is favorable and pleasing. That which is beneficial, though unpleasant, should be spoken to him when he is in private.

One who is not appointed should not seize wealth, nor should he overlook the king's honor. Likewise, the superintendent of the inner apartments should not adopt the dress, speech, or gestures of those who have been cast out due to enmity toward the king.
A servant should not enter into intimacy with the king and should guard his secrets;
having displayed some degree of skill, he should distinguish himself before the king.
One should not disclose to the world any secret that has been communicated by the king;
when another task is being commanded, one should say, "What shall I do?
and one should wear the clothing, jewels, and ornaments bestowed by the king.
One should not enter the presence of the King on unsuitable ground;
one should avoid yawning, spitting, coughing, anger, leaning against a support, frowning, flatulence, or belching in his vicinity. (3)
One should skillfully employ others to proclaim one's own virtues.
Deceit, greed, backbiting, atheism, meanness,
as well as fickleness— these must always be abandoned by one who serves a king.
Having united himself with learning, sciences, and arts through his own efforts, one who increases prosperity should finally engage in service to the king for the sake of his own welfare;
furthermore, he should always pay homage to the king’s beloved ministers as if they were his own sons.

One should not place trust in his ministers; one should act in a manner pleasing to the king's mind. A wise man should abandon one who is disaffected and seek his livelihood from one who is well-disposed.
Unless asked, he should not speak to him, though he may act as he desires in times of distress.
He is gracious, he grasps what is said, and he does not hesitate regarding secrets; he does not retain what is given by the king,
nor [does he accept] what is not specifically assigned.
One should avoid *ga*, *gha*, *ña*, and *ca* three times; likewise, one should avoid *ga*,
*gha*, *ja*, and *ṭa*.
4. *niyojayet* according to Ga., Gha., and Ña;
5. *bhūtivardhanīm* according to Ga. and Ṭa.
He offers inquiries regarding [the listener's] virtue and so forth, and provides a seat;
delighted by hearing his discourse, he welcomes even unpleasant words as if they were in the Nandana grove,
accepts even a small gift, and remembers it even amidst other conversations.

Thus, one who is devoted [to his master] should perform service; he should avoid serving anyone else. Thus ends the two hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Conduct of a Servant," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 221:
The Perfection of Fortifications (*Durgasaṃpatti*)
Puṣkara said:
I shall describe the perfection of a fortress; a king should dwell in a fortified region that consists mostly of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, and which is likewise impregnable to others.

A region that is somewhat associated with Brahmins, where many rituals are performed, which does not depend on rain for its sustenance, where water is available through irrigation, and which is praised as being free from oppression by others and endowed with flowers, fruits, and grain— is highly commended.
Impassable to enemy armies and free from wild beasts and thieves,
the powerful king should dwell there after constructing one of the six types of forts: a fort of bows, a fort of earth, or likewise a fort of men.
O Bhārgava, the forest-fortress, the water-fortress, and the mountain-fortress exist;
however, the mountain-fortress is the best of all, being impenetrable and capable of breaking through others. It is endowed with flowers, fruits, grain, and wealth.
And there, in front, [he sees] marketplaces and the like, as well as temples and other such dwellings of deities.
I shall now describe the protection of kings; a king must be protected from poison. An excellent fortress should be provided with engines of war and weapons, and supplied with water.
Śirīṣa, possessing five parts [roots, bark, leaves, flowers, and fruits], when ground with urine, destroys poison.
Śatāvarī, chinnaruhā, viṣaghnī, taṇḍulīyaka,
koṣātakī, kalhārī, brāhmī, citrapaṭolikā,
maṇḍūkaparṇī, vārāhī, dhātrī, and ānandaka.
Unmādinī, somarājī, and gems that destroy poison;
dwelling in a fortress endowed with the characteristics of a proper site, one should worship the gods,
protect the subjects, conquer the wicked, and cause gifts to be bestowed.
By stealing the property of the gods and the like, one shall dwell in hell for an eon; therefore,
a king devoted to the worship of the gods should construct temples for the gods,
protect the abodes of the deities, and install the divine images.

A temple made of wood is more meritorious than one made of clay; a temple made of bricks is more meritorious than one made of wood; a temple made of stone is more meritorious than one made of bricks; and a temple made of gold and jewels is more meritorious than one made of stone.
By playing and constructing such a divine abode, one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One who provides paintings, gifts of song, instrumental music, spectacles, and the like,
and who bathes the deity with oil, clarified butter, honey, milk, and other substances, shall go to heaven.
A king should honor and protect the Brahmins, and he must not seize the property of the twice-born.
One who steals a single piece of gold, a single cow, or even a single inch of land, goes to hell until the dissolution of all things at the end of the aeon;
yet one should not harbor hatred toward a person of evil conduct, even if that person is established in every kind of sin.
There is nowhere a sin more grievous than the killing of a brahmin;
they could make a non-divine being divine, and they could make a divine being non-divine.
For the brahmins are indeed highly fortunate; one should always pay homage to them.
A weeping brahmin woman destroys the family, the kingdom, and the subjects;
therefore, a righteous king should provide protection for virtuous women.
A woman should be joyful, solely diligent in her household duties,
keeping the utensils well-maintained, and not being wasteful with expenses; she should always serve him to whom her father gave her as a wife.
When her husband has died and ascended to heaven, a woman who remains steadfast in celibacy should not take pleasure in another's house, nor should she be prone to quarreling;
likewise, a woman whose husband is away on a journey should avoid adornment.
Devoted to the propitiation of the deities and intent on the welfare of her husband,
she should likewise wear some ornament for the sake of auspiciousness.
That woman who enters the fire with her husband shall also attain the highest state.
The worship of Śrī should be performed, as well as the sweeping and cleaning of the house;
on the twelfth day of the month of Kārttika, one should likewise give Viṣṇu and a cow with its calf.
A husband is protected by Sāvitrī through the vow of truthful conduct. (2) AP_221B.025ab)

Regarding the duties of kings,

The village headman shall pacify the faults that have arisen in the village;
if he is unable, he should go and report them to the leader of ten villages (*daśapāla*).
Having heard this, the leader of ten villages shall likewise apply the appropriate remedy in that matter.
Indeed, from a well-protected realm, a king obtains wealth and other such things;
one who possesses wealth attains dharma, and one who possesses wealth enjoys pleasure. For without wealth, [all these] are utterly destroyed.
Just as a river in summer has no specific distinction [of water], so it is for one who has fallen and is destitute in this world;
people do not accept food from the fallen, and the poor man does not give.
Even the wife of one devoid of wealth will not remain devoted;
a king who causes oppression to his kingdom dwells in hell for a long time.
Therefore, a king should always conduct himself like a woman who is pregnant, sharing the same nature as her unborn child.

For him whose subjects are well-protected, heaven is like his own home.
He whose subjects are unprotected has hell as his abode;
the king takes a sixth part of both their merit and their demerit.
Through protection comes the attainment of dharma, and through non-protection, he incurs sin.

Like a beautiful woman being devoured by royal favorites and thieves, the subjects must be protected, especially from the scribes (*kāyastha*s). When protected from those fears, the subjects truly belong to the king.

one should perform the suppression of the wicked and take the tax prescribed by the Teacher.
One should deposit half in the treasury and always give half to the twice-born.

But one who speaks falsely shall be fined an eighth part of his great wealth;

Within three years, the owner may reclaim [the property]; after that, the king shall take it. He who says "this is mine" and can prove his claim according to the rule—that owner is entitled to the goods, provided he establishes its form, number, and other characteristics.

Even at the point of death, one should not take taxes from Brahmins;
for that king in whose realm a Vedic scholar perishes from hunger,

She who does not welcome conversation with him,

Chapter 224:
Duties of Kings (Rājadharmāḥ)
Puṣkara said:
"The protector of the earth must provide protection for the prince;
he should instruct him in the treatises on Dharma, Artha, and Kāma, as well as in the science of archery."
He should have him trained in the arts by trustworthy persons who speak with false kindness;
under the pretext of protecting his person, he should appoint guards over him.
Furthermore, he must not allow him to associate with those who are angry, greedy, or insulted.
If it is impossible to instill virtues in him, one should bind him with [restraints] at his various entrances and employ him in all offices as a disciplined servant;
the king should abandon hunting, drinking, and gambling, for they lead to the ruin of the kingdom.
One should avoid sleeping during the day, wandering about aimlessly, harshness of speech, and slander; one should also abandon physical violence and the destruction of property.
Furthermore, one should refrain from the demolition of architectural features and the neglect of fortifications and other such works.
The corruption of objects has been described, as well as their being scattered; giving at the wrong place and time, and giving to an unworthy recipient. AP 224.007ab.
The corruption of wealth is said to be the engagement in improper actions;
one should therefore avoid lust, anger, intoxication, pride, greed, and arrogance.
Having thus achieved victory over his servants, he should then conquer the people of both the city and the countryside.
First, he should conquer external enemies; these external enemies are of three kinds: hereditary, adjacent, and artificial.
As previously stated, these are respectively paternal, ancestral, and neighboring. Likewise, one must consider the father’s and grandfather’s friend, as well as the enemy's vassal.

O highly fortunate one, an artificial friend is said to be of three kinds. O knower of dharma, sovereignty consists of seven limbs: the ruler, the ministers, the territory, the fort, the army, the treasury, and the ally; this is called the sevenfold kingdom.
The master is indeed the root; therefore, he must especially be protected, as is the kingdom.
One should strike down those who betray the constituents of the kingdom at the proper time, being harsh when necessary and mild otherwise.
In this way, the king secures both worlds; he should cause his servants to abandon all levity.
In this world, servants treat with contempt a king who is overly cheerful and fond of pleasant conversation;
therefore, for the sake of winning over the people, he should feign being addicted to vices. He should speak with a smile and act in a way that pleases the world.
For a king who procrastinates, the loss of his undertakings is certain—
whether regarding passion, pride, arrogance, malice, or sinful deeds.
Yet, when something unpleasant must be spoken, one who procrastinates is praised.
A king whose counsel is kept secret shall not suffer calamities;
therefore, [his] kingdom [shall endure].
Gha, Cha, Ja, Ña, Ṭa.
For it is known that the deed he has performed, not yet begun, will bring him sovereignty,
through his outward forms, gestures, gait, movements, and speech.
Furthermore, what is held within is perceived through the distortions of the eyes and the face.
A king should not deliberate on a secret plan with only one person, nor with many people together;
rather, the king may consult on plans with many individuals separately.
A minister should never disclose his counsel to anyone, even among other ministers;
for in this world, men are never to be trusted.
And likewise, a decision regarding counsel should be made by a single wise man.
Through lack of discipline a king may perish, but through discipline he may obtain his kingdom.
From those learned in the three Vedas, he should learn the triple knowledge and the eternal science of government (*daṇḍanīti*).
Having mastered the science of inquiry (*ānvīkṣikī*), the science of wealth (*arthavidyā*), and the undertakings of commerce (*vārtā*) from the world,
one who has conquered the senses is indeed able to keep the subjects under control.
All gods and twice-born (*dvija*) men are to be honored, and one should bestow gifts upon them.
Giving to a twice-born man is an inexhaustible treasure that cannot be destroyed by anyone;
never retreating in battles and the protection of subjects,
as well as gifts to Brahmins, constitute the supreme welfare of a king.
He should likewise provide for the welfare, security, and livelihood of the wretched, the helpless, the elderly, and widowed women.
He must establish the proper order of the social classes and stages of life, and perform the honoring of ascetics.
One should not trust everyone, yet one should trust ascetics;
and one should inspire confidence in others by means of a reason that accords with reality.

One should contemplate the meaning like a heron, exert valor like a lion,
snatch away like a wolf, and dart away like a hare.
And likewise, O King, a monarch should be firm in striking like a boar;
he should be versatile like a peacock, steadfast in devotion like a horse,
and sweet-spoken like a cuckoo.
One should always be as wary as a crow; one should dwell in a residence that is not known.
One should not touch food or a bed that has not been previously examined, nor should one approach an unknown woman, nor board an unknown boat.
One who oppresses the kingdom falls away from both his royal wealth and his very life.
Just as a calf, once nourished and grown strong, becomes fit for work,
so too, O highly fortunate one, a kingdom, when properly sustained, becomes capable of performing its duties.
All this action depends upon both destiny and human effort;
for while destiny is indeed inconceivable, human effort possesses the capacity for action.
The sovereignty, the earth, and the glory of a king arise from the affection of the people.
Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Duties of Kings," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 225:
Duties of Kings (Rājadharmāḥ)
Puṣkara said:
Know that what is called destiny is simply one's own karma acquired in another body;
therefore, the wise declare that human effort alone is superior in this world.
Likewise, adverse fate is overcome by human effort; however,
success may come even without human effort due to virtuous action performed in the past.
O Bhārgava, human effort bears fruit in due time through the perfection of destiny;
both destiny and human exertion bring results to a man,
for just as from the union of rain and cultivation, the attainment of fruits occurs in due season.
One should exert human effort consistent with righteousness, neither being indolent nor relying on fate.
All undertakings are accomplished through means such as conciliation and the rest;
these are conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and likewise punishment.
Illusion, indifference, and sorcery—these are the seven expedients; hear them.
Conciliation is said to be of two kinds: truthful and untruthful.
Even among those, untruthful conciliation serves only to provoke the anger of the virtuous.
For those of noble birth, who are upright, constant in dharma, and have conquered their senses, can be subdued by conciliation;
even Rākṣasas are won over by such means.
Likewise, there is a description of the various services rendered and the favors bestowed upon them.
But toward those who hate one another, who are angry, fearful, or insulted,
one should employ sowing of dissension; one should show them the supreme danger and point out hope for their own side, by means of whatever fault they fear.

One should alienate those very people by whom one has been defeated; indeed, one must protect the one who causes dissension among kinsmen. Having pacified the external treasury consisting of neighboring kings, as well as the ministers, sons, and others, and having also pacified the internal treasury, one should conquer that enemy.
Giving is the supreme skillful means; through giving, one partakes in both worlds.
Indeed, there is no one who does not become subject to the power of giving. (Note:
"One should show fear to another" refers to the *ñā* [mantra]).
2. [The commentary on] "ministers, kinsmen, younger brothers, and so forth" is as follows:

He should accomplish that which is unaccomplished by means of both punishment and its application;
for everything is established upon punishment, yet punishment, when improperly administered, brings destruction.
By punishing those who should not be punished, or by failing to punish those who deserve it, a king perishes.
Gods, Daityas, serpents, humans, Siddhas, spirits,
and birds would overstep their own boundaries if he did not maintain the rod of punishment;
for it is he who tames the untamed and punishes those who deserve punishment.
Because he restrains and punishes, the wise know him as *daṇḍa* (the rod of punishment).
Indeed, by his splendor, the king is difficult to behold like the sun;
therefore, by his appearance, he brings delight to the world like the moon.
Because he pervades the world through his spies, the king is the wind;
because he effects the restraint of faults, the lordly king is Vaivasvata (Yama).
When he consumes the wicked-minded, then he becomes the purifier (fire).
When one gives gifts to the twice-born, he becomes the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) from that;
because of raining down streams of wealth upon the gods and others, he is remembered as Varuṇa;
and by sustaining the worlds through forbearance, he becomes a true king (Pārthiva).
"Since Hari protects [the world] through his powers of energy, counsel, and so forth, therefore [he is called] Dhari.
Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Means of Conciliation and the Others," in the Agni Mahāpurāṇa.

[This applies to] a mother, a father, an elder brother, a father-in-law, or a teacher.
One who reviles [another] shall be fined one hundred [paṇas]; likewise, one who does not yield the path to his teacher.

However, if a person of the lowest caste (antyajāti) commits an offense against a twice-born man (dvijāti), the king shall immediately and without hesitation cut off that very limb with which he has offended.
The king shall cause both lips to be cut off from one who spits out of arrogance;
he shall cause the penis to be cut off from one who urinates [upon him], and the anus from one who utters abusive words.
For one who sits upon a superior seat while another is seated low, the lower part [of the offender] shall be cut off;
and whichever limb causes pain to another, that very limb of his shall be severed.
Those who kill cows, elephants, horses, or camels shall have their hands and feet amputated.
Having cut down a tree that bears no fruit, one deserves a fine of gold;
if a path, a boundary, or a reservoir is destroyed, he shall be made to pay double.
Whoever steals the goods of another, whether intentionally or even unintentionally, [shall be punished].
Having produced satisfaction for him, he should then give it to the king as a fine.
But he who takes a rope or a jar from a well, or destroys that water-station (*prapā*), shall receive punishment; he should be fined for one month at the place where living beings are harmed.
For one who steals more than ten *kumbhas* of grain, the punishment is death;
for stealing less than that, he should be assigned a fine eleven times the value.
For the theft of gold, silver, and the like, as well as for the abduction of men and women, the punishment is death.
Whatever limb a thief employs against men,
that very limb the king shall take away as a deterrent.
A Brāhmaṇa who takes a small amount of vegetables, grain, and the like, incurs no guilt.
One may kill a wicked man who steals the property of a god; likewise, one should slay one who attempts to seize a house or field, as well as one who approaches another's wife.
One should kill an arsonist, a poisoner, and likewise one with a weapon raised.
The king may execute those who practice sorcery against cattle and other such malefactors, as well as assassins;
he should not speak with another's wife, for she must not enter [the royal presence] if she is forbidden. A woman choosing her own husband should not be punished by the king.
A woman who serves a superior man but violates her inferior husband deserves death;
one who transgresses against her husband should be caused to be torn apart by dogs.
One should cause a woman defiled by a man of equal caste to subsist on mere alms;
a woman defiled by a superior man shall undergo tonsure.
Furthermore, for a Brāhmaṇa, there is penance upon approaching a Vaiśya woman, and for a Kṣatriya, upon approaching a woman of the lowest castes.
In the case of approaching a Śūdra woman, a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya should first be fined;
if a courtesan, having received her fee, goes elsewhere out of greed,
she shall pay double the fee as well as a fine equal to double that amount.
A wife, sons, slaves, a pupil, and a uterine brother—
when they have committed an offense, these may be beaten on the back with a rope or a split bamboo cane,
but one must not strike them on the head; for he who strikes them there incurs the guilt of a thief.
But those appointed for protection who violate their duty for the sake of their own livelihood—
having confiscated all their property, the king shall banish them. Likewise, those who, though appointed to their respective duties, obstruct the affairs of the workers;
The king should cause those who are merciless and cruel-minded to be deprived of their wealth;
and whichever minister or judge should decide a case unjustly,
the king should confiscate his entire property and banish him.
One should place the emblem of a female organ for violating the teacher's bed, a liquor-sign for drinking intoxicants,
a dog's foot for thefts, and a man's head for the murder of a Brahmin.
The king should execute wicked Śūdras and others, but he should banish wicked Brahmins.
One should hand over the wealth of those who have committed great sins to Varuṇa;
moreover, anyone in the villages who provides food to thieves, as well as those who supply them with goods and containers— all such persons he should cause to be executed.
In the realms, he should remove sinful local chieftains who hold office;
likewise, those thieves who commit robbery at night after having made a pact [with others].
Having cut off their hands, the king should impale them on sharp stakes;
the king should execute those who destroy tanks or temples.
He who, except in times of distress, discards filth upon the royal highway, [should be punished].
For he shall be fined one *kārṣāpaṇa* and shall clean up that impurity; those who break a bridge or a public monument shall pay five hundred.
Likewise, whoever deals unfairly with equals, or who acts dishonestly regarding the price, [shall be punished].
A man who, having taken goods from merchants, conceals them at an improper price, shall first or even a middle fine;
the king shall impose the highest amercement as a separate punishment for each such act.

He who adulterates substances and he who sells counterfeits shall receive the middle amercement; likewise, the forger shall receive the highest amercement. One who causes a quarrel must pay the value of the damage and a fine twice that amount.

Whether it be a Brahmin or a Śūdra who eats what is forbidden to eat, the fine is one kṛṣṇala; the same applies to one who forges scales, edicts, or a document of destruction. Furthermore, whoever transacts business with these persons shall be made to pay the highest fine.
One who administers poison or sets fire [to property], or one who causes the death of her husband, teacher, Brahmin, or child,
should be deprived of her ears, hands, nose, and lips, and banished with cattle.
Likewise, those men who destroy fields, houses, villages, or forests [should be punished].
One who has sexual intercourse with the king’s wife shall be burned in a fire of straw;
likewise, one who alters a royal edict by making it deficient or excessive,
and one who releases an adulterer or a thief, shall receive the highest punishment.
The punishment for one who mounts the royal vehicle or throne is the highest fine (uttamasāhasa).
He who, though defeated according to the law, thinks "I am not defeated," [is subject to this penalty].
Having defeated him as he approaches,
one should fine him double the penalty; the one who summons another when not summoned shall be subject to corporal punishment.
And he who, having escaped from the hand of the punisher, flees,
being deficient in manly effort— that wealth the punisher shall recover.
Thus ends the section titled "The Administration of Punishment" in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The two hundred and twenty-sixth chapter.
Chapter 227:
The Military Expedition (Yuddhayātrā)
Puṣkara said:
When a king perceives that he is being overwhelmed by a powerful rear-attacker due to his own cry for help, then he should undertake a military expedition.
"My warriors are well-nourished, my servants are maintained, and my forces are abundant;
being capable of protecting my base, I shall go with them and enter the camp."

Or one should march when the enemy is in calamity, or when the adversary is afflicted by divine portents such as earthquakes; or when an earthquake occurs in a certain direction, or when a comet has defiled that same quarter; or when the army is loathed by its enemies, or when internal dissension has arisen within it.
When auspicious throbbing of the body occurs, as well as when one sees a good dream, and when an auspicious omen or a favorable sign has arisen, one may march against the enemy's city.
(Note: "punarjitvā" is found in the manuscripts *ga*, *gha*, and *ja*.)
2. "Having been surrounded by them" is the correct reading.
3. "Filled with internal anger," according to the manuscripts *kha* and *cha*:
One should deploy an army consisting largely of infantry and elephants during the rainy season;
one crowded with chariots and cavalry during the late autumn and early winter;
and one endowed with all four divisions of the forces during the spring or at the onset of autumn.
An army with many foot soldiers always conquers its enemies. A throbbing on the right side of the body is auspicious; however, it is not auspicious on the left side, nor on the back or the heart.
A mole, a wart, and likewise a throbbing sensation—
these, when occurring on the left side in reverse order, are auspicious for women.
Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Journey," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter [X].
Chapter 128:
The Chapter on Dreams (Svapnādhyāya)
Puṣkara said:

I shall describe dreams that are auspicious and inauspicious, as well as those that remove suffering; however, the growth of grass or trees on any part of the body other than the navel [is inauspicious].
Dusting the head with powder, shaving the head of bronze vessels, nakedness, wearing soiled garments, anointing the body, being smeared with mud,
falling from a height, marriage, and singing; AP_228.002cd–228.003ab/
The diversion of stringed instruments, as well as riding on swings;
the acquisition of lotuses and metals, and furthermore, the killing of serpents.
And likewise, [the sight of] trees with red flowers, and that of a *caṇḍāla*, [are inauspicious]. (AP 228.004cd)
The act of mounting boars, horses, donkeys, and camels; the eating of the flesh of birds, of oil, and of *kṛśara*;
entering the mother’s womb; and likewise ascending a funeral pyre.
The falling of Śakra’s banner, the falling of the moon and the sun,
the appearance of celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial portents,
and even the provocation of gods, the twice-born, kings, and elders.
Dancing, laughing, marriage, and singing;
(2) the playing of musical instruments even when deprived of stringed accompaniment;
the downward flow of rivers and bathing with cow-dung water. (AP 228.008–009ab)
Likewise, [one should avoid] embracing young girls or having sexual intercourse with men, as well as the application of mud mixed with water or ink-water to the body,
the emaciation of one's own limbs, purging, and the act of vomiting.
Traveling toward the southern direction, being overcome by disease,
the loss of fruits, likewise the breaking of the bodily elements,
the collapsing of houses, and the sweeping away of one's home.
Even with playful piśācas, carnivorous beasts, monkeys, and the lowest of men; likewise, being overcome by others and the arising of calamities from that;
wearing saffron-colored robes and playing with such garments.

to "oil and *kṛśara* rice-and-meat porridge."

Drinking oil, immersion baths, red garlands, and ointments—these and other such dreams are inauspicious; however, not speaking of them is auspicious.
Likewise, sleeping on the bare ground, bathing, and the worship of Brahmins should be performed.
An oblation with sesame seeds, the worship of Hari, Brahmā, Śiva, and the Sun,
as well as the recitation of hymns and the chanting of the *Puruṣasūkta* and other mantras—
these [remedies apply] when dreams occur during the first watch of the night.
[The results] ripen after a year;
in the second [case], after six months; in the third, after three months;
in the fourth, after half a month; and in the fifth, after ten days at dawn.

If, during a single night, a dream occurs— whether auspicious or inauspicious— one should predict its fruition based on that which is seen last. Therefore, after having a favorable dream, subsequent sleep is not recommended.
Riding upon mountains, palaces, elephants, horses, and bulls is auspicious;
likewise, O twice-born one, climbing trees with white flowers or ascending into the sky is favorable.
So too is the appearance of trees or grass growing from the navel, as well as having many arms.
Likewise, there is the state of having many heads and the appearance of grey hair;
wearing very bright garlands and wearing very white garments;
and the seizing of the moon, sun, stars, and planets, as well as the act of wiping them away.
O twice-born one, there is also the embracing of Śakra’s banner, the act of raising a banner,
and the subduing of enemies;
likewise, victory in dispute, in gambling, and in battle.
The eating of raw meat, the eating of milk-rice (*pāyasa*), the sight of blood, or bathing with blood; [this occurs] in the first part. (Note 1: "In the first part" refers to the *kha* manuscript.)

The writhing on the ground with weapons, as well as the clear sky,
and the milking by the mouth of female buffaloes, cows, lionesses, female elephants, and likewise mares, are all auspicious.
O twice-born one, O Rāma, devotion toward the gods, the brahmins, and likewise toward one's gurus,
as well as an ablution with water fallen from the horns of cows or from the moon— that indeed should be known as bestowing sovereignty.
Likewise, there is the consecration to kingship, as well as the cutting off of the head,
death, the acquisition of fire, the burning of houses and the like by fire,
the attainment of royal insignia, and the sounding of stringed musical instruments.
He who sees at the end of a dream a king, an elephant, a horse,
gold, a bull, or a cow, his household increases;
likewise for one who dreams of climbing a bull, an elephant, a house, a mountain peak, or a tree, or of weeping.
Smeared with ghee or excrement, or likewise sexual intercourse with a forbidden woman;
white clothing, clear water, a fruit-bearing tree, and a cloudless sky—
thus ends the chapter on dreams, titled "The Dream Chapter," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The two hundred and twenty-eighth chapter.
Chapter 229:
Omens of Birds (Śakunāni)
Puṣkara said: "Medicinal herbs, black grain that is unwholesome,
cotton, dry grass, cow dung, and indeed wealth [are all things to be avoided]."
Charcoal, molasses, and *sarja* resin, as well as one who is shaven-headed and smeared with oil, and one who is naked; :p 333.
Iron, mud, leather, hair, a madman, a eunuch, outcastes such as Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas, men who are prison guards,
a pregnant woman, a widow, oil-cakes and the like, and a corpse— [these are not to be stepped over].
Husked grain, ashes, potsherds, bones, and broken vessels are inauspicious;
likewise, the sound of musical instruments is inauspicious when it is broken or discordant like a terrifying drum.
The sound "Come! is auspicious when heard from the front, but not from behind.
The word "go" uttered from behind is excellent, but from the front it is censured.
"Where are you going?", "Stop!", "Do not go!", and "What will you gain by going there?"— such unpleasant sounds, as well as carnivorous beasts appearing on banners and the like, portend death.
The stumbling of vehicles, the breaking of weapons,
a blow to the head by doors and the like, and the falling of umbrellas, garments, and so forth—
by worshipping and praising Hari, these inauspicious omens shall be destroyed.
But seeing a second [bird] contrary to that, one should enter the house;
[or if there are] white flowers, excellent, a full water-pot most excellent,
meat, fish, a distant sound, or an old goat.
Cows, waves, elephants, and the blazing fire; fresh durvā grass, cow dung, a courtesan, gold, silver, and gems;
vacā, white mustard seeds, medicinal herbs, mung beans, weapons, and swords.
An umbrella, a seat, royal insignia, a corpse free from weeping, fruit, ghee, curd, milk, unbroken grains, a mirror,
honey, a conch shell, sugarcane, auspicious speech, and the singing or playing of devoted musicians.
And [the words] "molasses and snakes" (guḍasarpau) are found in the manuscripts labeled Ga, Gha,
and Ña on page 334.
The deep rumbling of clouds and mental satisfaction from lightning—
on one side are all these signs, but on the other side is mental satisfaction alone.
Thus ends the chapter titled "Auspiciousness" in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The two hundred and twenty-ninth chapter.
Chapter 230:
Omens of Birds (Śakunāni)
Puṣkara said:
"When a man stands still while asking about his journey, the omens indicate his good or ill fortune regarding both the country and the city."
All [omens] that are blazing are declared by those who contemplate destiny to have evil results,
while those that are tranquil are proclaimed by the astrologers to have auspicious results; thus, six types of blazing among omens have been specified.
Due to differences in time, direction, place, action, sound, and species,
each preceding one among these should be understood as being more powerful than the one following it:
a day-roamer [is stronger] than a night-roamer, and likewise, a night-roamer [is stronger] than a day-roamer.
In the case of cruel signs, planets, and ascendants, the [direction] should be known as "blazing" (dīptā). That which the Sun is about to enter is to be known as "smoky" (dhūmitā);
that in which he is currently situated is "flaming" (jvalitā), and that from which he has departed is considered "charred" (aṅgāriṇī).
These three are known as "blazing," while five others are likewise "calm.
When the direction is blazing, an omen occurring in that direction is proclaimed to be "blazing."

O best of the twice-born, one who lives in a village while the forest is nearby, or who lives in the forest while being like a village-dweller, as well as one who disparages trees, should be known as a "blazing region" (deśadīpta) when residing in an inauspicious place. One who performs actions unbecoming of his own caste is designated as "blazing in action" (kriyādīpta).
That which is called "flaming by sound" is described as having a broken and terrifying resonance;
likewise, that which is "flaming by birth" should be known as one who eats meat exclusively.
Through all these distinctions, one should diligently determine whether a bird is flaming or tranquil.
A mixed omen is declared to be one consisting of various [animals]; its result, whether auspicious or inauspicious, should be stated as follows:
cows, horses, camels, donkeys, dogs, sarika birds, house-lizards, sparrows, hawks, tortoises, and others are said to be village-dwellers.
Goats, sheep, peacocks, and lordly elephants; the boar, buffalo, and crow—these are specified as both domestic and wild; all others are forest-dwellers.
The cat and the cock are domestic, yet they too are forest-dwellers.
Their consciousness indeed becomes eternal due to the distinction of their forms:
the Gokarṇa, the peacock, the ruddy goose, the donkey, the Hārīta bird,
the crow, the Kulāha, the wild cock, the hawk, the jackal, the Khañjana bird, and the monkey.
The *śataghna*, the *caṭaka*, the *śyāma*, the *cāsa*, the *śyena*, and the *kaliñjala*;
the *tittira*, the *śatapatra*, and likewise the three kinds of *kapota*;
the *khañjarīṭaka*, the *dātyūha*, the *śuka*, the *rājīva*, and the *kukkuṭa*.

The *bhāradvāja*, the *sāraṅga*, and others should be known as those that roam by day; while the *vāguri*, the owl (*ulūka*), the *śarabha*, the *krauñca*, the rabbit (*śaśaka*), the tortoise (*kacchapa*),
the *lomāsikā*, and the *piṅgalikā* are said to be those that roam by night.
And all the other forest-dwellers—swans, deer, cats, mongooses, bears, and serpents—as well as [the others mentioned]... (f. 336b).
Wolves, lions, tigers, camels, village pigs, humans, porcupines, bulls, jackals, wild dogs, cuckoos, and cranes;
horses, men wearing loincloths, and monitor lizards— these are indeed the amphibious beings.
In both the *bala* and *prasthāna* [movements], all those moving in front of the army are declared to bring victory, while those behind cause destruction. Furthermore,
when one goes from the house and speaks while standing in front, [the same result follows].
A peacock crying on the left portends dishonor from the king or a feast involving strife;
however, its appearance while traveling is auspicious, as is the throbbing of the left limb.
Furthermore, a peacock with a broken or discordant cry announces plunder by thieves.
O Rāma, for one who has set out on a journey, a deer appearing in front will be fatal to life.
Likewise, O Rāma, bears, rats, jackals, tigers, lions, cats, donkeys, and a donkey making a distorted sound are all inauspicious when encountered from the opposite direction.
The partridge is excellent when on the left, as is the one situated on the right; however, the tittiri bird on the back is of censured fruit and is not praised.
Deer, boars, and spotted antelopes, though auspicious on the left, become inauspicious when on the right.
Those that act contrary [to the right path] are always despised as harmful;
however, bulls, horses, jackals, tigers, lions, cats,
and donkeys should be known as fulfillers of one's desired aims when they move from the right to the left.
A jackal, a dark-faced female owl, a *śūcchū* bird, a tawny-colored lizard, a house-godhika, a sow, a cuckoo, and those with masculine names [are auspicious] when on the left.
The passage beginning with "1. *pratilomās tathā* etc.
and ending with "siṃhamārjāragardabhāḥ" is not present in the two manuscripts of Ja... and Bha....
The *strīsañjñā*, *bhāsakārūṣaka*, *piśrīkarṇa*, *chitkara*,
*ruru*, and *śyena* [birds] are the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) for the southern [fire].
The mention of the jātī flower, the ichneumon, the hare, the boar, and the lizard is auspicious;
thereafter, the sight of a monkey or a bear is not desired,
for a bird that flies against one as one sets out daily is a powerful omen that accomplishes one's purpose.
The wise should declare that its fruit will occur on that very day. O twice-born one,
those who desire food, children, and likewise those intent on enmity,
should be known as fruitless when they have entered within the boundary.
A female jackal (śivā) becomes auspicious with one, two, three, or four cries;
likewise, she is proclaimed inauspicious with five or six. With seven she is auspicious, but beyond that she becomes fruitless.
The flame-faced (Sūryamukhī), which causes the hair of men to stand on end and strikes terror into mounts, should be known as the increaser of fear; however,
if she is first seen upon a deer in an auspicious place, one should declare it to be auspicious.
For a human being, both the inauspicious and the auspicious [results] for a year are likewise [determined].
If a man sees a spotted antelope on the first day in such a manner,
he should understand that the fruit for the year will correspond to his own [condition].
Thus ends the two hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "Omens," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*. [Note 1]:
