Chapter Two Hundred and Thirty-One:
The Chapter on the Thirty-First [Additional] Hundred.
Puṣkara said: "By whichever path many crows enter the city..."
By that path, the capture of the besieged city shall come to pass.
If a crow, crying out while the army is encamped for the sake of lodging,
is on the left side, distressed by fear and trembling, it foretells an insurmountable danger.

If a crow crushes a shadow, a limb, a vehicle, sandals, an umbrella, clothing, or similar objects, death occurs; if it honors them, there will be honor; and if it performs a desired service for them, it is auspicious.
A crow that causes a traveler to return home by moving back and forth at the doorway brings good fortune.
If one throws a burnt red object into the fire within the house,
it indicates that [the deity] is offering blood;
furthermore, O Bhārgava, if one offers yellow substances, such as gold or silver, it foretells imprisonment.
One should predict the acquisition of whatever object is brought forward;
likewise, one should predict the loss of whatever object is taken away.
There shall be the acquisition of wealth if raw meat is vomited in front [of the subject].
If earth is thrown, there will be the acquisition of land; if a jewel is offered, there will be a great kingdom.
For a traveler, a crow that is favorable brings security and is capable of accomplishing tasks, though it should be known not as a bringer of wealth; one that is unfavorable brings fear.
If a crow approaches from the left while cawing, it will cause the failure of one's journey;
a crow on the left is considered auspicious, whereas one on the right brings about the destruction of wealth.
1. *Duṣkaram* (difficult to do), as in Kha, Cha, and Ca; 2. *Dakṣiṇo 'nnavināśakṛt* (the right [hand] causes the destruction of food), as in Ga, Gha, and Ña. (p.
The left [side] moving in the natural direction is best; the right is considered middling.
Moving in the reverse direction on the left portends the prevention of travel;
having returned home, it announces one's intended departure for a journey.
A crow with one leg raised, looking toward the sun, is terrifying;
dwelling in a hollow, it brings about great misfortune.
A crow is not auspicious in a saline wasteland, but one marked by mud is praised.
A crow with a mouth full of impurity is a "accomplisher of all aims" (sarvārthasādhaka);
other birds as well, O descendant of Bhṛgu, should be known to be like crows. Dogs stationed to the left of the military camp are destroyers of Brahmins.
If the dog barks at the place of Indra (the eastern quarter) in the city of a king, or at the gate-tower of a city governor,
or inside the house of a householder, it portends death.
However, if it sniffs the left side of a person, it shall lead to the accomplishment of that person's goals.
If it approaches facing him with its right limb and likewise its left arm, it causes destruction to the traveler's journey;
O Bhārgava, such a bird on the path announces thieves who obstruct the way.
One who has not obtained [alms], one with a face like a bone, one who is wicked, one with a face like a rope or rags,
one with shoes on his face, one whose mouth is full of meat,
as well as anything inauspicious or hair— these are likewise impure.
Whomever he urinates upon while proceeding, that person shall experience fear;
yet, having urinated upon a certain place or a tree, he proceeds toward auspiciousness. (Note 1:
"The accomplisher of one's purpose," and so forth.)
The reading "gṛhe gataḥ" does not exist in the interior of the *ṭa* manuscript;
the reading beginning with "koṭare" and ending with "sarvārthasādhakaḥ" is found in the *ṭa* manuscript.
Furthermore, there is no auspicious rite or material substance that could bring about the accomplishment of his purpose.
O Rāma, dogs and likewise jackals and other such animals are to be understood [in this manner].
The uncaused lowing of cows should be known as a source of fear for the master;
at night, it portends danger from thieves, and if it is distorted, it likewise portends death.
If a bull bellowing at night belongs to Lord Śiva,
it brings victory to the king;
likewise, cows that have been released, those being fed, and one's own cows bestow fearlessness.
Those who have abandoned affection for their own offspring, who are considered to cause the destruction of the fetus,
who strike the ground with their feet, and who are miserable, terrified, or terrifying, are inauspicious;
whereas those with moist limbs, bristling hair, and mud clinging to their hooves are auspicious.
All this should also be told by one who understands regarding the chief queen and others:
likewise, the mounting of another horse while his own is still bridled,
sitting in the water, and rolling about on the ground are not desired.
The sudden death of a horse, or its falling asleep for no apparent reason,
as well as a sudden aversion to barley and sweetmeats, is not auspicious. Furthermore,
the appearance of blood from the mouth and trembling are also not considered favorable omens.

If a single crow plays with pigeons and mynas while its eyes are filled with tears, it foretells death; if it licks its own feet with its tongue, it portends destruction. Likewise, if it scratches the earth with its left foot, [the same result follows].
Or if it sleeps on its left side, or during the day, it does not bestow auspiciousness;
likewise, one that urinates once or has a face clouded by sleep leads to fear.
[The term] *saparyārha* means "worthy of worship," which is a virtuous epithet.
2. [The reading] "vināśakṛt" is found in manuscripts Ja and Ṭa;
"If he does not grant an ascent, or if he goes home in opposition..."
If it touches its left side while neighing, it foretells an obstacle to the journey;
if it touches its foot, it brings victory over the enemy warrior.
If the elephant engages in mating while traveling through a village, it will bring about the destruction of the country.
If a female elephant in rut, having recently given birth, does not mount the king for his rest, or if she goes against him or returns home,
or if the elephant loses its rut, it shall become a slayer of the king.
If an auspicious bull,
horse, or elephant, while amidst the enemy army, tramples its left foot with its right foot and likewise rubs its right tusk with its trunk, it is inauspicious.
The army may meet with destruction due to a localized downpour from a fragmented cloud,
or from unfavorable planets and constellations, as well as from headwinds; likewise,
during the time of a march or in battle, the falling of the royal parasol and other such omens portend danger.
Joyful men and favorable planets are indeed the signs of victory;
the overwhelming of warriors by crows and the destruction of the army circle by carnivorous beasts portend defeat.
The eastern, western, northeastern, and northern directions are most beloved and auspicious.
Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "Auspicious Omens," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*. [Note:
1] Beginning with "left, right," and so forth.
The reading from "sammukhamāruta" up to "antaḥ" does not exist in manuscript Jha;
Chapter 232:
Considerations on Processions, Mandalas, and Other Matters.
Puṣkara said:
I shall now describe the entire procedure for a military expedition based on the principles of royal dharma;
[one should avoid setting out] when the sun has set, when it is in its debilitated state, when it is impaired, or when it is situated in an inimical zodiacal sign.
One should abandon a journey when Venus is retrograde or eclipsed;
likewise when Mercury is retrograde, or when the lord of the direction (the Sun) and other planets are so situated.
One should also avoid traveling during the *vaidhṛti*, *vyatīpāta*, *nāga*, and *śakuna* yogas.
One should likewise avoid setting out on a journey during the Catuṣpāda, Kintughna,
Vipatti, Naidhana, Pratyari, or Janman asterisms; one should also avoid traveling during the Gaṇḍa yoga and on the Riktā lunar days.
The northern and the eastern directions are likewise proclaimed as one;
and the western and the southern directions are likewise one.
One must not leap over the *parigha* (the atmospheric obstruction) arising from the directions of wind and fire;
furthermore, the days of the Sun, Moon, and Saturn are not auspicious.
The asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā belong to the east, and those beginning with Maghā belong to the south.
Furthermore, some say the directions beginning with Maitra (East), while others say those beginning with Vāsava (North-East).
All these gateways are praised; now I shall tell you the measurement of the shadow.
Twenty [aṅgulas] are to be known for the sun, and sixteen are proclaimed for the moon.
Fifteen [verses] are said for Mars, and likewise fourteen for Mercury;
one should avoid [the rest]. (Variant readings: *vivarjayet* is found in manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, and *ña*).
The eastern and northern directions are likewise;
thus, thirteen [days] are proclaimed for Jupiter, and twelve for Venus.
Likewise, eleven [periods] are proclaimed for all undertakings during the solar [transit].
A man should not go out when the birth-lagna is directly facing the rainbow (*śakracāpa*). One should set out for victory when the omens and other signs are auspicious, while remembering Hari.

After the consideration of the mandala, I shall describe that which is to be done for the protection of the king: the sovereign, the minister, the fort, the treasury, the army, the ally, and the territory; this is said to be the sevenfold kingdom.
A ruler of the earth should destroy those who create obstacles for the sevenfold kingdom; furthermore, prosperity should be pursued within all circles of states, and among these,
one's own circle of states should be considered the primary circle.
The neighbors of his circle [of kings] should be known as enemies;
the one who is allied with him should be known as a friend; beyond that, the enemy's friend;
then the friend's friend; and after that, the friend's friend's enemy.
This has been explained previously; now understand it from me once more:
first is the rear-enemy (pārṣṇigrāha), then the ally of the rear-enemy (ākranda); after that comes the supporter (āsāra), and the ally of the ally is called the ākrandāsāra.

O twice-born one, O bull among men, it is impossible to reach a certain conclusion even in this case regarding one who desires victory, one who is allied with an enemy, or one who has been released; yet,
one who is capable of both restraint and favor is proclaimed to be neutral.
"He who is capable of both punishing and favoring everyone, yet remains impartial—he is declared a powerful lord of the earth.
And regarding all the circles [of vassal kings], there is this half-verse: "For they are indeed equal to the lords of the gods."
The word "āsāraḥ" appears before this in manuscript Ṭa, but it is disconnected:
No one is inherently an enemy or a friend; enmity and friendship arise from causes.
This circle of twelve kings has been fully described to you.
Enemies are to be known as threefold: hereditary, neighboring, and artificial.
Among these, each preceding one is considered more difficult to treat than the next.
Even an immediate enemy is, in my view, merely artificial;
whereas those who seize the rear of an enemy, as well as his friends, become his true enemies.
One should pacify the rear-attacker by means of strategic methods; likewise, the ancients praise the destruction of an enemy through one's own ally.
Furthermore, an ally may become an enemy due to the proximity of neighboring states.
One who desires to conquer an enemy should uproot him himself, provided he is capable; by doing so,
no fear arises from that adversary even as his own power increases.
Just as the world would not be alarmed by him and just as trust would arise,
so should one who desires victory and triumphs through righteousness bring the world under his control.
Thus ends [the section] titled "Considerations on the Expedition and the Circle" in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The two hundred and thirty-second chapter.
Chapter 233:
The Sixfold Policy (Ṣāḍguṇya)
Puṣkara said:
"I have already explained conciliation and sowing dissension, as well as bribery and punishment;
punishment within one's own country has been described, and now I shall speak to you regarding that in a foreign land."
"One who desires to seize an enemy should cut him down"—thus [it is said] in the *Gha* and *Ña* recensions, p.
Punishment is said to be twofold: manifest and unmanifest. AP 233.002ab.
Plundering, the destruction of villages, the destruction of crops, setting fires, open assault, poison, fire, execution by various men,
the corrupting of virtuous people, and the defilement of waters.
The application of punishment has been declared; now hear, O Bhārgava, about indifference.

When a king considers that there will be no conflict for him in battle, yet [the enemy's] persistence would lead to misfortune, and likewise that peace could be achieved [through other means], [then he should remain indifferent].
If, having gained a foothold here, his giving causes the depletion of wealth and leads to the consequences of sowing dissension and punishment, then one should resort to indifference,
thinking: "He is not able to do me any harm or cause me any distress."
"And I cannot remain indifferent toward him;
he must be treated as an enemy by the king, for one who is struck down by contempt becomes a foe.
I shall describe a deceptive stratagem, proceeding with false portents."

O twice-born one, having attached a large firebrand to the tail of a stout bird while it is staying in the enemy's camp, one should cause it to fly away and thereby display the fall of a meteor to the enemy.
In this way, many other various portents should also be displayed;
likewise, one should cause terror among enemies through diverse deceptions.
Astrologers and ascetics should proclaim the destruction of the enemy.
A king desiring to conquer the earth should cause his enemies to tremble by means of that [power].
Furthermore, the favor of the deities should be proclaimed to the enemy:
"The force of our enemy has arrived; strike fearlessly!"
When battle has arrived, one should say: "All the enemies are broken!
One should utter war-cries and shouts of joy, and likewise declare: "The enemy is slain!"
Urged by the command of the gods, the king, fully equipped for battle, shall employ the *indrajāla* (magical illusion); he shall manifest Indra at the proper time.
The king shall provide a fourfold army to assist the inhabitants of heaven.
One should display strength when [the enemy] has arrived, as well as a rain of blood at the gates of Indra’s city;
one should show severed enemy heads atop the palace towers.
I shall now fully explain the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), among which are the two excellent options: peace (*sandhi*) and war (*vigraha*).
Alliance (*sandhi*), war (*vigraha*), marching (*yāna*), encampment (*āsana*),
double-dealing (*dvaidhībhāva*), and seeking refuge (*saṃśraya*) are proclaimed as the six measures of policy (*ṣaḍguṇāḥ*).
Alliance is traditionally defined as a formal agreement (*paṇabandha*), while war is understood as an act of injury (*apakāra*).

The marching of one desiring victory into the territory of the enemy is called *yātrā* (expedition). Remaining in one’s own country during a state of war is called *āsana* (sitting encamped). Marching with half of one's forces is called *dvaidhībhāva* (double-dealing or dividing the army).
One who is neutral or situated between two sides is known as a "doubtful" king due to his dependence;
he should seek an alliance with one who is equal or stronger,
while a king himself who is powerful should wage war against one who is weaker.
Even in that situation, one whose rear is secure should seek refuge with a stronger power when he is able to sit and cause an interruption of the enemy's operations; however,
a lord of the earth whose rear is insecure should remain engaged in hostilities.
A powerful king whose rear is not secure should resort to a dual policy; however, a monarch who has been attacked by a stronger power should undoubtedly [seek peace].
Therefore, he should state that dependence is the lowest of virtues;
for it is said: "One should display [virtues] at the pinnacle of a palace.
[Variant readings: *vigṛhītas tu* (in manuscript *kha*)].
Their vehicle is proclaimed to bring great gain; therefore, at that time, the king should take recourse in it.
But when deprived of all power, one should then seek refuge.
Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Sixfold Policy and Other Means," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 234:
Daily Duties of the King (*Prātyahikarājakarma*)
Puṣkara said:
I shall describe the perpetual duties that one should perform day by day.
O King, when two muhūrtas remain of the night, the king should abandon sleep.
Then, amidst the sounds of musical instruments, panegyrists, and songs, he should observe those men who are hidden—
those whose people cannot be identified by anyone—
and thereafter, the hearing of income and expenditure should be conducted according to the prescribed rule.
Then, having relieved himself, the king should go to the bath-house;
afterwards, the king should perform his bath preceded by the cleansing of his teeth, and having performed the twilight prayers and recitation, he should worship Vāsudeva.
One should offer purificatory oblations into the fire and satisfy the ancestors with water.
[Regarding the phrase] "in the event of great loss or expense," [the reading is found in the manuscripts] kha, cha, and ṭa.
[The passage beginning with] "seated, [one should avoid] the interruption of the ritual," etc., follows.
The reading ending with "rājā samāśrayet" is not found in manuscript *ja*;
page 348.
Accompanied by the benedictions of the twice-born, having been anointed and adorned, he should give away a cow together with a golden girdle; then, looking at his face in a mirror,
the king, holding gold, should hear the date and other details.

Having taken the medicine prescribed by the physician and performed the auspicious touching of the ritual objects, he should then approach his preceptor; having received the blessing bestowed by him, he should proceed to the assembly hall. Standing there, he should look upon the Brāhmaṇas, as well as the ministers and counselors.
O illustrious one, having heard that the subjects have been announced by the doorkeeper,
he should listen to historical accounts, attend to the affairs at hand and the determination of legal cases, then oversee judicial proceedings, and finally hold counsel with his ministers.
One should not deliberate with a single person, nor should one do so with many;
one should not act in secret or in public with fools or the untrustworthy. One should ensure that counsel is well-guarded, so that the kingdom is not harmed.
In discerning outward signs, the protection of counsel is considered paramount for a king.
Through physical gestures and subtle hints, the wise grasp the secret plan; he who delights in the words of astrologers, physicians, and ministers [is protected].
The king attains great power,
for they uphold him as their sovereign;
having performed the consecration ritual (*mantra*), he then exerted himself in vehicles and weapons.
Having bathed at the Niḥsattva and other sites, the king should behold Viṣṇu well-worshipped;

he should behold the sacrificial fire into which oblations have been offered, and he should behold the Brahmins who have been duly honored. He should conduct himself in a guarded and unobtrusive manner.
In place of the reading "ākāragrahaṇe rājño mantrarakṣā parā matā," the reading in the *ṭa* manuscript is "ākāreṅgitatattvajñaḥ kāryākāryavicakṣaṇaḥ."
One who is adorned with these [virtues] should partake of food that has been thoroughly examined for purity through acts such as giving; thus one attains sovereignty over kings.
One should eat food that is well-tested by means of gifts and other such measures.
Having eaten and taken betel, seated on his left side,
he should contemplate the scriptures; having inspected the warriors, the storehouses, and the armory, and having sat through the evening twilight, he should reflect upon his duties.
Having dispatched his spies and finished his meal, the king should remain within the inner apartments;
undistracted by other matters such as instrumental music and song, he should thus conduct himself daily.
Thus ends the [chapter] named "The Daily Routine" in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The two hundred and thirty-fourth chapter.
Chapter 235:
The Consecration for Battle (Raṇadīkṣā)
Puṣkara said:
I shall first describe the procedure for the march and the rules for battle,
when the king’s expedition is to take place after seven days.
Hari, Śambhu, and Vināyaka are to be worshipped with sweetmeats and other offerings.
On the second day, having fully worshipped the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), one should perform the ritual of the bed (śayana).
Either on the bed or before it, having honored the deities, one should then meditate upon the mantra.
Homage to Śambhu, the three-eyed one, to Rudra, and to the giver of boons;
homage to Vāmana, to Virūpa, and to the Lord of Dreams. One should go to sleep [thinking thus].
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, wielder of the trident, whose vehicle is the bull,
O Eternal One, tell me what is desired and undesired for me while I am asleep in a dream.
The priest should recite the mantra beginning with "yajjāgrato dūram.
On the third day, he should worship the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and those Rudras who are the lords of the directions.
On the fourth day, he should worship the planets (grahas), and on the fifth day, he should worship the two Aśvins.
On the road, one should perform the worship of the deities and of rivers and other such features;
likewise, there should be an offering (*bali*) to the gods dwelling in heaven, the intermediate space, and on earth.
At night, there is the worship of the hosts of spirits (*bhūtagaṇa*) and of Vāsudeva and the others.
One should perform the rites for Bhadrakālī and Śrī, and pray to all the deities:
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Nārāyaṇa, the lotus-born, Viṣṇu, Narasiṃha, and Varāha.
Śiva, Īśa, Tatpuruṣa,
Aghora, Sadyojāta, O Rāma;
and Sūrya, Soma, Kuja, Budha, Jīva, Śukra, and Śanaiścara.
Rāhu, Ketu, Gaṇapati, Senānī, Caṇḍikā, Umā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, the hosts headed by Brahmāṇī, the Rudras, Indra and the others, Vahni, the Nāgas, Tārkṣya, and other deities; AP 235.012ab.
May those dwelling in heaven, the atmosphere, and on earth bring about my victory;
may they crush the enemies in battle,
having accepted this offering.
Together with my sons, mother, and servants,
O gods, I have come to you for refuge.
1. "In front of that" (tat-purataḥ) is found in manuscript Kha.
2. The passage beginning with "at night" (rātrau) and ending with "born of truth" (satyajaḥ) is not present in manuscript Ga.
"May they crush my enemies," thus [in] *gha* and *ña*; "May they protect me; I am their servant," thus [in] *ja* and *ṭa*:
"Having gone behind these armies, O destroyers of enemies, homage be to you!
Having returned, I shall offer a tribute even greater than what was given."
On the sixth day, the victory-bath (vijayasnāna) should be performed like a consecration (abhiṣeka); and on the seventh day, the day of the procession, one should worship Trivikrama.
One should also worship the weapon and the vehicle with the mantras prescribed for the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
With the sounds of "Auspicious Day" and "Victory," one should listen to this mantra:
"May the gods dwelling in heaven, the intermediate space, and on earth grant you long life;
O God, may you attain success, and may your divine procession be auspicious."
Having heard, "May all the deities protect [me]," the king should depart,
taking up his bow along with arrows while reciting the mantra *dhanurnāga*, and then,
having muttered the mantra *tad viṣṇoḥ*, he should place his foot upon the face of the enemy.
Having mounted the right foot [of the chariot] in sequence upon the elephant, the chariot, the horse, and the draft-animals in the thirty-two directions beginning with the east,
he should proceed to the accompaniment of musical instruments; once mounted, he should not look back.
Having traveled for the distance of one *krośa*, he should halt, worship the deities and the twice-born,
and then proceed to the enemy's territory while protecting his own army;
thus the king, having reached the lord of the gods—
He should protect the protector of the land;
he should perform the worship of the gods and must not cut off the revenue there.
Having returned to his own city, he should not hold those people of that land in contempt.
1. "And may there be destruction of the enemy at the rear of the armies," thus [it is said] in the *Ṭa*.
2. "Having conquered the enemy, I shall bestow [the land]," thus [it is said] in the *Ṭa*. 3. "May the expeditions be victorious," thus [it is said] in the *Ṭa*.

4. "But having reached another country," according to Ga., Gha., and Ña; 5. "One should observe the customs of the country," according to Kha.; "One should protect [oneself] by means of the customs of the country," according to Ga. and Gha.
Having achieved victory, O King, the ruler should worship the gods and bestow gifts.
On the second day, when the battle is about to take place, one should bathe the elephants, horses, and other mounts; worship the divine lion among kings;
and at night, indeed, [worship] the royal insignia such as the parasol, the weapons, and the hosts.

Having worshipped Nṛsiṃha in the morning, along with his entire retinue of mounts and attendants, he should observe the fire into which the priest has offered oblations; having performed the sacrifice, he should honor the twice-born.
Then, taking up his bow and arrow, he should indeed mount an elephant or another vehicle and proceed.
Remaining invisible to his enemies in that region, he should organize his constituent elements; he should fight with few when they are concentrated, but may extend them at will when numerous.
When few are facing many, the battle array should be "needle-mouthed" (sūcīmukha).
Formations are proclaimed to be of two kinds: those in the shape of living beings and those in the form of material objects;
namely, the Garuḍa formation, the Makara formation, the Cakra, the Śyena, as well as the Ardhacandra, the Vajra, and the Śakaṭa formation.
The Maṇḍala, the Sarvatobhadra, and the Sūcīvyūha—these are the arrays for those men;
furthermore, among all these arrays, there is a fivefold arrangement of the army:
two wings, two flanks, and the fifth must necessarily be the center.
He should engage in battle with either one or two divisions,
while he should set aside a third division solely for their protection;
the king should never employ the formation of a battle array (*vyūha*).
If the root is severed, there will be total destruction; therefore, the king himself should not fight.
The lord of the earth should remain at a distance of one *krośa* behind the army;
staying there is prescribed for the purpose of rallying the warriors who have broken ranks.
If the main force is broken, the destruction of the entire army is ordained.
One should not arrange the warriors in the battle formation either too closely together or too far apart.
So that there may be no mutual clashing of weapons,
one who desires to break the enemy's army should break it while they are still united; likewise, even by the enemy, those who are united must be protected from being broken.
One should, according to one's will, form an array that causes division among the enemy arrays;
O twice-born one, there should be four foot-soldiers for the protection of the elephant's feet,
and likewise four horses and four shield-bearers for the chariot.
In battle, archers should be placed in front, equal to those bearing shields;
behind the archers should follow shield-bearers, and behind the shield-bearers should follow archers.
Behind the chariots should be placed elephants; these must be assigned by the ruler of the earth.
One should diligently attend to the religious duties of the infantry, elephants, and horses;
brave men should be placed at the front, while the host of cowards should merely display their shoulders to cause the enemy to flee. (1)
But those who tremble at the front must not be sent forward;
for brave men standing at the front encourage even the cowards in battle— those who are tall, those with auspicious marks, and those men whose eyes do not squint.
Those with closely knit eyebrows, who are wrathful and fond of quarreling,
yet always cheerful and exultant, should be known as brave and full of desire.
The act of removing [the dead] from the battlefield for those who were slain while gathered together,
as well as the counter-attack against elephants and the offering of water-libations (*toyadāna*) and so forth;
this is the cause for terrifying the enemy.
ga..., gha..., ña... ca 2; and those with squinting eyes, according to kha..., ga..., gha..., ña... ca.
The act of removing the *vala* (the protective covering) is performed;
furthermore, the bringing forward of weapons and the duties of the infantry are prescribed.
The task of the shield-bearer is proclaimed to be the protection of one's own army against enemies seeking to break through, as well as the breaking apart of those who stand in a compact formation;
likewise, it is said that his duty is to turn back archers in battle.

Retreating to a great distance is likewise called the movement of one who has struck a blow; terrifying the enemy forces is likewise called the work of the chariot. Breaking up those who are united, and uniting those who are divided—[these are its functions].

When [the enemy] has encountered [an army], the ground with broken walls, gate-towers, watchtowers, and trees is known as suitable for infantry; likewise, level ground is suitable for chariots and horses,
while ground that is muddy is declared to be the battlefield for elephants.
Having thus arranged the battle formation and positioned the sun behind him,
and likewise having favorable Venus, the sun, the guardians of the directions, and gentle winds,
he should rouse all the warriors by proclaiming their names, lineages, and heroic exploits.
Through victory there is the attainment of enjoyments, and for one who has died, the attainment of heaven;

by conquering enemies, there is the acquisition of pleasures, and for one who has died, the supreme goal. There is no means of atonement for the master’s funeral cake equal to the destiny found in battle.
The blood of heroes flows out, and by means of it they cast off their sins;
enduring the suffering of the bodily elements and so forth in battle is the highest austerity.
Thousands of excellent apsarases go to the hero who has died in battle.
The Lord takes away the merit of those who break their resolve and turn back;
it is said that for them, the fruit of killing a Brahmin accrues at every step.
Furthermore, he who abandons his companions and goes on alone brings about his own destruction.
The fruit of the horse sacrifice is proclaimed for heroes who do not retreat;
victory belongs to the king who is devoted to dharma.
Those of equal status should be fought with those of equal status;

elephants and other such units should not be struck by elephants and the like; nor should those who are fleeing, those who have entered as spectators, those who are unarmed, or those who are wounded be slain.
When [the enemy] is calm, overcome by sleep, or has half-crossed a river or forest; on a cloudy day, one should carry out ambushes for the sake of destroying the enemy.
Grasping his arms, he should cry out: "The others are broken! They are broken!"
A vast army and a friend have been gained, yet the leader here has been struck down; the commander-in-chief has been slain and the king himself has fallen into distress.
For the fleeing warriors, a blow to their front must now be dealt.
O knower of dharma, incense that is supremely intoxicating should be offered,
as well as banners and a collection of terrifying musical instruments;
having attained victory in battle, one should worship the gods and the brahmins.
When a battle has been waged by a minister, the jewels go to the king;
his women are not to be protected by anyone, whether they belong to him or to another.
Having encountered an enemy released in battle, one should protect him like a son.
Furthermore, he should not fight again; he should observe the local customs and traditions.
Then, having reached his own city, he should enter his home during a fixed asterism, perform worship of the gods and other deities, and protect the families of the warriors.
He should share what he has obtained with his servants;
this initiation for battle, which I have described to you, will surely lead to victory for the king.
Thus ends the section titled "The Initiation for Battle" in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The two hundred and thirty-fifth chapter.
1. "Victory is eternally rooted in Dharma" (as found in manuscripts *kha* and *cha*).
2. "One should worship the gods, the Brahmins, and the gurus" (as found in manuscripts *gha*, *ja*, and *ña*).
Chapter Two Hundred and Thirty-Six:
The Chapter on the Sixty-Four Yoginīs.
Puṣkara spoke this Śrī-stotra for the sake of stabilizing the royal fortune of Śrī, just as it was formerly recited by Indra.
Thus praise was offered; likewise, for the sake of victory, a king should perform praise.
Indra said:
"I pay homage to all the worlds."
You are Śrī, the lotus-eyed consort of Indra, who dwells upon the chest of Viṣṇu;
you are Siddhi, Svadhā, Svāhā, and Sudhā; O Purifier of the World, you are Sandhyā, Night, Radiance, Bhūti, Medhā, Śraddhā, and Sarasvatī.

O beautiful one, you are the science of sacrifice, the great science, and the secret science; O Goddess, you are the science of the Self that bestows the fruit of liberation. You alone are logic, the three Vedas, commerce, and the science of government.

O Goddess, this world has been filled by you with your gentle forms that are themselves gentle. O Goddess, who else but you could occupy this body of the God of gods, the wielder of the mace, which consists of all sacrifices and is conceivable only through yoga?

O Goddess, the entire triple world was abandoned by you and had become almost ruined; it has now been restored to prosperity by you. Wives, sons, as well as home, friends, grain, wealth, and so forth—
O highly fortunate lady, this [benefit] always accrues to men from the sight of you;
[the reading "of all beings" occurs in the manuscripts gha, ja, and ña].
2. [The mantra] "javanīm ambusambhavām" (is for one born of water).
Health of the body, sovereignty, the destruction of the enemy faction, and happiness—(1)
O Goddess, for men beheld by your glance, nothing is difficult to attain;
you are the mother of all beings, and Hari is the God of gods, our father. O Mother, this entire world, both moving and unmoving, is pervaded by you and by Viṣṇu.
O purifier of all, do not abandon pride, nor the treasury, nor the granary, nor the house, nor the retinue, nor the body, nor the wife;
do not abandon sons, nor groups of friends, nor livestock, nor ornaments.

O stainless one, those men whom you have abandoned would immediately abandon even my divinity through their goodness, truthfulness, purity, and likewise through virtues such as moral conduct— were it not for the fact that they have been forsaken by you.
Beheld by you, even men devoid of merit are instantly endowed with all virtues such as moral conduct, as well as noble lineage and sovereignty.
He is praiseworthy, he is virtuous, he is blessed, he is of noble birth, and he is wise.

O Goddess, beloved of Viṣṇu, he who has been gazed upon by you is truly a hero and a man of valor; yet all his virtues, such as good character and the like, immediately fall into disarray when you, the Mother of the World, turn your face away from him.
"Even the tongue of the Creator would not be able to describe your virtues.
Be gracious, O lotus-eyed goddess; never forsake us.
Thus spoke Puṣkara.
Thus praised, Śrī granted Indra his desired boon:
the firm stability of his kingdom, victory in battle, and so forth.
(Note: *kṣayaḥ* [decay] is read as *svayam* [himself] in manuscript *kha*.)

Acquiring wealth by righteous means, its increase, its protection,

Discipline is the root of policy, for discipline arises from the determination of the treatises.

Chapter 241:

Rāma said:

Having arrayed the sixfold army and having worshipped the gods, one should advance against the enemy; that army consists of hereditary troops (maula), recruited troops (bhūta), the rear-guard (śroṇi), allies (suhṛd), enemies (dviṣat), and forest-dwellers (āṭavika).

Among the calamities of the [six] constituent elements, each preceding one is more serious than the following; likewise, with the sixfold army consisting of counsel, treasury, infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants,
wherever there may be danger— in rivers, mountains, marshes, or fortresses— [one should act accordingly].
The general should proceed here and there with his forces drawn up in battle array;
the leader should march at the front, surrounded by pre-eminent warriors.
In the center are the women, the lord, and the treasury, as well as the weak troops; on both flanks are the cavalry, on the flanks of the cavalry are the chariots,
on the flanks of the chariots are the elephants, and on the flanks of the elephants is the forest force.
Thereafter, the general, having placed everything in front of him, should himself proceed skillfully with his arrayed host; he should march slowly, consoling those who are weary,
using a great crocodile formation when there is danger ahead.

With the wings spread like a hawk, or with a needle-like formation at the front of the heroes; when danger lies behind, one should employ the cart formation (*śakaṭa*); when danger is on the flanks, the formation known as the thunderbolt (*vajra*);
and when danger is on all sides, one should arrange the all-auspicious array (*sarvatobhadra*).
In mountain caves, in dense thickets, and in the narrow passes of rivers and forests;
exhausted by long journeys, with fatigue brought on by hunger and thirst; afflicted by disease, famine, and pestilence; and scattered by bandits— [He saw beings] in such states.
[The food] scattered on the path, gathered into a heap,
lying down, distracted by eating, not on the ground, or ill-placed;
terrified by fear of thieves or fire, or struck by rain and wind— [such food is unfit].
In such cases, he should protect his own army and strike down the enemy force;
for one who is superior in terms of place and time, whose disposition is not divided, and who is strong,
should indeed engage in open warfare, whereas in the opposite case, one should employ treacherous warfare.
At those times of assault, one should strike down the enemy while they are in a state of total confusion.
This is known as the "Vajra-Saṅkaṭa" (the adamantine strait).
One should strike down those who are out of position, those who are in their own position, and those who are born in their own territory—
those drawn by nature or by force— with the help of brave men using snares, such as forest-dwellers, through breaking, giving way, and dragging away.
Having first presented a frontal display so that the enemy's attention is fixed upon it,
one should then strike from behind with a swift and heroic force; or else, having thrown the enemy into confusion from the rear, one should strike them from the front with brave warriors.
By these two [methods], the attacks on the flanks are explained for fighting from ambushes; however, when the ground is uneven, the swift warrior should strike from behind.
In the same way, one should strike from the front or the rear when the ground is uneven, as well as from the flanks.

Having first engaged the forces of traitors, enemies, and forest-dwellers in battle, he should strike them when they are exhausted, demoralized, and without support, while his own mounts remain unwearied;
or else, being diligent, he should cause a feigned retreat using the forces of traitors and enemies.
Relying on secret counsel, one should strike down the enemy who has become confident, thinking "it is won," among the army camps,
cities, villages, crops, masters, subjects, and so forth;
being vigilant, one should destroy the hostile force as it becomes overconfident.
Alternatively, having drawn out that target by seizing cattle and blocking the roads,
one should strike it while it sleeps during the day— its soldiers being disoriented by sleep and exhausted from the vigil and worship performed at night due to fear of a sudden assault.

Surprise while [the enemy] is sleeping trustfully at night; leading the way during a march with elephants or swordsmen; entering forest strongholds; breaking up undivided armies; and rallying broken forces.
Causing terror, striking down gates, the work of guarding the treasury and elephants;
breaking the unbrokeable and the reconciliation of friends— these are the duties of the chariot.
The search for forest paths and directions; the characteristics of supplies and reinforcements; pursuit and retreat; the execution of urgent tasks;
the pursuit of the distressed; and the destruction of the flanks and the rear.
Furthermore, the duties of a cavalryman and a foot soldier include always bearing weapons,
clearing the camp and the paths, performing enema treatments,
and removing large stumps, anthills, trees, shrubs, and thorns.
Ground that is not too uneven is considered suitable for infantry, provided it has room for retreat;
it should have few trees and stones, its hills should be easily leaped over, and it should be firm.
Ground free of gravel and mud, and with space for retreat, is suitable for cavalry.
The ground for chariots was free of stumps, trees, and furrows; it was devoid of mud, crushable trees, and tangled thickets of creepers;

For one who receives back broken forces such as the *urasya* (chest) division is known as "receiving" (*pratigraha*), which is capable of managing other royal affairs; however,
a battle array that is depleted by him appears as if it were broken.
A wise man who desires victory should not fight without receiving reinforcements;
for where there is a king, there is a treasury, and sovereignty indeed depends upon the treasury. Therefore, he should give something to the warriors from that [treasury].
It is not appropriate [to set a fixed price];

Or indeed, they might fight back with horses, chariots, and elephants;

Just as there should be no crowding when withdrawing from physical exercise,

Moving through the object of experience with the flanks, wings, and chest,

Chapter 252:
An Exposition on Legal Proceedings (Vyavahāra)
Agni said:
"I shall declare the legal procedure, which provides the discernment between right and wrong;
it is said to have four feet, four bases, and four means."
It is proclaimed as having four benefits, four pervasions, and four functions;
likewise, it has eight limbs, eighteen sections, and a hundred branches;
furthermore, it has three origins, two applications, two doors, and two destinations.
Dharma, legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), custom (*caritra*), and royal edict (*rājaśāsana*)—
among these four pillars of legal proceedings, each subsequent one establishes the preceding.
Among them, Dharma is established in truth, while legal procedure rests upon witnesses.
In the *Caritra*, it is said: "The *saṅgraha* (compilation) of men's deeds [is the *varmiṇa*], while the royal decree is the *śāsana*. (Gha and Ña manuscripts, p. 407).
Because it is to be accomplished through the means of conciliation (*sāma*), it is called the "fourfold instrument" (*catus-sādhana*).
And because it protects the four stages of life (*āśrama*), it is the "fourfold benefactor" (*catur-hita*).
[It protects] the perpetrator, the witnesses, the truthful ones, and the king himself.
Because he pervades [all things] by means of his feet, he is therefore remembered as "the four-pervading" (caturvyāpin).
Because he brings about these four— dharma, wealth, fame, and the esteem of the world—
he is proclaimed as "the four-achiever" (catuṣkārī).
The king, his attendants, the court members, the legal treatise, the calculator, the scribe, gold, fire, and water—this is declared to be the eightfold assembly;
for it proceeds from these three: desire, anger, and greed.
Therefore, this triad is proclaimed as having three origins and being the cause of disputes.
Furthermore, a lawsuit is to be understood as twofold, arising from suspicion and from proof of the facts.
Suspicion arises from six sources through association, while proof of the facts is seen to be sixfold.
Because it is connected with two sides, it is declared to have two doors;

of these, the first side is the *pūrvavāda* (the proponent's position), while the subsequent one is the *pratipakṣa* (the opponent's counter-position). Because they follow either reality (*bhūta*) or quibble (*chala*), it is declared to have two courses.
That which is debt to be paid and that which is not to be paid, by whom, where, and in what manner,
as well as the law regarding giving and receiving— it is known as the legal title of "Recovery of Debt" (*ṛṇādāna*).
When one deposits one's own property with another out of trust, free from apprehension...
That which is called "deposit" (nikṣepa) is declared by the wise to be a head of legal dispute.
Where merchants and others perform work collectively, that they know as "partnership" (sambhūyasamutthāna), a head of legal dispute.
When one who has properly given away property desires to take it back again,
that is recorded in tradition as the legal dispute known as *apradānika* (non-delivery).

And when one who has undertaken service does not perform it, this legal title is called "Non-performance after Undertaking Service. The rules regarding the payment and non-payment of wages for servants are as follows.
The non-payment of wages is recorded as a subject of dispute.

When another person’s property— whether it be a deposit, something lost, or something found— is sold in the absence of the owner after having been seized, that is to be known as sale without ownership.
When, after selling a commodity for its price, it is not delivered to the purchaser, that is called the legal dispute of "non-delivery after sale" (*vikrīyāsampradāna*). When,
after purchasing a commodity for its price, the purchaser does not find it to his satisfaction...

When a buyer, having purchased a commodity for a price, considers it a bad purchase, this refers to the established practice (*sthiti*) of heretics, guilds (*naigama*), and so forth; such a convention is called a "compact" (*samaya*). The non-fulfillment of that compact is recorded in legal tradition as a ground for dispute (*vivādapada*).

Where determinations regarding embankments, field boundaries, and whether land is cultivated or uncultivated occur in matters concerning fields, that is a dispute arising from fields (*kṣetraja*). Where the rules for women and men pertaining to marriage are proclaimed, that is the section on marriage (*vaivāhika*).
The legal title known as the union of man and woman is recorded as that subject of dispute.
Furthermore, that which is arranged by sons regarding the division of their father’s property is called "inheritance" (dāya) by the wise; that is the subject of dispute.
Whatever act is performed impulsively by those arrogant of their strength is declared to be *sāhasa* (violence); it is called a title of dispute (*vivādapada*).
[That which] involves abuse of country, caste, family, and so forth, accompanied by [mention of] limbs...
Speech whose meaning is contrary [to others] is called verbal harshness (*vākpāruṣya*):
"Inflict injury upon the limbs of another with hands, feet, weapons, and so forth. (AP 252.028ab)
Assault with violence by means of fire and other such instruments is called *daṇḍapāruṣya* (physical violence). Gambling with dice, knucklebones, sticks, and the like is called *dyūta* (gambling).
Gambling with living creatures and betting on animals for sport;
furthermore, miscellaneous legal disputes (vyavahāra) that lack a formal basis;
as well as the defiance of the king’s commands and the failure to perform his duties.
Legal procedure consists of eighteen titles; their subdivisions indeed amount to one hundred.
Due to the diversity of human actions, it is said to have a hundred branches. The king, free from anger, should oversee legal proceedings together with wise Brahmins.
The members of the court should be impartial toward both enemy and friend, free from greed, and learned in the sacred scriptures.
If [the king] cannot find such persons, he may appoint a Brahmin to the seat of judgment out of necessity.
Those who act contrary to the legal codes out of passion, greed, or fear are not fit for this office.
The members of the court shall each be punished separately; the fine for the dispute is double that amount.
For when one who has been oppressed by others through a path deviating from the traditional law and custom brings a matter before the king, that indeed constitutes a subject of legal litigation.
The defendant must submit a written response in the presence of the plaintiff, exactly as it was understood by the claimant;
this document must be marked with the year, month, fortnight, day, names, caste, and other identifying characteristics,
and it should be presented once the meaning of the claim has been heard.
A petitioner who has been tormented by distress should immediately cause a document to be written that establishes the matter he has asserted;
if that is proven, he attains success, but otherwise the opposite occurs.
This four-footed judicial procedure has thus been demonstrated in disputes.
The reading "apaśyatā" is not correct:
"Without having discharged the charge, one should not bring a counter-charge against him. (AP 252.038cd)
One should not cause a defendant who has been summoned by another to abandon his case or undergo an improper change of state;
however, in cases of mutual assault or acts of violence, one may institute a counter-charge.
In both instances, a guarantor capable of ensuring the final resolution of the matter must be secured.
If he denies it, he should pay a fine to the king equal to that amount;

however, for a false accusation, he shall forfeit double the value of the claim. In cases of violence, theft, verbal abuse, false accusations, and the abduction of women, [the rule regarding the denial of a claim applies].
One should deliberate immediately; otherwise, time is said to be determined by one's own desire.
He goes from place to place, and he licks the corners of his mouth. His forehead perspires, and there is a change in the color of his face.
One who undergoes a change from his natural state through actions of mind, speech, or body,
whether during a legal proceeding or as a witness, is proclaimed to be "corrupt in speech.
Likewise, one who attempts to prove a doubtful matter on his own authority or who absconds is also considered corrupt.
If one who has been summoned says nothing at all, he is declared by the legal tradition to be liable for a fine.
When witnesses exist on both sides, the witnesses belong to the plaintiff; however, once the initial claim has been refuted, they belong to the defendant.
If the dispute should involve a group, the king shall cause the inferior party to pay [the fine].
Having caused the stake, the dwelling, and the wealth of the creditor to be paid,
the king should conduct the legal proceedings by dismissing the deceitful party through a messenger.
Even if the fact is true, it is lost in legal proceedings if it is concealed;
one who denies a claim that is entirely established by multiple witnesses, even if only a portion of it has been proven,
shall be made to pay the entire amount by the king, but he must not be made to pay what was not declared.
When there is a conflict between two legal traditions (*smṛti*), the principle is that one follows the established practice of the herdsmen;
for it is a settled rule that the *Dharmaśāstra* (the treatise on law) is more authoritative than the *Arthaśāstra* (the treatise on worldly affairs).
Written evidence, possession, and witnesses are declared to be the means of proof;
in the absence of any one of these, any one of the divine ordeals is prescribed.
In all disputes whatsoever, the subsequent mode of proof is the stronger.
In the case of a mortgage, a gift, or a purchase, the prior title is indeed more powerful;
however, for land, loss occurs after twenty years of possession by another who is seen and spoken to [of it],
while for other property, it occurs after ten years.
Except for property consisting of pledges, deposits, and that belonging to the mentally incapacitated or minors,
as well as the property of sealed deposits, the king’s women, and Vedic scholars— one should cause the person who misappropriates such property to pay it back to the owner.

And he should be made to pay that same amount to the king, or an amount according to his capacity; moreover, even a title-deed is superior to possession that has not been held through prior succession.
Even a title-deed has no strength where there is not even the slightest possession.
Possession attains the status of valid proof through pure title;
possession based on impure title does not attain validity.
However, he by whom the title was created must, when challenged, produce it.
Neither his son nor the son of his son [has a claim] there; possession is what is weightier in that case.
If one who was accused should die, one should recover that [property] from his inheritance.
In that matter, possession is not a valid ground when it is devoid of a legal title (*āgama*).
One should set aside legal transactions brought about by force or other such conditions:

those conducted at night, inside a house, or outside [the village], as well as those caused by enemies; and those instigated by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted, distressed, a child, or terrified.
Furthermore, a legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) conducted by one who lacks mindfulness does not succeed. (252.61ab)

The king shall cause wealth lost by more than one hundred [kārṣāpaṇas] to be restored to the creditor; if he cannot prove it through evidence, he ought to pay an amount equal to that. Furthermore, property stolen by thieves must be returned by the king to the people of the realm.
The interest per month shall be one-eightieth [of the principal] when there is security;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be two, three, four, or five percent.
For cattle and women, the maximum is seven percent; for liquids, it is eightfold.
For clothes, grain, and gold, the interest shall likewise be four, three, and two-fold respectively;
however, from another village it shall be ten percent, and from the sea twenty percent.
Or, all castes may pay whatever interest they have agreed upon among themselves.
One who has approached [the court] to accomplish his purpose should not be censured by the king;
however, if he departs for the king while his case is being adjudicated, he shall be punished and made to pay that wealth. Thus ends the section on legal procedure in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The two hundred and fifty-second chapter.
Chapter 253:
An Account of Legal Proceedings (*Vyavahārakathana*)
Agni said:
Once the debt has been established, the debtor should be made to pay it to the creditors in due order; having first given to a Brāhmaṇa, he should give it to the king thereafter.
The king shall cause the debtor to pay ten percent of the amount proven due; furthermore,
the creditor who has recovered his wealth shall be made to pay five percent.
One of low birth who has exhausted his debt should be made to work for its repayment;
however, a Brāhmaṇa who has exhausted his debt should be made to pay gradually according to his means.
He who does not accept the capital lent to him when it is being returned [should be compelled to do so].
That [debt] which has been established by a mediator shall not increase beyond that point.
One who inherits the estate, as well as one who marries the widow, must pay the debt;
likewise, a son whose property does not depend on others must pay for his father who is without heirs.
If a debt has been contracted for the sake of the family by those who have not separated from it,
the heirs shall pay it when the head of the household has died or gone abroad.
A wife is not liable for a debt contracted by her husband or son, nor is a father liable for one contracted by his son.

A husband shall not be liable for a debt contracted by his wife, except for what was incurred for the sake of the family; however, the husband of a cowherd’s wife, a liquor-seller’s wife, a fisherman’s wife, a washerwoman’s wife, or a hunter’s wife must pay their debts, because their livelihood depends upon him.

A debt contracted by a woman should be paid by her husband, or what was contracted together with him, or whatever debt she has incurred herself; no other woman is liable to pay it. Furthermore, [the debt] may be paid when the father is away on a journey, deceased, or overwhelmed by calamity.

A debt must be paid by sons and grandsons when it has been proven by witnesses in the event of a denial; however, a son shall not have to pay for his father’s debts incurred through liquor, lust, gambling, fines, judicial costs,
or for gifts made in vain.
Indeed, between brothers, between husband and wife, and between father and son— even when overwhelmed by calamity— [there is no separation].
It is recorded in the Smṛti that a surety (*pratibhāvya*) may be taken even by one who has not divided the inheritance.
A surety is prescribed for appearance, for trustworthiness, and for payment.
However, if the pledge (*ādhi*) is lost, those liable to pay shall be made to pay; this applies to the sons of the one who was a surety for loss as well.
Where a surety for appearance (*darśanapratibhū*) or a surety for confidence (*prātyayika*) has died, their sons need not pay the debt; however, those who stood as sureties for payment must pay it.
If there are many such sureties, they should each pay the debt according to their respective shares.
When these [debtor and surety] are under one and the same roof, the surety shall be made to pay the creditor whatever amount he desires;
and where the surety has publicly paid the debt to the creditor,
that amount shall be repaid by the debtors to him at double the value.
Grain from one's own lineage, including women and cattle, may be doubled;
clothing is said to be quadrupled, and liquids likewise eightfold.
If it is not released when the debt has become double, the pledge shall be forfeited.

What is lost through the passage of time perishes, but that which is to be enjoyed as fruit does not perish. A pledge intended for enjoyment is not subject to interest; likewise, no interest accrues on a beneficial pledge when it has been used. If such a pledge is lost or destroyed—provided it was not caused by acts of God or the king—it must be replaced by the debtor.
If, after the pledge has been accepted, it becomes worthless even though it was being protected, another pledge should be taken; or else, the creditor shall become a sharer in the debtor's wealth.
[The debtor] shall be made to pay the debt along with interest as a pledge based on good conduct (*caritra*).
One shall cause the debtor to repay double the value of any property for which a verbal pledge was made;
when the debtor is present, the pledge must be released, otherwise a fine shall be imposed. If the creditor has other assets, he may obtain a pledge from another member of the family.
Or it may remain there at its value fixed at that time,
without interest; for it is recorded in the Smṛti that a surety-debt and a witnessed-debt belong to one who is undivided [from his family].
Or even if he sells it in the presence of witnesses without the holder's consent;
but when the debt has indeed doubled upon the pledge, then— *AP_253.024ab*
A pledge must be released once the deposited wealth has doubled after it has been lent out.
That property which one should entrust to another's hand without disclosing that the recipient is in distress is called *upanidhi*; it must be returned in exactly the same manner.
If the property has been lost due to the king, fate, or thieves, he shall not be made to pay for it;
however, if he was commissioned to search for it and failed to do so when requested, he should be made to pay the value and a fine equal to that amount.
If he makes a living from it by his own will, he should be punished and made to pay the value along with interest.
This same rule applies to borrowed items, those held for delivery, deposits, and pledges.
Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "Legal Procedure," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 254:
An Exposition on Divine Measurements (Divyapramāṇakathana)
Agni said:
"Those who are ascetic, charitable by nature, of noble birth, speakers of truth,
devoted primarily to dharma, upright, possessed of sons, and endowed with wealth— "
Those engaged in the performance of the five sacrifices are declared to be witnesses—either five or three; all may serve as witnesses for all, according to their birth or caste.
However, women, the elderly, children, gamblers, those intoxicated, the insane, and those accused of crimes are excluded.
Those who stage plays, heretics, deceivers, those with impaired faculties,
those who eat the food of the fallen, kinsmen, companions, enemies, and thieves; AP_254.004ab/
One who is not a witness may yet be a witness to all matters; in cases of theft, verbal abuse, and violence, even a single person who knows the law may be a witness if agreed upon by both parties.
For a man who fails to testify regarding a debt becomes liable for that debt along with ten percent interest.
The king should cause that lowest of men— who, though knowing the truth, does not give testimony— to pay the entire amount on the forty-sixth day;
for he is indeed equal to false witnesses in both his sin and his punishment.
He should cause the witnesses, who stand in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, to hear [the following]:
"Those worlds which are for the doers of sins, as well as for those who commit the great sins (mahāpātaka),
those worlds which are for arsonists, and those which are for the killers of women and children."
He who gives false testimony incurs all those [sins];
know that whatever merit you have performed over hundreds of previous births, all of that belongs to the one whom you defeat through falsehood.
In a case of division, the testimony of the majority prevails; likewise, when the numbers are equal, that of those possessing superior qualities.
But when there is a division even among those of superior qualities, the testimony of those who possess the highest qualities should be accepted.
He whose claim the witnesses have declared to be true shall be the victor.
He for whom the speaker is otherwise is certain to suffer defeat.
Even when testimony has been given by witnesses, if others who are more virtuous or twice as numerous should state it otherwise, those [former witnesses] would be false.
The witnesses who were previously cited,
as well as those who give false testimony, shall each be punished individually; the fine for such false witnesses is double that of the dispute, and a Brāhmaṇa is ordained to be banished.
He who, having been made to hear the testimony from others, conceals it, being shrouded in darkness,
shall be made to pay a fine eightfold; however, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, he should be banished.
Indeed, where the death penalty would otherwise fall upon the members of the [four] castes, one may speak untruth as testimony.
However, for whatever matter is mutually agreed upon by the parties themselves,
a document should be executed with witnesses, preceded by the name of the creditor.
A document should be marked with the year, month, day, the name of the person to whom it is due, the names of the [debtor's] caste,
his own lineage, and his fellow-students, as well as the names of his father and other such identifiers.
When the matter is concluded, the debtor shall record his own name in his own hand.
"It is my opinion that what has been inscribed here belongs to such-and-such son;
and the witnesses, preceded by their fathers' names, should each write by their own hand: 'I, so-and-so, am a witness here. Thus they should all act."
He who is illiterate or a debtor should have his own intention recorded;
or a witness, in the presence of all the witnesses and by means of another witness, [should state]: "This was requested by both parties, and has been written by me, the son of so-and-so."
At the end, the scribe should write, "It has been written by so-and-so.
Even without witnesses, a document that is written in one's own hand is declared to be valid as evidence, with the exception of those executed through force or fraud.
A debt documented by a written instrument must be paid by three generations of persons alone;
however, the pledge is enjoyed as long as that [debt] is not repaid.
[The debt is discharged] when the debtor resides in another country, when the document is illegible, or when it is lost, effaced, or stolen.
If a document is torn, cut, or burnt, one should have another written; however,
that which is written in one's own hand for the purpose of clearing a doubtful matter may be accepted on the basis of logic, acquisition, performance, signs, connection, and title-deeds.
On the back of the document, one should write down what has been received from the debtor;
and the creditor shall deliver the receipt, marked with his own hand.
One should tear up the document for a debt that has been paid; for the sake of purification, one should cause another document to be made.
That which was executed with witnesses must be repaid in the presence of witnesses.
For the purpose of purification in this world, the ordeals are the balance, fire, water, poison, and sacred libation.
In cases of major charges, when the accuser has placed his head [as a stake], the other party may proceed according to their mutual consent;
otherwise, one party shall provide the head-stake.
Even without a head-stake, one may proceed in cases of treason against the king or in the event of a mortal sin.

One should not employ the ploughshare, the balance, or the poison for cases involving less than a thousand [paṇas]. In legal proceedings concerning matters of state, those who are pure should always administer the balance and other ordeals for amounts of a thousand; however, for smaller amounts, one should cause the ordeal to be administered in the royal treasury.
One who is pure should be made to pay fifty [paṇas]; one who is impure shall be subject to punishment.
Having summoned him while he is fasting and clothed, at sunrise, one should cause him to undergo the ordeals using a *darva* ladle in the presence of the king and Brahmins.
For women, children, the elderly, the blind, the lame, Brahmins, and the sick, the ordeal shall be by balance;
for a Śūdra, it shall be by fire, blazing or by seven grains of poison.
One who is accused and has resorted to the balance shall be weighed by experts skilled in the handling of the balance.
Having been brought down after being made level by means of a counterweight and marked with a line:
the sun, the moon, the wind, the fire, the sky, the earth, the waters, the heart, Yama,
day and night, both twilights, and Dharma know the conduct of a man.
O Tula, you were created by the gods of old as the abode of truth;
speak the truth, O auspicious one, and deliver me from this doubt.
"O Mother, if I am a doer of evil, then lead me downward;
if I am pure, lead me upward"—thus one should consecrate the scales.
Then, having marked the hands after they have been rubbed with rice grains, one should place them [upon the scales].
One should wrap the leaves of the seven-horsed fire-plant with thread that many times. "O Purifier, you alone move within all beings;
like a witness, speak the truth to me, O Fire, regarding my merits and sins."
When he has spoken thus, one should place upon both his hands a smooth iron ball weighing fifty palas and glowing with fire;
taking it up, he should run seven circles in a hundred [steps].
The mandala should be known as sixteen finger-breadths in extent; having left that much space from the fire, one who has rubbed the rice grains and remains unburnt attains purity.
If the ball falls in between or if there is doubt, one should perform the ordeal again.
"O purifier of purifiers, purify that which is to be purified;
O sanctifier, protect me with truth!"—with these words, [the priest] addresses the accused.
Standing in water reaching up to the navel, [the priest] takes hold of the thighs [of the accused] and enters the water.
If another man, having brought back the arrow that was released at the same moment,
should see his body submerged in it, he shall attain purification.
O Poison, son of Brahmā, you are established in truth and righteousness.
"Protect me from this curse; by truth, become nectar for me!
Having spoken thus, he should consume the *sārṅga* poison born of the snowy mountains;
if it is digested without its violent effects, one should declare him pure.
Having worshipped the deities and their attendants, one should take the water used for their ablutions;
having made [the recipient] listen to the mantra, one should cause them to drink three handfuls (prasṛti) of that water.
If, within fourteen days, no terrible misfortune caused by the king or by fate befalls him, he shall undoubtedly be proven innocent;
likewise [if there is no harm] to truthful speech, weapons, cattle, seeds, or gold.
"The deities, the feet of the guru, and the merits of sacrifices and charitable works—
these are declared to be easy oaths for cases of minor doubt. Thus ends the section titled "Divine Means of Proof" in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The two hundred and fifty-fourth chapter.
Chapter 255:
Exposition on the Partition of Inheritance (Dāyavibhāga)
Agni said:
"If the father should divide [the estate], he may divide the sons according to his will;
either by giving the eldest a superior share, or all may be equal sharers."

If he should give [the property] in equal shares, the wives whose *strīdhana* was not given by their husband or father-in-law must be made equal sharers; however, if he is capable and yet does not desire [to give], he may separate them after giving something to each.
If the division made by the father was unequal or contrary to the law,
the sons shall divide the inheritance and the debt equally after the death of both parents;
the daughters shall take the remainder of the mother's estate after her debts, and in their absence, the agnates.
Whatever else one may acquire by oneself without using the paternal estate—
whether it be a gift from a friend or a dowry received at marriage— that shall not belong to the heirs.
However, when property is acquired through joint effort, an equal division is ordained.

But for those who have many fathers, the allotment of shares is according to the fathers. Property acquired by the grandfather, whether it be a landed estate, a fixed endowment, or any other wealth; AP_255.007ab/
In that case, there may be equal ownership for both the father and the son; however, a son born after partition from a wife of the same caste is entitled to a share.
Alternatively, his share may be determined from the visible assets, after deducting income and expenses.
If one recovers property that was taken away which had come down in succession, he need not give it to the co-heirs; the same applies to what is acquired through learning.
Whatever was given to someone by his parents shall belong to him alone.

When dividing [the estate] after the father's death, the mother shall also take an equal share. Those [sons] who have not been initiated should be initiated by their brothers who have already been initiated;
and the sisters, having been given a fourth part from their own respective shares, [are considered as having received their portion].
The sons born of a Brāhmaṇa shall receive four, three, two, and one shares respectively according to their caste;
those born of a Kṣatriya shall receive three, two, and one shares; and those born of a Vaiśya shall receive two and one shares.
Furthermore, whatever property was taken from one another that is discovered after the partition has been made [shall be divided equally].
Furthermore, it is the established rule that they should divide that [property] into equal shares.
A son procreated through *niyoga* in the field of another by one who is childless is,
according to the law, the heir to the estate and the giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) for both [the biological father and the husband of the mother].
The legitimate son (aurasa) is one born of a lawful wife; equal to him is the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-suta).
The son born of the wife (kṣetraja), however, is one produced in the field by a kinsman of the same gotra or by another. The son secretly born in the house is known as the secret-born son (gūḍhaja).
One born of an unmarried girl is considered a *kānīna*, the son of his maternal grandfather.
A son born of a woman who has been remarried—whether she was previously deflowered or not—is a *paunarbhava*.
One whom the mother or the father gives away becomes a *dattaka* (adopted) son.
One who is purchased by both [parents] is a "purchased" son; one made by them is an "artificial" son;
one who has given himself is "self-given"; one found in the womb is "the son of a pregnant bride"; and one born with the wife is "the son received with the bride."
He who is taken up after having been abandoned is known as an *apaviddha* son;
he offers the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) and inherits a share among these [sons], each succeeding one in the absence of the preceding.
This rule regarding sons of the same caste has been declared by me.
Even one born of a Śūdra’s slave woman shall be an heir to a share by virtue of affection;
when the father has died, the brothers should give him half a share.
If he has no brothers, he shall take everything, except for the sons of the daughters.
The wife, the daughters, the parents, the brothers, their sons, a kinsman of the same lineage, a relative, a pupil, and fellow students—
in the absence of each preceding one among these, each subsequent one is the heir to the wealth.
For one who has died in heaven without a son, this rule applies to all social classes:
the heirs to the estate of forest-dwellers, ascetics, and lifelong students are,
in order, the teacher, a virtuous pupil, a spiritual brother, and a fellow student of the same sacred ford.
A reunited coparcener shall give and take the share of one who was reunited, whether that person has subsequently been born or has died; likewise, a uterine brother shall do so for a uterine brother.
However, a non-uterine brother who is reunited shall not take the property of a non-uterine brother.
Even if he is not reunited with the estate, a uterine brother may take the inheritance, and not any other agnate;
however, those who are outcasted, their sons, the impotent, the lame, the insane, the idiotic,
the blind, or those afflicted by incurable diseases and the like, must be maintained but are entitled to no share.
Their legitimate sons and those born of their wives are entitled to shares provided they are free from defects;
their daughters also must be maintained until they are given in marriage to husbands. Furthermore, the childless wives of these [deceased] men, if they have lived virtuously, must be supported.
Adulterous women,
as well as those who are hostile, shall be banished.
[Property] given by the father, mother, husband, or brother, or that which has come through the marriage fire (adhyagni),...
The woman’s property is declared to consist of the *ādhivedanika* (gift for supersession),
that given by her relatives, the *śulka* (dowry), and the *anvādheya* (subsequent gift).
When she dies childless, her kinsmen shall obtain it.
The property of a childless woman belongs to her brother, even in the case of the four forms of marriage beginning with the Brāhma;
however, if she has daughters, it goes to them, and if they have borne children, it goes to the father.
One who, having given away a daughter in marriage, takes her back, shall be punished and must pay the expenses along with interest.
Upon her death, he may take back what was given, after deducting both types of expenses.
In times of famine, for religious purposes, during illness, or when there is imprisonment,
the husband is not obliged to return the wife’s property that he has taken.

One should give an equal amount as compensation for supersession (*adhivedanika*) to a wife who has been superseded by another. If no separate property (*strīdhana*) was given to her, it is declared that half of what was given [to the new wife] shall be paid.
In cases of denial regarding partition, [the truth is established] by means of kinsmen, relatives, witnesses, and written records.
The contemplation of partition should be understood as applying to houses, fields, and separate property;
thus ends the two hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "Partition of Inheritance," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter Two Hundred and Fifty-Six.
The Decision on Boundary Disputes and Other Matters.
Agni said:
In a dispute concerning the boundary of a field, the neighbors, elders, and local groups [shall decide].
Cowherds, those who cultivate the boundaries, and all those who frequent the forests should demarcate the boundary by means of mounds, charcoal, husks, and trees;
it should be characterized by embankments, anthills, depressions, bones, shrines, and the like.
Or, neighboring village-headmen— four, eight, or even ten—
who wear red garlands and garments, shall lead [the boundary markers] to the border;
if they are false, they shall each be punished by the king with the middle amercement.
In the absence of marks indicating the knower [of the boundary], the king is the establisher of the boundary.
This same rule is to be understood regarding groves, temples, villages, water-reservoirs, gardens, and dwellings, as well as in the case of rainwater channels.
In cases of violating boundaries as well as seizing land,
those responsible for the boundary should be punished according to whether they are of low, high, or middle status.
However, a watercourse that causes little harm and brings about welfare should not be obstructed.
A well that carries water onto another's land is of little field but much water;
if one constructs an embankment in a field without informing the owner,
the produce belongs to the owner once it has arisen, and in his absence, to the king.
He who, even when a field has been ploughed, neither cultivates it himself nor causes it to be cultivated—
whether by four or ten [ploughs].
He shall be made to pay for the field that has not yet yielded fruit, and he must have it cultivated by another; however,
a female buffalo that causes damage through untruthfulness shall be fined for eight months' worth of loss,
a cow half as much, and a goat or sheep half as much again.
