For those who sit down after having consumed [the fodder], the fine shall be double that which was prescribed; this applies equally even in a pasture (*vivīta*). As long as the truth [of ownership] has not been destroyed, the owner of the field shall receive the fruit [of the damage].
The keeper shall be beaten, and the owner of the cattle deserves the previously mentioned fine.

There is no fault regarding a field on a path or at the edge of a village pasture. In the case of unintentional damage, there is no penalty; however, in the case of intentional action, one deserves a fine like that of a thief.

Cattle released for a great festival, a cow that has recently calved, one that is newly arrived, those whose herdsman has been swept away by gods or kings, and those that have strayed— these must be released.
In the evening, the herdsman shall return the cattle exactly as they were entrusted to him in the morning.
If [the livestock] perishes due to negligence, the keeper who has received his wages must pay for it;
however, in the case of destruction caused by the fault of the keeper,
a fine of twelve and a half paṇas is prescribed for the keeper, as well as the value of the property itself for the owner.
The grazing ground for cattle shall be according to the will of the village or by the authority of the king;
a twice-born man may take grass, firewood, and flowers from anywhere as his own. The area surrounding a village field should be one hundred bows in circumference.
A market town shall consist of two hundred [houses], and a city of four hundred.
One shall recover one's own property if it was sold by another; if the sale was not publicly announced, the fault lies with the buyer.
If a purchase is made from an inferior person, in secret, for an inferior price, or at an improper time, the buyer is a thief.
Having recovered property that was lost or stolen, one should cause the thief to be apprehended;
or, if there is a lapse of time or place, one should seize it oneself and hand it over.

Upon seeing the seller, the purchaser is cleared of blame; the owner recovers his property, the king receives a fine, and the purchaser must pay the price to him who was the seller there. Otherwise, a lost item may be recovered through legal title or possession. AP 256.021cd–256.022ab.

The fine for him is five times the value; and if that [stolen property] has not been recovered by the king, he who should recover from the hand of another any lost or stolen goods without reporting it to the king must be fined sixty *paṇas*.
If property that was lost or stolen is recovered by customs officers or local guardians, the owner recovers it within one year; after that, the king takes it.
One should pay four *paṇas* for a single-hoofed animal and five for a human being.
Two shares each for buffaloes, camels, and cows; one share each for goats and sheep—these should be given without detriment to one's own family, excluding the wife and sons.
When there is a lineage remaining, one's entire property must not be given away, nor that which has been promised to another.
The acceptance [of a gift] should be public, especially in the case of immovable property; what is promised as a gift must indeed be given, and once given, it should not be taken back again.
[The periods for returning a loan are] ten, one, five, seven days, a month, three days, or half a month.
Seeds, iron, draft animals, gems, women, milch cattle, and men are to be returned as they were received;
gold is not diminished when tested in fire, whereas [the loss] is two palas per hundred in silver,
eight in tin and lead, fifteen in copper, and [twenty] in iron.
In a hundred [palas], there is an increase of ten palas for woolen and likewise for cotton cloth;
it should be known that for medium quality there is an increase of five palas, while for fine quality, an increase of three palas is prescribed.
For woven silk and cloth with attached hair, a loss of one-thirtieth is prescribed.
There is neither decrease nor increase in silk or in bark garments;
having understood the place, the time, and the enjoyment, one knows the strength and weakness when [the garment] is lost.
Those skilled in matters of property should say without doubt that such a person must be made to pay restitution;
one who has been forcibly enslaved by thieves or even sold is liberated by saving his master's life, by abandoning his food, or by paying the ransom for him.
One who has been expelled from the order of renunciation becomes the king’s slave for life. Among the social classes, servitude may be according to the natural order, but never in the inverse order.
Even one who has mastered a craft shall dwell in the house of his teacher for the duration of the agreed time.
The pupil shall receive food from his teacher and give him the fruit of his own labor.
Having established a place for them in the city and settled the Brāhmaṇas there, the king should provide for those learned in the three Vedas and say: "Let your own dharma be protected."
That which is conventional and does not conflict with one's own dharma,
as well as any law enacted by the king, must also be protected with effort.
He who would seize the property of a corporation and he who would violate a formal agreement [should be punished].
Having confiscated all his property, he should be banished from the kingdom;
the words of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be followed by all.
Whoever therein acts contrarily shall be fined the first amercement.
Whatever one appointed to the affairs of the community may obtain, that he shall hand over;
if he does not hand it over himself, he shall be made to pay eleven times as much.
Those who contemplate the affairs [of the community] should be knowers of the Vedas, pure, and free from greed.
The word of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be carried out;
this same rule applies to guilds, merchant associations, heretical sects, and assemblies.
The king should guard against their internal dissension and protect their traditional way of life.
One who abandons work after having received wages shall pay double;
if he has not received wages, he shall be made to pay an equal amount. The tools and implements must be protected by the servants.
But he who, without having fixed the wages, causes work to be done, shall be made by the king to pay a tenth part of the profit from trade, cattle, or crops; likewise,
he who exceeds the stipulated place or time, or performs the work otherwise [than agreed].
In that case, however, it is at the master's discretion whether more should be given when extra work has been performed.
A person’s wages correspond to the extent of the work he performs.
If the task is impossible for both [master and laborer] to accomplish, then in a case where it can be accomplished, one should act according to what was agreed upon.
The carrier shall be made to pay for goods lost through no fault of the king or fate;

likewise, one who causes an obstruction to the journey shall be made to pay double the wages. If he abandons the goods while the journey has begun, he must pay a seventh part of the value; if he abandons them on the way, a fourth part.
The keeper of the gambling hall shall cause the person who abandons the game to pay the entire stake at the halfway point.
From a gambler who wins a hundred-fold increase on the wager, the keeper of the hall may take five percent;
from any other deceitful gambler, he may take ten percent.
Properly protected, he should give the king the share as determined;
he should cause the winner to take what was won and give truthful speech to the victor, being patient.
When the king has arrived at the established gambling circle and his share has been obtained—
A victory should be granted in a place where it was won fairly, and not otherwise.
For those who observe legal proceedings and the witnesses themselves— those who play with fraudulent dice or by means of deception— should be branded with a mark and banished by the king.
A single-headed game of dice should be conducted for the purpose of identifying thieves;
this same rule is to be understood as applicable to betting with living creatures and to challenges to combat.
Thus ends [the section] titled "The Decision on Boundary Disputes and Other Matters" in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The two hundred and fifty-sixth chapter.
Chapter Two Hundred and Fifty-Seven.
Then begins the two hundred and fifty-seventh chapter.
The section on verbal abuse and so forth; Agni said:
[This applies] to those who, through truthful, untruthful, or false praises, [cause harm to] those with deficient limbs or senses, or those who are diseased.
If one makes a false accusation, he shall be fined twelve and a half paṇas;
and if one swears, "I shall violate your sister or your mother," the king shall cause him to pay a fine of twenty-five paṇas.

Half [of the standard fine] shall be imposed for offenses against those of lower status, and double for offenses against the wives of others or those of higher status; the application of punishment must be determined according to the relative superiority or inferiority of the castes and classes.
In cases of defamation involving the reverse order of social hierarchy, the fines shall be doubled or tripled.
According to the direct order of the castes (*varṇas*), the fine is reduced by half from that [standard].
For verbal injury involving the destruction of the arms, neck, eyes, or thighs, the fine is one hundred;
for those involving the feet, nose, ears, hands, and so forth, it is half of that.
But one who is unable and speaks thus shall be fined ten *paṇas*.
Likewise, one who is able shall provide a guarantor for his safety.
For an insult involving a crime causing loss of caste, the fine is the middle *sāhasa*.

But one who is guilty of a minor offense (upapātaka) should be made to pay the first amercement. Insulting those learned in the three Vedas, the king, or the gods is an offense punishable by the highest amercement.
[Note: In the phrase "he shall give," it is more appropriate for the reading to be "he shall be made to pay."]
The middle [fine] applies to groups of kinsmen; the first [fine] applies to villages and districts.
In the case of a person killed without witnesses, [the truth is established] by physical marks, circumstantial reasoning, and the discovery of the body.
Legal proceedings must be conducted with caution due to the fear of forged marks.
It is ordained that for touching [another] with ashes, mud, or dust, the fine shall be ten paṇas;
for touching [another] with impure matter, the heel, or spittle, it is ordained to be double.
In the case of women who are equal [in status], the punishment is the same; for those of higher rank, it is double; for those of lower rank, it is half.
There is no punishment for acts committed through delusion, intoxication, and the like.
However, the limb that causes injury to a Brāhmaṇa shall be amputated, but this applies to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa.
For raising a weapon, the first amercement is the punishment; for actual contact, it is half of that.
For raising a hand or a foot, the fines are ten and twenty [paṇas] respectively.
But for all these acts against one another, the Middle Amercement is prescribed in the legal treatise.

For pulling at the feet, hair, or garments, or for seizing them by the hand, the fine shall be ten *paṇas*. For causing pain, dragging, wrapping with a garment, or pressing down with the foot, the punishment shall be one hundred;
likewise for a man who causes pain with wood or other implements without drawing blood.
He shall be made to pay thirty-two paṇas; double that amount if blood is seen, and likewise for the breaking or cutting off of a hand, a foot, or the ear and nose.

The middle amercement is prescribed for breaking open a wound, as well as for killing one who is nearly dead; likewise for obstructing movement, food, or speech, for piercing the eyes or other [sensitive parts],
and for fracturing the neck, arms, or thighs.
For those who strike one person or many, the fines shall be double as previously stated.
That which was stolen during a quarrel must be restored, and the fine is declared to be double.
Furthermore, he who causes another pain must pay the expenses incurred for the victim's recovery.
He shall be made to pay twenty-two paṇas as a fine, and whatever punishment has been prescribed for whichever specific quarrel.
A ferryman taking land tolls shall be fined ten paṇas;
the same penalty applies for failing to invite Brāhmaṇas or neighbors [to a meal].
Likewise, for striking, piercing, cutting, or intentionally causing the felling [of trees], [the same fine shall be imposed].

One who throws harmful substances, those that cause disease, or those that are life-threatening into another's house shall be made to pay fifteen, twenty, and thirty paṇas respectively; for throwing such things,
the first offender shall be made to pay sixteen paṇas, the second shall be fined the middle amercement.
In the case of causing pain, drawing blood, or cutting off a limb or member,

the fine for small animals shall be two paṇas and so forth in ascending order; for cutting off a male organ or killing [a small animal], the middle amercement and the value [of the animal] shall be paid.

For these [offenses] involving large animals, the fines are double; for cutting branches, stems, or destroying the entirety of trees that have sprouted branches, the fines are double those for twenty [smaller] trees that provide a livelihood.
He who causes a rash act to be committed shall be made to pay double the fine;
but he who, having said "I will give," causes it to be done, shall pay four times the amount.
One who insults a noble person, one who transgresses [the rules], and one who strikes his brother's wife [shall be punished].
One who fails to deliver a message as entrusted, one who breaks down a house situated by the sea,
and one who commits an injury against neighbors,
kinsmen, and others— the penalty for these is determined to be a fine of fifty paṇas.
One who approaches a widow of her own accord; one who does not run to the aid of someone crying out for help; one who cries out falsely; a *caṇḍāla* who touches those of the highest caste;
and a *śūdra* who feeds ascetics at rites for the gods or the ancestors.
The passage beginning with "prarohiśākhinām" and ending with "viṃśater dviguṇā damāḥ" is not present in manuscript *kha*.
One who makes an improper oath, one who is unfit yet performs the work of the fit,
one who obstructs the virility of bulls or small animals, one who denies a common property, and one who causes the destruction of a maidservant’s fetus; AP_257.030cd–257.031cd/

A father and son, a sister and brother, a husband and wife, or a teacher and pupil— anyone who abandons another from among these when they have not fallen from their caste shall be punished with a fine of one hundred [paṇas].
Furthermore, a washerman who wears another's garment shall be fined three paṇas.

In cases of sale, lease, pledge, or borrowing, [the fine shall be] ten *paṇas*. One who forges scales, royal edicts, measures, or coins, as well as anyone who conducts transactions with such forged items, shall be made to pay the highest fine.
One who declares a genuine coin to be counterfeit, or a counterfeit coin to be genuine,
that examiner of currency shall be made to pay the first amercement.
A physician who practices quackery among animals shall be made to pay the first fine.
Among humans, [the fine] is middling; likewise, among royal officials, it is highest for one who binds an innocent person or releases one who deserves to be bound.
Furthermore, one who binds a minor who has not yet attained legal capacity shall be made to pay the highest fine.
Whoever should take even an eighth part [of the value] by means of a measure or a scale,
shall be made to pay twenty-two paṇas; this is ordained for cases of increase or decrease in the case of medicines, oils, salt, perfumes, sugar, and so forth.
One who adulterates inferior goods with superior ones shall be made to pay a fine of sixteen paṇas.
For artisans and craftsmen who, acting in concert,
cause a decrease or an increase in the price of their wares by means of oppression, a fine of one thousand is prescribed.
Whatever profit is established by the king, whether through daily sales or purchases,
that surplus is traditionally held to be the merchant's gain.
A merchant may take five percent on goods of his own country and ten percent on foreign goods, provided the purchase and sale are immediate;
having calculated the expenses arising from the merchandise, these rates are to be applied to the value of the goods.
The purpose of the transaction is to provide benefit to both the buyer and the seller.
If one who has received the price does not deliver the commodity to the buyer, he must be made to pay it back with interest;
or, if the buyer has come from another region, he must be made to pay the profit derived from that region.
Even after it has been sold, the article may be returned if the previous buyer does not accept it;

if the loss was due to the fault of the buyer, that loss shall indeed belong to the buyer alone. However, if a defect arises in the merchandise due to injury caused by the king or by fate, [the seller shall bear the loss].
This loss falls solely upon the seller who does not deliver what has been requested; likewise,
if he sells to another hand what has already been sold, or if he sells what is defective as if it were non-defective,
the fine in that case shall be double its value.
A merchant who, being ignorant of the loss or increase of his merchandise, does not exercise regret after having purchased it, shall incur a fine of one-sixth [of the value] if he persists;
this applies to merchants acting in a collective association for the sake of profit.
Whatever profit or loss arises from goods, or whatever is determined by agreement, or what is forbidden or not specifically prescribed, or what is lost through negligence—
he who recovers it from a thief or from a forest-dweller is entitled to a tenth part of it.
The king shall take a twentieth part as toll for the inspection of goods;
however, that which is sold as unproven, or what is fit for the king, belongs to the king.
One who speaks falsely regarding the quantity or who evades the toll station [shall be punished].
And he who engages in fraudulent buying and selling shall be made to pay eight times the value.
When the owner has died while in another country, his heirs and kinsmen [shall take] the property.
Or his kinsmen may take it when they have arrived; in their absence, the king [should take it].
They should abandon one who is dishonest, but not one who is free from greed; if he is incapable, the king should have the work performed by another.
By this, the rule for officiating priests and laborers has been declared.

A thief is apprehended by his captors through stolen goods, or by his tracks, or because of a prior offense, or likewise because he is staying in an impure dwelling. Others also may be seized on suspicion due to their concealing their caste, name, and so forth.
Those addicted to gambling, women, and drink; those with parched and cracked faces and voices;

those who inquire about the property and houses of others; those who move about in secret; those who have no income yet spend lavishly; and those who sell goods that do not exist—[these are the spies].
If one who has been apprehended on suspicion of theft purifies himself,
the king shall have him pay back the stolen property and punish him with the penalty prescribed for a thief;
having compelled the thief to restore what was taken, the wise king shall execute him by various means.
Having identified the Brahmin by his distinctive marks, the king should banish him from his own kingdom;
if he has been killed or abducted, the guilt falls upon the village headman provided the victim did not escape.
The village, however, shall provide compensation within its own boundaries, or at the place where the tracks lead.
A group of five villages shall be situated beyond one *krośa*, and a group of ten villages beyond that. Alternatively, moreover,
those who capture prisoners, those who carry off horses and elephants,
and those who kill by force, these men he shall cause to be impaled upon a stake.
For those who commit the offenses of causing a monk to be expelled or breaking open a sealed storehouse, the punishment shall be the loss of one hand and one foot respectively;
for a second offense, they shall be deprived of one hand and one foot.
One should also confiscate their provisions, lodging, fire, water, ritual implements, and expenses.
For one who knowingly gives [poison] to a thief or a murderer, the highest fine is prescribed; likewise,
for causing an abortion by striking with a weapon, the highest fine is prescribed.
Whether he be high-born or low-born, in the case of killing a man or a woman,
one should bind a stone around the neck of the man-killer and cast him into the water; likewise for a woman who administers poison, sets fire [to a dwelling], or kills her own guru or her own child.
Having mutilated their ears, hands, noses, and lips, one should cause those who set fire to fields, houses, forests, villages, pastures, or threshing floors to be put to death by cattle;
likewise, one who has sexual intercourse with the king’s wife should be burned in a grass-fire.
A man shall be apprehended for adultery with another's wife by seizing her by the hair; if the woman is of his own caste, the highest fine is imposed, but if she is of a lower caste, the middle fine.
In the case of a man approaching a woman of a higher caste, there shall be death for the men and the cutting off of the ears for the woman.
For crushing the knot of the lower garment, the breasts, the covering, the navel, or the hair;
for conversing at an improper place or time; and for staying together [with a woman], a woman shall pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], while a man shall pay a fine of two hundred.
In the case of a prohibition against those two [acts], the punishment is the same as for adultery (*saṃgrahaṇa*):
one who has intercourse with animals shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred; for a woman of lower caste or cows, the middle amercement.
The same applies to female slaves kept in the household or female servants.
A man shall also be made to pay fifty paṇas for approaching a woman who is forbidden [to him].
For approaching a female slave by force, the fine is ordained as ten paṇas.
For approaching an outcaste woman or a female ascetic, he should be branded with the mark of a dog's foot and banished.
Whoever writes a royal edict with either omissions or additions,
or who releases an adulterer or a thief, shall receive the highest punishment. For one who defiles a Brahmin with forbidden food, the punishment is the highest amercement.
One who deals in counterfeit gold and one who sells forbidden meat shall be branded with a physical mark and made to pay the highest amercement.

For a master who is capable but fails to restrain fanged or horned animals shall pay the first *sāhasa* fine; likewise, if he is called out [by the victim], he shall pay double. One who accuses a person who is not a thief of being a thief shall be made to pay a fine of five hundred.

Having cut out the tongue of one who speaks what is displeasing to the king, as well as one who reviles him, a seller of the limbs of a corpse, one who strikes his guru, and a breaker of his secret counsel, the king shall banish them.
The punishment for one who mounts a royal vehicle or throne is the middle amercement.
Likewise, for one who plucks out both eyes, or who issues commands hostile to the king,
or for a Śūdra living by the profession of a Brāhmaṇa, the fine shall be eight hundred.
If one should think "I am unconquered" when he has been defeated according to the law, the king, having conquered him again as he approaches, shall punish him with double the fine.
That punishment which is taken by the king according to justice belongs to Varuṇa.
Having made it known, one should personally give thirtyfold more to the brahmins;
[for this] there is dharma, wealth, fame, standing in the world,
and support, as well as great respect from the subjects and an eternal station in heaven.
"And for a king who observes legal proceedings, there shall be seven virtues.
Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Section on Verbal Abuse and Other Matters," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter Two Hundred and Fifty-Eight: The [Chapter] on the [Deity] with Eight Arms and Five Faces.
Agni spoke the *Ṛgvidhāna*,
and Puṣkara proclaimed the *Ṛg-yajuḥ-sāma-atharva-vidhāna*.
"By reciting [this] one attains enjoyment and liberation; likewise, by performing oblations, one gains [them] for Rāma.
Puṣkara said:
"I shall now declare to you the duties and rites that must be performed according to each Veda."
First, listen to the *Ṛgvidhāna*, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation:
by performing recitation (*japa*) of one's heart's desire while submerged in water or during a fire sacrifice (*homa*),
Gāyatrī fulfills that wish, especially through the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
O twice-born one, for one who eats only at night and bathes frequently, ten thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī at that very place destroy all impurities; furthermore,
by reciting it one hundred thousand times while subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), he becomes a partaker of liberation.

The *praṇava* is indeed the supreme Brahman; its recitation destroys all sins. Standing in water reaching up to the navel, one who drinks water after having recited the syllable *oṃ* a hundred times is indeed freed from all sins.
He is completely liberated.
The three measures (*mātrā*), the three Vedas, the three gods, the three fires,
the seven great utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), the worlds, and the fire-oblation— this [collection] destroys all sins.

The *gāyatrī* is the supreme mantra to be recited, as are the *mahāvyāhṛtis*; likewise, O Rāma, the *aghamarṣaṇa* is prescribed for recitation while submerged in water. This hymn beginning with "agnim īḷe purohitam" has Agni as its presiding deity.
"He is indeed liberated from sins"—thus read in the manuscripts *ga*, *gha*, and *ña*.
438) "He who, bearing fire upon his head, should recite [the mantra] for a full year... (AP 258.009cd).

He should perform the fire-oblation at the three periods of the day, subsist on alms, and maintain the sacred fires. Beyond this, by constantly reciting with self-restraint the seven verses beginning with "Vāyu" that have been proclaimed, he attains his desired objects.
One who desires intelligence should daily recite the three-verse hymn beginning with "sadasanyam.
These nine verses, which destroy death, were proclaimed by Anvaya;
one who is bound or imprisoned should recite them, having Śunaḥśepa as the seer.
One is released from all sins, or even a sick man becomes free from disease;
he who desires eternal pleasure, a friend, wisdom, and sovereignty, should daily perform the *Indriya* rite with these sixteen *ṛc*-verses.
By reciting the hymn beginning with "hiraṇyastūpam," one repels enemies;
by reciting "ye te panthāḥ," a person becomes secure on his journeys;
and he who indeed praises Īśāna day after day with the six verses addressed to Rudra [becomes likewise secure].

Or one should prepare a *caru* offering for Rudra; his supreme peace will then be attained. By daily worshipping the Sun while reciting the hymn beginning with "Ud," one should cast seven handfuls of water; this is the destroyer of mental suffering.
Then, while reciting the half-verse beginning with *dviṣantam* and ending with *yad vipra*, one should meditate;
within seven nights, the wrongdoer shall fall into enmity.
One desiring health or a sick person should recite the final verse of the *Praskanna* hymn.
He should recite the first half-verse while seated in various postures;
at sunrise, he should recite it to obtain inexhaustible longevity, and at midday,
he should recite it to obtain splendor.
When the sun has set, by reciting the *na vayaś ca* hymns, one repels the enemy and subdues his foes.
One should prescribe the fulfillment of all desires through the eleven verses of Suparṇa;
by reciting these beginning with "ādhyātmikīḥ kaḥ," one shall attain liberation.
By means of the verse "ā no bhadrāḥ," one shall obtain long life.
With the hymn beginning "O Soma," one should behold the new moon;
approaching it with fuel in hand, one undoubtedly obtains garments.
Desiring long life, one should always recite the Kautsa hymn beginning with "This."
Having praised the Sun with the verse beginning "āpanaḥ śośucad," just as he releases his rays in the midst of the sky, so too does one release one's sin.
One should mutter the hymn beginning with "jātavedase" as a blessing for safety on the road.

One is liberated from all fears and shall attain well-being in one's home. Furthermore, when the night has dawned, one should recite this "Pramandinī" hymn, which destroys bad dreams and brings liberation for a woman in childbirth.
Reciting "Indram" while bathing, and likewise offering clarified butter while reciting the seven verses beginning with "Vaiśvadevam," a man is released from all sin;
and by constantly reciting "Imām," he obtains his desired objects.
Having fasted for three nights and being pure, one should offer oblations of *auḍumbara* fuel-sticks prepared with clarified butter while reciting the two verses beginning with "mā nastoke.
Having thus severed all the bonds of death, one shall live free from disease.

With his arms raised, having praised Sambhu with this very [hymn] and likewise with the verse beginning "mā nastoke," a man becomes invincible to all beings once the tying of the topknot has been performed; of this there is no doubt.
A man who, with sacrificial fuel in hand, constantly approaches the Sun at the three junctions of the day [reciting] "The wondrous one," shall likewise obtain his desired wealth.
Then, by reciting "atha svapne" at dawn, midday, and throughout the day,
one destroys all bad dreams and obtains auspicious food;
likewise, the mantra "ubhe pumān" is proclaimed as a destroyer of Rākṣasas.
By reciting the verse "ubhe vāsā," one shall obtain all desires;
by reciting "na sā gaṇ," one is released from those who would do him harm;
and by reciting "kayā śubhā," one shall attain preeminence among one's kin.
By reciting "imam ṛṣabham," one shall obtain all desires.
One should constantly stand near [the fire] with the mantra "pitaḥ" when wealth has arrived. And for one traveling on a journey, there should be an oblation of ghee with the hymn "agne naya."
He who constantly recites the *Suśloka* hymn attains heroic conduct;
by means of the *Kaṅkato na* hymn, one dispels all poisons.
By means of the *Yo jāta* hymn, one shall obtain all desires.
By means of the hymn beginning with "gaṇānām," one obtains unsurpassed affection;
and by the verse beginning with "yo me rājan," which pacifies bad dreams,
he who sets out on a journey shall see any risen enemy [subdued].
Whether for an unfavorable or a favorable purpose, one should indeed recite this;
by constantly reciting with self-restraint during the sacred festivals this unsurpassed twenty-two-verse hymn concerning the inner self, one attains all desired objects.
Reciting the hymn beginning with "kṛṇuṣva" and offering clarified butter while composed in meditation,
one shall obtain food for a hundred [days].
Ga..., gha..., ja... ca 2; "Food is always present," ka..., cha... ca:
It shall take away the lives of enemies and destroy even the *rakṣas* demons;
day after day, one should personally worship the fire with this *ṛc*.
The fire itself, facing every direction, protects him from all sides.
"Haṃsaḥ śuciṣat"— with this [verse], being pure, one should gaze at the sun;
and when entering upon agriculture, one should offer a *sthālīpāka* sacrifice according to the rules in the middle of the field with the five [mantras] ending in "svāhā."
For Indra and for the Maruts, for Parjanya and for Bhaga, the plowman,
according to their respective characteristics, should perform the ritual while wielding the plow. Then,
for the sake of grain and the furrow, he should recite the *Sunāsīra* hymn thereafter.
One should worship these deities with perfumes, garlands, and prostrations. When sowing, reaping, threshing, or clearing the furrows, one’s labor becomes unfailing, and agriculture always prospers.
Through the hymn beginning with "From the ocean" (samudrāt), one obtains all desires from the Purifier;
through the two verses beginning with "Viśvānara," he who is worthy of the sacrificial fire crosses over all calamities and attains imperishable glory.
One attains vast prosperity and achieves unsurpassed victory;
by praising with the hymn "agne tvaṃ," one obtains the desired wealth.
One who desires offspring should constantly recite the three mantras dedicated to Varuṇa as their deity.
One should always recite the three [verses] beginning with "Svastyā" in the morning; it is a great means of securing well-being.
Having uttered the verse beginning with "Svasti panthā," one travels on the road endowed with prosperity.
One who desires victory [should recite] "Vanaspate"; the enemies shall become afflicted with disease.
For a woman whose pregnancy has become obstructed, the extraction of the fetus is the best [remedy],
as it arises from the occurrence of disease.
One desiring rain should employ the hymn beginning with "acchāvada";
fasting and wearing wet clothes, he will cause it to rain before long.
A man desiring cattle should mutter this [hymn] beginning with "manasaḥ kāmaḥ";
one desiring progeny, being pure and observant of vows, should bathe with the hymn beginning with "kardamena";
and a man desiring sovereignty should bathe with the hymn beginning with "aśvapūrvāḥ."
A Brāhmaṇa should bathe upon a deerskin according to the prescribed rule;
a Kṣatriya on a tiger skin, and a Vaiśya likewise on a goat skin.
A fire-oblation of ten thousand [offerings] is proclaimed for each case.
With the hymn beginning with "āgāre," one should worship the cow, the mother of the worlds, in the pen; and if one so desires, those cows shall always be inexhaustible.
With three verses beginning with "upeti," one should consecrate the king’s drum.
One obtains splendor and indeed subdues the enemy.
One who holds grass in hand and is surrounded by robbers should recite the *rakṣoghna* hymn;
by reciting the verse beginning with "ye ke ca uma," one shall attain long life.
Likewise, one should consecrate the components of the army with the *Jīmūta-sūkta*;
then, according to the specific characteristic [of each], the king destroys his enemies in battle.
By means of the three hymns beginning with "āgneya," one obtains inexhaustible wealth.
One should station the spirits at night using the *amīvahā* hymn.
Whether in distress, in a difficult situation, or in a stronghold; or when released from captivity, or while fleeing, or when captured—one should likewise recite this hymn.
Having fasted for three nights with self-restraint, one should have a *pāyasa* caru prepared;
with that, one should offer a full hundred oblations with the verse beginning "tryambaka."
Having dedicated [the offering] to Mahādeva, one may live happily for a hundred years;
having bathed, one should worship the Sun with the verse beginning, “That eye.”
One who desires to live a long life should recite the hymn beginning with "udyantam" and "madhyagam";
this is declared to be the destroyer of enemies.
Furthermore, for one whose vow has been broken through delusion, or who has associated with outcasts (vrātyas), [this hymn is prescribed].
Having observed the fast, one should offer clarified butter with the mantra "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows," and by reciting the verse beginning with "āditya" and the *samrāj* mantra,
one shall be victorious in debate.
By reciting the four verses beginning with "mahī," one is liberated from great fear; indeed,
by muttering this verse beginning with "mahī," one shall obtain all desires,
and by muttering the forty-two verses addressed to Indra, one destroys one's enemies.
By reciting "vācaṃ mahī," one attains health;
and by reciting the two verses beginning with "śanno bhava," while being restrained and pure after eating,
and touching the heart with the hand, one is not overcome by diseases.
Having bathed and offered oblations with the hymn *uttamedam*, one should cause the destruction of an enemy.
By offering oblations with the hymn *śanno agne*, one shall obtain food.
A maiden is liberated from the evil influence of the quarters by means of the *vārarṣi* hymn.
When "yadatyakavyā" is uttered and recited, the world will surely come into being;
by reciting "yadvāk," one's speech becomes refined and perfected.
By reciting "vāco viditam," one attains mastery over speech.
The *pāvamānī* verses are considered the most purifying among all purifiers;
the thirty *vaikhānasa* verses are regarded as the supreme purifiers.
1. *ādityeti prasaṃmrājam* — as in manuscripts ga, gha, and ña. 2. *saṃsthiteti* — as in manuscripts ka, cha, and ca;
O best of sages, sixty-two *ṛc* verses beginning with "parasva" have been proclaimed for the destruction of all impurities, for purification, and for auspiciousness;
likewise, sixty-seven hymns (*sūkta*) beginning with "svādiṣṭyā" have been cited.
By muttering and offering oblations of these six hundred and ten *ṛc*s of the *Pāvamānī* hymns, one shall conquer the terrible fear of death.
Or, standing in water, one should mutter the verse beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭha" to destroy the fear of sin.
Restrained, one should recite the mantra *pradevann eti* while in the desert wastes;
when a life-threatening danger has arisen, one quickly regains longevity.
At night, one should mentally recite the single verse beginning with *prāveyām*.

When dawn has broken and the sun has risen, one shall obtain victory in gambling; and by reciting "mā pragāma," even a fool finds his way on the road. One should consider any dear friend to be as one whose life is exhausted.
Having bathed, he should touch his head with the mantra "yatteyam";
by doing so five times a day for a thousand repetitions, he attains a long life.
A wise man should offer ghee into the fire a thousand times with the mantra "idaṃ medhyā".
One desiring cattle should recite "vayaḥ suparṇa" while standing in a cow-pen; one desiring wealth should do so at a crossroads; by doing so, he indeed finds prosperity.
By practicing "haviṣyantīyam," one is liberated from all sins.
His diseases will perish and his bodily fire will likewise increase.
One who desires rain should employ this hymn beginning with "O Bṛhaspati," which consists of those medicinal herbs that are auspicious and destroy all maladies.
"In all these cases, the supreme peace is to be known, as well as the *pratiratha*;
O Sūta, the *sāṃkāśyapa* is always proclaimed for one desiring progeny.
By reciting "I am Rudra," a man becomes eloquent;
by muttering "Rātrī" during the nights, the wise man is not born again from a womb.
Reciting the Rātrisūkta at night, a man who seeks security shall conquer the night.
Reciting the hymn "kalpayanti" daily brings about the destruction of enemies;
likewise, one who is firm in his vows should recite the great Dākṣāyaṇa hymn, which bestows long life and luster, as well as the hymn "uta devāḥ," which destroys disease.
When there is danger from fire, one should recite this hymn beginning with "O Agni, this is your birthplace.
In the forest, one should recite the verse beginning with "Araṇyānī," which destroys that fear.
Having approached the two Brāhmaṇa Sūktas, one should recite the Brāhmaṇī Ṛc and the Śatāvarī.

By using separate waters or clarified butter for a month, one attains wisdom and prosperity; this [rite] destroys rivals and is for one desiring victory in battle. It is the fire of Brahmā, acting in concert, which wards off death from the fetus.
One who is pure should mutter the *Apah* hymn, which destroys bad dreams;
by muttering "yenedam," one indeed attains supreme meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
"Mayo bhūrvāta" is the supreme means for the well-being of cattle.
By this [mantra], one may ward off sorcery, Indra’s net, or illusion.
On the road, one should mutter for the sake of a safe journey: "May you be the lowest among the three worlds.
One should likewise mutter "To Agni, vidviṣan" as a destroyer of enemies.
One should worship the household deities with the Vāstoṣpati mantra;
this is declared to be the rule for recitation (japa), while it should be understood as being especially so when an oblation (huta) is performed.
At the conclusion of the fire-offering, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given, for through the oblation, the pacification of evil occurs.
The oblation is pacified by food through the gift of food and gold;
the blessings of the Brahmins shall be unfailing, and bathing outside [the village] is beneficial in every respect.
Siddhārthaka seeds, barley, grain, milk, and likewise ghee;
milky trees as fuel for the fire—these oblations indeed grant all desires.
[For malevolent rites: thorny wood, mustard seeds, blood, and poison.
In the case of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), O Mountain, eating stone, groats, milk,
curd, alms-food, fruit, and roots is declared as the procedure;
thus ends the *Ṛgvidhāna* in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The two hundred and fifty-eighth chapter.
Chapter 259:
The Ritual Procedure for the Yajus Mantras (Yajurvidhāna)
Puṣkara said:

"I shall declare the ritual procedure for the Yajus, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; listen, O Rāma! The Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis) are considered to be preceded by the syllable Om."
The wise one should propitiate the gods with a thousand oblations of clarified butter— [oblations] which destroy all impurities and likewise grant all desires—
thereby obtaining whatever is wished for by the mind, O Rāma, and bestowing the objects of desire sought by the mind.
One who desires peace should perform [the rite] with barley; with sesame seeds for the removal of evil;
likewise with grains and white mustard seeds, which grant all desires.
For one desiring cattle, fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood are recommended.
With curd for one desiring food, and with milk for one wishing peace;
but with fuel-sticks of *apāmārga*, for one desiring abundant gold.
One desiring a daughter should offer *jātī* flowers tied in pairs and smeared with clarified butter; one seeking a village should offer sesame seeds and rice;
and for the rite of subjugation (*vaśyakarman*), one should likewise offer *śākhoṭa*, *vāsā*, and *apāmārga*.
O Bhārgava, one who desires the destruction of enemies should, being filled with wrath, properly offer oblations of fuel-sticks mixed with poison and blood into the fire of Vyādhighāta;
O twice-born one, having fashioned an image of the king out of all types of grain.
If one performs the oblation a thousand times, the king shall come under one's control;
for one desiring clothing, flowers [are prescribed], and *darvā* destroys disease. For one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), *vāsogra* is ordained.
In rites of counter-attack (*pratyaṅgira*), one should offer oblations with the ashes of husks and thorns;
likewise, in rites of inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), one should offer the eyelashes of a crow and an owl,
as well as the ghee of a tawny cow (*kāpila*), O twice-born one, during a lunar eclipse.
Having brought that *vacā* root by means of a consecrated sprinkling (*sampāta*) with *vacā* powder,
a man who eats it after it has been empowered with a thousand recitations becomes possessed of great intelligence.
[One should also prepare] an eleven-finger-long iron or *khadira*-wood peg.
Reciting "dviṣato bandhosi," one should bury [the object] in the enemy's house;
this rite for the eradication of enemies has been described to you.
And by reciting "cakṣuṣyā," one whose eyes have failed shall regain his sight.
Having offered *dūrvā* grass with the mantra "upayuñjata" from this section, as well as "annadam," "tanūnapād agne," and "sat," one becomes free from distress; furthermore,
an oblation of curds and clarified butter with the mantra "bheṣajam asi" wards off calamities concerning cattle.
1. *khādiram eva vā* is found in manuscripts *ga*, *gha*, and *ña*.
2. *paśūpasargaḥ* is found in manuscripts *ka* and *cha*.
The oblation to Tryambaka increases good fortune;
by uttering the name of a maiden, it is the supreme means for obtaining a daughter.
By constantly reciting [this mantra] during times of fear, one is liberated from all fears.
By offering dhattūra flowers with clarified butter as an oblation, one shall obtain all desires;
and by offering guggulu, O Rāma, one beholds Śaṅkara in a dream.
By reciting the *Anuvāka* beginning with "yuñjate manaḥ," one shall attain long life;
it destroys all afflictions,
wards off demons, brings fame, and likewise bestows victory.
"Effortless is Agni"—this [mantra] bestows victory in battle;
"O Waters, carry this away"—this is for the bath that removes sin;
"O Viśvakarman, with the oblation... [is used for] a ten-finger-long iron needle.
One should bury a maiden at the door; she shall not be given to another.
O best of the twice-born, one who desires strength should offer this oblation with the mantra "O God Savitṛ.
O best of the twice-born, one who desires strength should offer it into the fire with the words "Svāhā!"
O knower of dharma, O twice-born one, by consecrating sesame seeds, barley, and the grains of the apāmārga plant a thousand times,
and likewise applying yellow orpiment as a tilaka mark, one shall become beloved by the people.
Likewise, the recitation of the Rudra hymns destroys all sins;
the fire-oblation (homa) accomplishes all rites and likewise bestows peace in every situation for goats,
sheep, horses, elephants, and cows.
O Bhārgava, [this applies] to humans, to lords of men, to children, and even to women; as well as to villages, cities, and even entire regions.
"viṣṇor virāṭam" is the reading according to Gha and Ña; "viṣṭor arāṭam" is the reading according to Ka,
Ja, and Ṭa.
O Knower of Dharma, for those who are afflicted, as well as those who are diseased,
when a plague has arrived, or likewise when there is fear born of enemies; AP_259.027cd–259.028ab.

The Rudra-homa is the supreme pacification; by means of milk-rice and ghee, one removes all sins through the Kuṣmāṇḍa-ghee-homa. O best of men, one should eat at night only barley-meal, barley-gruel, or alms-food.
One who is devoted to bathing outdoors for a month is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
by performing oblations with the mantra "madhu vātā," one obtains everything from the beginning. Having offered oblations with the mantra "dadhi krāvṇaḥ," one undoubtedly obtains sons.

Likewise, the hymn beginning with "ghṛtavatī" bestows longevity; however, that which begins with "ghṛtena tu" [is for prosperity]. The hymn beginning with "svasti na indra" destroys all afflictions, while "iha gāvaḥ prajyāyadhvam" increases nourishment.
Likewise, the destruction of *lakṣmī* occurs through a thousand oblations of clarified butter;
by offering *apāmārga* grain with the *śruva*-ladle while reciting "devasya tvā," one is quickly liberated from malevolent sorcery— of this there is no doubt.
With fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, one should offer oblations to Rudra; thus one shall obtain gold.
When there is a fire-omen, a man should offer oblations of rice while reciting "O Śiva, be [favorable]!
Furthermore, the hymn beginning with "Those armies... (*yāḥ senā*) removes the fear of thieves.
O twice-born one, a man who offers black sesame seeds by the thousands for us shall be liberated from malevolent incantations and deformities.
By offering food with the mantra "O Lord of Food," he shall likewise obtain food.
The mantra "haṃsaḥ śuciḥ sadi" chanted over water destroys all evil;
likewise, "catvāri bhaṅge" chanted over water removes all sins.
Having chanted "devā yajña," one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having offered clarified butter with the mantra "O Spring," one shall obtain a boon from the Sun;
and the ritual for the mantra "Suparṇo 'si" should be performed in the same manner as the *vyāhṛti* rites.
Having recited "namaḥ svāhā" three times, one shall obtain release from bondage;
by repeating the *drupadā* mantra three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sins.
"O cows, be born here"—this mantra increases the intellect.
One should offer oblations of clarified butter, curd, milk, or milk-rice;
and having offered them with the mantra beginning "śataṃ ya... and also with *parṇa* leaves and fruits, one obtains health, prosperity, and likewise a long life.
"O plants, rejoice!
[This act] is beneficial for cutting and shaving. Through an oblation of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) with the *aśvāvatī* verse, one shall obtain peace."
By the mantra beginning with *tasmāt*, one imprisoned in bondage is liberated;
by the mantra beginning with *yuvā suvāsāḥ*, one obtains excellent garments. May all curses be released from me—this is the destruction of the Ender (*Antaka*).
"Do not harm me"—this oblation of sesame and clarified butter destroys enemies.
(4) "Homage be to all serpents," and with clarified butter and milk-rice;
"Make him a king"—this [mantra] destroys malevolent spells. (5)
By offering ten thousand stalks of *dūrvā* grass while reciting the mantra "kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt," a person shall pacify the plague in a village or even an entire district;
one afflicted by disease is freed from disease, and likewise, one suffering from misery is freed from misery.
Regarding "śatañca" in the *ṭīkā*:
it is "śataṃ vā" according to *ka*.
2. "May we rejoice in the medicinal herbs," thus [it is] in Ja...
3. "The destroyer of all sins," thus in Gha... and Ña...
4. "The destroyer of obstacles," thus in Ka... and Cha...
O Rāma, by offering *auḍumbara* fuel-sticks a thousand times with the mantra "Sweet is our tree," a person obtains wealth.
One attains great good fortune, as well as success in the threefold worldly affairs. By offering oblations with the mantra "apāṃ garbha," one will certainly cause the god to send rain;
likewise, by offering curd, ghee, and honey with the mantra "apaḥ piba."
O Knower of Dharma, immediately thereafter he causes a great rain to fall.
This hymn beginning with "Obeisance to you, O Rudra" is the destroyer of all calamities;
it is declared to bring about all peace and to destroy even the greatest of sins.
By means of this [mantra] "adhyavocat," there is protection for one who is ill;
by scattering white mustard seeds (*siddhārthaka*) while reciting it on the road, one becomes happy, as it is a destroyer of demons, conducive to fame, and increases longevity and nourishment.
O knower of dharma, by reciting "asau yas tāmra" while constantly worshipping the Sun-god morning and evening without weariness,
one obtains inexhaustible food and attains a long life.
The mantra "pramuñca dhanvan" and so forth, consisting of six [verses], is a consecration of weapons that strikes fear into enemies; there is no need for deliberation regarding its use in battle.
The mantra beginning with "mā no mahāntaḥ" likewise brings peace to children.
One should recite the seven sections beginning with *namo hiraṇyavāhave* (AP 259.057ab).
By offering oblations of *rājikā* seeds soaked in pungent oil, one destroys enemies.
Furthermore, by performing one hundred thousand oblations of lotuses with the mantra *namo vaḥ kirikebhyaḥ*, a person [attains his goal] (AP 259.058ab).
One obtains royal fortune, and likewise, with *bilva* fruits, one obtains gold;
and from an oblation (*homa*) performed with sesame seeds while reciting "imā rudrāya," wealth is attained.
By another oblation of *dūrvā* grass, one becomes free from all diseases;
and with the mantra "The swift one, sharpening... (*āśuḥ śiśānaḥ*), for the protection of weapons.
O Rāma, destroyer of all enemies,
it is said that in battle one should offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter with the *rājasāman* mantra, O knower of dharma; thus, a twice-born man is liberated from eye disease.
In the house, a fire-oblation (*homa*) with the verse "śanno vanaspate" should be performed to remove defects of the dwelling site (*vāstu-doṣa*).
By offering clarified butter (*ājya*) with the verse "agna āyūṃṣi," one incurs no enmity from anyone.
By offering parched grain (*lāja*) with the verse "apāṃ phena," one shall attain victory.

By reciting "Bhadrā," one who is deficient in his senses shall become possessed of all faculties. "Agniś ca pṛthivī ca" is the supreme means for subjugation. By reciting the mantra "Adhvane," one shall be victorious in legal disputes.
The mantra "brahma rājanyam" brings success at the commencement of any undertaking;
by reciting "saṃvatsaro 'si" with a steady mind, one becomes free from disease through a hundred-thousand-fold oblation (lakṣahoma).
The mantra "ketuṃ kṛṇvan" increases victory in battle.
"Indra, Agni, Dharma"—this is the formula for binding the armor in battle.
"Dhanvā nāga" is the supreme mantra for taking up the bow.
Likewise, the mantra "yajīta" is to be known as the one for consecration.
"O fathers, come hither"— this is proclaimed as the swift mantra for the fires;
likewise, "they yoke the horses"— this is said to be the mantra for the yoking of the horses.
The verse beginning with "āśuḥ śiśānaḥ" is where the commencement is spoken of; [it is called] "the increase of dharma," and this is indeed the mantra for the arrows of the chariot.
The mantra "viṣṇoḥ krama" is the supreme one for mounting a chariot;
and "ājaṅgha" is cited as the mantra to be used when striking horses.
One should mutter the mantra "yāḥ senā abhitvarī" at the front of the enemy army;
likewise, the mantra "dundubhya" should be used for the beating of the drum.
By performing [the rite] with these mantras previously offered into the fire, one shall become victorious.
From the *koṭihoma* of the hymn beginning with "yamenadattam," the wise practitioner should quickly produce a chariot that grants victory in battle.
Likewise, the ritual for the hymn beginning with "ā kṛṣṇena" should be performed according to the procedure for the *vyāhṛti* mantras.
One shall obtain concentration of mind;
by offering five rivers and five hundred thousand oblations, one shall attain prosperity when the mantra has been consecrated with this mantra for the sake of the bridegroom Dakṣāyaṇa.
One should wear gold a thousand times over as a protection against enemies.
If one throws this [charm] toward living beings, or casts a stone or a clod of earth in the four directions within the house, then there shall be no fear of thieves for him at night.
This is the supreme method of subjugation:
a man who has come there to kill becomes submissive.
One should give him food, betel, flowers, and so forth, which have been consecrated with the mantra.

O Knower of Dharma, O Gentle One, he who quickly comes under one's control will always find peace everywhere through the recitation of "śaṃ no mitra" and by performing a fire-oblation at a crossroads after making you, the Lord of Hosts, the leader of the assemblies.

One shall undoubtedly bring the entire world under one's control by means of all types of grain; this is known as the *Śivasaṃkalpa* [mantra]. (Note: According to the *gha* and *ja* manuscripts, the reading is "this is the *Śivasaṃkalpa*"; according to the *ka* manuscript, it is "by means of the *parāṅganā-gāyana*").
The mantra "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ" is for the consecration;
likewise, "śanno devīrabhiṣṭaye" is the supreme bringer of peace.
By offering clarified butter in portions with the mantra *ekacakrā*, one obtains peace from the planets and their favor; of this there is no doubt.
By offering clarified butter with the two mantras beginning *gāvo bhagaḥ*, one shall obtain cattle.
The portion beginning with "sopaditi" is prescribed for the sacrifice to the domestic fire;
the portion beginning with "vanaspate" for the gods is prescribed for the sacrifice to the trees.

The Gāyatrī is to be known as belonging to Viṣṇu; "That supreme step of Viṣṇu" likewise pacifies all sins and fulfills all desires. Thus ends the section on the Yajur-vidhāna in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
The two hundred and fifty-ninth chapter.
Chapter 260: The Sāmavidhāna (The Ritual Application of the Sāman Chants)
Puṣkara said:
The ritual for the Yajus has been told; now I shall describe the ritual for the Sāmans.
Having recited the Vaiṣṇava Saṃhitā and performed the fire-oblation, one shall partake of all desires.
Having properly recited the Saṃhitā of the Chāndasas, one pleases Śaṅkara;
and by reciting the Skandī and the Paitryā Saṃhitās, one shall indeed become graced with his favor.
1. "bhāgata" is found in manuscripts ka, ga, cha, and ña.
2. "pravādīśaṃ sopaditi" is found in manuscripts kha and cha.
3. "It is so; it brings peace to all," as stated in the *Gha* and *Ña* recensions on page 455:
"Since we, O Indra, partake of that which destroys the fault of violence... (AP 260.003ab)
One who has broken his vow of celibacy is liberated by reciting "agnistigma" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.2.1).
It should be known that the "paritoya" hymn recited over those waters removes all sins.
Furthermore, having sold what ought not to be sold, one should recite the "ghṛtavatī" hymn.

O Rāma, having sprinkled ghee according to the prescribed rule with the mantra "ayāno deva savitar jñeyam duḥsvapnanāśanam" and "abodhy agniḥ," the binding of the girdle is performed with the remainder of that ghee.
O best of the Bhṛgus, for those women whose fetuses fall away,
one should immediately bind this jewel upon the newborn child;
by this means, King Soma is released from diseases.
One who employs the Sarpasāman shall not suffer from the bite of snakes;
and by offering oblations with the hymn "mādya tvā vādyata," a Brahmin who has bound on the *śatāvari* amulet shall not incur danger from weapons, even if he does so a thousand times.
Having offered oblations with the mantra *dīrghatamasorka*, one shall obtain abundant food;
by muttering *svamadhyāyanti*, one shall not die of thirst;
and by muttering *tvam imā oṣadhīḥ*, one shall not incur disease.
By reciting the *devavrata* hymn while on a journey, one is liberated from all fears.
The oblation offered with the verse "yad indro munaye tvā" increases good fortune.
Likewise, the application of collyrium to the eyes with the verse "bhago na citraḥ" is beneficial.
O Rāma, this increases good fortune; there is no need for deliberation here.
One should recite the group beginning with "Indrā" (indrādidevatā), which likewise increases good fortune.
[Note: This is joined with the mantra "parito yaṃ ayutaṃ," as recorded by Ja and Ṭa.]
2. "Thirsty," according to Gha and Ña:
for your performance is indeed dear to us. (1)
One should cause a woman to hear the *kāmyā* [hymn];
she will desire him, O Rāma—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
The *Rathantara* and *Vāmadevya* [sāmans] increase one's spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
One should daily cause the child to consume powdered *vacā* soaked in ghee, while reciting the *Indramidgāthin* hymn; thus he shall become a possessor of the Veda (*śrutidhara*).
Having offered oblations and recited the *Rathantara*, one obtains a son without doubt.
This mantra, "May there be prosperity in me," should be recited; it increases prosperity.
By constantly employing the eightfold [rite] of Vairūpya, one shall obtain prosperity;
by employing the sevenfold eightfold [rite], one shall attain all desires.
He who, unrestrained, constantly performs the ritual attendance upon cows at morning and evening with the mantra "gavyeṣuṇā"— for him those cows shall always remain in his home.
May the wind blow upon a drona-measure of barley smeared with clarified butter as a healing medicine.
By this, performed according to the rules, one dispels all illusion.
Having offered sesame seeds with the *pradeva* mantra while reciting the *dāsa* mantra, one effects the destruction of magical rites (*kārmaṇa*).

A wise person, having offered a thousand *vāsakedhma* oblations that grant victory in battle,

as well as their principal officers.

Having thoroughly steamed excellent flour-cakes and cut them into pieces with a razor, one who knows the mantras, while filled with wrath, should anoint them with mustard oil and recite this mantra: "O Hero, we praise you... AP_260.023ab.

or "paripriyā devakaviḥ" (as found in manuscripts *gha* and *ña*).
Having performed this rite with the mantra, the wise man shall obtain victory in battle.
The Gāruḍa, Vāmadevya, Rathantara,
and Bṛhadratha [Sāmans] are declared to be the pacifiers of all sins, without a doubt.
Thus ends the section titled "The Ordinance of the Sāmans" in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The two hundred and sixtieth chapter.
Chapter 261:
The Ritual Procedure for the Atharva Veda (Atharvavidhāna)
Puṣkara said:
The ritual procedure for the Sāman hymns has been told; now I shall speak of those belonging to the Atharvaveda.
By offering oblations to the group beginning with the Śāntātīya, a human being attains peace.
Having offered the *Bhaiṣajya* group, one dispels all diseases;
having offered this *Trisaptīya* group, one is liberated from all evils.
Having offered the *Abhaya* group, one never encounters fear anywhere.
O Rāma, by offering the *gaṇa* oblation, one is never defeated;
by offering the *gaṇa* that bestows long life, one wards off untimely death.
By offering the *svastyayana-gaṇa*, one attains well-being everywhere.
By offering oblations to the Śarma-vārma-gaṇa, one attains prosperity as well as protection;
by offering to the Vāstoṣpati-gaṇa, one dispels defects of the dwelling site (vāstu-doṣa);
likewise, by offering to the Raudra-gaṇa, one dispels all defects.
With these tenfold qualities, one should indeed perform the oblation in the eighteen pacifying rites:
the Vaiṣṇavī, Aindrī, Brāhmī, and likewise the Raudrī pacification.
The Vāyavyā, the Vāruṇī, the Kauverī, and likewise the Bhārgavī;
the Prājāpatyā, the Tvāṣṭrī, the Kaumārī, the one whose deity is Agni,
the Mārudgaṇā, the Gāndhārī, and likewise the Nairṛtakī with peaceful [mantras].
The *Śānti* belonging to Aṅgiras, that of Yama, and the earthly one grant all desires.
Indeed, for one who has muttered "You are Death" (*yastvāṃ mṛtyuḥ*), this destroys death; and having offered oblations with the mantra "Suparṇas tvā," one is not at all harmed by serpents.
"This which was given by Indra" (indreṇa dattam) shall fulfill all desires;
"This which was given by Indra" (indreṇa dattam) is the destroyer of all afflictions.
And the mantra "These goddesses" (imā devīḥ) is the supreme performer of all pacification.
"O gods, O Maruts"—this brings about the fulfillment of all desires.
"From the world of Yama"—this is the supreme pacifier of bad dreams.
And "Indra and the five merchants"—[this is likewise].

The oblation "Kāmo me vājī" offered by women increases their good fortune; likewise, the oblation "tubhyameva javīmān" offered ten thousand times shall result in the same increase of good fortune for women.
"O Agni, with cows..."— this [verse] increases intelligence;
"with the firm, the firm..."— when offered as a libation, it certainly brings about the attainment of one's station.
If a dog says, "Live by lac," it will bring about gains from agriculture;
if it says, "I am broken," this will increase one's good fortune;
and if it says, "The nooses that are mine," this will cause release from bondage.
By means of oblations and recitation [of the mantra] "May they curse me, O slayer," one shall destroy enemies.
[The mantra] "O Indra, the forest, the wood-cutter...
and "O Agni, [grant] prosperity... [are used].
The phrase "you are the most excellent" increases fame and intelligence;
just as the phrase "surpassing the deer" increases the good fortune of women.
The mantra "yenedam" and "idam eva" brings about conception;
"ayam te yoniḥ" brings about the birth of a son;
and "śivaḥ śivābhiḥ" increases one's good fortune.
May Bṛhaspati protect us on the path; may there be well-being.
The mantra "muñcāmi tvā" is taught as a warder-off of untimely death.
One who studies the Atharvaśiras is liberated from all sins.
But primarily, a certain rite for the mantras has been enjoined by you: first, sacrificial fuel from trees fit for sacrifice,
then clarified butter, rice grains, and likewise white mustard seeds.
O Bhārgava, unbroken grains, sesame seeds, curd and milk,
as well as darbha grass, dūrvā grass, bilva fruits, and lotuses—
these substances are said to bring about peace and prosperity in every respect.
O knower of dharma, one should employ oil, *kaṇā* seeds, mustard, blood, and poison,
along with thorny fuel-sticks, in malevolent rites (*abhicāra*). One who knows the application should perform [the rite] according to the Ṛṣi, the deity, and the meter.
Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Atharva-vidhāna," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*. [Note:
According to the manuscripts designated as Gha, Ja, and Jha, the verse reads, "One should pacify an angry king."]
Chapter Two Hundred and Sixty-Two.
Puṣkara said:
The Śrīsūkta, which should be known for each Veda, increases prosperity and pacifies portents.
The fifteen verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇā hariṇīm" belong to the Ṛgveda;
the four verses beginning with "ratheṣvakṣeṣu vāja" belong to the Yajurveda;
and the *Sāraṅga* chant as well as the *Śrīsūkta* belong to the Sāmaveda.
"O Creator, bestow prosperity upon me, as it was [bestowed] upon Prāktama Atharvaṇa.
Whoever recites the Śrīsūkta with devotion, having offered oblations, shall indeed possess prosperity.
Furthermore, by offering lotuses, bilva fruits, clarified butter, or sesame seeds, one attains prosperity."
One should recite the *Puruṣasūkta*, which bestows everything; indeed,
being free from sin, one should offer a handful of water with each verse of that hymn.
Having bathed and offered a single flower to Viṣṇu with each one, one becomes a destroyer of sins;
having bathed and offered a single fruit with each one, one shall possess all desired objects. By reciting the Puruṣasūkta, one becomes freed from both major and minor sins.
Purified through arduous penances, having recited [mantras], offered oblations, and bathed, one then partakes of all [merits].
Among the eighteen pacifications (*śānti*), three other pacifications are superior:
the Immortal (*amṛtā*), the Fearless (*abhayā*), and the Gentle (*saumyā*), which crush all portents.
Amṛtā has all deities as her presiding divinity; Abhayā has Brahmā as her deity; Saumyā has all deities as her presiding divinity; and there may be one [goddess] who grants all desires.
(Note: Regarding the phrase "hy ekaikaśa," the reading *ka...* suggests a variant or corruption.)
O best of the Bhṛgus, for Abhayā a jewel of gha, cha, and ña should be fashioned; likewise for Varuṇa.
The hundred-stalked *amṛtā*, the *saumyā*, and the conch-born gem (*śaṅkhaja-maṇi*),
as well as the mantras dedicated to those deities— by these, the binding of the gem shall lead to success.
These are the afflictions arising from celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial portents.
Listen to the threefold wonders—celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial—consisting of the abnormalities of planets and constellations; understand from me what is celestial and atmospheric.
The falling of meteors, the burning of the quarters, and likewise halos;
the city of the Gandharvas, and whatever rain is unnatural; as well as the occurrence of moving and stationary objects on the earth, and even earthquakes born of the ground.
If rain occurs within seven days [of an eclipse], it will be a portentous marvel causing fear;
without a rite of pacification (*śānti*), such a marvel will cause fear for three years.
They dance, tremble, and blaze forth.
They shriek and weep, perspire and laugh;
there is the pacification of the manifestations of the deity after having worshipped and offered oblations to Prajāpati;
and in that kingdom where fire blazes even without fuel, there is a great clamor.
If a kingdom possessing fuel does not burn, it is oppressed by rival kings;
O Bhārgava, the pacification of such abnormalities of fire is performed with fire-mantras. Trees that bear fruit out of season and exude milk or blood [portend misfortune].
Having worshipped Śiva, one should perform the rite for pacifying the calamity of trees;
excessive rain, drought, and famine are considered the two-fold dangers.
1. "By means of accomplishment" (siddhyā) — thus in manuscripts *gha* and *ña*. 2. "And the deities" (devatāśca) — thus in manuscripts *kha* and *cha*.
3. "They descend" (āvaṭanti) — thus in manuscript *kha*.
If rain begins on the third day during the non-seasonal period (anṛtu), it should be known as portending fear.
Through the worship of Parjanya, the Moon, and the Sun, the abnormalities of rain shall be destroyed;
rivers, lakes, and springs recede from the city and yet approach its vicinity, and they become tasteless.
When there is an anomaly in bodies of water, the Varuṇa mantra should be recited.
Likewise, when women give birth out of season, or fail to conceive at the proper time,
or when there is an abnormality in childbirth, such as the birth of twins and so forth.
If there is a deformity in the birth of women, one should worship a woman, a Brahmin, and other such beings.
If a mare, a female elephant, or a cow gives birth to twins,
or if they give birth to something of a different species or deformed, it will surely die within six months.
Or if they give birth to deformed offspring, there shall be fear of an enemy army.
In the event of such abnormalities at birth, one should perform fire oblations (*homa*), recite prayers (*japa*), and honor Brahmins and others.
Furthermore, whatever vehicles are unyoked, or those that are yoked do not move forward—
And when the sounds of musical instruments are heard in the sky and great danger has approached;
when wild beasts and birds enter the village,
or domestic animals go to the forest, or land-dwelling creatures go toward the water.

Auspicious jackals go from the water to the dry land, or [approach] the king’s gate and such places. If a cock cries out at night in its dwelling, or a jackal howls at sunrise; or if a house-pigeon enters [the home], or a carnivorous bird settles upon the head—[these are ill omens].
A crow, while engaged in copulation, may turn a sweet fly into honey when seen upon a palace, an archway, a garden gate, a rampart, or a house;
however, the falling of such firm structures without a visible cause portends the death of the king.
When the quarters of the sky are overwhelmed by dust or smoke,
when comets appear, when there is an eclipse, or when the moon and sun are spotted;

Wherever there is an abnormality in the planets or the constellations, one should predict fear in that very place. Where fire does not blaze and where clouds shed water, death, fear, and desolation shall be the fruit of such portents.
Peace is attained through the worship of the twice-born, the gods, and others, as well as through recitations (*japa*) and fire-offerings (*homa*).
Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Pacification of Portents," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Having bathed with the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā," one should offer the *arghya* water to Viṣṇu.

to Nandinī, Subhāgyā, and Sumaṅgalī, O Bhārgava.

One should offer to Dharma and Adharma at the two doors; to Dhruva in the middle of the house;

One should also offer to the Bhūtas outside, and to Dhanada in the shelter.
A man should offer [the oblation] to Indra and Indra’s attendants in the east;

and to Varuṇa and his attendants in the west.
One should offer [the oblation] to Soma and the Soma-puruṣas in the north immediately thereafter;

One should likewise offer it to Ākāśa above, and similarly to the Sthaṇḍila on the ground.
One should offer the *bali* outside every day, both in the daytime for those who roam by day and at night for those who roam by night; likewise,
one should perform the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa-nirvapaṇa*) in the morning, but not in the evening.
One should first offer to the father, then immediately after to his father;
then to the great-grandfather, and thereafter one should present [the offering] to his mother and the father’s mother.
One should thus worship the ancestors upon *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing south, while making offerings to their mothers as well.
"May those who belong to Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yama, or Nirṛti—
those crows— accept this ball of rice (piṇḍa) offered by me.
With this mantra for the "crow-ball," one should cause the ball for the dogs to be given.
Two dogs, Śyāva and Śabala, were born in the lineage of Vivasvat;

"May the cows, the mothers of the three worlds, accept my morsel.

‘You are the means of expiation, svāhā! To Agni Sviṣṭikṛt, svāhā! Oṃ, to Prajāpati, svāhā!’
The worship of Viṣṇu and the Vaiśvadeva bali have been described by me to you.
Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Worship of the Devas and the Vaiśvadeva Bali," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 264:
The Bathing of the Guardians of the Quarters and Others.
Agni said:

A wise man should cause the planets, Viṣṇu, and others to bathe on the bank of a river."

Chapter 265:
The Bathing of Vināyaka (Vināyakasnāna)
Puṣkara said: I shall describe the bath that accomplishes everything for those afflicted by Vināyaka;
Vināyaka has been appointed for the purpose of ensuring the successful completion of rites free from obstacles.
And regarding the leadership of the hosts, he excessively plunges into water in a dream along with Keśava, Īśa, and Pitāmaha, and he sees shaven-headed men.

One possessed by Vināyaka mounts upon carnivorous beasts; likewise, while walking, he imagines himself being pursued by others. Dejected and with his undertakings fruitless, he sinks into despondency without apparent cause.
A maiden does not obtain a husband, nor does a beautiful woman obtain offspring;
a learned priest does not attain the status of a teacher, nor does a student obtain his studies;
a wealthy man does not gain profit, nor does a farmer obtain success from his cultivation.
If a king does not obtain his kingdom, one should perform a ceremonial bath for him under the asterisms of Hasta,
Puṣya, Aśvinī, Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), or Vaiṣṇava (Śravaṇa), upon an auspicious throne.
Having anointed him with a paste of white mustard seeds mixed with clarified butter, [one should proceed].
Likewise, with his head anointed with all medicinal herbs and all fragrances,
he should be bathed with four jars into which have been placed all medicinal herbs from a horse stable, an elephant stable, an anthill, a confluence of rivers, and a lake.
One should place earth, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), fragrance, and *guggulu* resin into them;
with that which has been purified by the seers as the thousand-eyed, hundred-streamed [water], I sprinkle you with the purifying (*pāvamānya*) verses. (3)
May King Varuṇa, Bhaga, Sūrya, and Bṛhaspati purify you; may Indra,
Vāyu, and the Seven Seers grant you fortune.
"Whatever misfortune is in your hair, at the parting of your hair, or on your head;

Mita, Sammita, Śālakakaṇṭaka,
