one should offer rice grains both prepared and unprepared, as well as meat-rice,
fish, raw flesh, various flowers, and three kinds of liquor.
One should offer radishes, fried cakes (pūrikā), flour-cakes (pūpa), as well as sweetmeat balls (eṇḍavika),
garlands, curd-rice, milk-porridge, flour-mash, sweet balls (modaka), and molasses;
then one should worship Ambikā, the mother of Vināyaka.
Having offered the *arghya* of *dūrvā* grass, mustard seeds, and flowers, with hands full to the brim:
"O auspicious one, grant me beauty, grant me fame, grant me good fortune! Grant me a son, grant me wealth, and grant me all my desires!"
One should feed the Brāhmaṇas and give a pair of garments even to the Guru;
having worshipped Vināyaka and the planets, one obtains prosperity and the fruit of one's actions.
Thus ends the section on the Vināyaka-bath in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The two hundred and sixty-fifth chapter. [Variant readings:
"Endowed with the *vaṣaṭ*-call" (as found in manuscripts gha, ja, ña, and ṭa).]
Chapter Two Hundred and Sixty-Six: The Chapter on the Sixty-Sixth [of the Two Hundred and Sixty-Sixth] Section.

Puṣkara said: I shall describe the Māheśvara bath, as well as the *lakṣa-homa*, the *koṭi-homa*, and other rites, which increase the victory of kings and others. Now I shall explain the Māheśvara bath.
That which Uśanas formerly spoke to Bali, the lord of the Dānavas:
"Before the sun has risen, one should bathe [the deity] on the pedestal in the morning with jars [of water], saying:
*Oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya ca balāya ca*."
To him whose body is smeared with white ash:
"Victory! Victory! Conquer all enemies; silence [them] in quarrels, conflicts, and disputes; shatter them!"
Oṃ matha matha! Whatever travelers there may be who, at the time of the end of the eon, desire to burn this worship— may that fierce-formed Śukra, the thousand-rayed one, protect your life.
And may Śiva, the destroyer of Tripura, who is like the fire of universal destruction and who embodies all the gods,
protect your life— likhi likhi khili svāhā!
Having bathed in this manner with the mantra, one should offer oblations of sesame seeds and rice.
Having bathed the wielder of the trident (Śūlapāṇi) with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should worship him.
I shall now describe other baths for you, which always lead to victory.
Bathing with ghee is said to be the supreme increaser of longevity;
bathing with cow dung brings prosperity, while bathing with cow urine destroys evil.
Bathing with milk bestows strength and intelligence, and bathing with curd increases prosperity.
The end of evil is achieved through water infused with *kuśa* grass; one who partakes of all [merits] does so through the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Through the hundred-rooted plant (*śatamūla*), there is the attainment of everything; by means of water from a cow’s horn, one conquers sin.
A bath with *palāśa*, *bilva*, lotus, and *kuśa* grass bestows all things.
A bath with *vacā*, the two types of *haridrā*, and *musta* is supreme for destroying demons;
it promotes longevity, fame, and increases righteousness and intelligence.
With water from gold there is auspiciousness; likewise with water from silver and copper.
With water containing jewels there is victory; with all kinds of perfumes, good fortune.
With water from fruits there is health; and with water from *dhātrī* trees, supreme prosperity.
Through sesame and white mustard one gains fortune (*lakṣmī*) and good luck;
through *priyaṅgu* flowers, lotuses, blue lotuses, and *kadamba* flowers, one gains splendor (*śrī*); and through water from the *balā* tree, one gains strength.
Bathing with the water that has washed the feet of Viṣṇu is superior to all other baths.
Being alone,
one should perform the ritual according to the rules with the verse "To the one who desires the one," and one should bind an amulet on the hand while reciting the *Akrandaya* hymn.
Kuṣṭha, pāṭhā, vācā, śuṇṭhī, śaṅkha, loha, and other such gems; yet the Blessed Lord Hari is the master of all desires.
Through the worship of him alone, one attains all desires.

Having bathed [the image] with ghee and milk and having worshipped it, one becomes a destroyer of bile disorders. By offering an oblation of five kinds of mung beans, one is released from dysentery. Having bathed [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one shall destroy wind-related diseases.
Through bathing with the two unctuous substances (*dvisneha*), one destroys diseases of phlegm (*śleṣma*); and through excessive worship, [one gains merit].
Ghee, oil, and likewise honey constitute the supreme triple-essence (*trirasa*) bath;
the ghee-water bath is the *dvisneha*, while the bath containing both ghee and oil is *samala*.
Honey, sugarcane juice, and milk are known as the *trimadhura* bath;
ghee, sugarcane juice, oil, and honey are the *trirasa* for the sake of prosperity.
"1. For one desiring barley... [as noted by Ka and Cha on p.
As for the ointment, it consists of camphor, uśīra, and sandalwood, mixed with three parts of sugar.
With sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron,
one should apply the five-fold ointment (*pañcānulepana*) to Viṣṇu, which bestows the fruits of all desires;
likewise, the "three-fragrance" (*trisugandha*) consists of camphor along with sandalwood and saffron.
Mṛgadarpa with camphor, malaya-sandalwood which grants all desires,
nutmeg with camphor, and sandalwood— the three-fold cool—
these, when yellow or white in color, as well as those that are white, O Bhārgava, [are to be used].
One should designate black, red, and those of five colors; the blue lotus (*utpala*), the lotus-born (*padma*), and jasmine (*jāti*)—these three white flowers are for the worship of Hari.
Saffron (*kuṅkuma*), red lotuses, and the three-fold red *utpala* [are likewise prescribed].

Having worshipped Viṣṇu with incense, lamps, and other offerings, peace shall come to men; in a square pit one cubit in size, eight or sixteen Brahmins should perform a *lakṣahoma* or a *koṭihoma* with sesame seeds, clarified butter, barley, and grains.
"By worshipping the planets with the Gāyatrī mantra, all-encompassing peace shall come in due order.
Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Great Lord’s Bath, the Lakṣa-homa, the Koṭi-homa, and Other Rites," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 267:
The Ritual for the Nīrājana Lustration Ceremony

Puṣkara said: The king should perform the annual ritual for his birth-star (janmarkṣa), worshiping it month by month, as well as the deities such as the Sun and the Moon at every solar transit (saṃkrānti).
Upon the rising of Agastya, one should worship Hari during the four-month period of Agastya;
on the occasions of His lying down and waking up, one should observe a festival for five days.
During the bright fortnight of the month of Proṣṭhapada, beginning from the first lunar day in due order,
one should construct a palace for Śakra in the eastern direction from the camp.
Having installed the banner of Śakra there, one should worship both Śacī and Śakra.
On the eighth day, one should cause that staff to enter [the temple] accompanied by the sound of musical instruments;
on the eleventh day, having observed a fast, and on the twelfth day, one should worship the raised banner,
which is clothed in garments and placed within a water-pot.
O Lord of the Suras, O Śacī’s husband, O Indra, conqueror of enemies, slayer of Vṛtra, subduer of Pāka!
O God, O God of great fortune, for you have indeed come to dwell upon the earth.
"You are the Lord, eternal indeed, devoted to the welfare of all beings;
you are the King of infinite splendor, who increases fame and victory.
May these gods, and Śakra who brings forth good rain, increase your majesty."
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa; Kārttikeya and Vināyaka; the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, Bhṛgus, and the quarters;
the Maruts, Guṇas, world-protectors, planets, Yakṣas, mountains, and rivers.
May Samudrā, Śrī, Mahī, Gaurī, Caṇḍikā, and Sarasvatī cause your splendor to increase; be victorious, O Śakra, Lord of Śacī!
And by your constant victory, may auspiciousness be read aloud for me.
Be gracious toward the kings, the brahmins, and all subjects in every way;
through your favor, may the earth always be rich in crops. May there be auspiciousness and freedom from obstacles, and may calamities be thoroughly pacified.
"Located on a cloth," as found in the manuscripts ka and ga.
Having worshipped Indra with the mantra "cha... ja... ṭa... ca," one who has conquered the earth shall attain heaven.
Having painted Bhadrakālī on a cloth, one should worship her during the month of Āśvina for victory;
likewise, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, one should worship her weapons— the bow, the banner,
the parasol, and other royal insignia— along with weapons and so forth, using flowers and other offerings.
Waking at night, one should offer the *bali* oblation; on the second day, one should sacrifice again:
"O Bhadrakālī, Mahākālī, Durgā, remover of the distress of the difficult!
O Caṇḍī, victorious in the three worlds, be present for my peace and victory!"
I shall describe the ritual of *nīrājana*. One should prepare a temple in the northeast; there, one should always worship the deities at the three archways (*toraṇa*).
When the Sun, having left the constellation Citrā, enters Svāti, [the rite should be performed].
From that time onwards, [the rite] should be performed until the sun is situated in Svāti;
[the deities are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śambhu, and Śakra, as well as Anala and Anila,
Vināyaka, Kumāra, Varuṇa, Dhanada, and Yama.
One should worship the Viśvedevas, Vaiśravaṇa, and the eight elephants:
Kumuda, Airāvaṇa, Padma, Puṣpadanta, Vāmana, Supratīka, Añjana, and Nīla; worship should be performed in the house and other such places.

The domestic priest should offer oblations of clarified butter, fuel-sticks, white mustard seeds, and sesame seeds. Eight consecrated jars should be used to bathe the horses and the best of elephants;
the horses should be bathed first, and then one should offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to the elephants.
One should cause [the image] to be brought out through the archways, but one must not cross over the city gates and such;
then everyone should step forward, and one should worship the emblem of the King (Rājaliṅga) at home.
Having worshipped Varuṇa in the western quarter, one should offer the bali-oblation to the spirits at night, beginning with the *śekhara* [mantra].
When the sun has set, the king should reside in his hermitage;
on that day, he should especially adorn his vehicle.
And the royal insignia, having been worshipped, should be held in the hands of men.
O knower of Dharma, one who knows the proper time should consecrate with mantras the elephant, the horse, the parasol, the sword, the bow, the drum, the banner, and the flag;
having thus consecrated them all, he should then mount them upon the backs of the elephants.
The astrologer and the domestic priest should be mounted upon elephants;
having ascended the ministers as well, he should depart through the archway.
Having exited, he should mount an elephant and then depart through the archway.
Having distributed the sacrificial offering according to the prescribed rites, the king, mounted upon the back of an elephant, should,
with a well-composed mind, circumambulate three times the multitude of the mute, which illuminated the quarters of the sky.
Endowed with a fourfold army, making the earth resound with his entire host,
one should thus depart for home after offering the final libation of water; this rite known as *nīrājana* brings peace, prosperity, and the destruction of enemies.
Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual of Nīrājanā," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
(Note: *viśākhāntviti* appears in manuscripts *ka* and *cha*.)
Chapter Two Hundred and Sixty-Eight: The [Chapter on] the Sixty-Eight [Devas] of the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven.
Puṣkara said: I shall now declare the mantras for the parasol and other [emblems], by means of which, having worshipped them, victory and other [auspicious results] are attained.
By the word of truth of Brahmā, and by that of Soma and Varuṇa,
and by the power of the Sun, may you grow strong, O high-minded one!
You who resemble the color of white silk, possessing the beautiful luster of snow, the kunda flower, and the moon.
Just as a cloud covers this earth for the welfare of all,
so do you cover the king for the increase of his victory and well-being.
Born of the lineage of the Gandharvas, may you not be a defiler of your family.
By the word of truth of Brahmā, Soma, and Varuṇa;
by the power of the sacrificial fire, O horse, may you prosper!
And likewise by the splendor of the Sun and the ascetic heat of the sages.

"By the celibate discipline of Rudra and by the power of Pavana, remember that you are a prince; remember the Kaustubha jewel! Consider the destination to which one who kills a Brahmin, as well as one who kills his father or mother, must go."

O horse, may you swiftly go to that destination reserved for one who speaks falsehood regarding land and for a Kṣatriya who turns his back in battle; may that sin not be yours, and may you not suffer such a transformation on the path of war.
Slaying your enemies in battle along with your master, may you be happy!
O banner of Śakra, you of great heroism, the golden one has taken refuge in you; likewise, Vainateya, the king of birds and the standard of Nārāyaṇa, is here.
The son of Kāśyapa, the bringer of the nectar of immortality, the enemy of the Nāgas, whose vehicle is Viṣṇu;
he is immeasurable, invincible in battle, and the slayer of the enemies of the gods.
Possessing great strength, free from agitation, with a massive body and consuming nectar,
Garuḍa, who moves with the speed of the wind, is present and stationed within you;
for you have been established by Viṣṇu, the god of gods, for the sake of Śakra.
Be ever for my victory, for my prosperity, and for my strength;
protect our warriors along with their horses, armor, and weapons, and consume our enemies—
Kumuda, Airāvaṇa, Padma, Puṣpadanta, and Vāmana.
Supratīka, Añjana, and Nīla—these eight are the divine origins.
Their sons and grandsons have taken refuge in eight strengths:
Bhadra, Manda, Mṛga, Gaja, and Saṃkīrṇa.
Born in forest after forest, those great elephants whose origin is in passion—may the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts protect you!
O Lord of Nagas, guard your mate; let your covenant be upheld.
Mounted upon Airāvata, the wielder of the thunderbolt, Śatakratu,
this king of the gods who follows behind you, may he protect you; attain victory in battle and proceed always with well-being.
Obtain strength equal to Airāvata in battle;
may you have prosperity from Soma, strength from Viṣṇu, splendor from the Sun, speed from the Wind,
steadfastness from the Mountain, victory from Rudra, and fame from the god Purandara.
In battle, may the *nāgas* protect you, as well as the quarters of the sky together with their deities;
may the two *Aśvins*, along with the *gandharvas*, guard you from all directions;
and may the *Manus*, the *Vasus*, the *Rudras*, Vāyu, Soma, and the great seers [protect you].
The hosts of nāgas, kinnaras, gandharvas, yakṣas, and bhūtas, the seizing spirits (grahas),
May Śakra, the commander Skanda, and Varuṇa abide in you;
may they consume all enemies, and may the king attain victory. Whatever ornaments have been employed by the foes on every side, [may they turn against them].
Let the weapons of your enemies fall, destroyed by your splendor—
just as they did at the slaying of Kālanemi, in the battle that destroyed Tripura,
in the fight against Hiraṇyakaśipu, and in the killing of all the Asuras.
Thus you were adorned in the past; be adorned likewise today, remembering the sacred pledge.
Upon seeing these blue and white [flags], may the enemies of the king perish instantly, defeated in battle by various terrible diseases and by weapons.
Pūtanā, Revatī, Lekhā, and Kālarātri— these are recited.
O Banner, may you, having taken refuge in me, swiftly burn all enemies,
as [you were consecrated] by the trident-bearing God of gods at the great sacrifice of Sarvamedha.
You were fashioned from the very essence of Śiva and of the entire world;
remember yourself as the other form of Nandaka, O destroyer of enemies!
O Kṛṣṇa, dark as the petal of a blue lotus, you are the dispeller of evil dreams!
Asirviśasana, Khaḍga, Tīkṣṇadhāra, Durāsada, Augarbha, Vijaya, and likewise Dharmapāla—
these are the eight names of yours previously proclaimed by the Self-Existent One.
Your constellation is Kṛttikā; the god Maheśvara is your preceptor;
gold is your body, and Janārdana is your deity.
O sword, protect the king, along with his army and his city.
O God, you are my father and my grandfather; therefore, protect me always.
O armor, grant me security in battle; today, let there be glory for my army.
Protect me, protect me! I am worthy of your protection, O sinless one; homage be to you, O Dundubhi! By your roar, you cause the hearts of my enemies to tremble;
be so for the armies on the ground that you increase our victory.
Just as excellent elephants rejoice at the roar of a thundercloud,
so may your voice bring us joy and delight; yet,
just as fear arises in women at the sound of a thundercloud, [so may it not arise in us].
Thus, by your sound, may our enemies tremble in battle.
You should always be worshipped with mantras and employed for victory and other such purposes.
Furthermore, the consecration of Ghṛtakambala, Viṣṇu, and others should be performed once a year.
"The consecration of the king must be performed by the astrologer and the domestic priest.
Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Mantras for the Parasol and Other Regalia," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.

Chapter Two Hundred and Seventy-Eight:
Viṣṇu’s Armor.
Puṣkara said:
O best of the twice-born, in former times, when he was about to slay Tripura, the Viṣṇu-armor was prescribed for Śaṅkara by Brahmā for his protection;
and it was likewise [prescribed] by Vāgīśa for Śakra as he set out to destroy Bala.

I shall describe its essential nature; listen to the truth, O Jayādimat. Viṣṇu stands in the east bearing a discus, Hari in the south bearing a mace, Viṣṇu in the west bearing a bow, and Jiṣṇu in my north bearing a sword.
Hṛṣīkeśa is in the corners, Janārdana in those openings,
Hari in the form of a boar upon the earth, and Narasiṃha in the sky above me.
This stainless Sudarśana discus, with its razor-sharp edge, revolves here.
Her garland of rays is difficult to behold, intended to slay the preta-demons and night-stalkers;
and this mace, blazing like a thousand-rayed, kindled fire,
is the destroyer of rākṣasas, bhūtas, piśācas, and ḍākinīs.
And may the twanging of Vāsudeva’s Śārṅga bow utterly destroy my enemies— be they animals, humans, kuṣmāṇḍas, pretas,
and so forth.
May those who have been shaken off by the brilliance of the sword’s edge, though they were concentrated in mind, go forth and be instantly pacified, like serpents by Garuḍa—
those Kuṣmāṇḍas, ghosts, yakṣas, daityas, and night-stalkers.
May the hungry ghosts, the Vināyakas, the cruel ones, humans, the Jambhakas, birds,
lions and other beasts, and the biting serpents—
all become gentle, struck down by the sound of Kṛṣṇa’s conch.

Those who rob me of my mental composure, those people who steal my mindfulness, those who take away my strength and vigor, and those who cause the loss of my radiance; those who deprive me of enjoyments and those who destroy my auspicious marks.
May those *kuṣmāṇḍa* spirits perish, struck down by the roar of Viṣṇu’s discus;
may I attain stability of intellect, stability of mind, and likewise stability of the senses through the glorification of Vāsudeva, the God of gods.
May Janārdana Hari be present behind me, in front of me, to my right and left, and in the intermediate directions;
having prostrated before that worshipful Īśāna, the infinite Acyuta Janārdana, one does not perish.

Just as Hari is the Supreme Brahman, so too is Keśava the Supreme and the very nature of the world; by that truth, may my threefold inauspiciousness be destroyed through the chanting of the name of Acyuta.
Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Viṣṇu-Armor," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 270.
Now begins the two hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of the Branches of the Vedas.
Puṣkara said:
All mantras are benefactors and accomplishers of the four aims of life;
the number of divisions of the *Ṛg*, *Atharva*, *Sāman*, and *Yajus* is one hundred thousand,
consisting of the Sāṅkhyāyana as the first and the Āśvalāyana as the second.
Ten hundred [verses] of mantras and two thousand [brāhmaṇas] constitute the Ṛgveda according to its measure, as remembered by Dvaipāyana and others;
likewise, there are one thousand nine hundred mantras of the Yajus.
There are one thousand and eighty-six branches of the Brahmins:
those known as the Kāṇva and Mādhyandina, the Kaṭha and Mādhyakaṭha, as well as the Maitrāyaṇī and that designated as Taittirīya.

The Vaiśampāyanika and other branches are established within the Yajurveda; of the Sāmaveda there is one known as Kauthuma and a second as Ātharvaṇāyanī; furthermore, there are four Gānas, as well as the Āraṇyaka of the Veda.
The *ukthas* are said to be nine thousand with four hundred,
and the *brahmasaṅghaṭakas* have the fourth [section] as their *ūha*;
here, the measure of the *sāmans* is proclaimed to be exactly twenty-five.
Sumantu, Jājali, Ślokāyani, Atharvaka,
Śaunaka, Pippalāda, Muñjakeśa, and others [compiled] sixty thousand one hundred mantras and one hundred Upaniṣads.

In the form of Vyāsa, that Blessed One caused the division of the branches; the divisions of the branches and so forth— namely the Itihāsas and Purāṇas— originated from Viṣṇu through Vyāsa, and Sūta Lomaharṣaṇa received the Purāṇas and other works from him.
Sumati, Agnivarcas, Mitrayu, Śiṃśapāyana,
Kṛtavrata, and Sāvarṇi were his six disciples; these, beginning with Śāṃśapāyana, composed [the works].
The compendiums of the Purāṇas,
such as the Brāhma and others, consist of eighteen Purāṇas, including the Harividyā;
for in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa, Hari exists in the form of knowledge.
He possesses both conceptual proliferation and is free from proliferation; he assumes the nature of both the formed and the formless.
By knowing him, worshipping him, and praising him, one attains worldly enjoyment and liberation.
He is Viṣṇu, the Victorious, and the All-pervading, and he bears the forms of fire, the sun, and other deities.
In the form of Agni, Viṣṇu is the mouth of the gods and the supreme goal;
he is celebrated in the Vedas and Purāṇas as the embodiment of sacrifice.
Furthermore, the Purāṇa known as the Āgneya is a most exalted manifestation of Viṣṇu.
Janārdana is both the author and the listener of the Purāṇa called Āgneya;
therefore, this great Āgneya Purāṇa consists of all the Vedas,
is composed of all branches of knowledge, is meritorious, and is the most excellent repository of all wisdom.
Indeed, this form of Hari, which is the soul of all, bestows knowledge upon men who read or hear it while seeking knowledge; it grants wealth and fortune to those seeking prosperity;
it grants a kingdom to those desiring sovereignty; and it bestows dharma upon those who desire dharma.

He is the giver of heaven to those seeking heaven, the giver of sons to those desiring sons, the giver of cattle and other things to those desiring them, and the giver of villages to those desiring villages.
1. Śiṃśapāyana and others composed [it]; [this is indicated by] *kha* ... 2. "The supreme" [is indicated by] *ña* ... 3. "Bestowing glorious strength" [is indicated by] *ña* ... 4. *p* 4.
It grants desires to those who seek desires, bestows all good fortune, and confers virtue and fame upon men; it brings victory to those who long for victory,
gives everything to those who desire all things, and grants liberation to those who seek liberation.
This is the two hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of the Vedic Branches and Other Matters," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*, which destroys the sins of those who commit them.
Chapter 271:
The Greatness of Giving and Other Virtues
Puṣkara said:
One should cause to be written and bestowed that portion of the Brāhma [Purāṇa] which was previously declared by Brahmā to Marīci, consisting of fifty thousand verses.

On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one seeking heaven should give a golden lotus weighing twelve thousand *dhenu*s along with a water-cow; and on the full moon of Āṣāḍha, one should likewise give [a golden lotus] weighing twelve thousand *dhenu*s, as Parāśara has related concerning the history of the Varāha-kalpa.
One should recite and offer the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa, consisting of twenty-three thousand verses; by giving a water-cow on the full moon of Āṣāḍha, one attains the abode of Viṣṇu.
The Vāyavīya Purāṇa, beloved of Hari, consists of fourteen thousand verses.
In connection with the Śvetakalpa, Vāyu proclaimed these dharmas here;
one should give them to a Brahmin after having them written down, along with a cow made of molasses, on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa.
Where the expansion of Dharma is recounted with reference to the Gāyatrī— 5.1–2ab.
That which contains the slaying of the demon Vṛtra is called the Bhāgavata. One should give it during the month of Proṣṭhapada in the Sārasvata Kalpa;
it consists of eighteen thousand verses and is accompanied by a golden lion.
Where Nārada proclaimed the dharmas based on the Bṛhatkalpa,
that work consisting of twenty-five thousand verses is called the Nāradīya;
one should give it along with a cow during the month of Āśvina and obtain ultimate perfection.
In which the investigation of dharma and adharma concerning enemies is set forth;
one should then offer the *Mārkaṇḍeya* in nine thousand verses on the full moon of Kārttika.
That which was proclaimed by Agni to Vasiṣṭha is indeed the *Āgneya*.
Having written this book, he who gives it away during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa becomes a giver of everything;
[it contains] twelve thousand verses for the awakening to all branches of knowledge,
and fourteen thousand verses concerning the future arising of the Sun.
Bhava, however, spoke it to Manu; one should give [this Purāṇa], which contains jaggery and other offerings, on the full moon of Pauṣa.
The Brahmavaivarta was narrated by Sāvarṇi to Nārada;
it consists of eighteen thousand verses and recounts the history of the Rathantara.
One who recites the *Varāha-carita* during the month of Māgha shall attain the world of Brahmā;
therein, Maheśvara, stationed within the center of the fiery *liṅga*, proclaimed the sacred laws (*dharmas*).
That *liṅga* in the *Āgneya-kalpa* consists of eleven thousand verses.
By giving that [gift] on the full moon day of Phālguna, one attains auspiciousness through a sesame-cow;
[one also gains] fourteen thousand [verses] of the Vārāha [Purāṇa] as uttered by Viṣṇu,
concerning the deeds of the Boar on earth from the time of Manu’s manifestation.
On the full moon day of Caitra, one who possesses a golden *garuḍa* indeed attains the state of Viṣṇu.
The great *Skānda*, consisting of eighty-four thousand verses, was proclaimed by Skanda; it is the retention of all branches of knowledge.
One should dedicate the *Sadharmāḥ* to the *Tatpuruṣa-kalpa*;
one should give the story of Hari as the *Vāmana*, consisting of ten thousand verses, in the *Dhaumya-kalpa*;
and during the autumnal equinox, one should impart the knowledge of dharma, wealth, and other goals.
The *Kūrma* consists of eight thousand verses and was spoken by Kūrma in the subterranean realm (Rasātala);
one should bestow it along with the account of Indradyumna, as in the case of the *Hemakūrma*.
The *Mātsya*, beginning from the start of the Kalpa, comprises thirteen thousand verses.
For on the equinox, Matsya would indeed give the *Hemamatsya* to Manu;
and he would give the *Garuḍa*, consisting of eight thousand verses as spoken by Viṣṇu in the *Tārkṣakalpa*,
which describes the birth of Garuḍa from the cosmic egg, like the *Hemahaṃsa*.

That which Brahmā spoke concerning the majesty of the *Brahmāṇḍa* consists of twelve thousand verses; one should present that *Brahmāṇḍa* to a twice-born man at the conclusion of the section on Bhārata, along with garments, perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.

One should first honor the reciter and feed the twice-born with milk-rice; at every festival, one should give gifts such as cows, land, villages, and gold. When the *Bhārata* is completed, O Brahmin, one should worship the manuscript of the *Saṃhitā*.
Then, having established them in an auspicious place and covered them with linen cloth and other materials,
one should worship Nara and Nārāyaṇa and the books with flowers and other offerings;
thereafter, having given cows, food, land, and gold, and having fed [the brahmins], one should ask for their forgiveness.
Great gifts should be given, as well as various kinds of jewels;
one should cause two or even three *māsakas* to be bestowed month after month.
At the beginning of the [solar] transit, the gift for a disciple (*śrāvaka*) is prescribed first.
O twice-born one, all the listeners should perform worship toward the reciter;
he who bestows books of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas [attains great merit].
"By worshipping [it], one shall obtain long life, health, heaven, and liberation.
Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of Giving and Other Virtues," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 272:
The Glorification of the Solar Lineage (Sūryavaṃśakīrtana)
Agni said:
"I shall describe to you the solar dynasty, the lunar dynasty, and the lineage of kings.
From Hari, Brahmā was born from the lotus; Marīci was the son of Brahmā."
From Marīci came Kaśyapa; from him, Vivasvat; and his wives were Saṃjñā, Rājñī, Prabhā, and the three daughters of Raivata.
Prabhā gave birth to a son, Revanta; and Saṃjñā, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, bore to the Sun three children: her son Manu, and the twins Yamunā and Yama.
Chāyā, who was also Saṃjñā, bore the son Sāvarṇi, the Vaivasvata Manu.
Śani, Tapati, Viṣṭi, and the two Aśvins were born from Saṃjñā; moreover, there were the sons of Vaivasvata Manu, and indeed none were equal to him:
Ikṣvāku, Nābhāga, Dhṛṣṭa, and Śaryāti.
Nariṣyanta, Prāṃśu, Nābhāga, and others who were most excellent, as well as Karuṣa and the mighty Pṛṣadhra, [were born] in Ayodhyā.
And Manu had a daughter named Ilā; from her, by Budha, Purūravas was born.
Having begotten Purūravas, Śelā became Sudyumna.
From Sudyumna were born three kings: Utkala, Gaya, and Vinatāśva.
The kingdom of Utkala belongs to Utkala; the western direction belongs to Vinatāśva;
and Gayāpura belongs to Gaya, the best of kings.
By the word of Vasiṣṭha, Sudyumna indeed obtained Pratiṣṭhāna.

Having obtained the kingdom, Sudyumna gave it to Purūravas. The Śakas were the sons of Nariṣyanta, and Ambarīṣa was the son of Nābhāga; he was a devotee of Viṣṇu and a protector of subjects. From Dhṛṣṭa came the Dhārṣṭaka lineage.
From Śaryāti came Sukalpa; from Ānarta came Vairohi, who was the king of Ānarta. The region was called Ānarta, and its capital city was Kuśasthalī.
Reva’s son was the righteous Raivata, named Kakudmin.
The eldest son of the hundred sons, having obtained the kingdom of Kuśasthalī,
heard from Brahmā in the presence of the God that what had been but a moment for the deity had passed as many yugas in the mortal world, accompanied by his daughter.
Then he arrived with speed at his own city, Dvāravatī by name, surrounded by the Yādavas, many-gated and enchanting,
protected by the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas.
Having recognized that Revatī was irreproachable, he gave her to Baladeva with Vāsudeva at the head;
then, having performed austerities on the peak of Mount Sumeru, he went to the abode of Viṣṇu.
The two sons of Nābhāga were Vaiśyas who attained the status of Brāhmaṇas;
the descendants of Karūṣa, however, were Kṣatriyas fierce in battle, known as the Kārūṣas;
and Pṛṣadhra fell to the state of a Śūdra after having harmed his guru’s cow.
Then from Ikṣvāku, the son of Manu, came Vikukṣi, who became Devarāj. From Vikukṣi came Kakutstha, and his son was Suyodhana.
His son was named Pṛthu, and Viśvagaśva was the son of Pṛthu.
Āyu was his son, and Yuvanāśva was likewise his son. From Yuvanāśva came Śrāvanta; the ancient city of Śrāvantikā [was named after him].
From Śrāvanta, Vṛhadaśva arose, and from him came King Kuvalāśva.
In former times, he indeed attained the state of Dhundhumāra by the name of Dhundhu.
There were three kings of the Dhundhumāra lineage: Dṛḍhāśva, Daṇḍa, and Kapila.
From Dṛḍhāśva came Haryaśva and Pramodaka.
From Haryaśva was born Nikumbha; from Nikumbha came Saṃhatāśva;
both Akṛśāśva and Raṇāśva were the two sons of Saṃhatāśva;
Yuvanāśva was the son of Raṇāśva; and Māndhātṛ was born from Yuvanāśva.
Māndhātṛ’s son was Purukutsa, and Mucukunda was the second.
From Purukutsa was born Asasyu, who was begotten by Narmadā. Sudhanvan was the son of Sambhūta, and Tridhanvan was the son of Sudhanvan.
The son of Tridhanvan was the youthful Satyavrata;
from Satyavrata came Satyaratha, and Hariścandra was his son.
From Hariścandra came Rohitāśva, and from Rohitāśva, Vṛka was born.
From Vṛka came Bāhu, and from Bāhu came Sagara;
his beloved wife was Prabhā, who indeed became the mother of sixty thousand sons.
From King Tuṣita, through the grace of Daurva, she bore one son, Bhānu, whose son was Asamañjasa.
While digging the earth, many Sāgaras were consumed by Viṣṇu;
from Aṃśumat was born Asamañjas, and from him came Aṃśumān and Dilīpa.
From Dilīpa came Bhagīratha, by whom the Gaṅgā was brought down. (AP 272.030ab) [Note: According to some manuscripts, this is attributed to a sage.]
From Bhagīratha came Nābhāga; from Nābhāga, Ambarīṣa;
from Ambarīṣa, Sindhudvīpa; and Śrutāyu is known as his son.
From Śrutāyu was born Ṛtaparṇa, and his son was Kalmāṣapāda.
From Kalmāṣapāda was born Sarvakarman; from him came Anaraṇya; from Anaraṇya came Nighna; and from him came Anamitra and Raghu.
From Raghu was born Dilīpa, and from Dilīpa came King Aja.
From Aja came Dīrghabāhu, and from him was born Kāla; from Kāla, Ajapāla arose.
Likewise, Daśaratha was born, and he had four sons.
All were of the nature of Nārāyaṇa; Rāma was his eldest brother,
the king and best of the Raghus who brought about the end of Rāvaṇa in Ayodhyā,
whose life-story Vālmīki composed after hearing it from Nārada.
Rāma’s two sons, Kuśa and Lava, were born of Sītā and increased the lineage.
From Kuśa was born Atithi, and Niṣadha was his son.
From Niṣadha, Nala was born, and from Nala, Nabha was indeed born.
From Nabhasa came Puṇḍarīka, and from him Sudhanvan was born;
from Sudhanvan came Devānīka, and Ahīnāśva was his son. From Ahīnāśva came Sahasrāśva, and from him Candrāloka was born.
From Candrāvaloka came Tārāpīḍa, and from him Candraparvata;
from Candragiri came Bhānuratha, and his son was Śrutāyu. These are remembered as born of the Ikṣvāku lineage and as upholders of the Solar dynasty.
Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Glorification of the Solar Lineage," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
[Note: In the manuscripts designated as Kha, Cha, and Ca, the reading is "sakarmābhūt" (he became possessed of action).]
Chapter Two Hundred and Seventy-Three.
Regarding the description of the Lunar Dynasty,
Agni said:
"I shall proclaim the Lunar Dynasty, which, when recited, destroys all sins."
Brahmā was born from the navel-lotus of Viṣṇu; Brahmā’s son was Atri, and from Atri came Soma.
Soma performed the Rājasūya sacrifice and gave away the three worlds as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
When the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) was completed, those who desired to behold his form [approached] Soma.
With their limbs scorched by the arrows of desire, the wives of gods attended upon him;
Lakṣmī abandoned Narāyaṇa and Sinīvālī abandoned Kardama, while Dyuti left Vibhāvasu and Puṣṭi left the imperishable Dhātṛ.
Prabhā abandoned Prabhākara and went to Haviṣmān; Kuhū herself [chose] Jayanta as her husband; Vasu [chose] Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci;
and at that time, Dhṛti, abandoning her husband Nandin, took refuge with Soma.
Then Soma also desired them as if they were his own; yet,
when their husband had thus committed an offense against them, that host of husbands was unable to retaliate.
Furthermore, having regained the sovereignty over the seven worlds through his ascetic power despite curses, weapons, and other obstacles,
his mind— struck by misconduct instead of discipline— wandered astray.
Soma, indeed, having disregarded the son of Aṅgiras, forcibly abducted the illustrious Tārā, the wife of Bṛhaspati; thereupon,
that famous war known as the Tārakāmaya ensued.
Neither the gods nor the dānavas were able to prevent it; it was a great [conflict] that brought about the destruction of the world.
Brahmā, having restrained Uśanas, gave her to Aṅgiras.
Seeing that she was pregnant, the Guru said, "Abandon the fetus. When the fetus had been abandoned, it blazed forth and said, "I am born from Soma."
Thus Budha was the son of Soma, and his son was Purūravas;
having left heaven, the Apsaras Urvaśī chose him as her husband,
and the king lived with her for fifteen years.
Five, six, seven, eight, ten, and eight— O Great Sage, fire was originally one, but by him the Tretā age was set in motion.
Purūravas, devoted to yoga, went to the world of the Gandharvas.
Āyuṣmān, Dṛḍhāyu, Aśvāyu, Dhanāyu, Dhṛtimān, Vasu,
Divijāta, Śatāyu, and Urvaśī gave birth to these kings.
Nahuṣa was the son of Āyu, as were Vṛddhaśarmā and Raji.
Darbha was free from sin;
Raji had a hundred sons who became known as the Rājeyas, for Raji had received a boon from Viṣṇu.

Requested by the gods, he slew the Daityas in the war between the gods and the asuras. Having granted his sonhood to Indra who had approached him and having given him the kingdom, he departed to heaven.
Then, his kingdom having been seized by the sons of Raji, Śakra became deeply dejected.
Through the ritual for pacifying the planets and other rites, the Guru gave that [knowledge] to Indra;
having deluded the sons of Raji, they remained established in their own dharma.
Nahuṣa had seven sons, of whom Yati was the eldest and Yayāti was the most excellent.
Udbhava, Pañcaka, Śaryāti, Megha, and Pālaka—
these are known as the Pañcāgnis.
Even while still a youth, Yati attained Hari after meditating upon Viṣṇu;
at that time, Devayānī, the daughter of Śakra, became the wife of Yayāti.
Devayānī gave birth to five sons for Yayāti from Vṛṣaparvan’s daughter Śarmiṣṭhā: Yadu and Turvasu, and Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru— these were the sons born of Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.
Yadu and Pūru became the increasers of their lineages.
Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Lunar Lineage," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 274:
Description of the Yadu Lineage
Agni said:
Yadu had five sons; among them, Sahasrajit was the eldest—Nīlāñjaka, R̥dhu, Kroṣṭu, Śatajit, and Sahasrajit.
Śatajit, Haihaya, and Reṇuhaya—these three were the sons of Haya.
Dharmanetra was the son of Haihaya, and Saṃhana was the son of Dharmanetra.
Mahimā was the son of Saṃhana, and Bhadrasenaka was the son of Mahimā.
From Bhadrasena came Durgama; from Durgama came Kanaka.
From Kanaka came Kṛtavīrya, then Kṛtāgni, then Karavīraka, and Kṛtaujas was the fourth; from Kṛtavīrya came that Arjuna.
Datta bestowed upon Arjuna sovereignty over the earth with its seven continents,
as well as a thousand arms and invincibility against enemies in battle.
For one who abides in unrighteousness, death at the hands of Viṣṇu is certain.
O kings, that Arjuna performed ten thousand sacrifices;
by his mere remembrance, there was no loss of property in his kingdom.
"Surely no kings shall ever attain the state of Kārtavīrya through sacrifices, gifts, austerities, valor, or sacred learning. And Kārtavīrya had five hundred sons who were truly preeminent."
Sūrasena, Sūra, Dhṛṣṭokta, and Kṛṣṇa were his sons;
and there was a great king of Avanti named Jayadhvaja.
From Jayadhvaja came Tālajaṅgha, and from Tālajaṅgha, [there were] then sons.
There were five lineages of the Haihayas: the Bhojas, the Āvantyas, the Vītihotras, the Svayamjātas, and likewise the Śauṇḍikēyas.
From Vītihotra was born Ananta, and from Ananta came King Durjaya.
I shall proclaim the lineage of Kroṣṭṛ, in which Hari himself was born.
From Kroṣṭṛ came Vṛjinīvān; from Vṛjinīvān came Svāhā;
and the son of Svāhā was Ruṣadgu.
His son was Citraratha; from Citraratha came Śaśabindu, a universal monarch devoted to Hari. And of the hundred sons of Śaśabindu, there were one hundred [successive kings].

Pṛthuśravas was the preeminent son of those wise ones of beautiful form and great wealth and splendor; Suyajñaka was the son of Pṛthuśravas; Uśanas was the son of Suyajña; and Titikṣu was the son of Uśanas.
From Titikṣu was born Marutta; from him, Kambalabarhiṣa;
from Pañcāśatrukmakavaca came Rukmeṣu and Pṛthurukmaka.
And Viṣāṃśu; [Ja...]: 15 Haviḥ was Jyāmagha, and Jyāmagha was the destroyer of sin; he became one who was conquered by women.
From Jyāmagha was born Vidarbha; his son was Kauśika;
from the excellent Lomapāda came Kratha, and from Lomapāda was born Kṛti.
Cidi was the son of Kauśika; from him the kings known as the Caidyas are descended. From Kratha came the sons of Vidarbha, and from Kunti came Dhṛṣṭaka.
From Dhṛṣṭa came Nidhṛti, and his son was Vidūratha, also called Udarka.
Vyoma was the son of Daśārha; from Vyoma, Jīmūta is said to have been born. Vikala was the son of Jīmūta, and Bhīmaratha was his son.
From Bhīmaratha came Navaratha, and from him Dṛḍharatha was born.
From Dṛḍharatha was born Śakunti; from Śakunti came Karambhaka;
from Karambha was born Devalāta, and Devakṣetra was his son.
From Devakṣetra was born one named Madhu; from Madhu came Dravarasa.
From Dravarasa was born Puruhūta, and Jantu was his son.
Guṇin was King Yādava, and Sāttvata was the son of Jantu.
From Sātvata were born Bhajamāna, Vṛṣṇi, Andhaka, and Devāvṛdha; these four lineages are renowned. Of Bhajamāna, there were four sons:
Vāhya, Vṛṣṭi, Kṛmi, and Nimi.
From Devāvṛdha came Babhru; his verse is sung here:
"Just as we hear of his virtues from afar, so do we hear them from nearby;
Babhru is the best among men, and Devāvṛdha is equal to the gods."
Sama was [the son], and Vabhru had four sons who were kings devoted to Vāsudeva:
Dhṛti... [and others].
2. *devarāto 'bhūt* iti kha..., ga...,
gha...;
ja..., ña..., ṭa..., and ca 3 are "extended" (vistṛtā), according to ka... and cha... and ca.
Kuhura was the son of Bhajamāna,
and Śini was the son of Kambalabarhiṣ.
Kuhura’s son was Dhṛṣṇu, and Dhṛṣṇu’s son was Dhṛti.
From Dhṛti was born Kapotaroman, and his son was Tittiri.
Tittiri’s son was Nara, and his son was Candanadundubhi.
Punarvasu was his son, and Āhuka was the son of Āhukī. From Āhuka, Devaka was born, and from him Ugrasena arose.
Devavān and Upadeva are recorded as the sons of Devaka.
They had seven sisters, whom he gave to Vasudeva:
Devakī, Śrutadevī, Mitradevī, Yathodharā,
Śrīdevī, Satyadevī, and Surāpī as the seventh.
Ugrasena had nine sons, of whom Kaṃsa was the eldest:
Nyagrodha, Sunāman, Kaṅka, Śaṅku, the king Bhūmipa,
Sutanu, Rāṣṭrapāla, Yuddhamuṣṭi, and Sumuṣṭika.
The son of Bhajamāna was Vidūratha, the foremost of chariot-warriors; Rājādhideva was the heroic son of Vidūratha. Rājādhideva had two sons: Śoṇāśva and Śvetavāhana.
Śoṇāśva had five sons, Śamī, Śatrujit, and others.
Śamī’s son was Pratikṣetra; Pratikṣetra’s son was Bhojaka.
Bhoja’s son was Hṛdika, and Hṛdika had ten sons.
Kṛtavarman, Śatadhanvan, Devārha, Bhīṣaṇa, and others;
[and] Kukura and Bhajamāna— so it is said.
1. Sundara was a devotee;
2. [The son] of Kukura;
3. Śakrajit and others—thus [it is stated in] manuscript KHA.
From Devārha was born Kambalabarhis;
from Asamaujas were born Sudaṃṣṭra, Suvāsa, and Dhṛṣṭa.
Gāndhārī and Mādrī became the two bold wives.
Sumitra was born of Gāndhārī, and Mādrī gave birth to Yudhājit.
From Anamitra and Dhṛṣṭa was born Śini, and from him indeed came Devamīḍhuṣa.

Anamitrasuta was Nighna, and Nighna’s son was Prasenaka; Prasena was the son of Satrājit. Having obtained the Syamantaka jewel from the Sun, while he was wandering in the forest, a lion killed him and seized the jewel.
The lion was slain by Jāmbavat; Jāmbavat was defeated by Hari.
Therefore, having obtained the jewel and Jāmbavatī, he returned to the city of Dvārakā and gave [the jewel] to Satrājit; Śatadhanvan killed him.
Having slain Śatadhanu and taken the jewel, the glorious Kṛṣṇa should present that jewel to Akrūra in the presence of the foremost of the Bālayādas;
by reciting this, one casts off the false accusation against Kṛṣṇa and attains heaven.
Satrājit’s son was Bhaṅgakāra, and Satyabhāmā was the beloved wife of Hari. From Anamitra was born Śini, and Satyaka was the son of Śini.
From Satyaka was born Sātyaki, and from Yuyudhāna (Sātyaki) was born Dhuni.
Dhuna’s son was Yugandhara; Svāhya was the son of Yudhājita; his [Yugandhara’s] sons were Ṛṣabha and Kṣetraka; and from Ṛṣabha came Svaphalka.
Akrūra was indeed the son of Svaphalka, and from Akrūra came Sudhanvaka;
from Śūra came Vasudeva and others, while Pṛthā became the beloved wife of Pāṇḍu.
1. *sudhājitam* according to Kha and Cha;
2. *svāndhobhūt* according to Kha and Cha;
*sākṣobhūt* according to Ja.
From Dharma was born Yudhiṣṭhira; from Vāyu in Kuntī was born Vṛkodara;
from Indra in Mādrī were born Dhanañjaya, Nakula, and Sahadeva.
From Vasudeva and Rohiṇī were born Rāma, Sāraṇa, and Durgama.
From Vasudeva and Devakī, Susenaka was born first,
followed by Kīrtimān, Bhadrasena, Jārukhya, and Viṣṇudāsaka.
Bhadradeha and Kaṃsa slew these six embryos;
then came Bala, then Kṛṣṇa, the sweet-speaking Subhadrā,
Cārudeṣṇa, Śāmba, and others— the sons of Jāmbavatī born from Kṛṣṇa.
Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Yadu Lineage," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the two hundred and seventy-fifth chapter:
The Twelve Battles.
Agni said:
Kaśyapa became Vasudeva, and Aditi became the excellent Devakī. From Vasudeva and Devakī, Kṛṣṇa was born, endowed with ascetic power,
for the sake of protecting righteousness and for the removal of unrighteousness.
For the sake of protecting Surā and others, and for the purpose of churning the Daityas and others,
[he had wives such as] Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā— the beloved daughter of Nagnajit— and likewise Satyā;
Satyabhāmā was the consort of Hari, as were Gāndhārī and Lakṣmaṇā.
And the goddess Kālindī, as well as Jāmbavatī, Suśīlā, Mādrī, Kauśalyā, Vijayā, Jayā,
and Citravindā.
In this manner, there were sixteen thousand such goddesses;
and from Rukmiṇī were born Pradyumna and others, while from Satyabhāmā were born Bhīma and others.
From Jāmbavatī were born Śāmba and others; likewise,
there were other hundreds of thousands of sons for that wise one,
as well as eighty thousand Yādavas protected by Kṛṣṇa.
From Pradyumna and Vaidarbhī was born Aniruddha, who delighted in battle.
From Aniruddha were born the Yādavas headed by Vajra, who possessed great strength.
There were thirty million and six million Dānava-like Yādavas.
He became the destroyer of those obstacles that afflict humanity;
Hari is born as a human being in order to establish the order of karma.
There were twelve battles between the gods and the asuras for the sake of the inheritance.
The first was the Nārasiṃha battle, the second the Vāmana battle;
then the Varāha battle, the fourth the Amṛtamanthana,
the Tārakāmaya battle, and the sixth was indeed the Ājīvaka battle.
The slaying of Andhaka at Tripura was the ninth; then followed the destruction of Vṛtra, the conquest of Hālāhala, and the terrible battle of Kolāhala.
Long ago, he tore apart Hiraṇyakaśipu with his claws.

The divine protector Nārasiṃha made Prahlāda a king; and Vāmana, born of Aditi as the son of Kaśyapa, having deceived the powerful Bali during the war between the gods and the asuras, bestowed the kingdom upon Mahendra.
Having slain Hiraṇyākṣa, the Boar protected the gods;
praised by the gods of gods, he lifted up the earth,
making Mount Mandara the churning-stick and Vāsuki the rope.
Churned by the gods and asuras, it bestowed the nectar of immortality upon the gods.
Then, in the battle of the stars, the gods were protected;
having restrained Indra and the elder gods,
Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and Kaśyapa [protected] the Dānavas and the gods in the fray.
Having warded off the dānavas such as passion and hatred,
Hari, the protector of the gods and crusher of the daityas, took refuge in the Lord Brahmā— the driver on the chariot of the earth— and burned the triple city.
When Rudra was oppressed by Andhaka, who desired to seize Gaurī, Hari—
being devoted to Revatī— performed the destruction of the demon Andha;
having become composed of the foam of the waters, he carried away [the nectar] in the battle between the gods and the asuras.
Viṣṇu protected the divine duties by slaying Vṛtra, the seizer of the gods;
and Hari, as Paraśurāma, having conquered the Dānavas such as Śālva and others,
and having struck down the wicked Kṣatriyas, protected the gods and their followers.
Having warded off the Daitya Hālāhala poison from Maheśvara,
Madhusūdana dispelled the fear of the gods;
and in the battle between the gods and asuras, the Daitya Kolāhala was defeated by him.
And all the gods were protected by Viṣṇu through the preservation of dharma;
kings, princes, sages, and deities—
whatever has been told and whatever has not been told, these are the incarnations of Hari.
Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Twelve Battles," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Chapter 276:
Description of the Royal Genealogies (Rājavaṃśavarṇana)
Agni said:
"The son of Turvasu was Varga, and his son was Gobhānu; the son of Traiśāni was Karandhama."
From Karandhama was born Marutta, and Duṣmanta was his son.
Varūtha was the son of Duṣmanta, and from Varūtha came Gāṇḍīra.
From Gāṇḍīra came Gāndhāra; from him, five provinces arose.
The Gāndhāras, Keralas, Colas, Pāṇḍyas, and Kolās were of great strength.
From Druhyu came Vabhrusetu, and from Vabhrusetu came Purūvasu. From those Gāndhāras came Gāndhāra; from Gāndhāra, Dharma was born; and from Dharma, Ghṛta arose.
From that wise Ghṛta came Pracetas, who indeed had a hundred sons;
Ānadratha, Sabhānara, Cākṣuṣa, and Parameṣuka;
from Sabhānara was born Kālānala, and from Kālānala was born Sṛñjaya.
Purañjaya was the son of Sṛñjaya, and his son was Janamejaya. His son was Mahāśāla, and his son was Mahāmanas. From him, O Brahmin, came Uśīnara; from Ṛgāyā, however, came Nṛga.
From Nara came Nara, and from Kṛmi came the son Kṛmita;
his son was Śobhānu— thus [it is said] in the Kha[ndika].

In Daśārṇa, Subrata was born, as well as Śibi in Dṛśadvatī;

From Titikṣu came Uśīnara; from Titikṣu came Ruṣadratha. From Ruṣadratha was born Paila, and from Paila was born the son Sutapas.

Puṇḍra, Kaliṅga, Bāleya, Bali, Yogin, and Balānvita;

Chapter 277:
Description of the Lineage of Puru
Agni said:
Puru’s son was Janamejaya; his son was Prācīnvat.
From Prācīnvat came Manasyu, and from him was born King Vitamaya.
From Śundhu was born Vītamaya, and from Śundhu there was a son named Bahuvidha.
From Bahuvidha came Saṃyāti, and his son was Ahovādin. His son was Bhadrāśva, and Bhadrāśva had ten sons.
Ṛceyu, Kṛṣeyu, and likewise Sannateyu as his son;
Ghṛteyu, Citeyu, and the most excellent Sthaṇḍileyu; Dharmeyu, Sannateyu, Kṛceyu, and Matināraka.
From Taṃsur was born Pratiratha; from Pratiratha was born Matināraja;
from Patiratha was born Kaṇva; and from Kaṇva came Medhātithi.
From Taṃsurogha were born four sons: Duṣmanta, Pravīraka, [Śrutānta, and Anagha].
From this Anu was born the hero Sumanta, and from Duṣmanta, Śakuntalā gave birth to the powerful Bharata, after whom the descendants are called the Bhāratas;
for when Bharata’s sons had perished due to their mother’s anger, [he became the lineage's progenitor].
Then, having been brought by the Maruts, that son of Bṛhaspati,
Bharadvāja, was transferred [to him], and Vitatha became the performer of sacrifices.
And that Vitatha indeed begot five sons.
Śambhu was also possessed of various kinds of fearlessness;
likewise, there were Suhotra, Suhotṛ, Gaya, and Garga.
And Kapila [beheld] the high-souled Suketu and his two sons;
likewise Kauśika and Gṛtsapati, and the sons of Gṛtsapati—
the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas— and Dīrghatamas in Kāśī.
Sutā was born;
from him came Dhanvantari, and his son was Ketumān.
From Ketumān was born Hemaratha, who is known as Divodāsa.
From Divodāsa came Pratardana; from Pratardana, Bharga and Vatsa;
from Vatsa came Anarka, and from Anarka, Kṣemaka was born.
From Kṣemaka came Varṣaketu, and Vibhu is recorded as the son of Varṣaketu.
Vibhu’s son was Ānarta, and Vibhu’s son was Sukumāraka. From Sukumāra came Satyaketu, and from Vatsaka came Vatsabhūmi.
Suhotra’s son was Bṛhatputra, and Bṛhat had three sons.
Ajamīḍha, Dvimīḍha, and the heroic Purumīḍha were born; from Ajamīḍha and Keśinī was born the powerful Jahnu (3). From Jahnu was born Ajakāśva, and Balākāśva was his son.
From Valākāśva came Kuśika; from Kuśika came Gādhi, whose son was Indraka.
From Gādhi came a daughter, Satyavatī, and Viśvāmitra, the most excellent of sons.
Devarāta and Katimukha were those sons of Viśvāmitra.
Śunaḥśepha and another, Aṣṭaka, were born from Ajamīḍha; Śānti was born from Nīlinī, and Purujāti was born from Suśānti.
1. "Kāśadīrghatamas" according to Ja...; 2. "Suta" according to Kha..., Cha..., and Ja... Ca.
3. [He was] powerful (prabhāvavān), according to Kha...: p 25. From Purujāti came Vāhyāśva; from Vāhyāśva, five kings.
Mukula, Sṛñjaya, King Bṛhadiṣu,
Yavīnara, Kṛmila, and the Pāñcālas— these are the ones renowned as such.
The twice-born of the Maukulya lineage were the landholders of Mukula.
From Mukula was born Cañcāśva, and from Cañcāśva there arose a pair:
Divodāsa and Ahalyā. From Śaradvata, [Divodāsa] begot [Śatānanda] upon Ahalyā.
From Śatānanda came Śatānanda; from him, Satyadhṛt; then Mithuna; then Kṛpa and Kṛpī; from Kivodāsa came Maitreya; then Somapa;
from Sṛñjaya came Pañcadhanus, and his son was Somadatta.
Sahadeva was born from Somadatta, and from Sahadeva came Somaka; from Somaka was born Jantu, and Jantu’s son was Pṛṣata. From Pṛṣata came Drupada, and his son was Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
And from Ajamīḍha, Dhṛṣṭaketu begot Ṛkṣa through Dhūminī;
from Ṛkṣa, Samvaraṇa was born; and from that Samvaraṇa came Kuru, who, having departed from Prayāga, established Kurukṣetra.
From Kuru came Sudhanvan, also known as Sudhanu, and Parikṣit, the subduer of enemies.
From Sudhanvan was born Suhotra, and from Suhotra was born Cyavana.
Through the service of Vasiṣṭha, seven sons were born to Girikā.
From King Bṛhadratha were born the heroes Kuśa, Yadu, Pratyagraha, and Bala, as well as Matsya, Kālī, and Kuśāgra; from that Kuśāgra, son of Bṛhadratha, Vṛṣabha was born, whose son was Satyahita.
Sudhanvan was his son; from Urja was born Āsīca, and from him came Sambhava. Yavīnara was [the son] of Sambhava.
From Sambhava came Jarāsaṃdha, and his son was Sahadeva;
from Sahadeva came Udāpi, and from Udāpi came Śrutakarman.
The righteous Janamejaya was the heir of Parikṣit.
From Janamejaya came Trasadasyu; and the son of Jahnu was Suratha, as well as those known by the names Śrutasena, Ugrasena, and Bhīmasena.
Janamejaya had two sons, Suratha and Mahimān.
From Suratha was born Vidūratha, and from Vidūratha came Ṛkṣa.
The son of the second Ṛkṣa was Bhīmasena.

Pratīpa was born from Bhīmasena, and from Pratīpa came Śāntanu; Devāpi and Bāhlika were also [sons] of Śāntanu. From Śāntanu was born Somadatta. From Bāhlika were born Somadatta, Bhūri, Bhūriśravas, and Śala.
Bhīṣma was born to Śāntanu by Gaṅgā; Vicitravīrya was born to Kālī;
and Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, in the field of Vicitravīrya, begot Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and Vidura.
From Pāṇḍu were born Yudhiṣṭhira by Kuntī, as well as Bhīma and Arjuna— these three—

And from Arjuna was born Saubhadra, Parikṣit, from Abhimanyu.

From Bhīmasena and Hiḍimbā was born another, Ghaṭotkaca;
these kings of the past and those of the future are beyond counting.
