Chapter 278:
Siddha Medicines (Siddhauṣadhāni)
Agni said:
"I shall proclaim the Ayurveda, the essence that restores the dead to life, which the divine Dhanvantari spoke to Suśruta."
Suśruta said:
"Tell me the Āyurveda, which destroys the diseases of men, horses, and elephants;
[tell me] the perfected medical formulations and the perfected mantras that bring the dead back to life."
Dhanvantari said:

A physician, protecting the strength of one afflicted by fever, should cause him to eat parched grain gruel (lāja-maṇḍa) with dry ginger; likewise, boiled water that has ended the thirst and fever [should be given].
After six days have passed, one should certainly have him drink a bitter decoction made of *mustā*, *parpaṭaka*, *uśīra*, *candana*, *udīcya*, and *nāgara*;
thereafter, one should cause him to undergo purgation.
Old ṣaṣṭika rice, nīvāra, red śāli, and pramodaka—
these and similar preparations are desired in cases of fever, as are preparations of barley,
as well as mung beans, lentils, ṇaka beans, horse gram, and kuṣṭha.
//AP_278.006cd/:n 1 "The matured humors," thus [it is said in] Ña..
Āṭakyā, the various types of *nāraka*, *karkoṭaka*, *katolvaka*,
*paṭola* with its fruit, *nimba*, *parpaṭa*, and pomegranate [are used]; in fever,
emesis is recommended when the doshas move downward, and purgation when they move upward.
In cases of *raktapitta*, the six-fold drink (*ṣaḍaṅga*) should be taken without ginger; likewise,
parched grains of barley, wheat, and rice, along with roasted paddy,
lentils, *kuṣṭha*, chickpeas, green gram, and wheat-based foods, are beneficial as edibles.
Ghee and milk prepared with honey, *vṛṣa* juice, and honey are beneficial; likewise,
the consumption of aged *śāli* rice is recommended in cases of diarrhea,
as is food that does not cause internal secretions when combined with the bark of *lodhra*.
One should avoid exposure to the wind with great effort; in all cases of abdominal tumors (gulma), one should eat vāṭya with milk and vāstūka seasoned with ghee.
Furthermore, wheat, śāli rice, and bitter vegetables are beneficial for those suffering from abdominal enlargements (jaṭhara).
Wheat, rice, mung beans, the *brahmarkṣa* tree, khadira, abhayā,
the five spices (*pañcakola*), meat from wild animals, neem, āmalaka, patola, the juice of citron, nutmeg, dried radish, and rock salt.
Likewise, for those suffering from skin diseases (kuṣṭha), water boiled with khadira is recommended for drinking;
for gruel, lentils and mung beans are advised, as well as aged śāli rice; and for soups, the meat broth of wild animals served with vegetables such as nimba and parpaṭaka is likewise prescribed.
Viḍaṅga, marica, musta, kuṣṭha, lodhra, suvarcikā,
and manaḥśilā, along with vāleya, ground with urine, destroy skin diseases; likewise,
apūpa cakes, kulmāṣa, barley, and similar foods are beneficial for those suffering from urinary disorders.
Preparations of barley, mung beans, horse gram, and aged rice;
bitter and dry vegetables, and bitter greens. (278.17cd–278.18ab)

Oils derived from sesame, śigruka, vibhītaka, and iṅguda; mung beans along with barley and wheat; grain that has been stored for a year; and the broth of wild game are recommended for consumption by those suffering from rājayakṣman.
One may eat *kaulattha* or *maudga* beans prepared with *rāsnā*, dried radish, and meat from wild animals;
or with cakes (*pūpa*) or *viskara* preparations, cooked with curd and pomegranate,
and seasoned with the juice of *mātuluṅga*, honey, grapes, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), and other such ingredients.
One should feed the patient suffering from dyspnea and cough with barley, wheat, and rice.
Gruels, flour-based drinks, meat soups, and decoctions prepared with the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *balā*, *rāsnā*, and horse gram (*kulattha*) are remedies that ward off dyspnea and hiccups.
One suffering from swelling should consume aged barley, wheat, or *śāli* rice along with dried radish, horse gram (*kaulattha*), and the meat-juice of wild animals, together with *uśīra*.
Alternatively, one may eat *pathyā* (chebulic myrobalan) with jaggery, or jaggery with ginger.
Buttermilk and *citraka* both destroy diseases of the *grahaṇī*.
Old barley, wheat, and *śāli* rice, the meat-broth of wild animals (*jaṅgala*), as well as mung beans, *āmalaka*, dates, grapes, and jujubes [are likewise beneficial].
Honey, clarified butter, milk, Śakra, Nimba, Parpaṭaka, Vṛṣa,
and fermented preparations of buttermilk (takrāriṣṭas) are recommended for those suffering from wind disorders (vāta-roga).

Those suffering from heart disease should be purged; long peppers (pippalī) are beneficial for those with hiccupping. Buttermilk, balā, rock salt, and pearls dissolved in cold water [are recommended].
Pearls, sauvarcala salt, ajamoda, and so forth, as well as wine, are prescribed for alcoholism (madātyaya).
A person suffering from chest wounds should drink lac along with honey and milk.
2. *sadāmaye* is the reading of Ña; *damātyaye* is the reading of Ṭa:
One may overcome the depletion caused by a diet of meat broth by protecting the digestive fire;
for food, one should eat red *śāli* rice, wild *nīvāra*, *kalama*, and other grains;
as well as preparations of barley, meat, vegetables, *sauvarcala* salt, and *śaṭī*.

Likewise, *pathyā* (harītakī) is beneficial for hemorrhoids; as is the scum of boiled rice mixed with buttermilk and water. Furthermore, a plaster made from *mustā*, *citraka*, and *haridrā*, along with preparations of barley, *śāli* rice, *vāstūka*, and *suvarcalā*, are recommended.
Cucumber, gourd, and wheat, combined with milk, sugarcane juice, and ghee,
as well as thin gruel, wine, and other such drinks, are recommended for consumption in cases of dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra).
Likewise, parched grain, flour, honey, meat, and parūṣaka fruit are beneficial.
Foods that soothe the digestive fire, such as those prepared with vārtāku, and drinks that suppress vomiting;
Śāli rice with water or milk—either plain and warm, or boiled;
or a pill made of musta and jaggery held in the mouth to quell thirst.
Preparations of barley, cakes,
dried radish, and likewise vegetables such as patola and the tips of vetra stalks destroy urinary obstruction.

One should consume old wheat, barley, and *śāli* rice along with soups made from *mudga*, *āḍhaka*, and *masūra* lentils, combined with sesame, the juices of wild animals, rock salt, ghee, grapes, ginger, *āmalaka*, and *kola*. AP_278.037ab
For one suffering from erysipelas (*visarpa*), a drink consisting of grapes, pomegranate, and molasses mixed with sugar and honey is beneficial;
likewise, light foods such as red *yaṣṭikā*, wheat, barley, and mung beans;
and *kākamārī*, the tips of reeds, *vāstuka*, and *suvarcalā*.

For the destruction of *vātaśoṇita* (blood disorders caused by wind), white water mixed with honey is recommended; likewise, *pathyā*, the scum of *kāśa* gruel, buttermilk, and *vāruṇa* soup [are beneficial].
Ghee prepared with *dūrvā* grass is beneficial for diseases of the nose;
likewise, oil prepared in the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* or in the juice of *dhātrī* is also effective.

O Brahmin, fasting is desired for all diseases as well as for those arising from parasites in the head; likewise, the consumption of sesame seeds along with cold water and food is said to strengthen the teeth and provide supreme satisfaction.
A mouthful of sesame oil is the supreme means for strengthening the teeth;
powdered *viḍaṅga* with cow’s urine is effective everywhere for destroying worms;
furthermore, *dhātrī* fruits and clarified butter applied as a head-ointment are excellent.
For the destruction of diseases of the head, one should take unctuous and warm food; likewise,
oil or goat’s urine as an ear-drop is excellent for destroying earache, O twice-born one, or alternatively, all kinds of fermented acids (śukta).
Girimṛc-candana, lac, and jasmine buds—
when these are combined and made into a wick, it removes blood and semen from wounds.
Likewise, vyoṣa joined with triphalā, tucchaka, and water [are used for the same purpose].

Likewise, *rasāñjana* ground on a stone and fried in clarified butter, combined with *lodhra*, sour gruel (*kāñjika*), and rock salt, is beneficial for all eye diseases when used as an eye-drop (*āścyotana*) to eliminate them. It pacifies all disorders of the eyes.
An ointment made from mountain clay and sandalwood is recommended for external application to the eyes;
one who desires to live a long life should always practice the use of *triphalā* to destroy eye diseases, taking it at night with honey and clarified butter.
Milk and ghee prepared with the juice of śatāvarī are known to be aphrodisiacs;
likewise, milk and ghee prepared with kalambikā and mung beans are also aphrodisiacs.
Triphalā, when combined with madhuka as before, should be known as "all-white" (sarvaśuklā), which promotes longevity; thus it is stated in Kha...:p 32. AP_278.050cd.

O Brahmin, ghee prepared with *vacā* and the juices of the *madhuka* group destroys wrinkles and graying hair; it is an oblation that destroys the defects caused by malevolent spirits and bestows intelligence.
Likewise, an ointment prepared with the decoction of *valā* paste accomplishes all purposes; it is beneficial for massage.
Alternatively, oil prepared with *rāsnā* and *sahacara* is for those suffering from disorders of wind (*vāta*).

Food that does not cause secretions is recommended for wounds. Likewise, a bolus of roasted flour (śaktupiṇḍī) and sour substances are recommended for promoting suppuration. Furthermore, neem powder (nimbacūrṇa) is used for breaking up a suppurated wound and for healing it.
Likewise, the treatment of wounds with needles (2), the performance of special bali offerings, and the protection of women in childbirth are always beneficial for living beings.
Eating neem leaves is the remedy for one bitten by a snake;
a fumigation of palmyra leaves, neem leaves, hair, old oil, and barley-clarified butter,
or alternatively with peacock feathers and clarified butter, is for one bitten by a scorpion.
A plaster made from the seeds of the *palāśa* tree ground with the milk of the *arka* plant;
or black pepper (*kṛṣṇā*) combined with the fruit of the *śivā* tree for one afflicted by a scorpion sting; or equal parts of *arka* milk, sesame, oil, minced meat (*palala*), and jaggery.
By drinking it, one quickly overcomes even the most difficult-to-restrain dog venom;
likewise, by drinking the root of *taṇḍulīya* mixed with an equal amount of *trivṛt* and ghee,
one swiftly conquers even the most powerful poisons of snakes and insects.
Sandalwood, padmaka, kuṣṭha, latā, ambu, uśīra,
and pāṭalā are beneficial for the throat and indeed bestow growth.
2. And with the secondary offerings (pratyupacāra)—thus [in] Kha;
3. "Joined with the jar" (kalasaṃyutā)—thus [in] Ka.
Nirguṇḍī, śārivā, and selu constitute a remedy that destroys the poison of spiders;
O twice-born one, a head-purgative (śirovirecana) consisting of jaggery and ginger is recommended.
Likewise, for internal oleation and enemas, oil and clarified butter (ghṛta) are unsurpassed.
Fire is the supreme agent for inducing perspiration; cold water is the supreme agent for checking it.
Trivṛt is the best for purgation, and likewise, Madana is the best for emesis. Enema, purgation, emesis, oil, clarified butter, and honey [are likewise recommended].
The supreme medicine for wind, bile, and phlegm, respectively.
Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "Efficacious Medicines," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 279:
Medicines that Cure All Diseases
Dhanvantari said:
Diseases are considered to be bodily, mental, accidental, and innate.
Bodily diseases are fever, leprosy, and so forth; mental diseases are considered to be anger and the like.
Adventitious afflictions arise from external causes, while those born together with the body include hunger, old age, and so forth.
To destroy both physical and adventitious ailments, one should offer ghee, molasses, salt, gold, and a cake to a Brahmin on a Sunday.

If an oil-anointing is given to a Brahmin during the Moon [transit], one is liberated from all diseases. During the transit of Saturn, one should give oil; during Āśvina, one should give food with cow's milk.
By bathing the Liṅga with ghee and milk, one shall be freed from disease.
One should cause oblations to be offered into the fire with the Gāyatrī mantra, using *dūrvā* grass soaked in the three sweets;
on whichever lunar mansion one contracts a disease, on that [mansion] a bath and an offering should be performed for auspiciousness.
The hymn to Viṣṇu brings relief from mental ailments such as pain;
now listen likewise to the humors—wind, bile, and phlegm—and the bodily constituents.
O Suśruta, food that has been eaten passes from the stomach in two ways.
By one part it becomes dross, and by the other part it attains the state of essence (*rasa*).
The portion that is dross constitutes the waste therein: feces, urine, sweat, and rheum of the eyes;
as well as the mucus of the nose, earwax, and whatever bodily impurities there may be.
From the portion of the essence (*rasa*), the essence there becomes blood;
from blood comes flesh, from flesh fat, and from fat the formation of bone;
from bone marrow, from that semen, and from semen passion as well as vitality (*ojas*).
Having understood the region, the affliction, the strength, the capacity, the time, and the constitution, one should administer medical treatment according to the power of the medicine; likewise,
one should avoid the empty lunar days (riktās), the last day of the fortnight, Tuesday, and planets that are slow, dull, red, or fierce.
Having duly worshipped Hari, the cows, the twice-born, the moon, the sun, the gods, and others, O learned one, listen to this mantra; then one should undertake the preparation of the medicine:
"Brahmā, Dakṣa, the Aśvins, Rudra, Indra, Earth, Moon, Sun, Wind, and Fire..."
May the sages, the multitude of medicinal herbs, and the hosts of beings protect you; may this be for you as an elixir for the seers, as nectar for the gods,
and as the finest wine for the supreme Nāgas— may it be a medicine for you.

A region characterized by wind and phlegm, abounding in trees and water, is known as *anūpa*; a *jāṅgala* region is the opposite of that. A region with a moderate amount of trees and water is likewise considered *sādhāraṇa*.
The Jāṅgala region is known as moderate, characterized by an abundance of pitta;
its wind is dry, cold, and mobile, while its pitta is hot, and its pungent triad (kaṭutraya) is likewise hot.
They declare that [phlegm] is stable, sour, unctuous, sweet, and increases with strength;
their increase occurs through similar factors, while the opposite occurs through contrary ones.
The tastes—sweet, sour, and salty—are phlegm-provoking and destroyers of wind (vāyu).
Pungent, bitter, and astringent [tastes] increase wind (*vāta*) and destroy phlegm (*śleṣman*);
pungent, sour, and salty [tastes] should be known to likewise increase bile (*pitta*). Bitter, sweet, and astringent [tastes], on the other hand, destroy bile.
This is not a quality of the taste (*rasa*), but is held to be a property of the post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*).

Furthermore, O Suśruta, they perform their actions through their potency (*vīrya*) and their specific inherent power (*prabhāva*): those that are hot in potency destroy phlegm (*kapha*) and wind (*vāta*), while those that are cold destroy bile (*pitta*).
In the cold season, the spring, and likewise in the summer, the accumulation,
provocation, and pacification of phlegm are proclaimed respectively.
O Suśruta, [these also occur] in the summer, the rainy season, the night, and likewise in autumn.
The accumulation, provocation, and pacification of *vāyu* are proclaimed to occur respectively during the rainy season,
autumn, and early winter;
likewise, the accumulation, provocation, and pacification of *pitta* are proclaimed to occur in the same sequence.
The period beginning with the rainy season is emission (*visarga*), while those beginning with the winter season are likewise three;
similarly, the period beginning with the cool season is withdrawal (*ādāna*), consisting of the three seasons ending with summer.
Emission is proclaimed to be lunar (*saumya*), whereas withdrawal is fiery (*āgneya*).
Moving through the three seasons beginning with the rains, Soma produces the three tastes— sour, salty, and sweet— in their respective order;
moving through the three seasons beginning with the cool season, the Sun likewise produces the [other] tastes.
Likewise, one should gradually increase the bitter, astringent, and pungent [flavors],
so that as the nights increase, strength indeed increases accordingly.
Then, as the lifespan of human beings gradually diminishes, the duration of nights, the number of days, and likewise the span of life itself decrease.
At the beginning, middle, and end [of this period], phlegm, bile, and wind [predominate].
Their accumulation is said to occur during the period preceding their provocation;
their pacification is proclaimed to occur in the period following that provocation.
O Brahmin, this happens through excessive eating as well as through fasting.
For all diseases arise from the suppression of natural urges.
One should fill two parts of the stomach with food, one part with drink,
and likewise leave one part remaining as space for the movement of wind and other bodily humors.
Likewise, medicine that is contrary to the cause of the disease must be administered;
this alone is proclaimed by me here as the essential point.
[One should avoid] above the navel, below it, and likewise in the anus and the hips.
The locations of phlegm, bile, and wind within the body have been proclaimed;
nevertheless, these are all-pervasive throughout the body, with wind being especially so.
The heart is situated in the center of the body, and that is remembered as the seat of the mind.
One who is emaciated, has sparse hair, is fickle, talkative, possesses a turbulent digestive fire,
and likewise travels through the sky in dreams, is said to have a wind (vāta) constitution.
One who has premature gray hair, is prone to anger, perspires easily, and is fond of sweets [is said to have a bile (pitta) constitution].
One who sees radiant things in dreams is said to be of a pitta constitution;
whereas a man of a kapha constitution has firm limbs, a steady mind, a bright complexion, glossy hair, and sees pure water in his dreams.
O tiger among sages, humans are traditionally known to be of the nature of *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva*, and are composed of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*).
From sexual intercourse, from the performance of heavy labors,
from eating poor food, and from grief, the wind (vāyu) becomes provoked in the body;
likewise for those who consume burning foods, those who frequent fires, and those who travel on hot roads.

O twice-born one, bile (pitta) becomes provoked by fear; likewise, it is provoked in those who drink excessive water, eat heavy food, or sleep immediately after eating. Similarly, phlegm (śleṣman) becomes provoked in those people who are indolent.
Having recognized diseases arising from wind (vāta) and other humors through their symptoms, they are to be pacified:
breaking pain in the bones, an astringent taste in the mouth, dryness of the mouth,
yawning, and horripilation are the characteristics of a disease caused by vāta.
Yellowing of the nails, eyes, and veins, a pungent taste in the mouth, thirst, burning sensations, and heat are the indicators of a disease of *pitta*.
Furthermore, lassitude, excessive salivation, heaviness, and a sweet taste in the mouth [are also signs].
A desire for warmth is a characteristic of diseases caused by *śleṣman* (phlegm).
Unctuous and warm food, massage with oil, drinking oil, and so forth, alleviate *vāta*.
Clarified butter (*ājya*), milk, sugar and the like, and exposure to moonlight and similar cooling influences alleviate *pitta*.
Triphalā oil with honey, physical exercise and other such activities that remove phlegm,
as well as meditation on Viṣṇu and His worship, shall lead to the pacification of all diseases.
Thus ends the section on medicines that cure all diseases in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter two hundred and eighty-three:
[Regarding] meteors, heat, and those who travel on the path— thus [it is said] in the Kha manuscript,
folio 38.
Chapter 280:
[The Two Hundred and Eightieth Chapter]
Dhanvantari spoke on the characteristics of taste and so forth:
"I shall describe the characteristics of taste; listen to the qualities of medicinal substances."
A man who knows the tastes, potencies, and post-digestive effects should protect the king and others.
O mighty-armed one, the tastes—sweet, sour, and salty—are proclaimed to be born of Soma; likewise, pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes are fiery (āgneya).
The transformation of a substance is threefold, consisting of pungent, sour, and salty;
its potency is declared to be twofold, namely hot and cold;
and the specific power (*prabhāva*) of medicinal herbs, O best of the twice-born, is indescribable.
The sweet, the astringent, and likewise the bitter taste are declared to have a cooling potency; the remaining tastes are proclaimed to be hot.
In that regard, O giver of honor, although guḍūcī is bitter, it is hot due to its extreme potency;
likewise, although pathyā is astringent, it is hot;
and similarly, although meat is sweet, it is proclaimed to be hot indeed.

Lavaṇa (salt) and madhura (sweet) are traditionally held to have a sweet post-digestive effect (*vipāka*); the sour (*amla*) is likewise said to be hot, while the remaining [tastes] have a pungent post-digestive effect.
When there is a discrepancy between the potency (*vīrya*) and the post-digestive effect, certainty in that matter is reached through the specific power (*prabhāva*).
That which is proclaimed as honey is sweet but pungent in its digestion;
one should boil [the drug] in sixteen times the quantity of water until it remains four times the quantity of the substance.
Barley and honey (yavakṣaudra).
This is the rule for a decoction where no specific method has been stated:
the decoction water should be four times the amount of the fat;
having extracted the medicinal substance equal in weight to the fat, the wise physician should then add the fat.
One should then add a quarter-part of oil relative to the quantity of the medicinal substances;
whatever substance is used, it should likewise be an oily substance.
This is proclaimed as the method for cooking oils when the medicinal herbs have been combined.
But the consistency of a linctus (lehya) is equal to that [of a decoction], O Suśruta;
a clear decoction with few medicinal ingredients shall be as previously described.
One *akṣa* is prescribed for a powder (*cūrṇa*), and four *palas* for a decoction (*kaṣāya*).
This is considered the moderate dose; there is no fixed calculation for the dose.

O highly fortunate one, the determination of the dose should be made by carefully considering the age, the season, the strength, the digestive fire, the location, the substance, and likewise the disease.
In that regard, tastes are generally to be known as mild (*saumya*) and nourishers of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*);
sweet tastes, in particular, are to be known as nourishers of the constituents.
Furthermore, a substance whose qualities are equal to those of both the humors (*doṣa*) and the constituents is [beneficial].
That same [practice] should be known as leading to increase when done correctly, while the opposite brings about decline.
O best of men, these three supports have been declared for this body:
food, sexual intercourse, and sleep; one should always apply effort toward them.
Through non-cultivation and cultivation, [the body] may undergo absolute destruction. Nourishing that which is emaciated, reducing that which is corpulent,
and protecting the moderate body— these are considered the three types of bodily management.
1. And in the cooking of medicated oils (*sneha-pāka*), it possesses those same qualities;
2. its similarity is such that it becomes just as [described] by Suśruta.
Two types of therapeutic procedures (upakrama) have been taught: satiation (tarpaṇa) and non-satiation (atarpaṇa).
Furthermore, one should be a consumer of wholesome food, a consumer of moderate food, and likewise a consumer of digested food.

O best of men, there are five ways of preparing medicinal herbs: as a juice (*rasa*), a paste (*kalka*), a decoction (*śṛta*), a cold infusion (*śīta*), and a warm infusion (*phāṇḍa*). Juice should be known as that which is pressed out; a paste arises from what has been stirred.

That which is boiled is known as *śṛta*; that which has stood overnight is *śīta*; and that which is strained immediately after being boiled is called *phāṇṭa*. One hundred and sixty instruments are traditionally recorded.
He who knows this shall indeed be invincible; one should be well-versed in the science of relationships.
For the sake of the digestive fire, one should maintain purity of food, for the strength of men is rooted in the fire.
O virtuous queen, one should consume *triphalā* with rock salt, which bestows a healthy complexion.
A person with a predominance of wind (vāta) should prepare meat broth from wild game mixed with rock salt, curd, milk, and long pepper, making the liquid portion equal to the other ingredients;
massage is prescribed during the summer, while in the winter it should be moderate or abundant.
In spring, it should be known that [the massage] is moderate; in the summer heat, it is intense and crushing.
First, the skin is to be massaged, and immediately thereafter the limbs.
When the sinews, blood, and body [are reached], the bone appears as if it were full of flesh.
Likewise, the wise man should massage the shoulders, the arms, as well as the shanks together with the knees;
he should rub the collarbones and the chest as before,
and likewise exert great pressure upon all the joints of the limbs.
One should stretch the joints of the limbs, but neither by force nor out of sequence. A person should not exert himself when exhausted, nor after eating or drinking.
This should be done during the fourth part of the day, specifically in the latter half of the third watch.
One should not engage in physical exertion at all; one may bathe once with cold water, and warm water will remove fatigue. One should not suppress the breath held in the heart.
Physical exercise destroys phlegm (kapha), while massage destroys wind (vāta).

Bathing destroys an excess of bile (pitta), and after it, exposure to the sun is pleasant. Men who perform wholesome exercise at the beginning of activities that cause heat and fatigue [attain health].
Thus ends the two hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Taste and Other Qualities," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 281:
The Science of Arboriculture (Vṛkṣāyurveda)
Dhanvantari said:
I shall proclaim the Ayurveda of trees: a Plakṣa tree is auspicious in the north, a Vaṭa in the east, a mango tree in the south, and an Aśvattha in the west according to its ritual application.
In the southern direction, thorny trees have grown nearby;
there may be a garden in one's household residence,
or sesame seeds, or flowers in bloom.
One should take up and plant trees after having worshipped a twice-born man and the moon;
for the planting of trees, the constellations Dhruva, Vāyavya, Hasta, Prājāpatya, Vaiṣṇava, and likewise Mūla, are recommended.
One should cause the currents of rivers to enter, and have lotus ponds constructed.
Hasta, Maghā, Anurādhā, Puṣya, Jyeṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj,
and the three Uttarās are auspicious for the commencement of constructing reservoirs.
Having worshipped Varuṇa, Viṣṇu, and Parjanya, one should perform that rite.
[The trees used are] Ariṣṭa, Aśoka, Punnāga, Śirīṣa, along with Priyaṅgu;
as well as Aśoka, Kadalī, Jambu, Vakula, and Dāḍima.
Planted trees should be watered in the evening and morning during the hot season, on alternate days during the cold season, and whenever the ground dries up during the rainy season and at night.
The distance between them should be twenty cubits for the best variety and sixteen cubits for the middling variety.

One should move the trees from one place to another at least twelve times; otherwise, the trees will become fruitless. First, they must be cleared with a weapon, then smeared with a paste of *viḍaṅga* and ghee, and finally sprinkled with cold water.
In the event of the loss of fruit, one should always sprinkle with *kulattha*, black gram (*māsa*), green gram (*mudga*), barley, and sesame seeds,
using water mixed with ghee and cooled milk for the sake of fruit and flowers.
One should also apply the powder of sheep and goat dung, barley flour, and sesame seeds.

One should cause beef and water to remain for seven nights; sprinkling this upon all trees brings about an increase in fruits, flowers, and the like. By sprinkling with fish-water, the growth of the branched trees is likewise achieved.
Fish and meat combined with *viḍaṅga* seeds and rice-grains indeed satisfy the pregnancy-longing (*dohada*) for all trees without distinction and destroy their diseases;
thus ends the *Vṛkṣāyurveda* in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The two hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "Nāma."
Chapter Two Hundred and Eighty-Two.
Dhanvantari spoke of medicinal herbs that cure various diseases: one should consume a decoction of *siṃhī*, *śaṭī*, the two types of *niśā* (turmeric and black turmeric), and *vatsaka*.
This is recommended for all types of diarrhea in children and for disorders of the breast milk.
One should lick a powder of *śṛṅgī*, *kṛṣṇā*, and *ativiṣā* with honey;
furthermore, *ativiṣā* alone removes cough, vomiting, and fever in a child.
Vaca, taken with ghee or milk, or mixed with oil, should be used by children;
or a child should drink Yaṣṭikā or Śaṅkhapuṣpī combined with milk.
Thus, the child's speech, physical form, lifespan, intelligence, and prosperity increase.
In the morning, a child should drink for the sake of increasing intelligence a decoction of vacā, agniśikhā, vāsā, śuṇṭhī, kṛṣṇā, niśā, gada, yaṣṭi, and saindhava;
or [a decoction] of devadāru, mahāśigru, the three myrobalans (phalatraya), and payomuc.
A decoction of Pippalī with a paste of Mṛdvīkā removes all types of worms.
Sprinkling [the child] with the juices of Triphalā, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Viśvā, along with honey, ghee, ewe’s milk, and cow’s urine, is beneficial for a child suffering from disease.
In this case, the juice of *dūrvā* grass used as a nasal drop (*nasya*) is excellent for removing blood from the nose; likewise,
the juice of garlic, ginger, and *śigru*, or oil prepared with ginger and *jātī*, when used as an ear-drop, removes earache.
Regarding "siṃhī" and "ṣaṣṭī," [it is noted that] in the phrase "śūlahā," the masculine designation is an archaic usage (ārṣa).
3. It removes urine-retention and cures wasting diseases (śoṣa).
[End of page 44] Jātī leaves, its fruit, the three pungents (vyoṣa), a gargle, cow’s urine, and niśā.
Oil prepared with a decoction of milk and a paste of *abhayā* removes the affliction of the teeth.
For the pacification of the disease of the epiglottis (*adhijihvā*), one should prepare a gargle by boiling together paddy-water, coconut water, cow’s urine, *kramūka*, and *viśva*.
Oil prepared with the paste of *lāṅgalī* and the juice of *nirguṇḍikā*,
when administered as nasal drops (*nasya*), destroys *gaṇḍamālā* and *galagaṇḍa*.
[One should also use] the sprouts of *arka*, *pūtīka*, *snuhī*, *rugghāta*, and *jātī*.
One should perform anointment with cow’s urine using [substances] that destroy all skin disorders. Vākucī taken with sesame seeds destroys leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) within a year.
A bolus of *pathyā*, *bhallātaka*, oil, and jaggery, however, conquers leprosy.

Buttermilk mixed with the powder of *pūtīka*, *vahni*, turmeric, *triphalā*, and *vyoṣa* should be drunk for hemorrhoids; or *abhayā* with jaggery should be eaten; or else a decoction of *phala*, *dārvī*, and *viṣāṇā*, or the juice of *dhātrī*.
A paste of *rajanī* mixed with honey should be drunk by one suffering from *akṣaudra-prameha*;
likewise, a decoction of *vyādhighātaka* containing *vāsā* combined with castor oil should be drunk to remove *vāta-śoṇita*. Pippalī, when consumed, destroys the spleen disease (*plīhā*).
One suffering from abdominal enlargement (jaṭharin) should consume black iron powder (kṛṣṇā) that has been repeatedly saturated with the milky sap of the snuhī plant;
or, milk mixed with the paste of rājādana, agni, viḍaṅga, and vyoṣa;
or, pippalī, ugrā, abhayā, and kṛṣṇā, smeared with viḍaṅga and kept in ghee.

A decoction of the three fruits (*phalatraya*), *amṛtā*, *vāsā*, and *tiktabhūnimba* removes chronic fever, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), hemorrhoids, anemia (*pāṇḍu*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and worms;
likewise, that same decoction mixed with honey cures anemia accompanied by jaundice (*kāmalā*).
One suffering from *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders) should drink the juice of *vāsā* with sugar and honey;
or alternatively, milk boiled separately with *varī*, *drākṣā*, *balā*, and *śuṇṭhī*.
One suffering from consumption (kṣayaroga) should lick a mixture of varī, vidārī, pathyā, the three types of balā, and vāsaka, combined with śvadaṃṣṭrā, honey, and ghee.
Alternatively, one should take the bark and pith of pathyā, śigru, karañja, and arka, combined with honey and sea salt.
This formulation destroys fistula-in-ano and abscesses, and according to the experts in the treatises, it brings about their ripening.
A plaster consisting of *trivṛt*, *jīvatī*, *dantī*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, the two types of *śarvarī*, *tārkṣaja* (guggulu), and neem leaves is recommended for hemorrhoids (*bhagaṇdara*).
A wick made of cloth and combined with *rugghāta*, blue lac, powder, goat’s milk, and honey should be applied to a wound; it is purifying and destroys [excessive] discharge.
[Likewise, a wick may be prepared] with *śyāmā*, *iṣṭi*, *niśā*, *lodhra*, *padmaka*, blue lotus, and sandalwood.
Oil boiled with black pepper in milk serves as a healer for wounds.
Ashes from the leaves of the auspicious cotton tree (*karpāsa*), along with *phala*, *upala*, salt, and turmeric (*niśā*),
made into a paste and heated in a copper vessel with oil, is a remedy for injuries.
One should apply the essence of *kumbhī* mixed with milk and burnt with fire to a wound;

that very same [essence], when used as a wash with coconut powder and ghee, will destroy it. Equal parts of *viṣā*, *ajamoda*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), and the bark of *ciñcā*, together with *abhayā*, [should be used].
Water boiled with *vatsaka*, *ativiṣā*, *viśva*, *bilva*, and *musta* should be administered with buttermilk or warm water to destroy diarrhea caused by undigested matter (*āma*).
It should be given for chronic diarrhea accompanied by *āma* and for colic associated with *āma*.
One suffering from colic (śūla) should drink the *sugata* ashes burnt with charcoal dissolved in warm *sindhu* water; indeed, that same preparation, combined with *hiṅgu*, *kaṇā*, and *abhayā*,
and saturated with honey, [is likewise effective].
*kaṭurohā*, *utpalātaṅka*, and powdered parched rice (*lāja-cūrṇa*). (Ta...
A cloth soaked in a decoction of *pāṭhā*,
*āragvadha*, *jāti* leaves, grapes, and the three fruits (*triphalā*), applied to the mouth,
destroys thirst; this same decoction, prepared with honey and used as a gargle (*kavala*), removes diseases of the mouth.
A decoction of *kṛṣṇā*, *ativiṣā*, *tiktā*, *indrā*, *dāru*, *pāṭhā*, and *payomuc*, boiled in urine and mixed with honey, removes all diseases of the throat.
[Likewise, a preparation] of *pathyā*, *gokṣura*, *duḥsparśa*, *rājavṛkṣa*, and *śilājatu*... AP 282.034ab.
A decoction of *kaṣāya* drunk with honey removes dysuria;
a decoction of bamboo bark and *varuṇa* destroys gravel and stones;
and one who eats milk with a decoction of *śākhoṭaka* becomes free from elephantiasis.
Milk and oil from the bark of the *arka* tree mixed with honey and rock salt,
as well as ghee prepared with *jālakukkuṭa*, removes diseases of the feet; likewise,
ghee processed with the powder of ginger, *sīvarcalā*, and asafoetida along with ginger juice [is effective].
Know that this decoction removes pain and is effective for curing suppressed digestive fire.
A patient suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma) should drink buttermilk mixed with the juices of *sauvarcala*, *agni*, and *hiṅgu* along with *dīpyaka*, or combined with *viḍa* salt and *dīpyaka*.
A decoction of *dhātrī*, *paṭola*, and *mudga* with ghee cures erysipelas (*visarpa*).
Another remedy is a decoction of *śuṇṭhī*, *dāruharidrā*, and *akṣa* combined with urine.
Furthermore, a decoction of the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), iron filings (*ayorajas*), alkali (*kṣāra*), and *phala* removes swelling (*śotha*).
Jaggery, *śigru*, and *trivṛt* combined with the powder of rock salt,
or a decoction of *trivṛt* fruits mixed with jaggery, acts as a purgative.
Milk boiled with a decoction of *vacā* and *phala* (emetic nut) produces emesis.
One hundred palas of the three myrobalans (triphalā), each separately saturated with the juice of bhṛṅgarāja,
[should be taken] together with grapes, immortality fruit (mṛtaphala), and the three myrobalans.
Viḍaṅga and iron powder, combined in ten parts,
along with one hundred and twenty palas each of śatāvarī, guḍūcī, and agni.
One who licks [this] with honey, ghee, and sesame paste shall be free from wrinkles and grey hair;
indeed, such a person shall live for a hundred years, devoid of all diseases. Triphalā, when combined with honey and sugar, destroys all diseases.
Sugar, honey, and ghee combined with black pepper and the three myrobalans (triphalā), as well as the powders of harītakī, citraka, ginger, guḍūcī,
and muṣalī, when consumed along with jaggery, remove all diseases and grant a lifespan of three hundred years.
If one releases a small amount of powdered *javā* flower mixed with oil into water,
it will take on the appearance of ghee; likewise, a small amount of powder combined with water is seen as a wonderful incense when prepared with the placenta of a cat.
Furthermore, by means of the smoke of honey, he is seen just as before;
having ground [the root] of the *pāṭali* tree and smeared it upon both feet, a man may walk upon glowing coals.
Having arranged displays such as the rising of grass and so forth, he shows his wonder-working power,

which destroys the effects of poison, planetary afflictions, and diseases, as well as minor charms and desired objects; that is declared to be your sixfold activity, which rests upon two types of accomplishment.

Wherein mantras, meditations, medicinal herbs, discourses, mudrās, and worship are the secret methods, and the fruit of which is declared to be the fourfold aims of life— he who recites this shall go to heaven.
Thus ends [the section] titled "Medicinal Herbs that Cure Various Diseases" in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The two hundred and eighty-second chapter.
[Variant readings: 1. "Twenty-five" in manuscripts Ña and Ṭa; 2. "Camphor and *jahu-kā-taila*" in manuscript Kha.]
Camphor, nutmeg, and sesame oil:
Chapter 283.
Now begins the two hundred and eighty-third chapter,
on the description of medicinal herbs in the form of mantras;
Dhanvantari said:
The syllables beginning with Oṃ grant longevity, health, and the celestial realm.
Oṃkāra is the supreme mantra; by reciting it, one becomes immortal. Gāyatrī is the supreme mantra; by reciting it, one partakes in both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Oṃ, homage to Nārāyaṇa; this mantra accomplishes all aims. Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Vāsudeva, the giver of everything. Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Viṣṇu; this mantra and this supreme medicinal herb [are likewise effective].
By this, indeed, the gods and the asuras became possessed of splendor and free from disease;
likewise, the benefit of beings and righteousness are the great medicine.
One who practices the true Dharma is a possessor of Dharma; through these qualities, one becomes stainless.
Śrīda, Śrīṣa, Śrīnivāsa, Śrīdhara, Śrīniketana,
Śriyaḥpati, and Śrīparama— one shall obtain prosperity by means of these [names].
Kāmī, Kāmaprada, Kāma, Kāmapāla, as well as Hari,
Ānanda, and Mādhava— these indeed are the names of Hari for the sake of fulfilling desires;
and Rāma, Paraśurāma, Nṛsiṃha, and Viṣṇu likewise.
The names beginning with Trivikrama should be recited by those desiring victory;
Puruṣottama should be constantly recited by those practicing sacred knowledge (*vidyā*).
Dāmodara removes bondage, and Puṣkarākṣa cures diseases of the eyes.
Hṛṣīkeśa, the remover of fear, should be recited during the preparation of medicinal herbs; Acyuta and the Amṛta mantra [should be used] in battle for one who is unconquered.
One who desires safety should meditate on Nārasiṃha when crossing water;
one should remember the wielder of the discus, the wielder of the mace, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, and the wielder of the sword.
One should remember Nārāyaṇa at all times; Nṛsiṃha is the dispeller of all fears.
One should constantly recite the names of Garuḍadhvaja, Viṣahṛt, and Vāsudeva;
one should invoke Ananta and Acyuta when establishing grain and other goods in a dream;
and one should invoke Nārāyaṇa in the case of bad dreams, and Jalaśāyin in the event of a fire or similar calamity.
One seeking knowledge should worship Hayagrīva; one desiring a son should worship Jagatsūti; for the sake of Śauri’s purpose, one should worship Balabhadra—the single name that accomplishes all aims.
Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of Medicinal Plants in the Form of Mantras," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 284.
Now begins the two hundred and eighty-fourth chapter:
The Elixir of the Perfected Yoga for Reviving the Dead.
Dhanvantari said:
I shall further declare the perfected yogas that bring about the restoration of the dead—
divine teachings spoken by Ātreya, which crush all diseases.
Ātreya said:
In fever caused by Vāta, there should be a decoction of the five roots beginning with bilva;
or else, a purifying preparation of long pepper root, guḍūcī, or viṣvaja.
1. *vīrakārye* (in the case of a heroic deed), according to manuscript Kha; 2. *ekanāmātha sārthakam* (and then the single name is meaningful), according to manuscripts Kha and Ña; 3.
*sarvavyādhivināśakān* (the destroyers of all diseases), according to manuscript Kha.
Āmalakī, abhayā, kṛṣṇā, and vahnī are the destroyers of all fevers; so too are bilva, agnimantha, śyonāka, kāśmarya, pārī, and sthirā.
Trikaṇṭaka, pṛśniparṇī, bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārikā,
and kuśa root cure fever, indigestion, pain in the flanks, and cough; so too do guḍūcī, parpaṭī, musta, kirātatiktaka, and viśvabheṣaja.
This *pañcabhadra* is prescribed for fever caused by vāta and pitta.
A purgative decoction prepared with *trivṛt*, *viśālā*, *kaṭukā*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *āragvadha* should be drunk; it destroys all fevers.
This powder, equal in measure to sugar and combined with viḍaṅga, conquers the five types of cough.
[It is prepared] with daśamūla, śaṭī, rāsnā, pippalī, bilva, pauṣkara,
śṛṅgī, tāmalakī, bhārgī, guḍūcī, and nāgavallī.

A person should drink a decoction of barley prepared according to the prescribed method to pacify cough, heart disease, malabsorption syndrome, pain in the flanks, hiccups, and dyspnea; likewise, one may take licorice (madhuka) combined with honey, or long pepper (vipalī) mixed with sugar.
Nāgara combined with jaggery cures hiccups; the three salts (lāvaṇatraya),
kāravī, jīraka, marica, drākṣā, vṛkṣāmla, dāḍima,
sauvarcala, jaggery, and honey destroy all types of anorexia.
One should cause [the patient] to drink the juice of *śṛṅgavera* (ginger) together with honey;
it destroys loss of appetite, dyspnea, and cough, and puts an end to catarrh and phlegm.
[The paste of] *vaṭa*, *śṛṅgī*, *śilā*, *lodhra*, pomegranate, and *madhuka*, mixed with honey—
One should drink [this] with rice-water to ward off vomiting and thirst.
(Devadāru, balā, rāsnā, triphalā, vyoṣa, and padmaka— thus according to manuscript kha).
Guḍūcī, vāsaka, and lodhra, combined with pippalī and honey,
overcome blood [disorders] associated with kapha and remove thirst, cough, and fever.
Likewise, the juice of vāsaka, or the juice of copper [oxide] mixed with honey, acts similarly.

Black pepper infused with the fragrant essence of *śirīṣa* flowers is beneficial. Furthermore, *mūṣalī*, *taṇḍulīyaka*, *nirguṇḍī*, *sārivā*, *śelu*, and *raṅkola* remove all afflictions and destroy poison.
One should drink a decoction of mahauṣadha, mṛtā, kṣudrā, and puṣkara combined with kaṇā for fainting and intoxications; likewise,
one āḍhaka of ghee [should be cooked] with two palas each of hiṅgu, saurcala, and vyoṣa.
Ghee prepared with four times the amount of cow urine,
along with *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *vattā*, and *kuṣṭha*, and combined with the juice of *brāhmī*,
destroys epilepsy accompanied by insanity; it is an excellent promoter of intelligence.
Similarly, ghee prepared with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) combined with abhayā cures leprosy; likewise,
ghee processed with paṭola, triphalā, nimba, guḍūcī, dhāvanī, vṛṣa, and karañja is known as Vajraka ghee, which destroys leprosy.
One should take ten palas each of nimba, paṭola, vyāghrī, guḍūcī, and vāsaka, all finely ground;
these should be boiled in one droṇa of water until only one-quarter remains.
One should cook one *prastha* of clarified butter with an infusion of *triphalā* as its core;
this is known as *pañcatikta* ghee, which destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*),
as well as the eighty diseases born of wind (*vāta*) and the forty born of bile (*pitta*).
1. And *vaṅkola* (as in Kha, Ña, and Ca); 2. *puṣpaka* (as in Ja); 3.
*granthilodbhava* (as in Kha).
[The verse beginning with] "combined with triphalā and sugar" (as found in manuscripts Kha and Ña,
p.
52) [cures] twenty disorders arising from phlegm, such as cough, chronic rhinitis, hemorrhoids, and wounds.
Just as the sun indeed destroys darkness, this "dust of yoga" (yogarajas) destroys other [ailments];
with a decoction of *triphalā* and the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*,
one should perform the washing of wounds for the pacification of venereal sores (*upadaṃśa*).
Then one should dust it with the powder of *paṭīla* leaves, or with the powder of pomegranate shoots,
or even with the powder of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).

One should cook oil with triphalā, iron filings, yaṣṭimadhu, mārkava, utpala, and marica, along with rock salt; when used as an ointment, it cures vomiting. One should also [cook] two prasthas of mārkava juice with milk, madhuka, and utpala.
One should cook one *kuḍava* of oil [with these]; when used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), it removes graying hair.
*Nimba*, *paṭola*, *triphalā*, *guḍūcī*, *svadira*, *vṛṣa*, *bhūnimba*, *pāṭhā*, *triphalā*, *guḍūcī*, and red sandalwood—[these are the ingredients].
This pair of formulations destroys fever, leprosy, eruptive boils, and the like.
A decoction made from *paṭola*, *amṛta*, *bhūnimba*, *vāsā*, *ariṣṭaka*, and *parpaṭa*,
with *khadira* added at the end, brings about the pacification of eruptive boils and fever.
Daśamūlī, chinnaruhā, pathyā, dāru, punarnavā,
śigru, and viśvajit are beneficial for fever, abscesses, and swellings. An ointment made of madhūka and nimba leaves serves to purify wounds.
Decoctions of triphalā, khadira, dārvī, nyagrodha, atibalā, kuśā,
and the roots and leaves of nimba are beneficial for purification;
the juice of karañja, ariṣṭa, and nirguṇḍī destroys worms in ulcers.
"One might even be crushed by an elephant," so it is said in the manuscripts marked Kha and Ña,
page 53.
An ointment consisting of *dhātaki*, sandalwood, *balā*, *samaṅgā*, licorice, blue lotus,
along with *dārvī* and marrow, mixed with clarified butter, heals wounds.
Likewise, an application of *guggulu*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), the three pungents (*tryoṣa*), and *samāṃśa*, combined with clarified butter, [achieves the same].

One should consume Harītakī prepared with urine, combined with oil and salt, every morning; it removes fistula-in-ano, malignant ulcers, pain, and hemorrhoids, and it dispels diseases caused by Kapha and Vāta.
One should drink [this] with alkaline salt.
Purgation is indeed for those whose constitution is dominated by phlegm and wind; it removes the increase of phlegm.
[This is prepared] with long pepper, long pepper root, *vacā*, *citraka*, and ginger.
Or one should drink a decoction that destroys *āmavāta*.
One should drink *rāsnā*, *guḍūcī*, castor root, *devadāru*, and *mahauṣadha* for *vāta* affecting all the limbs, as well as for *sāma* conditions located in the joints, bones, and marrow.

Or one should drink a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) with water boiled with ginger (*nāgara*); a decoction of ginger and *gokṣuraka*, when consumed every morning, digests wind-related ailments and pain in the waist, destroys suffering, and alleviates illness.

By consuming for a long period the oil of *prasāraṇī* along with its roots, leaves, and branches, or the juice, paste, powder, or decoction of *guḍūcī* and *surasā*, one is liberated from *vātaśoṇita*.
One should consume either *pippalī* in increasing doses (*vardhamāna*) or *pathyā* with jaggery;
by drinking this prepared decoction, one quickly conquers *vātaśoṇita* accompanied by burning sensations.
1. "Destroying phlegm and wind" (kaphavātavināśinīm) — thus [it is read in] Ja. 2. "Trikaṭu, triphalā, and kuṣṭha" (trikaṭutriphalākuṣṭham) — thus [it is read in] Ña. 3.
"Prepared with paṭola, triphalā, abhaya, kaṭukā, and amṛta" (paṭolatriphalābhayakaṭukāmṛtasādhitam) — thus [it is read in] Kha, Cha, and Ña.
When [the fever] has become lukewarm or cold, one should administer *guggulu* with a decoction of *guḍūcī* and *triphalā*.
Balā, punarnavā, the two types of aṇḍavṛhatī, and gokṣura,
when drunk together with asafoetida and fresh ginger, immediately dispel diseases caused by wind (vāta).
One karṣa each of pippalīmūla and the five salts [should be used].

One should drink a pill the size of a *kola* fruit, composed of *pippalī*, *citraka*, *śuṇṭhī*, *triphalā*, *trivṛtā*, *vacā*, the two types of alkali (*kṣāra*), *śādvalā*, *dantī*, *svarṇakṣīrī*, and *viṣāṇikā*, mixed with *sauvīraka*.
When swelling has become suppurated, or when abdominal enlargements and similar conditions have increased, *trivṛt* is used;
milk is an excellent remover of swelling, as is *dāru*, along with *varṣābhū* and *nāgara*.
Likewise, sprinkling with a decoction of *arka*, *varṣābhū*, and *nimba* conquers swelling.

Clarified butter prepared with *vyoṣa* (the three pungents) in three times its quantity of alkaline water from *palāśa* ashes— when drunk by one who consumes it, the hemorrhoids fall away without a doubt;
likewise, salt prepared with *viśvaksenā* and *avanirguṇḍī*.
Oil prepared with four times its quantity of water and the pungent substances— viḍaṅga, anala, sindhūttha, rāsnā, agni, kṣāra, and dāru—
or with oil alone, cures gaṇḍamālā; when used as an ointment, it removes galagaṇḍa.
A decoction of *śaṭī*, *kuṭaja*, and *balā* combined with milk,
along with a paste of *payasyā*, *pippalī*, and *vāsā*, prepared [as a medicated ghee], is beneficial for *kṣaya*. [Likewise,
one should use] *vacā*, *viḍa*, *abhayā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *hiṅgu*, *kuṣṭha*, *agni*, and *dīpyaka*.

Powdered *pāṭhā*, *nikumbha*, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *agni* (citraka), prepared with water in the proportions of two, three, six, four, one, seven, and five parts respectively, when drunk, destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*), abdominal enlargement (*udara*), colic, and cough. (AP 284.056ab)
Then, in the case of burning and cold sensations,
pills made from the powder with cow’s urine destroy abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, and the like.
Vāsā, nimba, paṭola, and triphalā remove wind and bile;
one should lick viḍaṅga powder with honey to destroy worms.
Viḍaṅga, rock salt, and alkali, or even harītakī taken with urine [are also effective].
The barks of *śallakī*, *vadara*, *jambu*, *piyāla*, *āmra*, and *arjuna*,
drunk with milk and smeared with honey, separately restrain the flow of rut in elephants.
Likewise, equal parts of *bilva*, *āmra*, *ghātakī*, *pāṭhā*, *śuṇṭhī*, and *mocarasa* [achieve the same].
Yellow myrobalan (*harītakī*), when taken with jaggery and *takra*, stops even difficult-to-conquer diarrhea.
A decoction of *cāṅgerī*, *kola*, curd-water, ginger, and alkali,
combined with clarified butter, should be drunk to relieve pain from anal fissures.
Viḍaṅga, ativiṣā, musta, devadāru, pāṭhā, kaliṅgaka,
combined with marīca, destroys swelling and diarrhea;
or [it may be taken] with sugar, rock salt, and ginger, or with pippalī, honey, and jaggery.
One should eat two harītakī fruits twice [daily]; thus one shall live happily for a hundred years.
The same applies to *triphalā* combined with *pippalī*, along with honey and clarified butter. Alternatively, one may take the powder of *āmalaka* infused with that very *surasā*.
Having licked honey, ghee, and sugar combined together, a woman who desires offspring should drink milk.
Likewise, one should cook auspicious *pippalī* with equal parts of the powders of *māṣa*, *pippalī*, *śālī* rice, barley, and wheat.
Having consumed that, one should drink milk sweetened with sugar;
then, like a young sparrow, one will certainly pierce a woman ten times.
[One should also take] *samaṅgā*, *dhātakī* flowers, *lodhra*, and blue lotuses.
Three *palas* of this [substance] cure *amlapitta*;
it should be administered with milk to women to destroy *pradara*.
Vījaṅka, eraṇḍaka, madhuka, white sandalwood, the roots of the lotus and water-lily, madhuka, sugar, and sesame seeds—
this is the supreme remedy for extracting the fetus when it is being expelled.
A plaster consisting of *devadāru*, *nabha*, *kuṣṭha*, *nalada*, and *viśvabheṣaja*,
mixed with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) and oil, removes headache. (AP 284.070ab)
One should drink lukewarm *mindhūtya* strained through a cloth to relieve earache;
or one may drink separately the juices of garlic, ginger, *śigru*, or plantain;
or one should drink *balā*, *śatāvarī*, *rāsnā*, *amṛtā*, and *mairīyaka*.
Ghee prepared with triphalā is unsurpassed for destroying timira.
A person should drink ghee processed with triphalā, vyoṣa, and rock salt; it improves vision, clears the eyes, and is beneficial for the heart.
The filaments of the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), combined with the juice of cow dung,
form an illuminating pill-collyrium that cures eye diseases such as *kr̥cchra* and is beneficial for both day-blindness and night-blindness.
A decoction of nimba, stirred with a paste of yaṣṭīmadhu, vacā, kṛṣṇā seeds, and kuṭaja, is for inducing emesis;
for purgation, water boiled with yava should be given to one who has been lubricated and sweated.
If prepared otherwise, it causes weak digestion, heaviness, and loss of appetite; one should drink this powder with warm water—
it is the excellent purgative known as Nārāca, which destroys all diseases.
1. "Kṛṣṇa" according to manuscript *kha*;
2. "Kuṣṭha" according to manuscript *ña*.
3. These perfected formulations (*siddhayoga*), beginning with *pathyā*, *saindhava*, and *kuṣṭha*, which were revealed by Ātreya to the sages, [are now presented]. (AP 284.077cd)
"These [remedies] remove all diseases and are the foremost of all formulations, according to Suśruta.
Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Elixir Formulation for the Accomplishment of Reviving the Dead," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 285:
The Ocean of Kalpas (Kalpasāgara)
Dhanvantari said:
I shall now describe the Kalpāmṛtyu compound, which bestows longevity and destroys diseases;
this "Three Hundred" (triśatī) preparation, consisting of honey, ghee, triphalā, and amṛtā, should be used to eliminate ailments.
One pala, half a pala, or one karṣa of the entire triphalā,
as well as nasal drops (nasya) of bilva oil for a month, makes one a poet of five hundred [verses]; it conquers disease, untimely death, and old age— [this is] sesame.

Likewise, one should consume bhallātaka; by taking the powder of the five parts of vākūcī for six months with decoctions of khadira water, one conquers kuṣṭha, as does the powder derived from nīlakuruṇṭa.
One who consumes milk with honey or sugar and milk shall live for a hundred years;

by taking one *pala* of honey, ghee, and ginger every morning, one conquers old age and attains strength; and by drinking milk with the powder of *māṇḍūkī*, one lives free from wrinkles and grey hair.
A person who drinks a karṣa of uccaṭā with honey and milk overcomes death;
likewise, nirguṇḍī taken with honey, ghee, or milk conquers disease and death.
Regarding "oil":
one *karṣa* of *palāśa* oil should be drunk with honey for six months.

A man who subsists on milk alone for five hundred days shall live for a thousand years. One should drink the juice of *jyotiṣmatī* leaves with milk, or *triphalā* with milk; likewise, one should drink a *pala* of the powder of *śatāvarī* with honey and ghee.
Nirguṇḍī taken with honey, clarified butter, or milk conquers disease and death;

likewise, one *karṣa* of powdered *nimba* roots and five other parts (*pañcāṅga*), saturated with a decoction of *khadira* and then taken with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, conquers disease and one shall become free from fear.
One who eats *rudantikā*, ghee, honey, and milk conquers death.
By consuming the powder of *karṣa* soaked in *harītakī* and the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*,
along with ghee and honey, one attains a lifespan of three hundred years and overcomes disease.
Vārāhikā, the juice of Bhṛṅga, iron powder, and Śatāvarī with clarified butter— one Karṣa each;
[likewise] Pañcaśatī, powdered Kartarī, and Śatāvarī.
Copper that has been processed with Bhṛṅgarāja, honey, and ghee three hundred times, as well as mercury,
sulphur, and Kumārikā;
Having rubbed two *guñjā* seeds with juices, one lives for five hundred years;
with a *pala* of *aśvagandhā*, oil, clarified butter, and sugar, one lives for a hundred years;
furthermore, by drinking a *pala* of powdered *punarnavā* with honey, clarified butter, and milk, [one attains longevity].
One pala of *aśoka* powder with honey, ghee, and milk removes pain.
By using sesame oil with honey as a nasal drop (*nasya*), one gains black hair and lives for a hundred years.
Drinking one *karṣa* (or *akṣa*) of [the same] with honey, ghee, and milk, one attains a lifespan of a hundred years.
"He shall be free from disease and affliction" (ñ);
"all [this] with clarified butter" (kha).
3. *tāmrāmṛtam* (according to Kha);
4. *suratusyam* (according to Ja and Ña):
Having eaten *abhaya* with jaggery, ghee, honey, and other sweet substances,
one who consumes milk-rice will have black hair, remain free from disease, and live for five hundred years; likewise,
by drinking the powder of *palāṅkuṣmāṇḍikā* with honey, ghee, and milk.
One who eats milk-rice for a month becomes free from disease and lives for a thousand years.
A powder of *śālūka* with *bhṛṅga*, ghee, honey, and ghee makes one live for a hundred years;
an application of a karṣa of bitter gourd oil as a nasal drop makes one live for two hundred years.
Triphalā, pippalī, and śuṇṭhī, when consumed, grant a lifespan of three hundred years; the aforementioned formulation with śatāvarī produces a thousand-year life and surpassing strength;
likewise, the previous formulation with citraka, as well as that with śuṇṭhī and viḍaṅga.
It is prepared as pills, processed with the juices of iron, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *balā*, the five parts of the neem tree (*nimba-pañcaka*), *khadira*, *nirguṇḍī*, *kaṇṭakārī*, *vāsaka*,
and *varṣābhū*.
Whether with clarified butter, honey, molasses, or water, the King of Compounds (Yogarājaka), when taken with the mantra *oṃ hrūṃ saḥ*,
becomes the "Formula for Reviving the Dead," which conquers both disease and death.
Served by gods, asuras, and sages throughout the oceans of kalpas,
he taught the science of elephant medicine (*hastāyurveda*) to Pālakāpya, the king of Aṅga.
Thus ends [the section] titled "The Ocean of Kalpas" in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter Two Hundred and Eighty-Five:
Chapter {286}
Now begins the two hundred and eighty-sixth chapter on the medical treatment of elephants.
Pālakāpya said:
O Lomapāda, I shall now describe to you the characteristics and the medical treatment of elephants.
Those that have long trunks, deep breaths, great endurance,
twenty or eighteen nails, and those that exude rut during the cold season are highly praised.
Those whose right tusks are elevated and large like a rain-cloud,
and whose ears are broad with skin marked by fine spots— such elephants are to be kept; likewise, those that are dwarfed or have crooked tusks are not to be kept.
Female elephants with calves at their sides and even those elephants that are bewildered—
[if] an elephant possesses these seven qualities: color, temperament, strength, form, luster, firmness of limb, and speed, he shall be victorious in battle.
Elephants are the supreme ornament of the camp and the army;
indeed, the victory of the rulers of the earth depends upon the elephants.
And in all cases of *pākala* (elephant fever), an oil enema (*anuvāsana*) should be administered.
O kings, one should perform the processing of ghee and oil in a place free from drafts; likewise, the treatment for the aggregates (skandhas) should be carried out like that of a protector.
O twice-born one, in cases of jaundice (pāṇḍuroga), cow’s urine and ghee processed with the two types of turmeric (rajanī) [are prescribed].
In cases of constipation (*ānāha*), the administration of oil-enema is recommended for one who has been treated with oil.
For the purpose of a post-drink (*pratipāna*), *vāruṇī* wine mixed with the five salts is prescribed.
Thus spoke Dhanvantari.
2. *Mardanā* (rubbing/cleansing):
Gargles prepared with *viḍaṅga*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), the three acrids (*vyoṣa*), and rock salt (*saindhava*).

In cases of fainting, one should feed the elephant and cause it to drink honey-water. For pain in the limbs or the head, nasal medication (nasya) is highly recommended. One should treat the foot diseases of elephants with a poultice of medicated fats (sneha-puṭaka).
Afterwards, purification is prescribed with a decoction of *kalka*.
One whose body trembles should be fed with the juices of peacock, partridge, quail, and pigeon, combined with long pepper (*pippalī*) and black pepper (*marica*).

An elephant suffering from diarrhea should eat a bolus consisting of *bālabilva*, *lodhra*, and *dhātakī* mixed with sugar. For the seizing of the trunk, ghee combined with *layaṇa* should be administered as a nasal drop (*nasya*).
A gruel made from *māgadhī* and *nāgara* (ginger) prepared with *musta* should be given for *utkarṇaka*,
as well as the broth of boar meat; likewise,
[a preparation] cooked with the ten roots (*daśamūla*), horse gram (*kulattha*), sour liquids, and *kākamācī* should be administered.
Oil combined with asafoetida removes the disease of throat-obstruction (*galagraha*). One should cause [the patient] to drink clarified butter (*ghṛta*) mixed with the eight salts ground together,
or *prasannā* wine, or the boiled seed of the cucumber (*trapuṣa*) in cases of urinary obstruction (*mūtrabhaṅga*).
In cases of skin diseases, an elephant should drink a decoction of nimba or vṛṣa;
in cases of intestinal worms, cow's urine and viḍaṅga are recommended;
and milk boiled with ginger, long pepper, grapes, and sugar is beneficial.

A drink that causes the healing of wounds and consumption, as well as wholesome meat broth, and rice with mung beans combined with the three pungents (trivṛt, vyōṣa), is recommended for loss of appetite. [The following are also beneficial: trivṛt, vyōṣa, agni, dantī, arka, śyāmā, kṣīrī, ibhā, and pippalī.
With these, an unctuous preparation (sneha) that removes gulma is prepared, as well as another;
[these are administered] by means of purgation, liquefaction, massage, oleation, internal drinking of fats, and oil enemas (anuvāsana).
One should bring all these arisen discharges under control;
likewise, one should drink *yaṣṭīmadhu* with autumnal mung bean soup.
Likewise, an ointment made with *bālabilva* fruits is recommended for *phaṭūroga*.
One should cause [the patient] to drink boluses of *viḍaṅga*, *indrayava*, *hiṅgu*, *sarala*, and the two types of *rajanī* in the forenoon for the alleviation of all colic pains.
Among their principal foods are *yaṣṭikā* rice and *śāli* rice; barley and wheat are middling; the rest are inferior, as is the case for elephants.
Barley and likewise sugarcane increase the strength of elephants.
Dry barley is [prohibited] for elephants; likewise, substances that aggravate the bodily humors are forbidden.
For an elephant in rut, the drinking of milk is recommended.
Similarly, auspicious meat broth boiled with digestive stimulants is beneficial.
A crow, a dog, both a raven and an owl, and a monkey— these,
combined with honey, form a medicinal bolus for use in battle during times of great calamity. [Likewise, one may use] pungent fish, viḍaṅga, alkali, koṣātakī, and milk.
And with turmeric— this incense brings victory to the elephant.
Likewise, a sprinkling over the eyes with long pepper, rice, oil, wine, and honey is praised as a stimulant.
The excrement of a sparrow and likewise that of a pigeon,
along with the dried dung of milk-tree trees— this is the desired collyrium for clarity of vision.
1. "With mung-bean soup," according to Ja and Ña; 2. "For intoxication," according to Ña.
And the sprouts of milk-exuding trees (kṣīravṛkṣakarīra);
with these, one whose eyes are anointed brings about slaughter in battle.
Blue lotuses and *sustantagara* ground with rice-water are an excellent means for soothing the eyes.
When the nails grow long, they should be clipped and anointed with oil once a month.
His bedding and dwelling place should be made of dried cow dung and dust; likewise, sprinkling with clarified butter is desired during the autumn and the heat of summer.

Chapter two hundred and eighty-six:

Dhanvantari, the essence of those who ride horses, said:
"I shall now declare the essence of horsemanship and the medical treatment of horses."
The collection of horses should be carried out for the sake of achieving dharma, kama, and artha.
The constellations Aśvinī, Śravaṇa, Hasta,
and the three Uttaras are praised for the initial riding of horses.
During the winter, the cool season, and the spring, one may ride the horse;
however, riding is forbidden during the summer, autumn, and the rainy season. One should not strike the horse with harsh or excessive whips, nor should one do so in an improper place.
In a place crowded with stakes and bones, uneven and filled with thorns,
covered with sand and mud, and marred by one pit after another;
One who does not know the horse's mind and lacks skillful means may indeed attempt to ride it;
yet he, seated upon its back, is carried away by the horse itself.
Only some fortunate person, the best among the wise, would ever succeed in communicating his will to the horse.
Through practice and diligent application, the weapon-mantra becomes its own carrier;
then, for one who has bathed and is facing east, one should place the deities upon the body with their respective seed-syllables,
beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, in the proper sequence.
Brahmā resides in his mind, Viṣṇu in his strength, and Vainateya in his prowess; the Rudras are in his flanks, Bṛhaspati in his intellect, and the Viśvedevas in his vital organs;
the Moon and Sun are in the whorls of his eyes, and likewise the Aśvins in his ears.
The fire is in his belly, the *svadhā* offering in his sweat, speech in his tongue, and the wind in his speed;
the vault of heaven is on his back, all the mountains on the tips of his hooves,
the stars in the pores of his skin, and the lunar digit in his heart.
One should worship Agni in the radiance, Rati on the hips, and the Lord of the World on the forehead;
one should worship the planets in the neighing and likewise Vāsuki on the chest. Having fasted, the rider should worship the horse and mutter the *dakṣa-śruti* mantra.
O horse, you are a king of the *gandharvas*; listen to my words. Born as you are in the lineage of the *gandharvas*, do not be a defiler of your family!
By the truthful word of the twice-born, and by the power of Soma and Garuḍa.
By the power of Rudra, Varuṇa, and Pavana, and by the radiance of Hutāśana, remember your birth, O horse!
Remember that you are the son of a lord of kings; call to mind your truthful word.
Remember the maiden Vāruṇī; remember the Kaustubha jewel.
When the ocean of milk was being churned by the gods and the asuras, you were born there in the lineage of the gods; fulfill your own promise. Born in this family of horses, become my eternal friend.
Listen, friend, and be my perfected mount;
protect my victory and me in battle, and bring about success.
In the past, having mounted your back, the Daityas were slain by the gods.
"Now, having mounted you, I shall conquer the enemy host.
Having performed the *karṇajāpa* and likewise bewildered the enemies, the rider should bring the horse back; victory comes from such mastery in battle."
Generally, the defects that have arisen in their own bodies are eliminated by horses through great effort, whereas the virtues are [preserved] by the best of riders.
The virtues arising from a noble steed appear as if innate;
yet other riders destroy even those virtues that are born with them.
One person discerns the virtues, while another likewise perceives the faults.
Blessed is the wise man who understands the horse; the dull-witted one does not.

He who lacks knowledge of action, knows no means, is addicted to speed, and is excessively irascible—even if he is my own, he is not praised when he delights in heavy punishment and seeks out vulnerabilities.
Skilled in means, knowing the mind, pure, and a destroyer of faults,
he was constantly intent on acquiring virtues and proficient in all activities.
Then, having seized [the reins] with firm control, he entered the surface of the road.
It should be driven by its own rider through the distinction between left and right; thus it is said,
"together with the asuras," meaning those born together with the body.
Having mounted it suddenly, one must not strike the best of horses;
from being struck, it suffers both [pain], and from fear, delusion arises.
In the morning, the rider should move [the horse] by pulling up the reins with a gallop;
very slowly, without the bit, while holding the reins. On another day, it is said that "consoling" (*āśvasana*) is employed as a form of conciliation (*sāma*) toward the horse.

The punishment for biting and striking consists of a whip, a gift, and patience over time; however, when there is prior purification on a sacred day (*parvan*), one should apply increasingly severe measures.
On the surface of the tongue, one should employ the "no-yoke" method when mounting a horse.
One should cause the bit, along with the hundred virtues and the other, to sink into the corner of the mouth;
having made the mount forget [the bit], one should gradually loosen it for those that are slack.
For a horse lacking the tongue-limb, one should release the knot of the tongue.
One should release the tightness as long as one does not emit the *stobha*. One should perform the hundredfold armor-protection (*urastrāṇa*) and release it without faltering.
With the face turned upward, the armor-protection for that person is firm by its own nature.
Having prepared [the horse], the best of riders should lead it with a playful gaze.
His left [hand] joined with the left rein,
he should hold the right [rein] with that which grasps the hind leg.
He who performs this service by means of the left rein in this sequence will indeed have his very foot held fast;
for if the foot is released at the front, a very firm posture is produced.
The two who were carried off [were] Duṣkara and Moṭaka; likewise, Nāṭakāyana was deprived of his left side, Khalīkāra was struck by a blow, and Guṇana was similarly treated.
Indeed, the horse’s own nature was such that it turned its face away from him as he stood before it.
And it is not thus that the causes for seizing the feet of horses [are applied]; rather,
having observed the horse to be trusting, one should press the seat firmly.
Having restrained the foot in the mouth, seizing it for control is beneficial; having pressed firmly with the two lips and pulled the rein,
one is thus seized by that binding of the pair of feet.
In the same way, "speaking" is described as follows:
having restrained the feet with the bridle and then releasing the bridle, striking [the horse] at the desired spot is considered "striking."
Having understood this sequence for the prevention of collapse during the gallop,
this procedure is prescribed by means of the fourth [movement], the *moṭana*.
When a horse does not place its hoof on the ground in a small circle, [this method is applied].
One should seize the foot of the lord by means of the buttocks and the navel; when one proceeds after having firmly or gently grasped [the other],
that act by which one is seized is called *saṃgrahaṇa*.
Having struck the distracted horse on the side with a blow while standing his ground,
he pulled the bridle with his foot and seized the horse by the neck; then, as the horse rose up, he kicked it with his heel.
That which is seized after having been humiliated is considered a humiliation;
even among the three types of gait, one that takes a step without being desired is not truly desired.
For that place where one is seized by force after being struck is indeed a deep abyss.
Having struck the horse with the fourfold [whip] and with another rein, it is made to breathe out and is caught elsewhere; that, moreover, is called *ucchāsana*. [Note 1:
It refers to the non-arising of the time for battle and so forth.]
2. "But because of application on the outer side," according to manuscript *kha*. 3. "Having split the seat," according to manuscript *kha*.
4. "The extraction of the thorn of the grasper," according to manuscript *kha*.
Having directed his natural gaze toward that direction as it extends outward, one should cause him to grasp that; this is considered "turning the face. AP_287.049cd.
Then, having caused [the horse] to take the step in the three types [of gaits] in due order,

the wise man should gradually train it in the five flows and the circles and so forth; he should cause the horse to gallop with its face raised up to the sky, or he should cause it to gallop with a relaxed gait.
One should cause the horse to gallop as long as there is lightness in its limbs;
when it is gentle on the shoulder, light in the mouth, and relaxed in all its joints,
and is thus submissive to the rider, then one should restrain it.
One should not withdraw the hind leg until the horse has become steady;
then, an attraction should be performed here with both hands by means of a bridle-rein,
so that the horse stands in the *trika* posture with its neck extended and its face level.
When the two hind feet are on the ground and the two forefeet are supported in the air,
then one should apply the *sandharaṇa* maneuver and strike firmly with the fist; thus, even a horse that does not stop when suddenly pulled back will be brought under control.
One should train a horse that tosses its body by making it circle the mandala;
and one that kicks its rider on the shoulder should be restrained with the whip.

Cow dung, salt, urine, boiled earth, and [other substances] combined together— [Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of verse 56 from the *Aśvavaidyaka* (or *Aśvacikitsā*), attributed to Jayadatta. An ointment for the limbs destroys the exhaustion caused by the stinging of flies and other insects.
Indeed, a broth made from the *bhadra* and other species should be given to the horse in its midday meal.
Upon seeing a very sharp object, the horse becomes dispirited with hunger.
Just as they are obedient, so too do the training instructions perish if they are neglected;
yet, if not neglected, they do not fail. One should drive the horse with its face held high, pressing it firmly with both knees while maintaining a steady fist.
The *gomūtrākuṭilā*, the *veṇī*, the *padmamaṇḍalamālikā*,
and the *pañcolūkhalikā* should be performed; these are proclaimed as the *garvitās*.
Contracted, expanded, contracted-and-expanded, and as it is gathered; likewise, leaping and non-leaping—thus the sixfold [gait] is illustrated.
It extends for a hundred bow-lengths of the *vīthī*, or eighty, or ninety.
A noble horse is easy to train; a sluggish one is focused solely on the whip.
A deer-like horse is of mixed nature; a horse that eats sugar, honey, and parched grain, being fragrant and pure, is like a twice-born Brahmin.
A spirited Kṣatriya horse that is well-trained and intelligent,
and a Śūdra who is impure, fickle, dull-witted, deformed, ill-minded, and wicked;
a horse being held by a rein, and one that shows its saliva.
This [method] should be applied to the reins through the tightening, holding, and releasing of the grip.
I shall describe the characteristics of horses and other animals as Śālihotra has declared them. Thus ends the section titled "The Essence of Horse-Management" in the Agni Purāṇa.

Now begins the two hundred and eighty-eighth chapter:
The Treatment of Horses.
Śālihotra said:
I shall describe the characteristics of horses: one with missing teeth, one with extra teeth, one with a gaping mouth, one with a black palate,
one with a black tongue, one born twin-like, and likewise one whose testicles have not descended.
Likewise, there was Dviśapha, Śṛṅgin, Trivarṇa, Vyāghravarṇaka,
Kharavarṇa, Bhasmavarṇa, Jātavarṇa, Kākudī,
Śvitrin, Kākasādin, and Kharasāra.
One with eyes like a monkey, black bristles, and likewise a black private part;
one with a black snout, a porcupine, or one resembling a partridge;
one that is uneven, has white feet, and is devoid of the *dhruva* whorl.
A horse associated with a clockwise-rotating curl (āvarta) should be avoided.

Those that are golden-colored and glossy are always to be praised;
those with long necks and prominent eye-ridges, and those with short ears, are beautiful.
