One should therefore avoid Vijaya.
A horse that has been well-trained and tamed brings good fortune, whereas otherwise it brings suffering.
The Gandharvas are the sons of Śrī; horses are the supreme jewel.
In the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), however, the horse is offered because of its purity;
likewise, the bull, *nimba*, *bṛhatī*, *guḍūcī* with honey, *siṃhā*, *gandhakārī*, *piṇḍī*, and the fomentation (*sveda*) of the head.
Asafoetida, Puṣkaramūla, ginger, and sour Vetasa,
combined with long pepper and rock salt, destroy colic when taken with warm water.
Ginger, Ativiṣā, Musta, Anantā, Bilva, and Mālikā [are likewise used].
A horse should drink a decoction of these, which destroys all types of diarrhea.
Furthermore, by drinking goat’s milk boiled with *priyaṅgu* and *sārivā*,
and mixed with an adequate amount of sugar, a horse is freed from exhaustion.
An oil enema (tailavasti) should be administered into the rectum (droṇikā) of the horse;
furthermore, the vessel (śirā) arising from the abdomen (koṣṭha) should be pierced, by which his well-being will be restored.
Equal parts of dārvī, triphalā, vyoṣa, and jaggery (guḍa) [should be used].
This bolus should be administered to horses to destroy cough;
the horse should drink the juice of *vṛṣa* with *priyaṅgu*, *lodhra*, and honey,
or milk prepared with the "five pungents" (*pañcakola*) and other ingredients, for by this it is indeed freed from cough.

In all instances of excessive exertion, purification at the outset is best; for horses afflicted by fever, the prescribed course of treatment consists of oil massages, dry rubbings, unguents, nasal drops, and suppositories, while the primary regimen is indeed with milk.
The roots of *lodhra* and *kandhara*, along with *mātulāṅga*, *agni*, and *nāgara*— wherein the queen and the horse [are present].
This ointment of kuṣṭha, hiṅgu, vacā, and rāsnā mixed with ghee is a destroyer of swelling.
Mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, grapes, the two types of bṛhatī, red sandalwood, the seeds and roots of trapuṣī, śṛṅgāṭaka, and kaśeruka—
this [mixture] boiled with goat’s milk, well-cooled, and combined with sugar [is prescribed].
Having drunk [this], the horse, abstaining from water, is freed from *raktameha*.
Swelling of the vessels located in the neck, jaw, and throat, as well as lockjaw (*galagraha*),
[is treated] with anointing using pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*).
In that regard, among those very [remedies], it is recommended for a swelling in the throat caused by the disease *galagraha*. For a swelling generally located in the region of the throat,
*pratyakpuṣpī*, as well as *vahni*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and the juice of *saurasa* are used.
By applying these [medicines] mixed with black pepper and asafoetida as a nasal drop (nasya), one does not perish at night.
For the paralysis of the tongue, this application of jyotiṣmatī, pāṭhā, black pepper, kuṣṭha, and vacā, combined with honey, jaggery, and cow’s urine, is beneficial.
A medicinal paste (piṇḍī) prepared with sesame seeds, liquorice, turmeric, and neem leaves, combined with honey, acts as a purifier; when combined with clarified butter, it heals wounds.
Indeed, for those horses that limp due to injury and suffer from intense pain, [this remedy is prescribed].
For them, sprinkling with oil quickly removes the pain.
When [the abscess] has ripened and burst due to the provocation of the *doṣas* or by injury, the procedure for ulcers (*vraṇakrama*) applies;
[this involves] pastes of *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, *madhūka*, and *vaṭa*.
A decoction made with abundant water, lukewarm, purifies wounds when prepared with *śatāhvā*, *nāgara*, *rāsnā*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *kuṣṭha*, *saindhava*,
*devadāru*, *vacā*, the two types of *rajanī*, and *raktacandana*.
Oil prepared with a decoction of *guḍūcī* along with milk.

In all cases involving one who possesses the [auspicious] marks, this should be applied everywhere with *mrakṣa* and *vastināśa*. For eye diseases, blood-letting should be performed on the corners of the eyes using leeches;
and the treatment is accomplished with a decoction of *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *khādita*.
A paste made from equal parts of *dhātrī*, *durālabhā*, *tiktā*, *priyaṅgu*, saffron (*kuṅkuma*),
and *guḍūcī* is beneficial for one who has lost his grip on life;
it is likewise useful in cases of convulsions, when stones are heard falling, and in cases of dried-up semen.
In the case of a rapidly acting affliction, immediate incision is desired.
Rubbing with cow dung, mañjikā, kuṣṭha, turmeric, sesame,
and mustard seeds, ground together with cow urine, destroys itching.

A cold decoction mixed with honey and sugar, when administered as a nasal drop, cures *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders); likewise, it does so when drunk, prepared with *aśvakarṇa*. Salt should be given to horses every seventh day.
Likewise, after one has eaten, [a drink] should be given; however, in the case of excessive drinking, *vāruṇī* [liquor] should be used.
In autumn, the post-drink remedy (*pratipāna*) should consist of life-sustaining (*jīvanīya*) drugs combined with sweeteners, mixed with *mṛdvīkā*, sugar, long pepper (*pippalī*), and *padmaka*.
In the onset of winter, horses should be given a drink (pratipāna) prepared with viḍaṅga, pippalī, dhānyaka, śatāhvā, lodhra, saindhava salt, and citraka;
likewise, [a preparation] of lodhra, priyaṅgu, mustā, pippalī, and viśvabheṣaja.
In the spring, a post-drink (pratipāna) consisting of honey should be given to destroy phlegm;
in the summer, wine mixed with jaggery should be served as a post-drink along with *priyaṅgu*, *pippalī*, *lodhra*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *akṣa*, and *mahauṣadha*.
Regarding the statement "piercing is desired," [the manuscripts] Ja and Ña read as follows on page 74:
Lodhra wood, salt, long pepper, and ginger.
In the onset of the rainy season,

horses afflicted by bile provoked by the summer heat, those with abundant blood in autumn, and those with loose stools during the monsoon, should drink these [medicines] mixed with oil as a post-drink (pratipāna), or they should drink clarified butter.

Horses that have a predominance of phlegm (kapha) and wind (vāyu) should drink oil; however, for those in whom complications from oleation (sneha-vyāpad) have arisen, a drying treatment (virūkṣaṇa) should be performed. For three days, their food should consist of dry gruel (yavāgū) combined with buttermilk (takra).
Clarified butter is recommended in autumn and summer, oil in the cool season and spring;
during the rains and the cold season, a mixture of both is desired. One should avoid heavy, obstructive foods, physical exercise, bathing, and exposure to the sun.
Except for wind, one should avoid bathing and drinking for a horse that has been given oil, as well as the discharge of dung and urine, when the rains arrive; however,
at a time of excessive bad weather, a single drink is recommended.
In the season of moderate cold and heat, one should drink twice [daily] and bathe once;
in the summer, there should be three baths and drinks, along with prolonged immersion in water.
Four *āṭaka* measures of husked barley should be provided.
One should also cause chickpeas, rice, mung beans, or peas to be given.
For half a day and night, ten *tulās* of green fodder should be provided;
eight *tulās* of dry fodder, or four *tulās* of chaff.
Dūrvā grass destroys bile (pitta), barley destroys cough, and vūṣaka destroys the accumulation of phlegm (śleṣman).
Arjuna destroys asthma, and likewise māna destroys the loss of strength.
[These remedies apply to] disorders born of wind (vātika), bile (paittika), phlegm (ślaiṣmika), and those arising from the combination of all three (sānnipātika).
Diseases shall not afflict the horse that feeds on *dūrvā* grass;
there are two types of tethering-ropes for the wicked, pertaining to both sides.

A bow should be placed behind it, supported by a distant peg. They should be made to dwell in a prepared place that has been fumigated, where fodder is laid out, where lamps are provided, and which is well-guarded.
Cocks, goats, and monkeys, as well as deer, should be kept in the horse-stable.
Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Science of Equine Medicine," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 289:
The Pacification of Horses (Aśvaśānti)
Śālihotra said:
"I shall proclaim the pacification of horses (*aśvaśānti*), which crushes the disease of *vajī*. Listen, O Suśruta, to its threefold nature: the constant, the occasional, and the optional."
On an auspicious day, having worshipped Śrīdhara and Śrī, as well as that king of horses, Uccaiḥśravas, one should offer clarified butter with oblations to Savitṛ;
one should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born, and thus there shall be prosperity for the horse.
On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Aśvayuja, one should perform an external propitiatory rite (śāntika),
especially worshipping the two Nāsatyas and Varuṇa;
having then drawn [the mandala], one should surround the Goddess with branches.
One should offer jars filled with all the flavors and covered with cloths in the various directions;
having worshipped them, one should offer oblations of barley and clarified butter, and worship the horses along with the two Aśvins.
One should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins; now hear concerning the occasional rites (*naimittika*).
At the beginning of Capricorn (*makara*), one should worship Viṣṇu and Śrī with lotuses, as well as Brahmā, Śaṅkara, Soma, Āditya, and the two Aśvins.
He also [placed] Revanta, Uccaiḥśravas, and the guardians of the quarters upon the petals;

and on each side of the altar, in a place to the north, he placed a hundred offerings for each of the deities consisting of full jars, sesame seeds, unbroken rice, clarified butter, and white mustard.
And by one who has observed the fast, the ritual act that removes the horse's disease should be performed.
Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Pacification of Horses," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 290:
The Pacification of Elephants (Gajaśānti)
Śālihotra said:
I shall proclaim the pacification of elephants (*gajaśānti*), which destroys the diseases of elephants;
on the fifth lunar day, one should worship Viṣṇu, Śrī, and the elephant Airāvata.
Brahmā, Śaṅkara, Viṣṇu, Śakra, Vaiśravaṇa, Yama,
the Moon and Sun, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Agni, as well as Earth and Space.
The remaining mountains and elephants are those eight who are of divine origin:
Virūpākṣa, Mahāpadma, Bhadra, Sumanas,
Kumuda, Airāvaṇa, Padma, Puṣpadanta, and Vāmana.

The eight elephants—Supratīka, Añjana, and the others—are the oblation; furthermore, the sacrificial fee consists of elephants sprinkled with water of pacification. Now hear concerning the occasional rite for prosperity.
And for elephants, crocodiles, and so forth, outside the city in the northeast,
one should worship Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī upon a lotus on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), Brahmā in the center, the Sun and the Earth on the filaments (keśara), and indeed Skanda and Ananta.
[One should worship] Space, Śiva, Soma, Indra, and the others, as well as their weapons, in sequence upon the petals:

the thunderbolt (vajra), the spear (śakti), the staff (daṇḍa), the lance (tomara), the noose (pāśa), the mace (gadā), the trident (śūla), and the lotus; outside the stalks, [one should place] the discus (cakra), the sun, and likewise the two Aśvins.

Likewise, one should place the eight Vasus and the Sādhyas in the southern petal; then the Aṅgirasas, the Aśvins, the Bhṛgus, and the Maruts in the southwestern petal; the Viśvedevas in the western petal; and the Rudras in the northeastern mandala.
Then, one should worship the gods outside along the drawn line;
one should worship the authors of the Sūtras, the Ṛṣis, and Vāṇī in the east and other directions, and the rivers, mountains, and great elements in the corners, beginning with the northeast.
A lotus, a wheel, a mace, and a conch; then a square mandala with four doors, and from that, the water-pots (2);
and in the directions starting from the southeast, the banners (3).
At the gate, there are four archways with elephants such as Airāvata and others;
in the east and other directions, having worshipped the elephants with medicinal herbs and hundredfold oblations of clarified butter, one should circumambulate the separate vessels of the gods.
Having honored the elephants, the fire, the deities, and others with external offerings, they went to their own homes;
likewise, the horse-physicians and others should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the twice-born.
Then, having mounted a female elephant, one who knows the proper time should speak into its ear.
1. *Maruto 'nala* is *ja*.
2. *Catuḥkumbhā* is *ña*. 3. *Patākina* is *ja*.
O King of Nāgas, having performed the rite of peace for the deceased, one should recite the mantra over this [remains].
"O illustrious elephant, you have been made by the king the leader of his elephants;
the monarch will worship you with the finest garlands and choice foods,
and by his command, the world shall then offer worship to you."
The king must be protected by you in battle, on the road, and likewise at home.
Abandoning your animal state, remember your divine nature.
In ancient times, during the war between the gods and the asuras, the elephant Śrīgaja was restored to his celestial form by the thirty deities.
The glorious elephant named Ariṣṭa, the son of Airāvaṇa,
possesses the entire majesty of all auspicious elephants.
O lord of elephants, that majesty of yours is endowed with a divine nature.

"May she attend upon you; may she protect the king in battle"—with these words, the consecrated king should mount her on an auspicious day. Following him, they should proceed with new, well-trained elephants equipped with weapons.
In the halls, upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the form of a lotus, one should worship the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and others outside;
on the filaments (keśaras), one should worship Bala, Nāga, Bhū, and Sarasvatī;
and having worshipped Ḍiṇḍima in the centers with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Having offered oblations, a water-pot filled with mercury should be given to a brahmin.
One should honor the superintendent of elephants and five elephants, as well as one who is skilled in calculation.
He should give that [elephant] to the superintendent of elephants, and he too should cause the drum to be sounded.
Standing at the rear, one should offer salutations with auspicious and profound sounds.
Thus ends the two hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Pacification of Elephants," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
1. *kṛdvānyasmin* (or *kṛd vānyasmin*)—thus [read] in the manuscripts marked Kha, Ja, and Ña:
p. 79, Chapter 291.
Chapter Two Hundred and Ninety-One:
The Ayurveda of Peace.
Dhanvantari said:
The king must protect cows and Brahmins; I shall declare the rite for the peace of cows.
Cows are purifying and auspicious; the worlds are established upon cows. Their dung and urine are supreme, the ultimate destroyers of misfortune.
Scratching the cows, water from their horns that crushes the flood of sins,
cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, ghee, and gorocana—
this supreme sixfold limb [of the ritual] wards off bad dreams and other such evils when consumed.
Yellow orpiment destroys poison and demons; one who eats the fodder of cows goes to heaven.
That man in whose house cows suffer goes to hell.
One who eats the fodder of another's cow goes to heaven, while one who benefits cows attains the world of Brahmā.
By the gift of a cow, by chanting its praises, and by providing protection, one uplifts one's lineage;
the earth becomes purified by the breath of cows, and sin is destroyed by their touch.
Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass [are the five products of the cow].
A fast for one night and night may purify even a dog-cooker (śvapāka);
it was practiced of old by the lords for the destruction of all impurities.
And that which lasts for three days each [of the preceding penances] is known as the Mahāsāntapana.
This [practice] bestows all desires and crushes all that is inauspicious.
By subsisting on milk alone for twenty-one days, one performs the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penance;
through the attainment of all desires, they become stainless and bow down as the most excellent ones.
For three days one should drink warm urine, for three days one should drink warm ghee,
and having drunk warm milk for three days, one should subsist on air for the final three days.
The *taptakṛcchra* vow destroys all sins and bestows the world of Brahmā;
the *śītakṛcchra*, as declared by Brahmā, likewise bestows the world of Brahmā when performed with cold substances.
One should perform the bath with cow urine and maintain one's livelihood on cow's milk.
One who observes the cow-vow (govrata) should go to the cow-pen when the cows have eaten and eat only after they have eaten;
by one month [of this practice], he becomes free from sin, attains the world of cows (goloka), and goes to heaven.
Furthermore, by reciting the Gomatī-vidyā, one shall go to the supreme Goloka.
There, in a celestial chariot, he rejoices with songs, dances, and apsarases.
Cows are eternally fragrant; cows possess the scent of guggulu resin.
Cows are the foundation of all beings; cows are the supreme source of well-being.
Food indeed is supreme; cows are the highest oblation for the gods.
They purify all beings, and they both yield [milk] and speak.
With oblations purified by mantras, they satisfy the immortals in heaven.
Cows are employed in the fire-sacrifices of the seers during their oblations;
cows are the supreme refuge for all beings,
cows are the highest purifier, and cows are the most auspicious.
Cows are the stairs to heaven; cows are auspicious and eternal.
Homage to the glorious cows, to the daughters of Surabhi, and homage again and again to the pure daughters of Brahmā.
The Brahmins and the cows constitute a single family divided into two parts: on one side the sacred mantras abide, and on the other the sacrificial oblation abides.
The entire world is indeed always sustained by gods, brahmins, cows, virtuous men, and virtuous women; therefore, all of them are considered most worthy of worship.
For it is cows alone who drink from that sacred ford where the Gaṅgā and other rivers flow.

The greatness of cows has indeed been told; now likewise hear of their medical treatment. In cases of diseases affecting the horns of cows, one should administer oil prepared with rock salt and a paste of ginger, balā, and meat, along with honey.
In all cases of earache, oil prepared with mañjiṣṭhā, asafoetida, and rock salt, or alternatively with garlic, should be administered; likewise,
the roots of bilva and apāmārga, along with dhātakī and pāṭalā, [should be used].

An application of *kuṭaja* at the roots of the teeth destroys their pain. O Rāma, ghee cooked with substances that remove toothache should be known as a cure for diseases of the mouth; likewise, rock salt (*saindhava*) is effective for diseases of the tongue.
Ginger, the two types of turmeric, and the three myrobalans (triphalā) are recommended for throat obstruction,
as well as for heart pain, pain in the bladder, wind diseases, and consumption.
Furthermore, the three myrobalans mixed with clarified butter are praised when given to cows to drink.
In cases of diarrhea, one should administer the two types of *haridrā* and *pāṭhā*.
Likewise, in all diseases of the internal organs (*koṣṭha*) as well as in diseases of the peripheral tissues (*śākhā*),
one should administer *śṛṅgavera* and *bhārgī* for cough and dyspnea.
Priyaṅgu combined with salt should be administered for the healing of fractures.
Oil boiled with madhuyaṣṭī is used for pitta-type [fractures] that cause wind;
it should be prepared with vyoṣa and honey for kapha-type [fractures], and with puṣkara-rasa for hemorrhage.
One should offer oil, clarified butter, and yellow orpiment, as well as meat from an animal that is broken or wounded.
Likewise, one should give sesame seeds with wheat, the milk of cattle, and ghee for a month.
This mixture with salt, when given as a bolus to calves, bestows nourishment and strength; it is an incense for the destruction of the seizing of the horns,
consisting of devadāru, vacā, māṃsī, guggulu, hiṅgu, and mustard seeds.
This incense is beneficial for cattle, intended to destroy diseases caused by planetary influences and other ailments.
A bell should also be made for the cattle and adorned with this incense;
by means of *aśvagandhā* and white sesame seeds, the cow shall become a yielder of milk.
One who keeps *pinyāka* (sesame oil cake) and *rasāyana* in the house at night should always worship *Śānti* and *Śrī* upon the excrement on the fifth day;
one should also worship Vāsudeva with perfumes and other offerings— this is called another form of *śānti*.
On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Aśvayuja, one should worship Hari,
as well as Hara, Rudra, Aja, Sūrya, Śrī, and Agni with clarified butter.
Having consumed curd, honored the cows, and performed the circumambulation of the fire, the ritual should be completed.
One should arrange a fight among bulls outside [the city] to the sound of singing and musical instruments;
salt should be given to the cows, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brāhmaṇas.
On special occasions such as the month of Makara and others, one should worship Viṣṇu together with Śrī.
In the lotus on the sacrificial ground, one should worship the deities residing in the filaments located in the cardinal directions:
Subhadra, Rāja, Ravi, Bahurūpa, and Bali outside;
as well as Kha, Viśvarūpā, Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Śānti, and Rohiṇī.
The directions beginning with the East are indeed the poisoned cows; the Moon is the Lord (Īśvara).
One should offer oblations into the fire upon lotus leaves and in jars, using sacrificial fuel-sticks of milk-trees, mustard seeds, unhusked rice, and grains. AP 291.042ab.
One should give a hundred, a hundred pieces of gold, and vessels of bell-metal and so forth to a twice-born;
cows, accompanied by milk and other offerings, should be honored and released for the sake of peace.
Agni said:
Śālihotra taught the Ayurveda of horses to Suśruta,
and Pālakāpya spoke the Ayurveda of elephants to the King of Aṅga.
Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Ayurveda for Peace," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 291.
Now begins the two hundred and ninety-second chapter:
The Definition of Mantras.
Agni said:
I shall declare the Mantravidyā-Hari mantra, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
listen, O twice-born one! Mantras consisting of more than twenty syllables are known as *mālā-mantras*;
those with more than ten syllables, but fewer than that, are designated as *bījas*.
Indeed, these *mālāmantras* grant success in old age, while during youth,
other mantras consisting of more than five syllables grant success at all times.
The classes of mantras are threefold, according to whether they are feminine, masculine, or neuter.

Feminine mantras end with *vahnija* (svāhā) and conclude with *namaḥ*; neuter mantras are the remainder, while masculine ones are recommended for use in rites of eradication (*uccāṭana*) and the like.
Feminine mantras are also used for minor rites (*kṣudrakriyā*) and the destruction of diseases, whereas in other cases they are not.
Neuter mantras are those called Āgneya (fiery) and Saumya (lunar); one should recite the *tāra* (oṃ) at the beginning and end of both.
A mantra is considered Āgneya when it predominantly consists of the *tāra*, the final syllable, fire (*ra*), and space (*ha*).
The disciplined and gentle [planets] are praised for cruel and gentle rites respectively;
and [the gentle ones are used] for binding, eradication, and subjugation.
Two [syllables] are not here;
[the mantra] beginning with "kha" is on folio 84.
The mantra dedicated to Agni should generally be addressed to Soma and be accompanied by "namaḥ" at the end.
A mantra that is gentle or fiery, yet concluded with the syllable *phaṭ*,
does not grant success if it is merely asleep or just awakened;
O great-armed one, the time of sleep belongs to the dog, while the state of wakefulness flows toward the south.

One should know the time of awakening for both [Manus] from the reversal of this: for the Āgneya Manu and the Saumya Mantra, on both days of the month. One should avoid those Manus associated with malefic asterisms, zodiac signs, inimical colors, and so forth.

The letter *p* (pa), when joined with the vowel *a*, indicates that an enemy has begun for the sake of assisting in the acquisition of a kingdom; the letter *r* (ra) indicates that he has gone to the Kuru lands;
and the letter *u* (u) indicates that he has reached a cowherd’s hut.

These vowels are to be applied according to the sequence of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and the signs (*rāśi*), with the final two vowels (*e* and *o*) corresponding to the conjunctions of Revatī.
The vowels *velā*, *guru*, and *śoṇa* are distinguished by their functions;

these should be known as the letters of the script in the *vaśi* [positions]. One should also apply the lords of the sixth house and others to the script situated at the crossroads (*catuṣpatha*), within the intervals between the syllables and words of the name.
The *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *vairin* [mantras] are situated in the second position; one should thus determine the *siddha* and the others by their extreme qualities.
A *siddha* [mantra] is mastered through recitation (*japa*), while a *sādhya* is mastered through recitation, worship, oblations, and so forth.
Even when fully perfected through mere meditation, such an enemy mantra will destroy the practitioner.
Any mantra that abounds in malevolent syllables is censured by all;
yet, having entered the initiation according to the rules, ending with the consecration—
Having heard the tantra and received it from the guru, the wise, skillful, pure, and devoted practitioner, intent upon recitation, meditation, and so forth, should accomplish his desired mantra;
[this applies] even with the syllables of the *siddhi*, *yanti*, and *dalas*.
[The practitioner] who has completed the recitation, the full oblation, and so forth—
accomplished, ascetic, skilled, a knower of the tantras, and truthful in speech.
One who is capable of both restraint and favor is called a Guru.

A disciple is one who is tranquil, self-controlled, proficient, has observed celibacy, eats sacrificial food (haviṣya), performs service to the teacher, and possesses the zeal for spiritual accomplishment.
But he who is to be instructed, as well as a disciplined son or one who bestows wealth, may likewise receive it;
however, for the sake of perfect accomplishment, the preceptor should recite the mantra a thousand times.
A mantra heard by chance, or obtained through deceit or force, [is not to be taught].
If one should produce even a single meaningless verse situated upon a leaf,
or if one should accomplish a single mantra through numerous rites such as recitation, fire-offerings, and worship, it will be mastered by him with only a slight amount of practice.
For one who has correctly mastered even a single mantra, there is nothing in this world that cannot be accomplished;
what then can be said of a man who possesses many mantras? He is indeed Śiva himself. A single-syllable mantra becomes effective through one million recitations (*japa*).
One should adjust the recitation of other mantras by increasing the number according to the increase in syllables;
for *mālā-mantras*, the practice of recitation consists of repeating the mantra two or three times the number of its seed-syllables (*bīja*).
When no specific number is mentioned, one should perform one hundred and eight or one thousand recitations in rites such as *japa*.
In all cases, they know that the oblation (homa) should be one-tenth of the recitation (japa), accompanied by consecration (abhiṣeka).
When no specific substance is mentioned, clarified butter (ghṛta) is used for the oblation; for one who is unable [to perform the ritual], the recitation is always the substitute.
For the limbs (aṅga-mantras) and so forth, the recitation and other rites should be one-tenth of the root mantra (mūla-mantra).
Through the recitation of the mantra together with its power (śakti), the deity of the mantra becomes the granter of desires;
she becomes satisfied for the practitioner through meditation, fire-offerings (homa), worship, and so forth.
Whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is ten times more distinguished than loud recitation (uccair-japa).
Recitation with the tongue is said to be a hundredfold [more effective], while mental recitation is a thousandfold;
one should commence the ritual of mantra facing either east or downward.

All mantras begin with the *praṇava*; one should recite them while remaining silent, eating only as prescribed, and sitting down, viewing the deity and the preceptor as equal. Secluded places such as huts, temples, rivers, and lakes are suitable locations for this practice.
Upon success, one should recite the mantra on the lunar days and weekdays while consuming gruel, cakes, milk, solid food, or sacrificial oblation (haviṣya). //AP_292.031cd//
On the eighth and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight, during eclipses and the like, the practitioner [should know the presiding deities]: the Aśvins,
Yama, Anala, Dhātṛ, Śaśin, Rudra, Guru, Diti,
the Serpents, the Pitṛs, Bhaga, Aryaman, and the Moon and the Sun.
Tvaṣṭṛ, the Maruts, Indra and Agni, Mitra and Indra, Nirṛti, and Varuṇa;
the Viśvedevas, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Vāyus, and the Lord of Waters;
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pūṣan, and the deities of the Aśvinī constellation and the others.
Agni, Aśvin, Umā, Nighna, Nāga, Candra, Divākara,
Mātṛ, Durgā, Diśāmīśa, Kṛṣṇa, Vaivasvata, Śiva,
and Śaśāṅka are the lunar days (tithis); the Pitṛs are the deities of the fifteenth day.

Hara, Durgā, Guru, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Lakṣmī, and Dhaneśvara—these are the lords of the days beginning with Sunday. Now, the assignment of the letters (lipinyāsa) is described: [they are assigned] to the ends of the hair, the forehead, the two eyes, and the two ears.
The two [syllables] for the nose, cheeks, lips, and teeth, and two each for the head and face, respectively;
[these are the letters] of the five classes [of consonants],
located in the joints of the arms and feet.
One should place [the syllables] on the two sides, at the back, at the navel, and at the heart, in sequence.
(AP 292.039ab) [Note: "tara" is found in manuscript kha.]
One should place the five groups of vowels and [the consonants] beginning with *ya* in the heart; these shall be the seven constituents (*dhātu*).
Skin, blood, flesh, sinew, fat, marrow, and semen are the bodily constituents (*dhātavaḥ*);
likewise, fat, milk, and the garment are written as the lords of scripts (*lipīśvarāḥ*).
[The lords are] Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, and Amareśvara.
Agnīśa, Bhāvabhūti, Tithīśa, Sthānuka, Hara, Daṇḍīśa, Bhautika, Sadyojāta, Anugraheśvara,
Akrūra, and Mahāsena— these are the deities who provide refuge.
Then Krodhīśa and Taṇḍa, Pañcāntaka and Śivottama,
likewise Rudra and Kūrma, the Three-eyed One and the Four-faced One,
Ajeśa and Śarmasoneśa, as well as Lāṅgali and Dāruka.
Ardhanārīśvara, Umākānta, Āṣāḍhi, Daṇḍin,
Atri, Mīna, Meṣa, Lohita, and likewise Śikhī;
Chagalaṇḍa and Dviraṇḍa, along with Mahākāla and Vālin.

One should install in sequence, ending with "namaḥ," the Rudras who are embodiments of power (ātmaśakti), beginning with Bhujanga, Pinākin, Khaḍgīśa, Vaka, Śveta, Bhṛgu, Laguḍīśa, Akṣa, and Sambartaka.
One should assign all the limbs; indeed, mantras accompanied by their limbs grant success.
One should assign these limbs beginning with *hṛllekhā* and *vyoma*.
He who recites the heart-mantra and the others ending with the limb-mantras, saying "namaḥ" at the heart, [attains success].

One should perform the five-limbed assignment (pañcāṅga-nyāsa) as follows: *svāhā* on the head, *vaṣaṭ* on the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *hūṃ* on the armor (*kavaca*), *vauṣaṭ* on the eyes, and *phaṭ* for the weapon (*astra*).
Alternatively, one may perform the limbless assignment (*niraṅga-nyāsa*) by oneself; having performed these, one should recite [the mantra] one million times.
One should offer sesame seeds as prescribed for the goddess Vāgīśī with the two feet-mantras;
the Goddess of the Letters holds a rosary, a water-pot, a book, and a lotus.
One should assign [the letters] at the beginning of rituals and so forth for the sake of attaining success, such as poetic skill;
one who is pure and stainless becomes a Niṣkavi, and all mantras are perfected by the Mothers.
Thus ends the chapter titled "Exposition of Mantras" in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
The two hundred and ninety-second chapter;
now begins the two hundred and ninety-third chapter.
Agni spoke of the characteristics of the *nāgas*,
as well as the *nāgas* and other beings, the ten states of existence (*bhāva*), and karma.
"Sūtaka" (birth-impurity) and "daṣṭaceṣṭā" (the behavior of the bitten)— these are said to be the seven symptoms.
Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkaṭa, Abja, Mahāmbuja,
Śaṅkhapāla, and Kulika— these are the eight preeminent nāgas.
Two Brahmins, two Kshatriyas, two Vaishyas, and two Shudras are proclaimed among the Nagas, possessing respectively one hundred and eight, one hundred and five, three hundred, and one hundred heads;
their descendants number five hundred, and from them were born countless others.
The hooded snakes (*phaṇin*), the circular-marked (*maṇḍalin*), and the striped (*rājīla*) are composed of wind, bile, and phlegm respectively;
these intermediate species are known as *darvīkara* snakes when mixed with [other] humors.
The *gonasas* move slowly, are long, and are covered with various kinds of circular spots.
[They are] those who bear the discus, the plow, the mace, and the goad;
2. [they are] standing—thus [it is said]. *kha* manuscript.
The *rājila* snakes are variegated and glossy, with markings that run both transversely and vertically;
those with mixed marks are intermediate, while others belong to the earth, rain, fire, or wind.
These are of four kinds, comprising twenty-six varieties: sixteen are *gonasas*, thirteen are *rājīlas*, and the *vyantaras* are twenty-one;
those snakes that are born at unspecified times are known as *vyantaras*.
In four months, beginning from Āṣāḍha, the embryo develops; then, at two hundred and forty days, it is born.
Serpents devour the masses of offspring, with the exception of females, males, and neuters.
The eyes open after seven days; he emerges from the womb after one month;
he becomes conscious after twelve days; his teeth appear upon seeing the sun;
and after thirty-two days, twenty [teeth] appear, four of which are fangs.
Karālī, Makarī, Kālarātrī, and Yamadūtikā—
these are the venomous fangs located on the left and right sides; by [controlling] them,
one is freed from the skin after six months and shall live for two cycles of sixty years.

The seven Nāgas are said to be the lords of the days beginning with Sunday; during the day and night, they each preside over six consecutive days, while Kulika presides over all the junctions (sandhis),
or else his rising occurs together with Śaṅkha or Mahābja.
Or rather, when two *nāḍikās* of the mantra and the *mantraka* arise as the *kulika*,
that time is harmful everywhere, especially in the case of a snakebite.

The asterisms Kṛttikā, Bharaṇī, Svātī, Mūla, the three Pūrvas, Aśvinī, Viśākhā, Ārdrā, Maghā, Āśleṣā, Citrā, Śravaṇa, Rohiṇī, and Hastā; the days of Saturday and Tuesday; and the lunar dates (tithis) of the fifth and eighth.
"The sound of only a single *nāḍikā*," so it is stated in the Ña manuscript.
2. "One should point out," so it is in the Ka manuscript.
Kha, Ja, and Ṭa:
The sixth lunar day (ṣaṣṭhī) conjoined with the moon is Śivā; it is censurable [to perform rites on] the fifth and the fourteenth.

The four periods of twilight (saṃdhyā) are inauspicious, as are the burnt yogas and the zodiac signs; the bites may be single, double, or multiple; and there is the "pierced" bite and the "mutilated" bite.
Thus, the bite is of four kinds.
The bites are threefold, causing injury to two or one [limb], accompanied by pain and profuse bleeding;
at night, the bites sent by Yama resemble a single leg or a tortoise,
feel like the touch of ants, and are accompanied by swelling and pain in the throat.
A stinging insect that has been rubbed, a venomous one with its venom removed,
or one placed in a temple, an empty house, an anthill, a garden, or a hollow;
at a crossroads, in a cemetery, by a river, or at the confluence of rivers— AP_293.021cd–293.022ab.
On an island, at a crossroads, on a palace, in a house, or on a lotus; at the summit of a mountain, at the gate of a temple, in a ruined well, in a dilapidated dwelling, or against a wall;
under a *śigru*, a *śleṣmātaka*, or an *akṣa* tree; and under a *jambū*, a *ḍumbara*, or an *iṅguda* tree.

Gazing at the directions, flickering the tongue, shaking the body, and weeping;
the offering is as before with fish and other items, and for the incense and ointment, hiṅgu,
vacā, siddhārtha, and garlic are used for the one who seizes from above, the Mahāgraha.
One should fumigate and anoint the child with red sandalwood, kuṣṭha, and other such substances; [the symptoms are] agitation, upward gasping, and the gnawing of one's own two fists.
Incense made from the hair and nails of a monkey is for the *daśamī* seizure, which causes weeping.
Its symptoms are constant crying, a sweet fragrance, and a blue complexion.
One should smear [the patient] with incense made from nimba, bhūtograrājī, and sarjarasa.
One should offer an external oblation (bali) consisting of parched grain, fermented gruel, and rice mixed with meat.

This ritual of incense and other offerings should continue for thirteen days. The seizing spirit known as Māsika-vatsa-pūtanā causes the child to cry like a crow, experience labored breathing, emit the odor of urine, and close its eyes.
He should perform a bath with cow’s urine and fumigate him with a cow’s tooth; [and likewise] with incense and lamps. (Note: 1. *dhūpadīpe* according to ṭa;
2. *karakodanam* according to kha.)
One should offer yellow garments, red garlands and perfumes, and a lamp of oil;
as well as three kinds of milk-rice and liquor, and four kinds of sesame and beans.
For two months, one should offer a bali-oblation for seven days beneath a *karañja* tree in the direction of Yama; [the symptoms will be] a crown on the head, a cold body, a chill,
vomiting, dryness of the mouth, and [a desire for] flowers, perfumes, and fine garments.
In the third [watch], there is cake, boiled rice, a lamp, black water and so forth, incense, a cow-faced vessel, sleep, excrement, urine, and weeping;
[the food consists of] barley, *priyaṅgu*, meat, half-cooked grain, vegetables, and boiled rice.

In the first part of the day, one should offer milk; at midday, incense with ghee and the five-fold resin (*pañcabhaṅga*). That bath removes the affliction of Piṅgalā. [If the patient's] body is cold, has a putrid odor, and suffers from emaciation, he will certainly die.
The fifth [sign] is lalanā; there will be lassitude of the limbs and dryness of the mouth.
The downward breath (apāna) becomes yellowish in color, and offerings (bali) consisting of fish and other items are made on the right side.
After six months, there is the movement of mud-born [insects], weeping, and a distorted voice.
An offering (bali) consisting of fish, meat, liquor, cooked rice, flowers, perfumes, and so forth [is for the first day];
on the second, one should fast; on the third, there is a foul odor and toothache;
an offering should consist of flour-meat, liquor, and meat on the eighth day of Yamunā.
There may be boils, emaciation, and other such ailments; one should not perform medical treatment for these.
In the ninth [lunar mansion], one afflicted by Kumbhakarṇī suffers from fever and vomiting;
in Vaiśvaka, the offering consists of weeping, meat, fermented grain-porridge, wine, and so forth.
In the tenth [lunar day], the activity of an ascetic, fasting, and closing the eyes;
a bell, a banner, and flour are prescribed, along with an offering of liquor and meat for the *surā* [deity].
On the same [day], the eleventh is that of a *rākṣasī*, characterized by affliction and the inability to treat the eyes and other ailments.
On the twelfth day, Cañcalā is the breath; her activities include trembling and other such gestures.
The offering should be made in the east at midday with groats and the like, along with sesame seeds and so forth.
In the second year, however, there is suffering—suffering such as weeping and so forth.
An offering of sesame, meat, liquor, and flesh, along with ritual bathing and other rites, should be performed as before.
In the third year, there is weeping, trembling, crying out, and the discharge of blood and urine.
In the fourth [month], there is rice with molasses, cakes made of sesame, an image fashioned from sesame paste,
a sesame bath with five leaves, and incense made from the bark of the *rājaphala* tree.
There is also swelling of the throat and fever accompanied by a general prostration of all the limbs.

In the fifth year, Cañcalā [is propitiated] with an offering of fish, meat, sesame seeds, and so forth, as well as a ritual bath and incense; there is fever, terror, and a sense of physical exhaustion.
An offering of meat and rice should be made, and incense should be burned with a ram's horn.

In the sixth year, one who carries the leaves of the *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, and *bilva* will suffer from the drying up of the *dhāvanī* (urinary tract), a bad taste in the mouth, and exhaustion of the limbs.
For seven days, there should be offerings (*bali*) with the aforementioned substances, as well as fumigation (*dhūpa*) and bathing (*snāna*) with *bhaṅga* preparations.
On the seventh day, there is vomiting into the Yamunā, along with speaking, laughing, and weeping;
and offerings, bathing, and fumigation with meat, wine, liquor, and so forth.
In the eighth year, Jātavedas causes fasting and excessive weeping;
there should be an offering of *kṛsara*, cakes, curd, and so forth, as well as bathing and fumigation.
In the ninth year, Kālābda causes the slapping of the arms, thundering, and fear.
The oblation should consist of *kṛśara*, cakes, flour, *kulmāṣa* grains, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
In the tenth year, there will be a kalahamsī bird, burning sensations, emaciation of the limbs, and fever.
1. "Vaivarṇyam" is [the reading in] Ṭha...
2. "Bhāgakaiḥ" is [the reading in] Kha...

For five nights, one should offer a *bali* oblation consisting of *paulikā* cakes and curd-rice; on the eleventh day, the seizer is a *graha* who is cured by *nimba* incense and an ointment of *kuṣṭha*. Devadūtī speaks harshly; her *bali*, ointments, and other rites are as previously described.
On the twelfth day, the offering (bali) consisting of smearing with unguents and so forth is as before.

On the thirteenth day, there is the offering pertaining to Vāyu; one should bathe [the deity] with red food, perfumes, garlands, and the like, using five-petaled flowers, while applying ointments to the face and the limbs.
In the fourteenth [day], incense made from the petals of the *rājī* plant brings about a *yakṣiṇī*;
there is pain, fever, and burning, and the offering consists of meat-eaters and the like.
For the sake of pacification, bathing and other rites are performed as before; the affliction caused by *muṇḍikā* occurs in the fifteenth day.
One should constantly perform the treatment for the Mother [demoness], characterized by those movements and the constant flow of blood.
The sixteen-year-old Vānarī [demoness] falls to the ground; there is always fever.
For three nights, an offering (*bali*) consisting of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and other items should be made, along with bathing and other rites as previously described.
In the seventeenth [year], Gandhavatī [is the presiding deity]; there is trembling of the limbs and weeping.
An offering of sour gruel and other such items, as well as bathing, incense, and ointments, should be performed as before.
The lords of the day are those named Pūtanā, and the lords of the year are the Sukumārikās.
Oṃ, homage to all the Mothers! Consume, consume the affliction of children;
cut, cut! Shatter, shatter! Quiver, quiver! Seize, seize!
Drag forth, drag forth! Thus does the one who has attained perfection command: Hare, hare!
Make her free from defects—make the girl, the boy, the woman, or the man [free] through the application against all seizing spirits (*graha*).
O Cāmuṇḍā, homage to the Goddess! Hrūṃ hrūṃ hrīṃ! Depart, depart!
Hrūṃ! May the evil planets depart; Rudra commands the household spirits to go by another path. This mantra shall be effective for all desires regarding all child-seizing spirits.
Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed Lady Cāmuṇḍā! Release, release the *bali* offering, whether it be for a boy or a girl!
Accept, accept the *bali*! Victory, victory! Dwell, dwell!
In every offering of the *bali*, this protective mantra is recited:
"May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Skanda, Gaṇeśa, and Gaurī protect [him] from the onset of fever and release the boy!"
Lakṣmī, the Gaṇas, and others...
Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Bālatantra for Warding off Child-Spirits," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 299: The Heart-Mantras and Other Rituals for the Planets (Grahahṛnmantrādikam)
Agni said:
I shall now declare the mantras and other rites for the subduing of planetary influences (graha),
which destroy those influences arising from the consumption of forbidden or impure food, as well as from joy, desire, fear, grief, and the like.
Furthermore, from the provocation of one's guru, deities, and others, five types of insanity arise;
they are known as those born of the three *doṣas*, those from their combination (*sannipāta*), and the exogenous (*āgantu*).
Deities and other *grahas* have manifested in manifold ways from the wrath of Rudra.
In rivers, lakes, ponds, and the like; on mountains, in groves, and on bridges;
at the confluence of rivers, in empty houses, at the entrance of a burrow, and under a solitary tree—there the planetary spirits seize men and their fortunes.

Sleeping while pregnant, being near her time of delivery, being naked, or performing the ritual bath after menstruation; likewise, insulting men, enmity, obstacles, and the reversal of fortune— [these are the results].
The transgression of proper conduct toward deities, gurus, the Dharma, and so forth.
(AP 299.006ab) [Note: In the ña and ṭa manuscripts, the word "striyaḥ" (women) appears here. (p. 109)
A man who is being favored by the deity Hūṃkāra falls from mountains and trees, repeatedly shaking his hair; with bloodshot eyes, he weeps and dances.
He is agitated, afflicted by the burning pain of a spear, tormented by hunger and thirst, and suffers from a headache.
The man seized by the *balikāma* demon begs, "Give! Give! The man seized by the *ratikāma* demon desires women, garlands, enjoyments, and bathing.
Mahāsudarśana pervades the sky and has a nose like a tree branch.
The Caṇḍī-mantras, beginning with Pātālanārasiṃha and others, are destroyers of the seizing spirits (grahas).
[One should worship] the supreme beloved of Pṛśni, Hiṅgu, Vacā, Cakra, and Śirīṣa;
the God who holds a noose and a goad, and carries a rosary and a skull-cup.

Having worshipped the four-faced one, who holds a khaṭvāṅga, a lotus, and other emblems, who is situated upon a khaṭvāṅga and a lotus both internally and externally, and who is joined with Āditya and the others within the solar disc, one should offer the arghya water when the sun has risen.
Śvāsa, Viṣa, Agni, Vipra, Kuṇḍī, Hṛllekhā, Sakala, and Bhṛgu;
for the Sun: Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Jvālinī, Kula, Mudgara, Padmāsana, Aruṇa, Raktavastra, Sad-yuti, and Viśvaka.
Majestic, holding a lotus with his two arms, gentle, and adorned on all limbs;
the deities of the heart and other limbs are red, gentle, bestowing boons, and holding lotuses.
His garment resembles a mass of lightning; he is white and gentle, while Mars is reddish-brown.
Likewise, Mercury is described as such; Jupiter is yellow, Venus is white, Saturn has limbs like black charcoal, Rāhu is smoky-colored, and Ketu is said to be smoke-gray.
She has a beautiful left thigh, her left hand is at the end [of the arm], and her right hand bestows fearlessness.
Having purified one's hands with the weapon-mantra, those [mantras] beginning with one's own name are the seed-syllables.
:n 1 "Vipiṭanāsika" is the reading in manuscript Ña.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the thumbs and so forth, on the palms, and on the eyes; one should place the pervasive [placement] starting from the heart with the three root-syllables, and then perform the placement of the visualization of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) together with its limbs (*sāṅga*).
Having washed the vessel with the Astra-mantra and filled it with water using the Mūla-mantra,

one should place upon it fragrant paste, flowers, unbroken rice, dūrvā grass, and the arghya offering, and consecrate them with the mantra; then, having sprinkled oneself and the sacrificial materials with that water, one should certainly perform the worship.
One should arrange these— the abundant, stainless, essential, and supreme bliss worthy of attainment—
on the seats and so forth, with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) in the center and at the intermediate directions;
and upon the seat, one should likewise arrange them with the heart-mantra in the center, in the cardinal directions, and in the intermediate directions.
Upon the pedestal is a heart-lotus; in its filaments are the eight Śaktis:
Vāṃ Dīptā, Vīṃ Sukṣmā, Vuṃ Jayā, and Vūṃ Bhadrīkā.
Having worshipped *veṃ* as the manifestation (*vibhūti*), *vaiṃ* as the stainless (*vimalā*), *vom* as the lightning that destroys the darkness,
*vauṃ* as the one facing all directions (*sarvatomukhī*), and *vaṃ* as the seat (*pīṭha*), one should worship the Sun;
O observer of good vows, having invoked him, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings with the heart-mantra and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
The letter *kha* and the two staff-bearers (*daṇḍinau*) are fierce; marrow is joined with the teeth, and flesh is long.
This entire [mantra] of the Sun, together with the aged wind and the heart, bestows everything.
The heart and the other limbs are to be worshipped in the directions of fire, the lord (north-east), the rakṣas (south-west), and the wind (north-west).

Having worshipped the weapons-mantra in front and the moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus in the directions starting from the east, situated within the pericarp and the cardinal points respectively with their own mantras,
one should apply nasal drops, collyrium, and so forth, using goat’s urine which wards off the grahas.
Ghee cooked with an āḍhaka of goat’s milk and pāṭhā, apathyā, vacā, śigru, sindhu, vyoṣa, and the individual fruits [of the three myrobalans] removes all grahas.
So too do vṛścikālī, phalī, kuṣṭha, the salts, and śārṅgaka.
To destroy epilepsy, one should have the patient drink that water;
one should also have him drink milk produced from the decoction of vidārī, kuśa, kāśa, and ikṣu.
Ghee prepared with *droṇa*, liquorice, and the juice of *kuṣmāṇḍa*, as well as *pañcagavya* ghee, are likewise [effective]; now hear the application that removes fever:
*oṃ bhasmāstrāya vidmahe ekadaṃṣṭrāya dhīmahi tanno jvaraḥ*.
One suffering from dyspnea should lick a mixture of black pepper, long pepper, rāsnā, jujube, oil, and jaggery;
or alternatively, one should take bhārgī with yaṣṭimadhu, honey, and ghee.
One should lick *pāṭhā*, *tiktā*, *kaṇā*, and *bhārgī* with honey;
or one should lick this triad— *dhātrī*, *viśvasitā*, *kṛṣṇā*, *mustā*, *kharjūra*, and *māgadhī*— along with *pivara* and honey, which destroys hiccup.
One suffering from cough should drink the juice of *kāmalī*, *jīra*, *māṇḍūkī*, *niśā*, and *dhātrī*.
Having eaten equal parts of the powder of *vyoṣa*, *padmaka*, *triphalā*, *kiṇḍaka*, *devadāru*,
and *rāsnā* with sugar, one will certainly be cured of cough.
Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Heart-Mantras of the Planets and Other Rites," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 300:
The Worship of the Sun (Sūryārcana)
Agni said:
"The bed, the staff, the bull, the lord, the purifier, and the four-faced one—
this seed-mantra, which accomplishes all aims, is declared for the purpose of the *piṇḍa*."
One should oneself [place] the long vowels and so forth, and the limbs (aṅgas) in their entirety within the seed-syllables;
likewise, the void (khāta), the poison (viṣa), together with the bindu, and all [the other elements].
The five seed-syllables of the Gaṇa yield great fruit when seen individually:
"Obeisance to the Gaṇa," to Jayanta, to Ekadaṃṣṭra, to Acalakarṇin, to Gajavaktra,
and to Mahoharahasta.
The five-limbed rite is common to all; success shall come from reciting it one hundred thousand times.
One should worship the forms on the cardinal petals for Gaṇādhipati, Gaṇeśvara, Gaṇanāyaka, and Gaṇakrīḍa, as well as the five limbs as before.
One should worship these— Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadaṃṣṭra, Mahodara, Gajavaktra,
Vikaṭa, and Vighnarāja, who is smoke-colored—
in the cardinal and intermediate directions, as well as in the various parts of these worlds, using the appropriate mudrā.
With the thumbs placed between the middle and index fingers and the fists closed,
he has four arms, is rich with sweetmeats (modaka), and is equipped with a staff, a noose, and a goad;
he is red in color, holds a tooth and food, possesses a lotus, and is surrounded by nooses and goads.

One should worship him especially on the fourth lunar day and constantly thereafter. By offering oblations made with the root of the white *arka* tree, along with sesame seeds, ghee, rice, curd, honey, and clarified butter, there shall be the attainment of all things; good fortune and the power of subjugation will come to pass.

The one who destroys sound, blood, life-force, and the elements; the staff-bearer, the sun-like Bhairava; the creator of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation; he who is enveloped by the two halves of the cosmic egg—his five forms are short vowels, and his limbs are the long vowels.

In the northeast, one should worship the Sun, who is as red as vermilion and has his beloved consort as his left half; in the corners starting from the southeast are Mars, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu. Having bathed according to the rules and worshipped the Sun preceded by the offering of *arghya*, [one should proceed].
To Kṛtānta [offer] the remains of the offering; to Aiśa, splendor; to Caṇḍa, the kindled lamp;
and [to the others], yellow pigment, saffron, water, red perfumes, unbroken rice, and sprouts.
Having offered bamboo, parched grain, rice, *śyāmāka* millet, sesame, and mustard seeds, together with *javā* flowers, and holding those in vessels upon his head,
he should prostrate himself on the ground with his knees and present the *arghya* offering to the Sun.

Having worshipped the planets with nine jars consecrated by one's own vidyā-mantra for the sake of pacifying the planets and other influences, and having performed the ritual bath and recitation for the Sun, one shall obtain victory in battle; [one should worship] the seed-syllable together with the fire-vowel (ra) and the nasal bindu.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) from the head to the feet and having worshipped with the root mantra and the mudrā,
one should contemplate oneself as the Sun according to the prescribed arrangement of the limbs;
and for meditation, [the deity] is yellow in killing and paralyzing, and white in nourishing.
One who is constantly devoted to consecration, recitation, meditation, worship, and fire-offerings shall delude Kṛṣṇa like a rainbow; such a person,
radiant, victorious, and glorious, shall attain victory at the ocean and other such places.
Having placed this [mantra] upon the betel and other items and having recited it, one should offer the uśīraka;
touching with the hand while reciting the nyāsa-bīja is said to bring [the object] under control.
Thus ends the three-hundredth chapter, titled "The Worship of the Sun," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 301:
Various Mantras
Agni said:
"The boat is considered to be joined to the sides of speech and action, with the semen as its child;
this Sarasvatī, whose end is the oblation and whose color is that of the region, is the preeminent Vidyā."
1. "And it should be held" (dhāryaḥ) — thus [it is read] in manuscript Kha...
2. "In the procedure for the lightning-strike" (vidyutpātavidhau) — thus [it is read] in manuscripts Gha, Ja, Ña, and Ṭa.
One who possesses equanimity should recite the mantra of one hundred and fourteen syllables, consisting of one hundred thousand repetitions;
it begins with *atri*, followed by *savahni*, then the left eye (*vāma*), the dot (*bindu*), and *indra*, ending with the heart (*hṛt*).
One should invoke and worship Śakra, the yellow bearer of the vajra and lotus;
one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of clarified butter and sesame seeds and perform an ablution with them.
By this, a king or similar person who has lost their kingdom and so forth shall regain their kingdom, sons, and other blessings.

Having worshipped Śiva, one should recite the mantra of the power (Śakti) known as Hṛllekhā— who holds a discus, a noose, and a goad, and who bestows protection and boons— from the eighth day until the fourteenth day; she is called Śaktidevā, the fire that consumes defects, and the wielder of the staff of punishment.
Through fire oblations and other rites, one shall attain good fortune, poetic talent, and become a possessor of cities.
Oṃ hrīṃ oṃ, obeisance to Kāma, for the welfare of all people, for the enchantment of all people, the blazing one; make the hearts of all people go toward my own self, make them do so, oṃ.
By means of the recitation (*japa*) and other practices of this mantra, one may bring the entire world under one's control.
*Oṃ hrīṃ cāmuṇḍe, burn [so-and-so] twice, cook [him/her] twice, bring [him/her] under my power twice, ṭha 2*. This is proclaimed as the subjugation-mantra (*vaśīkaraṇa-mantra*) of Cāmuṇḍā.
One should wash the private parts with a decoction of the three fruits to gain mastery [over them].
A woman, however, [should do so] with aśvagandhā, barley, niśā, camphor, and so forth. [The recipe consists of] eight grains of long pepper, rice, and twenty black peppers.

An ointment of *vṛhatī* and *rasa* brings [the subject] under control until death; likewise, an ointment consisting of the root of *kaṭīra*, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), and honey will have the same effect. Snow, *kapittha*, *karabha*, *māgadhī*, *madhuka*, and honey [are also used].
When an ointment made from these is applied to a couple, it brings them well-being;
likewise, honey mixed with the juice of *kadamba* and sugar,
along with *sahadevī*, *mahālakṣmī*, *putrajīvī*, and *kṛtāñjali*, [brings similar results].
This powder, when applied to the head, brings even a lion under one's supreme control.
One *prastha* each of the decoction of *triphalā* and sandalwood, and two *kuḍavas* each [of the other ingredients], [should be prepared].
Honey from *cuñcuka* flowers, as much as is required, along with bhr̥ṅga, hemarasa, and doṣā;
niśā cooked with ghee and dried in the shade is used for coloring when applied as a paste.
Vidārī, together with uccaṭā and powdered māṣa, mixed with sugar—
He who drinks milk daily while reciting the *Gāthā* mantra shall approach a hundred women.

[One should take] a powder of *gulma*, black gram, sesame, and rice, combined with milk and sugar; likewise, the roots of the *aśvattha*, bamboo, and *darbha* grass, as well as those of Viṣṇu and Śrī.

A woman desiring a son should drink the roots of *dūrvā* and *aśvagandha* with milk; likewise, for three days during her fertile period, she should drink the fibers of *kauntī*, *lakṣmī*, *dhātrī*, *vajra*, *loghra*, and the sprouts of *vaṭa* with ghee and milk for the sake of obtaining a son.

One desiring a son should drink milk with the root of the *śrī* plant and its *vaṭa*-sprouts; she should also administer as a nasal drop the juice of the goddesses of the *śrī*, the *vaṭa*-sprouts, and the *devīs*. She should take the root of the *śrī-padmaka* along with milk and the superior root of the *aśvattha* tree.
Cotton-seed fruit and sprouts combined with water;
the tips of *apāmārga* flowers and fresh buffalo milk— these four formulations, together with five other herbs, have been proclaimed for the sake of obtaining a son.
Sugar, blue water-lily flowers, akṣa, lodhra, sandalwood,
and sārivā should be administered with rice-water when a woman’s fetus is leaking; or she should lick parched grain, liquorice, sugar, grapes, honey, and ghee.
Having separately smeared the roots of *aṭarūṣaka* and the stalks of *kākamācī* below the navel, a woman gives birth easily.
For the discharge of blood and semen, one should drink red and white *jāvā* flowers.
Keśara, the root of bṛhatī, gopīyaṣṭi, tṛṇotpala,
goat’s milk, and oil— eating this [mixture] causes the growth of hair.
And when the hair is falling out, this [remedy] should be applied:
one *prastha* of oil from the juice of *dhātrī* and *bhṛṅga*, and one *āḍhaka* of milk.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed Tryambaka! Pacify, pacify! *culu* 2! *mili* 2! *bhida* 2! O *gomāninī*!
Hrūṃ phaṭ to the wielder of the discus.
In this village, protect the herd of cows, grant peace, grant peace! Ghaṇḍākarṇa, the great general, the hero, the one proclaimed to be of great strength,
the destroyer of enemies— may that Lord of the World protect me.
One should also separately assign these two verses and these two Gorakṣaka mantras.
Thus ends the three hundred and first chapter, titled "Various Mantras," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 302:
The Worship of the Syllables of the Limbs (*Aṅgākṣarārcana*)
Agni said:
When the moon is situated in its natal asterism and the sun is in the seventh sign, that time is to be known as the period of Pūṣan; at that time, one should examine the eclipse.
If one's throat and lips move from their positions, and the nose is crooked and the tongue black, his life shall indeed last for only seven days; [the sequence is:
*tāra*, sheep (*meṣa*), poison (*viṣa*), *dantī*, man (*nara*), long (*dīrgha*), wound (*vaṇa*), and taste (*rasa*).
To Krūḍholka, Maholka, and Vīrolka, let there be the crest-mantra (śikhā).
To Hyalka and Rāholska, this is the Vaiṣṇava eight-syllable mantra.
One should sequentially place the eight-syllable mantra upon the joints of those eight fingers, beginning with the little finger, using the tip of the thumb; then,
when the middle finger is joined to the thumb, one should likewise place it there.
One should place the extraction of that [mantra] on the little toe, and then the extraction of the seed-syllable.
These three [syllables] are red, pale-yellow, smoky-grey, green, golden, and white;
one should place these syllables in sequence, visualizing them as having such forms and being awakened by meditative realization.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the limbs and the seed-syllables upon the hands and the body;
as it is done for oneself, so should the placement be performed for the deity, excluding the hands.
One should worship with perfumes and flowers the phonemes located in the heart and other stations.
One should place Dharma and so forth, Agni and so forth, and Adharma and so forth upon the limbs, the seat, and the lotus;
there, one should sequentially place the three mandalas— the sun, the moon, and the fire— which pervade the filaments and the pericarp, according to their respective divisions.
The qualities (guṇas), such as *tantra* and *sattva*, are located in the filaments, and the powers (*śaktis*)— namely Vimalā, Utkarṣaṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, and Yogā— are situated there in sequence.
Then, Prahvī, Satyā, Īśānā, and Anugrahā are likewise positioned in the center.
Having worshipped the yoga-pīṭha and invoked Hari, one should perform the sacrifice.
Water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, yellow garments, and ornaments—
this fivefold service (pañcopacāra) is all offered with the root mantra.
The four forms, Vāsudeva and the others, are to be worshipped in the cardinal directions;
one should worship Śrī, Sarasvatī, Rati, and Śānti in the intermediate directions.
[Note: According to manuscript *kha*, the sequence is heart, face, eyes, head, feet, knees, genitals, and hands.]

One should worship, in due order, the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the pestle, and the sword and the Śārṅga bow, together with the forest garland, in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Having worshipped Tārkṣya outside, one should worship Viṣvaksena and Someśa in front of the Deity, outside the enclosure;
by worshipping them along with Indra and the other attendants, one shall obtain everything.
Thus ends the three hundred and second chapter, titled "The Worship of the Syllables of the Limbs," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 303:
The Mantras for the Worship of the Five-Syllable and Other [Mantras]
Agni said: "Meṣa, saṃjñā, viṣa, sādyam, asti, dīrghodaka, rasa—
this five-syllable mantra bestows auspiciousness and is of the nature of Śiva."
By thoroughly worshipping Tāraka and the others, one shall attain divinity and other such states.

The Supreme Brahman consists of knowledge; it is the supreme intellect, Śiva, who resides in the heart as its power, the Lord of all, appearing distinct from the forms of Brahmā and the other deities.

The syllables of the mantra are the five elements, their corresponding mantras are the objects of the senses, as well as the five vital breaths beginning with *prāṇa* and the organs of knowledge and action;
everything is the five-syllabled Brahman, and likewise, it culminates in the eight-syllabled one.

One who has gathered the requisites produced according to the Tantra, having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rule, should sprinkle the site of initiation with cow products while impelled by the mantra.
In the middle [of the pavilion], outside the archways—according to the manuscripts Kha, Ja, and Ña:
"The scattering of rice and other rites [should be performed] with the mantras of the primary deity's limbs and vidyās. (p. 119)

Having prepared the *caru* and the milk, he should then divide it into three parts. Having offered one part and performed the oblation with another, the preceptor, together with his disciples, should consume the remaining portion.
Then, having sipped water and performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkṛtya*), the teacher should give [the remainder] to the disciple.
Having consecrated a tooth-stick produced from a milk-tree or similar source by reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
and having cleansed it, used it to clean the teeth, and rinsed the mouth, one of pure mind should cast it on the ground toward the east, north, or west; this is auspicious.
Furthermore, having secured that returning disciple with the child-binding (*śiśubandha*) and other protections,
the wise one should sleep upon a bed of *darbha* grass on the sacrificial altar together with him.

Having observed that he has fallen into deep sleep, the disciple should, at dawn, awaken the Guru with auspicious words of success and expressions of devotion; then, one should perform the worship of the mandala once again,
worshipping the mandala described as Bhadraka and so forth, which bestows all accomplishments.
Having bathed and sipped water, and having smeared his body with clay while reciting mantras,

a person should bathe in a sacred ford (śivatīrtha) preceded by the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite; then, having performed the ritual sprinkling of water on his hands, the wise man should proceed to the worship and other rites.
One should perform the lotus posture with the root mantra and, by means of it, practice inhalation (*pūraka*) and retention (*kumbhaka*).
Having joined the self upward to the end of the crest-lock at a distance of twelve finger-breadths,
one should dry up and burn one's own body and then drench it with nectar.
Having inflamed [the fire], one should lead the self back into that divine body.
By doing so, there shall be purification of the self; having performed this and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should begin the worship in sequence:
the mountains and other features are black, white, dark green, red, and yellow.
The syllables of the mantra are the limbs of Daṇḍin; within them reside all the forms.
[Note:
"The disciple, having sipped water," etc.]
Having assigned the limbs everywhere from the thumb to the little finger,
one should assign the syllables of the mantra to the feet, the private parts, the heart, the mouth, and the head.
Having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) starting from the head, one should perform the placement of the limbs (aṅga) using the root mantra.
One should place the feet of the pedestal—red, yellow, dark blue, and black—arising according to their respective times.
One should place the limbs of one's own body with the mantras, as well as Adharma and the others in the cardinal directions.

Therein, upon the lotus and the triad of maṇḍalas beginning with the solar, one should place the [nine] qualities; on the petals starting from the east and so forth are Kāmā and the others, nine in number,
and above the pericarp are Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and Kalavikāriṇī in sequence.
Balavikāriṇī, Arthabalapramathanī,
Sarvabhūtadamanī, and the ninth, Manonmanī;
white, red, black, yellow, dark-blue, and said to be like fire.
One should sequentially visualize those spears as having a blackish-red hue and the form of flames;
then, from the heart-lotus, one should invoke Śiva— who is crystal-like in luster, four-armed, and holds a fruit and a trident— upon the infinite yoga-seat (anantayogapīṭha).
[He is] with the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting, five-faced, and three-eyed.
On the petals, the five forms beginning with Tatpuruṣa are to be established;
in the east is Tatpuruṣa, who is white, and Aghora, who has eight arms and is black.

He has four arms and faces and is yellow; Sadyojāta is in the west. Vāmadeva, who delights in women, has four faces and arms and is reddish; he is in the north. In the northeast is Īśāna, the bestower of all, who is white and has five faces.

One should worship the infinite and subtle Lord of Siddhas, who has a single eye, with his desired limbs according to the prescribed rule; one should then worship [the deities] in the directions starting from the east:
Ekarudra, Trinetra, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin.
In the intermediate directions beginning with the northeast, these Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) are seated upon lotuses:
white, yellow, white, red, smoky, red, crimson, and white.
One should worship Śūla, Aśani, Śara, Īśvāsa, and Vāha; then the four-faced ones;
Umā, Vaṇḍeśa, Nandīśa, Mahākāla, Gaṇeśvara, Vṛṣa, Bhṛṅgiriṭi, and Skanda, starting from the northern direction and proceeding clockwise.
One should worship the vajra, the spear, the staff, the sword, the noose, the banner,

the mace, the trident, the discus, and the lotus, starting from the east; and having worshipped the deity, one should then have the consecrated disciple drink the five products of the cow (gavyapañcaka).
Having sipped water and sprinkled [the disciple] with the ends of his eyes, he should bind his eyes with a thread;
then he should lead the disciple through the door into the southern part of the pavilion, where the Guru, seated upon kuśa grass and other seats, shall purify him.
Having withdrawn the primordial principles (tattvas) in sequence into the ultimate reality (paramārtha),
the teacher should again cause the disciple to arise by way of emanation (sṛṣṭimārga).
Then, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the disciple, he should lead him in circumambulation.
Having led [the disciple] to the western door, one should cause him to cast a handful of flowers.
One should designate that name as his primary name upon which the flowers fall,
into a pit dug at the side of the sacrificial ground, provided it is equipped with a level girdle.
Having generated the Śiva-fire and performed the sacrifice, one should again worship it with the disciple;
then, having dissolved the disciple— who has become identical with oneself— into meditation through the process of dissolution,
and having regenerated him once more, one should place consecrated darbha grasses into his hand.
One should offer the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth into the fire by means of the [mantras] beginning with the heart (hṛdaya).
(Note: 1. "kamalānanā" is the reading in manuscript ña;
2. "sandhādimekhale" is the reading in manuscript kha.)
Having offered one hundred oblations for each [deity], one should perform the fire sacrifice with the root mantra of Vyoman.
Having performed the offering, one should make the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and offer eight oblations with the Astra mantra.
For the sake of purification, one should perform the expiation (prāyaścitta) and then complete the remainder;
having worshipped the consecrated jar (kumbha), one should sprinkle the disciple with its water while he sits upon the pedestal.
Having imparted the rules of conduct (samaya) to the disciple, one should honor one's own guru with gold and other offerings.
The initiation for the five-syllabled mantra of Viṣṇu and others is indeed declared in this very same way:
*e*. Thus ends the three hundred and third chapter, titled "The Mantras for the Worship of the Five-Syllabled [Mantra] and Others," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 304:
The Fifty-Five Names of Viṣṇu.
Agni said:
"That man who indeed mutters the fifty-five names of Viṣṇu partakes of the fruit of mantra-recitation and other rites, and his worship at sacred fords and such becomes inexhaustible."
One should worship Puṇḍarīkākṣa at Puṣkara, Gadādhara at Gayā, Rāghava at Citrakūṭa, and Daityasūdana at Prabhāsa;
likewise, Jaya at Jayantī and Jayanta at Hastināpura.
One should worship Vārāha at Vardhamāna, Cakrapāṇi in Kaśmīra,
Janārdana at Kubjāmra, Keśava in Mathurā,
Hṛṣīkeśa at Kubjāmra, and Jaṭādhara at Gaṅgādvāra.
One should worship Hari in the form of Mahāyoga at Śālagrāma, at Mount Govardhana;
the four-armed [Viṣṇu] at Piṇḍāraka, and the one bearing the conch at Śaṅkhoddhāra.
One should know Vāmana at Kurukṣetra, Trivikrama on the Yamunā, Viśveśvara at the Śoṇa, Kapila at the eastern ocean,
Viṣṇu in the great ocean, and [the Lord] at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
They know Vanamāla at Kiṣkindhyā, and the god Raivataka; Mahāyoga on the banks of Kāśī, and Ripuñjaya at Virajā;
Ajita at Viśākhayūpa, and Lokabhāvana in Nepāla.
One should know Kṛṣṇa to be at Dvārakā, Madhusūdana on Mount Mandara,
and one should remember Hari, the destroyer of enemies, at Śālagrāma;
one should remember Puruṣa at Pūruṣavaṭa and the Lord of the World at Vimala.
One should worship Ananta in the Saindhava forest, Śārṅgadhārin in Daṇḍaka, Śauri in Utpalāvartaka, the Lord of Śrī on the Narmadā,
Dāmodara on Raivataka, and Jalaśāyin in the Nandā.
One should know Gopīśvara in the Sindhu ocean, Acyuta on Mount Māhendra,
Devadeveśa on Sahya mountain, Vaikuṇṭha in the Māgadha forest,
Sarvapāpahara on the Vindhya mountains, and Puruṣottama in Oḍra.
Know the Self within your heart, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who recite its name.
Vaiśravaṇa is indeed in every banyan tree, Śiva at every crossroads,
Rāma on every mountain, and Madhusūdana everywhere.
Remembering Nara on earth, Garuḍadhvaja in the sky, and Vāsudeva everywhere— by recollecting Vaśiṣṭha— one partakes of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
By chanting these names of Viṣṇu, one shall obtain everything.
Whatever *śrāddha*, gift, recitation, or libation is performed in these sacred fields,
all that becomes multiplied ten millionfold; upon death, one becomes identical with Brahman.
Whoever should read or even hear [this], being purified, shall attain heaven.
Thus ends the three hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Fifty-five Names of Viṣṇu," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 305:
Mantras of the Nārasiṃha and Others.
Agni said:

Stambhana (paralysis), vidveṣaṇa (enmity), uccāṭana (expulsion), utsādana (destruction), bhrama (delusion), māraṇa (killing), and vyādhi (disease)—these are known as the six acts (kṣudrakarma); listen now as their release is described.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Mad Rudra! Bhrāma 2! Bhramaya 2! Terrify so-and-so!
Cause him to whirl about 2! With your fierce form, hūṃ phaṭ ṭha 2!
Having recited this at night in a cremation ground three hundred thousand times, one should offer oblations of honey.
The enemy is constantly tormented by the fire of the funeral pyre with fuel-sticks of *dhūrta* wood.
Having recited the mantra, one should pierce an image made of black gold-ore with golden needles at its throat or heart; thus the enemy shall die.
The ashes of a donkey, a young child, and a funeral pyre, along with *brahmadaṇḍī* and *markaṭī*—
one should cast this powder, consecrated by mantra, either into a house or upon the head to effect eradication.
*Bhṛgu*, *ākāśa*, blazing fire, *bhṛgu*, fire, *varma*, and *phaṭ*.

Thus, in the thousand-spoked [wheel]: *hūṃ phaṭ* for the Ācakra, *svāhā* for the heart; *śivaḥ* for the Vicakra, then the *śikhācakra*; then the armor (*kavaca*) for the Vicakra, and then the eye (*netra*).
The weapon of the discus is prescribed; the wheel of flames is as before.
The Śārṅga and Sudarśana are the destroyers of minor planetary influences and the means for accomplishing all goals.
One should indeed place the syllables upon his head, eyes, mouth, heart, secret place, and feet;
[one should meditate on him] seated upon a lotus within a wheel, with the luster of fire, possessing fangs and four arms,
holding in his hands a conch, a discus, a mace, a lotus, a rod, and a goad.
The archer with tawny hair and eyes, who pervades the three worlds with his bowstring—
when pierced by the fire from his navel, diseases, planetary afflictions, yellow discuses, red maces, and dark intermediate tones perish.
The rim is white, and there is a black-colored line on the outside; with these colors, one should draw two wheels in this manner, alternating between the spokes and the intervals between them.
First, having brought water from a jar and placed it within the field of vision.
Having offered the Sudarśana [mantra] there, one should perform oblations in sequence upon the southern wheel:
clarified butter, apāmārga twigs, unbroken rice, sesame, mustard seeds,
milk-rice, and cow’s ghee, each eight thousand times.
The one who knows the ritual procedure should throw the remnants of each substance into the pitcher;
he should place the *piṇḍa* prepared by way of departure into that same pitcher.
He should deposit Viṣṇu and all other [deities] right there, and likewise on the south side.
Homage to the followers of Viṣṇu, who bring peace to all! May they accept [this] for the sake of peace; homage!
With this mantra, one should offer the *bali* oblation with the water remaining from the fire-oblation.

Having placed a leaf of the milky tree (palāśa) upon a vessel fashioned from a wooden plank and filled with cow's products, the twice-born should perform two oblations in this manner in each of the directions;
