these two oblations, accompanied by sacrificial fees, destroy spirits and other such evils.
1. Regarding the two syllables [in the word *gavyākta*]:
according to Kha, it is extracted as *kṣudra* from the leafless [forms] written on leaves of the *gavyākta* tree. (p. 126)

With *dūrvā* grass for longevity, with lotuses for prosperity, with *uḍumbara* fruits for sons, with clarified butter in the cow-pen for the attainment of cattle, and with all kinds of trees for intelligence:
*Oṃ kṣauṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Nārasiṃha, who wears a garland of flames.*
To the one with blazing fangs, fire-eyes, the destroyer of all *rakṣasas*, the annihilator of all *bhūtas*, and the destroyer of all fevers: burn! burn! cook! cook! protect! protect! *hūṃ phaṭ*!
This is the mantra of Nārasiṃha, which wards off all sins and calamities.
By means of recitation (*japa*) and other rites, one may remove minor planetary influences, epidemics, poisons, and diseases.
A powder made from the flesh of a frog will cause the solidification of water and fire.
Thus ends [the section on] the *Nārasiṃha* and other mantras in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter Three Hundred and Fifth:
Chapter Three Hundred and Sixth.
Regarding the mantras for deluding the three worlds,
Agni said:
"I shall declare the mantra that deludes the three worlds for the sake of attaining the four aims of human life."
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ oṃ, obeisance to Puruṣottama, you who possess the form of the Supreme Person, abode of Lakṣmī, agitator of the entire world,
piercer of the hearts of all women, and creator of intoxication and madness throughout the three worlds.
Scorch, scorch! Inflame, inflame! Dry up, dry up! Slay, slay!
Paralyze, paralyze! Dissolve, dissolve! Attract, attract! O most fortunate one, bestower of all auspiciousness, granter of desires, kill [Name] with the discus, the mace, and the sword—[all]...!
:P 127 Pierce with arrows! Bind with the noose! Strike with the goad! Hurry! Hurry! What are you waiting for? Until then, my desired goal shall be accomplished! HŪṂ PHAṬ!
Homage!

Oṃ! To the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), who causes intoxication with passion throughout the three worlds, *hūṃ phaṭ*, homage to the heart! Draw [us] in, O one of great power, *hūṃ phaṭ*, homage to the weapon (*astra*) of the Lord of the Three Worlds!
Strike 2, shatter 2 the minds of all people, bring them under my control 2, HŪṂ PHAṬ!
To the Eye, O Enchanter of the Three Worlds, Hṛṣīkeśa of incomparable form,
Attractor of the Hearts of All Women, come 2, homage!
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as described for the root mantra using the *saṅgākṣiṇyāyaka*,
and having worshipped, recited [the mantra] fifty thousand times, and performed the consecration (*abhiṣeka*),
one should offer a hundred oblations into the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), the sacrificial fire (*agni*), and the divine fire (*devikavahni*).
Separately, one should offer curd, ghee, milk, sacrificial porridge with clarified butter, boiled milk,
unbroken rice, sesame seeds, barley, the three sweets, flowers, fruit, curd, and fuel sticks— each twelve times with the root mantra, and a thousand times with the *akṣata* mantra.

Having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he should cause the disciple to eat the remaining sacrificial porridge (*caru*) mixed with clarified butter; having fed the Brahmins, he should satisfy the preceptor (*ācārya*), and thus Manu succeeds.
Having bathed and sipped water according to the rules, he should enter the sacrificial hall while maintaining silence.
Having gone there and assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), one should dry the body according to the prescribed rite.
First, one should place the Sudarśana [mantra], which destroys demons and wards off obstacles, in the various directions.
Then, one should visualize the five-seeded [mantra] situated in the center of the navel, smoke-colored and consisting of fierce wind.

One should meditate on the seed-syllable *raṃ* situated in the heart-lotus as it separates all impurity from the body without exception; having recollected it, one should burn [the body] with its flames spreading upwards,
downwards, and across, and then drench the physical form at the crown of the head.

Having meditated thus, with the nectars flowing through the path of the suṣumnā both externally and internally, one whose body is thus purified should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) three times with the mantra.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) ending with the hands, one should place the *śakti* on the head and face,
in the secret parts, the throat, the cardinal directions, the heart, the armpits, and throughout the entire body;
having invoked [the deity] from the solar orb into the heart-lotus through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
With the syllable *Tāreṇa*, one should remember that Supreme Self, endowed with all auspicious marks:
"We know Him who deludes the three worlds; we meditate upon Smara; may that Viṣṇu inspire us."
Having performed self-worship according to the prescribed rite and having consecrated the sacrificial materials with pure vessels, one should worship Him upon a pedestal prepared for the ritual,
situated on a lotus atop Garuḍa.

Beautiful in every limb, having attained the fullness of age, grace, and youth; with copper-hued eyes rolling from intoxication, noble and overwhelmed by passion; adorned with divine garlands, garments, ointments, and ornaments, his face was graced with a smile.
Viṣṇu, who is adorned with various kinds of numerous retinues and attendants,
who bestows grace upon the worlds, who is gentle, whose splendor is like that of a thousand suns,
who carries five arrows, whose gaze is fixed on his attained desire, and who has two or four arms.
One should meditate upon [the deity] surrounded by celestial women, his eyes fixed upon the face of the Goddess,
holding a discus, a conch, a bow, a sword, a mace, a pestle, and a goad.
One should worship him holding a noose, from the invocation until the dismissal;

and one should worship Śrī, who stands upon his left thigh and shank, embracing her husband with one hand, holding a lotus and a fly-whisk in her other hands, full-bodied, and endowed with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem.
One should worship Hari, who wears a garland and yellow garments, and is adorned with the discus and other [emblems].
Oṃ Sudarśana, great king of wheels, terrifying to the wicked! Cut, cut! Rend asunder, rend asunder! Devour the supreme mantras! Eat them! Consume all spirits! Hūṃ!
:p 129 phaṭ oṃ jalacarāya svāhā / khaḍgatīkṣṇa chinda 2 khaḍgāya.
Homage! To the one with the spotted bow and arrow, Hūṃ Phaṭ!
We know the host of spirits; we meditate upon the fourfold; may that Brahman inspire us.
Sambartaka, blow away! Poṭhaya 2 hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Bind with the noose! Ākarṣaya 2 hūṃ phaṭ!

Having drawn [the weapons] with the hook, one should worship the weapons on the arms in sequence with these respective mantras: *oṃ pakṣirājāya hrūṃ phaṭ*. *Hūṃ phaṭ*. With these mantras, one should worship the weapons on the arms in order. *Oṃ pakṣirājāya hrūṃ phaṭ*.
One should worship Tārkṣya in the pericarp and the deities of the limbs according to the rule;
the Śaktis, such as Indra and others, are in the yantras, while Tārkṣya and the others hold chowries.
At the end, the Śaktis are to be employed, and at the beginning, Sureśa and the others, along with Daṇḍin.
Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī are yellow; Rati, Prīti, and Jayā are white;
Kīrti and Kānti are white; Tuṣṭi and Puṣṭi are dark blue, as declared by Smara.
One should worship the god Viṣṇu, ending with the lords of the quarters, for the attainment of desired goals.
Having meditated and recited this mantra, one should offer oblations and perform the consecration:
*oṃ śrīṃ krīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ trailokyamohanāya viṣṇave namaḥ*.
By means of this worship and other rites, one obtains all desires as before.
One should constantly satisfy [the deity] with waters and *sammohanī* flowers;
Brahmā, Śakra, and Śrīdaṇḍin are the seed-syllable that deludes the three worlds.
Having recited [the mantra] three hundred thousand times and having performed one hundred thousand oblations with *bilva* fruits mixed with clarified butter,
with rice grains, fruits, perfumes, and so forth,
or with *dūrvā* grass, one shall obtain long life.
For he who is pleased by such rites as consecration and fire-offerings is the bestower of desired fruits, [offered] with fruits, flowers, and so forth.
Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, the Boar, the Lord of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; O Lord of the Earth, grant me [the earth]—
svāhā to the heart!
By reciting this five-limbed mantra ten thousand times daily, one shall obtain long life and sovereignty.
Thus ends the three hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Mantra for Enchanting the Three Worlds," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 307:
The Worship of Trailokyamohanī, Lakṣmī, and Others.
Agni said:
"O Chest, O Carrier of the Fire, O Yāmā, O Eyes, O Staff-bearer, O Śrī, giver of all accomplishments!
Salutations to Mahāśrī, to Mahāsiddhi, to you who possess the radiance of a great lightning flash!"
Homage to the goddess Śrī Vijayā!
O Gaurī of great power, bind, bind! Homage! Hūṃ!
O you of great body, lotus-handed one, hūṃ phaṭ! Homage to Śrī!
To Śrī, phaṭ; obeisance to Śrī. To Śrī, phaṭ; śrīṃ, obeisance.
To Śrī, obeisance to the Giver of Fortune.
Svāhā svāhā śrī phaṭ!
Its limbs are said to be nine; one should rely upon even one among them.
Having recited it three hundred thousand times or one hundred thousand times with the beads of a rosary made of lotus seeds, it bestows prosperity.
By worshipping Śrī in the house of Śrī or in the house of Viṣṇu, one shall obtain wealth.
One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of rice grains smeared with clarified butter into a fire of khadira wood;
the king will become submissive, and there shall be ever-increasing prosperity and fortune.
By sprinkling mustard-seed water, all malevolent planets are destroyed.
By offering one hundred thousand oblations of *bilva* fruits, Lakṣmī is attained and an increase in wealth occurs.
Then, one should meditate upon the four-gated palace of Śakra within the heart.
One should meditate upon Balākā, who is short and dark-complexioned, holding a white lotus, with her two arms raised, playing at the gateway as before;
she holds a red lotus with her upraised hand.
One should contemplate Vanamālinī at the southern gate, white-limbed and green, holding a white lotus aloft with both arms;
one should meditate upon the messenger of Śrī named Vibhīṣikā at the western gate.
Outside the door of Śāṅkarī, in its center, there is an eight-petaled lotus;
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are to be meditated upon upon the lotus petals, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Those [elephants] with the luster of collyrium, milk, saffron, and gold, well-adorned with fine garments,
are located on the petals starting from the southeast; likewise, Guggulu, Kuruṇṭaka,
Damaka, and Salila— these female elephants have the radiance of silver.
One should visualize Śrī upon the pericarp; she holds golden jars, has four arms, possesses a golden luster, with her two upper hands holding lotuses,
her right hand displaying the gesture of fearlessness, and her left hand granting boons.
Having meditated upon her, who is clad in white perfumes and garments and bears a single garland of silver and weapons, and having worshipped her along with her retinue, one shall obtain everything;
however, one should not wear the flowers of the *droṇa* or *abja* nor the leaves of the *śrīvṛkṣa* on the head.
One should avoid salt and *āmalaka* fruit on the lunar days corresponding respectively to the serpent (*nāga*) and the sun (*āditya*).
Eating milk-rice (*pāyasa*), one should recite the *Śrīsūkta* and perform an ablution for Śrī.
Having visualized Śrī upon one's head through the ritual sequence beginning with invocation and ending with dismissal, one should worship her.
The separate application of bilva, ghee, lotus, and milk-rice leads to prosperity.
Poison, the buffalo, the beloved of the earth (the cow), fire, the udrija, light, and the two-faced one (the horse)—[these are the components].
Oṃ hrīṃ, O crusher of the great buffalo, ṭha ṭha! Homage to the root mantra that destroys the buffalo! Confound the enemy-buffalo, confound him! Hūṃ phaṭ!
ṬHA ṬHA! Make the buffalo neigh! HŪṂ! Strike the buffalo! O Goddess! HŪṂ! O Slayer of the Buffalo! PHAṬ!
This is declared to be the Heart of Durgā, complete with its ancillaries, which accomplishes all aims.
One should worship that Goddess as prescribed, as well as the pedestal situated within the limbs,
with the mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ durge rakṣaṇi svāhā* and *namaḥ durgāyai varavarṇyai*.
Homage to the Noble One, Kanakaprabhā, Kṛttikā, Abhayapradā, Kanyakā,
and Surūpā.
One should worship these forms situated upon the petals in sequence with the initial vowels:
to the Discus, the Conch, the Mace, the Sword, the Bow, and the Arrow;
one should worship this Durgā, ending with the World-Guardians, using the eighth vowel and the others.
The Durgā-yoga brings longevity, prosperity, and victory over one's enemies;
an oblation of sesame seeds with the Īśāna-mantra effects subjugation.
Victory is achieved with lotuses, peace with dūrvā grass, and desire with palāśa flowers.
Through the *kākapakṣa* [mantra], there shall be nourishment; death, hatred, and the like shall occur;
and Manu shall remove everything, including the onset of fear from Brahma and minor deities.
Oṃ Durge Durge Rakṣaṇi Svāhā!

Having meditated upon oneself as the goddess Śyāmā, four-armed, fierce in form, with three eyes, and holding a conch, discus, lotus, and trident, one becomes the protective Muditā, united with the limbs of Jayadurgā.
One should conquer these at the beginning of battle; one should worship them for victory with a sword and other weapons.
Thus ends the three hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Worship of Trailokyamohanī, Lakṣmī, and Others," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Three Hundred and Eight: The Chapter on the Eight [Qualities] (Aṣṭādhikatriśatatamo ’dhyāyaḥ)
Agni said:
"I shall now fully describe the limbs of Tvaritā, which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
Oṃ, salutation to the Support-Energy (Ādhāraśakti).
Oṃ Hrīṃ, twice, salutation to the Great Lion (Mahāsiṃha). Oṃ, salutation to the Lotus (Padma).
Oṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ khecachekṣaḥ / strīṃ oṃ hrūṃ kṣaiṃ hrūṃ phaṭ, obeisance to Tvaritā. Khe ca, obeisance to the heart.
*Cha* to the head, *namaḥ*;
*che-kṣaḥ* to the crest-lock, *namaḥ*; *kṣastrī* to the armor, *namaḥ*.
Strīṃ hrūṃ, salutation to the eyes;
hrūṃ khaḥ, salutation to the weapon, phaṭ; oṃ, may we know the Tvaritā-vidyā.
And we meditate upon the swift vidyā; may the Goddess inspire us.
Homage to Śrīpraṇītā! Homage to Hrūṃkārā!
Oṃ kheca, homage to the heart; homage to Khecarī;
Oṃ caṇḍā, homage.
Homage to Chedanī; homage to Kṣepaṇī;
homage to Strī, Hrūṃ, and Kāryā.
Protect [him] from Kṣemaṅkarī, Jayā, and Kiṅkara!
Oṃ, by the command of Tvaritā, be firm! Vaṣaṭ!
"Totalā," "Tvaritā," and "Tūrṇā"— thus is this Vidyā proclaimed.

[One should place them] in sequence upon the head, the forehead, the crown, the throat, the heart, the navel, the secret place, the two thighs, the two knees, the two shanks, the two calves, and the two feet.
Having placed the limbs and having placed the mantras, one should place the all-pervading [mantra] in its entirety.
Pārvatī and Śavarī are the sovereigns, with hands granting boons and fearlessness;
she has a peacock for her vehicle, a crest of peacock feathers, and garments of young sprouts.
Seated upon a lion throne, endowed with a parasol of peacock feathers,
the goddess is three-eyed, dark-complexioned, and adorned with a forest garland.
Having become one whose ornaments are Brahmin serpents, whose bracelets and armlets are [serpents],
whose waist-band is Vaiśya serpents, and whose anklets are made of Śūdra serpents—
one who has thus assumed this form should recite that mantra one million times.
In ancient times, Īśa assumed the form of a Kirāta and Gaurī likewise appeared as such;
one should recite her mantra, meditate upon her, and worship her, for she removes all obstacles, poisons, and the like.
She is to be worshipped on the eight lion-thrones, sequentially on the petals starting from the east.
One should worship these [deities] with the seed-syllable *Śrī*: Aṅgagāyatrī at the tips of the petals, Praṇītā and Hūṃkārā and so forth, and Phaṭkārī in front of the Goddess;
they possess the colors of the world-protectors' weapons, while Phaṭkārī holds a bow.
Jayā and Vijayā, holding golden staffs, are to be worshipped as the two door-keepers;
outside of them are Kiṅkarā, Varvarī, Muṇḍī, and Laguḍī.
Having worshipped thus with the appropriate materials, one should perform oblations in a fire-pit shaped like a womb (yoni).
With *arjuna* flowers one gains gold; with wheat, the abundance of nourishment;
with barley, grains, and sesame seeds, there is the attainment of all success and the destruction of calamities.
With *akṣa* fruits, one brings about the madness of the enemy; and with *śālmalī* flowers, his death.
With *jambu* flowers there is the acquisition of wealth and grain; with blue lotuses (*nīlotpala*), satisfaction;
with red lotuses (*raktotpala*), great prosperity; with *kunda* flowers, great success;
with *mallikā* jasmine, the agitation of the city; and with white water-lilies (*kumuda*), the gain of people.

Through *aśoka* flowers there shall be the gain of a son; through *pāṭala* flowers, an auspicious wife; through mangoes, long life; through sesame seeds, prosperity; through *bilva* fruits, glory; through *campaka* flowers, desired wealth;
and through *madhuka* flowers and *bilva* fruits, one may attain omniscience.
Through three hundred thousand recitations, all attainments are gained; likewise through burnt offerings, meditation, and sacrifice.
Having worshipped within the mandala with the Gāyatrī, one should offer twenty-five oblations.
One should offer three hundred [oblations] starting from the root; by means of the sprouts, one becomes initiated.
Having first drunk the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should always consume the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
Thus ends the three hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Worship of Tvaritā," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 309:
Now begins the three hundred and ninth chapter.
Agni, beginning with the mantra of Tvaritā, said:
"I shall now declare another Tvaritā-vidyā, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
In the pure Vajrākula mandala drawn with colored powders, one should worship the goddess in the center of the lotus,
the eight vajras in the cardinal and intermediate directions, and the pathway.
A man should quickly draw the beauty and ornamentation of the gateway and meditate [upon the goddess]:
she has eighteen arms, is seated upon a lion with her left leg firmly planted and her right leg doubled up, resting upon a footstool.
Adorned with serpent ornaments, he holds in his right hands a vajra, a skull-cup, a sword, a wheel, a mace,
a trident, an arrow, and likewise a spear, as well as the gesture of granting boons;
and in [his left hands] a bow, a noose, an arrow, a bell, and the threatening gesture.
On the left side, he holds the conch, the goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and likewise the boon-granting gesture as weapons;
by worshipping him, there shall be the destruction of enemies, and one conquers the kingdom with ease.
One shall possess long life and national prosperity, and partake in divine and other supernatural accomplishments.
(Note: "Vajrārgale" refers to the [mantra] Vajrārgalā.)
The thirteen netherworlds (pātālas), ending with the realm of the fire of time (kālāgni) at the end of the universe;
beginning from the vowel *oṃ* and extending to that which denotes the entire cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
From the syllable *oṃ*, one should cause [the breath] to revolve; thereafter come Tvaritā and Totalā.
I shall now declare the introductory section: one should write the group of vowels upon the ground.
The palate-group is the *ka*-group, and the third is that of the tongue and palate.
The fourth [is formed] at the palate and the tip of the tongue; the fifth is between the tongue and the teeth.
The sixth is endowed with eight folds; the seventh is the mixed class (the labials). The sibilants (ūṣman) constitute the eighth class. Then one should extract the mantra.
Mounted upon the sixth vowel, joined with the final of the sibilants (ūṣman) and the bindu,
and combined with the second letter of the palatal class (tālavya-varga) and the eleventh vowel—
this is the first [syllable], which arises solely from the contact of the tongue and the palate. AP_309.011cd–309.012ab/
And one should place that very same second [syllable] below;
it is joined with the eleven vowels, and the first [consonant] is from the palatal group (tālavya).
One should see the second [consonant] of the sibilants (ūṣman) joined below.
One should join the second of the sibilants (ūṣman) conjoined with the sixteenth vowel (au);
then, through the contact of the tongue and the teeth, one should place the first [consonant] below.
Furthermore, from the second of the mixed group (the labials), one should again place it below.
One should join the fourth vowel with the first letter of the palatal class;
one should place the second of the sibilants (ūṣman) below it.
Then, one should join the end of the sibilants with the eleventh vowel and include the bindu.
Mounted upon the five vowels by means of the union of the two lips is the second syllable; another [syllable] is at the tip of the tongue through its union with the palate. (Note:
The reading *ūṣmāṇasya* is not correct.)
First, these [syllables] extracted by half a vowel should be joined with the fifth [vowel];
beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, one should recite them during the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) accompanied by *svāhā*.

Oṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraḥ hṛdayaṃ (the heart); hāṃ hṛśceti śiraḥ (hāṃ hṛśceti is the head). Hrīṃ jvala jvala śikhā (hrīṃ jvala jvala is the crest-lock); syāt kavacaṃ hanudvayam (the armor is on the two jaws). Hrīṃ śrīṃ kṣūnnetratrayāya (hrīṃ śrīṃ kṣūṃ is for the three eyes); vidyānetraṃ prakīrtitam (this is proclaimed as the eye-mantra of the Vidyā). Kṣauṃ haḥ khauṃ.
"Hūṃ phaṭ! One should first assign the secret limbs for the weapon.
I shall now declare the limbs of Tvaritā; listen to me regarding the limbs of the Vidyā.
The first two are declared to be the heart, while three or four are desired as the heads."

The fifty-fifth and fifty-sixth are said to be the *śikhā*; the seventh and eighth are the *kavaca*. The ninth, characterized by half a syllable, becomes the *netra*, which is designated as *tota*; thereafter comes the *vajratuṇḍa*.
*Kha kha hūṃ*—these are the ten seed-syllables of Vajratuṇḍendradrūtikā;
*khecari jvālinījvāle khakheti* are the ten syllables of Jvālinī;
*varce śaravibhīṣaṇi khakheti* are likewise the syllables of Śavarī.
Che, chedani, karālini, khakhā, and also karālī; vakṣaḥśravadravaplavanī, kha, kha, dūtīplavaṃ, and khyapi.
Strībālakāre Dhunani, Śāstrī, Vasanavegikā;
Kṣe Pakṣe Kapile, Ha Sa Ha Sa, the messenger named Kapilā;
Hrūṃ Tejovatī, Raudrī, and Mātaṅgaraudridūtikā.

Puṭe puṭe kha kha khaḍge phaṭ is the mantra of Brahmakadūtikā. These ten syllables belong to Vaitālī; one should discard others like snake-skin or straw. At the beginning of the ritual placement (nyāsa) starting with the heart, the wise practitioner should place [the mantras] in the middle and then in the eyes.
From the feet up to the head, and from the head down to the feet;
[the body] flows, melts,
and dissolves into the chest.
From the feet, knees, thighs, and private parts, and from the regions of the navel, heart, and throat,
as well as from the upper and lower parts of the diamond-mandala, [one should visualize] the primordial seed-syllable.
From that, one should contemplate the form of the Moon, the cow who rains down a stream of the nectar of immortality.
The practitioner should visualize [the deity] entering through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
The mantra-knower should repeatedly place the primordial seed-syllable on the head, face, throat, heart, navel, secret parts, thighs, knees, and feet, as well as on the forefinger and so forth.
He who knows that the moon is above and the lotus is below, and that the body is the form of the seed-syllable— for him there shall be no death, nor diseases, nor fevers.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should sacrifice, recite, and meditate upon the Goddess one hundred and eight times.
I shall now describe the mudrās, beginning with the Praṇītā; the Praṇītās are remembered as being fivefold.
Having joined the two hands together, one should place the two thumbs in the middle.
One should place the threatening finger (tarjanī) joined to the top of the head;
this is proclaimed as "Praṇītā. One should bring it to the region of the heart;
the twice-born know it to be with the seed-syllable at the end, positioned above the middle of the little finger (kanyasā).

Having joined the two middle fingers together so that they touch at many points, one should place the tips of the two index fingers in the middle; this is proclaimed as the *Bhedanī*. Having bound it at the region of the navel, one should then raise the two thumbs.
The Karālī-mahāmudrā should be applied at the heart by the practitioner.
Then, as before, one should raise the Jyeṣṭhā finger while it remains locked;
this is declared to be the Vajratuṇḍā, which one should bind at the vajra-region.
One should bind the wrists with both hands,
extending each three fingers;
this is proclaimed as the Vajra-mudrā.
And [the term] *prasāryā* is [found] in the manuscript marked Ṭa...
on page 139:
"The staff (*daṇḍa*), sword (*khaḍga*), discus (*cakra*), and mace (*gadā*) are known as mudrās according to their form."
One should press with the thumb; the trident should be directed upwards, while the single middle finger raised above is prescribed as the *śakti* itself.
[The other hands hold] the arrow, the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), the bow, the noose, the burden, and the bell.
The conch, the goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the lotus— these eight and twenty [deities],
namely Mohanī, Mokṣaṇī, Jvālinī, Amṛtābhayā,
and Praṇītā, are the five mudrās which one should employ in worship and fire-oblation.
Thus ends the three hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Mantra of Tvaritā and Others," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 310.
Now begins the three hundred and tenth chapter,
concerning the root mantra of Tvaritā and so forth.
Agni said:
I shall now describe the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other rites, having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) upon a lotus surrounded by lions and vajras.
*He* 2 *huti*, O Vajradanta, *puru* 2 *lulu* 2 *garja* 2; homage to the lion-throne here! There should be four lines extending horizontally and four extending upwards.
The wise one should construct the squares by dividing [the area] into nine parts. One should accept the squares located in the cardinal directions and eliminate those in the intermediate directions.
Indeed, it is taught that there are eight external lines at the corners of the outer squares.
One should bring [the lines] inward from the outside of the outer chamber as far as the middle;
the middle prong of the vajra should be such that the outer line is divided into two halves.
The wise one should cause the outer line to be curved, forming two bends.
The central square shall be a lotus with a radiant yellow pericarp;
having drawn it with black powder, one should depict a vajra, a sword, and a sharp crescent moon.
On the exterior, the [mandala] should be square and marked with vajra-enclosures;
the mantra-practitioner should place four vajra-enclosures at the gates.
That which is named the lotus should be the left pathway, and it should be level.
The center is red and the filaments are likewise; women who have been initiated into the mandala shall conquer the kingdoms of others and swiftly attain sovereignty.
One should join the form, illuminated by the *praṇava*, with the syllable *hūṃ*.
O twice-born one, having recited the root-vidyā situated in the wind and the ether,
one should worship it again with the first [syllable] in the pericarp;
thus, having worshipped in circumambulation, one should worship each seed-syllable starting from the beginning.

In the interior, however, are the limbs of the Vidyā; in the southeast are five, in the southwest (nairṛta) [is one], and in the center is the Eye; the weapon of the directions is for the protection of the secret limbs. The oblations are located on the filaments, on the left and right sides.
Having fully worshipped the five [deities] five times, one should worship them with their respective mantras;
one should then assign the eight world-protectors (lokapālas) on the outside of the inner maṇḍala.
[The seed-syllable] ending in the letter *va* (the final consonant), mounted upon the fire (*ra*) and differentiated by the sixth vowel (*ū*), [is the seed-mantra].
One should join that which is occupied by the fifteenth [digit] with its respective names;
for the sake of prosperity, one should quickly worship it in the pericarp of the lion [mandala] with perfumes and other offerings.
1. "The Āgneya [should be] with the *annairṛta*," thus [it is in] Ña...
2. "Adorned with the highest tone (*jyeṣṭhasvara*)," thus [it is in] Kha... and Cha...
3. The reading "one should join them by means of their names" (*nāmabhir yojayet*) ought to be the correct one.
4. "Blue," according to Ña... 5. "Fortune," according to Ña...
One should encircle [the site] with eight jars consecrated with one hundred recitations of the mantra;
having recited the mantra one thousand and eight times, [one performs] the ten-part subsidiary rite (*daśāṃśaka*) for the limbs.
One should prepare the sacrificial pit and stir the fire with the fire-mantra;
one should deposit the fire with the heart-mantra and meditate upon the Śakti residing within the fire.
One should perform the oblations for the rites of conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), and the birth ceremony (jātakarma).
One should generate a hundred oblations with the heart-mantra and one secret oblation on the secret limb;
by means of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) of the vidyā, the fire of Śiva shall blaze forth.
One should perform the homa with the root-mantra a hundred times, and for the ancillary mantras (*aṅga*), one-tenth that amount.

Then one should offer [the oblation] to the Goddess and cause the disciple to enter. Having performed the striking with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should then assign the secret limbs. Once he is armored with the limbs of the Vidyā, one should join him to those very limbs of the Vidyā.
One should cause the disciple to cast flowers and lead him to the fire-pit;
with barley, other grains, sesame seeds, and clarified butter, one should perform a hundred oblations with the root-vidyā.
First, the state of being stationary [is attained] through the homa; after that, the state of a reptile.

The state of being a bird, a beast, or a domestic animal, as well as human birth, the state of Brahmā, the state of Viṣṇu, and finally the state of Rudra— these constitute the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Indeed, by means of that single oblation, the disciple becomes initiated.

Thus there shall be authority; hear now of liberation beyond this. When the practitioner of mantra, established on Sumeru, abides in the state of Sadāśiva, being self-abiding, he should offer into the supreme fire ten times one hundred acts of non-action.
By means of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), that yogi is no longer stained by merit or demerit;
he goes to liberation, the supreme state, having reached which he does not return.
Just as water poured into water becomes one with it, so too does the embodied soul [merge] with the Head.
One should perform the consecration with jars and shall partake of all things, such as victory and sovereignty;
a young girl and a Brāhmaṇa woman should be worshipped, and one should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and others.
Having performed worship day after day, one should sacrifice even a single thousand [times];
the goddess Śrī will become the granter of desires. She bestows abundant enjoyments and whatever else one may desire.
By reciting it one hundred thousand times, one shall become a lord of treasures;
by double that amount, one shall obtain a kingdom; by triple, a yakṣiṇī;
by quadruple, the state of Brahmā, and thereafter the station of Viṣṇu.
With six hundred thousand recitations, there is great accomplishment; with one hundred thousand, sins are destroyed.

By reciting it ten times for the purification of the body, one obtains the fruit of bathing at a sacred ford; by reciting it a hundred times, one should quickly worship [the deity] on a cloth, in an image, or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
A hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand recitations are prescribed for the *japa* and the *homa*.
Having performed the *japa* according to this rule, one should then perform the *homa* one hundred thousand times with the meat of a buffalo,
a goat, or a sheep, or with human flesh from the city.
Having performed the fire-oblation with sesame seeds, barley, parched grain, rice, wheat, mangoes, and bilva fruits mixed with clarified butter, one should observe the vow.
At the hours of midnight, fully equipped with sword, bow, arrows, and other weapons, one should remain vigilant.
Wearing a single garment that is multicolored, or red, yellow, or black,
or even blue, one should worship the Goddess with those very same [garments].
The wise one should proceed toward the southern direction and offer an oblation at the door.
1. "By means of an oblation of sesame seeds and ghee floating [on water]" (as found in manuscripts *kha* and *cha*);
2. "By means of floating" (*plavena*) (as found in manuscripts *kha* and *cha*).
By means of the *dūtī* mantra at the gateway and so forth, or at a solitary tree, or in a cremation ground,
the king thus attains all desires and enjoys the entire earth.
Thus ends the three hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Root Mantra of Tvaritā," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Then, in the three hundred and eleventh chapter,
[concerning] the Tvaritā-vidyā, Agni said:
I shall explain the introduction to the Vidyā, which grants the accomplishment of dharma, desire, and the other aims;
one discovers the divisions of the Vidyā through the arrangement of nine compartments,
by means of the forward and reverse orders, and through their combined and individual applications.
Through the application of Karṇā and Vikarṇā, and from that point upward by way of division,
and through the application of the triple-triad (tritrika), one whose body is armored by the Goddess knows the many mantras that bestow success and have emerged from the context.
Mantras are recorded in various scriptures, yet their practical applications therein are difficult to find.
The Guru is the primary letter; he is not described in the preceding day’s discourse, but in that context there were single letters, pairs of letters, triplets of letters, and so forth.
One should divide four lines each extending horizontally and vertically;
thus there will be nine compartments. Having thus established these in the center, one should then arrange them clockwise and subsequently differentiate the arrangement.
For that practitioner who, through the application of the sequence of the introductory chant, attains the introductory chant,
the accomplishments indeed rest in the palm of his hand.
The three worlds shall be at his feet, and he shall obtain the earth with its nine divisions;
having drawn the Śiva-tattva all around upon a skull,
or else upon a cloth from a cremation ground, the knower of mantras should go outside.
One should write his name situated upon the pericarp in the center;
having stepped upon a birch-bark leaf with one's feet, one should heat it with charcoal from the *khadira* tree.
Within seven days, one shall bring forth everything in the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving.
One should cause [the mandala] to be drawn within the interior of a vajra-enclosure on a twelve-spoked wheel;
in the center, one should place the name situated within the womb, interlaced with the mantra of Sadāśiva.
This should be done on a wall, a wooden board, or a stone slab, using turmeric.
Stiffness of the mouth, stiffness of the gait, and even the paralysis of an army occurs [when one] has drawn,
with poison and blood, a six-cornered diagram upon a skull-cup in a cremation ground, O wise one, intersected by staffs and joined on all sides with power-staffs (śaktis).
He shall slay the enemy in the cremation ground before long;

he effects the destruction of the kingdom by placing the enemy in the middle of the wheel. Having reduced the spear to the state of being a spoke of the wheel, one should destroy the enemy by means of the enemy's name.
One should inscribe the seed-syllable of Tārkṣya in the middle of a sword; then,
having written the name of the enemy using the *vidarbha* method upon charcoal from a cremation ground, one will subjugate that region within seven days by striking it with the ashes of a *preta*.
In acts of splitting, cutting, and even killing, one becomes Śiva;
this is taught as the Tāraka eye, which one should employ for pacification and nourishment.

having placed the Praṇava below that, one should again place the Ūhaka below it— [the mantra] consisting of the Praṇava and so forth, beginning with the throat and lips, situated within the universal form of Aṃśumān.
The mantra ending with *namaḥ* consists of four syllables; it is the universal form and the cause.
Struck by the measure of the sun, the limbs [of the mantra] are here as before in the Brahman-mantra.
One should extract the *praṇava* first, and then utter the two "throbbing" (*prasphurat*) syllables.
Thereafter, one should contemplate that form as most terrible;
having uttered the sound *caṭa* twice, one should then pronounce *pravara*;
and *daheti* should be performed twice, followed by *vameti* twice.
Having split [the mantra] into two with the words "ghātaya," one should recite it ending in "hūṃ phaṭ.
The Aghora-weapon is the Eye-mantra; now the Gāyatrī is being declared:
"We know that Great Lord; we meditate upon Mahādeva..."

There, may Śiva impel [the seeker]; Gāyatrī is the accomplisher of all goals. For victory in a journey and similar undertakings, one should worship the primordial host (pūrvagaṇa) for the sake of prosperity; first, the field is divided into twelve parts on all sides by the sun (twelve). AP_317.006–007cd.
One should draw a four-petaled lotus with three petals within a triangle in every direction.
Behind that, there is a path consisting of one square (padikā) with three petals joined by a horse;
the pedestal (pādapaṭṭikā) has three petals and is adorned with lotuses along with the sons of Vasudeva.
Above that, a pedestal (vedikā) should be provided, measuring only one *bhaga*.
The door is measured by a lotus, and the side-door (*upadvāra*) is described as being from a square cell;
the mandala, fashioned with doors and side-doors, is the destroyer of obstacles.

A reddish lotus should be in the center, with outer lotuses beyond that; the pathway (vīthikā) should be made white, and the doors as one desires. The pericarp (karṇikā) should be yellow in color, and likewise the filaments (keśarāṇi).

In the center of the maṇḍala called Vighnamarda, one should worship Gaṇapati; his name begins with "Sa," followed by "Varāka," and is joined with the word "Devāt" and "Śakra. His head is struck by Tatpuruṣa, beginning with "Oṃ" and ending with "Namaḥ."
Gajākhya, Gajaśīrṣa, Gāṅgeya, Gaṇanāyaka, Trirāvarta, Gaganagaṅgopati— these occupy the first row;
as well as Vicitrāṃśa, Mahākāya, Lamboṣṭha, and Lambakarṇaka.
Lambodara, Mahābhāga, Vikṛta, Pārvatīpriya,
Bhayāvaha, Bhadra, Bhagaṇa, and Bhayasūdana—
these twelve are in the tenth row; and Devatrāsa is in the west.
Mahānāda, Bhāsvara, Vighnarāja, Gaṇādhipa, Udbhaṭasvana, Bhaścaṇḍa, Mahāśuṇḍa, Bhīmaka,
Manmatha, Madhusūdana, Sundara, and Bhāvapuṣṭaka.
In the north, one should worship Brahmeśvara, Brāhma, Manovṛtti,
Saṃlaya, Layadūtyapriya, Laulya, Vikarṇa, Vatsala,
Kṛtānta, and Kāladaṇḍa, as well as Kumbha, according to the previous procedure.
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times and perform the fire oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that amount;
for the remaining [deities], one should cause the fire oblation to be performed with ten offerings for each recitation.
Having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*); everything is then accomplished.
A person should perform worship of the Guru with land, gold, horses, elephants, garments, and other such gifts.
Thus ends the three hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "Worship of the Gaṇas," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 318:
Now begins the three hundred and eighteenth chapter.
Regarding the worship of Vāgīśvarī, the Lord said:
"I shall now proclaim the worship of Vāgīśvarī along with her maṇḍala."
One should perform the *ūhaka* mantra joined with time (*kāla*) and endowed with the phonemes (*varṇa*), making the Lord Niṣāda like Manu, resembling the moon and the sun;
for it should not be given away in letters, but one should meditate upon her who resembles the jasmine flower and the moon.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, visualizing [the goddess] adorned with a garland of fifty letters like a string of pearls,
endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, holding a rosary and a book, and possessing three eyes;
[one should visualize] the garland of letters extending from the top of the head down to the shoulders.
One should visualize [the goddess] entering as if she were a young woman, starting from the letter *a* and ending with the letter *kṣa*.
For the purpose of initiation, the Guru should prepare a mandala; for the grasping of the mantra, a lotus is beneficial, having the sun at its apex and being divided by the moon into two parts.
1. "Joined with the moon" (candramasāyutam) is [the reading] in manuscript ña;
2. "performed" (kṛtam) is [the reading] in manuscript kha.
A path one square wide should be made; eight lotuses are placed on four squares.
Outside, there is a path one square wide, and the doors are two squares wide.
Having fashioned two strips for the secondary doorways and the binding of the corners,
nine lotuses are completed; their pericarp has the luster of gold,
the filaments are variegated, and one should fill the corners with red.
The space between the lines of the sky is black; the doors are measured according to the dimensions of Indra’s elephant.
In the center is Sarasvatī upon a lotus; Vāgīśī is in the eastern lotus, along with Hṛllekhā, Citravāgīśī, Gāyatrī, and Viśvarūpā.
The intellect of Śaṅkarī and Dhṛti, located in the east and other directions, are marked with their own seed-syllables, *hrīṃ*;
they should be meditated upon like Sarasvatī, and one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with tawny-colored clarified butter.
Through this, one becomes a poet in both Sanskrit and Prakrit, and a knower of poetry, the sciences, and so forth.
Thus ends the three hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Worship of Vāgīśvarī," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 318.
Chapter Three Hundred and Twenty-Nine: Mandalas.
Īśvara said:
O Guha, I shall describe the eight mandalas of Sarvatobhadra;
the wise man should establish the eastern direction at the equinox using a gnomon,
or else by means of a thread aligned between the constellations Citrā and Svātī.
Having stretched a cord extending from east to west, one should mark the center.
One should mark two points to the south and north from the center of those two extremes;
in the middle, one should draw two lines crossing each other from south to north.
One should indicate the meeting of the corners by means of half the measurement of a hundred fields.
Thus, from the expansion of the fourfold sūtra, a square is produced;
therein, one should construct an auspicious and beautiful *bhadra* with a sweating-enclosure (*svedaka*).
In a field divided into sixty-four parts, the pathway is one part.
The door, measuring two units, should have half a lotus on each side including the cheek-panels; there, one should fashion a two-unit space with various decorative bands.
The lotus is white, the pericarp is yellow, and the filaments are variegated.

There, a red pathway should be fashioned, and the door should have the form of Lokeśvara. In the rite for daily practice, the corners are red; now hear about the occasional lotus: it is of two kinds, unattached and attached, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
For those seeking liberation, it is unattached; for others, it is attached—thus it is threefold and distinct.
By name, they are the child, the youth, and the aged, who bestow the accomplishment of the fruit.
One should cast the threads in the cardinal and intermediate directions upon the lotus-field.
The five kalpas are circular and equal in extent to the lotus-field (*padmakṣetra*).
Therein, in the first [kalpa] is the pericarp (*karṇikā*), joined with nine lotuses;
then in the second and the third are twenty-four filaments (*keśara*).
The joint of the petal is like the frontal globe of an elephant, and the tip of the petal is situated within;
in the fifth [stage], the lotus is known to have the form of space (*vyoma*).
When the tips of the petals are not joined, one should divide them by their width according to the directions.
By abandoning two parts, one should fashion the petal with eight portions;
from its base, one should extend the petal along the line of the width of the joint.
In this manner, by following the sequence of right and left, it becomes increased;
or else, from the middle of the junction, one should rotate it like a half-moon.
Or, with a thread from the tips of the two junctions, it likewise becomes a "child-lotus" (bālapadma).
One should rotate it from behind with a measure of half the joint-thread;
a lotus with a sharp tip and a good wind grants both enjoyment and liberation.
For the increase of enjoyment, for subjugation (*vaśya*), and so forth, a "child" (*bāla*) lotus is equal [to the others].
It has nine naves and nine cubits, with its parts consisting of the essence of mantras;
in the center is a lotus whose seed-threads are measured according to the size of the door, and outside of that,
the neck, the sub-neck, and the pearl-band are established, while a walkway is considered to be on the exterior of that.
It is divided into ten parts on all sides; there are eight lotuses in the cardinal and intermediate directions, along with a gateway lotus and a walkway.
Outside of that is a five-paved walkway which is adorned.
The door-neck should be like a lotus, and the lip-neck one *padika*;
the cheek should be made one *padika*. Clearly, there are three doors in the cardinal directions;
the corner-binding should have three bands, while the two bands should be like a thunderbolt (*vajra*).
The central lotus is white;
[the others are] yellow, red, blue, yellow-white, smoky-grey, red, and yellow—these grant liberation.
One should recite the mantras of Śiva, Viṣṇu, and the others upon the eight lotuses starting from the east.
Having worshipped Śakra and the other deities upon lotuses and so forth in the center of the palace,

one should place the weapons on the outer pathway; then, for the sake of the horse sacrifice and during rites such as the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇa*), one should draw the great mandala.
One should first rotate an eight-cubit field by means of the six flavors (rasa) and the two wings (pakṣa).
[Note: "Measured in five parts" appears in manuscripts *kha* and *cha*.]
In the center is a two-petaled lotus, and from that, a path consisting of single squares;
then, one should arrange eight blue lotuses in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
These [eight] are equal in size to the central lotus, while those [other] thirty lotuses are likewise [of that same measure].
The petals are devoid of joints and are like blue lotuses;
behind them is a path of one square (*padikā*), and above that are eight *svastikas*, each consisting of two squares, fashioned from the divided sections.
One should draw svastikas there, and the pathways (vīthikā) outside should be as before.
The doors and the lotus should be provided with a border (upakaṇṭhya),
while in the maṇḍala, the corner is red, the pathway is yellow, and the lotus is blue.
O Guha, it should be variegated with svastikas and other designs, granting all desires;
it shall consist of five lotuses and five hands, divided into ten parts on all sides,
with two-padded lotuses, a pathway, a border-strip, and lotuses in the cardinal directions.
There are four [squares] at the back, a path of one square, and then two squares;
the doors are provided with necks and sub-necks, and there is a lotus in the center.
Indeed, in this five-lotus mandala, the eastern [lotus] is white and yellow.
The southern lotus has the luster of lapis lazuli, the western lotus has the luster of a kunda flower, the northern lotus has the luster of a conch shell, and all the others are multicolored.
I shall now describe the ten-handed mandala that grants all desires.
The fourth [section] is a square with modified proportions, and its door should consist of two parts.
In the center, there is a lotus as before; now I shall describe the destruction of obstacles.
Having made the city four-armed, one should likewise fashion Vṛtra with two hands.
The pathway, measuring one cubit [in width], is surrounded by many svastikas;
likewise, it is provided with upakaṇṭhas.
The doors shall be one cubit in measure, and the circle shall be adorned with lotuses;
one should worship five white lotuses in the center and the partless (niṣkala) deity as the object of worship.
One should indeed worship the heart-mantra and the others in the east and other cardinal directions, and the weapon-mantras in the intermediate directions.
And as before, I shall now describe the five Brahmans as the support for the intellect:
in the hundredth part and the lunar-day part, there is a lotus; in each direction, there are eight liṅgas joined with the girdle-parts, and the neck should consist of two parts.
The preceptor, relying on his intellect, should fashion the creepers and other elements;
the mandala consists of four, six, five, eight, and so forth, as well as those beginning with *kha* (space), *ā* (vowels), and *khikhā* (the head of space).
Everything resides in the sky, the eyes, the moon, and the sun, and indeed the sky and the eyes are described by the color of the moon.
Indeed, there are one thousand four hundred and forty mandalas of Hari, Śambhu, the Goddess, and the Sun.
Now hear concerning that which arises from the creeper-liṅga, divided into seventeen parts.
One should mark five, three, one, three, and five [units] in the directions;
in the upward direction, there is a two-unit [space] for the temple of the Liṅga, with two units in the middle between the side compartments, and then a lotus of one unit.
On both sides of the *liṅga*, O auspicious one, the two-pada door should not be omitted;
its side-ornaments (*pārśvaśobhā*) and six creepers (*latā*) should likewise be omitted. Above that, having omitted two padas, the eight auspicious features (*bhadra*) of Hari are prescribed.
The *raśmimān* is joined with the *samāyukta*, and from the omission of the *veda* comes the *śobhika*.
Then there is the twenty-five-fold lotus; thereafter, having protected two by two the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the non-pedestal (*apīṭhaka*), there are likewise eight *upaśobhās*.
The auspicious [syllable] that designates the Goddess and so forth is large in the middle and extremely small;
one should elide it, according to the reading "lopayet" found in the manuscript Ña.
One should erase [the lines],
as stated on page 166;
in the center is a nine-square lotus, and in the corners are four auspicious squares (bhadracatuṣṭaya).

The remaining thirteen steps are the support of the intellect; the mandala is a hundred-and-sixty-petaled lotus, the support of the intellect, located among the directions beginning with Hara. Thus ends the section on mandalas in the Agni Purāṇa.
Chapter three hundred and nineteen;
now begins chapter three hundred and twenty.
The Ritual for the Pacification of the Aghora Weapon and Others.
The Lord said: In all rites, the sacrifice of the weapon (astrayāga) must first be performed; it bestows success.
In the center, one should worship the weapon of Śiva and so forth; from the east onwards in sequence, one should worship the five wheels and the ten hands for victory in battle and similar occasions.
For the worship of the planets: the Sun is in the center, and the Moon and others occupy the directions starting from the east.
Through the worship of the planets, all [disturbances] shall remain in the eleventh house.
I shall now proclaim the rite for the pacification of weapons, which destroys all portents,
quells planetary afflictions and diseases, and crushes pestilence and enemies.

A person should recite the Aghora-weapon mantra, which destroys the afflictions caused by Vināyaka; by reciting it one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*), there will be the destruction of planetary influences and the like. In the event of a portentous calamity (*utpāta*), an oblation of sesame seeds should be performed.
For portents occurring in the heavens, one hundred thousand recitations are required, and for those occurring in the atmosphere, half of that amount.
In the case of terrestrial portents, it is beneficial to perform a hundred-thousandfold oblation (*lakṣahoma*) with ghee;
and by offering guggulu resin with ghee, all portents and the like are subdued.
By means of an oblation of *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice, and clarified butter, diseases are destroyed; furthermore, by a thousand offerings of clarified butter, bad dreams undoubtedly perish.
By ten thousand offerings of *javā* flowers mixed with clarified butter, the afflictions caused by planetary influences are destroyed.
The pacification of the affliction of Vināyaka is achieved by ten thousand oblations of clarified butter;
the pacification of spirits and *vedālas* is achieved by ten thousand oblations of *guggulu*;
and [the pacification] of wild beasts and *kaṅkas* is achieved by the breaking of branches of the *mahāvṛkṣa*.
When forest-dwellers enter while one is staying at home, [one should perform] oblations of *dūrvā* grass, clarified butter, and unbroken rice; likewise,
when a meteor falls or there is an earthquake, [one attains] welfare through oblations of sesame seeds and clarified butter.
In the case of blood-flowing [from trees], one should perform the *śānti* rite with ten thousand units of *guggulu* resin;

likewise for the untimely appearance of fruits and flowers, for the ruin of a kingdom, and for the killing of bipeds and others. When there is a plague (*māri*), one should perform it with fifty thousand units of sesame and clarified butter.
For the purpose of pacifying the plague of elephants (*hastimārī*), when the tusks of a female elephant are growing,

and when rut is seen in a female elephant, peace is desired through ten thousand recitations. Furthermore, in the case of a miscarriage at an improper time, or where a newborn dies, [the same rite is prescribed].
If deformed beings are born during the time of a journey, one should offer ten thousand oblations;
however, for the accomplishment of the highest siddhi, one should perform a hundred thousand oblations of sesame and clarified butter.
For the middling [siddhi], half of that amount is used, and for the lowest ones, a quarter of that.
As is the recitation, so shall be the fire-oblation; victory will be achieved in battle.
One should recite the Aghora-weapon mantra while meditating upon the powerful five-faced [Śiva] after having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
Thus ends [the section] titled "The Ritual for Pacification of the Aghora-Weapon and Others" in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

whose entire body is red; who resembles a mass of crushed collyrium; and who is fond of the vetālas of the cremation ground.

By reciting it just once, one shall destroy all obstacles;
by reciting it a hundred times, one shall overcome portents and achieve victory in battle and other such situations.
Furthermore, through the fire-oblation (*homa*) of ghee and *guggulu*, even those things considered impossible to accomplish [shall be achieved].

Chapter 322:
The Six Limbs of the Aghora Weapon-mantras
The Lord said: By means of the mantra "Oṃ hrūṃ haṃsa," death, disease, and other afflictions shall be subdued;
through one hundred thousand oblations of dūrvā grass, one shall accomplish peace and nourishment.
Alternatively, O Six-faced One, by means of the *praṇava* or by means of *māyā*,
there is the pacification of celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial portents and calamities: *Oṃ namo bhagavati Gaṅge Kāli 2 Mahākāli 2 Māṃsaśoṇitabhojane*.
O you with red and black faces, bring human beings under control, svāhā!
Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times and performed oblations with a tenth part of that number, one becomes a performer of all rites;
one brings even Śakra and others under control—what need is there to mention mere humans?
This is the lore (*vidyā*) that effects invisibility, as well as enchantment and yawning.
It brings enemies under control and deludes their hostile intentions;
this vidyā is proclaimed as the wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu) in its sevenfold form.
I shall now proclaim the king of mantras, which deludes enemies, thieves, and others.
In all great dangers, one should remember that which is worshipped by Hara.
Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, an oblation with sesame seeds should be performed; listen now to the *uddhāraka* for its accomplishment:
*oṃ hale śūle ehi brahmasatyena viṣṇusatyena rudrasatyena rakṣa mām*.
To Vāceśvara, svāhā!
Because she delivers one from distress (*durga*), the auspicious goddess is therefore considered *Durgā*.
Having washed the rice grains with this king of mantras: *Oṃ caṇḍakapālini dantān kiṭi 2 kṣiṭi 2 guhye phaṭ hrīṃ*, [one should proceed].
Having recited [the mantra] thirty times, one should cause those powders to be given to the thieves;
indeed, white powders fallen from the teeth serve for purification.

Oṃ! O you with blazing eyes, radiant with a mass of tawny matted hair, O terrifier, O subduer of the three worlds, *ḍāmara* 2, rend 2, whirl 2, seize 2, crush 2, shatter 2, burn 2, cook 2! Thus does Siddhirudra command, if [the spirit] has entered a planet, whether it be the heavenly world or the world of the gods.
"Even though he is as immovable as a pleasure grove or a monastery, I shall nevertheless cause him to turn; accept this offering!
I give it to you, O Svaha!
Having thus offered the *kṣetrapāla* bali, the practitioner should go to the reservoir where the planetary spirit (*graha*) has been deposited.
Enemies go to their destruction in battle, and the multitude of enmities comes to an end. By placing the seed-syllable *haṃsa*, one may remove the three kinds of poison.
Having prepared equal parts of agallochum, sandalwood, costus, saffron, nāgakeśara, nakha, and devadāru, one should then use this incense,
combined with honey, for fumigating the body, clothing, and other items.
It is auspicious for disputes, for enchanting women, for quarrels, and for strife;
it is used for the choosing of a bridegroom for a maiden and for good fortune when consecrated with the *māyā-mantra*:
*hrīṃ*. [One should apply] *rocanā*, *nāgapuṣpa*, saffron, and realgar.
Having applied a tilaka on the forehead, whoever one looks upon shall become submissive.
Powder of śatāvarī drunk with milk produces a son;

The mantra Mahāmṛtyuñjaya brings about nourishment through recitation and fire-offerings.
Oṃ haṃsaḥ hrūṃ hūṃ sa hraḥ sauṃḥ;

The mantras, headed by Īśāna, bestow dharma, desire, and the other goals of life.
Īśāna is the lord of all sciences, the lord of all beings, and the sovereign of Brahman; may that Śiva, Sadāśiva, be mine.
Oṃ, may we know that Puruṣa; may we meditate upon Mahādeva; may Rudra impel us toward that.
Oṃ, from the non-terrible, from the terrible, and from those who are both terrible and non-terrible, from all sides!
Salutations to you from all forms of Rudra.
Oṃ, salutations to Vāmadeva, salutations to Jyeṣṭha, salutations to Rudra.
Salutation to Kāla; salutation to Kalavikaraṇa; salutation to Balavikaraṇa; salutation to Balapramathana; salutation to Sarvabhūtadamana.
Homage to the one who transcends the mind; homage!
Oṃ, I shall proclaim the Sadyojāta mantra: "Homage indeed to Sadyojāta!

I shall declare [this mantra] which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation:

The Pacification of Rudra. The Lord said:
I shall proclaim the Śiva-śānti, preceded by the Kalpa-aghora;
[this] Aghora is the lord of seventy million [mantras], the destroyer of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin,
the abode of the highest and lowest attainments, and the dispeller of all diseases.
It is the subduer of celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial portents; the devourer of poisons, malevolent planets, and piśācas; the fulfiller of all desires;
the expiation for those afflicted by a flood of sins; and the destroyer of the pain of misfortune.
Having placed the Solitary Hero (Ekavīra), he should always be meditated upon as five-faced,
the crusher of Brahmā, Hari, and the others.

In rites for pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika), [the deity] is white; in subjugation (vaśya), red; in paralyzing (stambhana), yellow; in driving away (uccāṭana) and killing (māraṇa), black;
in attracting (karṣaṇa), tawny; and in bewildering (moha), one should worship [the deity] in thirty-two colors.

One should recite the mantra three million times and perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with one-tenth that amount, using guggulu resin mixed with amṛta. Whether already perfected or not yet perfected, it accomplishes everything.
There exists no other mantra than Aghora that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One who does not practice celibacy becomes a practitioner of celibacy; one who has not bathed becomes a *snātaka*.
These two, the Aghora-weapon and the Aghora [mantra], are both kings of mantras;
through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, they shall crush the enemy army in battle.
I shall proclaim the propitiatory rite of Rudra, which is auspicious and the means for accomplishing all goals:
for the sake of obtaining a son, for the destruction of malevolent planets, for the eradication of poison and disease,
for the pacification of famine and pestilence, and for the removal of evil dreams.
For the sake of attaining power and sovereignty, for the destruction of enemies,
for trees that bear fruit out of season, and for the subduing of all malevolent planets,
one should perform worship with prostrations; likewise, in the sacrificial oblation (havana), the mantra should end with "svāhā."
One should employ the *vaṣaṭ* call for nourishment and the *vauṣaṭ* call for prosperity; one should also perform the application of the mantra according to its specific lineage:

And to the worshipful Puruṣa, to Īśāna, to Pauruṣa—these five in the north;

Homage to Viśveśvara, the lord of the Piśācas of Akāla.
Indeed, Umā and Maheśvara are to be worshipped within the pericarp of the Śiva-tattva.

Oṃ, to the one who pervades the sky, whose form is the sky, to Śiva, the all-pervading, the infinite, the protectorless, the non-dependent, to Śiva! These are the nine words in the principle of Śiva (śivatattva).
Salutation to the one who pervades the sky, who is designated as the eternal, who is established upon the seat of yoga, the perpetual yogi whose sustenance is meditation.
Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, the source of all,
to Śiva whose head is Īśāna and who possesses the five faces beginning with Tatpuruṣa; O Guha, one should worship the nine-fold state called Sadāśiva on the eastern petal.
To the one whose heart is not terrible, whose secret is Vāmadeva, and whose form is Sadyojāta;
Oṃ, salutations again and again!
To the protector of that which is more secret than the secret, to the imperishable one,

One should worship, offer oblations, and recite [this mantra] in the northeast, within the primordial principle (*prākṛta-tattva*).

Chapter 324: On the Aṃśakas and Other Matters.
Īśvara said:
One should wear a bracelet of rudrākṣas that is firm, whether it be uneven or perfectly even;
one should wear those with one, three, or five faces, according to what is available.
One should wear a flawless [liṅga] with two, four, or six faces, possessing sharp ridges, on the right arm or at the beginning of the top-knot (śikhā); it is praised as being four-faced.
Even one who does not practice celibacy becomes a celibate, and one who has not bathed becomes a ritual bath-graduate (snātaka).
Or a golden ring should be worn,
having been consecrated with the Śiva-mantra.
Śiva, Śikhā, Jyotis, and Savitṛ— these are the spheres of activity. AP 324.004ab.
The family should be known as the *gocara*; by that [lineage] one is consecrated (*dīkṣita*).

O Protector of the Earth, in the auspicious (*śiva*) [tradition], there are the *prājāpatya*, the *kapota*, and the *granthika*; likewise, in the *śikhākula*, there are the *kuṭila*, the *vetāla*, the *padma*, and the *haṃsa*.
The Dhṛtarāṣṭras, Vakas, Kākas, Gopālas, those known as Jyotis, the Kuṭikas, the Sāṭharas, the Guṭikas, and others who are Daṇḍins—
Sāvitrī and Gocara likewise; thus each one is fourfold.
I shall now describe the divisions beginning with "Siddha," by which a mantra bestows excellent accomplishment.

The Mātṛkā letters should be written on the ground, excluding the *kūṭas* and the neuter (*ṣaṇḍa*) vowels; having separated the syllables of the mantra, one should place the *anusvāra* separately for each.
One should perform the analysis of the practitioner’s name;
one should join the letters of the practitioner at the beginning and likewise at the end of the mantra.
One should count the name in sequence as *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari*.

If a mantra has a *siddha* [seed-syllable] at the beginning and likewise at the end, it bestows success in a hundredfold measure; even one that is *antyasiddha* (successful at the end) becomes successful at that very moment. One should consider a mantra that is *susiddha* at the beginning and *susiddha* at the end to be like one that is already accomplished (*siddha*).
One should avoid from afar an enemy both at the beginning and at the end [of a mantra].
Siddha, Susiddha, Ari, and likewise Sādhya—these share a single purpose.
If a Siddha is situated at the beginning of the mantra, it remains exactly so at the end as well.
Indeed, even thousands of enemies in the midst [of one's path] do not lead to harm.
In the case of a well-known mantra, there is a division by means of the *māyā*, *prasāda*, and *praṇava* syllables;
the portion belonging to Brahmā is the *brahmavidyā*, while the portion belonging to Viṣṇu is indeed the *vaiṣṇava*.
He is remembered as a portion of Viṣṇu.
A hero possessing a portion of Rudra is dear to Īśvara; one with a portion of Indra has eyes fixed like a serpent; one with a portion of a Yakṣa is fond of ornaments;
one with a portion of a Gandharva is excessively devoted to song and the like; and one with a portion of Bhīma is of the nature of a Rākṣasa.
One who has a portion of the Daityas is fit for warfare; one with a portion of the Vidyādharas is honorable;

one with a portion of the Piśācas is overcome by impurity. Having observed [the disciple], one should impart the mantra; the mantra should consist of a single syllable ending in *phaṭ*, up to a maximum of fifty syllables.
The *bāla* [mantras] end with twenty syllables, and the *rudras* consist of twenty-two weapons; those mantras beyond that are the *vṛddha*, up to three hundred syllables.
From the letter *a* to the letter *ha*, they correspond respectively to the white and black fortnights.
Excluding the *anusvāra* and *visarga*, there are ten vowels;
the short ones are white, the long ones are dark, and the lunar days (*tithi*) begin with the first day (*pratipad*).
When [the breath] has risen, rites such as pacification (śāntika) are performed; when it has wandered, rites such as subjugation (vaśyaka).
When it has wandered, the two junctions (saṃdhyā) occur; in the state of hatred (dveṣa), there is eradication (uccāṭana), and in the state of obstruction (stambhana), there is cessation (asta).
Here, in the Āvaha [state], rites such as pacification are performed, and in Piṅgalā, rites such as attraction (karṣaṇa).
The rites of killing, expulsion, and so forth are performed separately in five ways during the equinoxes:
earth is in the lower house, fire above, liquid in between,
wind outside the openings on the sides, and Maheśvara pervades everything.
Stambhana (paralysis) is achieved through the earth element; Śānti (pacification) through water; Vaśya (subjugation) and so forth through fire;
Bhramaṇa (bewilderment) occurs in air; and Puṇya (merit) in the void. One should practice according to the time. Thus ends [the section] named Aṃśakādi in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.

Chapter 325:
The Worship of Gaurī and Others
Īśvara said:
I shall describe the worship of Umā for the sake of good fortune and other benefits, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
along with the mantra, meditation, the mandala, the mudrās, and the means such as the fire sacrifice (homa).

Having turned back from the other side the one beginning with *iḍā*— Citrabhānu, Śiva, Kāla, endowed with great power (*mahāśakti*), together with the Lord and his causal transformation— the second [form] is pervaded by Dvārakā and joined with the station that gladdens Gaurī.
The root-mantra of Gaurī should be formed in the dative case:
*oṃ hrīṃ saḥ śauṃ gaurīyai namaḥ*.
There, by means of these three syllables alone, conjoined with the [six] seed-syllables (*jāti*), the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) are established.
One should extract the seat (āsana) by means of the *praṇava* alone, and the form (mūrti) indeed by means of the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
Likewise, one should extract water, time, and the seed-syllable of Śiva;
the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is conjoined with the long vowels and endowed with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) along with the [six] classes of beings.
One should perform the placement of the seat here with the *praṇava* (Om) and the placement of the form (*mūrtinyāsa*) with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).

O child, the *yāmala* method has been explained; now I shall describe the *ekavīra* method, which is pervasive and conjoined with emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), using fire, *māyā*, and the sacrificial fire (*kṛśānu*).
The seed-syllable consists of Śiva and Śakti; this seed-syllable is devoid of [the specific mantras for] the heart and other limbs.

One should worship Gaurī, who is golden, silver, made of wood, or fashioned from stone and so forth—either as the five-lump (pañcapiṇḍā) form or as the unmanifest (avyaktā). The fifth [form] is in the center, while [the others are] in the corners.
Lalitā, Subhagā, Gaurī, and Kṣobhaṇī follow in order from Agni;
[the fifth is] thus [the fifth].
One should worship Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Kriyā, and Jñānā, starting from the east,
upon the circumference; and on the left side of the pedestal (pīṭha) of Śiva is his unmanifest form.
Manifested, with two eyes, consisting of three syllables, pure, or accompanied by Śaṅkara;
she may have two lotus seats, or Tārā may have two arms or four arms; she may be seated upon a lion or a wolf.
Or she may hold in her left hand a rosary of eight or eighteen beads, a flower bud, a cluster of blue lotuses at her throat, or some other object such as an arrow or a bow.
In the left [hands], one should place a book, betel, a staff, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and a water-pot;
and for Gaṇeśa, a mirror and a bow. These should be offered one by one in sequence.
Alternatively, the lotus-gesture (*padmamudrā*) may be formed on the seat, whether manifest or unmanifest.

The *tiṅga-mudrā* is said to belong to Śiva, while the *āvāhanī-mudrā* belongs to both with joy. The *śakti-mudrā*, however, is called the *yoni*; the mandala is square, and within the four central squares is a four-petaled lotus.

In the upper half of the triangle, there is a crescent moon; the two-pada [section] is doubled in sequence, as is the door-neck (*dvārakaṇṭha*) from the double-necked section; one should worship three doors in each of the directions, or else perform the sacrifice in the *bhadraka* [mandala].

Or else, having established [the deity] upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and worshipped with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the nectar [of the five elements], and so forth, one facing north should offer red flowers;
having offered a hundred oblations of nectar and clarified butter, the giver of the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) shall possess all supernatural powers (siddhi).
Having offered the *bali* oblation, one should feed three or eight young girls;

one should present the food offering (*naivedya*) to the devotees of Śiva and not consume it oneself. (Note 1: Regarding the reading *siṃhasthāvāhyasiṃhastheti*, [the manuscript] *kha* reads *siṃhasthāvāhya siṃhastheti*.)
Six, nine, eight, and two women, or eight, he should feed; thus [state] Kha and Cha:
One seeking a maiden shall obtain a maiden; one without a son shall obtain a son; the unfortunate shall obtain good fortune; a king shall obtain a kingdom and victory in battle;
and through eight hundred thousand recitations, there is perfection of speech, and gods and others shall come under one's control.
One should not eat without having offered [the food], nor should one worship with the left hand.
On the eighth, the fourteenth, and especially on the third lunar day, I shall describe the worship of Mṛtyuñjaya; one should worship him within the belly of the water-pot (kalaśa).
While the oblation is being offered, the Praṇava is the form of Ojas;
with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should display the *kumbha-mudrā* and perform the homa with milk, *dūrvā* grass, clarified butter, *amṛtā*, and *punarnavā*.
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times while offering milk-rice and sacrificial cakes;
[visualizing the deity] with four faces and four arms,
holding two water-pots with two hands, and granting boons and fearlessness with the other two, one should bathe with the *vaiṣṇava-mudrā*.
When meditated upon and worshipped, he is indeed marvelous— he who bestows health, long life through right conduct, and auspicious medicine consecrated by mantra, and who removes untimely death.
Thus ends [the section] titled "The Worship of Gaurī and Others" in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Chapter 326:
The Greatness of the Temple of the Devas (Devālayamāhātmya)

The Lord said: Having worshipped the Lords of Vows (Vrateśvaras) and those beginning with Satya, the dedication of the vow is prescribed for the pacification of misfortune; it is the auspicious leader of the ritual manual.
A great conch made of gold brings prosperity at night;
for killing, a conch-shell thread; and a pearl increases progeny.
Crystal [rosaries] bestow prosperity, those made of *kauśa* fiber grant liberation;
the *rudrākṣa* born from the eye of Rudra is the most excellent of all, according to the measurement of the fruit of the *dhātrī*.
One should recite the mental mantra, whether with or without the *meru* bead;
pressing the ring finger and the thumb, one should perform the recitation.
Pressing the index finger and the thumb, one should not cross over the *meru* during the recitation.
If the thread falls due to negligence, one should recite [the mantra] two hundred times.
A bell composed of all musical instruments brings about success when it is sounded.
[One should purify with] cow dung, urine, anthill earth, ashes, and water.
In this manner, the purification of the temple, the sacred image, and so forth is accomplished.
The mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya" (Salutation to Śiva), known as Skanda, is the accomplisher of all aims;
it is celebrated in the Veda as five-syllabled and in the world as six-syllabled.

Śambhu resides at the end of the syllable *oṃ*, like the seed of a banyan tree for the sake of the mudrās. They know that the mantras beginning with Īśāna, namely *namaḥ śivāya*, belong to the six-syllabled thread (*ṣaḍakṣara-sūtra*). From the commentary on this [thread], the entire collection of vidyās arises.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva"— this much is the supreme state.
With this one should worship the *liṅga*, because Śiva resides within the *liṅga* for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds, granting dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation.
He who does not worship the *liṅga* is not a recipient of dharma and the other goals of life.
Through the worship of the *liṅga*, one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation; therefore, one should worship it for as long as one lives.
It is better to give up one's life than to eat without having worshipped it.
Through the worship of Rudra, one becomes Rudra; through the worship of Viṣṇu, one becomes Viṣṇu. Thus it is said [in the Khaṇḍakhādya, folio 183].

From the worship of Sūrya one becomes Sūrya; from the worship of Śakti and others, a man obtains a fruit ten million times greater than that which is gained through all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, pilgrimages, and the Vedas, provided he installs a *liṅga*.
Whoever worships an earthen *liṅga* made of bilva wood at the three junctions of the day,
having uplifted one hundred and eleven generations of their lineage, shall become a dweller in heaven.
With devotion and according to one's means, one should construct a collection of such shrines.
Whether small or great, the fruit is equal for both the wealthy and the poor. One should allocate two parts of one's wealth for the sake of Dharma and one part for livelihood. (326.016cd–326.017ab)
Since life is impermanent,
one who builds a temple for the gods rescues twenty-one generations of their kin and partakes in the fruits of that merit;
the reward increases ten-millionfold according to the materials used— clay, wood, brick, stone, and so forth, in successive order.
One who builds a temple for the gods using eight bricks shall attain heaven;
even one playing with dust who constructs a temple for the gods partakes in the fruit of that merit.
Thus ends [the section] titled "The Greatness of Temples and Other Matters" in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter Three Hundred and Twenty-Six.
