Agni, whose essence is *chandas*, said:
"I shall explain *chandas* according to its roots, as taught by Piṅgala, in due order."

The groups [of syllables] for all [the meters] beginning with *madhyā* and *antā* consist of two *ml* groups, two *js*, and three *sts*; these are the groups. (Note 1: According to manuscript *kha*, there is only one *dhanas* and *annātha*.)
A short or long syllable at the end of a metrical foot becomes heavy due to its connection with a visarga,
an anusvāra, a consonant, or likewise a jihvāmūlīya.
A long vowel following an *upadhmānīya* is heavy; *glu* (a short vowel followed by a consonant) and *na* (a short vowel followed by two consonants) are the *gaṇas* here.
There are eight Vasus and four Vedas, due to the elision of *ādi* and *āditya*.
Thus ends the section titled "The Essence of Prosody" (*Chandaḥsāra*) in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter Three Hundred and Twenty-Seven.
Now begins Chapter Three Hundred and Twenty-Eight.
Agni, the essence of the meters, said:
"In the section concerning the meters, the goddess Gāyatrī consists of a single syllable."
That [gāyatrī] of the Yajus should consist of fifteen syllables; that of the Prajāpati [Yajus] should have eight syllables; that of the Sāmans should be twelve-syllabled;
and that of the Ṛks should be eighteen-syllabled, increasing by two [syllables] for each subsequent [meter].
The fourth [verse] of the *ṛcas* should increase, as should the fourfold set belonging to Prajāpati; in the remainder, one should omit one [syllable] at a time up to the fourth verse.
[The meters are] *uṣṇih*, *anuṣṭubh*, *bṛhatī*, *paṅkti*, *triṣṭubh*, and also *jagatī*.
These should be known in sequence as *gāyatrīs*, and they are indeed Brahman.
Three by three they are common, and each one is also noble.
These shall be the designations for the *ṛc*s and *yajus* verses; one should write them in sixty-four squares.
Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Essence of Prosody," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Chapter 329:
The Essence of Prosody (*Chandaḥsāra*)
Agni said:
"The quarter of the Gāyatrī for the fulfillment of misfortune is known as the Vasus;
the quarter of the Jagatī is the Ādityas, and the quarter of the Virāj is said to be the Directions."
From Viṣṇu, the Rudras constitute a quarter (pāda); the meter has one quarter and so forth.
The first [meter] has four quarters with four syllables each; sometimes it has three quarters with seven syllables each.
That is Gāyatrī; when its quarter is a *nīvṛt*, it is *Pratiṣṭhā* and so on—six [varieties] with three quarters.

Increasing by six, eight, and eight, it consists of three feet; with six, eight, and fourteen, it is the *gāyatrī* of three feet; with nine, nine, and six seasons, it is the *nīvṛt*; with six, twelve, and six, it is the *vārāhī*; and now follows the third meter.
The *uṣṇik* metre is recorded in the Veda as having two feet with twelve syllables each, while it is known as having three feet with eight syllables each;
that *kakub-uṣṇik* consists of exactly three feet with eight, twelve, and eight syllables respectively.
Furthermore, the *uṣṇih* consists of three feet with twelve,

eight, and seven syllables respectively; the *paroṣṇih* follows that [the *uṣṇih*] and consists of four feet, while the *anuṣṭubh* consists of eight syllables per foot, being either four-footed or occasionally three-footed.

It should have the brilliance of eight suns; it may occur in the middle or at the end. If the first [pāda] consists of three *gāyatrī* [feet], the third becomes *pathyā*, while the second is *kusāriṇī*.
The shoulders and neck are called *krauṣṭuka*; there may also be a *yakṣa* and a *syadva*, as well as a *vṛhatī*.
At the end of the *upariṣṭādvṛhatī*, there is again a *purastādvṛhatī*.
In some cases, there are four verses of nine syllables each in the cardinal and intermediate directions, colored with eight hues;
it may be a Mahāvṛhatī consisting of three Jāgata [feet], or a Sato-bṛhatī,
or according to Bhaṇḍila, it may be a Paṅkti meter.
With twelve, twelve, and eight syllables [respectively],
the first two are the *vedayuṅ* (the Vedic couplet), then the *paṅkti*, and then the two inverted forms.
The *prastārapaṅkti* has the [heavy] syllable at the beginning, while the *āstārapaṅkti* has it at the end.
A *padapaṅkti* consists of four groups of five syllables and two groups of fewer;
a *gāyatrī* consists of three groups of six syllables and one group of five;
and a *jagatī* consists of six groups of five syllables.
By one [verse], the *triṣṭubh* is called *jyotiṣmatī*, and likewise the *jagatī*.

There is *purastājyotis* when there is a light at the beginning; *madhyajyotis* when there is a light in the middle; and *upariṣṭājyotis* when there is a light at the end. This is likewise for each of the five [verses].
In the *ṣaṭka* (six-syllable) meter, *śaṅkumatī* is the desired form; in the three-footed meter, *kakudmatī* is desired.
That which has a middle like a young child (*śiśumadhyā*) is *pipīlikamadhyamā*.
When it is reversed, it is *yavamadhyā*; [the *trivṛt*] is devoid of one [syllable].
With one additional *bhūmija* [letter], it becomes *cirā*; with two fewer, it becomes *avarā*.
With two more, it is *sandigdha*. From the deity and so forth, certainty arises from the first quarter; the meter and the deity follow in sequence.
Agni, Sūrya, Śaśin, Jīva, Varuṇa, and Candra,
as well as the Viśvedevas and the musical notes beginning with Ṣaḍja, and the bull— these correspond in order.
Gāndhāra, Madhyama, Pañcama, and likewise Dhaivata;
Niṣāda, Śveta, Sāraṅga, and Piśaṅgaka are their colors.
Kṛṣṇa, Nīla, Lohita, and Gaurī are at the head of the Gāyatrī and the others; [the sequence] is "with the middle like an ant" (sapipīlikamadhyaga).
The compositions have the luster of a white lotus; their meters are indeed Jyotiś and Chanda;
the deity is Agni; the caste is Vaiśya; and the lineages (gotras) are said to be Kāśyapa, Gautama, Aṅgiras, Bhārgava, Kauśika, and Vāśiṣṭha, respectively.
Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Essence of Prosody," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 330: An Exposition on Prosody and Metre (Chandojāti)
Agni said:
"The *utkṛti* consists of four hundred [syllables]; one should omit four from the *ukṛti*.
The *pratyakṛti* is formed by further reduction; these indeed are the various *chandas*."
From *atyaṣṭi* and *aṣṭi*,
then *atiśarkarī* and *śarkarī*, as well as *atijagatī* and *jagatī*;
here the meter may be worldly (*laukika*), while that which consists of eleven syllables per foot is remembered as Vedic (*ārṣa*).
The *triṣṭubh*, *paṅkti*, *bṛhatī*, *anuṣṭubh*, and *uṣṇih* have been described;
the *gāyatrī* is the *supratiṣṭhā*, and with the middle [measure] it is the *pratiṣṭhā*.
The *atyuktā* and *atyukta* are the beginning, each being diminished by one syllable [respectively].
A quarter consists of four parts; the *gaṇa*-metres are now demonstrated.
There are as many *samudra* groups as there are [parts], occurring at the beginning, middle, end, and everywhere.
The *kṛti*, *anighṛti*,
and *vṛtti* [meters]— these four and five classes are said to be the characteristics of the *āryā*.

In an Āryā, half of the *svaras* (vowels) constitutes half of the verse; in the uneven [pādas], there is a *ja* (the syllable *jagaṇa*) at the sixth position, and in the second and subsequent pādas, it is preceded by *na* (the syllable *nagaṇa*).
At the end of the seventh [position], there is a *ca* (the syllable *cagaṇa*), and in the second and fifth [pādas], there is a *na* (the syllable *nagaṇa*).
In the first half-verse, the sixth foot shall consist of a single short syllable;
the Āryā is traditionally defined as having three *gaṇas* in each of its two halves.
Another type is the *vipulā*, while the *capalā* occurs when the *ja* and *gau* (*jagaṇa* and *guru*) are situated in the middle.
When the second and fourth [syllables] as well as the first are short, it is *mukhacapalā*;
when the second is short, it is proclaimed as *jaghanacapalā*.
When both [the first and second] are short, it is *mahācapalā*, which has a duration equal to half a measure of song or instrumental music.
The *upagīti* and *udgīti* are said to be formed by the last half-verse in reverse order.

In the half-verse, there are the *rakṣagaṇa*, the *āryā*, the *gīti*, and the *chandas*; furthermore, *vaitālīya* consists of two syllables (*svarā*) per foot, with *na-la* occurring in the even feet.
The Vasus (eight), the forest-dwellers (seven), and the cow-tail (one)—these constitute the *gopuccha* metre.
The *pāṭalikā* consists of the end of the *bhagaṇa*; in the remaining [syllables], it is as before.
Together with six, whether mixed or unpaired, the eastern tradition (*prācyavṛtti*) is thus demonstrated.
The fifth [foot] together with the first, and the third joined with the thousand;
this should be called the Udīcyavṛtti in the eastern direction, and it functions simultaneously.
It would be the Ayukcāruhāsinī, and it would be the Antikā simultaneously. (15) AP 330.014–015ab.
When there are seven *ar* and *vas*, it is called *mātrāsamaka*; when there are *na*, *la*, *va*, *ma*, and *la*, with twelve or nine syllables, it is *navāsikā*;
*viśvoka* consists of five *mas* and eight *las*; and *citrā* consists of *la*, *va*, *ma*, and *ka*, and is *cala*.
*Pucchalam* (variant *kha*) is [the term].

Agni said:
"One should declare that *vṛtta* is of three kinds: even, half-even, and uneven; having made them equal on all sides, one should treat the unmade as half-even."
The uneven [pādas] should be deficient or excessive, while the even ones should have four measures (glaucas). Other than these two, it is a vitānaka;
however, the first [pāda] should be curved, and on a Saturday, the first is not remembered [as such].
The *vālmīki* [meter] consists of the fourth syllable being light; the *pathyā* has even syllables heavy;
the *viparītapathyā* is the opposite of that; the *capalā* has even syllables light;

With *nau*, seven, and *roda-daṇḍa*, it would be *Caṇḍavṛṣṭipraghāta*. (1–2)
By the addition of the letter *repha* (*r*), there may be *ṇa*, *ṇa*, and *va*; these are known as the principal [varieties] beginning with Vyāla and Jīmūta.
In the remaining cases, they are to be understood as *pracita*. This is called the *gāthā-prastāra*. Thus ends the section titled "Description of Even Meters" in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter Three Hundred and Thirty-Four.
Now begins Chapter Three Hundred and Thirty-Five.
Regarding the determination of the prosodic arrangement,
Agni said: "In this context, the established meter is the *gāthā*, which consists of a foot entirely composed of long syllables."
The *prastāra* (metrical grid) is formed by omitting the first *gāthā*; then, that which follows is equal [to the preceding], and that which precedes it is likewise.
[In this system,] there are nine *vasus* (eight) from the *vasu* (eight), and thus it is called *caṇḍavṛṣṭiprayāta*.
In the case of a lost [number], if the sum is even, divide by two; if odd, add one and then divide by two.
For the reverse process, multiply by two and subtract one. This is the method for finding the original number from its doubled value.
In the case of two numbers, the form is half; in the case of zero, it is said to be doubled.
That [result] is multiplied by its own half, and at the end, it is reduced by two for each pair.
In the subsequent [stages], it becomes full, and in the further [stages], it becomes full; this occurs according to the Meru-arrangement.

The number of syllables in the verse and the number of lines, as well as the length in finger-breadths from bottom to top, are calculated by doubling the count and subtracting one; this is declared to be the essence of prosody (*chandaḥsāra*).
Thus ends the section titled "Description of the Prosodic Expansion" (*prastāranirūpaṇa*) in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter Three Hundred and Thirty-Four.
Now begins Chapter Three Hundred and Thirty-Five.
The Exposition of Phonetics:
Agni said, "I shall speak of phonetics; there are sixty-three letters, or forty-four."
There are twenty-one vowels and twenty-five consonants;

the letters from ya onwards are traditionally held to be eight, while the four semivowels are also traditionally held to be four; furthermore, there are the anusvāra, the visarga, and the two sibilants, pa and kha, together with their counterparts.
One should know that *duṣpṛṣṭa* consists of the letter *ḷ*, the protracted vowel (*pluta*),
as well as *raṅga*, *khe*, and *ara*; and the letter *ha* joined with the fifth [consonant].

for the purpose of unifying the meaning through the intellect of the self, it is joined with the mind by the desire to speak.

It produces the sound;
the connection with the morning libation (prātaḥsavana) rests upon the Gāyatrī metre.
At the throat, it is joined with the midday libation (mādhyandina), following the sun within the middle mantras.
The vital air (māruta), which follows the *jagatī* [meter] and resides in the head, being impelled and directed toward the head,
reaches the mouth and produces the phonemes (*varṇa*); their classification is traditionally held to be fivefold.
By way of tone, time, place, effort, and the delivery of meaning, there are eight locations for the phonemes: the chest, the throat, the head,
as well as the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate.

Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), expansion (*vivṛtti*), *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ra*; the root of the tongue (*jihvāmūla*), and the labio-dental (*upadhmāna*)—these are the eightfold movement of the sibilants (*uṣman*).
The state of being (*bhāva*), the connection (*prasaṃdhāna*), and that which begins with the vowel *u* constitute the supreme word (*parampada*).
One should know that which ends in a vowel to be of such a kind; anything else, apart from a sibilant (*ūṣman*), is burnt, devoid of color, and consumed.
Such pronunciation is sinful; such pronunciation is auspicious.
Wealth that has come from a non-sacred source, even if accompanied by traditional lore, well-ordered,
and delivered with a fine voice and eloquent mouth, does not shine before the King of Brahman.
One who is misshapen, one with hanging lips, one who is indistinct, or one who nasalizes his speech [is likewise excluded].
One who is hoarse or has many tongues is not able to utter the phonemes correctly.
Thus, the phonemes should be employed neither indistinctly nor with oppression.
1. "Only one measure" (mātra) — [variant] kha; 2.
"The third pressing ends with the [bhāva]" — [variant] kha;
3. "That which has come from a false path" — [variant] ṭa.
"Having come from the sacred ford of Kṣatīrtha"— thus [it is said];
by the correct application of syllables, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

The three accents are the acute (udātta), the grave (anudātta), and the circumflex (svarita); they are defined by duration as short (hrasva), long (dīrgha), and protracted (pluta). The letters *v*, *h*, *a*, *i*, *cu*, *ya*, and *śa* are produced in the throat; *o*, *ṣ*, *u*, and *pu* are produced at the palate; and *e*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and *ka* are produced at the lips.
The sounds ṛ, ṝ, and ṛsā are known as retroflex (mūrdhanya);
ḷ, ḹ, and lasā are remembered as dental (dantya).
The sound hva is said to be produced at the root of the tongue, while va is recorded by the wise as a labiodental (dantyoṣṭha).
The vowels *e* and *ai* are known to be produced from the throat and the palate; *o* and *au* are remembered as being produced from the throat and the lips.
For the vowels *e* and *ai*, there should be half a mātrā of the throat.
The *ayogavāha* consonants are to be understood as sharing the place of articulation of their respective supports.
The vowels are known to be unaspirated, while the *hal* consonants are slightly aspirated;
the remaining *hal* consonants are said to be fully aspirated— understand these here according to their primary characteristics.
The vowels *a*, *m*, the nasalized (*anunāsika*) sounds, and *n* and *k* are known as having no breath; *h*, *s*, and *ṣ* are remembered as having slight resonance (*nāda*).
The letters beginning with *pa*, *ṇa*, and *ya* are resonant (*ghoṣavat*), while those beginning with *tha* and *ka* are aspirated (*śvāsin*).
One should know the vowel sound to be slightly aspirated; this is declared to be "long."
Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Phonetics," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Chapter Three Hundred and Thirty-Six.
Then begins the three hundred and thirty-sixth chapter.
Agni spoke the definition of poetry and so forth;
now I shall describe the ornaments of poetry, drama, and the like.
Sound, phonemes, words, and sentences—this is considered the totality of speech, wherein the triad of scriptural treatises, historical narratives, and sentences finds its completion.
In the scriptural treatises, sound is predominant; in the historical narratives, there is a focus on the final meaning.
Because denotation is primary, poetry is distinguished from those two;
human birth is rare in this world, and learning is rare therein.
Among those, the capacity for poetry is rare, and within that, creative power is rare.
In that [state], proficiency is difficult to attain; in that [state], discernment is difficult to attain.
When sought by the ignorant, the entire scripture does not succeed.
The first letters, the second letters, the aspirated consonants, and the fourth [set]—these are [the components].

Within groups [of phonemes], there is a collection of letters (varṇavṛnda); a word (pada) arises from the distinction between nominal and verbal suffixes; in brief, a sentence (vākya) is a series of words delimited by a desired meaning;
and poetry (kāvyam) is that which possesses manifest ornaments (alaṅkāra), is endowed with qualities (guṇa), and is free from defects (doṣa).
The source [of speech] is the Veda and the world; food and so forth are established as not born from a womb.
For gods and others, it is refined (*saṃskṛta*); for humans, the natural (*prākṛta*) is threefold.
Poetry and the like are traditionally held to be threefold: prose, verse, and mixed.
A succession of words without feet is also called prose (*gadya*);
it possesses three forms according to the divisions of *cūrṇaka*, *utkalikāprāya*, and *gandhivṛtta*. It has very few compounds and is not excessively dense in its composition.
From a long compound, there arises what is called *cūrṇaka*;
from a medium composition, it becomes a *kalikā*, which does not have an excessively base structure.

This [work] is considered to be of five kinds: the *vṛtta* (verse), which possesses a rounded shadow and is intense with fragrance; the *ākhyāyikā*, the *kathā*, the *khaṇḍakathā*, the *parikathā*, and likewise the *kathānikā*; as well as prose poetry (*gadyakāvya*). AP_336.012ab–cd.
Where there is an extensive praise of the author's lineage in prose (gadya),
where there are the abduction of a maiden, battles, separations, and calamities,
and where the applications of the *rītis* and *vṛttis* are brilliant— [that is the *ākhyāyikā*].
Where there is a division by breaths (ucchvāsa), or where it is in prose (cūrṇaka) or verse (uttara),
or where it consists of Vaktra or Aparavaktra meters— that is known as an Ākhyāyikā.
Wherein the poet briefly praises his own lineage in verses, [that is a Kathā].
Wherever an intermediate story (*kathāntara*) may serve to introduce the meaning for the sake of the hero’s pleasure,

or wherever there should be no formal division (*pariccheda*), one should occasionally employ *ālambhakas*; that [intermediate story] is called a *kathā*, and within its core one should compose a four-line verse (*catuṣpadī*).

Know that *khaṇḍakathā* is that which is [called] *parikathā*; in both of these, they recognize either a minister, a merchant, or a brahmin as the hero. Know that in these two, the *karuṇa* (pathetic) sentiment consists of four types of *vipralambha* (separation).
Of those two, the former (kathā) does not follow the [same] narrative;
because of the mixture of *kathā* and *ākhyāyikā*, it is known as *parikathā*.
It possesses the *bhayānaka* (terrible) sentiment, is preeminent in *sukha* (pleasure), and has the *karuṇa* (pathetic) sentiment in its core.

The *adbhuta* [sentiment] occurs at the end; that narrative (*kathānikā*) is not in the *udātta* [meter], its meaning being well-constructed. Verse (*padya*) consists of four lines (*catuṣpadī*), and it is of three kinds: *vṛtta*, *jāti*, and *uktha*.
Among these, *vṛtta* is measured by the number of syllables (*akṣara-saṃkhyeya*); it arises from the remainder of the *kṛti* [class].
"Kāśyapa says that calculation by means of two hundred *mātrās* constitutes *jāti*;
according to Piṅgala, meter (*vṛtta*) is of three kinds: even, half-even, and uneven."
That science is a boat for those wishing to cross the deep ocean of poetry;
it consists of the mahākāvya, the kalāpa, the paryābandha, the viśeṣaka,
the kulaka, the muktaka, and the koṣa— this is the family of poetic forms.

A *mahākāvya* is a composition in cantos (*sarga*) begun in Sanskrit; whether it originates from historical narratives or other sources, it is not at all flawed provided it has a noble subject matter.
The journey of the messenger with the mantra should not be excessively long;
it should be composed in the Śakvarī, Atijagatī, or Atiśakvarī meters, as well as the Triṣṭubh,
using verses such as the Puṣpitāgrā, which are beautiful, uniform, and characterized by noble lineages.
But the *muktā* [meter], which has a different metrical structure, consists of cantos that are not excessively abbreviated;

one [canto] is composed with *atiśarkarī* and *aṣṭi* meters, another with *saṅkīrṇaka*, and yet another with *mātrā*; and the final canto among those praised for its excellence is likewise distinguished.
In that [state], an eon passes unnoticed; for the virtuous, there is no regard for distinctions [of time] through cities,
oceans, mountains, seasons, the moon, the sun, hermitages, and trees,
nor through gardens, water-sports, drinking bouts, amorous dalliances, or festivals.
By the arrangements of the messenger's words, which were extraordinary due to the conduct of unchaste women,
and by darkness, the wind, and other intense manifestations, [he was overcome].
(Kaśyapa is the name in the *ja*, *ña*, and *ṭa* recensions.)

4. *vyaktā* iti ña...
It is set in motion by all modes of expression, permeated by all aesthetic moods,
and nourished by all poetic styles and sentiments.
Because it is nourished by the ornaments of poetic qualities,
it is therefore called a *mahākāvya*, and its author is a *mahākavi*.
Even though verbal ingenuity (*vāgvaidagdhya*) is predominant here, aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) alone is the lifeblood of this work.
The body [of this work], produced by distinct efforts, possesses the grace of verbal artistry;
it has been explained everywhere as yielding the fruit of the four aims of life under the name of "Nāyaka," composed in a uniform meter and tender with the Kauśikī style.

In this [work], there is a *kalāpa*, a journey (*pravāsa*), and the sentiment (*rasa*) called "prior passion" (*anurāga*); it contains a *saviśeṣaka* and, through attainment (*prāpti*) and so forth, is composed in both *saṃskṛta* and the local dialect (*nētra*).
A *kulaka* consists of many verses, and that is what constitutes *sandānitakas*.

Each individual detached verse is capable of evoking wonder; this treasury, endowed with the beautiful, well-spoken words of lion-like poets and as vast as the infinite Brahman, is pleasing to the discerning man of taste.
And its power is like a reflection; in creation, it has a distinct mode of operation. It is known as twofold: the "mixed" (*miśra*) and the "scattered" (*prakīrṇa*).
The scattered is both audible and performable, consisting of all types of speech.
Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Poetry and the Like," in the section on Ornamentation within the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*. [Variant readings:
*juṣṭam* in manuscripts Ja and Ṭa.]
Chapter Three Hundred and Thirty-Seven.
Now begins the three hundred and thirty-seventh chapter.
Regarding the definition of drama,
Agni said:
"The *nāṭaka*, along with the *prakaraṇa*, the *ḍima*, and also the *īhāmṛga*."
The *samavakāra* and the *prahasana* are to be known; likewise,
the *vyāyoga*, *bhāṇa*, *vīthyaṅka*, *troṭaka*, *nāṭikā*,
*saṭṭaka*, *śilpaka*, *karṇa*, and the *ekaduḥmallikā*.
Prasthāna, Bhāṇikā, Bhāṇī, Goṣṭhī, Hallīśaka,
Kāvya, Śrīgadita, Nāṭyarāsaka, Rāsaka,
Ullāpyaka, and Preṅkṣaṇa— these constitute the twenty-seven [types].
The characteristic has a twofold course: it is either general or particular.
The general applies to all objects, while the remainder operates only in specific cases; once the preliminary stage is concluded, both time and place apply.
The sentiments (*rasa*), the emotional states (*bhāva*), the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), the dramatic gestures (*abhinaya*),

as well as the act (*aṅka*) and the structural setting (*sthiti*), constitute the general framework because they apply everywhere; however, the specific details should be stated according to the occasion, while the general principles are stated first.
They say that drama is the means for accomplishing the three aims of human life (trivarga),
and its procedure consists of the preliminary ritual (pūrvaraṅga) performed according to rule,
which includes thirty-two components beginning with the *nāndī*.
Salutations to the deities and praise for the gurus,
as well as benedictions for the cows, Brahmins, kings, and others, are sung at the end of the *nāndī*;
this is how the *sūtradhāra* is established in dramatic works.
One should point out these five: the lineage beginning with the guru, the praise of the tradition, the poet’s personal prowess, the connection, and the subject matter of the poem. AP 337.011ab.
Where the actress, the *vidūṣaka*, or even the *pāripārśvika*,
together with the *sūtradhāra*, engage in a dialogue among themselves using various verses arising from their own roles that suggest the subject matter to be presented; [that is the *prastāvanā*].

That should be known by the wise as the *āmukha* (prologue), and it is also called the *prastāvanā* (introduction). It has three divisions: the *pravṛttaka*, the *kathodghāta*, and the *prayogātiśaya*. These arise within the portions of the seed (*bīja*).
When the Stage Director describes a time that has already begun, and the entrance of a character occurs based on that [time], it is *pravṛttaka*;
or when there is a statement by the Stage Director, or the very meaning of a statement [spoken by him]. (AP 337.015)

Having taken [the cue], the actor enters; this is called *kathodghāta*. When the *sūtradhāra* describes an action within the performance itself, and then the actor enters, that is indeed *prayogātiśaya*.
The body of plays and other such works is said to be the plot (*itivṛtta*), which is traditionally held to have two divisions: the established (*siddha*) and the imagined (*utprekṣita*).
The established is that seen in traditional scripture (*āgama*), while the imagined is created by the poet.

The seed (*bīja*), the drop (*bindu*), the banner (*patākā*), the small banner (*prakarī*), and the purpose (*kārya*) are the five elements of the plot (*arthaprakṛti*); and likewise, the five stages of action (*ceṣṭā*) follow in order:
the commencement (*ārambha*), the effort (*prayatna*), the attainment (*prāpti*), and the realization (*sadbhāva*).

The attainment of the fruit is certain, and the union with the fruit is the fifth. Likewise, the Mukha (opening), Pratimukha (counter-opening), Garbha (embryo), Vimarṣa (deliberation), and Nirvahaṇa (conclusion) are the five junctures (*sandhi*) in their proper order.
That which is indicated as a mere small amount, yet spreads forth in many ways,
and which culminates in fruit— that indeed is called a seed.

That in which the production of the seed (*bīja*) occurs, giving rise to various meanings and sentiments (*rasa*), and which follows the body of the poem, is proclaimed as the *mukha* (opening). It consists of the composition of a desired theme and the non-omission of the narrative.
The attainment of passion, the concealment of secrets,
renown like that of a wonder, and the disclosure of what is manifest—
just as a man lacking limbs is not excellent, so too is poetry [deficient] in these respects.
No historical event whatsoever proceeds without place and time;
therefore, because of the necessity of specifying these two, a "pada" (foot/verse-quarter) is so called.
Among places, it is the land of Bhārata-varṣa; among times, it is the three ages beginning with the Kṛta-yuga.
Without those two [the *nāṭyaśāstra* and the *alaṅkāraśāstra*], the arising of pleasure and pain for living beings would never occur;
nor is there any fault in the fact that discussions concerning creation and the like are applicable within the context of dramatic performance.
Thus ends the section titled "Description of Drama" in the *Alaṅkāra* chapter of the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter three hundred and thirty-seven.
Now begins chapter three hundred and thirty-eight.
Regarding the description of the erotic and other sentiments,
Agni said:
"The supreme, imperishable Brahman is eternal, unborn, and all-pervading."
In the Vedāntas, they speak of the Lord as the singular light of consciousness;
his innate bliss is manifested at certain times.
That manifestation of his is called the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of the wonder of consciousness.
The first modification of that [Mahat] is known as *ahaṅkāra* (the ego-sense);
from it arises self-conceit (*abhimāna*), and within it these three worlds are contained.
From self-conceit arises *rati* (erotic passion), and when that has reached full development,
it is designated as *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment) because of its commonality with transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*) and so forth.
Its various subdivisions include the others, such as the comic (*hāsya*) and the rest, in manifold ways.

Arising from the specific qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, they possess the individual characteristics of their respective sounds; these emerge from the Supreme Self through the continuum of the *guṇas*.
From passion (*rāga*) arises the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), and from sharpness (*taikṣṇya*) the furious (*raudra*) arises.

The heroic (*vīra*) is born from firmness (*avaṣṭambha*), while the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) arises from contraction (*saṅkoca*). Laughter (*hāsya*) is considered superior to the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), and the pathetic (*karuṇa*) rasa arises from the furious (*raudra*).
The marvelous (*adbhuta*) is produced from the heroic, and the terrifying (*bhayānaka*) from the loathsome.

The eight aesthetic sentiments (rasas)— namely the erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, the terrifying, the loathsome, the marvelous, and the peaceful— are by their very nature fourfold.
Without renunciation, speech does not shine, just as the goddess Lakṣmī does not shine without charity.
In the shoreless universe of poetry, the poet alone is the Lord of Creatures;
for as he conceives the world, so does it transform.
If the poet is a lover of the erotic, the world born of his poetry becomes composed of that very sentiment.

If that poet is free from passion (*vītarāga*), then that [work] is clearly devoid of aesthetic flavor (*nīrasa*). There is no aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) devoid of emotional states (*bhāva*), nor is there an emotional state devoid of aesthetic flavor.
For it is by means of these that one cultivates the aesthetic flavors, and the aesthetic flavors are cultivated [by them].

There are eight stable emotions (sthāyins) beginning with love (rati), and [thirty-three] transitory states (vyabhicārins) such as paralysis (stambha). Love is defined as the experience of pleasure toward an object agreeable to the mind. Laughter is said to be the expansion of the mind through joy and similar causes.
They say that fear is the agitation of the mind arising from the sight of paintings and the like,
while disgust is the loathing of objects that bring misfortune.
Astonishment (*vismaya*) is an expansion of the mind resulting from the perception of an extraordinary object.
There are eight [faults], beginning with paralysis (*stambha*), which arise from *rajas* and *tamas*.
Paralysis is the obstruction of activity induced by fear, passion, and so forth.
The water of the body arises from internal agitation caused by passion for women and the like;
sweat [arises] from joy and the like; the exhalation of the body and the emergence of horripilation [arise from the same];
and the obstruction of speech and the breaking of the voice arise from joy and fear, respectively.
They define mental dejection as grief arising from the loss of what is desired and similar causes; anger is the awakening of harshness toward that which acts in opposition;
and that which aims at the accomplishment of the goals of human life is called enthusiasm.
Trembling is proclaimed to be the agitation and intensification of the mind;
discoloration is the loss of luster born from despondency and similar states;
and tears are well known as the water from the eyes produced by suffering, joy, and so forth.
The setting of the senses and their dissolution through such means as leaping and other physical exertions is called *nirveda*—
the weariness of the mind characterized by dispassion and the like. Furthermore, *sāda* is the exhaustion residing in the body, arising from mental anguish and similar causes.
Apprehension is the anticipation of an undesirable event; envy is malice or jealousy; intoxication is the delusion of the mind arising from the consumption of wine and similar substances;
and fatigue is the exhaustion produced within the body resulting from excessive physical activity.
Aversion toward activities such as the erotic and so forth is called mental indolence (*ālasya*).
(AP 338.024cd) [Note 1] "Arising from fear, passion, and so forth" is found in manuscript *kha*.
[Note 2] Page 207.

Dejection is the falling away from one's essential nature (*sattva*); the brooding over objects of thought is called delusion (*moha*), which consists in being obstructed from the means for what ought to be done. Memory (*smṛti*) is the reflection of an object previously experienced.
Intellect (*mati*) is the discernment of objects, brought about by the knowledge of reality.
A certain contraction of the mind arising from shame, passion, and so forth is [the state of] bashfulness (*vrīḍā*). Unsteadiness is fickleness; joy (*harṣa*) is the clarity of the mind.
Possession (*āveśa*), its remedy, exhaustion (*śaya*), and the failure of one's own mental power regarding what ought to be done— this is called dullness (*jaḍatā*).
Contentment (*dhṛti*) is the increase of prosperity resulting from the attainment of what is desired.

Pride (*garva*) is the disregard for others and the cultivation of a sense of superiority in oneself; despondency (*viṣāda*) is the frustration regarding a desired object caused by fate or other obstacles; and longing (*autsukya*) is a state of agitation due to the desire for something not yet attained.
The numbness of the mind and senses is epilepsy; immobility is a state of being fixed.
Fear is the terror caused by afflictions and the like in battle; repetition is the wonder of the mind.
Impatience is the lack of tranquility in anger; awakening is the arising of consciousness.
*Avahittha* is concealment pertaining to gestures and facial expressions.
They know *ugratā* (severity) as harshness of speech and punishment arising from anger.
*Ūha* is deliberation (*vitarka*), while *vyādhi* (disease) is an affliction of the mind and body.
Insanity arises from causes such as unspeakable chatter, intoxication, and the like;
the supreme tranquility of the mind results from the knowledge of reality and similar means.
These emotional states (bhāvas) are indeed to be employed by poets as aesthetic flavors (rasas) in poetry and other works.
For that in which love and the like are manifested, and that by which they are manifested, is called the *vibhāva* (the determinant);
it is of two kinds, consisting of the objective basis (*ālambana*) and the stimulant (*uddīpana*).
This group of emotional states (bhāvas), beginning with love (rati),
arises depending upon that which is called the objective determinant (ālambana-vibhāva), such as the hero (nāyaka) and others.
Thus, there may be the noble and dignified (dhīrodātta), the noble and haughty (dhīroddhata), and likewise the noble and playful (dhīralalita).
The hero (nāyaka) is thus remembered as being of four types: the steadfast and tranquil (dhīrapraśānta), the compliant (anukūla), the clever (dakṣiṇa), the deceitful (śaṭha), and the bold (dhṛṣṭa).
There are also three [types of companions]: the confidant (pīṭhamarda), the parasite (viṭa), and the jester (vidūṣaka).
In the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), the companions in jest (*narmasaciva*) are the secondary male leads (*anunāyaka*):
the *pīṭhamarda*, the *sambalaka*, the illustrious *viṭa* born in that same locality, and the *vidūṣaka* who is a jester; these are the eight types of male and female leads (*nāyaka-nāyikā*).

According to the Kauśikas, [the types of women] are one's own (*svakīyā*), another's (*parakīyā*), and a remarried woman (*punarbhū*). There is also the common woman (*sāmānyā*), who is not a remarried woman; thus they are divided into many categories.
These are the excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) that exist through various latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Those who do not feel revulsion toward the objects of perception,
whose sixty-four arts are twofold through actions such as singing and the like,
even their memory is generally a source of mockery and derision.
Through the manifestation of objects by means of conditioned entities that have been awakened,
and through the mind, speech, intellect, body, memory, desire, aversion, and effort,
the very undertaking [of action] is known as the "manifestation" (*anubhāva*) of the wise.
And that [pleasure] is experienced here, it comes into being, and indeed it is defined.
It is said to be primarily an activity of the mind, an undertaking of the mind.
Being of two kinds—masculine and feminine—it is established even in this manner.
Beauty, grace, sweetness, steadfastness, profundity, charm, magnanimity, and splendor— these eight are the masculine qualities.
The disparagement of the lowly, rivalry with the superior, valor, and the causes such as dexterity—
these constitute beauty in the qualities of the mind, just as a house shines when it is beautiful.
Furthermore, there are *bhāva*, *hāva*, *helā*, *śobhā*, and likewise *kānti*.
Radiance, sweetness, heroism, boldness, nobility,
steadfastness, and depth are said to be the twelve excitants (vibhāvas) of women.
Emotional state (bhāva), playful gesture (vilāsa), and coquetry (hāva)— the latter being a slight manifestation of joy arising from emotion— are also included.
The application of speech is the undertaking of speech, and it is twelvefold:

therein, *abhāṣaṇa* (non-speaking), *ālāpa* (conversation), *pralāpa* (idle talk), *vilāpa* (much speaking), *anulāpa* (lamentation, which is speech of suffering), and *asakṛdvacaḥ* (repeated speech).
*Saṃlāpa* is speech consisting of question and answer; *apalāpa* is speaking otherwise than the truth.
*Vārtā* is news; *prayāṇa* is a journey; *sandeśa* is a message; *nirdeśa* is instruction; *pratipādana* is demonstration.
*Tattvadeśa* is the teaching of reality; *atideśa* is extension [of a rule]; *apadeśa* is the description of something else.
Instruction (*upadeśa*) consists of the speech of training, the expression of artifice, and the designation;
this activity for the sake of awakening is held to be the undertaking of right intelligence.
Its three divisions are style (*rīti*), meter (*vṛtti*), and application (*pravṛtti*).
Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rasas, such as the Erotic (Śṛṅgāra), etc.," in the *Ālaṅkāra* section of the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Chapter Three Hundred and Thirty-Nine.
Regarding the definition of *rīti*,
Agniruci said:
"In the formal presentation of the science of speech (*vāgvidyā*), *rīti* is also fourfold."
The Pāñcālī, Gauḍīyā, Vaidarbhī, and Lāṭajā styles are as follows:
the Pāñcālī is characterized by figurative usage (upacāra), softness, and short compounds;
the Gauḍīyā has an unstable structure and long compounds.

The Vaidarbha style is devoid of excessive or redundant embellishments (*upacāra*), possesses a composition that is not overly soft, and is free from compound words (*vigraha*). The Lāṭīya style has a clear composition and does not have excessively prominent compounds.
Although it has been described through numerous refinements,
dramatic action (*kriyā*) is established as fourfold: the *Bhāratī*, the *Ārabhaṭī*, the *Kauśikī*, and the *Sāttvatī*, whose modes of conduct are not inconsistent with their respective functions.

Predominantly speech, consisting mostly of men, joined by women, and characterized by common parlance—because it was composed by Bharata, this is called the Bhāratī style (rīti). The Bhāratī has four components: the Vīthī and likewise the Prahasana.
The *prastāvanā* (prologue) and the thirteen elements (*vīthyaṅga*) of the *vīthī* [are as follows]:
the *udghātaka*, the *lapita* as the second,
*asatpralāpa*, and *vākśreṇī*.
The *nālikā*, the *vipaṇan*,
as well as the *chalāvaskandita*;
[and] the *vāgveṇī*.
2. *Vyāhāra* and *trigata*, as well as *gaṇḍa*, *mṛdu*, and the thirteenth, *acita*.

The *prahasana* (farce) consists of speech directed toward ascetics and others that is primarily intended for ridicule; the *ārabhaṭī* (boisterous performance) is known to abound in illusions, sorcery, combat, and the like; and there are also the *maṅkṣiptaka* and *āpāta*.
And the very raising of the subject matter.
Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Rītis," in the section on Ornamentation within the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 340:
Description of the Movements of the Limbs in Dancing and Other Arts.
Agni said:

"They generally maintain that the initiation of the body, as well as the specific movements of the limbs and sub-limbs and the actions of these two, depend primarily upon the former [the self], which rests within the weak [the body]."
Līlā, vilāsa, vichitti, vibhrama, kilakiñcita, moṭṭāyita, kuṭṭamita, vivvoka, lalita,
as well as vikṛta, krīḍita, and keli— thus it is twelvefold.
In the destruction of conventional concealment (*saṃvṛti*), the imitation of the gestures of beloved ones while displaying particular distinctions is considered by the wise to be *vilāsa* (coquetry).
The mingling of laughter, weeping, and so forth, is indeed called *kilakiñcita* (amorous agitation).
A certain transformation is *vivvoka*, while *lalita* arises from delicacy (*saukumārya*).
The head, hands, chest, sides, hips, and feet are known as the primary limbs (*aṅga*) in their respective order;
the creeper-like eyebrows and so forth are the secondary limbs (*pratyaṅga*).
And [the state of] having the hands and feet drawn together occurs without an action produced by effort in the limbs and their parts.
The application [of this term] is not always primary; in some cases it is secondary.
It is also used for that which is slightly shaken, shaken, agitated, and thoroughly shaken.
Parivāhita, mādhūta, avadhūta, then ācita, nikuñcita, parāvṛtta, utkṣipta, and adhoga,
as well as lalita— thus the head should be known to be of thirteen kinds.
The movement of the eyebrows is to be known as sevenfold: lowering, knitting, and the face with a frown.

Vision is threefold: that which pertains to rasa, the stable emotions (sthāyibhāva), and the transitory emotions (sañcāribhāva). Among these, the vision born of rasa is free from the thirty-six varieties and is eightfold.
The action of the pupils is ninefold, consisting of revolving, moving, and so forth;
the nose is known to have six functions, while exhalation is considered to be ninefold;
the sinful action of the lips is sixfold, and the activity of the chin is sevenfold.
The face is of six kinds, beginning with the *kaluṣa*; the neck is recorded as being of nine kinds;
and the hand is generally released [from bondage] as either unjoined (*asaṃyuta*) or joined (*saṃyuta*), namely:
the *patāka*, the *tripatāka*, and likewise the *kartarīmukha*.
The half-moon, the formidable [spear], the parrot-beak,
likewise the *suṣṭi*, the *śikhara*, the wood-apple, the shield-mouth,
the needle-mouth, the lotus-bud, the *śiras*, and those with the head of a deer.
And likewise the *caturabhramaru*;
the *haṃsāsya* and *haṃsapakṣa*; as well as the *sandaṃśa* and *mukula*; and [the mudrās] known as *ākalpita* and *kalpita*.
Regarding the two readings "kāṅgūlakālapadmau" and "kāṃmūlakālapadmau," both of these textual variants are incorrect.
The spider (*ūrṇanābha*) and the cock (*tāmracūḍa*), these twenty-four are declared to have unjoined hands; however, thirteen have joined hands.
The añjali, the kapota, the karkaṭa, and likewise the svastika;
the kaṭaka, the vardhamāna, as well as the asaṅga and the niṣadha; the dola, the puṣpapuṭa, and likewise the makara.
The *gajadanta* (elephant-tusk), *vahistambha* (external pillar), and *vardhamāna* (increasing) are the other hands.
The chest (*uraḥ*) is of five kinds, such as *ābhugna* (contracted) and *nartana* (dancing).
The abdomen (*udara*) is of three types: extremely emaciated (*atikṣāma*), *khaṇḍa* (fragmented), and *pūrṇa* (full).
The five actions for the sides, the fivefold action of the shanks,
and the manifold action of the feet are prescribed in dance and drama.
Thus ends the section on ornamentation in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Chapter 341:
Description of Gestures (Abhinaya) and Other Elements of Dramatic Performance.
Agni said:
"Abhinaya should be understood by the wise as the presentation of meanings through direct representation;
its origin is fourfold, based on internal being (sattva), speech, limbs, and gestures."

The *sāttvika* [emotions] begin with paralysis and so forth; the vocal begins with the undertaking of speech; the physical is the undertaking of the body; and the *āhārya* consists of the activities initiated by the undertaking of the intellect.
Now, the application of the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and so forth is explained according to their identification.
Without that [union], the independence of all these [elements] would be entirely purposeless;
for erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) is traditionally held to be of two kinds: union (sambhoga) and separation (vipralambha).
Furthermore, those two [types of love-in-separation] are each twofold: concealed and manifest.
That erotic sentiment termed *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) is fourfold: namely, that called "love at first sight," and those consisting of "parting" and "sorrow."
Arising from any one of these as characterized by enjoyment,
it evolves in exactly four ways and does not deviate from what preceded it.
Its emergence occurs within a woman and a man, and its fulfillment is pleasure.
All the *sāttvika* [emotions] are present there, except for change of color (*vaivarṇya*) and fainting (*pralaya*).
The erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is augmented by virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, as well as by specific focal objects (*ālambana*) and their particular variations, being thus continuous.

One should know that *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment) is of two kinds, consisting of speech, costume, and action; and *hāsa* (laughter) is of four kinds: *smita* is said to be that in which the teeth are not visible;
*hasita* is that in which the tips of the teeth are slightly visible and the eyes are wide open.

A laugh accompanied by sound is *vihasita*, while that which is crooked is *upahasita*. A laugh with sound is *pāpahasita*, and one without sound is *atihāsita*. Furthermore, that which is called the pathetic (*karuṇa*) sentiment is of three kinds.
Sorrow arises from the destruction of dharma as well as from the agitation of the mind;
thus, sorrow becomes the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*). Which one is considered the primordial permanent emotion?
Furthermore, the *raudra* (fierce) rasa is also threefold, consisting of [the emotions arising from] the limbs, costumes, and speech.
Its manifesting factors are anger, perspiration, horripilation, and trembling.
There are three types: the heroic donor (*dānavīra*), the heroic in righteousness (*dharmavīra*), and the heroic in battle (*yuddhavīra*).
And it is held that *utsāha* (exertion) is the cause of its accomplishment.
Wherever the heroic sentiment (*vīra*) persists throughout its commencement,
the sentiment called the terrifying (*bhayānaka*) arises, and fear is that which brings it about.
The *vībhatsa* (the loathsome) is traditionally held to be of two kinds: the agitating and the disturbing.
The agitating consists of leaping and such; the disturbing consists of blood and the like.
Its function is to initiate disgust, and its *sāttvika* (pure) constituent ceases.
They declare that *alaṃkāras* are those properties (*dharmas*) which produce the beauty of poetry;
and those who desire to adorn may adorn the word, the meaning, or both in three ways.
Those [properties] here which are capable of adorning the word through etymological derivation and so forth [are the verbal ornaments].
The learned experts of poetic analysis declare these to be the ornaments of sound (śabdālaṅkāra): Chāyā, Mudrā, Ukti, Yukti along with Gumphanā,
Vākovākya, Anuprāsa, Citra, and Duṣkara.
It should be known that there are nine ornaments of words because they do not overlap;
among them, *chāyā* (shadow) is the imitation of another's utterance, and it is also fourfold,
arising from the imitation of the speech of common people, clever persons, children, or a single individual.
Proverbs and popular sayings are common to all people;
the wise pursue such popular sayings, for they desire their shadow.
The "cheṭaka" are the clever, whose intelligence is skillful in the fine arts (*kalā*). 341.022–023ab.
The shadow of a poetical expression (*chāyā*) is desired by poets as that which evokes the essence of a clever saying (*chekokti*).
The speech of one who is unrefined is characterized by all as being like the speech of a child;
therefore, the shadow of a child’s speech is that which imitates such limited utterances.
The speech of one who is intoxicated— though its syllables may be disordered and its words indecorous—
is such that even when spoken as a mere shadow of itself, it shines with great beauty;
for, through a particular intentionality, it reveals the poet’s creative power.
That which bestows joy is the *mudrā*; in our view, that very thing is also the bed.
That is called an "utterance" (*ukti*) in which even a meaning that is [otherwise] impossible becomes plausible.
Through the method for the sake of worldly conduct, it delights the hearts of the virtuous.
Both injunction and prohibition, as well as restriction and non-restriction, along with option and exclusive specification— these are its sixfold modes of expression.

The wise have described reasoning as that which is employed to effect the connection between two things— namely, the signified and the signifier— which are, as it were, mutually unconnected; and this applies equally to the word and its meaning,
as well as to the sentence and its meaning.

Its scope consists of six types: the subject matter (*viṣaya*), the context (*prakaraṇa*), and the elaboration (*prapañca*). Composition (*gumphanā*) is the practice of arrangement within the domain of word, meaning, and sequence; it is threefold according to the sequence of words, meanings, or both.
A dialogue (*vākovākya*) consists of a statement and a reply; it is of two kinds according to the distinction between direct and indirect speech.
Among these, the first is natural speech;
it is further divided into two types: that which begins with a question and that which is preceded by a question.
"Vakrokti (crooked speech), however, arises from stylistic deviation; by means of that [deviation], it is made twofold through intonation (*kāku*).
Thus ends the three hundred and forty-first chapter, titled 'The Description of Gestures and the Like,' in the section on Ornamentation within the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*."
Chapter Three Hundred and Forty-Two.
Then begins the three hundred and forty-second chapter.
Regarding verbal ornaments:
repetition of syllables, words, or sentences constitutes alliteration (anuprāsa), which may be characterized by the brilliance of fire.
The quality of *varṇa* (phonetic texture) is twofold, arising from the recurrence of single phonemes (*ekavarṇa*) or multiple phonemes (*anekavarṇa*).
From the recurrence of single phonemes, five styles (*vṛtti*) are born:
the sweet (*madhurā*), the graceful (*lalitā*), the mature (*prauḍhā*), the auspicious (*bhadrā*), and the harsh (*paruṣā*).
In the Madhurā [rīti], after the final consonant of a class (varga), the two sounds *ra* and *ṇa* should follow, separated by a short vowel; there should be a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of two *na*s.
Furthermore, a repetition of letters from the same class (*vargya-varṇa*) should not occur more than five times.
Lalitā consists predominantly of *bala* (short syllables).
That which is born from the *paṇa* group is *prauḍhā*.
Above, the letters of the *naṭa* group, excluding the fifth, are joined with the letter *repha* (*r*).
That which remains in the Bhadrā is called the Paruṣā; that in which the *ūṣman* sounds are joined with their respective consonants,
excluding the letter *a*, and in which there is an exceedingly great repetition of vowels, [is the Paruṣā].
Anusvāra and visarga, when occurring without an interval, lead to harshness;
as do the letters śa, ṣa, sa, and ra when joined with the letter ra, and also the vowel ā in great measure.
