2. "Because of the conjunction of a *mahāprāṇa* [consonant] with *ūṣman*, and because of the following light [vowel], they are not separated"—thus [it is said regarding] *ṭa*.
3. "Lalitā is preponderantly forest"—thus *kha*;
"Lalitā is preponderantly calves"—thus *ṭa*.
A *ha* joined with these two [nasals] and the semivowels (*antasthā*) results in harshness; likewise,
a heavy syllable (*guru-varṇa*) remains so even when another consonant intervenes, provided that [intervening consonant] is not itself combined with another.
Among those [faults], the first is honored as *pāruṣya* (harshness), but not the fifth.
Even *paruṣā* (harshness) is employed in the case of verbal abuse and the imitation of sounds, such as:
"Karṇāṭī, Kauntalī, Kauntī, Kauṅkaṇī, Vāmanāsikā."
The *drāvaṇī* consists of the five vowels (*mādhavī*) followed by the semi-vowels (*antastha*) and sibilants (*ūṣman*) in sequence;
that which is surrounded by various letters and expresses distinct meanings is *yamaka*, and it is of two kinds: non-intervened (*avyapeta*) and intervened (*vyapeta*).
It is non-separate due to immediate succession, and separate due to intervention.
These two are of two kinds, and through the division of their positions and feet, they are fourfold,
by virtue of the application of one, two, or three [feet] at the beginning, middle, or end of the first foot.
If each subsequent quarter begins with seven syllables more than the preceding one, it is sevenfold;
if the beginnings consist of one, two, or three quarters respectively, it is sixfold, and the other type is equal [to that].
The third [type] is threefold, having as its scope the beginning, middle, and end of a quarter-verse;
it consists of *pādāntayamaka*, *kāñcīyamaka*,
and likewise *vikrāntayamaka*.
The *pādādiyamaka* (initial repetition of the verse-quarter), as well as the *āmreḍita* (repeated),
the *caturvyavasita*, and the *mālāyamaka*—
these ten types of *yamaka* are preeminent; there are many other varieties besides them.
The repetition of a word, whether independent or dependent on another, is of two kinds: [the first is] *bālavāsikā* (as found in manuscripts *kha* and *ṭa*),
and [the second is] *vanavāsikā* (as found in manuscript *ña*).
2. "By each preceding one" is found in the manuscripts Ja, Ña, and Ṭa; 3. "And also the *sambandhayamaka*" is found in the manuscript Kha (p.
People know that there is repetition (*āvṛtti*) of words with distinct purposes [in the case of *yamaka*].
When two words are repeated, it may occur as a compound (*samasta*) through composition;
when they are not compounded, it occurs separately (*vyasta*) within a single quarter-verse (*pāda*) due to its analysis (*vigraha*).

In this manner, the repetition of a sentence is also desired as far as possible; for alliteration and other figures of speech are worthy of being employed when they are light, moderate, and appropriate. Whatever is experienced as similar through any mode of expression [is considered an instance of alliteration].
The proximity of words such as *tadrūpa* (that form) and so forth, when accompanied by that [context], brings about aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
In a social gathering, a verbal puzzle studied out of curiosity is called *vāgbandha* (verbal bondage);
it is termed *praśna* (question), *prahelikā* (riddle), *gupta* (hidden), as well as *cyuta* (omitted) and *datte* (added), both of which.

There are seven types of riddles (*samasyā*), which are subdivisions based on the application of multiple meanings. That in which a response is given through the arrangement of identical syllables is a "question" (*praśna*), distinguished by the categories of single-question, double-question, and response.
When asked about one thing in two ways, it is twofold: both combined and separate. A *prahelikā* (enigma) is that in which the word is concealed for two meanings;
it is twofold: verbal and objective. Among these, the objective arises from the comprehension of the meaning.
They say that a verbal riddle (*śābdī prahelikā*) arises from the comprehension of words; it is of six kinds.

That in which a sentence component is concealed, yet the intended meaning is not ultimate, and which possesses the expectancy established by those very components—that is "concealed" (*gupta*), even though it is hidden (*gūḍha*).

Where there is the appearance of another meaning due to the displacement of a sentence-component and so forth, that [fault] is "displaced" (*cyuta*); it is of four kinds, characterized by the requirement [of the displaced element]. (342.027cd–342.028ab) [Note 1]: *Laghum api evam arhaṇāt*—thus [it is stated] in the *Ṭīkā*.
"Because even a small [act] is thus worthy of honor," i.e.,
because even a small [act], being thus worthy of honor...
Because it is merely a minor expansion, these three readings do not appear to be correct.

When a second meaning is perceived even though a constituent of the sentence— whether a vowel, a consonant, a nasal bindu, or a visarga— is displaced, that is called *datta* (the "given"); its sub-varieties are considered to be as previously described, based on the displacement of vowels and so forth.
When another letter is substituted in place of a removed syllable,
and a different meaning shines forth therein, that is called *cyutadatta*. When a single well-composed verse is constructed from the parts of various other verses, [that is called *prahelikā*].
Because of the confusion of agency— whether it belongs to me, to another, or to both self and other—
this work is exceedingly difficult to compose, signaling the poet’s mastery;
though it may seem flavorless, it is a great festival for the connoisseurs.
It is threefold: by *niyama*, by *vidarbha*, and by *bandha*.
The *niyama* of a poet whose composition is delightful is traditionally held to be threefold: by position (*sthāna*), by vowel (*svara*), and by consonant (*vyañjana*).
Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is defined precisely by its direct and inverse orders;
this direct and inverse order arises through both word and meaning.
It is an artistic contrivance consisting of the arrangement of phonemes repeated in manifold ways.
The binding of various well-known objects is thus designated as eightfold:
the *gomūtrikā*, the *ardhabhramaṇa*, the *sarvatobhadra*, the *ambuja*,
the *cakra*, the *cakrābjaka*, the *daṇḍa*, and the *muraja*.
When there is one intervening syllable between each half-verse and each quarter-verse,
it is called *gomūtrikā*. Others say the former is *aśvapadā*,
while they call the latter *dhenu-gomūtrikā* and *jālabandha*.
One should perform the arrangement of these two using half-verses and half-lines; [this is called] the "knee-binding" (jānubandha).
Of the syllables placed here one below the other in successive order,
one should lead from the syllable situated at the very bottom up to the fourth quarter;
one should lead from the fourth quarter upward by half a quarter in reverse order.
That very *sarvatobhadra* is a threefold lotus;
from that, the obstacle [is placed] on the four petals, and on both sets of four petals.
Now, at the head of the first quarter, there are the syllables of the three quarters.
At the end of all the quarters, that [syllable] arises;
the final syllable of the preceding quarter [is placed] at the beginning of the subsequent quarter in reverse order,
and the final syllable of the last quarter [is placed] at the beginning of the first quarter as two syllables.

On a four-petaled [lotus], there should be eight petals; furthermore, on a sixteen-petaled one, there should be three colors. If there is a single syllable at intervals, one should weigh the pericarp above the row of syllables in the form of petals.
One should cause [the syllables] to enter into the pericarp of a four-petaled lotus.
One should write one [syllable] in the pericarp, and two each in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should arrange the entry and exit in the cardinal directions within the eight-petaled lotus.
In the midst of a sixteen-petaled lotus, which possesses rows of petals of various colors on all sides, there is the arrangement of equal syllables; therein,
the first wheel is four-spoked and twice [the size of] that [second].
In the first half, the syllables of the first and fifth positions of each quarter are identical;
likewise for the odd-numbered quarters, and also for the fourth and eighth positions of the even-numbered quarters.
Furthermore, this applies respectively to the northern, eastern, southern, and western sections of its upapāda.
There may be four quarters and a half-measure at the navel; one should lead its first syllable as far as the western spoke, while the remaining two quarters [occupy] these two [positions].
If the first two syllables at the end of the fourth quarter are both identical to those at the beginning of the third quarter,
and if the tenth syllable of all three quarters is also identical;
and if six syllables of that [third quarter] are identical to those of the first and last [quarters], [it is called a *pratyāpīḍa*].
Then the two intermediate [sections] and the large [section] are proclaimed as the *krama*.
One should write each foot in succession on the two faces;
however, one should place the tenth syllable at the navel and the fourth foot on the rim.
If the first, last, and tenth syllables of the verse are identical, and the first and last syllables of the two even quarters are identical;
and if the fourth and fifth syllables at the beginning of the odd quarters are identical;
and if the third syllable arises by following the second syllable in reverse order—[this is the Vaitālīya].
One should place the foot of the petal; the handle of the lotus is formed by the two second [parts] on the eastern petal, which are equal, and likewise the two seventh [parts].
The two northern petals are similar to the two second [parts], and then there are the two halves.
The second and sixth [syllables] are similar, as are the fourth and fifth; likewise, the first and last quarters are equal, as are the seventh and those of the latter half.
One should apply the fourth and fifth [quarters] in their respective order.
In the same manner, two *turya* syllables are to be joined at the ends of the petals of the two successive quarters;
however, in the *muraja*, both the final and the first syllables of the two halves are identical.
A syllable falling within a quarter or a half-verse may occur either in reverse or in direct order.
One should bind the last [syllable] up to the fourth from the beginning here;
from the fourth foot, whatever is the first, from the ninth and even from the sixteenth syllable,
there are four syllables in the middle of the *puṭaka*.
Having fashioned it, one should act so that it takes the shape of a *muraja* drum;
the second [wheel] possesses the excellence of the *cakravikrīḍita* and *śārdūlavikrīḍita* meters.
The *gomūtrikā* may be composed in all meters, while other poetic figures (*bandhas*) are generally in the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
If the names of these [figures] do not belong to the poet or the poem,
friends are not pleased by them, nor does an enemy feel distressed.
Arrows, bows, the sky, swords, mallets, and spears;
two, four, and three-pointed figures, the thunderbolt, pestles, and hooks;
the footprint of a chariot, that of an elephant, lotus ponds, and dagger-blades.
These and other such bonds are to be understood by the wise for themselves in this manner.
Thus ends the three hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Verbal Figures of Speech," in the section on Ornamentation within the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 343:
Figures of Sense (Arthālaṅkāra)
Agni said:
"The ornament of wealth is desired as the ornament of meaning;
without it, even the beauty of words is not captivating."
Devoid of the ornaments of meaning, Sarasvatī is like a widow;
[she possesses] essential nature, similarity, poetic fancy, and even hyperbole.
Elimination, contradiction, and the reason are each eightfold.
The very nature of entities is designated as their "own-being" (*svabhāva*);
it is declared to be of two kinds: innate and adventitious.
Intrinsic, constant, occasional, and likewise adventitious;
[it exists] only in the state of disjunction.

Similarity (*sādṛśya*), which is the commonality of attributes (*dharmasāmānya*), is of four kinds: simile (*upamā*), metaphor (*rūpaka*), hyperbole (*mahokti*), and corroboration (*arthāntaranyāsa*).
That which is called "simile" (*upamā*) is that in which there exists [a comparison] between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*).
And although existence (*sattā*) is connected with intermediate universals (*antarasāmānya*),
worldly activity proceeds by taking up some intended similarity (*sārūpya*).
That [activity] is twofold, according to whether the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is expressed in a compound or not.

Following the analysis (*vigraha*) of the expression, there is another type [of *upamita* compound] with a prefix, formed from the word indicating the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the word denoting the object of comparison (*upameya*), and the word expressing the indicator of comparison (*upamādyotakapada*). From the analysis of these two, it is threefold; and from the last one, with its prefix, it is again threefold.
There are eighteen distinct types of simile that become increasingly refined,
wherein a common attribute is either explicitly stated or merely implied;
because of the predominance of either the attribute (*dharma*) or the object (*vastu*), these two are known as the *dharmopamā* and the *vastūpamā*.
Where two subjects are compared with each other as being exactly equal, that would be *parasparopamā* (mutual comparison), since otherwise those two [would not be] well-known [as such].
That would be *viparītopamā* (inverse comparison); [and] *niyamopamā* (restrictive comparison) [arises] from exclusion.
But because it persists elsewhere as well, there may be "unrestricted simile" (*aniyamopamā*).
It is distinct from "cumulative simile" (*samuccayopamā*) due to the mention of a plurality of other attributes; for even when many attributes are similar, a distinction is intended to be expressed.
That which is called "excessiveness" is the simile of contrast (*vyatirekopamā*). Where there may be a comparison with many similar things, that is the "multiple simile" (*bahūpamā*).
If the attributes (*dharmas*) are different for each object of comparison (*upamāna*), that is indeed the "garland simile" (*mālopamā*).

Comparison by means of a modification of the standard of comparison is *vikriyopamā*. Having superimposed upon the object of comparison some indescribable quality that does not exist in the three worlds...

That which is compared by a poet and yet remains celebrated as something marvelous is the *adbhutopamā* (marvelous simile). When, having superposed the correlate (*pratiyogin*), one speaks of the object of comparison (*upameya*) as being non-different from it,
that is *mohopamā* (delusive simile), a statement characterized by error.
When there is doubt due to the lack of certain determination regarding the true nature of both the subject and the object of comparison, it is *saṃśayopamā* (simile of doubt).
When certainty is reached after having doubted the object of comparison (*upameya*), it is *niścayopamā* (simile of certainty).
And when one sentence is compared to another sentence by way of being the standard of comparison, it is *vākyārthopamā* (simile of the meaning of a sentence).

When a comparison based on self-similarity possesses a commonality that exceeds the norm, it is considered an "excessive simile" (sādhāraṇyatiśāyinī). When one thing serves as the object of comparison for another, and that [second] thing in turn becomes the object of comparison for yet another, this is known as the "sky-like simile" (gaganopamā).

Praise, censure, and likewise the "imagined" (kalpitā), as well as the "similar" (sadṛśī) and that which should be known as "partially similar" (kiñcitsadṛśī)— these are the five types of simile (upamā) mentioned previously.
That in which the nature of the object of comparison (upameya) is represented by means of a standard of comparison (upamāna) [is the simile].

Having observed the equality of qualities, they know that as *rūpaka* (metaphor); it is either a simile in which the distinction has vanished, or it is simply a metaphor. *Sahokti* (conjoint expression) is the narration of things possessing common attributes by means of their coexistence.

That would be *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle) when followed by a subsequent similarity; otherwise, when the mode of being of a sentient or insentient entity is presented in one way, but is conceived in another way,
they call that *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
The description of a thing's property as exceeding the limits of worldly experience is called *atiśaya* (hyperbole);
it is of two kinds, according to whether [the property] is possible or impossible.
It occurs where there is a perception of the deficiency of qualities (*guṇa*), genus (*jāti*), actions (*kriyā*), and so forth.
That is called *viśeṣokti* (the statement of distinction) precisely for the purpose of showing a distinction.
[Note: "pavanopamā" is found in manuscript *kha*;
"gamanopamā" is found in manuscripts *ka* and *ṭa*.]
When, by the exclusion of a well-known cause,
some other cause or even "inherent nature" (svābhāvikatva) is to be imagined in a given case, that is *vibhāvanā* (the description of the extraordinary).
The bringing together by means of reasoning of two things that are not [otherwise] connected,
preceded by a state of contradiction, is known as "contradiction" (virodha).
It serves as the probans for the purpose one intends to establish.
That [cause] also arises in two ways: as the producer (*kāraka*) and as the indicator (*jñāpaka*). That which is called the producer operates prior to the birth of the effect;
it is known as the "prior remainder" (*pūrvaśeṣa*) in relation to those very two specific states.
Either through the relation of cause and effect, or through an inherent nature that acts as a regulator,
there exists a distinction for that which is called an "indicator" (jñāpaka), such as the sight of a river in flood.
For the rule of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is established through the observation of inseparable connection.
Thus ends the three hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Figurative Meaning (Arthālaṅkāra)" within the section on Ornamentation in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 344.
Now begins the three hundred and forty-fourth chapter:
Figures of Sound and Sense.
Agni said:
The ornament of both word and meaning adorns them both equally;
it is like a necklace placed upon one spot that adorns both the breast and the neck of a woman.
[These qualities are: praise, beauty, propriety, conciseness, and precision of expression.
"Manifestation" (abhivyakti) means that which is manifest; its six varieties are awake [in this context].
Praise (praśasti) belongs to one who performs the act of melting the vitals of others.
That expression of speech is twofold, distinguished as expressions of love and hymns of praise.
*Premokti* (loving speech) and *stuti* (praise) are synonyms for the praising of virtues;
*kānti* (splendor) is the fitness of expression that is pleasing to the minds of all. (AP 344.004)
As is the subject matter, so is the style; as is the mode of expression, so is the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). From a composition that is either forceful or gentle, propriety (*aucitya*) arises.
*Saṃkṣepa* (conciseness) is the condensation of a vast meaning by means of few expressive words.
The state of being neither deficient nor excessive is the "appropriateness of the word to its object.
Manifestation is "evidentness," which also includes "direct hearing" (*śruti*) and "implication" (*ākṣepa*).
These are its two divisions; therein, "direct hearing" is the word's presentation of its own primary meaning.
That [denotation] is of two kinds only: indicative (*naimittikī*) and technical (*pāribhāṣikī*).

Conventional agreement (*saṅketa*) is called "technical" (*paribhāṣā*); therefore, the technical [denotation] is twofold—primary (*mukhyā*) and metaphorical (*aupacārikī*)—and each of those two is further twofold.

That function of a word by which it denotes a non-primary meaning through some cause, while its own primary denotation falters, is metaphorical (*aupacārikī*). It is further divided into the indicative (*lākṣaṇikī*) and the secondary (*gauṇī*), according as it arises from connection with the indicated (*lakṣaṇā*) or from connection with a quality (*guṇa*).
Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is said to be a cognition that is inseparably connected with the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*).
Due to its connection with the expressed meaning, its proximity, its inherence,
its contrariety, and its association with action, indication is considered to be fivefold.

Because the qualities of secondary meanings are infinite, [the resulting expression] is infinite according to the speaker's intention. When a property belonging to one thing is correctly applied to another by one who conforms to worldly convention, that is remembered here as *samādhi*.
Since an object not obtainable from the literal expression appears as something endowed with consciousness,
that is *ākṣepa* (suggestion by implication), and it is called *dhvani* because it is manifested by *dhvani*.
Where a meaning, having itself effected its own acquisition through either the word or the expressed sense, [is further suggested]...

When there is a negation of something desired for the sake of expressing a particular quality, they call that *ākṣepa* (paradoxical assertion); furthermore, this [present case] is praise through praise (*stutastotra*).
When praise is expressed for another object that is not the subject under discussion,
and where the intended meaning is understood through shared qualifiers (*samāna-viśeṣaṇa*),
that is called *samāsokti* (abbreviated expression) by the wise because it conveys its sense in a concise manner.
Apahnuti (concealment) consists in concealing something while suggesting another meaning;
paryāyokta (circumlocution) is that which is expressed by means of another mode. Because these [three] are exclusively of one kind, they are designated as "dhvani" (suggestion).
Thus ends the three hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Verbal and Semantic Figures of Speech," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the section on Ornamentation (*alaṅkāra*).
Chapter 345:
The Discrimination of the Qualities of Poetry (Kāvyaguṇaviveka)
Agni said:
Even when adorned, a poem devoid of merit cannot bring delight;
on the ungraceful bodies of women, a necklace becomes nothing but a burden.
Nor should it be said that merit and defect will simply be states of being;
for merits such as *śleṣa* (conciseness) and defects such as *gūḍhārtha* (obscure meaning) have been treated separately.
That which bestows a great luster upon poetry through its excellences (guṇas) is of two kinds: the general (sāmānya) and the particular (vaiśeṣika).
That which has become common to all is considered the general.
That which attains both word and meaning and becomes common to all three [types of poetry] by relying upon the word as its body is the quality of that [poetry].

Cohesion (*śleṣa*), elegance (*lālitya*), lack of depth (*agāmbhīrya*), delicacy (*saukumārya*), loftiness (*audāratā*), and etymological fitness (*yaugikī*)— these are the seven qualities of sound (*śabda*). Cohesion is said to be the state of words being arranged in close conjunction.
That wherein a syllable previously connected to a word is joined [with another] by means of grammatical substitution (*guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, etc. is not at all cited as *lālitya* (gracefulness);
it is merely a superficial composition marked by the delineation of specific characteristics.

The Noble Ones describe profundity as that very quality which consists of sound in others; gentleness is the state of being composed mostly of non-harsh syllables. [This is achieved] through clear words and praiseworthy qualifiers endowed with nobility.

Vigor (*ojas*) is the abundance of compounds; it is the lifeblood of verse and other forms of composition. From the Creator down to a blade of grass, the human character of any object being described is expressed by means of whatever word may be used.
That which brings about excellence is called a *guṇa* (excellence).
Sweetness (*mādhurya*), compactness (*saṃvidhāna*), softness (*komalatva*), loftiness (*udāratā*),
maturity (*prauḍhi*), and conventionality (*sāmayikatva*)— these six shine forth as its varieties.
Anger, envy, profoundity, personal sweetness, steadfastness, and depth constitute the "preparatory equipment" (parikara) for the accomplishment of what is desired.
That which is characterized by a specific arrangement free from hardness and the like [is the "form" (rūpa)].
Having set aside softness (*mṛdutā*), that which shines as delicacy (*komalatā*) is perceived there as the characteristic of the manifestation of generosity (*sthūlalakṣatva*);
that is *audārya* (nobility), the supreme excellence of intention.
Since they establish the demonstration of what is intended, the arguments containing logical reasons (*hetu*) are cited as being either mature or immature.
Whether independent or dependent, through the internal and external conjunction [of the senses],
that which is the comprehension of the meaning therein is called "conventional" (*sāmayikī*).
That which assists both the word and the meaning is traditionally known as the name (*nāman*), possessing the qualities of both.

Its clarity (*prasāda*), charm (*saubhāgya*), sequential order (*yathāsaṅkhya*), excellence (*praśastatā*), maturity (*pāka*), and passion (*rāga*) are elaborated as the sixfold expansion by the wise;
that which possesses well-known meanings and words is proclaimed as "clarity" (*prasāda*).
Wise men declare that *udāratva* (magnificence) is a certain quality of excellence which is perceived when [a word] is uttered; it is what they call *saubhāgya* (gracefulness).
The general rule (*sāmānya*) is extended by way of analogy to the enumeration (*anuddeśa*) according to their respective order (*yathāsaṅkhya*).
When a thing that is harsh, even if it is worthy of description,
is described as excellent by means of a non-harsh word—
such as when a certain high transformation is designated by the term "ripening" (pāka)— that is called *pākalya*.
There are four types of *pāka* (culinary transformation) based on the differences between grapes (*mṛdvīkā*) and coconut water (*nārikelāmbu*).

That which possesses sweetness at both the beginning and the end is specifically called grape-transformation (*mṛdvīkā-pāka*). Whatever distinction arises through the poet’s creative intent is celebrated as "with passion" (*sarāga*).
Cultivated through practice, it maintains even its innate brilliance.
This [attachment] is of three kinds: that which is like turmeric, that which is like saffron, and that which is like indigo.
That which has the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object is to be understood as the particular (*vaiśeṣika*).
Thus ends the three hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Discrimination of the Qualities of Poetry," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Chapter 346:
The Discernment of Faults in Poetry (Kāvyadoṣaviveka)
Agni said:
"The fault that causes agitation among the members of the assembly is sevenfold,
arising from the application of one, two, or three [defects] to the speaker, the expressive medium, and the subject matter."
In that regard, the speaker known as a poet (kavi) is celebrated as being fourfold according to his distinctions:
the doubtful, the ill-mannered, the ignorant, and the knower.
[He speaks] through etymological derivation and technical terminology, expressing the meaning through contact with the referent.
The division of that [speech] is twofold: word and sentence; thus the definition of both has been stated.
There are only two points of defeat regarding words: ungrammaticality (*asādhutva*) and non-usage (*aprayuktatva*).
The wise know that ungrammaticality is that which is contrary to the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*). (AP 346.004)

By those who are proficient, it is said that there are five kinds of defects: lack of connection (*anibaddhatva*), lack of usage (*aprayuktatva*), archaism (*chāndasatva*), obscurity (*avispaṣṭatva*), harshness (*kaṣṭatva*), non-idiomaticity (*asāmayikatva*), and vulgarity (*grāmyatva*). (AP 346.005–006ab)
The state of being Vedic [is not a fault] in the vernacular because it is not clearly understood due to lack of awareness.
Obscurity of meaning, perversity of meaning, and doubtfulness of meaning—these are the varieties; among them, "obscurity of meaning" (gūḍhārthatā) is as follows: AP_346.007cd.

Where the meaning is to be experienced as suffering, there is again the state of having a perverted meaning; the states of having another meaning and being incapable both approach this very [state] through the intellect.
They say that having a meaning which is subject to doubt constitutes ambiguity;
it entails the status of a fault except when it serves to alarm the virtuous.

The sages have declared that these [faults] consist of being difficult to pronounce, being harsh, deviation from convention, and being non-conventional; furthermore, vulgarity is defined as conveying a base meaning or being contemptible. AP 346.011ab–cd.
That [defect] is threefold: from the utterance or even the mere recollection of vulgar speech that ought to be spoken;
and it is twofold as a defect of the meaning, being either common or specific.

The "objection regarding multiple parts" (anekabhāgupālambha) is known as the common fault (sādhāraṇa). Furthermore, the loss of action and agent, the lack of euphonic junction (visandhi), tautology (punarukta),
and disjointed connection (vyastasambandhatā)— these five are considered common faults.
Inactivity, the failure of action, and furthermore, the loss of agency;

the absence of the agent and other grammatical factors (*kāraka*s), and the breach of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*)—that is, the corruption of *saṃdhi*—is of two kinds: either the *saṃdhi* is absent or it is contrary [to the rules]. (346.015cd–346.016ab)
The ambiguity of a compound arises from the emergence of a different meaning due to a difficult word-break;
tautology occurs through repetitive expression, which is of two kinds: repetition of meaning and repetition of words. Repetition of meaning is also of two kinds. (AP 346.017cd)
Likewise, [the meaning is conveyed] by means of another word;
when there is a repetition of words, it is not the repetition of the words themselves that occurs, but rather the repetition of what is expressed by them.
There is a loose connection due to separation, whereas there is a firm connection through mediation.
Because of the manifestation of another relation and because of the production of another relation,
[the afflictions] are called "impurities."
2. From the sequence of a different meaning due to the difficulty of the words... (Ṭa...
3. By means of the word previously employed... (Ja... and Ña...):
Even in the absence of those two, that [suggestion] is threefold due to internal intervention;
furthermore, it is twofold through the distinction between the word and the sentence.
Because it is sought after as the meaning to be expressed, it is twofold within both words and sentences.
The [reason] is divided into that which has its previously stated meaning already established and that which is yet to be established.
The reason may be characterized by the contradiction of what is intended, or it may be ineffective;
likewise, it may be unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Thus, the state of having a counter-argument (satpratipakṣatva) and the confusion with the "mistimed" (kālātīta) fallacy [are avoided];
for that [reason], the absence of the reason in the subject and its presence in the similar instance, as well as its presence in the dissimilar instance,
would not be painful even to those present in an assembly of poetic works.
He does not falter in the face of difficult tasks and the like;

he causes suffering [only] to those who recognize their faults. He does not obscure the hidden meaning in what is difficult to understand, nor does he cause agitation through vulgarity, because he conforms to what is well-known in both the world and the scriptures.
There is a mark [of a fault] due to the omission of an action, by virtue of the necessity of supplying that action;

for when a case-role (kāraka) has been lost, it is supplied through the force of implication (ākṣepa). However, in the case of a *pragṛhya* vowel, no defect whatsoever is perceived, as the hiatus (*vigatasandhi*) is accepted as such.

In difficult recitation, the absence of euphonic conjunction (*visandhi*) is not considered unfortunate when it occurs at the beginning of a hard-to-speak passage; likewise, the repetition of words (*padāvṛtti*) is auspicious in alliteration (*anuprāsa*). There is no fault in the summary of meaning (*arthasaṃgrahaṇa*), nor is it tainted by transpositions and the like.
Where there is no agitation among the wise regarding case-endings, technical names, or genders, there may be a difference in number between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison.
Likewise, the beautiful [simile] occurs when one is compared to many, or many to many.
This conduct of the sage is celebrated as "convention" (samaya).
It is the state of being free from the eleven [faults].
It is twofold, being both general and specific, like *dharma*;
for there is no dispute among established scholars, systematizers, and poets regarding that which is well-known as "general"—this is considered the convention (*samaya*). (AP 346.031–346.032ab)
That by which all established doctrines proceed without error,
or even that by which only some do so, is the common [doctrine];
it would be different from the doctrine of the Chedas, as might occur through the delusion of certain individuals.
Whose is the knowledge of logic? Whose is the doctrine of momentary flux? Whose is the view that consciousness arises from the elements? Whose is the clear illumination of knowledge?
Likewise, whose is the doctrine of the Arhat regarding the non-absolutism of words and the grossness of what is known?
The views of the Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, Śāktas, Sauras, and Siddhāntins are that Brahman is the cause of the world; for the Sāṅkhyas, it is [Brahman] together with Pradhāna.
Moving about in this world of Sarasvatī, they debate with one another.
When they perceive it as distinct, they bind themselves;
that [bond] is said to arise from the grasping of the non-existent and the non-grasping of the existent.
As this [bond] is being analyzed, its twofold nature is proclaimed.
The wise know that which is sublated by means of valid cognition, such as direct perception, to be non-existent;
that which is grasped by them is the luminosity of knowledge.
Only that which performs a causal function is ultimately real.
Whether through ignorance or through knowledge, Brahman alone is the ultimate reality;
Viṣṇu is the cause of heaven and other realms, possessing the nature of sound, ornament, and form.
There is both lower and higher knowledge; by knowing that, one is liberated from worldly existence.
Thus ends the three hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Discernment of Defects in Poetry," in the *Ālaṅkāra* section of the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Chapter 347:
The Designation of the Single Syllable (Ekākṣarābhidhāna)
Agni said:
"I shall tell you the name consisting of a single syllable ending in *mātṛkā*:
*a* is Viṣṇu, while *ā* is the negation in the two statements of the Grandfather."
Furthermore, *a* is indeclinable; it occurs in the sense of "until" (*ā bhavet*) and in anger or affliction (*saṃkrodhapīḍayoḥ*).
*i* is used for desire (*kāma*), pleasure (*rati*), and fortune (*lakṣmī*). *ī* is used for Śiva; *ū* for a protector (*rakṣaka*) and so forth.
(1) *ṛ* is used for sound (*śabda*) and the beginning (*ādi*); *ṝ* would be used similarly. *ḷ* and *ḹ* are indeed used for the two types of *diti* and for Guha.
E is the goddess, Ai is the Yoginī; Syādo is Brahmā, and Au is Maheśvara.
Aṅkāma is Aḥ, which is praised;
Ko is at the beginning of Brahmā, and Ku denotes that which is contemptible.
*Kha* signifies the void, the sense-faculties, a rhinoceros, and a *gandharva* in the context of a leader (*vināyaka*).
*Gaṅgīte* [is used for] a cow and a singer; *gho* [is used for] a bell and the opening of a small bell (*kiṅkiṇī*);
*ṅa* [is used] in the sense of striking, longing, and the terrifying (*bhairava*).
The syllable *ca* is used for "evil person," "pure," "cutting," and likewise for "victory";

Kāraka Sukanda said:
I shall now fully explain the grammatical factors (*kāraka*) together with the meanings of their case-endings:
"There is a village here named Hemahārka; I bow to Viṣṇu along with Śrī.
The independent agent (*kartṛ*) is that which possesses sovereignty; the wise worship Him until the end of knowledge.
The causal agent (hetukartṛ) indeed brings about what is beneficial for the object-agent (karmakartṛ);
the one of ordinary intellect breaks [the wood] himself, and the tree itself is cut down. When the agent is expressed, it is superior; when the agent is not expressed, it is inferior.
Just as the unexpressed agent (*kartṛ*) and its property (*dharma*) are explained to the disciple, so too has the fivefold agent been declared; now hear of the sevenfold object (*karman*).
For example, the ascetic (*yati*) places his faith in Hari as the desired object (*īpsita-karman*).
An unintended object of action is, for example, a snake when one leaps over it;
neither intended nor unintended is the dust when one eats milk. Furthermore, that which is not explicitly mentioned [as the object] is as in: "The cowherd milks the cow for milk."
Just as a teacher leads a student to a village, he should lead the disciple toward the object of action;

for when the object is expressed [by a verb], worship is performed for the sake of Hari’s glory. When the object is not expressed [by a verb], one should perform a hymn of praise to Hari, which bestows everything.
The instrument (karaṇa) is said to be of two kinds: external and internal.
One perceives form with the eye, which is external; one cuts that [grass] with a sickle. The recipient (sampradāna) is said to be threefold: the instigator, as in "the cow for the Brahmin."
A virtuous man should offer flowers to his master, even if he has caused them to be given by a servant acting under his authorization, provided they were not withheld from him.
Apadāna is said to be of two kinds: moving, as when one runs after a horse;
and non-moving, as when that Vaiṣṇava returns from the village on foot.
Adhikaraṇa is fourfold: pervasive, as clarified butter in milk.
Oil in sesame seeds is said to be *aupśleṣika* (inherent) for the sake of the gods;
a monkey staying in a house is like the *vaiṣayika* (objective) [location], as is a fish in water; and a lion in a forest is said to be like the *sāmīpyaka* (proximate) [location].
"A sound dwells in the Ganges"—such usage is metaphorical (*aupacārika*).
Likewise, when not already expressed by another verbal form, either the third or the sixth case is prescribed; for example:
"Viṣṇu is worshipped by people," or "the goal is to be reached by him."
One should bow to Hari when the agent or the object is expressed by the nominative case;

the instrumental is used for the cause, as in "he dwells with food" (annena) or "water for the tree" (vṛkṣāya); the dative is prescribed for the sake of something (tādarthye), and the ablative is used with prepositions such as *pari*, *upa*, and *ā*.
When used with *yoge*, it means "rained upon"; when used with *pari*, it means "around the village. This god was formerly very powerful.
Without Viṣṇu, there is no liberation for others from Hari.
With words such as *pṛthak* and *vinā*, the third and fifth cases may likewise occur.

The second case occurs through connection with words designated as *karmapravacanīya*, such as "separate from" (*pṛthak*) used with a village, "without" (*vinā*) used with a monastery, "prosperity" (*śrī*) used with prosperity, and "on account of" (*śriyaḥ*) used with actions;
likewise, it is taught that "the warriors [fought] facing the enemy" (*anvarjunam*) and "all around the village" (*abhito grāmam*).

The fourth case ending is used after words such as *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *svasti*, and *vaṣaṭ*. It is also used after a word expressing the sense of "for the sake of" (*tum-artha*) that denotes an action, as in *namo devāya* ("salutation to the god") or *te svasti* ("may it be well with you"). Furthermore, the third case ending is used in connection with the word *saha* ("with"), as in *pākāya* or *paktaye yāti* ("he goes for the sake of cooking").
The third case is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*), for a contemptible limb, and as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); as in:
"The father went with his son," "blind in one eye," and "Hari [is distinguished] by his mace."
A servant should reside according to his purpose; the locative cases are used for time and state.
When one bows to Viṣṇu, liberation occurs; having gone there in spring, he reached Hari.
He is the master of men, the lord among men, the sovereign of men.
May he be the lord of the virtuous;
may he be a witness among men, a witness for men, a protector among cattle, the master of cattle,
a progenitor of cattle, a progenitor of cattle, and here on earth, the heir of kings.
The sixth case is used for the cause of food (annasya), for the object of a verb meaning "to remember" (mātuḥ smarati), and it should always be used for the agent and the object; however,
in the case of "the breaker of waters" (apāṃ bhettā) and in formations such as the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), the sixth case is not used even for the object.
Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Case-Relations," in the section on Grammar within the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 354.
Now begins the three hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Summary.
Skanda said:

I shall explain the sixfold compound, and furthermore the twenty-eightfold [compound], which is twofold by way of the division between the obligatory (*nitya*) and the non-obligatory (*anitya*), and again twofold by way of elision (*luk*) and deletion (*lopa*).
The potter (*kumbhakāra*) is an obligatory [compound], as are the goldsmith (*hemakāra*) and others.
The compound *rājapumān* means "the king's man"; furthermore, this is an obligatory (nitya) compound.
[This is stated] because of the meaning... [fragmentary].

The *luksamāsa* (compound with elision) is based on difficulty [to understand], such as *kaṇṭhekāla* ("the one with Kāla at his throat") and others; however, there is no elision (*aluk*) in certain cases.
Thus, the *tatpuruṣa* compound is of eight types, formed with the first case (*prathamā*) and the other case endings (*sup*).
This is a *prathama-tatpuruṣa* compound, as seen in the analysis of "the front part of the body" (*pūrva-kāyasya*):
namely, *pūrvakāya*, *aparākāya*, and *adharottarakāyaka*;
likewise, half of a grain is *ardhakaṇā*, and such is the case with "alms and musical instruments" (*bhikṣātūryam*).
Likewise, the second [year] is one where one has fallen into a precarious livelihood and is dependent on others;
the third is one where the harvest is enjoyed for a year and grain is acquired for wealth;
the fourth would be one where offerings are made to Viṣṇu; and the fifth is one characterized by fear of wolves.
*Rājñaḥ pumān* (the king’s man) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*); *vṛkṣaphalam* (the fruit of the tree) is likewise;
*akṣaśauṇḍaḥ* (addicted to dice) is a locative compound (*saptamī-tatpuruṣa*); and *nañ-samāsa* (negative compounds) are those that are not beneficial.
The *karmadhāraya* is remembered as being of seven types, beginning with *nīlotpalam* (the blue lotus).
Likewise, there are compounds where the qualifier comes first and the qualified follows,

such as *vaiyākaraṇakha-mūci* (the grammarian with nails like claws), the auspicious two-word compound *śītoṣṇaṃ* (cold and heat), and also those where the object of comparison comes first, such as *śaṅkhapāṇḍaraḥ* (white as a conch).

A compound with a word of comparison as the final member is, for example, *puruṣavyāghra* ("tiger-like man"); one with a word expressing excellence (*sambhāvanā*) as the first member is, for instance, *guṇavṛddhi*. Here, "quality" (*guṇa*) is to be understood as "increase" (*vṛddhi*), just as *suhṛt* (friend) is indeed *suvandhuka* (one who binds well).

The *bahuvrīhi* compound with an initial restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) is of seven kinds. The two-word *bahuvrīhi* is exemplified by "the man who has ascended the palace" (*ārūḍhabhavano naraḥ*). This [type] is proclaimed as the "many-footed" (*bahvaṅghri*) when it has an honored word as its prior member, such as "one whose feet have been worshipped" (*arcitāśeṣapūrvaḥ*).
These [words] such as *vipraścopadaśaḥ* have a numeral as their final member (*saṅkhyottarapada*).
Just as there are examples with numerals as both members (*saṅkhyobhayapada*), such as *dvitrāḥ* (two or three) and *dvyekatrayo narāḥ* (men who are two, one, or three),
this [type of compound] may also have "together" (*saha*) as its prior member (*sahapūrvapada*), as in *samūloddhṛtakaḥ taruḥ* (a tree uprooted along with its roots).
The term *vyatihāra* signifies mutual exchange; *keśākeśi* and *nakhānakhi* denote hand-to-hand and nail-to-nail combat respectively.
The direction indicated is south-east (*dakṣiṇapūrvā*). A *dvigu* compound is stated to be of two kinds.

The dual compound (*dvandva*) is of two kinds: that which functions as a singular (*ekavadbhāvin*), such as *dviśṛṅga* ("two-horned"), and that which remains plural, such as *pañcamūlī* ("the five roots").

Indeed, the *dvandva* compound is twofold: the *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) and the *samāhāra* (collective). *Rudraviṣṇū* is an example of the former, while *bherīpaṭaha* ("kettle-drum and tabour") is an example of the latter.

The *avyayībhāva* compound is said to be of two kinds: that which has a noun as its prior member, such as *śākaprati* (a bit of vegetable), and that which is preceded by an indeclinable (*avyaya*), such as *upakumbham* (near the jar) and *uparathyam* (along the road). It is primarily fourfold.

The *dvandva* compound has the meaning of the final member as its primary sense, while the *dvandva* may also have both members as primary; the *avyayībhāva* has the first member as its governing sense, and the *bahuvrīhi* has its external referent as its primary sense. Thus ends the section on compounds in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*, within the treatise on grammar.
Chapter three hundred and fifty-four.
Now begins chapter three hundred and fifty-five.
Skanda said:
"I shall explain the *taddhita* suffixes; they are of three kinds, and their general function is as follows."

With the suffix *ilac*, *vyaṃsala* means "deceitful" and *vatsala* means "affectionate"; with *ilac*, *phenila* means "foamy. With the suffix *śa*, *lomaśa* means "hairy," while with *ina*, *pāmāna* means "scabby. With *ilac*, *picchila* means "slimy. With the suffix *aṇ*, *prājña* means "wise" and *ārcaka* means "devout"; from *danta*, with the suffix *urac*, *dantura* means "having protruding teeth."
With *re*, it would be "sweet" (*madhura*); with *re*, it would be "having a fine hollow" (*suśira*); with *re*, it would be "such a filament" (*keśara*).
With *ve*, it would be "gold" (*hiraṇya*); with *ve*, the Mālavas; and with *valaci*, it would be "dusty" (*rajasvala*).
The word *dhanī* is derived from *dhana* with the suffix *ini*; *dhanika* is said to be formed with the suffix *ṭhan*.

*Payasvī* is formed with *vin*, while *māyāvī* is formed with *ūni*. *Urci* is said to be formed with the suffix *yu*. *Vāgmo* is formed with *mini*, and *vācāla* is said to be formed with *ālaci* and *aṭac*.

*Phalinaḥ*, *barhiṇaḥ*, *kekī*, *vṛndārakaḥ*, and likewise *kani*; [the suffix] *āluc* forms *śītāluḥ*, one who does not endure cold; *śvāluḥ* is similar; and *himāluḥ* may also occur with *āluc*, one who likewise does not endure snow.
*Rūpa* may mean "wind" or *vātādu*, while *vātula* refers to one who is childless.
*Vāśiṣṭhaḥ* means a descendant of Kuśika (*kauravaḥ*), and *vāsaḥ* means a person from Pañcāla (*pāñcālaḥ*) who resides there; thus he is a resident (*vāsakaḥ*).
One who lives there is *māthuraḥ*, and one who knows or studies [it] is *cāndrakaḥ*.
The suffix *krama* denotes one who knows the sequence; *kauśaka* means one who has stepped out. The field where *priyaṅgu* plants grow is called *praiyaṅgavīna*;
likewise, *maudgīna* and *kaudravīṇa* denote fields of *mudga* and *kodrava* respectively. And *vaidehaka* refers to one who is childless.
In *iñ*, there is Dākṣi; in *dāśarathi*; in *kac*, Nārāyaṇa and so forth;
in *āśvāyana*; in *phañ*, [there is] Yajña; in *yac*, Gārgya and Vātsaka; in *ḍhaka*, Vainateya and so forth; and likewise in *ai* (or *airak*), Aṭakera.
In *ḍhra* there is the form *gaudheraka*; *gaudhāra* is proclaimed as *cārakīrita*.
In *kṣatriya*, *gha*, *kulīna*; in *kha*, *ṇya*, and *kairavya* and others are recorded.
In *yati*, *mūrdhanya*, *mukhya*, and so forth; *sugandhi* is the illustrative form (*rūpaka*).
From *tāraka* and other such words, the suffix *itac* is applied, as in *tārakitādayaḥ* (the sky and others having become starry).
When the suffix *anaṅ* is applied, there are forms such as *kuṇḍodhnī* (having breasts like jars) and *puṣpadhanvā-sudhanvanau* (the one with a flower-bow and the one with a good bow).
In the sense of "one who deceives wealth" (*vittavañcuḥ*), the word *cañcup* would be used for that person whose wealth is being deceived.
There may also be *caṇa*, as in *keśacaṇa*; and *rūpa*, as in *paṭarūpaka*. There is also *īyasun*, as in *paṭīyān*; and *tarap*, as in *akṣatara* and so forth.
The suffix *tarap* may follow even after *pacatitarām*, and *tamap* may follow even after *aṭatitamām*.
There may be *mṛdvītamā*, as well as *indrakalpaḥ* and *arkakalpakaḥ*.
In the case of *deśīya*, there are forms such as *rājadeśīyaḥ*, *deśīyaḥ*, and *deśyaḥ*.

The suffix *jātiya* is used after the words *jāti*, *jānu*, *mātrā*, *dvayasa*, and *daghna*; for example, *pañcajātīyaḥ*, *jānumātrīyaḥ*, *mātracīyaḥ*, *dvayaso’yaḥ*, *dvayasacīyaḥ*, *ūrudaghnaḥ*, and *ūrudaghnīyaḥ*. The suffix *tayaṭ* occurs as in *pañcatayaḥ*; and the suffix *ṭhak* is prescribed after *dauvārika*, as in *dauvārikaṣṭhakīritaḥ*.

Next, the general usage [of these suffixes] has been stated, as well as the taddhita suffixes termed "indeclinables" (avyaya): namely, *sili* in the sense of *yasmāt* and *yataḥ*, and *tral* in the sense of *yatra* and *tatra*;
furthermore, there are *adhunā*, *asya*, and *idānīm* in the sense of *asmin kāle*.
In all cases and at all times, the suffix *rhi* is prescribed after that [time word];
thus, *tarhi*, *ho*, *asmin kāle*, *iha*, *karhi*, and *kasmiṃś cit kālake*.
Likewise, *thāli*, *thami*, and *katham* are used; for example, one might collect [something] in the eastern direction.
*Astāti* is used for the preceding year; *purastāt* means one should move or go forward from the east, as it is said, "in the same day";
*parut* is used for the previous year, and *parāri* for the year before that.

*Aiṣamaḥ* means "in this year"; *ceritam* means "performed. *Edayuḥ* and *paredyavi* refer to what is said regarding the day after tomorrow; *parasmim ahani* means "on the following day. *Adya* means "on this day," while *dye* refers to the day before yesterday (*pūrvedyus*) and likewise to the day after tomorrow (*edyuṣi*).
One should dwell in the southern direction from both the south and the further south;
one should dwell in the northern direction from both the north and the further north.
One should dwell above from what is above, and one would become free from misfortune by being situated in the zenith.
And to the north, it was said by the Father: "There shall be *ācī* and *dakṣiṇā*;
in *āhau* there is *dakṣiṇāhi*, which dwells in two ways and is established in two forms."
Make the two ends meet as one; if you wish to join the two ends, there are these two ways:
[first], so that it is more firmly fastened.
The suffixes called *taddhita* are declared to be *nipātas*; the *taddhita* suffix expressing a state (*bhāva*) is as follows:
the state of being clever (*paṭu*) is *paṭutva*, while *paṭutā* is said to be formed with *tal*.
Similarly, *prathimā* is from *pṛthu*, and *saukhya* is said to be formed from *sukha* with the suffix *ṣyañ*.
And *steyam* belongs to a thief; that which is called friendship is *sakhyaṃ*. *Kāpeyam* is the state of a monkey (*kapin*); *sainyam*, *pathyam*, and *yakīritam* [are derived similarly].
*Āśvam*, *kaumārakam*, *cāṇi*, *rūpam*, *cāṇi*, and *yauvanam* [follow the same pattern].
The suffix *kaṇ* is prescribed after [the word] *ācārya*; in this same manner, other secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) are also formed.
Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Formed Secondary Derivatives," in the section on Grammar within the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 356: The Form Derived from the *Uṇādi* [Sutras]
The youth said:
"The *uṇādi* suffixes will now be explained as affixes following verbal roots (*dhātu*).
With the suffix *uṇ*, one becomes a craftsman (*kāru*) or an artisan (*śilpī*); furthermore, *jāyu* and *māyu* refer to bile (*pittaka*)."
In the Vāyu Purāṇa, the *uṇādi* suffixes occur frequently;
this reading is marred by the fault of tautology, whereas the reading "yathā" [as found in] Ja... is far more excellent.

*Āyuḥ* means life; *svāduḥ* means sweet; *hetu-ādyāḥ* refers to causes and so forth; *kiṃśāruḥ* is the awn of grain; *dhānyaśūkakaḥ* is likewise the beard of corn; *kṛkavākuḥ* is a cock; *gurūḥ* means a teacher or a husband; and *maruḥ* is a desert.

Chapter Three Hundred and Fifty-Seven.
Now begins the three hundred and fifty-seventh chapter.
The youth, having established the forms of the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ-vibhakti*), said:
"I shall now explain the verbal suffixes as well as their substitutes in brief."
The *tiṅ* suffixes occur in all three [voices]: in the impersonal (*bhāva*), the passive (*karman*), and the active (*kartṛ*).
Those [verbal roots] that take an object (*sakarmaka*) and those that do not (*akarmaka*) are traditionally held to occur in the active voice (*kartari*) in two forms.
Furthermore, the substitutes for those [suffixes] occur in the passive (*akarmani*) for the transitive roots, and likewise [in the active] for the intransitive ones.

The verbal suffix termed *laṭ* is prescribed for the present tense; the *liṅ* is said to be used for the sense of injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth. For injunction and the like, as well as for benediction (*āśis*), the *loṭ* is used; and for the immediate past (*anadyatana-bhūta*), the *laṅ*. For the remote past (*parokṣa-bhūta*), the *luṅ* and *liṭ* are used; and for the immediate future (*anadyatana-bhāvin*), the *luṭ*.

In the sense of benediction (*āśis*), the *liṅ* is used; in other remaining cases, the *laṭ* will occur, and the *lṛṅ* would occur when there is non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*) upon the presence of conditions for the *liṅ*.
In the subsequent [section], there are nine *ātmanepada* endings; the first person masculine is *ti*, *tas*, and *anti*, which are the first nine *parasmaipada* endings.
The second person (*madhyama*) consists of *sip*, *tha*, and *s*; the first person (*uttama*) consists of *mi*, *vas*, and *mas*.
Among these, *ta*, *ātām*, and *anta* are for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), while *thas*, *āthām*, and *dhvam* are for the middle voice as well; *i*, *vahi*, and *mahi* are for the first person.
The roots beginning with *bhū* are traditionally known as *dhātus*.
The roots *bhū*, *edh*, *pac*, *nand*, *dhvaṃs*, *śraṃs*, *pad*, *tvar*, and *śī*;
as well as *krīḍ*, *hu*, *hā* (jahāti), *dhā*, *div*, *svap*, *nah*, *su* (sunoti), and *vas*. AP_357.008ab–cd

The verbal roots *tud*, *mṛś*, *muñc*, *rudh*, *bhuj*, *tyaj*, and *tan*, as well as the root *kṛ* (to do), take the suffix *mani* when followed by a vikaraṇa such as *śap* and so forth. AP 357.009ab–cd.

The verbal roots *krīḍ* (to play), *vṛṅ* (to choose), *grah* (to seize), and *cur* (to steal) take the suffix *i*; likewise, *pā* (to drink), *nī* (to lead), and *arc* (to praise) are leaders [of their respective classes].
On the earth, the personal endings (*tiṅ*) are as follows: *bhavati* (he is), *saḥ* (he); *bhavataḥ* (they two are), *tau* (they two); *bhavanti* (they are), *te* (they).
*Bhavasi* (you are), *tvam* (you); *yuvām* (you two are), *bhavathaḥ* (you two); *yūyam* (you all are), and also *bhavatha* (you all). *Aham* (I am).

I am, we two are, and we are; indeed, the family prospers, the two of them prosper, and likewise they prosper; you indeed prosper through wisdom; and you two prosper, you all prosper, for you prosper; indeed, we two prosper through our intellect.
"May we prosper through devotion to Hari"—forms such as *pacati* (he cooks) and others are explained as before.

In the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), with the suffix *yak*, it becomes *bhūyate* or *anubhūyate*. Likewise, in the form *vubhūṣati* (he desires to become), and similarly with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), one forms *bhāvayati īśvaram* (he causes the Lord to be).
When the *yaṅ* [intensive] suffix is applied, it becomes *vobhūyate*; when the *yaṅ* is elided (*yaṅluk*), it becomes *vobhūte*.
Similarly, from the root *putra*, one forms *putrīyati* and *putrakāmyati*; likewise, from *paṭat*, one forms *paṭapaṭāyate*.
Furthermore, with the causative (*ṇic*) and the desiderative (*san*) suffixes, one forms *ghaṭayati* and *bubhūṣayati rūpakam*.
*bhavet*, *bhavetām*, and *bhaveyuḥ* [are used] in the optative (*liṅ*); *bhaveḥ* and *pare*; *bhavetam* and *bhaveta*; likewise *bhaveyam*, *bhaveva*, and *bhavema*;
and *edheta*, *edheyātām*, and *edheran*—[may one prosper] through the mind and through prosperity.
And *edhethās*, *edheyāthām*, *edhadhvam*, *edheya*, *edhevahi*, *edhemahi*. Let it be so; now for the imperative (*loṭ*), there are: *bhavantu*, *bhavatāt*, *bhava*;
*bhavatam*, *bhavata*; *bhavāni*, *bhavāva*, and *bhavāma*.
*edhata*, *amedhata*, *medhanta*, *medhai*, *pacāvahai*, *pacāmahai*; likewise, *abhyanandat*, *apacata*, *acann*, *apacas*;
*abhavataṃ*, *abhavatāṃ*, *apacam*, *apacāva*, and *apacāma*.
*aidhata*, *aidhetām*, *aidhadhvam*, *aidhe*, and *aidhāmahi*— this is the [form of] the root *indh*.
*abhūt*, *abhūtām*, *abhūvan*, *abhūḥ*, and *abhūvam*— this is the *luṅ* (aorist).
*aidhiṣṭa*, *aidhiṣātām*, *narau aidhiṣṭhāḥ*, *aidhiṣīta*—such forms occur in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*). *babhūva*, *babhūvatuḥ*, *babhūvuḥ*;
*babhūvitha*, *babhūvathuḥ*, *babhūva*; *babhūviva*, *babhūvima*.
*pece*, *pecāte*, *pecire*; likewise, *edhāñcakṛṣe*;
*edhāñcakrāthe*; *pecidhve*; *pece*; and likewise *pecimahe*.
In the *luṭ* [future tense], [the forms] are *bhavitā*, *bhavitārau*, *bhavitāraḥ*, and so on for *hara* and the others.
"I shall be," "you two shall be," "we shall be"—so too shall we [be].
You are the cooker, you two are the cookers, you all are the cooks; you shall cook the auspicious *odana*;
you shall cook, I shall cook, and we shall cook the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) for Hari.

In the optative mood expressing a benediction (*āśis*): may there be happiness; may Hari and Śaṅkara both be [prosperous]; may they all be [prosperous]; may you be [prosperous]; may the two of you be [prosperous]; may the lords be [prosperous];
may you all be [prosperous]; may I be [prosperous]; may we always be [prosperous].
For in the *liṅ* [optative] one says *yakṣīṣṭa*, *edhiṣīyāstām*, *yakṣīran*, *edhiṣīya*, *yakṣīvahi*, and *edhiṣīmahi*; and in the *lṛṅ* [conditional],
*ayakṣyata*, *ayakṣyetām*, *ayakṣyanta*, *ayakṣye*, and *ayakṣyethām* (for you two).
*ayakṣyadhvam*, *aidhiṣyāvahi*, *aidhiṣyāmahi*, and *arervayam*;
in the *lṛṭ* [future tense], *bhaviṣyati* occurs, as does *edhiṣyāmahe*; they will thus manifest forms such as *bobhaviṣyati*.
One should likewise form *ghaṭayet* and *paṭayet*, and also *putrīyati* and *kāmyati*.
Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Formation of Verbal Derivatives," in the section on Grammar within the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter Three Hundred and Fifty-Six.

The youth, having completed his form, said: "It should be understood that the *kṛt* suffixes occur in all three [voices]: in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), and the agent (*kartṛ*)."

The suffixes *aj*, *lyuṭ*, *ktin*, and *ghañ* are used in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*), as are those ending in *yuk*. Furthermore, with the vowel *ac*, [the following forms denote] the discipline (*vinaya*) of Dharma, its accumulation (*utkara*), and likewise its excellence (*prakara*). [With the suffix] *lpuṭ*, the forms *deva*, *bhadra*, and *śrīkara* signify a beautiful form.

In the *ktin* suffix, there are forms such as *vṛddhi*, *stuti*, and *matī*; in the *ghañ* suffix, the abstract state (*bhāva*); and likewise in the *yuc* suffix, forms such as *kāraṇā* and *bhāvanā*. Furthermore, with the suffix *akāra*, there is *cikitsā*.
Similarly, with the suffixes *tavya* and *anīya*, there are forms such as *kartavya* and *karṇīyaka*.

The suffixes *deya*, *dhyeya*, *yat*, and *ṇyat* denote that which is to be done; the *kṛtya* suffixes and those beginning with *kta* are to be understood as denoting the agent (*kartari*), and occasionally the abstract state (*bhāve*) or the object (*karmaṇi*). For example:
"He went to the village" (*gato grāmam*), "He went to the village" (*gato grāmaḥ*), and "The teacher was embraced by you" (*āśliṣṭo guruḥ tvayā*).

The suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* form the words *bhavan* and *edhamāna*; likewise, from all verbal roots, the suffixes *vuṇ* and *tṛc* form *bhāvaka* and *bhavitṛ*. The suffix *kvip* forms *svayambhū*, while in the sense of the past (*bhūte*), the suffixes *liṭ*, *kvasu*, and *kānac* are applied.

*babhūvivān*, *pecivān*, *pecānaḥ*, and *śraddadhānakaḥ* [are examples]; in the sense of the past tense (*bhūte*), forms such as *kumbhakāra* and others are traditionally taught as belonging to the *uṇādi* group; furthermore, it is stated that in the Vedic language (*chandasī*), [the suffixes] are applied diversely (*bahulam*), as in *vāyuḥ*, *pāyuḥ*, and *kāruḥ*.
Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Accomplishment of Verbal Derivatives," in the section on Grammar within the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Chapter 359: The Section on Heaven, Pātāla, and Other Realms.
Agni said:
I shall describe to you that Hari who is characterized by the names Svarga and so forth. Svaḥ, svarga, nāka, tridiva, dyo, div, and dve are synonyms for heaven; tripiṣṭapa is another.
The gods—Vṛndārakas, Lekhas, Rudras, and other host-deities (gaṇadevatās);
the Vidyādharas, Apsarases, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras; the Piśācas, Guhyakas, Siddhas, and Bhūtas: these are the divine origins (devayonayas).
The enemies of the gods are the asuras and daityas; the Sugata is the Tathāgata;
Brahmā is the Self-born, the eldest of the gods; Viṣṇu is Nārāyaṇa and Hari;
Revatīśa is Halī Rāma; and Kāma is Pañcaśara and Smara.
Lakṣmī is Padmālayā and Padmā; Śiva is Sarva and Sarveśvara.
His matted hair-knot is called Kaparda; his bow is Pināka, also known as Ajagava.
The Pramathas are his attendants (pāriṣadas); Mṛḍānī, Caṇḍikā, and Ambikā are names for his consort.
Dvaimātura, Gajāsya, Senānī, Agnibhū, Guha;
Ākhaṇḍala, Sunāsīra, Sūtrāman, Divaspati; and Pulomajā, Śacī, Indrāṇī—the goddess who is his beloved.
The palace of Indra is called Vaijayanta, Jayanta, or Pākaśāsani.
Airāvata, Abhramātaṅga, Airāvaṇa, and Abhramuvallabha are names for his elephant.
Hrīdinī and Vajra are feminine terms for the thunderbolt; it is also called Kuliśa, Bhidura, and Pavi.

A celestial vehicle is called *vyomayāna* or *vimāna* (the latter not being feminine); *pīyūṣa*, *amṛta*, and *sudhā* denote nectar; *sudharmā* is the assembly hall of the gods; and *svargaṅgā* is the celestial river.
In the feminine gender, when plural, they are *apsarasaḥ*; the celestial courtesans, headed by Urvaśī;
and the Gandharvas, Hāhā and Hūhū. Agni is *vahniḥ*, *dhanañjayaḥ*, *jātavedāḥ*, *kṛṣṇavartmā*, *āśrayāśaḥ*, and *pāvakaḥ*.
Hiraṇyaretas, Saptārcis, Śukra, Aśuśukṣaṇi, Śuci, Appitta, Aurva, Vāḍava, and Vaḍavānala are names of fire.
Of the two [terms] for fire, jvālā, kīla, arci, heti, and śikhā denote flame; of these, śikhā is feminine.
In three [meanings], *sphuliṅga* means a spark of fire; *dharmarāja*, the king of the departed;
*kāla*, the end-maker; *antaka*, the wielder of the staff; *śrāddhadeva*, the god of ancestral rites; and then the *rākṣasa*, *kauṇapa*, *asrapa*, *kravyāda*, *yātudhāna*, and *nairṛti*.
Precetā, Varuṇa, Pāśin, Śvasana, Sparśana, Anila, Sadāgati, Mātariśvan, Prāṇa, Marut, and Samīraṇa [are names of the wind].
Java, Raṃhas, Taras, Laghu, Kṣipra, Ara, and Druta [denote speed].
*Satvara*, *capala*, *tūrṇa*, *avilambita*, and *āśu* all mean "quickly.
*Satata*, *anārata*, *aśrānta*, *santata*, *avirata*, *aniśam*, *nitya*, *anavarata*, and *ajasram* mean "continuously" or "unceasingly. Furthermore, *atiśaya* means "excess" or "intensity."
*Ati*, *vela*, *bhṛśa*, *atyartha*, *atimātra*, *udgāṭa*, and *nirbhara*;
*tīvra*, *ekānta*, *nitānta*, as well as *gāḍha*, *vāḍha*, and *dṛḍha*.
Guhyakeśa, Yakṣarāja, Rājarāja, and Dhanādhipa.

A *kinnara* is a *kiṃpuruṣa*, a horse-faced being, or a *mayu*. A treasure is a *nidhi* or a *sevadhī*. The sky is *vyoman*, *abhram*, *puṣkaram*, or *ambaram*; it is also *dyau*, *div*, *antarīkṣam*, *kham*. The quarters are *kāṣṭhā*, *śākhā*, *kakubh*, or *diś*.
The innermost region is the Cakravāḍa circle;
Taḍitvān, Vārida, Megha, Stanayitnu, and Valāhaka are synonyms for a cloud.
Kādambinī is a mass of clouds; *stanita* and *garjita* mean thundering.
*Śampā*, *śatahradā*, *hrādinī*, *airāvatī*, and *kṣaṇaprabhā* refer to lightning.
*Taḍit*, *saudāminī*, *vidyut*, *cañcalā*, and *capalā* are also [names for] lightning.
*Sphurjathu* is the crashing of thunderbolts; *vṛṣṭighāta* is the cessation of rain; *avagraha* is drought.
*Dhārāsampāta* is a downpour; *āśāra* is a heavy shower; *śīkara* is known as water droplets.
*Varṣopala* is hail (*karakā*). A day when the sky is covered by clouds is called *durdina*.
*Antardhā*, *vyavadhā*, and *antardhi* (masculine) denote concealment,
as do *apavāraṇa*, *apidhāna*, *tirodhāna*, *pidhāna*, and *cchadana*.
*Abja*, *jaivātṛka*, *soma*, *glau*, *mṛgāṅka*, and *kalānidhi* are names for the moon.
Vidhu and kumudabandhu denote the moon; bimba and maṇḍala (which is not feminine) mean a circle or orb, used in three genders;
kalā is the sixteenth part; bhitta, śakala, and khaṇḍaka mean a fragment or piece; candrikā, kaumudī, and jyotsnā mean moonlight; and prasāda and prasannatā mean clarity or brightness.

*Lakṣaṇa*, *lakṣmaka*, and *cihna* mean a mark; *śobhā*, *kānti*, *dyuti*, and *chavi* mean luster; *suṣamā* and *paramā śobhā* mean supreme beauty. *Tuṣāra*, *tuhina*, *hima*, *avasyāya*, *nīhāra*, *prāleya*, *śiśira*, and *himam* all mean frost or snow.
*Nakṣatra*, *ṛkṣa*, *bha*, *tārā*, *tārakā*, and *uḍu* are feminine terms for a star.
*Guru*, *jīva*, *āṅgirasa*, *uśanas*, *bhārgava*, and *kavi* refer to Jupiter. *Vidhuntuda*, *tamas*, and *rāhu* refer to Rāhu. *Lagna* is known as the rising of the zodiacal sign (*rāśyudaya*).
The Seven Sages, headed by Marīci and Atri, are the Citraśikhaṇḍins;
[so too are] Haridaśva, Vṛhaspati, Pūṣan, Dyumaṇi, Mihira, and Ravi.
A halo, however, is called paridhi or upasūryaka within its circle.
*Kiraṇa*, *asra*, *mayūkha*, *aṃśu*, *gabhasti*, *ghṛṇi*, and *dhṛṣṇi* are synonyms for a ray of light;
*bhānu* and *kara* are masculine, while *marīci* and *dīdhiti* may be used for both genders, though *dīdhiti* is feminine.

*Prabhā*, *rug*, *ruci*, *tviṭ*, *bhās*, *bhā*, *chavi*, *dyuti*, *dīpti*, *rociḥ*, and *śociḥ* are synonyms for light; the last two are feminine, while *prakāśaḥ*, *dyotaḥ*, and *ātapaḥ* are masculine.
*Koṣṇam*, *kavoṣṇam*, *mandoṣṇam*, and *kaduṣṇam* mean slightly warm; these are used in the three genders when qualifying a noun.
*tiryañc*, *tīkṣṇa*, *khara*, as well as *diṣṭa*, *anehas*, and *kāla*;

*ghasra*, *dina*, and *ahar* (all meaning day); *sāyaṃsandhyā* (evening twilight), which is the progenitor of the ancestors (*pitṛprasū*); *pratyūṣa*, *aharmukha*, *kalya*, *uṣas*, and *pratyūṣas* (all meaning dawn).
Forenoon, afternoon, and midday constitute the three junctions (*trisandhya*).
Furthermore, night is called *śarvarī*, *yāmī*, *tamī*, and *tamisrā*; when accompanied by the moon, it is *jyotsnī*.
When joined with the day of the future or the present, the night is termed *pakṣiṇī*.
Ardharātra and niśītha denote midnight; pradoṣa and rajanīmukha denote the beginning of the night.

The junction of the lunar phases (parvasandhi) is the interval between the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad) and the fifteenth day (pañcadaśī). The two fifteenth days at the end of the fortnights are both called pañcadaśī, while the full-moon day is specifically termed pūrṇimā.
When the moon is deficient in its digits it is *sānumati*; when full, it is *rākā*.
The new moon is called *amāvāsyā*, *amāvasyā*, or *darśa*, marking the conjunction of the sun and the moon.
When the moon’s crescent is visible, it is *sinīvālī*; when its digits have vanished, it is *kuhū*.
*Saṃvarta*, *pralaya*, *kalpa*, *kṣaya*, and *kalpānta* denote the dissolution [of the world].
*Kaluṣa*, *vṛjina*, *enas*, *agha*, *aṃhas*, *durita*, and *duṣkṛta* denote sin.
*Dharma* is used in the masculine; *puṇya*, *śreyas*, and *sukṛta* denote merit; and *vṛṣa* [is also used for merit].
Delight, joy, gladness, and rapture; exhilaration, exultation, and intoxication of spirit;
bliss, ecstasy, and well-being; comfort, peace, and happiness; as well as supreme good, auspiciousness, welfare, prosperity, fortune, and goodness.
Bhāvuka, bhavika, bhavya, kuśala, and kṣema (which are not feminine) denote fortune; daiva, diṣṭa, māgadheya, and bhāgya denote destiny; and niyati and vidhi are feminine.

The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Self (ātman), the Person (puruṣa), Pradhāna, and Prakṛti are synonyms for Nature; in the feminine gender, they are called Hetu, Kāraṇa, Bīja, Nidāna, and Ādikāraṇa.
Furthermore, Citta, Cetas, Hṛdaya, Svānta, Hṛt, Mānasa, and Manas are synonyms for the mind.
Buddhi, manīṣā, dhiṣaṇā, dhī, prajñā, śemuṣī, mati, prekṣā, upalabdhi, cit, saṃvit, pratipad, jñapti, and cetanā; dhī that possesses retention is medhā; and saṅkalpa is mental action (mānasaṃ karma).
Numbering is *saṅkhyā*; investigation is *vicāraṇā*; deliberation is *carcā*; while doubt is *vicikitsā*.

Liberation (*mukti*) is synonymous with *kaivalya*, *nirvāṇa*, *śreyas*, *niḥśreyasa*, and *amṛta*.

Liberation is *apavarga*; ignorance is *avidyā* or *ahammati*. In the feminine, it refers to the fragrance arising from rubbing that is enchanting to people; it is called *parimala*. That which is exceedingly pervasive and pleasing to the nose is *āmoda*, while *surabhi* is the fragrant scent.

*Śukla*, *śubhra*, *śuci*, *śveta*, *viśada*, *śvetapāṇḍara*, *avadāta*, *sita*, *gaura*, *valakṣa*, *dhavala*, and *arjuna* [denote white]; *hariṇa* and *pāṇḍura* denote pale-white; while *pāṇḍu* denotes slightly pale, and *dhūsara* denotes greyish-white.

*Kṛṣṇa*, *nīla*, *asita*, *śyāma*, *kāla*, *śyāmala*, and *mecaka* denote black; *pīta*, *gaura*, and *haridrābha* denote yellow; *pālāśa*, *harita*, and *harit* denote green; *rohita*, *lohita*, and *rakta* denote red; and *śoṇa* denotes the color of a red lotus.
That which has an unmanifest redness is *aruṇa*; *pāṭala* is white-red;
*śyāva* is brownish; *kapiśa* is tawny; and *dhūmra* and *dhūmala* are dark red.
*Kaḍāra*, *kapila*, *piṅga*, *piśaṅga*, *ukadru*, and *piṅgala* denote reddish-brown;
*citra*, *kirmīra*, *kalmāṣa*, *śavala*, *eta*, and *karvura* denote variegated.
*Vyāhāra*, *ukti*, and *lapita* denote speech; *apabhraṃśa* and *apaśabdaka* denote corrupt words.
A collection of nouns and verbs is poetry (*kāvyam*), or it is an action (*kriyā*) accompanied by its factors of action (*kāraka*).
History (*itihāsa*) is what has occurred in the past; the *purāṇa* has five characteristics.
A narrative (*ākhyāyikā*) is that which has a known subject matter, while a composition (*prabandha*) is a fiction (*kalpanā*); such is a story (*kathā*).
*Samāhāra* and *saṃgraha* mean collection; *pravahlikā* and *prahelikā* mean a riddle. *Samasyā* refers to a condensed meaning; *smṛti* is remembered as a compendium of law (*dharmasaṃhitā*).
*Ākhyā*, *ākhyā*, and *abhidhāna* mean a name; *vārtā* and *vṛttānta* are said to mean news or an account.
*Hūti* is summoning or calling; *upanyāsa* is the opening of speech.

*Vivāda* is legal dispute (*vyavahāra*); *prativākya* and *uttara* are synonyms. *Upoddhāta* is an introduction; *udāhāra* is an illustration; *arthamithyābhiśaṃsana* is a false accusation regarding a matter.
*Abhiśāpa* (imprecation), *yaśas* (glory), *kīrti* (fame), *praśna* (question), *pṛcchā* (inquiry), and *anuyogaka* (interrogation);
*āmreḍitam* refers to what is spoken twice or thrice; *kutsā*, *nindā*, and *garhaṇa* denote censure and reproach; *ābhāṣaṇa* is conversation (*ālāpa*); and *pralāpa* is meaningless speech.
*Anulāpa* is speaking repeatedly; *volāpa* is lamentation;
*vipralāpa* is contradictory speech; *saṃlāpa* is conversation between two people; *supralāpa* is eloquent speech; and *apalāpa* is concealment. (AP 359.064–065ab)
Even pleasant speech that is unwholesome, though it may be agreeable, heart-pleasing,
exceedingly sweet, and consoling, would be incoherent, useless,
harsh, vulgar, and coarse; whereas even a pleasant truth, O beloved, is indeed [wholesome].

*Satya*, *tathya*, *ṛta*, and *samyak* mean "truth" or "reality. *Nāda*, *nisvāna*, and *nisvana* denote sound; likewise do *ārava*, *ārāva*, *saṃrāva*, and *virāva*. Furthermore, *marmara* refers to a rustling sound.
The rustling of garments and leaves, the tinkling of ornaments, the resonance of a lute, the sound of birds, the cry of animals,
a tumultuous noise, a confused clamor, singing, and chanting— these are all synonymous.
*Strī* refers to a woman; *pratiśrut* and *pratidhvāna* refer to an echo; *nisādaka* is that which produces sound from strings or the throat.
*Kākalī*, however, denotes a faint and subtle sound; *kala* refers to a sweet yet indistinct sound.
*Mantra* refers to a deep sound; *tāra* refers to one that is very high-pitched. These three [terms] apply to all three genders. //70//
The *ekatāla* has a uniform tempo; the *vīṇā*, however, is the *vallakī*. That same instrument with seven strings is the *vipañcī*, while one that modulates its pitch is the *parivādinī*.
Instruments such as the *vīṇā* are classified as *tata* (stringed), while those such as the *muraja* (drum) are *ānaddha* (membranous).

Wind instruments such as the *vaṃśī* (flute) and others are classified as *śuṣira* (hollow), while solid instruments such as the *kāṃsya* (cymbals) and *tāla* (clappers) are *ghana*; these four types of musical instruments are known by the names *vādya*, *vāditra*, and *ātodya*.
Among the drums, there are three varieties of *mṛdaṅga* or *muraja*: the *aṅkya*, the *āliṅgya*, and the *ardhaka*.
The *yaśaḥpaṭaha*, *ṭakkā*, *bherī*, *ānaka*, and *dundubhi* are synonyms;
the *ānaka*, *paṭaha*, *jharjharī*, *ḍiṇḍima*, and so forth are its varieties.
The *mardala* and *paṇava* are equivalent, while *tālaka* refers to the rhythmic timing (*kriyāmāna*).
*Laya* is equilibrium; *tāṇḍava* is dramatic dance (*nāṭya*), while *lāsya* is dancing (*nartana*).
The triad of music, song, and instrumental performance is called *tauryatrika*. This triad constitutes drama (*nāṭya*). A king is called *bhaṭṭāraka* or *deva*, as is his consecrated queen.
The aesthetic sentiments (rasas) are the erotic, the heroic, the pathetic, the marvelous, the comic, the terrifying, the loathsome, and the furious. The erotic is pure and radiant;
the heroic increases enthusiasm; and compassion, pity, and tenderness constitute the pathetic.
*Kṛpā*, *dayā*, *anukampā*, and *anukrośa* denote compassion; furthermore, *hasa*, *hāsa*, and *hāsya* denote laughter. *Vībhatsa* and *vikṛta*—this pair [of terms] is used in three genders.
Vismaya, adbhuta, āścarya, and citra; furthermore, bhairava,
dāruṇa, bhīṣaṇa, bhīṣma, ghora, bhīma,
and bhayānaka.

*Bhayaṅkara*, *pratibhaya*, *raudra*, and *ugra*—these four terms denote the terrifying. *Dara*, *trāsa*, *bhīti*, and *bhī* denote fear. *Sādhvasa* and *bhaya* denote dread. A mental transformation or state is *anubhāva*, which is the manifestation of an inner emotion. //68B//AP_359.068Bcd/
Pride (*garva*) is self-conceit (*abhimāna*), egoism (*ahaṅkāra*), and the inflation of the mind (*māna*).

Disrespect (*anādara*) is contempt (*paribhava*), humiliation (*paribhāva*), and disparagement (*tiraskriyā*). Shame (*vrīḍā*) is modesty (*lajjā*), bashfulness (*trapā*), and decorum (*hrī*). Covetousness (*abhidhyāna*) is the longing for wealth.
*Kautūhala*, *kautuka*, *kutuka*, and *kutūhala* are synonyms for curiosity.
//70B// *Vilāsa*, *vivvoka*, *vibhrama*, *lalita*, as well as *helā* and *līlā*—these are the *hāvas*, actions born of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-bhāva*). //71Bab//
*Drava*, *kelī*, *parīhāsa*, *krīḍā*, *līlā*, and *kūrdana* denote playful sport.
*Āchuritaka* is laughter accompanied by sarcasm (*sotprāsa*) and a slight smile (*samanāksmita*).
*Adhaḥbhuvana*, *pātāla*, *chidra*, *śvabhra*, *vapā*, and *śuṣi* denote the netherworld or a cavity.
*Garta* and *avaṭa* mean a hole or pit in the ground; *śvabhra* means a chasm. *Tamiśram*, *antimiraṃ*, and *tamaḥ* mean darkness.
*Sarpaḥ*, *pṛdākuḥ*, *bhujagaḥ*, *dandaśūkaḥ*, and *vileśayaḥ* mean a snake. *Viṣam*, *kṣveḍaḥ*, and *garalam* mean poison. *Nirayaḥ* and *durgatiḥ* (which is feminine) mean hell.
*Payaḥ*, *kīlālam*, *amṛtam*, *udakam*, *bhuvanam*, *vanam*—these denote water.
*Bhaṅgaḥ*, *taraṅgaḥ*, *ūrmiḥ*, or *kallolaḥ*—both of these also mean a wave or surge. *Pṛṣanti*, *binduḥ*, and *pṛṣataḥ* denote drops. *Kūlam*, *rodhaḥ*, and *tīrakam* denote a bank.
That sandy bank (pulina) is that which has arisen from water; jambāla, paṅka, and kardama refer to mud; parīvāhas are overflow waters; and kūpakas are holes or pits.
The ferryman is the *tāraka*, and the fare for crossing is the *tarapaṇya*; a wooden water-carrier is a *droṇī*.

Turbid water is *āvila*, while clear water is *accha* or *prasanna*. Furthermore, *gabhīraka* and *agādha* both mean deep; a fisherman is a *dāśaka* or *kaivarta*, and *śambūkas* are aquatic bivalve shells.
*Saugandhika* is *kahlāra*; the blue lotus is *indīvara* or *kaja*. *Utpala* and *kuvalaya* refer to the same; the white varieties are *kumuda* and *kairava*.
Their bulbous root is *śālūka*. *Padma*, *tāmarasa*, and *saṃkaja* denote the lotus.
The blue lotus is called *nīlotpala* or *kuvalaya*; the red lotus is known as *kokanada*.
