The root-stock is *karahāṭa*, the fiber is *śiphā*, and the bulb is *kanda*. The filament is *kiñjalka* or *kesara* (the latter not feminine). A mine is *khani* (feminine) or *ākara* (masculine). The foothills are *pādāḥ* or *pratyantaparvatāḥ*.
The ground near the base of a mountain is called *upatyakā*, while the ground above it is *adhityakā*.
Listen now to the various meanings of terms such as those belonging to the categories of heaven (*svarga*) and the underworld (*pātāla*).
Thus ends the section on the categories of heaven, the underworld, and so forth, in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter Three Hundred and Sixty:
Chapter Three Hundred and Sixty-One.
Now begins the three hundred and sixty-first chapter.
The section on indeclinables:
Agni said:
The prefix *ā* occurs in the sense of "slightness," "pervasion," and "limit" when joined with verbal roots.
The particle *ā* is used as a protracted form (*pragṛhya*) when expressing memory; it may also be used in a sentence. *Āstu* is used in the senses of anger and affliction.
*Ku* is used in the senses of evil, contempt, and "a little"; *dhik* is used in the senses of loathing and reproach.
*Ca* is used for subsequent mention (*anvācaya*), collection (*samāhāra*), mutual conjunction (*itaretara*), and simple conjunction (*samuccaya*).

The word *svasti* is used for blessings, welfare, merit, and so forth; *ati* is used for excellence and transgression; *svid* is used for inquiry and deliberation; and *tu* is used for distinction and emphasis.
*Sakṛt* means "once" or "at one time"; *ārāt* signifies "far" or "near";

*paścāt* denotes "in the west," "last," or is used for alternatives (*uta api artha-vikalpayoḥ*); *punar* and *sat* signify "again"; *śaśvat* means "always"; and *sākṣāt* means "directly" or "evidently."
*vata* is used for weariness, compassion, contentment, wonder, and address;
*hanta* is used for joy, compassion, the beginning of a sentence, and dejection;
*prati* is used according to usage for representation, substitution, repetition (*vīpsā*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and so forth.
The word *iti* is used in the senses of cause, context, manifestation, and conclusion;
*prācī*, *purastāt*, *prathama*, and *puraḥ* denote the sense of "in front" or "first";
and *yāvat* and *tāvat* are used for totality, limit, measure, and restriction.
The word *atha* is used for auspiciousness, immediate succession, commencement, inquiry, and totality; likewise, *otha* [is used similarly].
*Vṛthā* means "in vain" and "without purpose"; *nānā* means "various," "many," and "both.
*Nu* is used for inquiry and alternative; *anu* is used for "afterwards" and "resemblance."
The particle *nanu* is used in the senses of questioning, ascertaining, granting permission, conciliation, and addressing;
it is also used in censure, conjunction, inquiry, doubt, and possibility;
and in the senses of comparison, alternative, "together with," "half," and contempt.
*Amā* means together or near; *kam* means water or the head.
*Iva* is used for these two meanings; likewise, *evam* is used for such a thing and for certainty of meaning.
*Nūnam* is used for conjecture and for certainty of meaning; *joṣam* is used for silence and for happiness. *Kim* is used for inquiry and for loathing.
The word *nāman* denotes manifestation, possibility, the onset of anger, and reproach; *alam* expresses ornamentation, sufficiency, capability, and prohibition.

*Hūṃ* is used for deliberation (*vitarke*) and inquiry (*paripraśne*), as well as for the end and the middle of a *samaya*. It is also used for "again" (*punar*), for that which is not first (*aprathame*), for a division (*bhede*), for certainty (*nirniścaye*), and for negation (*niṣedhe*). *Purā* is used for continuity (*prabandhe*), for what is long past (*cirātīte*), and for what is near or coming (*nikaṭāgāmike*).
*Urari*, *urī*, and *corarī*—these three denote expansion and acceptance. *Svar* is used for heaven, the other world, news, and possibility;
*kila* is used for negation, poetic ornament, and an occasion of inquiry; and *khalu* is likewise used [for these].
*Abhitaḥ* is used in the senses of nearness, on both sides, quickly, entirely, and facing;
*prāduḥ* is used for manifestation and name; *mithas* and *anyonyam* mean mutually, as well as in secret;
*tiras* is used in the sense of disappearance and across; and *hā* is used in the senses of despondency, grief, and pain.
*Ahaha* is used for wonder, sorrow, cause, and emphasis.
*Cirāya*, *cirarātrāya*, *cirasya*, and so forth, express long duration.
*Muhuḥ*, *punaḥ punaḥ*, *śaśvat*, *abhīkṣṇam*, and *asakṛt* are synonyms meaning "again and again."
*srāk*, *jhaṭiti*, *añjasā*, *āśu*, *sapadi*, *drāk*, *maṅkṣu*, and *drute* (quickly);

*balavat*, *suṣṭhu*, and *kim uta* (how much more so) are used in the sense of intensity; *vikalpe* (in the sense of an alternative), there are *kiṃ*, *kim uta*, *tu*, *hi*, *ca*, *sma*, *ha*, and *vai*;
these are used for filling out the verse (*pādapūraṇe*), as well as for expressing praise (*pūjane*). Furthermore, *ati* is used in the same way.

*Divā* means "by day" and *doṣā* means "at night"; *naktaṃ* also means "at night. *Sāci* and *tiras* mean "obliquely" or "aside. Now, the words used for addressing others are *pyāṭ*, *pāṭ*, *aṅga*, *he*, *hai*, and *bhoḥ*. *Samayā*, *nikaṣā*, and *hiruk* [mean "near" or "without"].
But *atarkite* means suddenly; *puraḥ*, *purataḥ*, and *agrataḥ* mean before.
*Svāhā* is used for the offering of oblations to the gods; *śrauṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *vaṣaṭ* are sacrificial exclamations; *svadhā* is for ancestral offerings.
*Kiñcit*, *īṣat*, and *manāk* mean slightly or a little. *Pretya* and *amutra* refer to another state of existence after death.
*Jijñāsānunaya* (inquiry and conciliation) is expressed by *ña*;
likewise, *yathā* and *tathā* are used for similarity; and *aho* and *ho* are used for wonder. (AP 360.024cd)
*Maunam*, *tūṣṇīm*, and *tūṣṇīkam* denote silence; *sadyaḥ*, *sapadi*, and *tatkṣaṇe* denote the present moment;
*diṣṭyā*, *śam*, *upajoṣam*, and *cait* are used for joy; furthermore, *antarā*, *antare*, and *antareṇa* signify the middle or interval; and *prasahya* has the sense of force or compulsion.

The two [particles] *yukte* and *sāmpratam* signify "properly" (*sthāne*). *Abhīkṣṇam*, *śaśvat*, and *anāratam* signify "repeatedly. *Abhāve* signifies "non-existence. *Nahi*, *no*, and also *mā sma* and *mā alaṃ* signify prohibition (*vāraṇe*).
*Cet* and *yadi* signify an alternative (*pakṣāntare*). *Addhā* and *añjasā*—these two—signify reality (*tattve*).
*Prāduḥ* and *āviḥ* are used in the sense of manifestation; *om*, *evaṃ*, and *paramam* are used in the sense of assent;
*samantataḥ*, *paritaḥ*, *sarvataḥ*, and *viśvak* are used in the sense of "on all sides.
*Kāmam* is used for reluctant assent, while *astu* is used for the acceptance of something with disapproval.
Now, "nanu" is used in expressing contradiction; "kaccit" in making a request;

"niḥṣamam" and "duḥṣamam" in what is censurable; "yathāsvam" and "yathāyatham" mean "as each is"; and "mṛṣā," "mithyā," and "vitatha" mean "untrue"; whereas "yathārtham" and "yathātatham" mean "according to the fact."
The words *syāt*, *evam*, *tu*, *punar*, *vai*, and *vā* are expressive of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
*Prāk* has the sense of "past"; *nūnam* and *avaśyam*—these two—are used for certainty (*niścaye*);
*saṃvat* means "in a year"; *avara* means "later" or "below"; *arvāk* means "before"; *evam* means "thus"; and *svayam* means "by oneself."
*Alpa* means "small"; *nīcaiḥ* means "low"; *mahat* means "great"; *prāyas* means "mostly" or "for the most part"; *bhūman* means "abundance"; *adruta* means "not fast"; *śanais* means "slowly";

*sanā* means "eternal"; *bahiḥ* means "outside" or "external"; *smāt* means "past"; *asta* means "disappearance" or "setting"; *asti* is used for existence; it is used when speaking angrily; *ūm* and *um* are used in questioning; and *tvayi* is used in conciliation.
*Hūṃ* is used for deliberation; *uṣā* at the end of the night; *namaḥ* in salutation; *aṅga* in the sense of "again" or in censure; *duṣṭhu* and *suṣṭhu* in praise;
*sāyam* and *sāye* mean evening; *prage* and *prātaḥ* mean morning; and *nikaṣā* means near.
*Parut*, *parāri*, and *aiṣamaḥ* denote years; *pūrve* and *pūrvatare* denote past times.
In expressions such as *adya*, *atratya*, and *ahni*, as well as *pūrvedyuḥ* and so forth, the words *pūrva*, *uttara*, and *para* [are used].

Likewise, *adharēdyaḥ*, *anyatarēdyaḥ*, *itarēdyaḥ*, and *pūrvēdyaḥ* [are used]; *ubhayēdyaḥ* means "on both days," while *parēdyaḥ* means "on the following day. *Hyas* refers to a day gone by or past; *śvas* to a day not yet come or future; and *paraśvas* to the day after tomorrow. *Śvaḥpare 'hani* means "on the day after tomorrow."
*tadā*, *tadānīm*, *yugapat*, *ekadā*, *sarvadā*, *sadā*; *etarhi*, *samprati*, *idānīm*, *adhunā*, *sāmpratam*—likewise. Thus ends the section on indeclinables in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
The three hundred and sixty-first chapter;
now begins the three hundred and sixty-first chapter.
Regarding the various groups of meanings, Agni said:
"The word *nāka* refers to space, the third heaven (*tridiva*), and the world; it also refers to a dwelling and to people."
*Śloka* refers to verse and fame; *sāyaka* to an arrow and a sword; *ānaka* to a drum, a kettledrum, and a large drum; *kalaṅka* to a mark and a scandal;
*kaḥ* (the letter *ka*) to wind, Brahmā, and the sun (in the masculine); and *kaṃ* to the head and water.
*Pulāka* may refer to chaff, a concise summary, or a grain of boiled rice.
*Kauśika* refers to Indra, guggulu resin, an owl, a snake-catcher, or a mongoose.
A *śālāvṛka* is both a monkey and a dog. *Māna* signifies a means of measurement.
*Sarga* is used in the senses of creation, inherent nature, liberation, certainty, chapter, and emission;
*yoga* is used in the senses of girding oneself, means, meditation, conjunction, and reasoning.

*Bhoga* means enjoyment, happiness, or the maintenance of women and so forth; *abja* refers to the conch and the moon; *karaṭa* refers to a crow or the temples of an elephant; *śipiviṣṭaka* refers to one with a skin disease;
*riṣṭa* denotes well-being, misfortune, or non-existence; whereas *ariṣṭa* denotes both the auspicious and the inauspicious.

*Vyuṣṭiḥ* denotes fruitfulness and prosperity; *dṛṣṭiḥ* denotes knowledge, the eye, and vision; *niṣṭhā* denotes completion, destruction, and peace; *kāṣṭhā* denotes excellence, a limit, and a direction;
*bhū*, *go*, *vāk*, *tviṭ*, and *ilāḥ* denote the earth; *pragāḍham* denotes intensity and difficulty.
*Bhṛśa* and *pratijñā* mean "firmly"; *vāḍham* means "certainly. *Śakta*, *sthūla*, and *dṛḍha* are used in three genders (masculine, feminine, and neuter).
*Vyasta* and *saṃhata* mean "arranged" or "formed in array," while *vyūḍha* refers to one who is "well-built" or "broad-chested. *Kṛṣṇa* refers to Vyāsa, Arjuna, and Hari (Viṣṇu).
*Paṇa* refers to a stake in gambling and so forth, as well as wages, price, and wealth.
The word *maurvī* refers to a bowstring, as well as to qualities such as goodness (*sattva*), whiteness, and the morning twilight;
it also denotes an excellent person or a leader. *Ghṛṇā* signifies both loathing and compassion. *Tṛṣṇā* means longing, desire, and thirst. *Vipaṇi* refers to a marketplace or the path of merchants.
*Tīkṣṇa* refers to poison, disease, and metals; it is neuter, but masculine when meaning "sharp.
*Pramāṇa* means cause, limit, expectation, measure, and the knower. *Karaṇa* refers to the field, the body, and so forth. *Īriṇa* means a desert, a wasteland, and saline soil.
*Yantṛ* means a driver, *hastipaka* an elephant-keeper, and *sūta* a charioteer; *vahni-jvālā* (fire-flame) and *hetayaḥ* (weapons).
*Sruta* refers to that which has been heard; *avadhṛta* and *yuga-paryāpta* mean "fixed" and "sufficient" respectively.

*Kṛta* means "done"; *khyāta* means "famous. *Hṛṣṭa* means "delighted," while *pratīta* means "understood. *Abhijāta* means "well-born" or "of noble family," as well as "wise. AP_361.013ab AP_361.014ab
*Vivikta* means pure, solitary, or fainting; *mūrchita* means stupefied or increased.
*Artha* refers to that which is signified, wealth, an object, purpose, or cessation.
*Tīrtha* refers to a source, a sacred scripture, water frequented by sages, or a teacher.
*Kakuda* is used in the sense of preeminence, a royal insignia, or the hump on the shoulder of a bull; it is not feminine.
*Sambit* is used in the senses of knowledge, conversation, action, form, and name.
*Upaniṣad* refers to the secret doctrine within the *Dharma*; *śarad* means both a year and autumn.
*Pada* denotes resolve, protection, place, a mark, a foot, and an object.
*Madhura* and *svādu* mean sweet; *mṛdu*, *atīkṣṇa*, and *komala* all mean soft.
The word *sat* is used in the sense of truth, what is good, that which exists, what is praiseworthy, and what is venerable;
*vidhi* denotes a rule, fate, or even a divine ordinance; *praṇidhi* means a vow, a request, or conduct;
*vadhū* refers to a wife, a daughter-in-law, or a young woman; and *sudhā* means a plastering with lime, nectar, or the *snuhī* plant.
*Spṛhā*, *sampratyaya*, and *śraddhā* denote longing; *paṇḍitammanya* and *garvita* denote one who considers himself learned or is arrogant;
*brahmabandhu* denotes one who insults; *bhānu* refers to both a ray and the sun; *grāvāṇa* refers to both a mountain and a stone; and *pṛthagjana* refers to both a fool and a low-born person.
*Taru* and *śaila* denote peaks; *tanu*, *tvac*, and *deha* denote the body.
*Ātman* denotes effort, fortitude, intellect, inherent nature, Brahman, and the physical frame.
In the science of human endeavor (*pauruṣa-tantra*), *utthāna* means exertion, while *vyutthāna* means obstruction.
*Niryātana* means the clearing of a feud, as well as the handing over of a deposit in the context of giving;
*vyasana* refers to calamity, misfortune, ruin, or the vice arising from desire or anger; [the latter being] hunting, gambling, sleeping by day, slander, women, and intoxication.
The triple symphony (song, dance, and instrumental music), and idle wandering— this is the group of ten born of desire.
Backbiting, violence, malice, envy, finding fault,
and harshness of speech and punishment— this is also the group of eight born of anger.
*Akarma* refers to the secret; *kaupīna* to a loincloth; *saṅgati* to sexual union; and *rata* to pleasure.
*Pradhāna* is the primary cause; *paramārtha* is the ultimate truth; *dhī* is intellect; and *prajñāna* is wisdom, as well as the signs of the Buddha.
*Krandana* means weeping or calling out; *varṣma* means the body or measurement.
*Ārādhana* may mean accomplishment, attainment, or pleasing;
*ratna* refers to the best of its kind, while *lakṣma* denotes a mark or that which is preeminent.
*Kalāpa* refers to an ornament, a peacock’s tail-feathers, a quiver, and also a collection;
*talpa* refers to a bed and a turret; *ḍimbha* refers to an infant and a fool;
*stambha* refers to a pillar and stupor; and *sabhā* refers to a member of an assembly and an assembly hall itself.
*Kiraṇa* and *pragraha* mean rays; *dharma* refers to merit, restraint, and so forth;
*lalāma* means a tail, a sectarian mark, a horse, an ornament, a preeminent thing, or a banner;
*pratyaya* is used for dependence, an oath, knowledge, trust, and a cause. (AP 361.031ab)
*Samaya* refers to an agreement, an oath, conduct, time, a philosophical doctrine, or a convention;
*atyaya* means transgression or hardship; *satya* denotes both an oath and truth;
*vīrya* signifies strength and power; and *rūpya* refers to silver as well as that which is excellent.
*Durodara* refers to a gambler, a stake, or gambling itself;
*kāntāra* denotes a great forest or a difficult path, and is both masculine and neuter;
*hari* refers to Yama, Anila (the Wind), Indra, Candra (the Moon), Arka (the Sun), Viṣṇu, a lion, and so forth.
*Dara* (masculine) means fear or a pit; *jaṭhara* means hard as well as the belly;
*udāra* means a donor or great; *itara* means other or low;
*cūḍā*, *kirīṭa*, and bound hair—these three are synonyms for a crown.
*Bali* refers to offerings such as those made with the hands, or to strength found in the steadfastness of an army;
*nīvī* refers to the knot of a woman’s waist-cloth and also to a stake in a wager;
*vṛṣa* refers to semen, a rat, a bull, and merit.
*Ākarṣa* refers to a gambling die, a chessboard, or a magnet; *akṣa* denotes a sense organ, a component of a game, a weight (*karṣa*), or the *kali* tree.
*Ūṣṇīṣa* occurs in the sense of a crown or similar headgear, while *karṣū* is a term for a small irrigation channel.
When perception is the subject, *adhyakṣa* means a supervisor; *vibhāvasu* refers to the sun and fire;
and *rasa* denotes the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and others, poison, potency, a quality, passion, and liquid.
*Tejas* refers to luster and excrement; *āgas* to sin and offense;
*chandas* to verse and desire; *sādhīyas* to that which is more excellent and to a good person;
*vyūha* to a multitude and also to Vṛtra; and *ahis* to Vṛtra as well as the sun, moon, and fire, which dispel darkness.
Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Section on Various Meanings," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 362.
Now begins the three hundred and sixty-second chapter:
The Categories of Earth, Forests, Herbs, and so forth.
Agni said:
I shall describe the earth, cities, mountains, forests, medicinal herbs, lions, and other such things.
Earth is known as *anantā*, *kakṣamā*, *dhātrī*, *kṣmā*, *apyāku*, and *dharitrī*. Furthermore, *mṛt*, *mṛttikā*, *mṛtsā*, *mṛtsnā*, and *mṛttikā* denote excellent soil.
*Jagat*, *trapiṣṭapa*, *loka*, *bhuvana*, and *jagatī* are synonyms for the world.
*Ayana*, *vartman*, *mārga*, *adhvan*, *pathin*, *padavī*, *sṛti*, *saraṇi*, *paddhati*, *padyā*, *vartanī*, and *ekapadī* are synonyms for a path.

*Pūḥ*, *strī*, *purī*, *nagarī*, *pattana*, *puṭabhedana*, *sthānīya*, and *nigama* are synonyms for a city; however, any town that is distinct from the primary capital city is called a *śākhānagara*. A *veśa* is a brothel, which is a place of resort for courtesans.
A shop is *niṣadyā*, while *vipaṇi* and *paṇyavīthikā* refer to a market street;
a carriage road is *rathyā*, *pratolī*, or *viśikhā*. A mound or rampart is *caya* or *vapra* (the latter not feminine).
An enclosure wall is *prākāra*, *varaṇa*, *śāla*, or *prācīra*; a fence at the edge is *vṛti*.
A wall is feminine; it is called *kuhya* or *meḍūka* when it has no internal framework of bones (*nasta-kīkasam*).
A dwelling is a *kūṭa*, which is masculine or neuter; a hall is a *śālā*; and this [same type of structure] is a *sabhā* or a *sañjavana*.
A four-winged dwelling for sages is called a *parṇaśālā* or an *uṭaja* (the latter not feminine);
*caitya* and *āyatana* are synonyms. A stable for horses is a *vājiśālā* or *mandurā*.
The residence of the wealthy, such as a *harmya*, is a *prāsāda*, which belongs to gods and kings.
The word *strī* (feminine) refers to a door; *pratīhāra* is also a term for a door. *Vitardi*, however, means a raised platform or altar (*vedikā*).
The *kapotapālikā* (dovecote) is called *viṭaṅka*, which is both masculine and neuter. *Kavāṭa* and *advāra* are synonyms for a door-panel. *Niḥśreṇi* and *adhirohiṇī* refer to a ladder or staircase.
*Sammārjanī* and *śodhanī* mean a broom; *saṅkara* and *avakara* likewise mean refuse or rubbish.
*Adri*, *gotra*, *giri*, and *grāvan* mean a mountain or rock. *Gahana*, *kānana*, *vana*, and *ārāma* denote a forest. *Upavana* refers to an artificial grove, which is simply a cultivated garden.
This very pleasure grove, fit for the inner apartments, might be so;
for *vīthī*, *āli*, *āvali*, *paṅkti*, *śreṇī*, *lekhā*, and *rāji* all mean a row.
A tree that bears fruit through flowers is called *vānaspatya*, while one that bears fruit without flowers is a *vanaspati*.
Herbs end with the ripening of their fruit; *drudruma* and *āgama* refer to leaf-bearing trees.
*Sthāṇu*, *vāna*, *dhruva*, and *śaṅku* denote a trunk or stump. *Praphulla*, *utphulla*, and *saṃsphuṭa* mean fully blossomed.
*Palāśa*, *chadana*, and *parṇa* mean a leaf. *Idhma*, *edha*, and *samit* (the latter being feminine) mean sacrificial fuel.
The *bodhidruma* is *caladala*; *dadhittha*, *grāhī*, and *manmatha* are synonyms for it.
In that [same category], *dadhiphala*, *puṣpa*, *phala*, and *dantaśaṭha* are also included.
*Uḍumbara* is *hemadugdha*, and *kovidāra* is *dvipatraka*.
Saptaparṇa, viśālatvak, kṛtamāla, and suvarṇaka;
ārevata, vyādhighāta, sampāka, and caturaṅgula;
dantaśaṭha is found in the jambīra tree, and tiktaśāvaka in the varuṇa.
The *putrāga* is called *puruṣa*, *tuṅga*, *keśara*, and *devavallabha*.
The *pāribhadra* is the *nimbataru*, while the *mandāra* is the *pārijātaka*.
*Vañjula* and *citrakṛt* are synonyms; furthermore, there are two types of *pītanaka*: *pītanaka* and *kapītana*.
*Āmrātaka* is known as *guḍapuṣpa* and *madhudruma*. *Madhūka* is called *guḍaphala* and *sraṃsī*. *Nādeyī* and *ambuvetasa* are synonyms for the aquatic reed.
*Śobhāñjana*, *śigru*, *tīkṣṇagandha*, *kākṣīra*, and *mocaka* are synonyms for the drumstick tree;
the red variety is called *madhuśigru*. *Ariṣṭa* and *pheṇila* are equivalent terms.
*Gālava*, *śāvara*, *lodhra*, *tirīṭa*, *tilva*, and *mārjana* are synonyms for the *lodhra* tree.
Śelu is śleṣmātaka; śīta is uddāla and bahuvāraka; vaikaṅkata is śruvāvṛkṣa; granthila is vyāghrapād;
tinduka is also sphūrjaka; kāla is nādeyī and bhūmijambuka.
*Kākatindu* is *pīluka*; *pāṭali*, *mokṣa*, and *muṣkaka* [are synonyms]; *kramuka* is called *paṭṭika*; *kumbhī*, *kaṭarya*, and *kaṭphala* [are synonyms];
*vīravṛkṣa*, *aruṣkara*, and *agnimukhī* refer to the *bhallātaka* tree; these three [names] apply to all three genders.
The *savarjaka*, *asanajīva*, and *pītasāla* trees, as well as the *mālaka*;
the *sarja*, *aśvakarṇa*, *vīrendra*, *indradru*, *kakubha*, and *arjuna*;
the *iṅgudī*, the ascetic’s tree (*tāpasataru*), the *mocā*, and the *śālmali* tree.
*Ciravilva*, *naktamāla*, and *karaja* are synonyms for the *karañjaka* tree;
*prakīrya*, *pūtikarañja*, *markaṭī*, and *aṅgāravallarī* are also names for it.
*Rohī*, *rohitaka*, *plīhaśatru*, and *dāḍimapuṣpaka* refer to the same plant.
The *gāyatrī*, the *bālatanaya*, and the *khadira* are used for cleaning the teeth.
*Arimeda* is found in the *viṭkhadira*; *kadara* is found in the white *khadira*. Also [used are] the *pañcāṅgula*, the *vardhamāna*, the *cañcu*, and the *gandharvahastaka*.
Piṇḍītaka, maruvaka, pītadāru, and dāru; devadāru, pūtikāṣṭha, and śyāmā, which is called mahilāhvayā.
Latā, govandanī, gundā, priyaṅgu, phalinī, and phalī;
maṇḍūkaparṇa, patrorṇa, naṭa, kaṭvaṅga, and ṭuṇṭuka; śyonāka, śukanāsa, ṛkṣa, dīrghavṛnta, and kuṭannaṭa.
Pītadru and sarala; then nicula, ambuja, and ijjala; kākoḍumbarikā, phalgu, ariṣṭa, and picumardaka;
sarvatobhadraka and nimba; and śirīṣa, which is also called kapītana.
Vakula is said to be vañjula; picchilā, aguru, and śiṃśapā [are synonyms];
jayā, jayantī, tarkārī, kaṇikā, and gaṇikārikā [are synonyms];
āparṇa would be agnimantha; vatsaka is girimallikā.

*Kālaskandha* is *tamāla*; *taṇḍulīya* is *alpamāriṣa*. *Sindhuvāra*, however, is *nirguṇḍī*, and that same plant growing in the forest is *āsphotā*. *Gaṇikā*, *yūthikā*, *ambaṣṭhā*, *saptalā*, and *navamālikā* [are synonyms].
*Atimukta* is *puṇḍraka*; *kumārī*, *taraṇi*, and *sahā* are synonyms for it.
Among those, when red it is *kuruvaka*, and when yellow it is *kuruṇṭaka*.
*Jhiṇṭī* is blue; furthermore, *bāṇā*, *bhiṇṭī*, and *sairīyaka* apply to both [the red and yellow varieties].

The *kuruvaka* is red, while the *sahacarī* is yellow; both [are names for] these two. *Dhustūra*, *kitava*, and *dhūrta* refer to the thorn-apple (*dhattūra*). *Rucaka* refers to the citron (*mātulaṅga*).
*Samīraṇa*, *maruvaka*, *prasthapuṣpa*, and *phaṇijjhaka* [are synonyms].
Kuṭheraka is a synonym for parṇāsa; furthermore, āsphota is used for vasuka and arkaka.
Śivamallī is pāśupata, while vṛndā, vṛkṣādanī, jīvantikā, vṛkṣaruhā, guḍūcī, tantrikā, and amṛtā are synonyms [for the same plant].
Somavallī, madhurnī, and likewise mūrvā, moraṭī,
madhulikā, madhuśreṇī, gokarṇī, and pīluparṇī; (283) AP_362.041cd–042ab.
Pāṭhā, ambaṣṭhā, viddhakarṇī, prācīnā, vanatiktikā,
kaṭu, kaṭumbharā, cakrāṅgī, śakulādanī,
ātmaguptā, prāvṛṣāyī, kapikacchu, and markaṭī.
Apāmārga, śaikharika, pratyakparṇī, mayūraka, phaṇijjhaka, brāhmaṇī, bhārgī, dravantī, śambarī, vṛṣā,
maṇḍūkaparṇī, bhaṇḍīrī, samaṅgā, and kālameṣikā.
Rodanī, kacchurā, anantā, samudrāntā, durālabhā,
pṛśniparṇī, pṛthakparṇī, kalaśī, dhāvanī, guhā, nidigdhikā, spṛśī, vyāghrī, kṣudrā, together with dusparśā.
Avalguja, somarājī, suvalli, and somavallikā;
kālameṣī, kṛṣṇaphalā, vakucī, and pūtiphalī;
kaṇā, uṣaṇā, upakulyā, śreyasī, and gajapippalī are synonyms.
Cavya and cavikā, kākaciñcī and guñjā (also called kṛṣṇalā);
viśvā, viṣā, and prativiṣā; vanaśṛṅgāṭa and gokṣura; nārāyaṇī, śatamūlī, kāleyaka, and haridrā.
Dārvī, pacampacā, dāru, śuklā, haimavatī, vacā,
vacā, ugragandhā, ṣaḍgranthā, golomī, śataparvikā,
āsphotā, girikarṇī, siṃhāsya, vāsaka, and vṛṣa.
Miśī, madhurikā, chatrā, kokilākṣa, ikṣuraka, and kṣura;
viḍaṅga—also called kṛmighna—is not feminine; vajradru, snuh, and snuhī are synonyms for sudhā; mṛdvīkā, gostanī, and drākṣā refer to the grape; and valā as well as vāṭyālaka are synonyms for sārivā.
Kālā, masūravidalā, tripuṭā, trivṛtā, and trivṛt; madhuka, klītaka, yaṣṭimadhuka, and madhuyaṣṭikā.
Vidārī, kṣīraśuklā, ikṣugandhā, and kroṣṭrī are synonyms for the white variety;
gopī, śyāmā, and śārivā refer to the blue variety; and anantā, utpalaśārivā, mocā, rambhā, kadalī, bhaṇṭākī, and duṣpradharṣiṇī are synonyms for the plantain.
*Sthirā*, *dhruvā*, and *sālaparṇī* are synonyms; *śṛṅgī*, *vṛṣabha*, and *vṛṣa* are synonyms;
*gāṅgerukī*, *nāgabalā*, *muṣalī*, and *tālamūlikā* are synonyms;
and *jyotsnī*, *paṭolikā*, *jālī*, *ajaśṛṅgī*, and *viṣāṇikā* are synonyms.
*Lāṅgalikī*, *agniśikhā*, *tāmbūlī*, and *nāgavallī* are synonyms for betel vine.
*Hareṇū*, *reṇukā*, *kauntī*, *hrīvera*, and *divyanāgara* are synonyms for *kālānusārya*. Furthermore, *vṛddha*, *aśmapuṣpa*, and *śītaśiva* are also synonyms for it.
Śaileya, tālaparṇī, daityā, gandhakuṭī, and murā;
granthiparṇa, śuka, and barhi; balā, tripuṭā, and truṭi; śivā, tāmalakī, hanu, and haṭṭavilāsinī.
Kuṭa, naṭa, daśapura, vāneya, paripelava;
tapasvanī, jaṭāmāṃsī, pṛkkā, devī, latā, laśū, karcuraka, drāviḍaka, gandhamūlī, and śaṭhī are recorded [as synonyms]. AP 362.060ab–061ab.
*Syaddṛkṣagandhā*, *chagalāntrā*, *vegī*, *vṛddhadāraka*,
*tuṇḍikerī*, *raktaphalā*, *bimbikā*, *pīluparṇī*,
*cāṅgerī*, *cukrikā*, *ambaṣṭhā*, *svarṇakṣīrī*, and *himāvatī*.
Sahasravedhī, cukra, and amlavetasa are synonyms for Śatavedhī; likewise,
jīvantī, jīvanī, and jīvā are synonyms for Bhūminimba, which is also called kirātaka,
kūrcaśīrṣa, madhukara, candra, and kapivṛka.
Dadrughna is eḍagaja; varṣābhū is śīthahāriṇī;
kunandā is nikumbhatrā.
Yamānī, vārṣikā, as well as laśuna, gṛñjana, ariṣṭa, mahākanda, rasonaka,
vārāhī, badarā, gṛṣṭi, and kākamācī (vāyasī).
Śatapuṣpā, sitacchatrā, aticchatrā, madhurā, misi; avākpuṣpī, kāravī, and saraṇā, which is prasāraṇī;
kaṭambharā, bhadrabalā, and karvūra, which is indeed śaṭī.
*Paṭola*, *kulaka*, *tikta*, *kāravella*, and *kaṭillaka* are synonyms for the bitter gourd.
*Kuṣmāṇḍaka* and *karkāru* refer to the pumpkin gourd; *irvāru* and *karkaṭī* are feminine terms for the cucumber.
*Ikṣvāku* refers to the bitter melon (*kaṭutumbī*), while *viśālā* and *indravāruṇī* denote the white gourd.
The *śūraṇa* tuber is a destroyer of hemorrhoids (*arśoghnah*); likewise are *mustaka* and *kuruvindaka*.
In the bamboo family (*vaṃśa*) are found *tvaksāra*, *karmāra*, *veṇu*, *maskara*, and *tejana*.
*Chatrā* and *aticchatrā* are destroyers of *pālaga*; so too are *mālātṛṇaka* and *bhūstṛṇa*.
*Tāla* is called *tṛṇarāja*; *ghoṇṭā*, *kramuka*, and *pūga* refer to the betel nut tree; *śārdūla* and *dvīpin* denote the tiger; *haryakṣa*, *keśarin*, and *hari* denote the lion;
*kola*, *potrī*, and *varāha* denote the boar; and *koka*, *īhāmṛga*, and *vṛka* denote the wolf.
The *lūta* and *ūrṇanābha* are synonyms for a spider; likewise, *tantuvāya* and *markaṭa* are synonyms for a monkey.
A scorpion is called a *vṛścika* or a *śūkakīṭa*; *sāraṅga* and *tokaka* are synonyms.
A cock is called a *kṛkavāku* or a *tāmracūḍa*, while a cuckoo is known as a *pika* or a *kokila*.
The crow is called *karaṭa* and *ariṣṭa*; the heron is cited as *baka* and *kaḍva*.
The ruddy goose is the *koka*, *cakra*, and *cakravāka*; the *kādamba* is the *kalahaṃsaka*.
The *pataṅgikā* is the *puttikā*; the *saraghā* is the honey-bee (*madhumakṣikā*).
1. *Sakuladantī* is [also called] *nirdaṃṣṭrā*.
*Dvirepha*, *puṣpaliṭ*, *bhṛṅga*, *ṣaṭpada*, *bhramara*, and *ālī* [are synonyms for the bee].
The cry of a peacock is *kekā*; a bird is called *śakunti*, *śakuni*, or *dvija*.
The root of a wing is *pakṣati* (feminine), as is *pakṣamūla*. The beak is *cañcu* or *toṭi* (both feminine).
Flight is *gati*, *uḍḍina*, or *saṇḍīna*. A nest is *kulāya* or *nīḍa* (not feminine).
A fleshy sac is a *peśī*; when two [stages] are lacking, it is an *aṇḍa* (egg); a young one is called a *pṛthuka*, *śāvaka*, *śiśu*, *pota*, *pāka*, *arbhaka*, or *ḍimbha*.
A collection, an array, a group, a cluster, a multitude, a mass, a heap, a flock, a swarm, a thicket, or a cluster is termed a *nikuramba* or a *kadambaka*.
*Saṅghāta*, *sañcaya*, and *vṛnda* denote a multitude; whereas *puñja*, *rāśi*, and *kūṭaka* denote a heap.
Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Section on the Earth, Forests, Herbs, and so forth," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 363:
The Classes of Men, Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
Agni said:
"I shall now declare by name the classes of men—Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. O mortal, they are called *nara*, *pañcajana*, *martya*, *yoṣā*, *avaṃlā*, and *vadhū*."
A woman who goes to a rendezvous seeking her lover is called an *abhisārikā*.
A wanton woman, one who has abandoned her husband, an unchaste woman, a naked woman, and a female servant are all termed *koṭavī*.
A woman who is half-grown and who goes to the houses of others is called a *sairindhrī* or *kātyāyanī*.
A woman who has not reached puberty is called *asiknī*, while one who is stained with menstrual blood is *malinī*.
A courtesan is a *gaṇikā* or *veśyā*. The wives of one's brothers are *yātaraḥ*; the husband’s sister is *nanāndā*. Those who share the same funeral cake (*sapiṇḍa*) are *sanābhayaḥ*.
*Samānodarya*, *sodarya*, *sagarbha*, and *sahaja* are synonyms.
*Sagotra*, *bāndhava*, *jñāti*, *bandhu*, *sva*, and *svajana* are also synonyms.

*Dampatī*, *jampatī*, *bhāryāpatī*, and *jāyāpatī* are terms for a husband and wife. The *garbhāśaya* is the womb; it may also be called *jarāyu* or *ulba*. *Kalala* (referring to the embryo in its earliest stage) is not feminine. *Garbha* and *bhrūṇa* are synonymous terms for the fetus. *Śaṇḍa* and *napuṃsaka* are neuter terms for a eunuch or one lacking virility.
A child lying on its back is called *uttānaśaya*; a young boy is known as *bāla* or *māṇavaka*.
One with a large belly is *piciṇḍila* or *vṛhatkukṣi*; one with a flat nose is *avabhraṭa*. One with deformed limbs is *pogaṇḍa*; health is *ārogya* or *anāmaya*.
The term *eḍa* may refer to one who is deaf; *gaḍula* refers to one who is humpbacked; and *kuni* refers to one with a withered hand.

*Kṣaya*, *śoṣa*, and *yakṣmā* denote consumption (tuberculosis). *Pratiśyāya* and *pīnasa* both mean catarrh. *Kṣut* and *kṣutam* are feminine, while *kṣava* is masculine; *kāsa* and *kṣavathu* are masculine and denote coughing.
*Śotha*, *śvayathu*, and *śopha* mean swelling; *pādasphoṭa* and *vipādikā* mean cracked feet;
*kilāsa*, *sidhmaka*, *cchāntu*, *pāmā*, *vicarcikā* mean scabies;
*koṭha*, *maṇḍalaka*, and *kuṣṭha* mean leprosy; *śvitra* means white leprosy; and *arśas* means hemorrhoids.
Anāha is constipation; grahaṇī-ruk is dysentery.
Seed, potency, and faculty refer to semen. Palala, kravya, and āmiṣa refer to flesh. Vukkāgra-māṃsa is the heart-flesh. Hṛdaya is the heart. Medas is fat; vapā is suet; vasā is muscle-fat.
The posterior neck is the *śirā*; the *manyā* is the tendon; the *nāḍī* is the artery; the *śirā* is the vein.
The *tilaka* is the mole; the *kloma* is the lung; the *mastiṣka* is the brain; and the *drūṣikā* is the impurity of the eyes.
The *antra* is the intestine; the *purītat* is the mesentery; the *gulma* is the spleen, which is masculine; and then there is the *vasnasā*, the muscle-tendon.
The word *snāyu* (sinew) is feminine; *kālakhaṇḍa* and *yakṛt* (liver) are both neuter.
*Karpūra*, *kapāla*, *kīkasa*, *kuṇya*, and *asthi* (bone) are used for bone in general.
*Kaṅkāla* refers to the bones of the body, while *kaśerukā* refers specifically to the vertebrae of the spine.
The skull is the *karoṭi* (feminine); the ribs are the *parśukā*. A limb, a member, or a part is called *aṅga*, *pratīka*, or *avayava*; while the body is termed *śarīra*, *varṣma*, or *vigraha*.
*Kaṭaḥ*, *nā*, *śroṇiphalakam*, *kaṭiḥ*, *śroṇiḥ*, and *kakudmatī* refer to the hip;
*paścānnitambaḥ* refers to the buttocks at the rear of a woman's waist. *Jaghanam* is used for the front of the waist and is neuter.
The two depressions situated on the buttocks are called *kūpau*; when devoid of hair, they are termed *kakundare*.

In a woman, the two fleshy parts of the hips are called *sphic* or *kaṭiprotha*; the private parts are *upastha*, while *bhaga* and *yoni* refer to the vulva in both genders. The male organ is called *śiśna*, *meḍhra*, *mehana*, or *śephas*.
The belly is *piciṇḍa*, *kukṣi*, *jaṭhara*, *udara*, or *tunda*; the breasts are *kuca* or *stana*.

The nipple is the tip of the breast; *kroḍa* is the chest or the space between the arms; the shoulder is the head of the arm, called *aṃsa*, which is not feminine; its two joints are the *jatruṇī*; furthermore, *punarbhava*, *kararuha*, *nakha*, and *nakhara*—the latter two being non-feminine—refer to the fingernail.

When the thumb is extended together with the index finger and the others, it is a *pradeśa*; with the little finger also extended, it is a *tāla*. A *gokarṇa* consists of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
When the fingers are spread out in the hand, it is a *vitasti*, a *peṭa*, a *pratala*, or a *prahasta*.
His hands have clenched fists, his forearms are long, and he possesses the smallest fingers.
His neck is like a conch shell with three lines; the hollow of the nape, the back of the neck, the lower jaw below the lips, the cheeks, the throat, and the chin are all well-formed.

The outer corners of the eyes are the *apāṅga*; a sidelong glance is *apāṅgadarśana*. *Cikura*, *kuntala*, and *bāla* refer to hair. *Pratikarma* and *prasādhana* denote grooming or decoration. *Ākalpa* and *veṣa* refer to attire; *nepathya* refers to dress, while *pratyakṣa* refers to that which arises from the application of dramatic performance (*khelayoga*).
The *cūḍāmaṇi* is a crest-jewel; the *tarala* is that which is situated in the middle of a necklace; the *karṇikā* is a palm-leaf ornament; the *lambana* is a pendant;
the *mañjīra* and *nūpura* are anklets on the foot; and the *kiṅkiṇī* is a small bell.
Length is *āyāma*, height is *āroha*, circumference is *pariṇāha*, and breadth is *viśālatā*.
A *paṭaccara* is a worn-out garment; a *saṃvyāna* is an upper garment (*uttarīya*).
"Racanā" (arrangement), "parispanda" (movement), "ābhoga" (expansion), "paripūrṇatā" (fullness),
"samudgaka" (a small casket), "sampuṭaka" (a box), "pratigrāha" (a vessel for receiving), and "patadgraha" (a spittoon)—
thus ends the three hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Group of Humans," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 364:
Now begins the three hundred and sixty-fourth chapter.
The Section on Brahmins:
Agni said:
"Vaṃśa, anvavāya, and gotra are synonyms for lineage; kula, abhijana, and anvaya are also used in this sense."

The teacher who provides the exposition of the mantra is the *ādeṣṭṛ*; in the sacrifice, the one observing the vow is the *vratin*, and the sacrificer is the *yajamāna*. "Commencement" (*upakrama*) refers to the undertaking after having gained knowledge;
those with a common preceptor are *satīrthyas*; and likewise, those in an assembly are *sabhyas* or *sāmājikas*.
The members of the assembly are the *sabhāsadas* and *sabhāstāras*; the sacrificial priests are the *ṛtvijas* and *yājakas*.
These are, respectively, the *adhvaryu*, *udgātṛ*, and *hotṛ*, who are experts in the Yajur, Sāman, and Ṛg Vedas.
Furthermore, the *caṣāla* is the ring at the top of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*); and *sthāṇḍila* and *catvara* both mean a level piece of ground.
*Āmikṣā* is that which results from curdling milk with the addition of yogurt while it is warm; *pṛṣadājya* is ghee mixed with yogurt; *paramānna* is rice cooked in milk (*pāyasa*).
That animal is called *upākṛta* which, having been consecrated with mantras, is slain in a sacrifice.
*Paramparāka*, *samana*, and *prokṣaṇa* are for the purpose of killing;
*pūjā*, *namasyā*, *apaciti*, *saparyā*, *arcā*, and *arhaṇā* are synonyms.
*Varivasyā*, *śuśrūṣā*, *paricaryā*, and *upāsana* are synonyms for service.
*Niyama* and *vrata*—the latter being neuter—refer to meritorious acts such as fasting and the like.
The primary method (*mukhya-kalpa*) is the first alternative, while the secondary method (*anukalpa*) is inferior to it.
In this context, "kalpa" and "vidhi-krama" are to be understood as the ritual procedure; "viveka" is the state of being distinct.
"Upākaraṇa" is the formal commencement of Vedic study preceded by the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
A mendicant (*bhikṣu*) is also called a *parivrāj*, a *karmandin*, a *pārāśarin*, and a *maskarin*.
The sages are those whose speech is truth; the *snātaka* is one who has completed his vows by ritual bathing.
Those who have conquered the collection of their senses are *yatins*, and they are also *yatayas*.
That action which is constant and dependent upon the body as its instrument is *yama*.
But that which is a rule (*niyama*) is that action which is impermanent and has adventitious means;
[the result] is becoming Brahman, the state of Brahman, or even union with Brahman (*brahmasāyujya*).
Thus ends the section titled "The Class of Brahman" in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter Three Hundred and Sixty-Four.
Now begins Chapter Three Hundred and Sixty-Five.
The classes of Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
Agni said:
The Kṣatriya is consecrated on the head (mūrdhābhiṣikta), born from the arms, the ruler (rājanya), and the sovereign (virāj).
A king to whom all vassals are prostrate is a sovereign;
a universal monarch is a ruler of the entire earth, while any other king is a lord of a single province.
A minister is a counselor of intellect, an official, or a high state functionary; these are the chief officers.

Among those who oversee legal proceedings, the *prāḍvivāka* (judge), *akṣadarśaka* (witness-observer), *bhaurika* (treasurer), and *kanakādhyakṣa* (superintendent of gold) are [distinct], whereas the *adhyakṣa* (superintendent) and the *adhikṛta* (official) are synonymous.
The person appointed over the inner apartments is called an *antarvaṃśika*;
they are also known as *sauvidalla*, *kañcukin*, *sthāpatya*, and *sauvida*.
A *ṣaṇḍha* and a *varṣavara* are synonymous; these are servants, dependents, and those who live under others.
The king whose territory is immediately adjacent is the enemy; beyond him is the friend; further beyond is the neutral; behind is the rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāha*);
the spy is the "touch" (*sparśa*); the secret agent is the "subsequent" (*uttara*); and time is the "future" (*āyati*).
The present time is *tadātva*; the future result is *udarka*.

The unseen [omens] are fire, water, and so forth; the seen [omens] are those arising from one's own or another's army, as well as the auspicious jar (*bhadra-kumbha*), the full jar (*pūrṇa-kumbha*), the water-pot (*bhṛṅgāra*), and the golden vessel (*kanakālukā*).

*Prabhinna*, *garjita*, *māta*, *vamathu*, and *karaśīkara* [denote the rutting state of an elephant]. *Śṛṇi* is feminine; *aṅkuśa* (goad) is not feminine (*astrī*). *Paristoma* and *kutha* (an elephant’s housings) are both masculine and feminine (*dvayoḥ*).
*Karṇīratha*, *pravahaṇa*, *dolā*, *preṅkhā*, and so forth [denote a swing or litter]; these are feminine (*striyām*).
Ādhoraṇa, hastipaka, hastyāroha, and niṣādin denote elephant-riders;
bhaṭa, yodha, and yoddhṛ denote warriors. Kañcuka and vāraṇa (not feminine) denote armor for the head; śīrṣaṇya and śiras-tra also denote head-armor. Tanutra, varma, and daṃśana denote body armor.
*Āmukta*, *pratimukta*, *pinaddha*, and *apinaddha* denote one who has put on armor.

*Vyūha* is the arrangement of an army; *cakra* and *anīka* (which is not feminine) denote a military force. A single elephant, a single chariot, three horses, and five foot-soldiers constitute a *patti*.
By successively tripling all the constituent parts of the infantry, the designations of the army units are as follows: *senāmukha*, *gulma*, *gaṇa*, *vāhinī*, *pṛtanā*, *camū*, *anīkinī*;
ten *anīkinīs* constitute an *akṣauhiṇī*, [calculated] by means of elephants and the other components.
The words *dhanus*, *kodaṇḍa*, and *iṣvāsa* denote a bow; its tip is known as the *koṭi*; the middle of the bow is the *nasta*; and *maurvī*, *jyā*, *śiñjinī*, and *guṇa* denote the bowstring.
*pṛṣatka*, *bāṇa*, *viśikha*, *ajihmaga*, *khaga*, and *āśuga* denote an arrow.
*Tūṇa*, *upāsaṅga*, *tūṇīra*, and *niṣaṅga* denote a quiver; *iṣudhi* denotes both [a quiver and its contents].
*Asi*, *ṛṣṭi*, *nistriṃśa*, *karavāla*, and *kṛpāṇa* denote a sword.
Like a sword (*kṛpāṇa*);
the hilt of a sword is the *sarū*, while the blade is the *īlī* or *karapālikā*.
A battle-axe is called a *kuṭhāra* or *sudhiti*; a small knife is a *churikā* or *āsiputrikā*.
A *prāsa* is to be known as a spear (*kunta*), and a *tomara* is a javelin, not feminine. *Vaitālikas* are those who awaken [the king]; *māgadhas* and *vandins* are those who offer praise.
*Saṃśaptakas*, however, are those who by agreement do not retreat from battle.

*Patākā*, *vaijayantī*, *ketana*, and *dhvaja* denote a banner; the last term is not feminine. *Ahaṃpūrvikā* is used in the feminine for the sense of "I first, I first," while *ahamahamikā* refers to that mutual display of egoism.
*Śakti* is prowess, *prāṇa* is vitality, *śaurya* is heroism, *sthāna*, *sahas*, and *bala* are synonyms for strength.
*Mūrchā*, *kaśmala*, and *moha* are synonyms for fainting. *Avamarda* is oppression, while *abhyavaskandana* and *abhyāsādana* refer to an assault. *Vijaya* and *jaya* both mean victory.
Nirvāsana, saṃjñapana, sāraṇa, pratighātana, pañcatā, kāladharma, diṣṭānta, pralaya, and atyaya are synonyms for death.
Viśas, bhūmispṛśas, and vaiśyas are synonyms for the merchant class; vṛtti, vartana, and jīvana refer to livelihood.

Livelihoods such as agriculture and the like should be known; *kusīda* is living by interest, while *uddhāra* is the lending of wealth. *Kaṇiśa* is the ear of grain, and *kiṃśāru* is the awn of the grain. A cluster of grass and the like is called a *stamba* or a *guccha*.
Grain to be threshed includes rice, *stambakari*,
and chaff; beans and the like are known as pulse-grains (*śamīdhānya*), while barley and the like are awned-grains (*śūkadhānya*).

Grass-grains are *nīvāra*; a winnowing basket is known as *śūrpa*; a winnowing fan is *prasphoṭana*; a woven basket and a sack are *syūta* and *praseva*; a large basket and a small one are *kaṇḍola* and *piṭa*; and a mat and a straw-mat are *kaṭa* and *kiniñjaka*.
Furthermore, *rasavatī*, *pākasthāna*, and *mahānasa* are synonymous terms for a kitchen.
The superintendent of the kitchen is the *paurogava*; the cooks are *sūpakāras* or *vallavas*.

The *ārālikas*, *āndhasikas*, *sūdas*, *audanikas*, and *guṇas* are all terms for cooks. The word *ambarīṣa* is neuter; *bhrāṣṭra* is masculine; and *karkari*, *ālū*, and *galantikā* denote a small water-pot.

Āliñjara and maṇika denote a large water-jar; suṣavī refers to black cumin (kṛṣṇajīraka); āranāla is fermented grain-water; kulmāṣa refers to half-cooked grains; vāhlīka, hiṅgu, and rāmaṭha denote asafoetida;
niśā and haridrā denote turmeric; pītā is a feminine term for the same; and matsyaṇḍī and phāṇita refer to types of candied sugar.
*Kūrcikā* is a preparation of milk; *snigdha*, *masṛṇa*, and *cikkaṇa* mean unctuous and smooth;
*pṛthuka* is flattened rice; *dhānā* refers to parched barley grains; *jemana*, *lepa*, and *āhāra* denote eating or food; and *māheyī* and *saurabhī* are terms for a cow.
The bearers of yokes and the like are those yoked to vehicles; a *prasāṅgya* is one that has lost its vigor.
A cow that has long since calved is called a *vaṣkayaṇī*; a cow that has recently given birth is a *dhenu*.
A cow covered by a bull is a *sandhinī*; one that destroys the embryo is a *vehad*.
A merchant who lives by trade is called *paṇyājīva* or *āpaṇika*; a deposit is *nyāsa*, while a sealed deposit is *upanidhi*.
A man who haggles is *vipaṇa*, and selling is *vikraya*. Numerals from one up to ten agree in gender with the number they count (*saṅkhyeya*).
From twenty onwards, all numerals are always singular and may agree in gender with either the number counted or the counting word itself.
The dual and plural numbers exist for the purpose of denoting number; among those [categories], everything up to ninety is feminine.

A *paṅkti* consists of ten, a *śata* of one hundred, a *sahasra* of one thousand, and so on, each increasing tenfold in sequence. As for measurement, it is by means of finger-breadths (*aṅguli*) and *prastha*s; five *guñjā*s constitute the first *māṣaka*.
Sixteen *akṣas* make one *karṣa*, which is not feminine; four *karṣas* make one *pala*.
A *suvarṇa* and a *vista* are measures of gold; a *kuruvista*, however, is a *pala* of that [gold].

A *tulā* is a hundred *palas* in weight for a female measure; twenty *tulās* constitute a *bhāra*. A *kārṣāpaṇa* is that which weighs one *karṣa*; when made of copper, it is called a *paṇa*. Wealth, property, fortune, inheritance, patrimony, riches, and treasure are synonyms for wealth (*dhana*).
*Rīti* (in the feminine) and *ārakūṭa* are names for brass; *tāmraka*, *śulva*, and *audumbara* refer to copper. *Tīkṣṇa*, *kāla-ayas*, and *ayas* denote iron.
*Kṣāra*, *kāca*, *capala*, *rasa*, *sūta*, and *pārada* are terms for mercury.

Garala is poison; māhiṣa is buffalo-horn; trapu is tin, sīsaka is lead, and piccaṭa is a type of mineral; hiṇḍīra is sea-foam, abdhi-kapha is ocean-slime, and pheṇa is froth; madhūcchiṣṭa is beeswax, while sikthaka is the same; raṅga is vermilion, vaṅga is tin, and picusthūla is cotton; kūlaṭī, however, is realgar (manaḥśilā). AP 365.042ab.
Barley-alkali should be boiled; bamboo-manna and *vaṃśalocanā* [are used].
The *vṛṣalas*, those born of the lowest castes, the *śūdras*, the *caṇḍālas*, and the *antyajas* are the offspring of mixed unions (*śaṅkaras*).
A craftsman is an artisan; a guild consists of those of the same caste joined together.
A painter is one who lives by colors; a carpenter, a turner, and a builder are synonyms. A reed-worker, a goldsmith, a barber, and a low-caste scavenger are also mentioned.

One who lives by goats is a *jāvāla*; a *devājīva* is a *devala*. One who lives by his wife is a *śailūṣa*, as is a *bhṛtaka* or one who subsists on wages. A *vivarṇa*, a *pāmara*, a *nīca*, a *prākṛta*, and a *pṛthagjana* are all terms for the low-born.
One who has failed to perform the *upasad* rites is called a *jālma*; a servant is termed a *bhṛtya*, a *dāsera*, or a *ceṭaka*.

A clever person is known as *paṭu*, *peśala*, or *dakṣa*; a hunter is remembered as a *mṛgayu* or a *lubdhaka*. A *cāṇḍāla* is called a *divākīrti*; and *pusta* refers to work such as plastering and the like.
*Pañcālikā* refers to a doll or puppet; *varkara* is a young animal;
*mañjūṣā*, *peṭaka*, and *peḍā* denote a chest or basket; and *tulya* and *sādhāraṇa* are synonyms meaning equal or common.
"A *pratimā* (image) is a representation; the classes beginning with Brahmā are traditionally known as *vargas*.
Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Classes of Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 366:
General Names and Gender Markers (Sāmānyanāmaliṅgāni)
Agni said:

Now I shall speak of common names and gender markers; listen to that. A *sukṛtin* is one who has performed meritorious deeds, while a *puṇyavān* is one who possesses merit. A *dhanya* is one who is fortunate, whereas a *maheccha* is one of great aspirations, and a *mahāśaya* is one of noble character.
*Pravīṇa*, *nipuṇa*, *abhijña*, *vijña*, *niṣṇāta*, and *śikṣita* denote one who is skilled or learned.
*Vadānya*, *sthūlalakṣa*, *dānaśauṇḍa*, and *bahuprada* denote one who is generous or munificent.
*Kṛtī*, *kṛtajña*, and *kuśala* denote one who is capable or clever; while *āsakta*, *udyukta*, and *utsuka* denote one who is attached, diligent, or eager.
A wealthy man is called *ibhya*, *āḍhya*, *parivṛḍha*, *adhibhū*, *nāyaka*, or *adhipa*;
he is also *lakṣmīvān*, *lakṣmaṇa*, *śrīla*, *svatantra*, and *svairyapāvṛta*.
A *khalapū* is one who does much work; a *dīrghasūtra* is one who is slow in action. A *jālma* is one who acts without reflection; a *kuṇṭha* is one who is dull in his duties.
One who is a hero in labor is called *karmaśūra* or *karmaṭha*; a glutton is a *bhakṣaka*, *ghasmara*, or *admara*.
*Lolupa*, *gardhala*, and *gṛdhru* denote one who is greedy; likewise, *vinīta* and *praśrita* denote one who is humble.
*Dhṛṣṭa*, *dhṛṣṇu*, and *viyāta* denote one who is bold. *Nibhṛta* denotes one endowed with presence of mind.
*Pragalbha* denotes one who is confident. *Bhīruka* and *bhīru* denote one who is timid. *Vandāru* denotes one who offers salutation.
*Bhūṣṇu*, *bhaviṣṇu*, and *bhavitā* mean "one who will be"; *jñātṛ*, *vidura*, and *binduka* mean "one who knows";
*matta*, *śauṇḍa*, *utkaṭa*, and *kṣība* mean "intoxicated"; and *caṇḍa* means "extremely wrathful."
He who moves toward the gods is *devadryañ*; he who moves toward all is *viśvadryañ* or *viśvagañ*.
He who moves together is *sadhryañ*; he who moves across is *tiryañ*.
One who is skillful in the application of speech is *vāgmī*, and one who speaks much is *vāvadūka*.
One who talks much is a *jalpaka*, *vācāla*, or *vācāṭa*; one whose speech is highly censurable is *bahugarhyavāk*.

One who is reviled is *apadhvasta* or *dhikkṛta*. When bound, one is *kīlita* or *saṃyata*. A speaker of auspicious words at a festival is called *varaṇa*, *śabdana*, *nāndīvādī*, or *nānvīkara*; these terms are synonymous.
*Vyasanārta* and *uparakta* both mean "afflicted by calamity"; *baddha*, *kīlita*, and *saṃyata* all mean "bound.
*Vihista* and *vyākula* are synonyms for "distressed. *Nṛśaṃsa*, *krūra*, and *ghātuka* denote "cruel" or "murderous.
*Pāpa*, *dhūrta*, and *vañcaka* mean "wicked," "rogue," or "deceiver. *Mūrkha*, *vaideha*, and *vāliśa* refer to a "fool."
*Kadarya* means miserly or stingy; *kṛpaṇa* and *kṣudra* mean base or mean. *Mārgaṇa*, *yācaka*, and *arthin* denote a beggar or one who seeks.
One who possesses egoism is called *ahaṃyuḥ*. *Śubhaṃyuḥ* refers to one endowed with auspiciousness.
*Kāntam*, *manoramam*, *rucyam*, and *hṛdyam* refer to what is beautiful, delightful, pleasing, and cherished; while *abhīpsitam* refers to that which is desired.

Asāra, phalgu, and śūnya mean "pithless" or "insubstantial"; mukhya, varya, vareṇya, śreyas, śreṣṭha, and puṣkala denote "foremost," "best," or "excellent. Prāgrya, agrya, agrīya, and agrima signify "preeminent" or "first. Vaḍra, uru, vipula, pīna, and pīvan denote "broad," "vast," or "stout. Sthūla and pīvara denote "large" or "corpulent."

*Stoka*, *alpa*, and *kṣullaka* mean small; *sūkṣma*, *ślakṣṇa*, *dabhra*, *kṛśa*, and *tanu* mean thin; *mātrā*, *kuṭī*, *lava*, and *kaṇā* mean a minute particle; while *bhūyiṣṭha*, *puruha*, and *puru* mean abundant.

*Akhaṇḍa* means whole or complete; *upakaṇṭha*, *antika*, and *abhitaḥ* mean near or in the vicinity; *sannidha* and *abhyāsa* mean proximity; *nediṣṭa* and *susamīpaka* mean very close; *daviṣṭha* means very far; and *vṛtta*, *nistala*, and *vartula* mean round or circular.
*Ucca*, *prāṃśu*, *unnata*, and *udagra* mean high; *dhruva*, *nitya*, and *sanātana* mean eternal.
*Āviddha*, *kuṭila*, *bhugna*, *vellita*, and *vakra* also mean crooked. (Note:
This reading is defective due to the fault of tautology.)
Fickle and tremulous, as well as harsh, flat-bellied, and firm; fresh, brand-new, novel, recent, newly made, and young.
Single-minded and focused on nothing else, it was fierce and without delay;
varied and manifold in its many forms, as well as crowded and thick with obstacles;
sluggish, motionless, and drenched, characterized by persistent application and firm resolve.
*Sphāti* means increase; *prathā* means renown; *samāhāra* and *samuccaya* mean collection;
*apahāra* means decrease; *vihāra* means wandering;
*pratyāhāra* means taking back; and *nirhāra* means extraction.
Vighna, antarāya, and pratyūha are synonyms for an obstacle; āsyā, āsana, and sthiti denote remaining or staying;
sannidhi and sannikarṣa denote proximity; saṃkrama denotes a difficult passage; upalambha and anubhava denote experience; and pratyādeśa and nirākṛti denote rejection.
*Parirambhaḥ*, *pariṣvaṅgaḥ*, *saṃśleṣaḥ*, and *upagūhanam* denote an embrace.

*Anumā* (inference) [is characterized] by the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and so forth. *Bhrama* and *raviplava* refer to a swarm of bees. Knowledge of an object not in contact [with the senses] arising from a word is indeed called *śābda* (verbal cognition).
From the perception of similarity, there arises a cognition regarding what is similar; this is the result of comparison (*upamāna*).

When one sees an effect and [infers] its cause even in the absence [of direct observation], that is presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). The cognition of another's mind is inference for others (*parārthānumāna*).
When the counter-correlate is not perceived on the ground, the cognition "it does not exist" is non-apprehension (*abhāva*).
Thus, Hari has been described by means of names and gender signs for the sake of human understanding.
Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "General Names and Gender Signs," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Three Hundred and Sixty-Seven.
Then begins the three hundred and sixty-seventh chapter.
Regarding the constant, occasional, and elemental dissolutions, Agni said:
"Dissolution is indeed fourfold; that which is the dissolution of living beings is the constant one."
The constant destruction of all things that have been born is the occasional dissolution of Brahmā (*brāhma-naimittika-laya*).

At the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas, there is the elemental dissolution (*prākṛta-laya*). Through knowledge, the ultimate dissolution (*atyantika-laya*) occurs when the self merges into the Supreme Self.
I shall describe to you the form of the dissolution at the end of the aeon for the sake of one who perceives signs:
when a thousand cycles of four yugas have passed and the surface of the earth is nearly exhausted,
an exceedingly fierce drought occurs that lasts for a hundred years.
From that, the destruction of beings occurs; then Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World,
stationed within the seven rays of the sun, drinks up the waters and brings the water of the earth,
the netherworld, the oceans, and so forth, to its end.
Then, through its power, those very seven rays, augmented by the intake of water, arise as seven suns.
O twice-born one, they burn the entire triple-world together with the depths of the nether regions.
The earth becomes like the back of a tortoise; then, from the impact of the breath of the serpent Śeṣa, Kālāgnirudra burns the netherworlds below.
From the netherworlds Viṣṇu burns the earth, and from the earth he burns the heaven.
The entire three worlds then shone like a frying pan;
consequently, the inhabitants of both worlds were overcome by that heat.
They go to Maharloka, and from Maharloka they go to Jana; then,
having burnt the world in the form of Rudra, from the breath of Hari's mouth there arise clouds of various forms accompanied by lightning.
Raining for a hundred years, they extinguish the risen fire;
yet when the water stands having reached the abode of the Seven Sages, O Maruts,
the breath from the mouth of Viṣṇu brings those clouds to destruction.
Having drunk the wind, the Lord Hari reclines upon Śeṣa in the single ocean;
assuming the form of Brahmā, he is praised by the Siddhas and water-dwelling sages,
established in his divine yogic sleep consisting of his own *māyā*.

Contemplating himself as the one called Vasudeva, Madhusūdana sleeps for a kalpa; then, having awakened, he creates in the form of Brahmā. Thereafter, O twice-born one, the manifest world dissolves into primordial nature (prakṛti) at the end of two parārdhas.
When each place is multiplied by ten from one position to the next, the eighteenth place is designated as *parārdha*.
When that *parārdha* is doubled, it is known as the primary dissolution (*prākṛta-pralaya*).
O twice-born one, when the blazing fire has been produced by contact with the fire of drought,
and when the dissolution has arrived— brought about by the will of Kṛṣṇa— there occurs the destruction of the entire transformation beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas.
Water indeed first devours the quality of fragrance and the rest belonging to earth;
then, through its own quality of fragrance, earth becomes fit for dissolution. And water remains as that which consists of taste, for taste is the quality of those waters.
When those [waters] have perished, fire shines by means of light;
furthermore, wind devours the quality of light, which is form, as well as the sun.
When light has perished, the great wind blows with force;
then space swallows the quality of wind, which is touch.
When the wind has perished, O twice-born one, space remains devoid of sound.
Then the source of the elements (bhūtādi) swallows the sound of space and space itself;
the Great One (mahat) swallows space, which consists of ego-consciousness (abhimāna), and the source of the elements;
the earth goes to dissolution in water, and water proceeds into light (jyotis).

O twice-born one, wind dissolves into air, and air into space; that [space] dissolves into the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), and the ego-principle into the Great Principle (mahattattva). Nature (prakṛti) devours the Great Principle;
and Nature, which is both manifest and unmanifest, is the dissolution of the manifest into the unmanifest.
The Person is the single, pure syllable; he too is a portion of the Supreme Self.
Both Prakṛti and Puruṣa dissolve into the Supreme Self, wherein the Lord of All there are no conceptual constructions of name, genus, and so forth.
When the object of knowledge consists of mere existence, and the supreme Self is of the nature of consciousness, [then one attains the Self].
Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Eternal, Occasional, and Elemental Dissolutions," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 368:
Description of the Ultimate Arising from the Womb of *Laya* (Dissolution)
Agni said:
I shall speak of absolute dissolution; through knowledge, there is absolute dissolution.
Having understood the afflictions of the internal self and so forth, one attains it through detachment from one's own [self].
Internal suffering is twofold: physical and mental.
O twice-born one, hear now of that physical suffering, which consists of many varieties.
Having abandoned the body of enjoyment, the living being attains a womb through its karmas;
indeed, O twice-born one, there arises a body known as the *ātivāhika*.
This belongs exclusively to humans when the time of death has arrived.
O best of the twice-born, O sage, that body of living beings among humans is led along the path of Yama by the messengers of Yama;
thereafter, it goes to heaven or to hell, wandering like a water-wheel.
O Brahmin, this is known as the land of action, while that is remembered as the land of fruition.
Yama examines the wombs and the hells according to one's karma;
by that very same [karma], those who behold Yama are to be filled [with their retribution].
Indeed, living beings become like the wind and enter the womb;
however, a human being is led there by the messengers of Yama and sees it.
By that [vision], the righteous one is honored, while the most wicked one is beaten at home.
Citragupta shall examine his good and evil deeds;
while the body remains in a state of impurity, he dwells indeed in the *ativāhika* (transitional) body.
O knower of dharma, he then leads [the deceased] by means of the food consisting of the offered funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).
Having abandoned that preta-body and obtained another from the world of pretas,
that man shall dwell there joined by hunger and thirst, subsisting on the food of an *āmāśrāddha* offering, for he lacks the *pretapiṇḍa* offerings intended for the *ātivāhika* body.

For a man does not attain liberation; rather, he continues to consume funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) in that very world of the departed (*pretaloka*) even after one year has passed since the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite was performed.
Having completely cast off the body of a preta, one attains a body for enjoyment;
both types of bodies for enjoyment are said to be designated as "inauspicious" and "auspicious."
Having enjoyed [the fruits] with that body of experience, one is cast down from the bondage of karma;
thereafter, night-stalkers devour that body.
O twice-born one, if one remains in sin, then heaven has been enjoyed by him.
Then he takes a second body for the enjoyment of sinners;
having exhausted that sin, he who previously enjoyed the celestial realm is born after falling from heaven in the house of the pure and the prosperous.
If merit remains while sin is being experienced, then that [merit] will come into effect;
once that body has been consumed, one assumes an auspicious form.
But when only a small residue of karma remains, one is liberated even from hell.

Once released from hell, he goes to the womb of an animal; of this there is no doubt. Having entered the womb, the living being remains as a *kalala* (a jelly-like mass); in the second month it becomes a *ghana* (a solid mass), and in the third, the limbs [develop] from that.
In the fourth [week], the bones; in the fifth, skin and flesh;

in the sixth, the emergence of hair; and then in the seventh, while still enveloped by the fetal membrane, the living being experiences suffering in the body and joins its palms in reverence at the crown of its head.
The neuter remains in the middle, the female on the left, and the male is situated on the right;
he stands in the region of the belly facing the back,
and he knows without doubt whichever womb he occupies.
And he knows every account beginning from the birth of man; he goes—
so it is said.
In darkness and great suffering, the human being experiences what has been drunk in by his mother's food during the seventh month;
likewise, in the eighth and ninth months, he is intensely agitated.
During sexual intercourse, one experiences suffering; likewise during the mother's exertion.
If she is diseased, there will be disease [for the child]; for a moment, it is as if a hundred years have passed.
Then, tormented by its own karmas, it forms desires.
O Brahmin, having emerged from the womb, he will attain the knowledge of liberation. Overwhelmed by the winds of birth, he emerges from the mechanism of the birth canal;
being oppressed for about a month, he suffers from the touch of hands.
From the syllable *kha* [arise]: the minor channels in the body, the sense of hearing, distinctness, inhalation and exhalation, the movement of the wind, as well as the touching of the mouth;
likewise, the form of fire, vision, heat, the row [of teeth], and the bile.
From water in the body arise intelligence, complexion, strength, luster, brilliance, valor, sweat, and the sense of taste; likewise,
moisture, fat, plasma, buttermilk-like fluids, semen, urine, phlegm, and so forth are produced.
From the earth come the sense of smell, hair, nails, heaviness, and firmness;
from the mother are born the soft parts— skin, flesh, and heart—
as well as excrement, fat, moisture, and the stomach.
The veins, the sinews, and the semen are born from the father; however,
desire, anger, fear, joy, as well as the nature of righteousness and unrighteousness, physical form, voice, complexion, and the organs of excretion and so forth, are born of the self.
1. Inhalation and exhalation, together with their cessation, constitute external contact.
(Ña... 2. The navel and the penis...
(Kha... and Ña...: p. 304)
Likewise, the qualities of tamas are ignorance, negligence, laziness, thirst, hunger,
delusion, envy, deficiency, grief, exhaustion, fear,
lust, anger, valor, the desire for sacrifice, and loquacity.
Egoism, contempt for others, and passion— these, O great sage, are the qualities of *rajas*.
The desire for righteousness, the longing for liberation, supreme devotion to Keśava, courtesy, and perseverance— one should designate these as the qualities of *sattva*.
Fickle, irascible, timid, talkative, and fond of strife—
a man under the influence of much wind becomes one who travels through the sky even in his dreams.
One with premature gray hair, wrathful, highly intelligent, and fond of battle— [is characterized by fire].
A man with an abundance of bile will see radiant things in his dreams;
one with an abundance of phlegm will have steady friends, steady energy, firm limbs, and be endowed with wealth,
seeing water and white objects in his dreams.

Taste, moreover, is the life-force within the bodies of living beings, as is blood; it serves as an ointment for the flesh and provides moisture to the fat. It sustains the bones, while marrow fills them and increases virility.
For *ojas* produces semen and virility; it sustains the vital breath and maintains the stability of life.
*Ojas* is more essential than semen; when absorbed, it reaches the heart. It is said to reside in six locations: the two thighs, the two arms, the head, and the abdomen.
Just as there are six layers on the outside— the one that holds blood,
another that maintains grace, the fourth that holds the hollows,
the fifth which is the site of abscesses, and the sixth considered to be the sustainer of life— so too [is the body].
The seventh [vein] is the carrier of flesh, the second is the bearer of blood;
another has its seat in the liver and spleen, while yet another is the bearer of fat and bone.

The sixth [dhātu] is the bearer of marrow, phlegm, and feces, located in the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya); the seventh is the bearer of bile; and another is the bearer of semen, located in the receptacle of semen. Thus ends the description of the production of the embryo as the ultimate dissolution in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Three Hundred and Sixty-Eight:
[The Name] And now, Chapter Three Hundred and Sixty-Seven.
The limbs of the body;
Agni said:
"The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, the nose, the intellect, and the vital breath."
The elements are earth, water, fire, air, and ether;
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their qualities, residing respectively in ether and the others.
Furthermore, the anus, genitals, hands, feet, and speech constitute the instruments of action.
That [activity] consists of the actions of excretion, pleasure, procreation, grasping, movement, speech,
and so forth; here there are the five organs of action and the five organs of cognition,
as well as the five objects of the senses, the great elements, and the mind as their presiding lord.
The Self, the Unmanifest, and the twenty-four principles constitute the Supreme Person;
they are both conjoined and disjoined, like a fish and water.
Here, the qualities of passion (rajas), goodness (sattva), and darkness (tamas) are dependent upon the Unmanifest.
The inner person is the individual soul (jīva); he is the Supreme Brahman, the cause.
He who knows the supreme person attains the highest abode.
Seven receptacles are recorded in the body; one is the receptacle for blood.
The receptacle for phlegm is the fifth, while the receptacle for undigested matter and bile is the sixth;
the receptacle for wind and urine is the seventh, and for women, the receptacle for the fetus is the eighth.
From bile (pitta) comes the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya), and from fire (agni) comes the womb (yoni), which is expanded in its radiance.
The uterus (garbhāśaya) is like a lotus; therein it holds the semen mixed with blood. From one's own semen, the limbs arise, and over time, the hair (kuntala) grows there.
Therefore, O Sage, the semen that has been deposited in the womb does not enter the uterus (*garbhāśaya*).
Even during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), if the womb is obstructed by wind, bile, or phlegm,
then its expansion will never occur within it.

O highly fortunate one, *bukka*, *pukkasa*, *kaplīha*, *kṛtakoṣṭha*, *aṅgavraṇa*, and *taṇḍaka* are considered to be bound within the receptacle (*āśaya*). For embodied beings, [these arise] from the essence (*sāra*) of the nutrient fluid (*rasa*) as it is being digested.
O Knower of Dharma, from the froth of blood arise the spleen and the liver;
likewise, from blood and bile arises that which is known as the *taṇḍaka*.
And it is taught that the *vukka* originates from the spreading of fat and blood.
And from the expansion of blood and flesh, the intestines of embodied beings arise;
one should specify that those of men measure three and a half *vyāmas*,
while people learned in the Vedas declare those of women to be three *vyāmas* long.
The arising of the *kāmeśya* [wind] is said to result from its conjunction with the blood-wind (*raktavāyu*).
Through the spreading of phlegm (*kapha*), the heart becomes like a lotus;
it is downward-facing and hollow, wherein the living soul (*jīva*) is situated.
All states of being are pervaded by consciousness and are established therein;
likewise, the spleen is on its left side, and the liver on its right.
Furthermore, the *kloma* is on the right; thus has the lotus been described.
And those channels in this body that carry phlegm and blood—
their existence as sense organs arises from the inference of their constituent elements.
The white circle of the eyes arises from phlegm (kapha) and is paternal;
the black circle arises from wind (vāta) and is likewise maternal;
the skin-circle is known to originate from both the mother and the father, being produced from bile (pitta).
The tongue is born from flesh, blood, and phlegm; the testicles are born from fat, blood, phlegm, and flesh. These ten should be known as the seats of the vital breath (prāṇa):
the head, the heart, the navel, the throat, the tongue, semen, and blood.
The anus, the bladder, and the ankles—these sixteen are said to be the knotty joints (*kaṇḍurā*).
There are two in the hands, two in the feet, four on the back, and four in the neck;
thus, there are sixteen networks (*jālāni*) throughout the body from the feet to the head.
Flesh, sinews, veins, and bones— these four are each bound separately to one another at the wrists and the ankles;
six "tufts" (kūrca) are recorded here as being present, three in the hands and three in the feet respectively.
The wise have stated that there are likewise four muscular cords attached to the spinal column at the neck and the penis,
as well as ninety muscles that serve as their binders.
There are likewise seven neck vertebrae, five of which are situated at the head;
there is one each for the penis and the tongue, and three hundred and sixty bones.
Including the minute ones, there are sixty-four teeth and twenty nails.
There are also the longitudinal bones of the hands and feet; their four locations consist of sixty finger-bones, two in the heels, four in the ankles,
and likewise four bones each in the forearms and the shanks.
One should likewise indicate that the portions arising from the knees, cheeks, and the surface of the thighs [each] consist of two [units],
as do the positions of the eyes, the parts of the hips, and the surface of the buttocks.
There are thirty-six bones in the pelvis, forty-five in the back,
and likewise bones in the neck; there are two collarbones,
and the roots of those [shoulder blades] are situated in the forehead, eyes, cheeks, nose, and chin.
The ribs, together with the palates and the arbudas, number seventy-two;
there are two temporal bones (śaṅkhaka) and likewise four cranial plates (kapāla) in the head.
The chest consists of seventeen bones, and there are two hundred and ten joints.
There are sixty-eight branches, sixty minus one,
and indeed eighty-three intermediate ones;
there are nine hundred and two hundred and thirty ligaments, and seventy in the internal channels.
There are exactly six hundred ascending [channels], while the branches are said to be forty ascending; furthermore,
there are four hundred in the branches, and sixty in the two intermediate channels.
In women, there are twenty-four veins in total;
ten are in the breasts, thirteen in the womb,
and four are for the fetus and the channels of embodied beings.
Thirty-nine million and fifty-six thousand [channels] flow within the body,
like irrigation ditches in a field, carrying moisture, mucus, and other secretions.
Likewise, O great sage, there are seventy-two crores of cavities here in this body, O twice-born one: of marrow, of fat, of grease,
as well as of urine, bile, phlegm, and excrement.
"There are five hundred layers of flesh here" (as found in the manuscripts marked kha and ña,
In this regard, the handfuls (añjali) of blood and plasma are considered to increase progressively;
each subsequent one is deemed to be half again as much as the preceding handful.
The amount of semen is half a handful, and that of *ojas* is half of that.
Likewise, four [periods] for women arising from *rajas* have been declared by the wise.
Having understood the body—consisting of impurities, defects, and the like—to be a mere mass, one should renounce it within the Self.
Thus ends the [chapter] titled "The Limbs of the Body" in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter Three Hundred and Seventy:
Chapter 370.
Chapter Three Hundred and Seventy-One.
Regarding the description of the hells, Agni said:
"The paths of Yama have been described; I shall now speak of the death of men."
The heat (*ūṣman*), provoked within the body and impelled by a violent wind,
obstructs the body and indeed blocks all the humors (*doṣa*);
it further severs the seats of the vital breaths as well as the vital points (*marman*).
Then, provoked by cold, the wind seeks out an opening:
the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils,
and likewise the seven openings above, with the mouth as the eighth.
By these [openings], the vital breath generally departs for those of meritorious deeds;
for those who have performed unwholesome deeds, it departs through the anus and the generative organ.
Having formed a lump [of consciousness], one should then deposit it.

When the time of death has arrived and the vital breath (prāṇa) has reached the downward breath (apāna), the individual soul (jīva) then departs at will after piercing through the crown of the head of the yogin.
When knowledge is enveloped by darkness and the vital points (marmans) are obstructed,
that life-force (jīva), no longer having a basis in the navel, is moved by the wind;
and being thus afflicted, it withdraws the eightfold functions of the vital breaths (prāṇavṛttis).
The Siddhas and the gods perceive with their divine eye him as he is passing away, being born, or entering into wombs;
at that very moment, through yoga, he assumes a subtle, transportive body (*ativāhika-śarīra*).
Space, wind, and fire ascend above the body;
water and earth are said to return to their fivefold state when a person has attained dissolution.
However, the messengers of Yama lead away that subtle, transportive body (*ātivāhika-deha*).
Being led along the most terrible southern path extending eighty-six thousand [yojanas],
he partakes of the food and water provided by his kinsmen;
having seen Yama, he experiences the consequences as recounted by Citragupta at Yama’s command.
The righteous person attains heaven by means of the auspicious paths, while the sinner falls into the terrible hells;
I shall describe those hells and their torments, which are experienced by the wicked.
There are twenty-eight crores of hells situated below the earth.
At the end of the seventh level, situated in terrible darkness, is the first peak called Ghora; below that is Sughorā;
then Atighorā, Mahāghorā, and the fifth is Ghorarūpā.
The sixth is named Taralatārā, and the seventh is Bhayānakā;
then Bhayotkaṭā, Kālarātrī, Mahācaṇḍā, Caṇḍayā, Kolāhalā, the one called Pracaṇḍā, Padmā, and Narakanāyikā.
Padmāvatī, Bhīṣaṇā, Bhīmā, Karālikā,
Vikarālā, Mahāvajrā, Trikoṇā, and Pañcakoṇikā.
It is long, circular, seven-storied, and possesses excellent floors;
it is ablaze with twenty-eight crores of illusory manifestations that inflict suffering upon the wicked.
Within those twenty-eight crores, there are five leaders for each.
One hundred and forty-four hells beginning with Raurava,
namely Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava, the Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana), and likewise Lohabhāra.
The Kālasūtra hell, and likewise the Mahānaraka; the Sañjīvana, the Mahāvīci, the Tapana, the Sampratāpana;
the Saṅghāta, along with the Kākola, the Kudmala, and the Pūtimṛttika.
Know that there are iron spikes, parched husks, the principal Śālmalī river, and millions of hells of terrifying appearance;
those who have committed evil deeds are cast into each one of them, as well as into many others.
They have faces like those of cats, owls, jackals, vultures, and the like;
having thrown men into vats of oil, they ignite the fire,
and others they cast into frying pans and still others into copper vessels.
Others are cast into iron vessels and into those with many sparks of fire;
others are impaled on the points of pikes, while still others are cut up in hell. They are beaten with whips and made to eat balls of iron.
The messengers of Yama force men to drink dust, excrement, blood, phlegm, and the like,
as well as boiling liquor; they tear men apart again,
crush them in machines, and have them devoured by crows and other scavengers.
They are drenched with hot oil and their heads are cut in many ways;
crying out, "Alas, father!", they gnaw upon their own ears— such is your karma.
Having reached the terrible and censured hells born of great sins,
those who have committed great sins are reborn here upon the exhaustion of their karma;
a killer of a Brahmin enters the wombs of deer, dogs, pigs, and camels.

A drinker of intoxicants becomes a Kharapukkaśa Mleccha; a stealer of gold becomes a worm, insect, or moth; one who violates his Guru’s bed becomes a grass or shrub; a killer of a Brahmin suffers from consumption; and a drinker of intoxicants has black teeth.
A stealer of gold has deformed nails; one who violates the teacher’s bed has a skin disease;
whoever comes into contact with any of these is born with the corresponding mark.
A stealer of food becomes deceitful, and a stealer of speech becomes mute.
