By stealing grain one becomes extra-limbed; by slandering others, one has a foul-smelling nose; by stealing oil, one becomes an oil-drinker; and by being a backbiter, one has a foul-smelling mouth. Having abducted another's wife and having stolen the property of a Brahmin, [one suffers these consequences].
In a desolate forest region, he is born as a *brahmarākṣasa*.

One who steals jewels is born of a low caste; one who steals auspicious perfumes becomes a muskrat; having stolen leaves or vegetables, one becomes a peacock; and a stealer of grain becomes a noisy crow.
A goat [indicates] livestock; a crow, milk; a camel, a vehicle; a monkey, fruit;
a gadfly, honey; a vulture, fruit; and a house-crow, household utensils.
Śivatrī, Vastra, Sārasa, Jhallī, and Lavaṇahāraka—these are mentioned.

Internal suffering (ādhyātmika-tāpa) has been described; that caused by weapons and the like is external (ādhibhautika); and that caused by the afflictions of planets, fire, and deities is said to be supernatural (ādhidevika).
One should destroy the threefold suffering of cyclic existence through the yoga of knowledge. AP 370.039cd.
"By means of arduous penances, vows, gifts, and the like, as well as the worship of Viṣṇu and other rites, a man [attains liberation].
Thus ends the three hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of Hells," in the Agni Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 371:
Restraints and Observances (Yama-niyama)
Agni said:
For the sake of liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra, I shall declare the knowledge of the eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅgayoga), which reveals Brahman.
Yoga is one-pointedness of mind therein;

it is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, and the supreme identity of the individual soul (jīva) with Brahman. Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness [are its limbs].
The five restraints (yamas) are traditionally held to bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation through their observance:
purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and worship of the Lord. Indeed, non-injury—defined as causing no pain to living beings—is the supreme dharma.
Just as all other footprints of those who walk upon a path are encompassed within the footprint of an elephant,
so too is everything for the sake of Dharma declared to be contained within non-violence.
For causing agitation, violence, and likewise producing torment;
causing the breaking of limbs, the shedding of blood, and likewise the practice of backbiting;
and the manifestation of the Brahman—this is knowledge.
2. Just as [the tracks] of others [are not seen] in the footprint of an elephant...
3. "...of those who go on foot," according to Kha and Ja;
The excessive prohibition of what is beneficial, the exposure of vital points (marmans),
the denial of happiness, and confinement— these constitute its tenfold bondage.
Speech that is ultimately beneficial to living beings is the defining characteristic of truth.
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak an unpleasant truth, nor should one speak a pleasant falsehood—this is the eternal dharma.
The renunciation of sexual intercourse is celibacy (brahmacarya), and it is eightfold.
Recollection, narration, play, gazing, secret conversation,
intention, determination, and the actual performance of the act—
these the wise declare to be the eightfold sexual union.
Celibacy is the root of spiritual practice; otherwise, practice is fruitless.
Vasiṣṭha, Candra, Śukra, the preceptor of the gods, and Pitāmaha—even they, though advanced in austerity and advanced in age, were deluded by women.
Surā is to be known as threefold: that made from molasses (gauḍī), that made from flour (paiṣṭī), and that made from honey (mādhvī);
the woman herself is to be known as the fourth surā, by whom this world is deluded.
One becomes intoxicated upon seeing a beautiful woman, but one becomes intoxicated only after drinking [the other] surā.
Because a woman intoxicated by lust is thus seen, one should not gaze upon her;
likewise, a man who forcibly seizes any kind of another's property or consumes an oblation that has not been offered into the fire will inevitably go to the state of an animal.
One may accept a garment to cover the private parts, a patched cloak to ward off the cold, and even sandals; one should not make a collection of anything else.
One’s possession of clothing and such items should be solely for the purpose of maintaining the body.
The body, which is joined with dharma, must be protected with great effort;
likewise, purity is said to be twofold: external and internal.
External purity is said to consist of water and earth, while internal purity consists of the purification of one's disposition;
he who is pure by both means is truly pure, and no other is pure.
Contentment is said to be satisfaction with whatever is obtained by any means whatsoever.

The one-pointed concentration of the mind and the senses is called austerity (*tapas*). Mastery over them is said to be superior to all other dharmas; that is the supreme dharma. Vocal austerity consists of the recitation of mantras and the like, while mental austerity is the abandonment of passion.
The bodily austerity consists of the worship of the gods and so forth; all austerity is threefold.
From it [arise] the Vedas beginning with the *praṇava*, and they are established within the *praṇava*.
The *praṇava* is composed of speech; therefore, one should practice the *praṇava*.
The letter *a*, the letter *u*, and the letter *m* with its half-measure (*ardhamātrā*)—
these three measures are the three Vedas, the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, the qualities (*guṇas*),
the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, and Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Pradyumna, Śrī, Vāsudeva, and all that is the syllable Oṃ, which is Kāraka in sequence;
it is without measure, with its measures destroyed, the departure from duality, and auspicious.
He by whom this Oṃ is known is a sage, and no other is a sage.
The fourth measure, Gāndhārī, when applied, is perceived at the crown of the head; that is the fourth, the supreme Brahman, like a lamp of light within a jar.
Thus, a person should constantly meditate upon that which resides in the lotus of the heart and recite its mantra.
The *praṇava* is the bow, the self is the arrow, and Brahman is said to be its target; one should pierce it with undistracted mind, and like the arrow, become absorbed in that.
This single syllable is Brahman; this single syllable is the supreme.
Having known this single syllable, whatever one desires, that belongs to him;
its meter is the goddess Gāyatrī, and Antaryāmin is remembered as its seer (ṛṣi).
The deity of this [mantra] is the Supreme Self; its application is for the sake of enjoyment and liberation.
"Bhūḥ" to the Ātman of Fire is the heart; "Bhuvaḥ" to the Ātman of Prajāpati is the head;
and "Svaḥ" to the Ātman of the Sun is said to be the crest-lock and the armor.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the armor (*kavaca*) with *oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ* for the self of truth, and then the weapon (*astra*), one should worship Viṣṇu and recite [his mantra] for the sake of enjoyment and liberation.
One should also offer oblations of sesame, clarified butter, and so forth; thus everything is accomplished for the person.

But for one who performs the recitation twelve thousand times every day, the Supreme Brahman manifests after twelve months. Through ten million recitations, powers such as *aṇimā* are attained; through one hundred thousand, eloquence (*sārasvata*) and other qualities are gained.
The sacrifice of Viṣṇu is of three kinds: Vedic, Tantric, and Mixed.
One should worship Hari according to whichever one of these three methods is desired.
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, one who worships with a salutation—
The goal that one attains cannot be reached even by hundreds of sacrifices;
for him who has supreme devotion to the Divine, and as to the Divine so to the Guru— for that high-souled one, these truths thus explained become manifest.
Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "Restraints and Observances," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Chapter 372:
Posture, Breath Control, and Withdrawal of the Senses (Āsana, Prāṇāyāma, and Pratyāhāra)
Agni said:
Having assumed that posture prescribed for the lotus-seat and others,
one should meditate upon the Supreme after establishing one's own firm seat in a pure place.
Neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, an antelope skin, and kuśa grass—
having made the mind one-pointed there, and having restrained the activities of the mind and senses,
one should sit upon that seat and apply oneself to yoga for the sake of self-purification.
Holding his body, head, and neck straight, remaining motionless and steady,
he should gaze at the tip of his nose without looking in any direction,
while protecting his testicles with his heels and likewise his generative organ.
Having placed the arms across the thighs with effort,
one should place the back of the right hand upon the sole of the foot;
then, slowly raising the face and supporting it in front, one should fix the gaze.

Prāṇa is the wind born from one's own body; its *āyāma* is its restraint. By pressing the nostril with a finger and likewise with the other [hand], one should carefully exhale the air; because of this exhalation, it is known as *recaka*.

Just as one might fill a leather bag with external air, so too should one remain full; because of this filling, it is known as *pūraka* (inhalation). One neither consumes nor grasps the air situated internally or externally.
That *kumbhaka* in which one remains motionless like a full jar is the *kanyaka*;
it consists of a single upward expulsion (*udghāta*) and lasts for twelve *mātrās*.
The medium [breathing] has two exhalations and consists of twenty-four measures;
the superior has three exhalations and consists of thirty-six tāla-measures; and the most superior produces sweat, trembling, and convulsions.
If one does not conquer [the breath], one should not ascend the ground; likewise, hiccups, labored breathing, and other ailments arise.
When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is conquered, indeed, there arises little excrement, vigor, urine, and so forth, as well as health, swift movement, enthusiasm, and excellence of voice.

The fruit [of this practice] is strength, complexion, clarity, and the destruction of all defects. Recitation and meditation without the "womb" (agarbha) constitute the wombless; that which is endowed with them is the womb (sagarbha). For the sake of conquering the senses, one should maintain that supreme womb.
By means of knowledge and dispassion, and through the power of breath control (prāṇāyāma), having completely conquered the senses, everything indeed becomes conquered.
For both heaven and hell are nothing other than the senses themselves.
When restrained or unleashed, these lead respectively to heaven or to hell.
They say that the body is a chariot; the senses are its horses;
the mind is declared to be the charioteer; and breath-control is the whip.
It is taught that the mind,
when restrained by the two rays of knowledge and dispassion and unified through breath control (prāṇāyāma), gradually attains a state of immobility.
He who drinks a drop [of water] from the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month for more than a hundred years—prāṇāyāma is equal to that.
Having entered the ocean of sense-objects, the senses become attached; [therefore, one should restrain them].
1. *Kanyasa* is ña... 2. *Prāṇāyāma* is the hook (*aṅkuśa*), according to the Jha school;
That which draws back and restrains [the senses] is called withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). One should uplift oneself by means of the self, as one would rescue a person sinking in water;
one should take refuge in the tree of knowledge (*jñānavṛkṣa*).
Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Posture, Breath Control, and Withdrawal of the Senses," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Then, in the three hundred and seventy-third chapter,
Agni spoke on meditation (*dhyāna*).

The verbal root *dhyai* is traditionally understood in the sense of "thinking"; meditation (*dhyāna*) is defined as the repeated contemplation of Viṣṇu with an undistracted mind by one who possesses a mind,
yet for whom all residual impressions have been liberated.
The power that is equal to the contemplation of Brahman is called meditation (*dhyāna*).
For one who is established in the object of meditation and possesses a homogeneous cognition,
a cognition free from any other intervening thought is called meditation.
For one whose mind is established upon the object of meditation, in whatever place it may be, this is declared to be *dhyāna*: the single-pointed cultivation of the mental support (*pratyaya*).
Thus, he who, endowed with such *dhyāna*, should abandon his own body—
Having uplifted his family, kinsmen, and friends, he becomes Hari.
Even he who meditates upon Hari with faith for but a moment or half a moment attains that destination which cannot be reached by all the great sacrifices.
1. Regarding the phrase "by means of entering the river of enjoyments" (bhoganadyabhiveśena):
the meditator, the meditation, as well as the object of meditation and whatever is the purpose of meditation— [all these are the river of enjoyments].
Having understood these four, the knower of reality should practice yoga.
Through the practice of yoga, liberation and the eightfold great sovereign powers arise;
one who is endowed with knowledge and dispassion, possessed of faith, and filled with forbearance [attains this].
A devotee of Viṣṇu who is ever-energetic meditates thus; such a person is known as a true Puruṣa.
For the meditation upon Hari is the contemplation of the Supreme Brahman, both with form and without form.
Hari, the omniscient and supreme, is to be known as both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala).
The mastery of qualities such as *aṇimā* and liberation are the purposes of meditation;
therefore, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, who connects [the practitioner] with the fruit—
whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, or even opening and closing the eyes.
Whether pure or impure, one should meditate upon the Lord of the Hundred;
having established Keśava within the mind at the end of the abode of one's own body,
one should worship Him through the yoga of meditation in the center of the pedestal of the heart-lotus.
The sacrifice of meditation is supreme, pure, and free from all defects; by performing it, one attains liberation, for this is not achieved through external sacrifices purified by ritual.
Because it is free from the defect of violence, its purity is the means for accomplishing the mind.
The sacrifice of meditation is superior to that, for it bestows the fruit of liberation.
Therefore, having abandoned external means which are impure and impermanent—
having abandoned ritual acts such as sacrifice— one should practice yoga with great intensity.

One should first contemplate the unmanifest (avyakta), which is free from modification and endowed with the objects of enjoyment and the act of enjoying; then, at the beginning, one should contemplate the three qualities (guṇatraya) in their proper order:
having concealed tamas by means of rajas, one should then conceal rajas by means of sattva.
Regarding "by way of the path of meditation" (dhyānamārgeṇa):
one should first meditate upon the three mandalas in sequence as black, red, and white.
The twenty-fifth principle, the Puruṣa, transcends the qualities conditioned by sentient beings;
having abandoned this impure object of meditation, one should contemplate the pure.
Above the Puruṣa is situated a divine lotus of sovereignty.
The stalk, twelve finger-breadths in width, pure, expanded, and white,
is eight finger-breadths long; from its navel-center emerges a lotus with eight petals, which should be known as the eight qualities beginning with *aṇimā*.
One should contemplate the lotus as having the pericarp and filaments of supreme knowledge and detachment, and its stalk as the dharma of Viṣṇu; that supreme lotus consists of dharma,
knowledge, detachment, and the sovereignty of Śiva.
Having understood the entire lotus posture, one shall attain the end of all suffering.
Within the center of that lotus’s pericarp, one should meditate upon the Lord as the syllable Oṃ— spotless, the size of a thumb, and having the form of the flame of a pure lamp.

One should meditate on the Lord (Īśvara), who is the primordial principle (pradhāna) transcending the person (puruṣa), seated upon a lotus, appearing like a star in the shape of a *kadamba* bud, or shining on all sides with a network of rays.

One should constantly meditate upon and recite the syllable Oṃ, the supreme imperishable; desiring the steadiness of the mind, they seek gross meditation as a preliminary step. Once that [mind] has become such—that is, become motionless—it attains stability even in the subtle.
The stalk situated at the navel-base is ten finger-breadths in length;
by means of that stalk, there is an eight-petaled lotus twelve finger-breadths in width.
1. Keśava, who is always united with the limiting adjunct of the sentient being (*sattvopādhi*), is to be meditated upon—thus [it is said] in the Kha manuscript.
2. "Having assumed the form of the flame of a lamp"—thus [it is said] in the Kha and Ña manuscripts;
Upon a lotus with a pericarp and filaments, there are the orbs of the sun,
moon, and fire; situated in the center of the orb of fire is Viṣṇu, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, holding a lotus, four-armed— or else Hari, eight-armed.
Wearing the Śārṅga bow, the lotus, and bracelets, holding the noose and the goad, he is supreme; golden-hued and white-hued, marked with the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem,
wearing a forest garland and golden necklaces, his makara-shaped earrings are shimmering.

Wearing a crown radiant with jewels and clad in yellow garments, the Great One is enriched with all ornaments; he may extend himself as far as he desires. "I am Brahman, the light, the Self, Vāsudeva, the liberated—Oṃ!"
When weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra; when weary from recitation, one should contemplate.
For one engaged in recitation, meditation, and so forth, Viṣṇu quickly becomes propitious.
Indeed, all other sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation.
Diseases, mental afflictions, and malevolent spirits do not approach the one who recites [the mantra].
Through recitation, one shall obtain the fruits of enjoyment, liberation, and victory over death.
Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "Meditation," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Agni said:
Concentration (dhāraṇā) is the stability of the mind upon the object of meditation; like meditation (dhyāna), it is of two kinds.
Hari is attained through meditation on Hari in His formed and formless aspects and through the concentration of the mind.
When the mind does not waver from the object situated externally, that stability of the mind within its specific locations for a certain duration is called *dhāraṇā*.

When the mind, confined within the body for a limited duration of time, does not deviate from its object, that is called *dhāraṇā* (concentration). Twelve *āyāmas* constitute one *dhāraṇā*, and twelve *dhāraṇās* constitute one *dhyāna* (meditation).
Meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) up to the twelfth stage is designated as *samādhi*.
If one whose self is disciplined through the practice of *dhāraṇā* is liberated from the vital breaths (*prāṇa*),
having delivered twenty-one generations of his lineage, he goes to heaven, the supreme state.
In whichever limb of the yogis a disease may arise,
one should pervade that very limb with the intellect and maintain the concentration on reality (tattvadhāraṇā)— namely,
the fiery, the watery, the divine, and that which consists of nectar.
O best of the twice-born, the crest of Viṣṇu, ending with *phaṭ* and accompanied by fire, should be fashioned;
one should pierce the auspicious, divine, and formidable tip of the trident through the channels,
extending from the big toe to the skull, surrounded by a circle of rays.
"He goes himself to the supreme state. (kha manuscript, p.
O Great Sage, the lord of practitioners should contemplate that [light] proceeding with extreme brilliance toward the horizontal, downward,
and upward directions until his entire body has been reduced to ashes; and then he should withdraw it back once more.
O twice-born ones, cold, phlegm, and other ailments, as well as sin, are destroyed;
one should meditate on the head, the *dhīra* and *kāra* syllables, and the throat while facing downward.
With a mind whose thoughts are uninterrupted, one should meditate further with that very self;
having filled the entire universe on earth with streams of snow-bearing water produced by the touch of shimmering droplets, one should contemplate it.

Having entered the *suṣumnā* from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) down to the circle of the foundation (*ādhāramaṇḍala*) through agitation, one should inundate that which has its abode in the full moon with water of frost-like touch, which is the very form of nectar.
Afflicted by the intense heat of hunger, thirst, and exhaustion, one may hold the Vāruṇī mantra even without formal constraints for the sake of satisfaction;
this is called the Vāruṇī-dhāraṇā. Now hear the Aiśānī-dhāraṇā.
When the prāṇa and apāna have ceased in the lotus within the ether that is Brahman,
one should meditate on the grace of Viṣṇu until thought itself has come to an end;
then one should recite the Mahābhāva-mantra, whereby the Lord becomes all-pervading.

As long as one has not seen from the mouth of the Guru that form which flows forth from oneself— the supreme half-moon, the utterly peaceful, the non-manifest, and the stainless— then all this world of moving and unmoving things appears as both unreal and real.
When that supreme reality has been perceived, [everything] from Brahmā down to the moving and unmoving world [is seen as one].

The knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge; the visualization of the heart-lotus for meditation;
and all such acts as recitation, fire-offerings, and worship—all these are like a mother’s sweetmeat.
Or one may perform the concentration on nectar (amṛta-dhāraṇā) with the Viṣṇu-mantra;
one should meditate upon a lotus resembling the full moon situated within the hollow of the fist,
and one should diligently contemplate it as being located in the head, possessing the splendor of ten thousand moons.
One should meditate upon the full orb in the sky, filled with the waves of Śiva, and likewise within the heart-lotus; in its center, one should contemplate one's own body.
Through such concentration (dhāraṇā) and other practices, the practitioner becomes free from afflictions.
Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "Dhāraṇā," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 375:
Samādhi (The Meditative Absorption)
Agni said:
When meditation remains as mere self-luminosity, like a motionless ocean,
and is characterized by the nature of pure consciousness, that is called samādhi here.
The yogi who remains motionless and steady, having fixed his mind in meditation, is proclaimed to be established in *samādhi*, like a lamp in a windless place.
He does not hear, nor does he smell; he does not see, nor does he taste.
He does not perceive touch, nor does the mind form conceptualizations;
he does not conceive of anything, nor is he conscious of anything, like a piece of wood.
Thus, merged in the Lord, he is said to be established in samādhi.
Just as a lamp in a windless place does not flicker— this is the simile recorded for that yogin who meditates on Viṣṇu, the Self, in samādhi.
Divine portents arise, indicating the attainment of supernatural powers;
the faculty of hearing is suspended, and sensations occur in the teeth and limbs.
Moreover, the gods entreat that yogin with divine enjoyments.
Through gifts of land he becomes kings, and through wealth he becomes lords of great riches;
all the scriptures, beginning with the Vedas, proceed spontaneously from him,
as does poetry composed in his desired meters.
He acquires all divine elixirs (*rasāyana*) as well as divine medicinal herbs;
he masters all crafts and all arts; and he attains such qualities as the daughters of the lord of gods, as well as intuitive genius (*pratibhā*) and the like.
Viṣṇu is pleased with him who abandons [worldly ties] like a blade of grass;
having revealed knowledge to his disciple, he— possessing the sovereignty of qualities such as *aṇimā*—
enjoys pleasures as he desires and then casts off his body from that abode.
One should abide in one's own self, in consciousness, bliss, Brahman, the Lord;
for just as a soiled mirror is incapable of [reflecting] the knowledge of the Self,
so the embodied soul experiences sensation within its own body, which is the locus of all.
But one who is disciplined in yoga does not experience sensation through the yoga of all [beings].
For just as the single space appears distinct within jars and other vessels,
so too is the Self one, though present in many, like the sun reflected in various receptacles of water.
Brahman, ether, wind, fire, water, and the element of earth—
these are the worlds, this is the Self, and from it proceeds all that is moving and unmoving.
Just as a potter makes a jar through the conjunction of the rod, the wheel, and his effort, or as a house-builder constructs a house with grass, clay, and wood,
so too does the agent, taking up the instruments of action, [produce effects] within various wombs here in this world.
Thus, the self, having come together with the instruments of action, cleanses itself;
yet by its own will, through action, it becomes bound by defects and delusion.
Through knowledge the living being is liberated, and through dharma the yogi is free from disease.

Just as the stability of a lamp depends on the combination of the wick, the vessel, and the oil, so too is its transformation observed; likewise, the premature exhaustion of the vital breaths occurs when one who stands with a lamp-like light in the heart [is deprived of these supports].
His rays are infinite, like those of a lamp.
White, black, tawny, blue, brownish-red, yellow, and crimson—
among these, one stands upright; having pierced the solar disc and transcended the world of Brahmā, by that path one goes to the supreme goal.
That other hundred of rays of his which are established upwards by means of them he reaches the abodes of the hosts of gods;
while those rays of his below, which are of many forms and of soft luster—
For here, it indeed wanders about for the sake of experiencing karma by means of those [faculties]:
all the organs of perception, the mind, the organs of action,
as well as the ego-sense, the intellect, and the elements beginning with earth.
The unmanifest Self is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) and the Field (kṣetra) of this [universe];
it is the Lord of all beings, being both existent and non-existent, as well as both existent and non-existent.
From the Unmanifest arises the birth of the intellect (buddhi), and from that, the emergence of the ego (ahaṅkāra).
Therefore, the elements beginning with space arise with each successive quality added;
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their respective qualities.
Whichever of these [qualities] is dependent upon which [element], that very one dissolves back into it.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are proclaimed to be its very qualities;
indeed, when possessed by rajas and tamas, it whirls like a wheel.
That which is both beginningless and yet possesses a beginning is the Supreme Puruṣa;
that which is apprehended by means of the marks and the senses is declared to be a modification (vikāra).
From Him [proceed] the gods, the Purāṇas, as well as the sciences and the Upaniṣads.
The Ślokas, Sūtras, Bhāṣyas, and whatever else may be sacred literature,
as well as the region between the Pitṛyāna path and that of Agastya—
by that [path] those who maintain the sacred fires and desire progeny go toward heaven.
And those eighty-eight thousand sages who were householders, devoted to generosity and endowed with the eight qualities,
became the seeds for rebirth and the promoters of the Dharma.
And those who have taken refuge in the world of the gods along the path of the Seven Sages are likewise [seven] sages, entirely free from all undertakings;
they [attain this] through austerity, celibacy, renunciation of attachment, and wisdom.
Wherever they abide until the dissolution of all things,
the recitation of the Vedas, sacrifices, celibacy, austerity, self-restraint,
faith, fasting, and truthfulness are the causes for the knowledge of the Self.
He is to be meditated upon through all the stages of life (*āśrama*) in this very manner;
furthermore, He is to be seen, reflected upon, and heard by the twice-born.
Those who find Him in this way, as well as those who have resorted to the forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*), [attain Him].
The twice-born, endowed with supreme faith, worship the Truth;
in due order, they pass through the light, the day, the bright fortnight, and likewise the northern solstice.
Then a person born of the mind approaches those [beings] who belong to the world of Brahmā— the world of light, the sun, and the lightning— and makes them inhabitants of the world of Brahmā;
for them, there is no returning again to this world.
For those people who have conquered heaven through sacrifice, austerity, and gifts,
[they proceed] through smoke, night, the dark fortnight, and the southern solstice;
then to the world of the ancestors, the moon, the sky, the wind, water, and the earth.
In this world, they arise in succession and then return once more;
he who does not understand these two paths of the self will become a venomous snake, a moth, an insect, or a worm.

Through meditation on Brahman as a lamp within the heart, the individual soul becomes as if dead [to worldly existence]. Even a householder is liberated if he possesses wealth acquired by righteous means, is devoted to the knowledge of reality, is fond of guests, performs ancestral rites, and speaks the truth.
Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "Samādhi," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Chapter 376:
The Knowledge of Brahman (Brahmajñāna)
Agni said:
I shall proclaim the knowledge of Brahman for the sake of liberation from the ignorance of saṃsāra; by realizing "This Self is the Supreme Brahman, I am That," one is liberated.
The body is not the self, because it is an object of perception, like a jar and so forth.
Furthermore, when one is in deep sleep or at death, the self is certainly known to be distinct from the body.
If the body were the self, it would continue its activity even then, appearing as if it were subject to transformation and other such states.

The sense organs, such as the eye and so forth, are certainly not the self, for they are instruments; likewise, the mind and the intellect are not the self, for like a lamp, they are instruments. Even the vital breath is not the self, because of the presence of consciousness during deep sleep.
In the waking and dreaming states, consciousness is not perceived because it is intermingled [with objects].
Since the vital breath (prāṇa) devoid of discernment is known in deep sleep, the sense organ is therefore not the Self;
thus, the senses and so forth do not belong to the Self.
The ego as well is certainly not the self, because it deviates [from its nature] just like the body.
This self, distinct from those [previously mentioned], resides in every heart;
it is the seer of all and the enjoyer, like a lamp shining brightly in the night.
And at the time of commencing meditative concentration, the sage should reflect thus:
"From Brahman comes space; from space, wind; from wind, fire;
from fire, water; from water, earth; and from that, the subtle body."
Since the fivefold-combined elements arose from the non-fivefold-combined elements,
one should meditate upon the gross body and contemplate its dissolution into Brahman.
The five elements in their quintuplicated form and their effects are known as the Virāj;
this is indeed the gross body, which is fashioned by the knowledge of the Self.
Furthermore, the wise know that cognition through the senses is the waking state.
One should have confidence in this triad, which is the non-agent;
the unquintuplicated elements and their effect are called the *liṅga* (the subtle body).
Joined with the seventeen [principles], it is designated as Hiraṇyagarbha.
The subtle body of the self is called the *liṅga*;
dream-cognition, which arises from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the waking state and consists of objects,
serves as its analogy, for the *taijasa* self is indeed devoid of manifoldness (*aprapañcata*).
For the single cause of the two bodies known as the gross and the subtle is the Self and knowledge with its manifestation; that is said to be superimposed upon it.
It is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it both existent and non-existent, and it is not possessed of parts.
It is not devoid of parts, nor is it non-different, but rather different;
for that which is both different and non-different, being inexpressible, is the cause of bondage and saṃsāra.
That one Brahman is attained through realization, and certainly not by means of ritual actions.
Indeed, the complete withdrawal of the senses, which are of the nature of causes,

into the intellect (buddhi) constitutes the state of deep sleep (suṣupta); the Self that possesses the conceit of these two is the "wise one" (prājña), and these three together are remembered as the letter 'M' of the Praṇava.
The letter *a*, the letter *u*, and this very letter *m*—
I am the witness, pure consciousness alone, of the states of waking, dreaming, and so forth;
there is neither ignorance nor its effects, such as the bondage of saṃsāra and the like.
I am Brahman— eternally pure, free from bondage, true, blissful, and non-dual; I am Brahman, the supreme light, liberated, Om.
"I am Brahman, the supreme knowledge; samādhi is the destroyer of bondage.
For a long time, Brahman has been bliss; it is truth, knowledge, and infinite.
And: "This Self is the supreme Brahman; you are that Brahman."
Awakened by the Guru, the living self indeed realizes: "I am Brahman externally;
he is that Person in the sun; he is that indivisible I, Om.
The knower of Brahman is liberated from this essence-less saṃsāra and becomes that Brahman.
Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Knowledge of Brahman," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

"I am Brahman; I am Brahman with full consciousness, liberated, Om!

Chapter Three Hundred and Seventy-Eight.
Agni said:
"Through sacrifices one attains the gods; through austerity, one attains the state of Vairāja."
Through the renunciation of action, one attains dissolution into primordial nature (prakṛti) from detachment;
through knowledge, one attains absolute liberation (kaivalya). These five are recorded as the destinies.
Dispassion is the cessation of pleasure, pain, despondency, and the like.

Renunciation (*sannyāsa*) is the abandonment of actions, both those performed and those unperformed; herein, transformation—which begins with the unmanifest (*avyakta*) and ends with the specific (*viśeṣa*)—comes to an end.
Knowledge is said to be the realization of the difference between the conscious and the unconscious.
The Supreme Self, the support of all, the Supreme Lord,
is celebrated among the gods and in the Vedāntas by the name Viṣṇu;
indeed, as the Lord of Sacrifice and the Person of Sacrifice, He is worshipped by those engaged in ritual action.

By those who have desisted through the yoga of knowledge, he who is the embodiment of knowledge is perceived. O great sage, that Supreme Person is the speech consisting of short, long, and protracted vowels;
and both knowledge and action are said to be the means for attaining him.
Thus, knowledge is said to be twofold: that which is derived from scripture and that which arises from discernment.
The Brahman of Sound consists of scripture, while the Supreme Brahman is born of discernment.
Two Brahmans are to be known: that which is the Brahman of Sound and that which is the Supreme.
For the knowledge of the Vedas and so forth is indeed the lower imperishable (akṣara), while the supreme Brahman is the ultimate reality.
This very [Brahman] is to be expressed by the word "Bhagavat" through metaphorical application in worship; otherwise, it is [expressed as follows]:
the syllable *bha* is endowed with two meanings: "the sustainer" (*sambhartṛ*) and likewise "the supporter" (*bhartṛ*).
O Great Sage, this letter *ga* signifies the leader, the one who causes [beings] to go, and the creator;
it represents complete sovereignty, heroism, fame, and splendor.

Because knowledge, detachment, and the six [perfections] reside in Viṣṇu, He is designated by the term *bhaga*; likewise, all beings reside in Him, and He is the source (*dhātṛ*) whose nature is threefold.
Thus, the word *bhagavān* applies primarily to Hari alone, while its application elsewhere is merely figurative.
He who knows the origin and the dissolution of beings, their coming and their going,
as well as knowledge and ignorance— he is to be called the Blessed One (Bhagavān).
[He possesses] knowledge, power, supreme sovereignty, heroism, and splendor in their entirety.
In ancient times, Keśidhvaja taught Yoga to Khāṇḍikya Janaka, [defining] that which is denoted by the word "Bhagavat" as being devoid of qualities and the like that are to be abandoned:
"That which is the notion of self in what is not-self, and that thought which regards [the non-self] as 'mine'— "
Ignorance and the arising of existence are this twofold, stable seed;
within the body composed of the five elements, the embodied soul, shrouded in the darkness of delusion,
possesses the foolish intellect that loudly proclaims, "I am this."
And thus, toward his sons and grandsons, as well as those born from his own body,
the wise man maintains equanimity regarding the non-self physical frame;
a human being performs action for the benefit of all bodies.
When the body is distinct from the person, then that [body] leads to bondage;
however, this self consists of liberation, consisting of knowledge, and is stainless. Suffering, ignorance, and unrighteousness belong to *prakṛti*, but not to the self.

Indeed, water has no contact with fire, yet it acquires the properties of sound and so forth due to its contact with the cooking pot; O great sage, in that same way, the self, through its attachment to *prakṛti*, becomes adorned with egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and other such qualities.
For he is distinct from those common dharmas and is immutable;
the mind, when attached to sense objects, leads to bondage, but when free from sense objects, it leads to wisdom.
Drawing him away from sense objects, one should meditate on Hari, who has become Brahman;
O Sage, he leads that meditator upon Brahman to the state of the Self,
just as a magnet attracts iron according to its own power through investigation.
The union of that distinguished movement of the mind, which depends upon one's own effort,
with Brahman is designated as *yoga*. One who is established in *samādhi*, being free from all vibration, attains the supreme Brahman.

Through the observances (yamas) and the secondary observances (niyamas), by means of steadiness, withdrawal, and the conquest of the vital breaths through breath control (prāṇāyāma), and by means of withdrawal (pratyāhāra) whereby the senses are brought under control,
one should then cause the mind to abide in the auspicious substratum.
Brahman is the support of the mind, existing in two forms: the embodied and the unembodied.
Sanandana and others are endowed with the contemplation of the nature of Brahman, while others, from the gods down to the immovable beings, are characterized by the contemplation of karma.
In the case of Hiraṇyagarbha and others, meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) is said to be twofold—consisting of knowledge and action—and threefold; thus the universe is worshipped as Brahman.
That which is devoid of all distinctions, pure existence alone, and beyond the reach of the senses...
That knowledge which is self-evident through words is designated as Brahman;
and that is the supreme form of Viṣṇu—formless, unborn, and imperishable.
Since it is impossible to meditate upon that first [nature], one should therefore contemplate the embodied forms and so forth.

Then, having attained the state of true being, he becomes non-different from the Supreme Self; and any differentiation that exists for him would be produced by ignorance. Thus ends the knowledge of Brahman in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.

Chapter Three Hundred and Eighty-Three.
Agniveśa said: "I shall declare the knowledge of non-dual Brahman, which you have spoken of."
At Śālagrāma, he performed austerities, devoted to the worship of Vāsudeva and other rites;
having become a deer through association with deer, at the time of death, remembering a deer,
that deer— possessing the memory of his former births— cast off his body and by his own yoga became [a man] once more.
Having become one with the non-dual Brahman, he moved through the world like an insentient object;
that charioteer of King Vīra considered himself fit for the labor of service.
Urged by the words of the charioteer, he carried the palanquin.
The wise man, having been taken as a forced laborer, carried it for his own destruction;
he went with a sluggish pace, while the others who had gone quickly looked back.
Seeing those who were swift and moving rapidly, the king [saw] him who was not swift.
The king said:
"Are you weary? You have carried my palanquin only a short distance."
"Are you not capable of exertion? You appear to be stout.
The Brahmin said:
"I am not stout, nor indeed have I carried this palanquin of yours."
"I am not weary, nor is there fatigue; you are not to be carried, O Lord of the Earth.
The pair of feet is established upon the ground; the two shanks rest upon the two feet;
the two thighs rest upon the two shanks; and the belly is likewise supported by them."
The chest, the arms, and the shoulders situated upon the belly—
this palanquin rests upon my shoulders; what effort have I made in this matter?
If this body situated upon the palanquin is what you perceive as "you," then I am also there; yet if it is said that "I" am here [in the driver], then it is otherwise:
both I and you, as well as others, are carried along by the elements (bhūta).
O King,
this aggregate of qualities indeed falls into the stream of the qualities;
and these qualities, beginning with *sattva*, O Lord of the Earth, are subject to the power of karma.
Karma is accumulated through ignorance, and that exists in all living beings;
yet the Self is pure, imperishable, tranquil, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature.
Among all living beings, there is neither increase nor decrease for this single [Self].
O King, when there is no accumulation for it and no depletion,
by what reasoning have you stated, "You are fat," regarding that which resides in the arms,
shanks, feet, hips, thighs, belly, and so forth?
"O King, at that time, the existence of this palanquin was entirely dependent upon you;
yet by the act of raising the palanquin, it was supported by other living beings.
Whether it originated from the substance of stone or from the earth itself,"

O King, just as a man’s separation from his material instruments is a great burden to be endured, which of these two is the greater burden for me, O Lord of Men? Whatever substance this palanquin consists of, such is the aggregate of the elements.
"By you, this entire world of mine has been uplifted through your equanimity.
Having heard that, the king took hold of his feet, asked for forgiveness, and said:
"Be gracious; leave this palanquin and speak to one who listens."

"Whatever you are, for whatever purpose, or whatever the reason for your coming—" the Brahmin said: "Listen; it is not at all possible to say 'Who am I?'"* 19ef–20ab* 1: n* (Note: *The asterisks indicate line breaks from the source text.)

thus spoke Rajas.
"O Brahmin, why can it not be said, 'I am he who exists'?
O twice-born one, for one who uses the word 'I' with respect to the Self, there is no fault.
The Brāhmaṇa said:

The notion "I am sound" leads to error; likewise, it does not apply to the Self. When the single Person is established within all bodies, the cognition of the Self in what is not the Self—whether by means of sound or otherwise—is characterized as a delusion.
For at that time, the words "Who are you? and "Who am I? are fruitless.
"You are the king, this is the palanquin, we are the bearers, and these are your attendants"—O King, this world of yours is not real; this is what is said.

This conscious Great King does not say, 'I am mounted upon a tree.'"

No one says to you, "O all-inclusive wood, you have become a palanquin. This palanquin is merely a collection of wooden parts held together by a specific arrangement; O best of kings, seek it out by breaking it apart.
"Man, woman, this cow, horse, elephant, bird, or tree— O King, these worldly designations applied to bodies are to be understood as having karma as their cause.
The tongue says 'I am,' as do the teeth, the lips, and the palate."
Since all these are merely causes for the application of words,
why does she say "I am speech" herself by means of these reasons? Even so, it is not unreasonable to say that "I am not speech," for what has been stated would otherwise be false.
Since this body, characterized by the head, anus, and so forth, is distinct from the person, O King, why then do I apply this notion of "I" to it?
O best of kings, if there were anyone else other than myself, then it would be appropriate to speak thus: "This one is I, and this other is another.
But in the ultimate sense, there is no distinction between a mountain, an animal, or a tree.
These bodies and their various distinctions, which have their origin in karma;
that which is called "king" in the world, and that which consists of the king's soldiers— O King, all this and whatever else there is is not truly real, nor is it free from affliction.

You are the king of all the world, the son of your father, the enemy of your foe, the husband of your wife, and the father of your son; O King, what can I say to you? Is this your head, or is it your head, and likewise your belly?
How much more so, O Lord of the Earth, regarding your feet and other limbs? Are you indeed these, or are you distinct from all your constituent parts?
Having become discerning in this regard, reflect carefully: "Who am I? O King.
Having heard that, King Hari spoke to that avadhūta twice-born man;
Rajī said:

"You are a portion of that seer Kapila; for my sake, you are the giver of knowledge upon this earth.
Since you are one who surges with waves of wisdom, tell me that which is the highest good.
The brahmin said:
"You ask again what is the highest good, yet you do not ask about the ultimate truth, O King; for all other forms of excellence are indeed non-ultimate.
Having performed the propitiation of the deities, one desires the attainment of wealth."
O King, he desires sons and sovereignty; what indeed is better for him than that?
But for the discerning one, union with the Supreme Self is the highest good.
Ritual acts such as sacrifice would not exist, nor would there be the production of material substances.
The union of the ultimate reality with the self is held to be the ultimate truth;
it is one, all-pervading, equal, pure, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
The Self is devoid of birth, growth, and so forth; it is all-pervading and immutable.
It consists of supreme knowledge, is unattached, and is sovereign over qualities, classes, and the like.
O twice-born one, listen as I speak of that dialogue between Nidāgha and Ṛtu. (1)
Ṛtu, the son of Brahmā, was a man of knowledge; his disciple, Nidāgha, the son of Pulastya, having acquired learning from him, resided in a city in that town.

After a thousand divine years had passed, he went to visit Nidāgha.
At the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, having eaten his meal, Nidāgha said to his disciple:

Ṛtu said:
"O Brāhmaṇa, hunger exists for one who finds satisfaction upon eating food;
no hunger has arisen in me, so why do you ask about my satiety?"
"Hunger and thirst are known as properties of the body, O twice-born one; since these do not belong to me, I shall answer what I have been asked by you:
I am indeed always satisfied."
Since this person is all-pervading and omnipresent like space,
how could there be the sense "I am the inner self"? [If that were so,] he would be a wanderer.
You do not come from elsewhere, nor do you have a dwelling in any single place;
you are not one thing, nor am I another, nor am I anything other than you.

I am Ṛtu, your teacher, O twice-born one, come here for the sake of bestowing wisdom upon you. I shall now depart; the ultimate truth has been declared to you.
"Know this entire world to be thus one; there is no duality.
It is the very nature of the Supreme Self, designated as Vāsudeva.
At the end of a thousand years of seasons, he went once again to that city.
The season of summer spoke to Nidāgha as he stood in a secluded spot on the outskirts of the city: "Nidāgha, why do you stand in this solitude?
Nidāgha replied:
"O Brahmin, this great commotion of people, O lord of men, is because they wish to enter the beautiful city; for that reason I am staying here.
Ṛtu said:
"O best of the twice-born, tell me: who here is the lord of men, and who is the other person? You are knowledgeable, O most excellent of the twice-born.
[Tell me] about this one who [seized] the lord of elephants, intoxicated and risen like a mountain peak..."
"This king has mounted [the elephant], and so has his retinue and the others. "O Brahmin, this elephant that is below is he, and this one above is the lord of the earth.
Ṛtu said, "Who here is the elephant? and Nidāghaka said, "The king."
"The season Ṛtu has ascended; look at the illustration: I am like the king above, and you are like the elephant below.
Ṛtu said to Nidāgha: "Which one among you shall I call 'you'?"
Having bowed to him, Nidāgha said: "You are certainly my guru.

The mind, conditioned by the latent impressions of duality, does not perceive [the truth] in such a way from anything else; thus Ṛtu spoke to Nidāgha when he had come for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman.
"The ultimate reality, which is the essence and non-duality, has been shown by me.
The Brahmin said:
"Nidāgha, too, through that instruction, became devoted to non-duality."
He beheld all beings as non-different from himself;
through that knowledge he attained liberation, and in the same way you shall attain liberation. For you, I, and Viṣṇu are one, since [the Self] is omnipresent.
"Just as the single sky is seen as divided by distinctions such as yellow and blue,
so too is that single Self perceived as distinct and separate by those with deluded vision," Agni said.
For the king attained liberation from you through the essence of knowledge;
contemplate that Brahman is the knowledge which is the enemy of the tree of ignorance in saṃsāra.

The Essence of the Gītā.
Agni said:
I shall proclaim the essence of the Gītā, the most excellent among all songs.
Kṛṣṇa said to Arjuna that which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
the Blessed Lord said:
"Whether its life-force has departed or not, the embodied being is unborn and is not to be grieved for."
The self is undecaying, immortal, and indivisible; therefore, one should abandon sorrow and the like.
(From knowledge [comes this realization]). From *kha* and *ña*: "The King of Sauvīra";
from *kha*: "Bestowing enjoyment and liberation upon those who recite it."
For a person dwelling on sense-objects, attachment to them arises;
from attachment comes desire, from that anger, and from anger, delusion itself.
From delusion comes the loss of memory; from the destruction of the intellect, one perishes.
The abandonment of evil company comes from association with the virtuous; and from that, the desire for liberation arises.
By the renunciation of desire, one becomes established in the Self; at that time, one is called a man of steady wisdom.
That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man keeps watch;
that wherein beings keep watch is night for the sage who sees.
And for him who is content in the Self alone, no duty remains to be performed.
For him there is no purpose whatsoever in action here, nor any in inaction;
for the knower of truth, O mighty-armed one, regarding the distinction between the qualities and their functions,
he does not become attached, realizing that "it is the qualities that act upon the qualities."

One shall cross over all evil by the boat of knowledge alone. O Arjuna, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes for him who acts by dedicating his actions to Brahman and abandoning attachment.

He is not stained by evil, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. With his self disciplined through yoga, he perceives the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self; thus, he sees with equal vision everywhere.
One who has fallen from yoga is born into the house of the pure and the prosperous;
for no one who performs good deeds, my dear, ever goes to a miserable state.
Indeed, this divine illusion of mine, consisting of the gunas, is difficult to overcome.
Those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion.

O bull of the Bharatas, there are four kinds of people who worship Me: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom; yet the man of wisdom, established in oneness, is superior.
The syllable *oṃ* is the supreme Brahman; its inherent nature is called the *adhyātma*.
The emission (*visarga*) that brings about the arising of the existence of beings is designated as *karman*.
The perishable state is the *adhibhūta*, and the Puruṣa is the *adhidaivata*;
and I alone am the *adhiyajña* here in this body, O best of embodied beings. At the time of death, remembering Me, one undoubtedly attains My own state.
Whatever state one contemplates at the end while casting off the body, that very state one shall attain;
by fixing the vital breath between the eyebrows, one attains Me, the Supreme, at the end.
Thus, uttering the single-syllable Brahman "Om" while casting off the body, [one likewise attains the goal].
All beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, are my manifestations; all living creatures, glorious and powerful, are known as portions of me.
Knowing "I alone am the one who possesses all forms," one is liberated.
He who knows the field, the body, is proclaimed as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
That which is the knowledge of both the field and the Knower of the Field—that, in my opinion, is true knowledge.
The great elements, ego-consciousness, intellect, and the unmanifest; the ten senses and their single locus, as well as the five objects of the senses;
desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the composite body, consciousness, and fortitude.
This field has been briefly described along with its modifications.
