Detachment from the objects of the senses and indeed the absence of egoism; the contemplation of the defects of suffering inherent in birth, death, old age, and disease;
and lack of attachment and non-attachment toward children, wife, home, and so forth.
And there is constant equanimity of mind toward the occurrence of both the desirable and the undesirable.
And unwavering devotion to me through the yoga of exclusive concentration;
resorting to solitary places; a distaste for the assembly of people; steadfastness in the knowledge of the Self; and constant contemplation upon the knowledge of reality.
This is declared to be knowledge; ignorance is that which is otherwise than this.
I shall now declare that which is to be known, by knowing which one attains immortality:
it is called the beginningless, supreme Brahman, which is Being (sattva).
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere,
and with ears everywhere in the world, He stands encompassing all.
Shining with the qualities of all the senses, yet devoid of all senses.
It is unattached yet the sustainer of all; devoid of qualities yet the experiencer of qualities.
It is both outside and inside of all beings, moving and yet unmoving.
Because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible; though it is far away, it is also near.
It is undivided, yet it exists as if divided among all beings;
it is to be known as the sustainer of beings, the devourer, and the source of creation.
It is the light even of lights, and is said to be beyond darkness.
Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and that which is attainable through knowledge— residing in the hearts of all—
some perceive the Self within the self by means of meditation;
others by the yoga of Sāṅkhya, and still others by the yoga of action.
But others, not knowing this, worship having heard it from others;
they too, being devoted to what they have heard, quickly cross over death.
From *sattva* arises knowledge, and from *rajas* arises greed alone.
Negligence and delusion arise from *tamas*, as does knowledge itself;
he who remains established in the thought that "the qualities merely revolve" does not waver.
He who is equal toward honor and dishonor, friend and foe, and who practices renunciation—he is free from qualities.
They speak of the imperishable *aśvattha* tree as having its roots above and its branches below; the Vedas are its leaves—he who knows it is a knower of the Veda.
There are two types of creation of beings in this world: the divine and the demonic.
Non-violence and so forth, as well as forbearance, arise from the divine endowment of men;
neither purity nor right conduct arises from the demonic endowment.
Because it arises from hellish states, one should therefore abandon these three: anger, greed, and lust.
Sacrifice, austerity, and likewise charity are said to be of three kinds according to the qualities of goodness (sattva) and the rest.
Food that promotes longevity, vitality, strength, health, and happiness is of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
Food that causes pain, grief, and disease, and which is pungent or dry, is rajasic; food consisting of impure, leftover, or putrid items, as well as that which is tasteless and so forth, is tamasic.
A sacrifice performed according to the prescribed rules by one free from desire is sattvic.
A sacrifice performed for the sake of fruit, characterized by hypocrisy, is said to be *rājasa* or *tāmasa*.

Physical austerity (*śārīra-tapas*) is defined as that which is prescribed by rules regarding faith, mantras, and so forth; austerity consisting of speech (*vāṅmaya-tapas*) is defined as the worship of gods and others, or [the recitation of] hymns of praise.
Speech that causes no agitation, truthfulness, the regular recitation of sacred texts,
mental purity, gentleness, and restraint of pride constitute *sāttvika* austerity. On the other hand, austerity performed for the sake of rewards and the like is *rājasa*.

Giving for the sake of harming others is said to be *tāmasa*; giving for the sake of benefit is called *sāttvika*. Giving at a specific place and time out of a sense of obligation is *rājasa*; giving with contempt for the recipient and so forth is declared to be *tāmasa*.
The designation of Brahman is traditionally remembered as threefold: *Oṃ*, *Tat*, and *Sat*.
Ritual acts such as sacrifice and charity, when performed with these, bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men.
The threefold fruit of action— unpleasant, pleasant, and mixed—
is experienced after death, but never for renunciants.
Through the connection with action born of tamas, and out of delusion, distress, fear, and so forth...
The passionate and the pure, as well as that which is without desire— these five are the causes of action:
the locus, the agent, the various instruments,
the diverse activities, and the divine as the fifth among them.
Knowledge that is unified is *sāttvika*; knowledge that is divided is *rājasa*; knowledge that is contrary to reality is *tāmasa*. Action performed without desire is *sāttvika*;
action performed for the sake of desire is *rājasa*; but action performed out of delusion is *tāmasa*.
The agent who is equal toward success and failure is *sāttvika*; the *rājasa* is even more so;
the *tāmasa* would be deceitful and lazy. Furthermore, the intellect regarding action and so forth is *sāttvika*;
that which is for the sake of the task is *rājasa*; but that which is contrary to this is *tāmasa*.
Mental fortitude born of *sattva* is characterized by joy; that born of *rajas* is characterized by desire;

but that born of *tamas* occurs in states such as grief. Happiness resulting from *sattva* persists until the end; happiness resulting from *rajas* is present at the beginning but ends in sorrow; and that resulting from *tamas* is sorrowful even at its onset.
Therefore, by worshipping Viṣṇu— who, through his own action, has pervaded all this— the activity of all beings proceeds, and one attains perfection;
always and in all states, through action, mind, and speech.
It occurs for those who are not yogis (as stated in Kha... p.
"He who knows the world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, as well as Viṣṇu..."
The devotee of the Blessed One, the follower of the Lord, certainly attains perfection.
Thus ends the three hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Essence of the Gītā," in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 381:
The Song of Yama (Yamagītā)
Agni said:
I shall proclaim the song of Yama, which was spoken for the sake of Naciketas;
it is for the enjoyment of those who recite it and for the liberation of virtuous people who seek release.
Yama said:
Alas! Being himself unstable, he desires through extreme delusion a seat, a bed, vehicles, clothing, a house, and so forth, as if they were perfectly stable.
Constant mastery over enjoyments as well as the contemplation of the self—this indeed is the supreme welfare for human beings, as proclaimed by Kapila.
Seeing all things with equanimity, freedom from pride, and non-attachment; AP 381.003–004ab.

Indeed, the song sung by Pañcaśikha is the supreme good for human beings; it is the knowledge of the various stages of life, beginning from the womb, birth, and childhood. The song sung by Gaṅgā and Viṣṇu is the supreme good for human beings.
The remedy for internal and other forms of suffering from beginning to end, as well as that which was sung by Janaka, is indeed the supreme good for human beings.
That cognition which creates a distinction between the two—the self and the other—which are actually non-different; AP_381.007ab/
That which is known as the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman*— the ritual action that must be performed— is declared by Brahmā to be the supreme excellence, characterized by ultimate peace.
It is sung by Jaigīṣavya that one should cultivate attachments for the sake of the highest good;
the abandonment of all desires to act is the cause of the self's happiness. This supreme welfare of human beings has been proclaimed as the song of the gods.
Through the renunciation of desire, however, one attains consciousness, bliss, Brahman, and the supreme state;
for those possessed by desire, there is no such consciousness—this is indeed what was sung by Sanaka.
He who is devoted to action spoke of both the path of worldly engagement (*pravṛtta*) and the path of withdrawal (*nivṛtta*).
For this is the highest of all excellences: liberation from action (naiṣkarmya), which is Brahman, that Hari, and the Supreme Person.
O best of men, once knowledge has been attained, he no longer perceives duality with respect to Brahman, who is known as Viṣṇu, the supreme and immutable.
Through austerity, one obtains everything that the mind desires: knowledge, discernment, faith, good fortune, and supreme beauty.
There is no object of meditation equal to Viṣṇu, and there is no austerity superior to fasting.
There is no blessing equal to health; there is no river equal to the Gaṅgā.
There is no kinsman whatsoever—above, below, or before one, whether at the head of the body, the senses, or the mind—who is superior to Viṣṇu, the Teacher of the World.
Thus remembering this, whoever should renounce their life-breaths shall become Hari—
that which is Brahman, from which all proceeds, in which all is established,
which is ungraspable, indefinable, well-foundationed, and supreme.
Viṣṇu, existing in the form of both the supreme and the non-supreme, resides in the heart of all.
Some desire that supreme being as the Lord of Sacrifice (Yajñeśa) or the Person of Sacrifice (Yajñapuruṣa);
some [desire] Viṣṇu, some Hara, some Brahmā, and some Īśvara.
Some call the Sun and Soma by the names of Indra and others;
they declare that Viṣṇu is the world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
That Viṣṇu is the supreme Brahman, from which one does not return again;
one may attain him through great gifts such as gold, by bathing at sacred fords,
through meditations, vows, worship, and by hearing the Dharma.

Know the self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot itself. Know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as the reins. They say the senses are the horses, and the objects of the senses are the paths for their arrows.
The wise say that the self, when joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer.
But he who is devoid of discernment and whose mind is always uncontrolled does not attain the state of the Good, but instead enters into the cycle of rebirth.
But he who possesses discernment and always has a disciplined mind attains that state from which one is not born again.
The man who has discernment as his charioteer and holds the reins of the mind—
He reaches that supreme path, that highest step of Viṣṇu; for the objects of the senses are beyond the senses, and the mind is beyond the objects;
the intellect is beyond the mind, and the Great Self is beyond the intellect.
Beyond the Great is the Unmanifest; beyond the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa. There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal.
Hidden within all these beings, the Self does not shine forth.

But it is seen by those of subtle vision with a subtle and supreme intellect. The wise man should restrain speech in the mind; he should restrain that [mind] in the intellect; he should restrain the intellect in the Great Self, in the peaceful Self.
Having realized the union of Brahman and the Self through the restraints (yamas) and other practices, one becomes Brahman.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness— these are the [restraints].

The five restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) are purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and worship of the Lord; the posture (*āsana*) is the lotus-posture and so forth; breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is mastery over the vital airs; and withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) is self-restraint.
O twice-born one, that which is the steadfast fixing of the mind upon a single auspicious object is called *dhāraṇā* by the wise, because of its immovability;
it is the repeated fixing of the mind upon those very same objects.
Dhyāna is traditionally defined as samādhi, which is the state of abiding in the Self as "I am Brahman.

Just as space remains undivided from the sky even after the destruction of a jar, so the liberated individual soul (jīva) becomes one with Brahman; indeed, that which is real is Brahman, and he becomes Brahman.
The individual soul (jīva) realizes itself as Brahman through knowledge, and not otherwise;
for the jīva, when liberated from ignorance and its effects, becomes free from old age and death.
Agni said:
O Vasiṣṭha, this Yamagītā, when recited, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is declared to be the ultimate dissolution, consisting of the realization of Brahman through Vedānta.
Thus ends the three hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Song of Yama," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter [Number] on Meditation.
Now begins the three hundred and eighty-second chapter.
Regarding the majesty of the Āgneya Purāṇa,
Agni said:
"O Brahman, this Āgneya Purāṇa has been narrated by me to you."
One should know that the great [reality], consisting of the non-dual knowledge, is both with conceptual proliferation (*saprapañca*) and free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).

Knowledge is called the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, *Sāman*, and *Atharvan*; Viṣṇu is the source of the world; and there are the [six] limbs known as phonology (*chandas*), phonetics (*śikṣā*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), lexicography (*nighaṇṭu*), and astronomy (*jyotiḥ*).
Etymology, the treatises on Dharma, and so forth; Mīmāṃsā and the expansion of Nyāya; that which is called Āyurveda and the Purāṇas; the expansions of Dhanurveda and Gandharvaveda;
and that very science known as Arthaśāstra—all these, ending with the Vedas, are the Great Hari.
Thus, this is another knowledge, the supreme knowledge of the Imperishable;
for one whose entire being is Viṣṇu, the Kali age brings no affliction.
Even without having performed the great sacrifices or offered the ancestral *svadhā* oblations, [he is liberated].
One who worships Kṛṣṇa with devotion shall not become a vessel for sin;
meditating upon Viṣṇu, the ultimate cause of all, one does not perish,
even if the mind is drawn toward sense objects due to defects arising from other systems and the like.
Even having committed a sin, one is liberated from sins by meditating on Govinda;
that meditation is where Govinda is present, that is the discourse where Keśava is present,
and that is the action which is for His sake— what is the use of much other talk?
O twice-born one, neither a father to his son nor a teacher to his disciple should ever speak that supreme ultimate truth which I have declared to you;
for in this cycle of existence, sons, wives, wealth, and property are all obtainable by one wandering through saṃsāra.
Likewise, there are no other friends; such is the instruction for the twice-born: what is the use of sons, wives, or friends? What is the use of friends, fields, or kinsmen?
Instruction is the supreme kinsman for one who seeks liberation.
This path of reality is twofold: divine and demonic.
That which is devoted to devotion to Viṣṇu is divine; that which is the opposite is demonic.

This Purāṇa, which belongs to Agni, is sacred, health-bestowing, auspicious, and a destroyer of evil dreams; it brings happiness and joy to men and grants liberation to those in whose houses it is written, as proclaimed by me.
The book shall always remain there, and no calamities shall prevail.
Of what use are pilgrimages, or the gifting of cows, or sacrifices, or fasts,
for those men who listen to the Āgneya [Purāṇa] day after day?
He who gives a prastha of sesame seeds and a māṣaka of gold,
and hears even a single verse of the Āgneya [Parvan], shall obtain that same merit;
moreover, the recitation of this chapter is superior to the gift of a cow.
The sin committed during a day and night perishes for one who desires to hear this; indeed,
by reciting the Āgneya Purāṇa, one obtains the same fruit that would result from giving a hundred tawny cows at Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara.

One should know that the Dharma, consisting of both the path of worldly engagement (*pravṛtta*) and the path of withdrawal (*nivṛtta*), is not equal to this *Āgneya Purāṇa*, a scripture whose essence is the dual knowledge (*vidyā*).
By constantly reciting or even listening to this *Āgneya* Purāṇa, [one attains the goal].
A person devoted to Vasiṣṭha is liberated from all sins;
there shall be no calamities, no misfortunes, and no fear of thieves or enemies in that house where a manuscript of the Āgneya Purāṇa resides.

In that house where this ancient *Āgneya Purāṇa* resides, there is no fear of female spirits who steal embryos, nor do child-seizing demons dwell; furthermore, there is no fear of *piśācas* or similar beings.
By hearing this, a Brahmin becomes a knower of the Vedas, a Kshatriya becomes a lord of the earth, and a Vaishya attains prosperity; and a Shudra attains health—
whoever reads or hears this constantly, with an even-mindedness and a mind fixed on Vishnu.
In that ancient *Brahmāgneya Purāṇa*, all calamities—
whether celestial, atmospheric, or terrestrial, including evil dreams and malevolent spells—
are destroyed; indeed, Keśava destroys every other kind of misfortune whatsoever.
For a man who recites, listens to,
or honors this great Āgneya Śrī Purāṇa during the winter season,
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, he shall indeed obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
For one who recites this during the winter, the fruit is that of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice; in spring, that of the Aśvamedha;
in summer, that of the Vājapeya; and during the rainy season, that of the Rājasūya;
and in autumn, the fruit is that of a thousand cows.
O Vasiṣṭha, he who recites the Āgneya Purāṇa first with devotion before Hari shall worship Keśava here through the sacrifice of knowledge.
Victory indeed belongs to him who possesses a manuscript of this Āgneya Purāṇa.
"Written and worshipped in the home, enjoyment and liberation are indeed in one's hand"—
thus was it sung to me by Hari in the form of Kālāgni in the past. For this Āgneya Purāṇa is indeed the locus of the two-fold Brahma-vidyā.
"O Vasiṣṭha, you shall proclaim these two vidyās to your devotees.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Vyāsa, this Āgneya Purāṇa is your very form, consisting of the nature of these two vidyās."
It was told by Agni to Brahmā and Viṣṇu,
and likewise to the gods and sages; it reveals all goals to me.
O Gautama, whoever should read or hear this ancient Āgneya Purāṇa, which is well-measured by Brahmā; or who should write it, cause it to be written, recite it,
cause it to be recited, worship it, or even preserve it— [he shall attain the highest goal].
Freed from all sins and having attained his desires, he shall go to heaven;
he who, having had this Purāṇa transcribed, gives it to the Brahmins,
attains the world of Brahmā and shall uplift a hundred lineages.
Whoever recites even a single verse is liberated from the mire of sin.
Therefore, O Vyāsa, this Purāṇa, which reveals all truths, should always be heard by disciples together with Śuka and other sages who desire to hear it.
The Āgneya [Purāṇa], when recited and meditated upon, shall be auspicious, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
salutations to that Agni by whom this ancient [work] was sung.
Vyāsa said:
O Sūta, this which was sung by Vasiṣṭha in the past has been declared to you by me:
the nature of higher knowledge and lower knowledge, the supreme state,
and the form of Agni which is difficult to attain, yet is reached by those endowed with good fortune.
Meditating upon the ancient Brahman and Agni, they have come to Hari;
likewise, those seeking knowledge have attained it, and those seeking a kingdom have attained their kingdom.
The childless have become possessed of sons, and those without refuge have found shelter.
Those seeking good fortune attained good fortune, and those seeking liberation attained liberation;
by writing or having it written, they became free from sin and attained prosperity.
O Sūta, [I have heard] the Āgneya Purāṇa from the mouths of Śuka, Paila, and others.
Contemplate the Rūpa; you shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, without a doubt.
And you should cause this Purāṇa to be heard by your disciples and devotees.
Sūta said:
O sages, Śaunaka and the others, through the grace of Vyāsa, the Āgneya Purāṇa has been heard by me with reverence; for the Āgneya is indeed the very form of Brahman.
"O sirs, while you were performing sacrifices to Hari, the Lord, in the Naimiṣa forest and remained endowed with faith,
this Agni Purāṇa— spoken by Agni, equal to the Vedas— was proclaimed to you."
Endowed with the two-fold knowledge of Brahman, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; there is no essence higher than this, no friend greater than this,
no scripture more exalted than this, and no goal superior to this.

There is no scripture superior to this; there is no revelation superior to this; there is no knowledge superior to this; there is no traditional teaching superior to this; for there is no sacred tradition higher than this, and indeed, there is no wisdom higher than this.
There is no philosophical conclusion higher than this; there is no greater auspiciousness than this;
there is no Vedānta higher than this; and indeed, there is no Purāṇa more supreme than this.
On this earth, no rare object exists that is superior to this.
For in this Āgneya Purāṇa, all branches of knowledge are demonstrated;
all [the accounts] beginning with the Fish Incarnation are shown here, as are the Gītā and the Rāmāyaṇa,
the Harivaṃśa and the Mahābhārata, and the nine creations are displayed.

The Vaiṣṇava Āgama has been sung [here], including worship, initiation, consecration, the rite of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa), and so forth; the characteristics of images, the characteristics of temples, and the like; and the mantras which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The Śaiva Āgama and its meaning, as well as the Śākta and Saura [Āgamas],
the mandalas, the sacred sites (vāstu), various mantras,
the secondary creation (pratisarga) that has been sung, and the spherical expanse of the universe (brahmāṇḍaparimaṇḍala).
The treasury of the worlds (*bhuvanakoṣa*), including the continents, regions, and rivers, has been sung;
and the greatness of sacred sites (*tīrtha*) such as Gayā, Gaṅgā, and Prayāga has been proclaimed.
The wheel of luminaries beginning with the stars was sung, as well as the *Yuddhajayārṇava* (Ocean of Victory in Battle).
The beginnings of the *manvantaras* were sung, as well as the duties (*dharma*) of the social classes (*varṇas*) and others.
Impurity, the purification of objects, and expiation (*prāyaścitta*) were demonstrated.
The duties of kings, the laws of giving, various vows, legal procedures, means of pacification, the prescriptions of the *Ṛgveda* and other Vedas,
the solar lineage, the lunar lineage, the science of archery, and medicine.

The Gāndharvaveda, the Arthaśāstra, Mīmāṃsā, the expansion of Nyāya, the enumeration and majesty of the Purāṇas, prosody, grammar, rhetoric, Vighaṇḍu, and Śikṣā and Kalpa are declared and remembered here.
The occasional dissolution, the natural dissolution, and the absolute dissolution;
the Vedānta, the knowledge of Brahman, and Yoga with its eight limbs as proclaimed;
the hymns, the greatness of the Purāṇas, and the eighteen sciences are thus remembered.
For here, the Rigveda and others are indeed the lower [knowledge], while the higher knowledge is the supreme Imperishable;
the form of Brahman is said to be both with and without phenomenal expansion.
This [Purāṇa] consists of fifteen thousand [verses], with an extent of one hundred crores.
In the world of the gods, it is always recited by the deities;
having been sung in brief by Agni out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
"All is Brahman"— know this, O sages headed by Śaunaka.
O King, one who is self-restrained should listen to it or cause it to be heard, read it or cause it to be read,
write it or cause it to be written, apply its teachings, or even proclaim it;
likewise, he should honor the reciter of the Purāṇa with devotion.
By honoring him with gifts of cows, land, and gold, as well as garments, ornaments, and offerings of food,
one obtains the very same fruit that comes from listening to the Purāṇas.
And at the conclusion of the Purāṇa, one must certainly provide a meal for the twice-born;
thus stainless, having attained all goals, and together with his family, he shall attain heaven.
One should provide a mechanical device, a book, a thread, or a collection of leaves for the sake of the manuscript.
He who gives cloth for binding the covers and other such items shall attain heaven;
he who gives a book shall dwell in the world of Brahmā. In whosever house there is a book, there is no fear of calamities, and he shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
"Remember the ancient, fiery, and divine form of the Lord.
Thus addressed, Sūta departed after being honored by them; Śaunaka and the others then went to Hari.
Thus ends [the section] titled "The Greatness of the Āgneya Purāṇa" in the Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa.
The three hundred and eighty-second chapter.
The Āgneya Purāṇa is completed;
now follows the supplement (pariśiṣṭa) to the Agni Purāṇa.

Among the ten manuscript copies of the *Agnipurāṇa* marked with the letter 'Ka', in nine of these manuscripts, the text is complete following the chapter on the *Yamagītā* with the chapter on the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the Purāṇa.
In the manuscript marked with the letter *ga*,
however, there are thirty-three additional chapters, beginning with the section on cosmogony (*sṛṣṭiprakaraṇa*), following the chapter on the *Yamagīta*.

The authenticity of the mentioned chapters is doubtful because they are not found in the nine manuscript copies; even if their authenticity were established, it would be restricted to specific locations.
Relying upon a manuscript marked with a single *gacihna* (gap-marker) that was corrupt in its syllables and lacked clarity, I was unable to edit and publish the chapters mentioned as being in excess;
however, for the purpose of this notification, [I have included] what remains in excess from the manuscript alone bearing the *gacihna*.
A few chapters have been edited to the best of my ability and printed as a supplement,
based on the manuscript marked with the letter Ga.
Because of the loss of syllables and because it is not entirely pure, there are incorrect readings in many places in this remaining portion. —
Chapter 1.
The First Chapter.
Sūta said:
Having become Brahmā for the creation of the world, Narasiṃha proceeds [with his task].
I shall tell it to you in that manner; O Bharadvāja, listen to me.
The Blessed One named Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the World, having come into existence, is carried away by the service of beloved gods who are fond of pleasure.
This reading cannot be corrected by omitting the letters of the manuscript:
"By his own measure, his lifespan is recorded as one hundred years. (AP 1.003ab)
Time is Viṣṇu; by him the lifespan of all other beings— whether moving or unmoving— is calculated,
O best of men, as well as that of the earth, the clay, the oceans, and all things without exception.
Eighteen *nimeṣas* are proclaimed to be one *kāṣṭhā*;
thirty *kāṣṭhās* are known as one *kalā*, and thirty *kalās* are the measure of one *muhūrta*. A human day and night (*ahorātra*) is said to consist of that same number of *muhūrtas*.
A month consists of as many days and nights as that [year], being composed of two fortnights.
Six such months constitute an *ayana*; there are two *ayanās*, the southern and the northern.
The southern *ayana* is the night of the gods, and the northern is their day.
Two solstices and one year are proclaimed for mortals;
a month of men is declared to be a day and night for the ancestors (Pitṛs).
A human year is remembered as a day and night for the Vasus and other [gods].
Understand from me the division of that period known as Kṛta, Tretā,
and so forth,
which consists of four, three, two, and one thousand divine years respectively.
Those who know the past say that there are thousands of divine years in the ages (yugas);
the preceding twilight (sandhyā) is said to be of a measure equal to one hundred of those [years],
and the subsequent portion of the twilight (sandhyāṃśaka) is likewise equal to that, following immediately after the age.

O twice-born one, that period which exists between the two junctions (saṃdhyā) and the two partial junctions (saṃdhyāṃśa) should be known as being called a "yuga. The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the four yugas.
O twice-born one, that thousandfold period is declared to be a single day of Brahmā;
O Brahmin, during the day of Brahmā, there are fourteen Manus.
And their auspicious measure determined by time consists of the Seven Sages, the gods, Śakra, Manu, and his sons who are kings;
for they are created at one and the same time and are withdrawn in the same manner as before.
O twice-born Sūta, seventy-one times the number of four yugas constitutes a *manvantara*,
the period of a Manu, as well as that of Śakra and the others;
by divine reckoning, it consists of eight hundred thousand [years].
O Sage, this period is recorded as being fifty-one thousand years, plus another seven thousand and twenty thousand more;
thus is the day of Brahmā to be known, as has been fully proclaimed.
Indeed, having created by means of his mind these— gods, as well as ancestors,
Gandharvas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Guhyakas,
as well as Ṛṣis, Vidyādharas, humans, and animals— in this [world].
Having created birds, stationary beings, ants, and serpents, as well as the fourfold social order (cāturvarṇya) and assigned them to their respective lower duties,
that Lord, at the end of the day, withdraws the three worlds.
The Imperishable One lay upon the couch of Ananta for that entire night;
at its conclusion occurred the great kalpa renowned as Pādma,
in which the Fish Incarnation appeared for the purpose of churning the great ocean.
In the same way, the third eon is conceived as the Varāha-kalpa;
therein, Viṣṇu himself assumed the body of a boar. (Note:
This reading is not correct.)
Having created the world, the sky, the earth, and the waters, the Lord likewise created all living beings.
In the dissolution known as *naimittika*, Hari, the primordial deity, having withdrawn everything, remains in repose;
thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Section on Creation," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 2:
Then the second chapter;
Sūta said:
Here, from the navel of the sleeping God, a lotus was born.
O fortunate one, upon that lotus was born Brahmā, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. He was addressed by him [the God]: "O high-minded one, create living beings."
Having spoken thus, the Lord Nārāyaṇa vanished.
Brahmā, reflecting upon the god Viṣṇu who had departed after saying "So be it," remained for a while, yet he did not perceive anything whatsoever that could serve as the cause of the world.
At that moment, a great anger arose within the high-souled Brahmā;
from that, Rudra was born upon his lap, produced by his wrath.
Weeping, he was addressed by Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest:

"Give me a name," he said; to him, Rudra gave the name "Rudra. He, too, being told by him, "Create this world again," undertook asceticism and repeatedly created this world from the waters of the dissolution.
When that Prajāpati had sunk into the water,
Brahmā, the Lord of Beings, created another Prajāpati from his right side.
From that [union], Dakṣa arose on the left side;
he begot his wife, and she gave birth to the lord Manu Svāyambhuva. From him, the creation of living beings was thus brought forth by Brahmā.
"Thus has the creation been described by me to you, O best of sages, as the Lord of the World was creating. What more do you wish to hear?
Bharadvāja said:
“O Lomaharṣaṇa, this has been told by you to me in brief;
O high-minded one, tell me again in detail about the primordial creation.
Sūta said:
Likewise, at the end of that cosmic staff (the dissolution), the Lord Brahmā, arisen from sleep during the nights and overflowing with the quality of goodness (sattva), then beheld the empty world;
he is Nārāyaṇa, worthy of worship by the highest, the progenitor even of those who came before.
The Blessed One is of the nature of Brahman, beginningless, and the source of all;
and those who possess bodies should recite this verse concerning Nārāyaṇa.
The Lord, whose nature is Brahman, is the source and the imperishable of the world.
Water is called "nārāḥ," for water is indeed the offspring of Nara;
since that was his primordial abode (ayana), he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
As he contemplated creation as it was in the beginning of the kalpas, there appeared before him,
preceded by non-increase, a great mass of fire known as darkness (tamas),
delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha), gloom (tāmisra), and so forth.
Five types of ignorance appeared among those former great-souled ones;
this reading cannot be corrected due to the loss of letters in the manuscript.
This reading is not correct:
"The creation, existing in fivefold form, arises from the awakening of the one who meditates. (AP 2.017ab)
That should be known as the primary creation by the wise who understand the process of creation; furthermore, as he was meditating upon another supreme creation,
there arose the "animal-stream" (tiryakśrotas) creation.
Those such as animals are remembered as being well-known as those who follow the wrong path;
considering even that to be ineffective, the four-faced one [Brahmā] directed the flow toward the animal realm.
The third was the upward-streaming (ūrdhvaśrotas), which moved upwards from the earth;
from that arose the gods who move above, born together with the creation.
When he was satisfied and no longer desired further creation, then Prajāpati remained still.

Considering those born from the primary creation to be ineffective, he then reflected; thus, O Brahmin, he is remembered as the one with downward-streaming senses (*arvāk-śrotas*). Those humans who were likewise born with downward-streaming senses are regarded as effective (*sādhaka*).
And they carry light, are born from the quality of darkness (tamas), and are dominated by passion (rajas).
Therefore, they carry suffering and act again and again. These creations have been described to you there, O best of sages.
The first is the creation of Mahat; the second is that of the subtle elements (tanmātras);
the third is known as the Vaikārika (the egoic) creation, which is accompanied by the senses;
and the fourth is the Mukhya (principal) creation.
The immobile beings are considered the fourth;
that which is called the transverse-stream is the fifth, the animal womb;
then the upward-stream is the sixth, and the creation of the gods is the seventh.

Following that, the seventh creation, which is the foremost of those involving the downward flow of the senses and pertains to humans, is the eighth, the Anugraha creation; it is indeed characterized by both *sattva* and *tamas*.
Then there is the ninth, the Rudra creation; these are the nine creations of Prajāpati.
These five are known as the modified creations (*vaikṛta-sarga*), while the primary ones (*prākṛta*) are considered dear;
both the primary and the modified are indeed the root causes of the world.
When the creation was produced by Brahmā as he was creating, those which were uttered by me [the Vedas] arose;
thereafter, through his power, Nārāyaṇa— the sole lord of the world who assumes all forms— entered into that supreme manifestation and created everything, assuming the forms of Brahmā and others.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Section on Creation," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 3.
Now begins the third chapter, the Section on Creation.
Bharadvāja said:
"The ninefold creation was produced from Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest.
O Sūta, tell me now: how did that [creation] increase?
Sūta said:
First, those rich in asceticism were created by Brahmā for the sake of Rudra;
likewise, Sanaka and the others were created, as were Marīci and the rest—
namely Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Furthermore, the highly resplendent Tvashtar, Pracetas, Bhrigu,
Nārada as the tenth, and the immensely radiant Vasiṣṭha— these,
along with Sanaka and the others, were appointed to the path known as Nivṛtti.
Regarding that which is called "active engagement," Marīci and others are the sole means to liberation; the sage Nārada is he who was born from the body of Dakṣa, the Prajāpati.
Through his daughter's lineage, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings—
the gods, the dānavas, the gandharvas, the serpents, and the birds—
were all born from the daughters of Dakṣa as supremely righteous beings.
The four kinds of beings, both stationary and moving,
having attained growth, are those very ones born from the creation of Manu;
and the creators of that creation of Manu are the great seers, Marīci and the others.
The highly fortunate Vasiṣṭha and others, born from the mind of Brahmā, [are his sons]; and that Supreme Self alone, in the course of time, creates beings beginning with Viyat during the creations,
and afterwards [he withdraws them].
"The infinite one creates both in the form of kingship and in the form of a sage.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Section on Creation," in the Agni Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 4:
The Section on Creation (Sṛṣṭi-prakaraṇa)
Bharadvāja said:
O high-minded one, tell me in detail about the creation of Rudra;
and how did Marīci and the others, in turn, bring forth their secondary creation?
How could Vasiṣṭha’s status as the son of Mitra and Varuṇa come to be,
O one of great intelligence, given that he was previously born from the mind of Brahmā?
Sūta said:
I shall describe the creation of Rudra and his progeny, as well as the secondary creation (pratisarga) of the sages; listen as I speak of it in detail.

Then, at the beginning of the kalpa, as the Lord was meditating upon a son equal to himself, there appeared from his body a youth who was blue-and-red (Nīlalohita). He possessed a form that was half-male and half-female, and he was fierce and endowed with a magnificent physique.
Illuminating all the cardinal and intermediate directions with his splendor,
Prajāpati, seeing him blazing with brilliance, replied: "O high-minded one, at my command, you must today divide yourself."
Thus addressed by Brahmā, the powerful Rudra there then made his female state and male state separate from one another;
he divided his male state into ten parts and likewise into one part.
I shall state their names; listen to me, O best of the twice-born:
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Kapālī, and Rudra; Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, and Aparājita.
Vṛṣākapi, Śambhu, Kaparda, and likewise Raivata—
these eleven are declared to be the Rudras, the lords of the three worlds. And Rudra, who is indeed the state of womanhood, divided himself tenfold and onefold.
She, assuming many forms, was established as his wife.
Long ago, when he lay supine after performing severe austerities in the water,
the powerful god Rudra created her there.
O best of Brahmins, by the power of his asceticism, he [subdued] various beings,
as well as Piśācas and Kaśmalas with the faces of lions, camels, and crocodiles.
On Kailāsa, he created thousands of others, headed by Vetāla, who remained there as embodiments of Brahman; likewise,
he created twenty-five million Vināyakas and Rudras.
He also created Skanda for the destruction of those called hell-beings.
Thus has that Lord Rudra been described by me to you;
now learn from me as I describe the secondary creation (anusarga) of Marīci and the others.
When all these creatures, from the gods down to the immovable beings, had been created by the Self-existent One, they did not multiply for that wise being;
then he created mind-born sons who were like himself.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, and Mahāmati.
Regarding these nine Brahmās, the Purāṇas have reached a firm conclusion:
O illustrious one, at the time of creation, both Agni and the Pitṛs were the mind-born sons of Brahmā [who established] the Svāyambhuva Manu’s Dharma.
Having created the maiden Śatarūpā, he gave her to Manu;
and from that man, the goddess Śatarūpā gave birth to Priyavrata,
Uttānapāda, and a daughter named Prasūti.
Manu Khāyambhuva gave his daughter Prasūti to Dakṣa;
and then Dakṣa begot twenty-four daughters from Prasūti. Listen now to their names from me.
Faith, procreation, fortitude, contentment, nourishment, intelligence, and likewise action—
this reading is not correct.
The Lord Dharma accepted thirteen daughters of Dakṣa as his wives for the sake of offspring: Buddhi, Lajjā, Vapuḥ, Śānti, Siddhi, and Kīrti.
From Śraddhā and the other wives were born sons such as Kāma;
through the sons, grandsons, and further descendants of Dharma, the lineage of Dharma was greatly expanded.
Among them, there were others who were younger; I shall now proclaim their names.
O best of the twice-born, Sambhūti, Anubhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, Kṣamā, Sannati, Satyā, Urjā, Khyāti,
Svāhā as the tenth, and Svadhā is remembered as the eleventh.
These were given by Dakṣa to the sages of purified souls, beginning with Marīci; and I shall tell you who their sons were.
From Marīci was born Sambhūti, who gave birth to the sage Kaśyapa.
Smṛti was the wife of Aṅgiras, and she gave birth to daughters:
Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and likewise Anumati.
Similarly, Anasūyā bore to Atri sons who were free from blemish.
To Soma, Durvāsas, and the yogin Dattātreya [he gave them].
To Pulastya’s wife Prīti, Dānāgni was born as their son.
Viśravas was his son, and Rāvaṇa and others were his sons.
The Rākṣasas who dwell in the city of Laṅkā have been described; for their destruction in the worlds, Viṣṇu, requested by the gods led by Brahmā, took an incarnation here in the ocean of milk.
Kardama, Ambarīṣa, and Sahiṣṇu were the three sons;
these were born of Kṣamā, the wife of the patriarch Pulastya.
Kratu’s wife, Satvati,
gave birth to sixty thousand Vālikhilyas— sages with vital energy drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas), the size of a thumb-joint, and possessing the brilliance of the blazing sun.

Then, from Satyā, the wife of Pracetas, three sons were born who were true to their vows; their sons and grandsons were born by the hundreds and thousands. Furthermore, seven sons were indeed born to Vasiṣṭha from Urjā.
Rāja, Ūrdhvabāhu, Saraṇa, and Anagha—these were the last;
Surūpa and Śukra—all these became the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis).
From Bhṛgu and Khyāti was born Lakṣmī, who became the consort of Viṣṇu.
Likewise, Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ were born as the two sons of Bhṛgu under the asterism Khāti;
Āyati and Niyati were the two beautiful daughters of Meru.
Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ had those two as their wives, and from them both sons were born.
Prāṇa, Ṛkaṇḍu, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Mṛkaṇḍuja—
the latter by whom death was conquered, O Brahmin, when it was formerly offered to Nārāyaṇa—
from him Devaśivā was born, and she also became the daughter of Prāṇa.
His son was Sañjaya, renowned as Dyutimān; from him, O illustrious one, the lineage of Bhṛgu expanded. And he who was named Agni was the first-born son of Brahmā.
From him, Svāhā obtained three sons of noble vigor, O twice-born ones:
Pāvaka, Pavamāna, and Śuci, who feeds upon water.
I shall now describe their lineages, which are said to number forty-six.
This reading is impure due to a defect in the manuscript.
These are frequently recounted as the father and his three grandsons;
thus, forty-nine in the lineage have been proclaimed.
These Pitṛs were created by Brahmā, as I have explained them to you.
From them was born Svadhā, and from her Menā, the upholder of the earth.
O best of beings, hear from me how Dakṣa, having been previously commanded by the Self-born One to "create progeny," brought forth all living creatures.
O good son, Dakṣa first created the elements with his mind;
at that time, he created the gods, the ṛṣis, along with the gandharvas, asuras, and pannagas.
When the creatures being created by him did not multiply,
then that sage Prajāpati, having reflected upon the purpose of creation, desired to create various offspring through the very law of sexual union.
When the dark, great maiden Vīraṇī was the daughter of Prajāpati,
Dakṣa begot sixty daughters by her, according to our sacred tradition;
he gave ten to Dharma and thirteen to Kaśyapa.
Twenty-seven [lines] were for Soma; four for Viṣṇunemi;
two for the son of Buddha, and then two for Aṅgiras.
Two were for the learned Kṛśāśva; now hear from me about his offspring.
The Viśvedevas were born from Viśvā; the Sādhyas from Asādhyā.
The Marutvats were born from Marutvatī, and the Vasus are remembered as being born from Vasu.
The Bhānus were born from Bhānu, and the Muhūrtajas were born from Muhūrtā.
Ghoṣa was born in Nadyāyā, and the sons of Jāmī were born in Nāgavīthī;
formerly, Arundhatī gave birth to Pṛthivīviṣaya.

O high-minded one, in the sacrifice, Saṅkalpa was the son of Saṅkalpa. Those who possess manifold wealth and vital breaths, led by Devajyotis, are declared to be the eight Vasus; hear their names from me.
Āpa, Dhruva, Soma, Dhara, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus;
their sons and grandsons are by the hundreds and thousands.
Many daughters were proclaimed, and their sons numbered in the thousands:
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Ariṣṭā, Surasā,
as well as Surabhi, Vinatā, Tāmrā, Krodhā, Khasā, and Irā.
O sage who knows the dharma, hear from me about Kadrū and her offspring.
Twelve beautiful sons were born to Kaśyapa by Aditi;
I shall name them for you, so listen as I speak.
Mārga, Aṃśu, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa,
Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, Vivasvat, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, Indra, and likewise Viṣṇu— these twelve are said [to be the suns], O Great-minded One.
We have heard that two sons were born to Diti from Kaśyapa:
Hiraṇyākṣa, who was of massive body and slain by the Boar,
and many other mighty Daityas, the sons of Diti.
From Ariṣṭā, the Gandharvas were born;
and from Surasā, many hosts of Vidyādharas were produced.
Furthermore, the sage Kaśyapa begot cows from Surabhī.
Vinatā had two famous sons, Garuḍa and Aruṇa;
Garuḍa [became] the vehicle of Viṣṇu, the god of gods, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
Aruṇa, the charioteer of the Sun, became his vehicle out of affection.
Now learn from me of the six sons born to Tāmrā from Kaśyapa:
horses, camels, donkeys, elephants, gayals, and deer.
Likewise, from Krodhā were born the beasts and the wicked species;
from Irā, the various kinds of trees, creepers, vines, grasses, horses, and female offspring;
and from Khasā, the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and likewise the Apsarases of the sage.
O twice-born one, the twenty-seven sons of Kadrū who were mentioned— the great nāgas, the biters with venomous fangs, and those of excellent vows who became the wives of Soma—
had as their sons the great beings beginning with Budha.
The offspring of the wives of Ariṣṭanemi were sixteen here;
from Tāmrā, the learned Vahuputra had [sons] such as Vidyu and others.
These were the eminent sons of Pratyaṅgiras, sages honored by sages.
The sons of the divine seer Kṛśāśva were the celestial weapons;
indeed, at the end of a thousand yugas, they are born once again.
These descendants of Kaśyapa, comprising both the stationary and the moving, have thus been described.
Through their sons, grandsons, and descendants, the creation of the Lord of Creatures increased; such are the manifestations of the wise and steadfast god Nārasiṃha.
O Brahmin, these incarnations have been recounted by me to you.
I have related to you the lineage of the offspring of Dakṣa’s daughters;
he who remembers these with faith shall possess a lineage of glory.
I have described to you in brief the primary creation (sarga) and the secondary creation (anusarga) for the purpose of explaining the expansion of the world.
Those twice-born men who, devoted to Viṣṇu, always recite this [text], become pure.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Section on Creation," in the *Āgneya Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 5:
The Narration of Vasiṣṭha’s Sonship to Mitra and Varuṇa
Sūta said:
O twice-born one, I have described to you the creation of the world by Viṣṇu,
and how the gods, dānavas, yakṣas, and others were produced by that Great-Souled One.
Regarding that which you previously asked me in the presence of the sages— how Vasiṣṭha became the son of Mitra and Varuṇa—
I shall relate that ancient and meritorious narrative.
Listen with a one-pointed mind, O Bharadvāja, to what is spoken by me:
there was a Prajāpati named Dakṣa, who knew the true meaning and reality of all dharmas, who was the best among all knowers, and who had reached the further shore of all sciences.
Thirteen auspicious daughters were given by him to Kaśyapa;
I shall now state their names, so listen to me.
O Sage, they were Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kāṣṭhā, Muhūrtā, and Siṃhikā.
Śrutā, Kroṣṭrī, Surabhi, Vinatā,
and Surasā; Kadrū, Surasā, Yātudhānī, and Śunī are recorded as the daughters of Dakṣa, whom he gave to Kaśyapa.
Among them, the eldest and most excellent was Aditi by name;
Aditi gave birth to twelve sons whose splendor was equal to that of fire.
I shall declare their names; listen, O best of the twice-born, by whom this night of Vāsava is perpetually observed in succession:
Bharga, Aṃśu, Aryaman, Mitra, and likewise Varuṇa.
O one of great intelligence, Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, Vivasvat,
Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, Indra, and Viṣṇu is remembered as the twelfth;
these indeed are the twelve Ādityas who rain down and fall.
Her middle son was named Varuṇa by name;
renowned as a world-protector (lokapāla), he is celebrated in the western quarter.
He reigns over the western ocean in the western direction.
There is a glorious mountain made of gold named Asta;
that auspicious mountain, composed of various jewels and endowed with peaks made of every kind of gem along with flowing mineral veins, shines resplendent.
With caves possessing great bellies and resounding with the roars of lions and tigers,
frequented by gods and gandharvas in various secluded terrains;
when the sun has departed, the world is filled with darkness.

Upon its peak is a great, divine, and auspicious city named Sukhāvatī, made of Jāmbūnada gold; it is beautiful, constructed by Viśvakarman with pillars of jewels, and enriched with all means of enjoyment.
In that [region], Varuṇa Āditya, blazing with his own splendor,
protects all these worlds, having been appointed by Brahmā himself.
Being attended by Gandharvas as well as by throngs of Apsarases,
his limbs radiant with divine fragrance and adorned with celestial ornaments,
Varuṇa once went to the forest accompanied by Mitra.
In Kurukṣetra, in the auspicious forest always frequented by Brahman-sages,
endowed with various flowers and fruits and possessed of various objects of value,
hermitages are seen belonging to sages of sublimated vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*).
Resorting to that sacred ford, which abounded in many flowers, fruits, and water,
the two of them, wearing bark garments and black antelope skins, performed supreme austerity.
There, in a certain part of the forest, was a pure and auspicious lake.
Overgrown with many shrubs and creepers, frequented by various birds,
covered by diverse groves of trees, and adorned with lotus ponds;
it was known as Pauṇḍarīka, and was inhabited by fish and tortoises.
The two brothers, the celestial sages Mitra and Varuṇa, were celibate students who,
wandering at will from one region to another, arrived at that place.
There, the excellent Apsaras Urvaśī was drawn toward them by their splendor.
That fair-faced woman, bathing together with her companions, was singing and laughing; she was lovely, possessed of a sweet voice,
fair-complexioned like the interior of a lotus, and had glossy black hair.
With large eyes like lotus petals, red lips, and soft speech;
with teeth as white as a conch, jasmine, or the moon, even and without gaps;

Holding red lotuses in her hands and feet, endowed with discipline,
